While solutions utilizing fully-connected layers (MLPs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have successfully generated and controlled diverse movements involving close-range environmental interactions, fully-connected layers suffer from high computational and memory costs, potentially leading to sub-optimal performance. This study applies pruning algorithms to compress an MLP-MoE network for interactive character animation, thereby reducing parameter count and accelerating computation, albeit with a trade-off regarding motion quality. The results demonstrate that a pruned model, maintaining the same number of experts and parameters as a dense model, produces fewer motion artifacts while retaining similar high-level learned motion features.

We present the inaugural experimental proof of strange nonchaotic attractors (SNA) within the natural dynamics of a self-excited, laboratory-scale system. While prior experimental observations of SNA emergence were limited to quasiperiodically forced systems, this study marks the first report of such evidence in an autonomous laboratory setup. Specifically, we identify SNA situated between quasiperiodic and chaotic attractors, emerging via a fractalization pathway in a thermoacoustic system. These observed transitions from order to chaos through SNA have been validated using multiple nonlinear characterization techniques specifically designed for SNA detection.

We introduce a route choice model that frames traveler behavior as a utility-maximizing flow assignment across the entire network, subject to flow conservation. Route substitution is determined by the degree of overlap between paths. The model is estimated using the complete set of route alternatives without the need for choice set generation; notably, the estimation process relies solely on linear regression and is highly efficient. Predictions are derived through convex optimization, allowing for straightforward computation even in large-scale networks. We validate and estimate the model using an extensive dataset of 1,337,096 GPS traces from trips within the Greater Copenhagen road network.

We introduce the Sequential Aggregation and Rematerialization (SAR) scheme, a distributed method designed for full-batch Graph Neural Network (GNN) training on large-scale graphs. While recent large-scale GNN training has primarily relied on sampling-based approaches or non-learnable message passing, SAR enables direct distributed training of any GNN architecture on an entire large graph. The core innovation of SAR is a distributed sequential rematerialization strategy that reconstructs and subsequently releases segments of the excessively large GNN computational graph during the backward pass. This approach yields superior memory scaling, reducing memory consumption per worker linearly as the number of workers increases, even for densely connected graphs. Leveraging SAR, we achieve the largest full-batch GNN training applications reported to date and demonstrate substantial memory reductions with increased worker counts. Additionally, we propose a general optimization technique utilizing kernel fusion and attention-matrix rematerialization to enhance both runtime and memory efficiency in attention-based models. When combined with SAR, these optimized attention kernels deliver significant speedups and memory savings for attention-based GNNs. We have made the SAR GNN training library publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/IntelLabs/SAR}.

The ring-imaging Cherenkov detectors within the LHCb experiment underwent performance evaluation throughout the LHC Run 2 period, spanning 2015 to 2018. This assessment quantified the temporal stability of the Cherenkov angle resolution and photon detection counts under varying operational conditions. Analysis of the data confirmed that the particle identification capabilities meet the necessary criteria for the experiment's physics goals.

This study addresses the challenge of pre-training models to serve as universally reusable backbones for downstream tasks. Our proposed pre-training approach constructs an agent-environment interaction model by learning domain-invariant successor features from extensive agent experiences across diverse tasks, subsequently discretizing these features into behavior prototypes that form an embodied set structure. To ensure general reusability for downstream learning, we introduce two mechanisms: (1) embodied feature projection, which preserves prior knowledge by mapping new task observation-action pairs onto the embodied set structure, and (2) projected Bellman updates, which introduce learning plasticity tailored to new task settings. Preliminary results demonstrate that downstream task learning leveraging this pre-trained embodied set structure effectively adapts to unseen variations in task objectives, environmental dynamics, and sensor modalities.

Azimuthally-differential femtoscopic measurements offer crucial insights into system evolution dynamics and the nature of the source by probing both its spatio-temporal properties and collective velocity fields at freeze-out. Recent findings show that while HBT radius oscillations relative to the second harmonic event plane primarily reflect spatial geometry, those relative to the third harmonic event plane are mainly governed by velocity fields. This Letter reports the first azimuthally-differential pion femtoscopy results relative to the third harmonic event plane, analyzed as a function of pion pair transverse momentum $k_{\rm T}$ across various centralities in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV. We observe that the $R_{\rm side}$ and $R_{\rm out}$ radii, which describe the pion source size perpendicular and parallel to the pion transverse momentum, oscillate in phase with the third harmonic event plane, consistent with 3+1D hydrodynamical calculations. These observed oscillations definitively indicate collective expansion and anisotropic velocity fields. Furthermore, comparing the measured oscillations with Blast-Wave model predictions reveals that the initial triangularity is washed out by the time of freeze-out.

This article presents two analytical formulas for determining the mutual inductance between a circular filament and an arbitrarily positioned line segment, derived respectively via the Mutual Inductance Method (MIM) and Babic's Method (BM). Leveraging the principle that any curve can be approximated by a series of line segments, a new approach—the Segmentation Method—is introduced to calculate mutual inductance between a circular filament and filaments of arbitrary shapes. The validity of both the derived formulas and this proposed method was numerically confirmed using FastHenry software and benchmark examples from existing literature. Notably, the Segmentation Method was effectively utilized to compute mutual inductance for various specific curves, including circles, circular and elliptic arcs, ellipses, spirals, helices, and conical helices. All calculated results demonstrated strong agreement with the reference data.

As deep learning gains prominence in automatically classifying three-dimensional point cloud data, a primary bottleneck is the scarcity of high-quality training data, particularly when contrasted with the abundance available for two-dimensional images. While using synthetic data for network pre-training offers a potential remedy, the extent to which models can generalize from synthetic to real-world point clouds remains underexplored. Nevertheless, a vast array of 3D virtual environments exists that could be leveraged if proven effective, underscoring the significant value of research in this area. This paper introduces SynthCity, an open dataset designed to facilitate such research. SynthCity comprises a full-color Mobile Laser Scanning point cloud containing 367.9 million points, with every point labeled into one of nine categories. The point cloud was generated using the Blender plugin to simulate a typical urban or suburban setting.

We emphasize recent advances in calculating higher-order scattering amplitudes that involve massive internal propagators. The Feynman integrals contributing to these calculations frequently result in specific function classes, such as those linked to elliptic curves. As amplitudes incorporate additional scales, it becomes essential to deepen our comprehension of these integrals and leverage state-of-the-art technologies to manage the escalating analytic and algebraic complexity. Specifically, we begin by examining two-loop scattering amplitudes for top-quark pair production and finish by outlining crucial steps toward deriving next-to-next-to leading-order corrections for five-point processes.

Throughout multiple years, stars follow helical paths across the sky resulting from the interplay of proper motion and parallax. While gravitational influences from invisible companions are known to distort these tracks, the Gaia astrometric mission is expected to detect numerous new exoplanets, stellar binaries, and compact object companions with orbital periods ranging from tens of days up to the mission's full duration. This study utilizes simulated astrometric data to show that Gaia can also identify and characterize black hole companions to bright stars with orbital periods exceeding Gaia's operational lifetime. These long-period astrometric binaries do not complete full orbits; instead, they are detected via the curvature in their characteristic helical trajectories. By jointly measuring the radius of this curvature and the orbital velocity, constraints on the true orbit can be established. We calculate the precision of Gaia's orbital acceleration measurements and apply these to model the population of stellar-neighborhood black holes. Although orbital degeneracies suggest that accelerations from hidden black holes might mimic those of faint low-mass stars, we explain how Gaia data alone can confidently confirm the nature of specific putative black hole companions.

This study tackles challenges related to clustering and non-global logarithms within jet shapes during the production of Higgs or vector bosons accompanied by a single hard jet at hadron colliders. We present an analytical fixed-order calculation accurate to second order in the coupling constant, alongside an all-orders estimate for the invariant mass distribution of the highest-$p_t$ jet across various jet algorithms. Derived in the eikonal (soft) limit, our results achieve next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy. We match the resummed distribution to next-to-leading order results from MCFM and benchmark our findings against Monte Carlo event generators Pythia 8 and Herwig 7. Following the inclusion of non-perturbative effects, we compare our predictions with experimental data from the CMS collaboration regarding $Z$ + jet production, observing consistent agreement across a broad range of the observable.

A core challenge in Web science and social network analysis involves identifying a set $S$ of nodes that, with high probability, includes all nodes with a PageRank of at least $\Delta$ while excluding any node with a PageRank below $\Delta/c$, given an approximation factor $c>1$. This task is termed the {\sc SignificantPageRanks} problem. We present a nearly optimal local algorithm that solves this problem in $\tilde{O}(n/\Delta)$ time for networks with $n$ nodes, matching the theoretical lower bound of ${\Omega}(n/\Delta)$ and thus achieving optimality up to logarithmic factors.

Our approach relies on two primary technical innovations. First, we introduce a multi-scale sampling scheme for a fundamental matrix problem, which may have independent significance. In this abstract setting, one accesses an unknown right-stochastic matrix via row queries, where the cost and accuracy depend on a precision parameter $\epsilon$. For a cost proportional to $1/\epsilon$, the query returns $O(1/\epsilon)$ entries and their indices that $\epsilon$-approximate the row. The objective is to identify a set containing all columns with a sum of at least $\Delta$ and omitting those with a sum less than $\Delta/c$. Our scheme resolves this in $\tilde{O}(n/\Delta)$ time, whereas conventional sampling methods require $\Theta((n/\Delta)^2)$.

Second, we propose a novel local algorithm for approximating personalized PageRank. This method is more robust than previous approaches found in \cite{JehW03,AndersenCL06} and demonstrates high efficiency, especially in networks with large in-degrees or out-degrees. By combining this algorithm with our multi-scale sampling technique, we achieve an optimal solution to the {\sc SignificantPageRanks} problem.

Grasping objects amidst clutter presents a significant challenge for robotics. To address this, pre-grasping maneuvers like pushing and shifting can disperse items, simplifying the task. We introduce a Fast-Learning Grasping (FLG) framework based on deep reinforcement learning, which integrates pre-grasping actions with grasping to retrieve objects from cluttered environments with reduced real-world training requirements. This approach assigns rewards based on changes in environmental clutter and employs a hybrid triggering method to facilitate data-efficient learning and synergy. Additionally, an extended fully convolutional network provides a pixel-level value function for the workspace, enabling precise estimation of grasp probabilities for each action. A mask function is also incorporated as prior knowledge to guide agents in focusing on accurate pose adjustments, thereby enhancing training data collection and learning efficiency. The FLG model undergoes pre-training in a simulated environment before being transferred to the real world with minimal fine-tuning. Experimental outcomes show a 94% grasp success rate and the capability to generalize to new objects. Compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, the proposed FLG framework achieves comparable or superior success rates with significantly less real-world training. Supplementary video material is accessible at https://youtu.be/e04uDLsxfDg.

It is widely acknowledged that Everett's quantum mechanics theory is currently untestable because verifying it would require manipulating the observer in ways beyond our technological reach. We propose an alternative method to test this theory that avoids any operations on the observer. By assuming the observer has finite dimensions, we demonstrate that Everett's theory predicts unique characteristics for the observed system, and these differences are experimentally verifiable.

Composite axion models provide a solid theoretical basis for a high-quality Peccei-Quinn symmetry. We introduce a novel class of realizations naturally situated within Grand Unified Theories (GUTs), which maintain asymptotic freedom across all gauge groups and safeguard the axion symmetry against operators up to dimension 12. This framework yields several unique low-energy signatures. First, it predicts additional composite scalars; certain among them could serve as viable dark matter candidates for axion decay constants that are too small to account for QCD axion abundance. Second, the Standard Model gauge couplings undergo approximate unification at the axion scale, while genuine quark-lepton unification remains at much higher energies. This scenario implies the presence of GUT relics possessing Standard Model gauge quantum numbers at potentially observable energy scales.

Imputing missing data is a critical operation in various scientific and engineering fields. These gaps often stem from sensor limitations or post-processing errors in experimental data, or from numerical and algorithmic constraints in computer simulations. This paper focuses on the latter, specifically addressing numerical simulations of storm surges. The simulation generates time-series predictions across multiple geographic points, creating a spatio-temporal imputation challenge characterized by high spatial and temporal correlations among surge points and randomly distributed missing regions. Recently, machine learning approaches, particularly neural networks, have been utilized for such tasks, with Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs) gaining prominence as an unsupervised solution. This study enhances the performance of Generative Adversarial Imputation Nets (GAIN) by replacing fully connected layers with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to better capture data correlations and leverage adjacent surge points. Furthermore, the coordinates of the points are incorporated as additional features to enrich the information available to the convolutional layers. This adapted approach is termed Convolutional Generative Adversarial Imputation Nets (Conv-GAIN). The study evaluates Conv-GAIN against the original GAIN and other techniques, demonstrating that the proposed method achieves superior performance on storm surge data.

This article introduces a new computational framework for integrating one-dimensional (1D) fibers with the two-dimensional (2D) surface of a three-dimensional (3D) solid. The fibers are represented as 1D Cosserat continua (beams), each possessing six local degrees of freedom: three for position and three for rotation. A kinematically consistent coupling scheme is developed to address this specific problem type by managing both positional and rotational degrees of freedom along the beams. Positional coupling is achieved by maintaining a constant normal distance between points on the beam centerline and their corresponding points on the solid surface; this approach necessitates a consistent definition of the solid surface normal vector field to ensure fundamental mechanical properties, such as the conservation of angular momentum. While a previous study addressed the coupling of beam rotations with rotation tensors representing local orientation in a Boltzmann continuum, this work extends that methodology by constructing rotation tensors that reflect local surface orientations. Several numerical examples validate the consistency, robustness, and accuracy of the proposed method. Furthermore, a fluid-structure interaction case study involving a vascular stent illustrates the method's applicability to multi-physics systems of practical significance.

Laboratory test results represent a critical, high-dimensional element within patient Electronic Health Records (EHRs). We developed embedding representations using Word2Vec and GloVe for LOINC codes derived from the EHRs of approximately 80,000 cancer center patients. To incorporate data on test outcomes, we also trained embeddings on concatenated LOINC codes paired with symbols denoting normal or abnormal results. Our analysis revealed several clinically significant similarities among the LOINC embeddings. Specifically, for embeddings combining LOINC codes with abnormality indicators, we assessed their effectiveness in mortality prediction tasks and their capacity to maintain ordinal properties, ensuring that a test with a normal result is more similar to an abnormal one than to a severely abnormal one.

We present a family of equations of state (EoS) for hybrid neutron star matter, constructed via a two-zone parabolic interpolation that bridges a soft hadronic EoS at low densities with stiff quark matter EoS at high densities across a specific chemical potential range ($\mu_H < \mu < \mu_Q$). By fixing the hadronic component to the APR model and selecting a color-superconducting, nonlocal NJL model for the quark phase with two adjustable parameters, we conducted Bayesian analyses using this two-parameter EoS family. The study employed three distinct observational constraint sets: Set 1 required the mass of PSR J0740+6620, the tidal deformability from GW170817, and the mass-radius relation of PSR J0030+0451 (from NICER); Set 2 added the potential upper mass limit from GW170817; and Set 3 considered the possibility that the lighter component of the asymmetric binary merger GW190814 was a neutron star. Our results consistently indicate that the quark matter phase must be color superconducting, with the dimensionless diquark coupling $\eta_D$ approximately satisfying the Fierz relation ($\eta_D \approx 0.75$). Furthermore, the most probable solutions demonstrate a proportionality between $\eta_D$ and $\eta_V$, the coupling of the repulsive vector interaction necessary to sustain a sufficiently large maximum mass. Utilizing fictitious measurements within the Bayesian framework, we explored the implications of varying radius predictions for the massive $2~M_\odot$ pulsar PSR J0740+6220. Ultimately, incorporating the actual NICER radius measurement for PSR J0740+6220, we concluded that the most likely hybrid EoS cannot support a maximum mass as high as $2.5~M_\odot$, thereby implying that the event GW190814 involved a binary black hole merger.

Gaussian processes (GPs) have emerged as a standard method for constructing terrain representations due to their ability to model map uncertainty, thereby providing a reliability metric for map areas that can be directly integrated into Bayes filtering algorithms for robot localization. A crucial observation is that this uncertainty can account for the inherent noise in terrain surveying by leveraging the capacity of GPs to train on uncertain inputs (UIs). However, current techniques for generating GP maps with UIs are limited regarding the form and extent of input noise. This letter introduces a flexible and efficient framework for constructing large-scale GP maps with UIs using Stochastic Variational GPs and Monte Carlo sampling of UI distributions. We validate this mapping approach on extensive bathymetric survey data collected by an AUV, comparing its performance against methods using deterministic inputs (DI). Furthermore, we demonstrate that utilizing UI SVGP maps results in more accurate particle filter localization compared to DI SVGP maps during a real-world AUV mission over a fully predicted area.

Entering prompts like "a sea otter with a pearl earring by Johannes Vermeer" or "a photo of a teddy bear on a skateboard in Times Square" into OpenAI's DALL-E-2 text-to-image generator yields delightful and strikingly accurate results. This capacity to create highly realistic visuals, seemingly limited only by human imagination, promises numerous exciting and innovative applications. However, it also presents fresh challenges for the photo-forensic community. Driven by the observation that text-to-image synthesis does not rely on explicit geometric modeling—and considering that the human visual system often overlooks even obvious geometric errors—we offer an initial investigation into the perspective consistency of DALL-E-2 generated images to assess whether geometry-based forensic methods can effectively identify this new type of synthetic media.

Neural mass models are fundamental to large-scale brain simulations, typically defined at the node level as systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) featuring sigmoidal nonlinearities. By utilizing structural data from brain atlases to form networks, researchers investigate the emergence of functional dynamic states, such as synchrony. We demonstrate that the Wilson-Cowan neural mass model can be rigorously analyzed at both node and network levels by approximating the classic sigmoidal nonlinearity with a piecewise linear version. At the node level, periodic orbits are constructed by combining matrix exponential solutions, with stability assessed via Floquet theory. For networks governed by circulant interaction matrices, the stability of the synchronous state is determined through a low-dimensional Floquet problem parameterized by the interaction matrix's eigenvalues, a linear algebra approach that predicts the onset of spatio-temporal patterns resulting from synchronous instability. We further examine a discontinuous nonlinearity where the sigmoid is replaced by a Heaviside function, creating a continuous-time switching network. This setup permits unstable sliding periodic orbits at the node level. Stability analysis for these orbits employs a modified Floquet theory that accounts for perturbations evolving through switching manifolds using saltation matrices. At the network level, analyzing the stability of the synchronous state is significantly more complex; consequently, we apply concepts originally developed for Glass networks to evaluate the stability of periodic states in neural mass models with discontinuous interactions.

Neutron and proton scattering off deuterons or stable alpha particles can be treated as two-body systems. This study computationally derives inverse potentials directly from scattering phase shift (SPS) data for light nucleon-nucleus interactions, employing the Morse function as a reference potential. Within an optimization framework, the phase equation for different angular momentum ($l$) channels was solved numerically using the 5th-order Runge-Kutta (RK-5) method to refine Morse function parameters, aiming to minimize the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). The resulting inverse potentials for the S-wave in neutron-deuteron and proton-deuteron systems yielded MAPE values of 1.95% and 2.05%, respectively. For the P and D channels in neutron-alpha and proton-alpha systems, the MAPE was determined to be below 1.53% and 2.17%, respectively. Experimental resonance energies for the $p_{1/2}$ and $p_{3/2}$ states, extracted from partial cross-section plots, are 4.1(4) and 0.93(0.89) MeV for the n-alpha system, and 5.21(5) and 1.96(1.96) MeV for the p-alpha system. While the calculated total cross-section for n-alpha aligns well with existing literature, the p-alpha cross-section exhibits the correct physical trend.
This brief essay explores core findings regarding scalar curvature and the two primary methodologies employed to prove them.

Addressing the multimodality often produced by intricate statistical models continues to pose significant challenges. Existing Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approaches for this issue rely on ensembles of chains targeting products of power-tempered distributions. Although theoretically sound, these methods often exhibit poor mixing and sluggish convergence in practice due to their high computational demands. This study explores innovative extensions of the t-walk algorithm—a cost-effective, affine-invariant MCMC technique—to handle multimodal distributions. We recognize that the performance of our proposed method may vary depending on the specific problem and could face difficulties in highly complex scenarios; to address this, we introduce a post-processing strategy grounded in pseudo-marginal theory to integrate isolated samples.

This paper replicates the experimental findings from our previous study, "Describing Subjective Experiment Consistency by $p$-Value P-P Plot," which was presented at the 28th ACM International Conference on Multimedia. Our goal is to validate the reliability of those earlier results and to assist others in utilizing our software framework. We provide artifacts that enable the reproduction of all tables, figures, and data generated from raw subjective responses included in our prior work, thereby demonstrating the reproducibility of our findings. Furthermore, we encourage the broader community to adopt our software framework for analyzing subjective responses, extending its use beyond mere reproducibility initiatives.

Conventional AI methods for personalized contextual pricing typically presume that the data distribution during live pricing aligns with that seen during training. In practice, this assumption often fails due to the fluidity of customer purchasing behaviors, especially when unforeseen system shocks like the COVID-19 pandemic occur. This study examines shifts in customer behavior within a major airline during the pandemic by treating it as a problem of covariate shift and concept drift detection. By employing (i) Fast Generalized Subset Scanning and (ii) Causal Forests, we pinpoint which customers altered their travel and purchasing habits and identify the specific attributes driving these changes. Through experiments involving both simulated and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the application of these two techniques via qualitative analysis.

Recently, Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) has garnered significant research interest owing to its promising applications in fields like healthcare, education, and human resources. This paper introduces DialogueGCN, a graph neural network approach designed for ERC that utilizes both self and inter-speaker dependencies to model conversational context. By employing a graph network, DialogueGCN resolves context propagation limitations found in existing RNN-based techniques. Empirical results demonstrate that this method not only mitigates these issues but also surpasses current state-of-the-art performance across several benchmark emotion classification datasets.

This study investigates the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for three-dimensional compressible Euler equations. Employing Smith-Tataru's method \cite{ST}, we establish the local existence, uniqueness, and stability of solutions under the conditions that the initial velocity and density belong to $H^s$ and the specific vorticity belongs to $H^{s_0}$, with $2 < s_0 < s$. This work provides an alternative and streamlined proof of the results previously presented by Q. Wang in \cite{WQEuler}.

Van der Waals forces arise from dipole interactions, just as quadrupole-quadrupole forces stem from quadrupole interactions. This study concentrates on the forces between two dipoles or two quadrupoles. Classically, a Rydberg atom is modeled as a dipole, with the excited outer electron and the ion core forming the two poles. Quantum mechanically, these are treated as Rydberg transition dipoles; thus, dipole-dipole interactions represent the forces between two Rydberg atoms. Since Rydberg atoms also possess quadrupole characteristics, their mutual interactions include quadrupole-quadrupole components. This article investigates both the dipole-dipole and quadrupole-quadrupole contributions to the interactions among ultracold Rydberg atoms. The findings demonstrate that quadrupole-blockade has been observed, a phenomenon crucial for developing more compact quantum computers, quantum electronic devices, and quantum sensors.

High-dimensional, streaming datasets are now commonplace across modern applications, spanning finance, e-commerce, biomedical research, and neuroimaging. Consequently, numerous new algorithms have been developed to tackle the challenges these data present. This study focuses on $\ell_1$ regularized linear models applied to potentially non-stationary streaming data. Recent observations emphasize that selecting the regularization parameter is critical in such models; several methods have been introduced to iteratively adjust this parameter over time, thereby enabling the estimated model's sparsity to adapt. Furthermore, in many contexts, inferring the regularization parameter itself is valuable, as it reflects the model's underlying sparsity. However, this work highlights and provides extensive empirical evidence showing that various statistical properties—often unrelated—can also drive changes in the regularization parameter. Specifically, through synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that shifts in the parameter can be caused by variations in true sparsity, signal-to-noise ratio, or model misspecification. Therefore, the goal of this letter is to identify and catalog the statistical factors that induce changes in the associated regularization parameter. We conclude by presenting two applications involving financial and neuroimaging data, where these insights are particularly relevant.

This paper tackles a specific design challenge: determining the shape of a plate and its corresponding pre-stress that can relax into a specified three-dimensional shell. While isometric transformations preserve Gaussian curvature and thus cannot generate non-developable three-dimensional shells solely through plate relaxation, this geometric limitation can be bypassed. However, approaches that include small strains and large rotations are currently restricted to small areas. This study removes the small-area constraint to fully cover three-dimensional shells by employing shell-strips. Because shell-strips introduce an additional geometric parameter, we demonstrate that, under specific assumptions linking strip width to shell curvature, arbitrary shell surfaces can be designed by covering them with these strips. To illustrate this, we present optimized sphere covers using various relaxed plate-strips with homogeneous and isotropic pre-stress. Furthermore, we propose designs for a torus, a helicoid, and a non-developable Möbius band, which necessitate inhomogeneous and anisotropic pre-stress.

The FELiChEM facility, currently under construction, is an infrared free-electron laser (FEL) comprising two oscillators that produce middle-infrared and far-infrared radiation spanning 2.5 to 200 ${\rm{\mu m}}$. This paper presents a numerical investigation into the output properties of the middle-infrared oscillator, specifically focusing on precise cavity length detuning. The study highlights the temporal structure of micropulses and their associated spectral bandwidths. Using radiation wavelengths of 5 ${\rm{\mu m}}$ and 50 ${\rm{\mu m}}$ as case studies, the results demonstrate that adjusting the cavity length detuning allows the output pulse duration to be tuned between 1 and 6 ps, with corresponding spectral bandwidths ranging from 0.2% to 13%. Furthermore, the analysis discusses the emergence of a comb structure in the optical pulse, which occurs when the normalized slippage length is significantly less than one. These findings offer valuable insights for operating the FELiChEM facility and similar FEL oscillators.

Recent developments in variational autoencoders (VAEs) have facilitated the learning of latent manifolds structured as compact Lie groups, such as $SO(d)$. Because this methodology presumes that data resides on a subspace homeomorphic to the Lie group, we examine the validity of this assumption regarding images derived from projecting a $d$-dimensional volume with an unknown pose within $SO(d)$. By evaluating various theoretical candidates for the group and image spaces, we demonstrate that defining a group action on the data space typically fails, as it necessitates more rigorous geometric constraints on the volume. Through experiments utilizing geometric VAEs, we confirm that this constraint is essential for accurate pose inference and discuss the implications of these findings for future applications and research.

Mixed-initiative visual analytics systems utilize established design principles to enhance users' problem-solving capabilities. However, while these systems evaluate when to act autonomously to meet user objectives, many currently handle the risk of cognitive bias in human decision-making statically. This approach relies on predefined actions rather than dynamically identifying, communicating, and correcting biases as they arise. We contend that mixed-initiative design should integrate cognitive bias mitigation strategies directly by embedding specific techniques within the system to address biases in real time. To explore this, we examine domain experts in machine learning who apply visual analytics and systems that already employ mixed-initiative principles, assessing their capacity to support bias mitigation. This analysis leverages the unique insights of these experts within existing user-centered systems that effectively apply cognitive theory-based design principles. Based on these findings, we propose opportunities for domain experts to proactively address cognitive biases, building on their current contributions to the field. Finally, we outline open questions and future research directions for designers aiming to create visual analytics systems that incorporate bias-aware initiatives.

This study investigates lepton-flavor violating Higgs boson decays into $\mu\tau$ and e$\tau$ pairs, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at the LHC, achieved at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. No significant excess was observed, leading to the derivation of upper limits on the corresponding lepton-flavor violating branching fractions. At a 95% confidence level, the observed and expected upper limits for $\mathcal{B}($H $\to\mu\tau)$ are both below 0.15%, while those for $\mathcal{B}($H$\to$e$\tau)$ are below 0.22% (0.16% expected).

Completing knowledge triplets holds significant potential for various downstream tasks. Effective knowledge graph completion relies heavily on both structural and semantic information. Departing from prior methods that utilize only one of these aspects, we introduce a framework that jointly embeds semantic content from natural language descriptions alongside structural data. Our approach fine-tunes pre-trained language models using a probabilistic structured loss to facilitate graph completion; specifically, the model's forward pass processes semantic information while the loss function reconstructs structural elements. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we show that leveraging semantics allows our approach to substantially enhance performance in low-resource settings. The associated code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/pkusjh/LASS.
We calculate the twisted Koecher-Maass series of both the first and second kind for the Ikeda type lift associated with the exceptional group $E_{7,3}$. Consequently, we establish their rationality.

We introduce a novel superalgebra for $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity in $D=3,4$ dimensions, which incorporates a $U(1)$ generator. This algebra is based on the Soroka-Soroka framework and is generated by Lorentz ($J_{ab}$) and Lorentz-like ($Z_{ab}$) transformations, translations ($P_a$ and $T$), and two supercharges ($Q^I_\alpha$), representing the unique realization for this specific generator set. Furthermore, we develop a corresponding 3D Chern-Simons supergravity model based on this superalgebra and examine its significance.

We calculate the effective diffusion coefficient for a Brownian particle moving within a piece-wise linear periodic potential under spatially varying temperature, a system referred to as the Büttiker-Landauer motor. Our study derives analytical formulas for both the current and diffusion coefficients, which are then validated against numerical simulations.

Jet is a distributed, high-performance stream processor developed over the past five years at Hazelcast as an open-source project. Its primary design objective is to achieve millisecond latency at the 99.99th percentile. Initially conceived as an execution engine for applying complex business logic to streams from Hazelcast's In-memory Data Grid (IMDG)—which consists of high-performance, partitioned, and replicated in-memory data structures—Jet has since evolved into a comprehensive, scale-out stream processor capable of handling out-of-order streams and ensuring exactly-once processing. With end-to-end latencies measured in milliseconds and throughput reaching millions of events per CPU core, this paper details the key design choices made to optimize performance per core, shares lessons learned, and provides an empirical performance evaluation.

This abstract summarizes current experimental limits on $CPT$ violation within neutral meson mixing. Updated values for the $CPT$ asymmetry in the $B^0$ and $B_s^0$ sectors are derived from recent data released by BaBar, Belle, and LHCb. Through specialized analyses, LHCb is poised to tighten constraints on $CPT$ violation in the $D^0$, $B^0$, and $B_s^0$ systems. Because $CPT$ violation necessitates Lorentz invariance violation in local interacting quantum field theories, any observed asymmetry should display variations dependent on sidereal time and velocity boosts. These $CPT$- and Lorentz-violating phenomena are modeled using the Standard-Model Extension (SME) framework. The significant boost of neutral mesons generated at LHCb yields heightened sensitivity to the associated SME coefficients. Utilizing current LHCb data, we have precisely determined the non-sidereal-varying SME coefficients for the $B^0$ and $B_s^0$ systems. A comprehensive sidereal analysis will allow LHCb to enhance existing SME bounds in the $D^0$, $B^0$, and $B_s^0$ sectors by up to two orders of magnitude.

A freely moving fly traverses approximately 100 stereotyped states in a sequence that is strongly non-Markovian. To investigate these dynamics, we extended the information bottleneck method to compress the extensive set of behavioral states into a concise representation that optimally retains correlations between consecutive states. Remarkably, compressing the data into merely two states while preserving short-time correlations successfully captures the long-range correlations present in the raw data. Once the behavior is reduced to a binary sequence, we model its distribution using an Ising model featuring pairwise interactions, which represents the maximum entropy model consistent with two-point correlations. As we match correlation functions over increasingly longer timescales, the resulting model converges toward an Ising model characterized by inverse-square interactions and a near-zero magnetic field. The emergence of this statistical physics framework from the analysis of real animal behavior data is surprising.

Production garbage collectors often sacrifice performance to achieve shorter pause times, consuming significantly more CPU and memory than earlier, simpler designs. Concurrent copying collectors, such as C4, ZGC, and Shenandoah, face three primary constraints: 1) The inherent cost of concurrent copying, which demands high memory bandwidth and expensive read/write barriers; 2) Scalability issues arising from their reliance on tracing, which fails to scale effectively in practice; and 3) Lack of immediacy, as they delay reclaiming older objects, leading to high memory overhead.

We introduce LXR, which optimizes responsiveness and throughput by drastically reducing concurrent work and overhead. First, LXR minimizes copying by utilizing the Immix heap structure to reclaim most memory, reserving limited stop-the-world copying only to handle fragmentation. Second, it employs reference counting to ensure both scalability and immediacy, allowing for the prompt reclamation of both young and old objects, while using concurrent tracing solely to detect cyclic garbage. Third, to enable efficient copying of mature objects without excessive pauses, LXR implements remembered sets for reference counting and concurrent decrement processing. Fourth, it features a novel, low-overhead write barrier that integrates coalescing reference counting, concurrent tracing, and remembered set maintenance.

Consequently, LXR delivers exceptional responsiveness and throughput. When tested on the Lucene search engine with a large heap, LXR achieved six times higher throughput and reduced the 99.9th percentile tail latency by thirty times compared to the default configuration of the popular Shenandoah production collector.

This study addresses the optimal allocation of a measurement budget for particle filtering, specifically minimizing the expected mean square error. We introduce three distinct optimal intermittent filters, with their optimality criteria varying based on the information accessible during decision-making. The first, the stochastic program filter, uses a policy to determine measurement timing based on previously acquired data. The second, the offline filter, solves a combinatorial optimization problem beforehand to fix all measurement times simultaneously. The third, the online filter, recalculates the next measurement time upon receiving new data to incorporate all currently available information. We demonstrate that, regarding expected mean square error, the stochastic program filter outperforms the online filter, which in turn surpasses the offline filter; however, these exact filters are generally computationally intractable. Consequently, we approximate the filter estimate using a particle filter and employ a Monte-Carlo approach to estimate the mean square error. Furthermore, we compare various algorithms—including random trial, greedy forward and backward methods, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithms—to approximately solve the underlying combinatorial programs. Finally, the efficacy of these proposed methods is demonstrated through two examples: a tumor motion model and a standard particle filtering benchmark.

This study investigates special Lagrangian submanifolds within $\mathbb{CP}^3$, treated as a nearly K\"ahler manifold, through two distinct lenses: intrinsically via a moving frame approach and extrinsically by employing $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ moment-type maps. We present novel homogeneous examples derived from both viewpoints and provide a classification of totally geodesic special Lagrangian submanifolds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any special Lagrangian in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ or the flag manifold $\mathbb{F}_{1,2}(\mathbb{C}^3)$ possessing a symmetry associated with an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ subgroup of nearly K\"ahler automorphisms is necessarily homogeneous.

We report the outcomes of a model-driven search for continuous gravitational waves from the low-mass X-ray binary Scorpius X-1, utilizing data from the third observing run of the Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA detectors. This semicoherent approach leverages signal model specifics to coherently integrate data segments separated by a configurable coherence time, allowing a trade-off between sensitivity and computational expense. The analysis spanned gravitational-wave frequencies from 25Hz to 1600Hz, incorporating orbital velocity, frequency, and phase ranges derived from observational data. No significant detection candidates emerged, leading to the establishment of frequency-dependent upper limits. The tightest constraints, found between 100Hz and 200Hz, indicate an amplitude ($h_0$) of approximately $1 \times 10^{-25}$ when marginalized isotropically over the neutron star's unknown rotation axis inclination, or better than $4 \times 10^{-26}$ under optimal orientation assumptions. Current sensitivity now reaches amplitudes predicted by torque balance equilibrium models. Under the standard conservative model of surface accretion, our isotropically-marginalized upper limits approach predicted amplitudes between 70Hz and 100Hz, while limits assuming the neutron star spin aligns with the most probable orbital angular momentum fall below conservative torque balance predictions from 40Hz to 200Hz. Considering a wider array of accretion scenarios, our direct limits on gravitational-wave amplitude explore the relevant parameter space across a broad frequency spectrum, extending to 500Hz or higher.

The paper classifies Lie symmetries associated with the Schrödinger-Pauli equations for charged particles and quasirelativistic Schrödinger equations, notably identifying a novel superintegrable system that incorporates spin-orbit coupling.
We respond to the remarks made by H. Schuermann and V. Serov in arXiv:2204.05846 regarding our earlier work published in Physical Review A, Vol. 101, 023843 (2020).

Colorectal cancer has emerged as a critical threat to global health in recent years, making deep learning techniques essential for classifying colorectal histopathology images. While current methods predominantly emphasize end-to-end automatic classification, this paper introduces the IL-MCAM framework, which integrates attention mechanisms with interactive learning. This framework operates in two phases: an Automatic Learning (AL) stage and an Interactivity Learning (IL) stage. During the AL phase, a multi-channel attention model comprising three distinct attention channels and convolutional neural networks extracts diverse features for classification. In the IL phase, the framework employs an interactive strategy to iteratively incorporate misclassified images into the training set, thereby enhancing the MCAM model's classification capabilities. Performance was validated through experiments on a custom dataset and the HE-NCT-CRC-100K dataset, yielding classification accuracies of 98.98% and 99.77%, respectively. Furthermore, ablation and interchangeability tests confirmed the efficacy and substitutability of the three attention channels. Overall, the results demonstrate that the IL-MCAM framework achieves superior performance in colorectal histopathological image classification.

Directly embedding group symmetry into the learning process serves as a powerful principle for architectural design. Group-equivariant convolutional neural networks (G-CNNs) leverage this by generating features that transform covariantly with respect to input group actions, thereby achieving superior generalization in tasks possessing inherent symmetry. While existing theories and implementations of G-CNNs have addressed planar images under rotation or scaling individually, this paper introduces the Roto-Scale-Translation equivariant CNN (RST-CNN). This model guarantees joint equivariance across rotation, scaling, and translation through coupled group convolutions. Furthermore, acknowledging that real-world symmetry transformations are often imperfect and subject to input deformation, we conduct a stability analysis of representation equivariance under distortion. This analysis motivates the use of truncated expansions for convolutional filters based on pre-defined low-frequency spatial modes. The resulting model provably achieves deformation-robust RST equivariance, meaning the symmetry is approximately maintained even when transformations are corrupted by nuisance data deformations—a critical property for out-of-distribution generalization. Numerical experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and STL-10 demonstrate that the proposed model delivers significant performance improvements over prior methods, particularly in low-data regimes where both rotation and scaling variations are present.

Kurz et al. recently demonstrated that infinite $\lambda$-trees with a finite number of free variables, considered modulo $\alpha$-equivalence, constitute a final coalgebra for a functor within the category of nominal sets. In this work, we examine the rational fixpoint of this functor. We establish that it comprises all rational $\lambda$-trees, defined as those $\lambda$-trees possessing only a finite number of subtrees up to isomorphism. This result provides a corecursion principle, enabling the definition of operations like substitution on rational $\lambda$-trees.

While risk assessment is applicable across all workplaces, the inherent unpredictability associated with flammable and hazardous materials means that simply detecting a fire is insufficient. This limitation is evident in jet fires, where intense heat fluxes can strike nearby equipment, significantly raising the likelihood of a catastrophic domino effect. Consequently, characterizing such incidents is vital for effective risk management, particularly through the segmentation of radiation zones within the flame. This paper presents an exploratory study comparing traditional computer vision and Deep Learning segmentation techniques to address this challenge. Using a dataset of propane jet fires, the study trains and evaluates various approaches, incorporating specialized loss functions to mitigate data imbalance caused by differing zone distributions and backgrounds. Furthermore, performance metrics are correlated with expert manual rankings to ensure alignment with professional criteria. The research identifies the Hausdorff Distance and Adjusted Random Index as the most correlated metrics, with the UNet architecture combined with Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss yielding the best results. These findings offer a foundation for future work to extract additional geometric details from segmentation masks or to adapt the methods for other fire-related accidents.

Dimensional data reduction techniques are essential for analyzing and visualizing large datasets, yet unsupervised exploration demands methods that are simple, flexible, and scalable. Existing approaches often suffer from complex parameterization and computational bottlenecks when handling large-scale data structures. This work focuses on the t-SNE algorithm, demonstrating that a streamlined setup relying solely on the perplexity parameter can effectively balance the visualization of both local and global data structures. Additionally, we introduce a "chunk&mix" protocol to efficiently parallelize t-SNE, enabling the exploration of data across a significantly broader range of scales. Our parallel implementation of BH-tSNE, called pt-SNE, achieves global embeddings comparable to state-of-the-art solutions; however, the chunk&mix protocol introduces minimal noise and slightly reduces local-scale accuracy. We show that simple post-processing can effectively restore local visualization without compromising global precision. We anticipate this strategy will be applicable to other faster embedding algorithms, such as FIt-SNE or UMAP, thereby advancing the state of the art and facilitating more comprehensive data analysis and visualization.

This paper demonstrates that for a sequence of oriented, complete, pointed $3$-manifolds $(M_i, g_i, p_i)$ which are uniformly asymptotically Euclidean and possess non-negative integrable scalar curvature ($R_{g_i}\geq 0$), the condition that their mass $m(g_i)$ approaches zero implies that, after removing subsets $Z_i\subset M_i$ with boundary area $|\partial Z_i|\leq C m(g_i)^{1/2}$, the manifolds $(M_i \setminus Z_i, g_i, p_i)$ converge to Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$ in the pointed metric topology up to diffeomorphisms. This result validates Huisken-Ilmanen's conjecture within the flat metric topology. Furthermore, under the additional assumption of a uniform lower bound on Ricci curvature, $Ric_{g_i}\geq -2 \Lambda$, the original sequence $(M_i, g_i, p_i)$ converges to $\mathbb{R}^3$ in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology.

The origins and evolution of the 1/f power law seen in the energy spectra of solar coronal and solar wind fluctuations at hourly scales remain incompletely understood. Although various theories involving both linear and nonlinear mechanisms have been proposed, the highly inhomogeneous nature of the solar corona and solar wind is frequently neglected. This study examines the linear evolution of pure and surface Alfvén waves as they propagate through a plasma that varies inhomogeneously across magnetic field lines. We model this density inhomogeneity as two-dimensional colored noise with power spectral slopes between -2 and -1. When Alfvén waves travel independently along separate magnetic field lines, phase mixing eventually causes them to become completely out of phase, resulting in unrealistic spectra. However, when the interaction between the inhomogeneous background and the waves is fully considered, transverse waves—specifically surface Alfvén waves (also known as kink or Alfvénic waves)—emerge. These waves exhibit collective behavior among neighboring field lines with varying Alfvén speeds. We demonstrate that the linear cascade of surface Alfvén wave energy, driven by phase mixing and resonant absorption, produces a perpendicular wave energy spectrum that converges toward the perpendicular power spectrum of the background density. Consequently, our model suggests that a 1/f perpendicular density power spectrum in the solar corona can generate, through linear processes, the 1/f spectrum of fluctuations observed at the largest scales.

This study comprehensively evaluates the performance of variable-rate hybrid automatic repeat request with incremental redundancy (HARQ-IR) within Beckmann fading channels. The Beckmann model specifically captures the effects of line-of-sight (LOS) paths, temporal correlation in fading, and disparities in means and variances between in-phase and quadrature components. The combination of this sophisticated channel model and the variable-rate transmission strategy renders performance analysis highly complex, as the joint distribution of channel coefficients takes a cumbersome form that hinders exact analysis. Consequently, asymptotic analysis is employed to derive tractable results, leading to closed-form expressions for outage probability and long-term average throughput (LTAT) that offer clear theoretical insights. Moreover, the simplicity of these derived formulas facilitates the optimization of LTAT subject to an outage constraint by selecting optimal transmission rates. Specifically, leveraging the increasing monotonicity and convexity of outage probability relative to transmission rates, a suboptimal algorithm is developed by alternating between iterative optimization and concave fractional programming. This proposed method achieves lower computational complexity compared to exhaustive search techniques.

We introduce a solution concept for supergames modeled after finite automata. In this framework, an equilibrium is characterized as a cycle of state transitions, while a supergame represents an infinite trajectory through the states of a finite stage game. We demonstrate that when the stage game exhibits local non-cooperation and utility declines monotonically with the number of defecting agents, the symmetric multiagent prisoners' dilemma supergame is guaranteed to possess at least one symmetric equilibrium and may also admit asymmetric equilibria.

This work contributes to the investigation of superintegrable Hamiltonian systems with magnetic fields in three-dimensional Euclidean space ($\mathbb{E}_3$) within the framework of quantum mechanics. Despite increasing interest in complex electromagnetic fields among mathematicians, driven by their physical relevance confirmed in experiments [X. Peng et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 114 (2015)], such fields have remained largely unexplored in the literature on superintegrability. We address this gap by seeking additional first-order integrals of motion for integrable systems of cylindrical type. Our analysis reveals that known systems can be extended into this domain by incorporating complex coupling constants. Furthermore, we identify a novel system whose integrals of motion also involve complex constants. All identified systems exhibit multiseparability. However, rigorous mathematical analysis is complicated by the non-Hermitian nature of these systems and the loss of gauge invariance. We proceed formally and leave the resolution of these issues as an open challenge.

We develop and numerically resolve a model for surface-active nematodynamics. The numerical method is validated using a spherical geometry, after which we examine how hydrodynamics affects the oscillatory behavior of topological defects. For ellipsoidal surfaces, we investigate the impact of geometric forces on these motion patterns by incorporating both intrinsic and extrinsic curvature effects. The numerical experiments reveal that extrinsic curvature contributions lead to a stronger coupling with geometric properties, offering a means to regulate flow and defect dynamics through surface characteristics.

This note serves as a concise introduction to dimensional analysis within the contexts of Lorentzian and general relativity, as well as differential geometry. It aims to resurrect the concepts of 'intrinsic' or 'absolute' dimension for tensorial quantities, originally proposed by Dorgelo and Schouten. Unlike coordinate-dependent dimensions, intrinsic dimension reflects the physical and operational significance of a tensor, remaining independent of the coordinate system's units. The text summarizes the dimensional analysis of key tensors and operations, demonstrating that tensor components do not necessarily share the same dimension. Notably, it establishes that the Riemann (once contravariant, thrice covariant), Ricci (twice covariant), and Einstein (twice covariant) curvature tensors are dimensionless. Furthermore, the discussion explores the relationship between dimension and operational meaning for the metric and stress-energy-momentum tensors, reviewing various conventions for their dimensions, including Einstein's constant $\kappa$, with special attention to the intriguing case where $\kappa = 8\pi G$ excludes factors of $c$.

Our theoretical investigation into two-dimensional exciton-polariton lattices predicts the emergence of non-Hermitian topological corner modes driven by non-resonant pumping. Extending the concept of the non-Hermitian skin effect, our model results in the localization of all eigenstates at the two corners. This represents a higher-dimensional topological configuration compared to existing proposals in exciton-polariton systems. We demonstrate that this setup enables signals propagating through the bulk to navigate around defects—a capability absent in both one-dimensional topological lattices and two-dimensional lattices featuring Hermitian edge states. Moreover, because all polariton states remain localized away from the excitation site, the system facilitates more precise measurements of polariton-polariton interaction strengths, as the pump-induced exciton-reservoir is spatially distinct from the polariton states.

The anthropic principle suggests that life can only arise and persist within a limited range of fundamental constants (FCs). We extend these anthropic arguments to scenarios involving transient fluctuations in FCs, a regime typical of clumpy dark matter models where FCs inside dense regions can deviate drastically from their standard values. We demonstrate that the transit of such a macroscopic clump through Earth would render the planet uninhabitable, causing the periodic table of elements to be incomplete and preventing water from functioning as a universal solvent. Leveraging the anthropic principle allows us to tighten current astrophysical constraints on specific dark matter model couplings by a factor of one hundred thousand.

Service federation within 5G and B5G networks allows providers to orchestrate services across various domains, making admission control a critical challenge. For each incoming request, the admission controller must either select a deployment domain or reject it to maximize long-term average profits, without knowledge of future demands. This paper first derives an optimal admission control policy under the assumption of known demand arrival and departure rates by modeling the scenario as a Markov decision process and solving it via policy iteration. As a practical alternative for scenarios where these rates are unknown, we employ Q-Learning and R-Learning algorithms to approximate the optimal strategy. Extensive simulations demonstrate that these learning methods surpass greedy policies; while Q-Learning's performance is sensitive to the discount factor, the R-Learning algorithm achieves an optimality gap of no more than 3–5% regardless of the system configuration.

While the primary aim of text simplification (TS) is to lower complexity for human readers, this study explores a secondary application: aiding machines in natural language processing (NLP) tasks. We assessed neural TS through two approaches: simplifying input texts during prediction and augmenting training data to supply machines with extra information. Our results show that the data augmentation approach significantly enhances machine performance across two datasets. Specifically, applying TS to training data boosted the accuracy of LSTM (by 1.82–1.98%) and SpanBERT (by 0.7–1.3%) extractors on TACRED, a challenging, large-scale relation extraction benchmark. Additionally, this method improved matched and mismatched accuracies for a BERT text classifier on the MNLI dataset by up to 0.65% and 0.62%, respectively.

The well-established Tai mapping between two rooted labeled trees, $T_1(V_1, E_1)$ and $T_2(V_2, E_2)$, establishes a bijective node correspondence that maintains ancestor relationships. However, determining a maximum-weight Tai mapping for unordered trees is an NP-complete problem. In this study, we introduce the concept of an "anti Tai mapping," denoted as $M \subseteq V_1 	imes V_2$, which is a binary relation between two unordered labeled trees where no pair of elements $(x, y)$ and $(x', y')$ in $M$ satisfies the ancestor condition simultaneously. Specifically, for an ancestor order $x < x'$, the condition requires that $(x \le x' \iff y 
ot\le y') \vee (x' \le x \iff y' 
ot\le y')$. This maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem is critical for applying the cutting plane method within integer programming approaches to solve the original Tai mapping problem. We present an efficient polynomial-time algorithm to find such a mapping when one of the trees is a path. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to extend this approach to derive a polynomially computable lower bound for the optimal anti Tai mapping between two general unordered labeled trees. This extension relies on a restricted subclass of anti Tai mappings defined by the condition $x \sim x' \iff y 
ot\sim y'$, where $\sim$ indicates that two nodes lie on the same root-to-leaf path. For this specific class, we provide an efficient algorithm that solves the problem directly on two unordered trees with a time complexity of $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$.

This paper investigates smooth nonlinear mappings between Banach and Hilbert spaces that transform small balls into convex sets, assuming the ball radius is sufficiently small. This characteristic holds significant relevance for various applied problems. Specifically, for smooth and regular mappings in Hilbert spaces, the convexity of ball images and the preservation of convexity through linear approximations reveal profound geometric properties of the underlying space. The current study concentrates on establishing mild sufficient conditions for local convexity in nonlinear mappings of Banach spaces. Unlike the Hilbert space scenario, where local convexity relies on the strong convexity of a ball $B_{r}(a)\subset X$, local convexity in Banach spaces depends on more intricate properties of both the mapping and the space itself. Particular emphasis is placed on locally convex functions within Banach spaces, where the authors address a reformulated local convexity problem. The solution involves the interaction between the function's modulus of smoothness and the Banach space's modulus of convexity, derived from a comprehensive examination of local regularity in nonlinear mappings and associated convexity features. Several findings presented herein appear novel and significant even in finite-dimensional contexts. Furthermore, the study formulates open problems concerning the local convexity property for nonlinear mappings in Banach spaces.

The growing ability of large language models to produce human-like text has driven their widespread use in applications facing the public. Concurrently, these advancements have sparked intense debate regarding the potential societal risks, whether accidental or intentional. While various studies have pinpointed the sources of these harms and advocated for the creation of safer, more equitable models, this work goes further by surveying practical methods to address these threats. Leveraging existing taxonomies of language model risks, we offer a structured overview of strategies for detecting and mitigating various types of harm. By connecting diverse research areas, this survey serves as a practical guide for both researchers and practitioners, detailing the motivations behind mitigation techniques, their limitations, and unresolved challenges for future inquiry.

This paper presents the definitions of central vertex corona, central edge corona, and central edge neighborhood corona based on the central graph, and subsequently determines their adjacency, Laplacian, and signless Laplacian spectra. Our findings demonstrate that infinitely many pairs of cospectral graphs can be generated with respect to the adjacency, Laplacian, and signless Laplacian matrices. Furthermore, as a practical application, we compute the number of spanning trees and the Kirchhoff index for these constructed graphs.

Nanoelectromechanical systems (NEMS) combine electrical and mechanical functions at the nanoscale. Due to individual electron tunneling, these systems exhibit complex, self-generated, and highly non-linear dynamics. Theoretically, we demonstrate that rotor shuttles—fundamental NEMS lacking intrinsic frequencies—can rectify oscillatory bias voltages in a highly controlled way across a broad spectrum of external parameters, despite stochastic electron tunneling and thermal noise. Supported by a straightforward analytic model, we distinguish various operational modes of charge rectification. Remarkably, the current's direction is highly sensitive to external parameters.

We provide a comprehensive characterization of the Bridgeland stability manifold associated with the bounded derived category of holomorphic triples on a smooth projective curve of genus 1, describing it as a connected, four-dimensional complex manifold.

One of the most difficult and essential challenges in laboratory, astrophysical, and space plasma physics involves understanding how nearly collisionless plasmas relax into quasi-stationary states and the resulting electromagnetic turbulence. Recent arguments suggest that solar wind plasma $\beta$ and temperature anisotropy are controlled by kinetic instabilities—including the ion-cyclotron, mirror, electron-cyclotron, and firehose modes—and that magnetic fluctuations align with Fluctuation-Dissipation theorem predictions, even well below kinetic instability thresholds. Utilizing in-situ magnetic and plasma data from the THEMIS satellite mission, we demonstrate that this regulatory mechanism also operates within the Earth's magnetotail plasma sheet at both ion and electron scales. Despite the distinct differences between solar wind and magnetotail environments, our findings indicate that spontaneous fluctuations and their collisionless regulation are intrinsic characteristics of space and astrophysical plasmas, implying that these processes are universal.

Analyzing plaque deposits within the coronary vasculature remains a critical focus in contemporary clinical research. While numerous new algorithms for specific sub-tasks, such as centerline extraction or vessel and plaque segmentation, are currently being proposed, clinical application requires a comprehensive software solution that facilitates manual corrections, offers detailed visual feedback, and supports tissue analysis. To address this need, we introduce an integrated software platform capable of robust automatic centerline extraction and both inner and outer vessel wall segmentation, alongside user-friendly manual correction tools. Additionally, the system enables lesion annotation along centerlines for further tissue composition analysis. It also supports future research directions by accommodating dual-energy CT scans with specialized plaque analysis and automated quantification of fatty tissue surrounding the vasculature.

Principles governing the composition of reduced moduli are generalized from two dimensions to domains within $n$-dimensional Euclidean space for $n > 2$. This generalization yields analogues of the extremal decomposition theorems established by Kufarev, Dubinin, and Kirillova for the planar case.

We examine a wide range of non-classical states formed by superposing squeezed and displaced number states, analyzing their phase space structure with an eye toward Heisenberg-limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Suitable squeezing and displacement parameters are determined such that the state fidelity relative to a metrologically sensitive compass state exceeds 99%. Furthermore, the variance in measurements of small shifts is found to be identical for both the proposed states and the compass states, exhibiting comparable behavior as the average photon number changes. In terms of metrological applications, the low number variance of the compass state at low coherent amplitudes indicates its potential for estimating the damping parameter.

Techniques like Extra Corporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) cannulation and Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) present significant technical challenges even for experienced medical professionals. This study details the foundational technologies of a teleoperated system designed to facilitate femoral vascular access, a critical yet often limiting step in the broader adoption of these life-saving procedures in field settings. The system integrates a kinematic manipulator, diverse sensing capabilities, and a user interface. Furthermore, we assessed the system's performance using both surgical phantoms and in-vivo porcine models. These evaluations achieved, to our knowledge, the first instances of robot-assisted arterial catheterizations, marking a pivotal advancement toward the ultimate objective of fully automated catheter insertion via the Seldinger technique.

The non-Hermitian skin effect typically arises from asymmetric hopping between forward and backward directions, causing all system modes to localize at a single edge of a finite one-dimensional lattice. However, implementing such asymmetry in optical setups is highly challenging. We theoretically demonstrate that a finite chain of 1D exciton-polariton micropillars, which features symmetric hopping, can exhibit a bi-skin effect due to the system's intrinsic nonlinearity, resulting in mode localization at both edges. Furthermore, we calculate the winding number to reveal the topological origin of these modes.

This study extends distributionally robust newsvendor models by integrating moment constraints, maintaining Wasserstein distance as the ambiguity metric. It formulates the infinite-dimensional primal problem and utilizes moment problem duality to obtain a simplified finite-dimensional dual. A central inquiry examines how distributional ambiguity influences optimal order quantities and associated profits or costs. To address this, the paper develops relevant theory and presents an auto sales case study. The work concludes with observations on potential avenues for future research.

The Mermin-Wagner theorem posits that long-range magnetic order cannot exist in one- or two-dimensional isotropic magnets with short-ranged interactions. As a cornerstone in magnetism, this principle has guided the investigation of recently discovered 2D van der Waals (vdW) magnetic materials, from fundamental theory to practical applications. In these systems, magnetic ordering is usually explained by significant magnetic anisotropy, which creates a spin-wave gap and bypasses the theorem's primary assumptions. However, we demonstrate that in finite-size 2D vdW magnets typically encountered in laboratory settings (e.g., within millimeters), short-range interactions can be sufficiently strong to stabilize magnetic order at finite temperatures without requiring any magnetic anisotropy for practical use. We show that magnetic ordering can emerge in 2D material flakes regardless of lattice symmetry, driven by the intrinsic nature of spin exchange interactions and finite-size effects in two dimensions. Surprisingly, we find that the crossover temperature, marking the shift from a superparamagnetic state to a completely disordered paramagnetic regime, shows weak dependence on system size; consequently, observing the vanishing of magnetic order at cryogenic temperatures as predicted by the Mermin-Wagner theorem would require system lengths on the scale of the observable universe (~10$^{26}$ m). These findings highlight exchange interactions as the primary mechanism stabilizing short-range order in 2D magnetism and expand the potential for exploring low-anisotropy compounds at the atomic scale.

This paper examines the creation of vortex structures when an electron beam reflects off the double layer within Jupiter's ionosphere. It further investigates how these vortices affect the generation of dense upward electron fluxes, which are accelerated by the double layer potential along the Io flux tube, potentially enabling a phase transition to the cyclotron superradiance mode. The study analyzes the conditions required for the formation of these vortex perturbations and derives a nonlinear equation to describe their dynamics, subsequently exploring the resulting consequences.

The movement of noncircular two-dimensional vortices is demonstrated to rely on a specific interaction between vortex ellipticity and the fluid density gradient. This method adopts the viewpoint that an elliptic vortex can be modeled as the projection of a hypothetical circular vortex whose symmetry axis is angled relative to its propagation direction. The derived kinetic equation provides understanding regarding the simultaneous evolution of vortex tilt and velocity within few-body nonequilibrium systems, such as the nucleation and annihilation of vortex pairs. Developed and applied to optical vortices, the model's predictive capabilities are confirmed through optical experiments. Furthermore, this framework remains valid across both quantum fluid and classical hydrodynamic contexts.

In cricket, the coin toss result is widely considered a key factor influencing match outcomes. Teams that win the toss often choose to bat first to capitalize on favorable pitch conditions and establish a substantial target, which can hinder opponents from performing optimally in the second innings due to factors like deteriorating pitches and the pressure of chasing high scores. While existing literature and expert opinions highlight the benefits of batting first, there has been insufficient investigation into how batting and bowling orders affect match results to address potential biases. This study introduces a probability theory-based model to analyze venue-specific scoring and chasing patterns across different outcomes. An analysis of 1,117 One-Day International matches from ten major venues reveals a significant scoring advantage and higher likelihood of success when the winning team bats first. The findings indicate that if such a team were to chase instead, they would be highly unlikely to achieve or defend the same high scores. Consequently, the coin toss decision may inadvertently favor one side over the other. To rectify this, a Bayesian model is proposed to adjust target scores for each venue, ensuring equal probabilities of winning and scoring regardless of the toss outcome. The dataset and source code are made publicly available to support future research aimed at fostering competitive matches by neutralizing the advantage of batting order.

The LHCb experiment analyzes proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $13 \, \mathrm{TeV}$, utilizing an integrated luminosity of $6 \, \mathrm{fb^{-1}}$, to determine the ratios of effective decay widths for $D^0 \to \pi^-\pi^+$ and $D^0 \to K^-K^+$ relative to $D^0 \to K^-\pi^+$ decays. These measurements yield the charm mixing parameters $y_{CP}^{\pi\pi} - y_{CP}^{K\pi}$ and $y_{CP}^{KK} - y_{CP}^{K\pi}$, with results of $(6.57 \pm 0.53 \pm 0.16) \times 10^{-3}$ and $(7.08 \pm 0.30 \pm 0.14) \times 10^{-3}$, respectively, where the first uncertainties are statistical and the second are systematic.
