We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite.

The ALICE ITS3 upgrade initiative and CERN's EP R&D on monolithic pixel sensors are evaluating the viability of Tower Partners Semiconductor Co.'s 65 nm process for future vertex detectors. The ITS3 design intends to utilize wafer-scale Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors thinned to 20–40 µm and bent into cylindrical half-barrels. A primary step in realizing this detector involves validating the sensor technology through comprehensive characterization in laboratories and via in-beam tests. The Digital Pixel Test Structure (DPTS), produced as a prototype in the initial sensor submission, has undergone a systematic measurement campaign detailed in this article. The findings confirm that detection efficiency and resistance to both ionising and non-ionising radiation meet the anticipated requirements for ALICE ITS3. Additionally, the DPTS demonstrated operation at +20°C with 99% detection efficiency after an irradiation dose of $10^{15}$ 1 MeV n$_{\mathrm{eq}}$/cm$^2$. Furthermore, spatial, timing, and energy resolutions were assessed across various configurations and irradiation levels.

Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks represent a critical cyber threat, making their mitigation within cloud environments a persistent and significant security challenge that continues to attract research attention. Fog computing, an evolution of cloud computing, has been leveraged to enhance cloud security. Moving Target Defense (MTD) is an emerging proactive defense strategy designed to counter DDoS attacks by rendering systems dynamic and unpredictable through continuous alterations to the attack surface, thereby confusing adversaries. This paper introduces a novel DDoS mitigation framework called CFPM, which integrates the MTD technique with a Cloud-Fog Platform. CFPM implements migration-based MTD at the fog layer to defend against cloud DDoS attacks. It proactively identifies attackers among legitimate users at the fog layer and isolates them from benign clients. Furthermore, CFPM employs an efficient request handling mechanism for load balancing and attacker isolation, aiming to minimize service disruption for both cloud and fog servers. The framework's efficacy is assessed by analyzing system behavior before and after attacks across various scenarios. This approach proves effective by capitalizing on the synergistic advantages of MTD and the fog computing paradigm within cloud environments.

This work addresses the challenge of detecting multiway block structures within large, noisy tensors, a task critical to fields like genomics, recommendation systems, topic modeling, and sensor network localization. We introduce a tensor block model alongside a unified least-squares estimation method, providing theoretical accuracy guarantees for multiway clustering. Our analysis establishes the statistical convergence of the estimator and demonstrates that the resulting clustering procedure achieves partition consistency. Furthermore, we develop a sparse regularization technique to pinpoint blocks with elevated means. The proposed framework accommodates diverse data types, including binary, continuous, and hybrid observations. Through simulations and analysis of two real-world datasets, we show that our approach outperforms existing methods.

This document presents a compilation of six contributions from the 2021 ICRC conference by the CORSIKA 8 Collaboration, detailing the project's current status. Individual validations of secondary hadron and electromagnetic cascades are highlighted, alongside a review of existing results. A new framework for simulating radio emissions is introduced, leveraging CORSIKA 8's modular architecture to accommodate both the CoREAS and ZHS formalisms. Additionally, preliminary Cherenkov emission calculations are displayed, utilizing CORSIKA 8 integrated with a GPU-based Cherenkov code. Finally, a powerful new feature is demonstrated that allows for a comprehensive analysis of the complete genealogy of air shower particles.

Obtaining labels for supervised learning is often costly. To enhance the sample efficiency of neural network regression, we investigate active learning strategies that adaptively choose batches of unlabeled data for annotation. We introduce a framework for building these strategies using (network-dependent) base kernels, kernel transformations, and selection techniques. This framework covers numerous existing Bayesian approaches based on Gaussian Process approximations of neural networks, as well as non-Bayesian methods. Furthermore, we suggest substituting the standard last-layer features with sketched finite-width Neural Tangent Kernels and integrating them with a new clustering approach. To assess various methods, we establish an open-source benchmark featuring 15 large-scale tabular regression datasets. Our proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark, scales effectively to large datasets, and operates out-of-the-box without requiring modifications to network architecture or training code. We also provide open-source code containing efficient implementations of all kernels, transformations, and selection methods, enabling the reproduction of our results.

This research investigates the qualitative and quantitative analysis of chaotic systems through symbolic descriptions. By examining two well-known models—the Lorenz and Rössler systems and their characteristic attractors—we demonstrate that, when an appropriate symbolic partition is selected, three complexity metrics (Shannon source entropy, Lempel-Ziv complexity, and Markov transition matrices) effectively characterize the degree of chaos and accurately identify stability windows within the parameter space. Additionally, this study highlights the practical application of symbolic dynamics by introducing a fidelity test for reservoir computing to simulate chaotic properties in replicas of both models. These findings are corroborated by comparing the results of the proposed measures against one-dimensional return maps and established complexity metrics.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense, and unresolved radio flashes that originate beyond the Milky Way. Although the source of these enigmatic events remains unidentified, their extreme luminosity and fleeting nature have generated significant theoretical debate. The revelation that FRB 121102 is a repeating source allowed for multiwavelength follow-up observations, successfully pinpointing its host galaxy. VERITAS conducted observations at the FRB 121102 location, including simultaneous monitoring with Arecibo. This paper presents findings from a search for steady very high-energy gamma-ray emission, alongside the methodology employed to detect transient optical and very high-energy gamma-ray signals on short timescales.

Distributed certification, encompassing methods like proof-labeling schemes and locally checkable proofs, addresses the challenge of validating whether a distributed system adheres to a specific boolean predicate. In this framework, a non-trustable oracle assigns a certificate to every process, which are then verified locally by the processes themselves. This system must satisfy two key properties: completeness, ensuring all processes accept any valid instance with an appropriate certificate assignment, and soundness, guaranteeing that at least one process rejects every invalid instance regardless of the certificate assignment. The design goals require that verification be rapid and certificates remain compact. While numerous studies have developed specific certification mechanisms for particular predicates, this paper introduces a general "meta-theorem." We demonstrate that for any boolean predicate on graphs expressible in monadic second-order (MSO) logic, a distributed certification mechanism exists for graphs with bounded treewidth. This mechanism utilizes certificates of size $O(\log^2n)$ bits for $n$-node graphs and employs a verification protocol requiring only a single round of neighbor-to-neighbor communication.

This paper introduces a method for detecting 3D objects monocularly from a single RGB image, utilizing a new disentangling transformation for both 2D and 3D detection losses alongside a novel, self-supervised confidence metric for 3D bounding boxes. Our disentanglement strategy offers two key benefits: it streamlines training dynamics by mitigating complex parameter interactions and avoids the difficulty of balancing independent regression terms. By isolating the specific contributions of parameter groups to a loss function without altering its fundamental nature, our approach resolves these challenges. Additionally, we extend this disentanglement technique to a new loss function driven by a signed Intersection-over-Union criterion, further enhancing 2D detection performance. Beyond methodological contributions, we critically examine the AP metric used in KITTI3D, the primary dataset for benchmarking 3D detection. We identify and correct a flaw in the 11-point interpolated AP metric that has biased all prior results, particularly affecting monocular 3D detection. Through extensive experiments and ablation studies on KITTI3D and nuScenes, we achieve new state-of-the-art results for the "car" category by significant margins.

We introduce a new relativistic density-functional framework for modeling quark matter that incorporates a confinement mechanism. Within this approach, the quasiparticle treatment of quarks naturally suppresses them through a substantial quark self-energy, even at the mean-field level. We establish that our method is mathematically equivalent to a chiral quark model featuring medium-dependent couplings, with chiral symmetry restoration dynamically guaranteed by the density functional's construction. By integrating vector repulsion and diquark pairing, the model generates a hybrid equation of state (EoS) for cold compact-star matter. We investigate the relationship between this hybrid EoS and stellar mass-radius relations as well as tidal deformability, comparing the outcomes against multiple observational constraints. These include the NICER radius measurement of PSR J0740+6620 and tidal deformability limits derived from GW170817. Our results demonstrate consistency with these constraints, while noting that further refinement is possible by tuning the vector repulsion and diquark pairing coupling parameters.

Recent years have seen numerous adversarial training techniques proposed to enhance the robustness of machine learning models against input perturbations. However, despite significant advancements, these methods often result in a decline in standard test accuracy. This has sparked research interest in the tradeoff between standard accuracy (generalization) and robust accuracy (robust generalization). This paper revisits that tradeoff for latent models, arguing that it is alleviated when data exhibits a low-dimensional structure. Specifically, we examine binary classification under two generative models—the Gaussian mixture model and the generalized linear model—where features reside on a low-dimensional manifold. We present theoretical evidence demonstrating that this manifold structure enables the development of models that are nearly optimal for both standard and robust accuracy. Furthermore, we validate our theory through numerical experiments, including training a Mixture of Factor Analyzers (MFA) model on the MNIST dataset.

This guide serves as a tutorial designed for students and professionals to understand the underlying models and methods of tools used for electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations. Adopting an introductory approach, it illustrates the EMT methodology from a circuit-theory standpoint using two straightforward examples, while expecting readers to deepen their expertise through further study. Nevertheless, this document constitutes an excellent starting point for anyone interested in the field, particularly those aiming to develop their own simulation tools.

We introduce CPO, a rapid and resilient algorithm designed to localize a 2D panorama relative to a 3D point cloud, even when the scene undergoes changes. Instead of relying on traditional feature point matching, our method leverages the spatial context inherent in panorama images to robustly manage scene variations. Specifically, we develop an efficient color histogram generation technique followed by robust localization via score maps. By exploiting the unique equivariance of spherical projections, we enable swift color histogram creation for numerous camera poses without explicitly rendering images for every candidate. We accumulate the regional consistency between the panorama and point cloud into 2D/3D score maps, utilizing these to weight input color values and enhance robustness. This weighted color distribution rapidly identifies favorable initial poses, ensuring stable convergence for gradient-based optimization. Lightweight and effective, CPO achieves reliable localization across all tested scenarios, maintaining stable performance despite challenges such as scene changes, repetitive structures, and featureless regions, which are common obstacles in visual localization using perspective cameras.

Puckered-layer two-dimensional (2D) materials represent promising prospects for next-generation opto-electronic applications due to their anisotropic reaction to external stimuli and the ability to tune their band gaps across varying layer counts. Specifically, PdSe2 is an emerging 2D transition-metal dichalcogenide exhibiting a band gap that shifts from 1.3 eV in monolayers to predicted semimetallic behavior in bulk form. This study employs angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy with high energy and momentum resolution to investigate the electronic band structure of PdSe2. Our findings confirm the semiconducting character of the bulk material. Additionally, constant binding-energy maps of reciprocal space demonstrate a notable sensitivity to atomic arrangement and symmetry at specific sites. Supported by density functional theory calculations, we attribute this phenomenon to the intrinsic orbital character of the electronic bands. These outcomes not only deepen the understanding of PdSe2's electronic configuration but also highlight further capabilities of photoemission spectroscopy.

We establish that a minimum of $\Omega(n^{0.51})$ hyperplanes are required to intersect every edge of an $n$-dimensional hypercube. This result yields two applications: a lower bound on the computational complexity of parity and a lower bound on the cover number of the hypercube using skew hyperplanes.

Compounds of the type $A$B$_{2}$ (where $A$ is K, Rb, or Cs) adopt a cubic Laves phase structure with $Fd\bar{3}$m symmetry. This geometric arrangement facilitates chiral phonons, characterized by atoms circulating around their equilibrium points. However, the presence of both inversion and time-reversal symmetry causes the total pseudo-angular momentum (PAM) of the system to be zero. We demonstrate that doping these materials induces a transition to a new phase with $F\bar{4}3$m symmetry. The newly proposed systems, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, are dynamically stable and lack soft modes. The breaking of inversion symmetry in these doped variants allows chiral phonon modes to possess a non-zero total PAM. In both system types, these chiral phonons occur at wavevectors located at the Brillouin zone boundary. This research investigates chiral phonon engineering through doping, predicts two novel materials, and suggests a new avenue for exploring the phonon Hall effect.

This study introduces a machine-learning solution to the persistent challenge in quantum many-body physics known as analytic continuation. For decades, this notoriously ill-conditioned task of deriving spectral functions from imaginary-time Green's functions has driven the development of novel methodologies. We demonstrate the efficacy of contemporary machine-learning strategies, specifically convolutional neural networks and stochastic gradient descent optimizer variants. Crucially, our machine-learning continuation kernel operates without any pre-existing "domain knowledge," meaning no physical priors are incorporated into its construction; instead, the neural networks acquire necessary insights solely through training. This approach yields superior results for both metallic and insulating band structures. Compared to conventional methods, our technique delivers more accurate spectra regarding peak positions and magnitudes while exhibiting greater robustness against noise—a critical requirement for successful continuation. Additionally, it achieves a computational speedup of $10^4$ to $10^5$ times over the maximum entropy method.

This paper investigates the network coding challenge involving sum-networks with three sources and $n$ terminals (denoted as 3s/nt sum-networks) for any positive integer $n$. We establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for the solvability of a specific class known as terminal-separable sum-networks. Crucially, determining whether a network belongs to this class and assessing its solvability can both be accomplished in polynomial time. Building on this, we propose an alternative necessary and sufficient condition that enables a more efficient algorithm with $O(|E|)$ complexity for determining the solvability of 3s/3t sum-networks, improving upon the $O(|E|^3)$ approach by Shenvi and Dey ([18]). To achieve these findings, we extend the region decomposition technique from [22] and [23] and generalize the decentralized coding method introduced in [21]. These advancements offer novel, efficient methodologies for addressing multiple-source, multiple-sink network coding problems.

This study investigates the pathways to significantly enhance broadband connectivity in next-generation 6G wireless networks. The analysis encompasses various use cases, including scenarios requiring peak data rates of up to 1 Tbps. Achieving these ambitious connectivity targets necessitates a combination of enablers across infrastructure, spectrum, and protocol/algorithmic domains. Infrastructure-level solutions include ultra-massive MIMO (potentially via holographic radio), intelligent reflecting surfaces, user-centric cell-free networking, integrated access and backhaul, and the fusion of space and terrestrial networks. Regarding spectrum, the network must leverage sub-6 GHz bands for broad coverage and spatial multiplexing of numerous devices, while higher frequency bands are primarily reserved for maximizing the peak rates of point-to-point links. Finally, at the protocol and algorithmic level, advancements in coding, modulation, and waveforms are essential to deliver lower latency, higher reliability, and reduced complexity.

This paper introduces a novel class of hemivariational inequalities involving the Laplace operator on locally finite graphs, coupled with multivalued, nonmonotone nonlinearities formulated via Clarke's subdifferential. Initially, we establish and demonstrate key results regarding the subdifferentiability of nonconvex functionals defined on graphs. Subsequently, we examine an elliptic hemivariational inequality on these graphs, proving the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions through the application of the surjectivity theorem for pseudomonotone mappings. Finally, the study addresses parabolic-type hemivariational inequalities on locally finite graphs and establishes the existence of their weak solutions.

We examine the collection of points exhibiting high pointwise emergence for $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphisms that maintain a hyperbolic measure. We establish a lower bound for the Hausdorff dimension of this collection relative to the unstable Hausdorff dimension of the measure. Furthermore, when the measure is an SRB, we demonstrate that the set of points with high emergence attains full Hausdorff dimension.

We introduce ConceptX, a new framework designed to investigate how latent concepts are embedded in representations from pre-trained language models. By employing clustering to uncover these concepts and aligning them with extensive human-defined categories, we gain explanatory insights. Our analysis of seven transformer models highlights three key findings: i) the overlap between latent spaces and various linguistic concepts varies significantly; ii) lower layers primarily capture lexical concepts like affixation, while core linguistic structures such as morphological and syntactic relations are more prominently represented in middle and higher layers; iii) certain encoded concepts are multi-faceted and defy adequate explanation through existing human-defined concepts.

This study introduces a new approach designed to significantly lower the energy usage of Optical Line Terminals (OLTs) within Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) Passive Optical Networks (PONs), including EPON and GPON. Since OLTs represent a major source of energy consumption in PONs—a key component of FTTx infrastructure—reducing their power draw is essential for environmental sustainability. This need is increasingly critical as OLTs support higher data rates, which typically correlate with increased energy use. We propose a novel energy-efficient OLT architecture that ensures end-user services while minimizing the number of active line cards. Specifically, the system adjusts the count of powered-on line cards based on real-time incoming traffic. Furthermore, to prevent service interruptions caused by shutting down line cards, the OLT is equipped with appropriate optical switches that dynamically manage communication between line cards and ONUs.

Unlike classical deep learning architectures, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) feature neurons that communicate via electrical impulses, or spikes, mimicking biological neurons. This design makes SNNs attractive for AI applications, particularly because they can be deployed on energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. Nevertheless, they typically achieve lower accuracy compared to their analog equivalents. This report investigates several regularization and normalization methods aimed at enhancing surrogate gradient learning within SNNs.

This study examines the scattering of time-harmonic point sources by an infinite, locally rough interface containing bounded obstacles within the lower half-space. The model is first transformed into an equivalent integral equation defined over a bounded domain, establishing well-posedness in $L^p$ through classical Fredholm theory. Subsequently, a global uniqueness theorem is established for the inverse problem of determining the locally rough interface, the embedded obstacles, and the wave number in the lower half-space using near-field data collected above the interface.

We examine a non-factorizable charming-loop correction in two contexts: an exclusive FCNC $B$-decay expressed via the 3-particle Bethe-Salpeter amplitude (3BS) of the $B$-meson, $\langle 0| ar q(x)G_{\mu
u}(z)b(0)|B(p)angle$, and the associated correction to the $B$-meson semileptonic form factor. Despite shared characteristics, these corrections exhibit significant distinctions. The form factor correction is primarily driven by the collinear light-cone configuration of the 3BS, defined by $z_\mu= u x_\mu$, $0 < u < 1$, and $x^2=0$. Conversely, the FCNC amplitude is dominated by a distinct configuration featuring non-collinear arguments, where $x^2=0$ and $z^2=0$, yet $(x-z)^2
e 0$ (implying $z_\mu
e u x_\mu$).

This study explores a late-fusion method for piano transcription that integrates a robust temporal prior implemented as a handcrafted Hidden Markov Model (HMM). The proposed network architecture is both parameter-efficient and straightforward to train using gradient descent. In the final stage, outputs are aggregated over time to generate note segmentations via an HMM, where transition probabilities are derived from ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) envelope models typically used in sound synthesis. Subsequently, a binary decision rule filters out note segment hypotheses that are too weak. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MAPS dataset, significantly outperforming existing methods in predicting complete note regions from onsets to offsets.

Medical dialogue summarization demands coherent outputs that encompass all clinically pertinent details; however, training effective models typically necessitates vast quantities of labeled data, which are difficult to acquire. We introduce an algorithm designed to generate synthetic training data with a specific emphasis on retaining medically significant information. By employing GPT-3 as the foundational model, our method scales just 210 human-labeled examples to achieve performance comparable to models trained on 6,400 examples—a thirty-fold increase—through the application of low-shot learning and ensemble techniques. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that this strategy yields high-quality synthetic data which, when integrated with human-labeled datasets, produces summaries that significantly outperform those generated by models trained exclusively on human data, exhibiting superior medical accuracy and coherence.

Recently, researchers have focused significantly on the fairness of machine learning (ML) algorithms. Most ML approaches exhibit bias against protected groups, restricting their use in various domains such as crime rate forecasting. Furthermore, missing data in datasets can exacerbate fairness issues if not managed correctly, yet the impact of imputation techniques on fairness remains underexplored. This study investigates how different embedding and neural network-based imputation methods affect fairness within graph data, specifically regarding node attributes. Experiments across six datasets reveal substantial fairness problems associated with missing data imputation in graph node classification tasks. Additionally, our findings indicate that the selection of an imputation method influences both fairness and model accuracy. These results offer critical insights into ensuring fairness in graph data and suggest efficient strategies for handling missing values, while also outlining potential avenues for future theoretical research on fairness in graph structures.

We introduce a supersymmetric radiative seesaw model incorporating modular $A_4$ symmetry. Leveraging the contributions of supersymmetric partners within one-loop diagrams that generate neutrino masses, we achieve a successful fit to neutrino data and derive specific predictions for the normal hierarchy within a minimal framework unattainable in non-supersymmetric scenarios. Furthermore, we present multiple predictive figures and illustrate a best-fit benchmark point via $\chi^2$ analysis.

A novel concept of integrability, termed multi-dimensional consistency, is defined for integrable systems possessing a Lagrangian 1-form structure within the geometric framework of quantum mechanics. The zero-curvature condition, which ensures this consistency, serves as a pivotal relation, such as for Hamiltonian operators. Consequently, the presence of this condition directly guarantees the path-independence of the mapping, exemplified by multi-time evolution in the Schrödinger picture. Furthermore, a continuous multi-time propagator is formulated. Utilizing this new propagator introduces a fresh perspective on summing over all possible paths, requiring consideration not only of trajectories in the space of dependent variables but also those in the space of independent variables. When the semi-classical approximation is applied to this multi-time propagator—expressed via the classical action and its fluctuations—the resulting extremum propagator ensures path independence across the space of independent variables, thereby securing the system's integrability.

Leveraging BERT pre-training to enhance phoneme encoders in text-to-speech (TTS) has gained significant traction. However, existing approaches utilize character-based units for pre-training, creating a mismatch with the phoneme-based input required during TTS fine-tuning. While pre-training exclusively on phonemes resolves this input discrepancy, it struggles to capture rich semantic information and representations due to the restricted phoneme vocabulary. To address this, we introduce MixedPhoneme BERT, a novel BERT variant that integrates both phoneme and sup-phoneme representations to boost learning capabilities. Specifically, we combine the original phoneme sequence with a merged sequence of adjacent phonemes (sup-phonemes) as model inputs, thereby expanding the model's capacity to learn rich contextual features. Experimental results indicate that MixedPhoneme BERT substantially improves TTS performance, achieving a 0.30 CMOS gain over the FastSpeech 2 baseline. Furthermore, it delivers a threefold increase in inference speed while maintaining voice quality comparable to the previous TTS pre-trained model, PnG BERT.

High-eccentricity migration is a probable formation pathway for numerous hot Jupiters, especially those exhibiting significant misalignment between the star's spin axis and the planet's orbital angular momentum. In a specific variant of this mechanism, an inclined stellar companion triggers von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai (ZLK) eccentricity oscillations in a cold Jupiter, after which tidal dissipation shrinks and circularizes the orbit. This process can cause the stellar spin to evolve chaotically, yielding highly misaligned hot Jupiters. While prior population studies of this mechanism assumed the stellar spin was aligned with the planetary orbital angular momentum at the onset of ZLK oscillations, the presence of a binary companion may significantly excite the star's obliquity during the protoplanetary disk's dissipation. We computed the stellar obliquities generated during the protoplanetary disk phase and employed these values to conduct an updated population synthesis of ZLK-driven high-eccentricity migration. Our results indicate that the resulting obliquity distribution of hot Jupiter systems is primarily retrograde, featuring a broad peak near 90$^\circ$. This distribution aligns intriguingly with the recently observed abundance of perpendicular planets in close proximity to their host stars.

Data privacy has become a prominent concern in the digital age, prompting significant challenges in the collection, management, processing, and publication of data. Consequently, personal information has gained substantial attention, leading to the enactment of regulations such as the GDPR in the European Union and the LGPD in Brazil. These frameworks aim to safeguard user data against misuse and breaches while granting individuals the right to demand explanations from corporations. During crises like the COVID-19 and Ebola pandemics, the exchange of health data across organizations was vital for curbing infection rates and reducing fatalities. Nevertheless, data subjects must retain the right to inquire about data usage purposes, request anonymization, and demand data deletion. In response, permissioned blockchain technology offers a solution to empower users by ensuring data ownership, transparency, and security through an immutable, distributed ledger governed by smart contracts. While current blockchain governance discussions often focus superficially on first-layer models (public and permissioned), they frequently overlook regulatory compliance. To address this, we have developed a second-layer data governance model for permissioned blockchains, grounded in the Governance Analytical Framework principles utilized during pandemic responses. This model structures the relationship between data owners and stakeholders, including companies and government entities, while preserving user privacy and duties. Legally, the model is anchored in the EU GDPR to address data privacy concerns.

This study presents simulations assessing the potential of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Next Generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) to identify and resolve substructures caused by terrestrial planets and Super-Earths in nearby protoplanetary disks. Building on global 2-D hydrodynamical planet-disk simulations that model gas and dust dynamics around embedded planets, our work tracks the joint evolution of these components over thousands of planetary orbits. We demonstrate that extended integrations with the ngVLA, lasting several tens of hours, can detect and spatially resolve dust features associated with low-mass rocky planets within the terrestrial planet formation zones of nearby disks (at stellocentric radii of $r = 1 - 3$ au), provided the disk viscosity in these regions is low ($\alpha \le 10^{-5}$). In contrast, ALMA lacks the resolution to discern these structures in the same disk regions. Furthermore, we show that high-resolution ngVLA observations spaced several days to weeks apart would enable the detection of the proper motion of the azimuthally asymmetric structures anticipated in terrestrial planet formation zones.

The rise of outsourced training and machine learning as a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice.

We introduce a new method for reconstructing sparse signals from cross-correlated data, a scenario prevalent in imaging disciplines like optics, holography, and seismic interferometry. Unlike traditional sparse recovery using linear measurements where the unknown is a vector, this problem involves a matrix representing the cross-correlation of the signal, causing the number of unknowns to increase quadratically and creating an inversion bottleneck. Our strategy mitigates this by reducing the problem's dimensionality, focusing solely on recovering the diagonal of the unknown matrix, which scales linearly with problem size. Central to this methodology is an efficient {\em Noise Collector} that absorbs data derived from off-diagonal elements, which do not contribute additional information regarding the signal's support. This transforms the challenge into a linear problem with computational costs comparable to those of standard linear measurements. Theoretically, our approach guarantees exact support recovery when noise levels are moderate and ensures zero false positives regardless of noise intensity. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that utilizing cross-correlated data enhances recoverable sparsity, which grows nearly linearly with the data volume. Numerical experiments included in this study validate these theoretical predictions.

The Metaverse has recently garnered significant interest from both academic and industrial sectors due to its profound potential for seamlessly merging the physical and digital realms. By synthesizing virtual reality (VR), edge computing, and advanced wireless communications, a robust, intelligent, and multidimensional wireless edge Metaverse is established for future society. This paper proposes a privacy-preserving targeted advertising framework designed for this environment. Specifically, a Metaverse service provider (MSP) allocates bandwidth to VR users via edge access points to facilitate their access. To safeguard user privacy, covert communication techniques are employed in the downlink, enabling the MSP to deliver high-quality services and increase profitability. Drawing on the concept of "covert" operations, the study utilizes targeted advertising to promote bandwidth sales while ensuring the strategy remains undetectable to competitors attempting counter-offers or attackers seeking to disrupt services. Leveraging the Vidale-Wolfe model and Hamiltonian function, we derive the optimal advertising strategy regarding budget allocation. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric called Meta-Immersion to quantify user experience. Performance evaluations demonstrate that the MSP can significantly enhance its revenue through an optimal targeted advertising approach, particularly when compared to scenarios without such advertising.

We introduce a novel formulation of quantum decoherence theory based on conditional wave theory (CWT), a framework initially established in molecular physics under the name exact factorisation. This study applies CWT to a standard model of collisional decoherence involving a free particle interacting with environmental particles, analyzed within a long-wavelength limit. Generally, the CWT equation of motion for the particle is non-linear, with this non-linearity arising from CWT gauge fields. For Gaussian wave packets, the analytic solutions derived from CWT equations precisely match those obtained using the density matrix formalism. We demonstrate that the CWT gauge terms, which govern the dynamics of the particle's marginal wave function, correspond to a Taylor series expansion of the particle's reduced density matrix. Approximate solutions to these equations yield a linear-time approximation that accurately reproduces the ensemble width across both short and long time scales, as well as the long-term evolution of the coherence length. Utilizing this approximation, the non-linear equation of motion for the marginal wave function can be recast as the logarithmic Schrödinger equation. Furthermore, the CWT formalism offers the potential for computationally efficient decoherence calculations, as it operates with wave-function level terms rather than evolving a density matrix through a master equation.

This paper details the LHCb collaboration's current measurements of the CP-violating phase $\phi_s$, examining results from decay channels including $B_s^0\to J/\psi\phi$, $B_s^0\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$, and $B_s^0 \to \psi(2S)\phi$. For the first time, the observation of the $B_s^0\to\eta_c\phi$ decay mode is reported, offering a pathway to measure $\phi_s$ using the expanded datasets anticipated over the next several years. The document concludes by outlining the projected improvements in measurement precision for $\phi_s$ expected from LHCb over the coming decade.

We present ShortcutGen, a novel data poisoning attack that employs a learned generator to create sample-specific, error-reducing perturbations. Its primary innovation lies in utilizing a randomly initialized discriminator to supply the spurious shortcuts essential for poison generation. Unlike previous iterative approaches, ShortcutGen produces perturbations through a single forward pass without requiring labels. Compared to the existing generative method, DeepConfuse, ShortcutGen offers a simpler, faster training process while maintaining competitive performance. Furthermore, we show that incorporating a basic augmentation strategy enhances ShortcutGen's resilience to early stopping, and the combination of augmented and non-augmented techniques achieves new state-of-the-art results in final validation accuracy, particularly within challenging transfer scenarios. Finally, by analyzing its operational mechanism, we hypothesize that learning a more general representation space could enable ShortcutGen to function effectively on unseen data.

The gravitational wave field is advancing quickly, driven by significant improvements in detector sensitivity that have made binary black hole mergers detectable. Among the most intriguing systems for future space-based detectors are extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs). This study examines an EMRI system where the central object is a spherically symmetric, static braneworld black hole possessing a tidal charge ($Q$). We analyze how this tidal charge influences the total gravitational wave flux and orbital phase as a non-spinning secondary inspirals around the primary. Furthermore, we discuss the observational consequences of tidal charges within EMRI waveforms. Our results indicate that LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observations will impose far tighter constraints on this parameter than black hole shadow imaging or ground-based gravitational wave detectors, potentially offering a means to probe the existence of extra dimensions.

This article establishes, for any degree $d\geq 1$, an embedding $\Phi_d$ that maps the connectedness locus $\mathcal{M}_{d+1}$ associated with polynomials of the form $z^{d+1}+c$ into the connectedness locus of degree $2d+1$ bicritical odd polynomials.

Matrix-valued asymmetric truncated Toeplitz operators arise as compressions of multiplication operators defined between two potentially distinct model spaces. In this paper, we provide a characterization of these matrix-valued asymmetric truncated Toeplitz operators by utilizing compressed shifts.

The decay process $H\to \ell^+\ell^- \gamma$, where $\ell$ represents electrons or muons, arises from two loop-induced sources: the resonant channel $H\to Z[\to \ell^+\ell^-] \gamma$ and a non-resonant component. We outline a gauge-independent method to disentangle these sub-processes, define the decay width $\Gamma(H\to Z\gamma)$, and derive it from differential branching ratios of $H\to \ell^+\ell^- \gamma$. Specifically for $\ell=\mu$, the tree-level decay rate, governed by the muon Yukawa coupling, plays a significant role. We introduce optimized kinematic cuts designed to isolate these three contributions, thereby facilitating key milestones: (i) the discovery of $H\to Z \gamma$, (ii) the observation of the tree-level $H\to \mu^+\mu^- \gamma$ decay, and (iii) the characterization of new physics within both the effective $H$-$Z$-$\gamma$ and non-resonant $H$-$\ell^+$-$\ell^-$-$\gamma$ couplings.

The decays $B_d^0\to J/\psi K^0_{\text{S}}$ and $B_s^0\to J/\psi\phi$ are fundamental for measuring the mixing phases $\phi_d$ and $\phi_s$ of $B^0_q$-$\bar B^0_q$ ($q=d,s$) systems. The accuracy of extracting these parameters is constrained by doubly Cabibbo-suppressed penguin topologies, which can be accounted for via control channels leveraging $SU(3)$ flavour symmetry in strong interactions. By employing current data and a novel simultaneous analysis, we evaluate the current understanding of these effects and incorporate them into the derived $\phi_q$ values. We critically examine Standard Model predictions for these phases and assess the potential space for new physics. Looking toward the high-precision era of flavour physics, we demonstrate that signals for physics beyond the Standard Model could be detected with a significance exceeding five standard deviations. Furthermore, we calculate effective colour-suppression factors for $B_d^0\to J/\psi K^0$, $B_d^0\to J/\psi K^0_{\text{S}}$, and $B_d^0\to J/\psi\pi^0$ decays, serving as benchmarks for QCD computations of the underlying dynamics, and introduce a new method utilizing information from the semileptonic decays $B_d^0\to\pi^-\ell^+\nu_{\ell}$ and $B_s^0\to K^-\ell^+\nu_{\ell}$.

Born effective charges in insulators characterize the electric polarization generated by shifting individual atomic sublattices. While this concept initially appears inapplicable to metals and doped semiconductors—where macroscopic polarization lacks a clear definition—we demonstrate that, within clean conductors, moving beyond the adiabatic approximation yields well-defined nonadiabatic Born effective charges in the low-frequency regime. Furthermore, we observe that the sum of these nonadiabatic charges over sublattices does not vanish as it does in insulators; instead, it scales proportionally with the Drude weight. These theoretical findings are substantiated by density functional perturbation theory calculations performed on Al, electron-doped SnS$_2$, and SrTiO$_3$.

Scientific disciplines ranging from biology and health to education and social sciences increasingly rely on machine learning (ML) for large-scale data analysis. Yet, researchers creating sophisticated ML techniques often fail to offer detailed guides on their application. Current tutorials frequently impose high costs, demand extensive programming expertise, and lack specificity for particular fields. To democratize access to ML, we launched a free, year-long online series designed to teach advanced natural language processing (NLP) methods to scholars in computational social science (CSS). Collaborating with fifteen subject matter experts, two organizers created one-hour sessions featuring practical Python code covering various ML applications, from data pre-processing to tracking temporal language shifts. While live attendance was lower than anticipated, survey results indicated that participants' perceived knowledge increased by nearly one point on a 7-point Likert scale. Moreover, attendees asked insightful questions during the sessions and actively engaged with the material afterward, evidenced by 10,000 total views of recorded tutorials. This report outlines our organizational approach and extracts five principles for democratizing ML+X tutorials, with the hope that future organizers will build on these insights to further reduce barriers to ML skill development across all research fields.

Combining camera and LiDAR data has become the standard approach for 3D object detection. Existing methods typically use LiDAR point clouds as queries to extract features from images, but this reliance renders them ineffective when the LiDAR malfunctions, even slightly, thereby restricting their use in real-world autonomous driving. In contrast, we introduce BEVFusion, a novel yet straightforward fusion framework where the camera stream operates independently of LiDAR input, overcoming the limitations of prior approaches. Our experiments demonstrate that BEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art methods under standard training conditions. Furthermore, under robustness training that simulates various LiDAR failures, our framework significantly exceeds current benchmarks, achieving an improvement of 15.7% to 28.9% in mAP. To our knowledge, BEVFusion is the first solution capable of handling realistic LiDAR malfunctions and deploying directly in practical scenarios without additional post-processing. The source code is available at https://github.com/ADLab-AutoDrive/BEVFusion.

Identifying the optimal Virtual Machine (VM) configuration is essential for minimizing costs and maximizing throughput, which are the two main challenges in cloud-based distributed neural network (NN) training. Selecting the ideal VM within user-defined limits necessitates efficiently exploring a vast search space while accounting for performance variability caused by sharing cloud instances and networks. This paper analyzes such variance specifically for distributed NN training and reports on an extensive study of throughput and cost-efficiency across numerous instance types to narrow down the optimal VM search space. Leveraging insights from these studies, we developed Srifty, a system that integrates runtime profiling with learned performance models to accurately forecast training performance and identify the best VM option that adheres to user constraints, including support for heterogeneous setups and spot instances. We incorporated Srifty into PyTorch and tested it on Amazon EC2, followed by a large-scale generalization evaluation covering over 2,000 training configurations. Our findings demonstrate that Srifty achieves an 8% error rate in iteration latency prediction, and its VM recommendations deliver substantial improvements in throughput and cost savings while meeting user constraints, outperforming existing solutions in complex, real-world environments.

As human civilization exerts a growing influence on the Earth system, Earth observations have become an indispensable tool for evaluating and mitigating adverse effects. To address this, accurately detecting specific changes on the planet's surface is crucial, and we introduce an effective solution. Our proposed change detection and segmentation method innovatively integrates millions of available, off-the-shelf, unlabeled remote sensing images from various observation programs into the training pipeline using denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs). Specifically, we utilize a pre-trained DDPM to extract information from these uncurated datasets, then leverage the multi-scale feature representations from the model's decoder to train a lightweight classifier capable of identifying precise changes. Experiments conducted across four public change detection datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of F1 score, Intersection over Union (IoU), and overall accuracy. The code and pre-trained models can be accessed at: https://github.com/wgcban/ddpm-cd

In the field of automatic speech translation (ST), traditional cascaded methods, which separate transcription from translation, are being surpassed by increasingly robust and competitive direct approaches. By bypassing intermediate transcription steps, direct ST models can retain critical input information—such as vocal characteristics—that is typically discarded in cascaded frameworks. While this capability has proven beneficial for gender translation, direct ST systems remain susceptible to gender bias, a challenge also present in cascaded ST, machine translation, and various other natural language processing tasks. Furthermore, relying exclusively on vocal biometrics as a gender indicator can be inappropriate and potentially detrimental to specific user groups. This paper extends beyond speech signals to compare various strategies for informing direct ST models about speaker gender, evaluating their performance in translating gendered terms from English into Italian and French. To achieve this, we manually annotated large datasets with gender labels to simulate diverse real-world scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that gender-aware direct ST solutions significantly outperform powerful but gender-agnostic models. Specifically, incorporating gender information can boost the accuracy of translating gender-marked words by up to 30 points while maintaining overall translation quality.

Generative models have achieved significant success in synthesizing image data, particularly in sampling quality, diversity, and feature disentanglement. However, time series generative models currently lack these advantages because they are missing a representation capable of capturing temporal dynamics and enabling inversion for sampling. To address this, the paper introduces the intertemporal return plot (IRP) representation, which adapts image-based generative adversarial networks for time series generation. This representation effectively captures time series characteristics and, compared to alternatives, offers invertibility and scale-invariance. Empirical benchmarks validate these properties and demonstrate that the IRP allows an off-the-shelf Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty to generate realistic time series that outperform specialized RNN-based GANs while simultaneously reducing model complexity.

Precisely estimating ferroelectric polarization in ferroelectric-dielectric stacks is vital for materials science and essential for advancing ferroelectric-based electronic devices. This study re-examines the theoretical framework and practical application of the PUND technique within Metal-Ferroelectric-Dielectric-Metal (MFDM) structures through analytical derivations and numerical simulations. In MFDM architectures, the outcomes of PUND measurements can significantly diverge from the actual polarization switched within the stack, which itself differs from the remnant polarization of the ferroelectric layer. Consequently, the primary obstacles preventing PUND from accurately quantifying polarization switching in these stacks are analyzed. Examining physical quantities that are often unattainable in experimental settings offers valuable insight into the principal sources of error in the PUND technique, thereby elucidating the complex interaction between the depolarization field and charge injection/trapping mechanisms in MFDM stacks featuring a thin dielectric layer.

This paper introduces a technique for estimating the pose of a vehicle-mounted sensor as the vehicle traverses its environment, a critical capability for autonomous driving. Leveraging standard automotive sensors accessible via communication buses like CAN or FlexRay, we detail a process that integrates planar odometry from wheel data with a suspension model derived from linear suspension sensors to achieve a more precise camera pose estimation. We further discuss the application of this method in both visualization and computer vision contexts.

We introduce random linear embeddings that map finite point sets in $D$-dimensional space under the 1-norm into a $k$-dimensional space equipped with a novel metric. This approach ensures that for any pair of points not too close to each other, the distance between their embedded images follows a strictly concave, increasing function of their original distance, subject to multiplicative error. To guarantee these results with high probability, the target dimension $k$ only needs to scale quadratically with the logarithm of the point set's size. These embeddings utilize random matrices populated with standard Cauchy random variables, and their proofs depend on Chernoff bounds for sums of independent and identically distributed variables. The resulting metric is translation invariant but does not arise from a norm.

We establish a large deviation principle for the point process of $k$-element connected components in $\mathbb R^d$ under connectivity radii $r_n$ that diverge to infinity. The random points originate from a homogeneous Poisson point process, requiring the sequence $(r_n)_{n\ge1}$ to satisfy $n^kr_n^{d(k-1)}\to\infty$ and $nr_n^d\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, which characterizes a sparse regime. The rate function derived from this principle is expressible as relative entropy. Furthermore, we apply these findings to deduce large deviation principles for diverse functionals and point processes within stochastic geometry and topology. Specific instances of topological invariants examined include the persistent Betti numbers of geometric complexes and the count of Morse critical points associated with min-type distance functions.

Although the variable and hard-to-quantify baseline transcription level complicates the normalization of comparative transcriptomic data and remains biologically underappreciated, we demonstrate that this often overlooked factor is crucial for regulating gene network multistability and cellular differentiation. Basal expression correlates with chromatin loosening, as measured by DNA accessibility, and consistently drives cellular dedifferentiation according to transcriptomic signatures, regardless of the molecular or cellular tools employed. Formal modeling of gene network motifs central to developmental bifurcations reveals that non-specific expression levels restructure Waddington's epigenetic landscapes, rendering the attractors of progenitor and differentiated cells mutually exclusive. This mechanism is universal and applies to various genes, provided multistable circuits are accurately modeled with autonomous basal expression. These findings clarify long-standing connections between gene expression noise, chromatin decondensation, and cellular dedifferentiation, while underscoring the vital role of heterochromatin maintenance in preventing pathological reprogramming, age-related diseases, and cancer.
We present an alternative proof of Lyubeznik's result regarding the annihilator of local cohomology in characteristic zero.

The application of video-based facial expression analysis to infer health conditions, such as depression and pain, has grown significantly. While deep learning models designed for multiscale spatiotemporal processing have demonstrated strong potential in capturing facial dynamics, their high computational complexity hinders practical deployment. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel technique for decomposing the extraction of multiscale spatiotemporal features. This approach introduces the Decomposed Multiscale Spatiotemporal Network (DMSN), featuring three distinct variants: DMSN-A, DMSN-B, and DMSN-C. The DMSN-A block captures multiscale representations by examining spatiotemporal features across various temporal ranges, whereas DMSN-B analyzes features across multiple temporal ranges, and DMSN-C focuses on multiple spatial scales. By integrating these variants, our DMSN architecture effectively explores diverse multiscale spatiotemporal features, enhancing adaptability to different facial behaviors. Extensive experiments on challenging datasets reveal that the DMSN-C block is particularly effective for depression detection, while the DMSN-A block excels in pain estimation. Furthermore, the results indicate that the DMSN architecture offers a cost-effective solution for analyzing expressions ranging from minimal temporal variations, as seen in depression, to significant variations, as observed in pain estimation.

This paper presents a novel numerical approach for addressing multi-marginal optimal transport problems involving pairwise interaction costs. Typically, the computational complexity of such problems grows exponentially with the number of marginals, $m$. We propose a one-parameter family of cost functions that bridges the original cost function with a specialized variant where complexity scales linearly with $m$. We demonstrate that the solution to the original problem can be retrieved by solving an ordinary differential equation with respect to the parameter $\epsilon$, initialized with the solution corresponding to the specialized cost function. Finally, we provide simulation results utilizing both explicit Euler and higher-order explicit Runge-Kutta schemes to solve the ODE and, consequently, the multi-marginal optimal transport problem.

The text introduces a formula for Schur $Q$-functions that characterizes the action of Virasoro operators. Specifically, for strict partitions, it establishes a succinct expression for $L_{-k}Q_{\lambda}$, where $L_{-k}$ (with $k\geq 1$) represents the Virasoro operator.

Program synthesis refers to the automatic generation of software from a given specification. While most current methods treat program synthesis as a search problem involving discrete parameters, this paper introduces a new approach that frames it as a continuous optimization problem, solved using a state-of-the-art evolutionary technique called Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES). We also propose a mapping mechanism to translate this continuous formulation into executable code. Our system, named GENESYS, is compared against various recent synthesis techniques operating in both discrete and continuous domains. The results demonstrate that GENESYS generates a higher volume of programs within a fixed time budget than existing methods. Specifically, for programs with a length of 10, GENESYS produces 28% more solutions than competing schemes under identical time constraints.

This paper establishes a connection between the prime factors of the order of a Sylow normalizer and the degrees of characters that take values in certain small cyclotomic fields, noting that this relationship is particularly robust for solvable groups.

Although tunneling is a physical phenomenon, it remains enigmatic because wave packets cannot be formed beneath the barrier, rendering group velocity undefined. While particles can be detected on either side of the barrier, their properties within it have remained unprobed due to quantum measurement challenges. We demonstrate that these obstacles can be circumvented in mesoscopic systems, allowing for the derivation of an expression for the quantum mechanical current under the barrier. A general framework is established to obtain this expression for any arbitrary system, with mesoscopic phenomena enabling both theoretical and experimental validation. As an illustration, we analyze an ideal one-dimensional quantum ring with Aharonov-Bohm flux $\Phi$ connected to a reservoir. This model provides clear evidence of propagation under the barrier, yielding a non-invasively measurable current that is theoretically verifiable. Although time-reversed states are involved, there is no indication of causality violation. Given that evanescent states are notably stable and robust against phase fluctuations, they represent promising candidates for device applications, underscoring the importance of formalizing current under the barrier.

A promising avenue for hybrid quantum computing lies in the strong coupling between impurity spins and superconducting resonators. One method to control and boost this interaction is by preparing the resonator in a non-classical state, such as a squeezed state. In this study, we theoretically investigate how these states influence the spin's coherence. We derive an analytical framework using the Schrieffer-Wolf transformation to quantitatively predict both the coupling strength and the spin's dephasing rate, which we subsequently validate numerically. Our findings indicate that while squeezing can strengthen the resonator-spin coupling, it simultaneously amplifies photon noise and increases spin decoherence. Consequently, our work highlights a significant obstacle to employing squeezing to achieve the strong-coupling regime.

General Relativity has successfully withstood numerous observational tests, having been rigorously examined in the weak-field regime through Solar System experiments and binary pulsar observations. Recent progress has significantly advanced the study of the strong-field regime, now accessible via gravitational waves, X-ray data, and millimeter Very Long Baseline Interferometry. This work provides a summary of the current state-of-the-art regarding tests of General Relativity using black hole X-ray data, highlighting recent breakthroughs and outlining future directions.

We investigate the relationship between divergences in ground state entanglement entropy and emergent zero-modes within the Hamiltonian, focusing on one-dimensional Bosonic and Fermionic chains. Beginning with a system of coupled Bosonic degrees of freedom, we demonstrate that while zero modes are a prerequisite for entanglement entropy divergences, they are not sufficient on their own; we subsequently outline conditions that do guarantee such divergences. Our analysis then extends to Bosonic chains, revealing that zero modes of the entanglement Hamiltonian serve as a distinct signature for these divergences, independent of the entanglement Hamiltonian itself. We further generalize these findings to one-dimensional Fermionic lattices, specifically examining a staggered Fermion chain as a discretized Dirac field. We establish that the methods developed for Bosonic systems have direct Fermionic counterparts and support this with a numerical investigation of entanglement in the Fermionic chain. Finally, we contextualize our findings in relation to the factorization algebra theorem.

Single-layer graphene subjected to periodic lateral strain functions as an artificial crystal capable of sustaining boundary spectra with inherent polarity. These systems are examined by contrasting the impacts of periodic magnetic fields and strain-induced pseudomagnetic fields, which respectively break and maintain time-reversal symmetry. In the presence of magnetic fields, a Chern classification of superlattice minibands—under conditions of zero total magnetic flux—mandates that a single set of counter-propagating modes traverse each bulk gap across opposite boundaries of a nanoribbon. Conversely, with a pseudomagnetic field, pairs of counter-propagating modes shift to the same boundary, establishing well-defined valley-helical transport channels along a single zigzag edge. The discussion concludes with potential implementation strategies and their corresponding experimental signatures.

This paper introduces non-abelian Hodge techniques applicable to complex quasi-projective manifolds $X$ across both archimedean and non-archimedean settings. Within the non-archimedean framework, we extend a result by Gromov and Schoen: given a Zariski dense representation $\rho:\pi_1(X)\to G(K)$, where $G$ is a semisimple algebraic group over a non-archimedean local field $K$, we establish the existence of a $\rho$-equivariant harmonic map from $X$ to the Bruhat-Tits building $\Delta(G)$ of $G$, exhibiting appropriate asymptotic properties. Additionally, when the image of $\rho$ is unbounded, we construct logarithmic symmetric differential forms on $X$. Our primary archimedean result demonstrates that any semisimple representation $\sigma:\pi_1(X)\to\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb{C})$ is rigid if $X$ lacks logarithmic symmetric differential forms. Moreover, such a $\sigma$ is conjugate to a representation $\sigma':\pi_1(X)\to\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathcal{O}_L)$, where $\mathcal{O}_L$ denotes the ring of integers of a number field $L$, rendering $\sigma'$ a complex direct factor of a $\mathbb{Z}$-variation of Hodge structures. As a consequence, we show that a complex quasi-projective manifold $X$ possesses nonzero global logarithmic symmetric differential forms whenever there exists a linear representation $\pi_1(X)\to\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb{C})$ with an infinite image.

This paper addresses the optimal strategy for leveraging additional data—whether unlabeled data from the same task or labeled data from a related task—to learn a specific objective. The authors formalize this inquiry using the framework of reference priors, which are objective, uninformative Bayesian priors designed to maximize mutual information between the task and model weights. These priors allow the task to exert maximum influence on the Bayesian posterior; notably, reference priors adapt to the available sample size, favoring low-complexity models in the hypothesis space when sample sizes are small. This work provides the first demonstration of reference priors applied to medium-scale deep networks and image-based datasets. The authors extend the theory of reference priors and apply them to two distinct problems. First, they utilize unlabeled data to construct reference priors, creating new Bayesian semi-supervised learning approaches that maintain effectiveness even with very few samples per class. Second, they employ labeled data from a source task to generate reference priors, establishing a novel pretraining method for transfer learning that ensures data from the target task maximally shapes the Bayesian posterior. Empirical results validating these methods are presented on image classification datasets, with code accessible at https://github.com/grasp-lyrl/deep_reference_priors.

The equilibrium between a black hole and ambient thermal radiation is a fascinating subject. Primordial black holes, which originated in the early universe's thermal radiation era, form when gravity causes this radiation to collapse. Given the complexity of real-world scenarios, we adopt a simplified model that focuses solely on the system's thermodynamic properties: an isolated container of thermal radiation. By varying the initial temperature within a reasonable range, it becomes evident that a portion of the radiation inevitably collapses to form a black hole, eventually reaching thermal equilibrium in accordance with the second law of thermodynamics. However, incorporating both black hole quantization and the microscopic states of thermal radiation into this equilibrium yields a surprising result: thermodynamic fluctuations become unavoidable. Conversely, if only one of these factors is considered, the system satisfies both energy conservation and the second law of thermodynamics, thereby preventing such fluctuations. This finding offers a novel perspective on understanding the microscopic origins of thermodynamic fluctuations.

The Logic of Information Flows (LIF) has recently emerged as a broad framework within knowledge representation, capable of modeling procedural tasks in a declarative, logic-based manner. This paper addresses the challenge of query processing under limited access patterns—a well-established issue in database research—demonstrating that LIF is highly effective for this purpose. To achieve this, we introduce a first-order variant of LIF termed "forward" LIF. We define FLIFio, a syntactic subset of forward LIF, which precisely aligns with the "executable" fragment of first-order logic identified by Nash and Ludächer. Additionally, we establish that general FLIF expressions can be transformed into io-disjoint form. Central to the definition of FLIFio is the categorization of free variables within an expression into "input" and "output" roles. These findings rely on inertia and determinacy laws specific to forward LIF expressions, which are notable for their formulation in terms of input and output variables.

Saddle fixed points serve as the core of complex dynamical behavior in a system, with their one-dimensional stable and unstable manifolds being essential for comprehending such dynamics. Although sketching the unstable manifold is straightforward, calculating the stable manifold proves to be significantly more challenging. While various algorithms currently exist for determining the stable manifold of saddle points, they often face constraints, particularly in non-invertible systems. This paper introduces a novel algorithm designed to compute the stable manifold for two-dimensional systems, offering a solution that also accommodates non-invertible cases. Following an explanation of the algorithm's underlying logic, we illustrate its results through several examples.

Business process modelling languages generally utilize graphical symbols to depict process models, though these symbols vary based on the language's verbosity, paradigm, and specific focus. To clarify the distinct constructs and rules of individual languages and to connect them across different frameworks, meta-models have been introduced in academic literature. These meta-models serve as a vital repository of knowledge regarding the elements that current research deems essential for describing business processes. The objective of this study is to conduct a comprehensive systematic literature review (SLR) of such meta-models. This SLR seeks to address four research questions: (i) the types of meta-models found in the literature; (ii) the common constructs they include; (iii) their intended purposes; and (iv) how they have been evaluated.

Detecting subtle movements from small objects amidst noise, a critical requirement for vital sign monitoring, is inherently difficult; however, this task can be significantly enhanced through magnification. We introduced a sophisticated Gabor filter-based decomposition approach designed to amplify phase variations across different spatial wavelengths, thereby magnifying motion and isolating 1D signals for fundamental frequency analysis. These phase-derived outputs from the complex Gabor filters are processed to train machine learning models capable of predicting respiration and heart rate with improved precision. Our results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms traditional temporal FFT-based techniques in diverse clinical environments, including sleep labs and emergency departments, and remains effective across various human postures.

This study evaluates the security benefits of common functional programming features by assessing them against established information security principles. By contrasting imperative and functional code, the paper illustrates several specific scenarios. Ultimately, while there is a strong argument for adopting functional languages due to their potential for enhanced security, empirical research is required to substantiate this claim.

An individual's physical appearance, identity, and nonverbal signals significantly shape how they are perceived by negotiation partners, often affecting the final outcome. Recent technological advancements now allow for the modification of these cues during live video interactions. In some instances, a person's physical presence is explicitly substituted with 2D or 3D representations in interactive media. Conversely, technologies like deepfakes can subtly and implicitly adjust numerous nonverbal elements—including appearance and identity—in real-time. This article examines cutting-edge technologies capable of both explicit and implicit alterations to nonverbal cues, discusses their impact on the negotiation landscape, and underscores ethical considerations that require sustained attention from all stakeholders.

Coupling a topological insulator (TI) with an $s$-wave superconductor (SC) represents a compelling material system for creating topological superconductors, enabling the development of Majorana-based, topologically protected qubits. Through a computational investigation of the interface between Niobium (Nb) and Bi$_2$Te$_3$, we examine both the advantages and limitations of this platform for Majorana applications. Contacting the TI film with Nb induces charge doping from the superconductor to the insulator, shifting the Fermi level into the TI's conduction band. In thicker TI films, this shift causes band bending, resulting in the occupation of trivial quantum-well states at the interface. Within the superconducting regime, we find that the topological surface state acquires a substantial superconducting gap at the interface, a feature that remains robust against Fermi energy fluctuations. Additionally, our results indicate that the trivial interface state undergoes only marginal proximitization, which may hinder the successful implementation of Majorana-based qubits in this specific material configuration.

This work defines Vafa-Witten invariants for projective surface Deligne-Mumford stacks, extending Tanaka-Thomas's construction for projective surfaces based on the S-duality conjecture. We present calculations for a root stack over a general type quintic surface and for quintic surfaces featuring ADE singularities. Additionally, we examine the connection between the Vafa-Witten invariants of quintic surfaces with ADE singularities and those of their corresponding crepant resolutions.

This study examines the relationship among three frameworks for deforming rational surface singularities: the picture deformations introduced by de Jong and van Straten, Kollár's P-resolutions, and Pinkham's smoothings of negative weights. We present a concrete procedure to derive deformations in alternative theories from a given deformation in one, ensuring they parameterize identical irreducible components of the singularity's deformation space. The semi-stable minimal model program is utilized extensively for this aim. As a result, we validate Kollár's conjecture for various classes of sandwiched surface singularities.

Astrophysics urgently requires precise and autonomous methods for spectral classification. This thesis details the training of a convolutional neural network (ConvNet) to identify object categories—specifically quasars, stars, and galaxies—using solely one-dimensional spectra. The author created various scripts and C programs to handle dataset preparation, preprocessing, and postprocessing. Leveraging the EBLearn library developed by Pierre Sermanet and Yann LeCun, the ConvNet was constructed. Applying this model to a dataset exceeding 60,000 spectra achieved a success rate of approximately 95%. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the significant potential of convolutional neural networks and deep learning techniques within the field of astrophysics.

This study focuses on developing efficient numerical techniques for linear transport equations characterized by random parameters and diffusive scaling. We adapt the bi-fidelity stochastic collocation method, previously detailed in [33,50,51], to this specific context. The high-fidelity transport model utilizes an asymptotic-preserving scheme [29] for every stochastic realization, while the low-fidelity model employs the straightforward two-velocity Goldstein-Taylor equation to enhance the convergence rate of the uncertainty quantification procedure. This selection is driven by the shared diffusion limit between the high- and low-fidelity models. Computational efficiency is realized through the strategic selection of collocation points and the relative approximation of the high-fidelity solution. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy, including in non-diffusive regimes, alongside empirical error bound estimations as discussed in [16].

Locally repairable codes facilitate rapid recovery from node failures in distributed storage systems. By distributing codeword symbols across various storage nodes, these codes allow for the restoration of a failed disk by interacting with only a small subset of nodes; the count of nodes involved in this repair process is defined as the locality. This study focuses on locally repairable codes capable of recovery even when multiple nodes fail simultaneously. A local code is defined as the punctured version of the original code, formed by excluding symbols outside a specific repair group. The objective is to construct a code where every local code achieves a specified minimum distance, ensuring local repairability as long as the total number of failures remains below a certain tolerance threshold. Specifically, we examine linear locally repairable codes over a finite field of size four (characteristic 2), which is suitable for practical applications. We categorize all quaternary locally repairable codes that meet the Singleton-type upper bound for minimum distance and provide explicit constructions for every set of achievable code parameters.

We introduce Model-Predictive Interaction Primitives, a robot learning framework designed for assistive motion in human-robot collaboration that explicitly considers the biomechanical effects on the human musculoskeletal system. First, we expand upon Interaction Primitives to incorporate predictive biomechanics, enabling the forecast of a human partner's future biomechanical states based on current observations and planned robot control inputs. This capability is then utilized within a model-predictive control strategy to anticipate the ergonomic and biomechanical consequences of potential robot actions. Consequently, optimal control trajectories are chosen to reduce future physical stress on the human body.
