When the interface shifts, small-scale structures of the displaced phase are embedded into the adjacent phase using a second diffusion equation featuring a modified coefficient that vanishes at the interface to block cross-interface diffusion. Additionally, a pressure-like equation enforces incompressibility within the coarse velocity field. The approach demonstrates various coarsening levels, and simulations show that treating small scales as a homogeneous mixture in a coarse model yields results comparable to the filtered fully resolved field during the early stages of Rayleigh-Taylor instability.

To explain the surprisingly high thermoelectric performance in the thin-film Heusler alloy Fe$_2$V$_{0.8}$W$_{0.2}$Al, we investigate the magnon drag effect arising from a tungsten-derived impurity band as a potential cause, drawing parallels to phonon drag in FeSb$_2$. By assuming that the alloy's conduction band couples with this impurity band created by tungsten substitution, we calculate the electrical conductivity $L_{11}$ using the self-consistent t-matrix approximation and determine the thermoelectric conductivity $L_{12}$ due to magnon drag via linear response theory. We then estimate the temperature-dependent electrical resistivity, Seebeck coefficient, and power factor. Finally, comparing our theoretical predictions with experimental data for the thin-film alloy suggests that the exceptional thermoelectric properties stem from magnon drag associated with the tungsten-based impurity band.

This paper establishes a parabolic analogue of the Littlewood-Paley inequality for a broad class of time-dependent operators, encompassing both local and non-local types of arbitrary order. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this inequality provides a crucial estimate within the $L_p$-theory of stochastic partial differential equations.

The Bose-Fermi superfluid mixture serves as a valuable platform for investigating diverse macroscopic quantum phenomena. A recent study by Yao et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 145301 (2016)] realized a $^{41}$K-$^{6}$Li superfluid mixture, where rotating the system generated coupled quantized vortices and revealed several unconventional behaviors attributable to boson-fermion interactions. This work offers theoretical insights into these anomalous vortex lattice behaviors observed experimentally. Utilizing orbital-free density functional theory—whose validity was established by comparing predictions with full microscopic theory for vortex lattices in strongly interacting Fermi superfluids—we predict further experimentally accessible phenomena. These include novel vortex lattice structures within phase-separated Bose-Fermi mixtures and attractive interactions between vortices of the two superfluid components.

Accurately mapping the population of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) is essential for comprehending the evolution of supermassive black holes throughout cosmic history, yet locating heavily obscured AGN remains a major hurdle. This study establishes new demographic constraints for this elusive population by integrating X-ray spectral data with multiwavelength observational priors. Specifically, we selected X-ray AGN from the Chandra COSMOS Legacy survey and modeled their $2.2-500\mu m$ spectral energy distributions using galaxy and AGN templates to isolate the mid-infrared ($6\mu m$) luminosity of the AGN component. By applying empirical correlations between X-ray and $6\mu m$ luminosities, we inferred the intrinsic accretion luminosity at X-ray energies for each object. These inferred values served as priors in a Bayesian X-ray spectral analysis to estimate physical characteristics, including line-of-sight obscuration. This method resolves the degeneracy between accretion luminosity and obscuration that typically plagues X-ray spectral fitting, especially for Compton-Thick AGN with low photon counts. Combining these spectral results with the survey's selection function yielded an AGN space density and a Compton-Thick fraction of $21.0^{+16.1}_{-9.9}\%$ for redshifts $z<0.5$. For higher redshifts, the analysis provides upper limits on the Compton-Thick fraction of $\le 40\%$. These findings, which fall at the lower end of previously reported ranges, highlight the critical role of multiwavelength techniques in addressing the challenges of studying heavily obscured AGN demographics.

Developer interactions vary from face-to-face hallway conversations to comment threads on bug reports. Identifying discussions that address software design would significantly aid in documentation and refactoring efforts. Design mining applies machine learning methods to classify discussion artifacts, such as pull requests, as either related to design or not. This paper illustrates a basic example of design mining functionality, followed by an analysis showing that conclusion stability is weak across different artifact types and projects. We present two techniques—augmentation and context specificity—that substantially enhance both conclusion stability and cross-project applicability. Our proposed approach yields an AUC of 0.88 for within-dataset classification and 0.80 for cross-dataset classification.

This study derives two enhanced Amati correlations for Gamma-Ray burst (GRB) data using the copula statistical method. After calibrating these improved correlations with low-redshift GRB observations under a fiducial $\Lambda$CDM model ($\Omega_\mathrm{m0}=0.3$, $H_0=70~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$) and extrapolating to high-redshift data, we construct the GRB Hubble diagram. When applied to constrain the $\Lambda$CDM model, the copula-based improved Amati correlation yields results consistent with $\Omega_\mathrm{m0}=0.3$, unlike the standard and extended Amati correlations. These findings suggest that, when calibrated via low-redshift data, the improved Amati correlation renders GRBs a viable cosmological probe. However, the Bayesian information criterion slightly favors the standard Amati correlation due to its fewer model parameters. Moreover, simultaneous fitting methods do not provide clear evidence that the improved correlation outperforms the standard one. Consequently, further research is required to better compare the various Amati correlations.

Collective motion expanding across larger scales serves as a hallmark of liquid vitrification. We present evidence of distinct static and dynamic length scales emerging near the free surface of fully equilibrated glass-forming liquid films and their relationship to bulk system properties. Unlike the static correlation length, which grows monotonically, the dynamic correlation length—which quantifies the penetration of accelerated surface dynamics into the bulk—exhibits a notable non-monotonic evolution with temperature. This behavior remains robust despite variations in specific interatomic interactions. The peak in dynamic correlations identifies a cross-over temperature ($T_*$) that aligns with a morphological transition in the cooperative rearrangement regions (CRR) of fast-moving particles within the bulk. This transition occurs at a temperature exceeding the critical temperature ($T_c$) predicted by mode-coupling theory (MCT). We associate this point with the onset where fast-particle motion decouples from structural relaxation, a phenomenon rigorously defined within a recent extension of MCT known as stochastic $\beta$-relaxation theory (SBR).

The MAGIC Collaboration has recently identified VHE emission from the distant GRB 201216C with a statistical significance of approximately $5\sigma$. Although such remote GRBs are expected to be significantly attenuated by the extragalactic background light (EBL), the source of their VHE emission remains unexplained. This study introduces a numerical model to analyze the afterglow of GRB 201216C, which solves the continuity equation for electron distribution evolution. The model demonstrates that the broad-band observations can be accounted for by synchrotron and synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) radiation from the forward shock. Even under strong EBL absorption, the predicted 0.1 TeV flux is estimated to be between $\sim 10^{-9}$ and $10^{-10}\rm erg ~ cm^{-2} ~ s^{-1}$ at times $t \sim 10^3 -10^4 \rm s$, making detection by the MAGIC telescope feasible. Comparisons using this model reveal that the shock parameters of GRB 201216C align with those of other Sub-TeV GRBs (GRB 190114C and GRB 180720B), suggesting shared characteristics: high burst energy, low circum-burst medium density, and a low magnetic equipartition factor. Treating GRB 201216C as a representative case, we estimate that MAGIC can detect GRBs up to a redshift of $z \sim 1.6$. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the VHE photon energies from such distant events are capped at approximately 0.1 TeV. Consequently, enhancing the low-energy sensitivity of VHE telescopes is crucial for detecting Sub-TeV emissions from these remote GRBs.

Existing control plane verification tools fail to scale in large networks due to the intricate challenge of reasoning simultaneously about the behaviors of all nodes. This paper introduces a modular verification strategy where end-to-end network properties are validated through purely local checks performed on individual nodes and edges. Specifically, the method targets safety properties within BGP configurations, offering robust guarantees against arbitrary external route announcements from neighbors and random node or link failures. We have formally proven the correctness of this approach and implemented it in a tool named Lightyear. Experimental results demonstrate that Lightyear scales significantly better than previous control plane verifiers. Furthermore, we employed Lightyear to verify three properties of a major cloud provider's wide area network, which comprises hundreds of routers and tens of thousands of edges; to our knowledge, no prior tool has delivered such guarantees at this magnitude. In addition to these scaling advantages, our modular verification framework simplifies the localization of configuration errors and facilitates incremental re-verification as configurations are updated.

This study examines the holographic bound within the context of de Sitter space, focusing on a homogeneous, isotropic, and non-relativistic neutral hydrogen gas. Specifically, we integrate de Sitter holography with the quantum deformation of the hydrogen atom via quantum groups, utilizing the $\mathcal U_q(so(4))$ quantum algebra to build a finite-dimensional Hilbert space for the atom. Due to this quantum deformation, the Rydberg constant is shown to depend on the de Sitter radius, $L_\Lambda$. This insight allows us to derive a finite-dimensional Hilbert space for the entire ensemble of hydrogen atoms in the de Sitter universe, the dimension of which satisfies the holographic bound. Furthermore, we establish relationships between the hydrogen atom mass ($m_\text{atom}$), the total number of atoms ($N$), and the bulk Hilbert space dimension ($\text{Dim}{\mathcal H}_\text{bulk}$) with the de Sitter entropy ($S_\text{dS}$), Planck mass ($m_\text{Planck}$), electron mass ($m_\text{e}$), and proton mass ($m_\text{p}$), yielding the following approximations: $m_\text{atom}\simeq m_\text{Planck}S_\text{dS}^{-\frac{1}{6}}$, $N\simeq S_\text{dS}^\frac{2}{3}$, and $\text{Dim}{\mathcal H}_\text{bulk}=2^{\frac{m_\text{e}}{m_\text{p}}\alpha^2S_\text{dS}}$.

We employed seven distinct techniques to determine the broad-line and continuum reddening in NGC 5548. Our analysis evaluated two potential reddening curves for active galactic nuclei (AGNs): the relatively flat mean AGN curve proposed by Gaskell & Benker (2007) in the ultraviolet, and a curve that rises sharply into the ultraviolet, similar to that of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), alongside a standard Milky Way curve. Across all models, we determined a total reddening approximately 14 times higher than the minimal dust-induced reddening observed in the solar neighborhood. UV-to-optical ratios specifically exclude a steep SMC-like reddening curve for NGC 5548. Both the Milky Way and Gaskell & Benker curves yield a mean reddening of E(B-V) = 0.25 +/- 0.02. Four non-hydrogen-line indicators suggest that intrinsic hydrogen line ratios align with Baker-Menzel case B values. Furthermore, the unreddened optical-to-UV spectral energy distribution matches predictions for an externally illuminated accretion disc. The derived reddening for NGC 5548 is consistent with prior estimates for type-1 AGNs. Ignoring internal extinction results in a sevenfold underestimation of the luminosity at 1200 Angstroms, leading to an underestimation of the accretion disc's size scale by a factor of approximately 2.6. This finding mirrors the accretion disc size discrepancy identified during the 2013 AGNSTORM campaign and lends support to Gaskell's (2017) proposal that this discrepancy stems primarily from neglecting reddening.

The W boson mass measurement from the Tevatron CDF experiment showed a 7$\sigma$ deviation from Standard Model predictions. This paper explores potential interpretations and their implications for collider physics. We conduct electroweak global fits across different frameworks and assumptions, specifically examining three effective-field-theory scenarios: the $S$-$T$, the $S$-$T$-$\delta G_F$, and an eight-parameter flavor-universal model. We analyze the tensions among various $m_W$ measurements as reflected in these fits and the resulting shifts in parameter central values. Using these fit results, we evaluate several model classes and their consistency with the data. Our findings indicate that while single gauge boson extensions can address the $m_W$ anomaly, they are heavily constrained by direct LHC searches unless the $Z'$ is fermiophobic (or leptophobic), a scenario achievable through mixing between extra vector fermions (or leptons) and Standard Model counterparts. Additionally, vector-like top partners can partially account for the necessary shifts in electroweak observables. We also investigate top squark compatibility in detail, discovering that non-degenerate soft masses for top squarks increase the required operator coefficients, allowing for an explanation consistent with current LHC limits. Ultimately, further theoretical and experimental progress is urgently needed to uncover the underlying physics of this discrepancy.

We examine two distinct models: one involving massive fermions interacting with a massive scalar field, and the other featuring fermions within an electrical field (QED2). Chiral condensates are computed using the one-loop approximation. Our results indicate that for the Yukawa interaction between fermions and the scalar field, the chiral condensate remains non-zero even as the fermion mass approaches zero. Conversely, in QED2, the chiral condensate vanishes when the fermion mass is zero.

Current state-of-the-art neural entity linking models utilize attention-based bag-of-words context representations and pre-trained entity embeddings derived from word embeddings to evaluate topic-level compatibility. Nevertheless, these approaches often overlook latent entity type information within the immediate context, leading to frequent linking errors where mentions are associated with entities of incorrect types. To address this limitation, we propose injecting latent entity type information into entity embeddings using pre-trained BERT. Furthermore, we incorporate a BERT-based entity similarity score into the local context model of a leading framework to more effectively capture latent type information. Our approach significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art models on the standard AIDA-CoNLL benchmark. Detailed experimental analysis confirms that our model corrects the majority of type errors generated by direct baselines.

This paper presents H-STREAM, an evaluation engine designed for large-scale stream and data processing pipelines. It proposes treating stream processing operators as micro-services to facilitate the analysis and visualization of Big Data streams originating from Internet of Things (IoT) environments. These H-STREAM micro-services integrate stream processing and data storage techniques, dynamically tuned based on the volume of IoT devices generating streams, their production rates, and the available physical computing resources for real-time processing and delivery to consumers. Deployed within a cloud environment, H-STREAM offers stream processing and visualization micro-services that can be composed to execute specific stream aggregation analysis pipelines as queries. The study provides experimental validation using Microsoft Azure as the deployment platform to test H-STREAM's ability to address velocity and volume challenges in two scenarios: a neuroscience experiment and a social connectivity analysis conducted on IoT farms.

We introduce a novel conceptual framework for Earth's glacial-interglacial cycles, yielding governing equations characterized by a vector field with a hyperplane of discontinuities. Building upon classic Budyko- and Sellers-type energy balance models, this study removes the conventional assumption of equatorial symmetry to account for temperature-albedo feedback. The dynamics of distinct Northern and Southern Hemisphere ice caps are linked to an equation describing the annual global mean surface temperature. The system incorporates a discontinuous switching mechanism grounded in mass balance principles for the Northern Hemisphere ice sheet. We demonstrate that the resulting Filippov system possesses a unique, nonsmooth, and attracting limit cycle that captures the transition between glacial and interglacial states. Given the disparate time scales involved, the model constitutes a nonsmooth geometric perturbation problem; we apply specialized mathematical techniques to derive the periodic orbit. Our findings indicate that climatic shifts in the Northern Hemisphere induce synchronous changes in the Southern Hemisphere, aligning with observed Earth behavior on orbital time scales.

Floquet modulation is extensively employed in optical lattices to achieve coherent control of quantum gases, notably for creating artificial gauge fields and modeling topological phenomena. Yet, this modulation generates heating that can drown out quantum dynamic signals in ultracold atomic systems. In this study, we demonstrate that thermal motion, rather than acting merely as noise, serves as a novel control parameter within Floquet-modulated superradiance lattices—momentum-space tight-binding lattices formed by collectively excited atomic states. By combining Doppler shifts with Floquet modulation, effective forces can be generated along arbitrary directions within the frequency and momentum dimensions of the lattice. Consequently, dynamic localization, dynamic delocalization, and chiral edge currents can all be detected simultaneously from a single transport spectrum of superradiance lattices involving thermal atoms. This research opens pathways for simulating Floquet topological matter in room-temperature atoms and supports their integration into photonic applications.

This study introduces a framework for multimodal sentiment analysis and emotion recognition that utilizes convolutional neural networks to extract features from both textual and visual inputs. By integrating visual, textual, and audio data, we achieve a 10% performance gain over current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we address several often-overlooked challenges in this field, including the significance of speaker-independent models, the relative importance of specific modalities, and the issue of generalizability. Consequently, this paper establishes a new benchmark for future research and highlights the critical dimensions that must be considered when conducting such analyses.

Determining the specific function of individual buildings is vital geo-data for numerous applications, yet it remains challenging to acquire. A promising solution is predicting building uses directly from ground-level imagery. Since social media platforms host billions of photos featuring diverse perspectives, including street views, this study introduces a filtering pipeline to extract high-quality ground-level images from massive social media collections. This pipeline guarantees that all selected images possess complete and accurate geotags along with compass directions, enabling the alignment of visual content with spatial map objects. We evaluated our approach using a culturally diverse Flickr dataset comprising over 28 million images from 42 global cities. The resulting dataset was assessed for a three-class building function classification task involving commercial, residential, and other categories. Fine-tuned state-of-the-art models achieved F1-scores reaching 0.51 on the filtered images. However, our analysis indicates that performance is heavily constrained by the quality of labels sourced from OpenStreetMap; metrics improved by 0.2 when using only human-validated labels. Consequently, we regard these labels as weak and are releasing the filtered images alongside their corresponding buildings as a weakly labeled dataset.

Recent advances in deep learning have shown promise in predicting 3D protein structures from inputs like sequences and Cryo-EM images; however, these approaches often fail when dealing with protein complexes (PCs), which involve multiple proteins. This study investigates deep learning methods augmented by Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) to predict the 3D structures of PCs. Since AFM images capture proteins in various random orientations, these multi-view images offer a viable pathway for training neural networks to reconstruct complex structures. Yet, acquiring real AFM datasets is time-consuming and impractical. To address this, we developed a virtual AFM imaging pipeline that converts 'PDB' files into multi-view 2D virtual AFM images via volume rendering, resulting in a dataset of approximately 8,000 proteins. We trained a neural network named Pix2Vox++ for 3D reconstruction using these synthesized images. Evaluations across different view counts yielded an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.92 on the training set and 0.52 on the validation set. We anticipate that this methodology will significantly enhance the prediction accuracy of protein complex structures.

Segmenting brain tumors is essential for effective patient management. To automate and standardize this process, we developed several U-net-based neural networks, utilizing deep supervision and stochastic weight averaging, trained on the BraTS 2020 dataset. We created two independent ensembles from distinct training pipelines, each generating a segmentation map. These maps were combined by considering each ensemble's performance on specific tumor subregions. On the online validation set with test-time augmentation, we achieved Dice scores of 0.81, 0.91, and 0.85, and Hausdorff (95%) distances of 20.6, 4.3, and 5.7 mm for the enhancing tumor, whole tumor, and tumor core, respectively. Similarly, on the final test dataset, our results yielded Dice scores of 0.79, 0.89, and 0.84, along with Hausdorff (95%) distances of 20.4, 6.7, and 19.5 mm, placing us in the top ten. We explored more complex architectures and training methods, but these did not significantly improve performance while substantially increasing training time. Ultimately, our approach delivered balanced and strong results across all tumor subregions. The solution is available as open source at https://github.com/lescientifik/open_brats2020.

This paper establishes a non-trivial bound for the weighted average of the shifted convolution sum involving $GL(3)\times GL(2)$, specifically showing that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $X^{1/4+\delta} \leq H \leq X$ with $\delta > 0$, the inequality
\[
\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^\infty \lambda_f(h) V\left(
\frac{h}{H}\right)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \lambda_{\pi}(1,n) \lambda_g (n+h) W\left(
\frac{n}{X} \right)\ll X^{1-\delta+\epsilon}
\]
holds, where $V$ and $W$ denote smooth, compactly supported functions, and $\lambda_f(n)$, $\lambda_g(n)$, and $\lambda_{\pi}(1,n)$ represent the normalized $n$-th Fourier coefficients of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ Hecke-Maass cusp forms $f$ and $g$, as well as the $SL(3,\mathbb{Z})$ Hecke-Maass cusp form $\pi$, respectively.

Over time, stars drift from their origins through radial migration, obscuring the chemical and kinematic signatures essential for reconstructing the Milky Way's history. Consequently, a primary objective of Galactic Archaeology is to identify stellar birth clusters within the disk using chemical tagging. This study demonstrates that stellar birth radii can be determined directly from observational data with minimal assumptions regarding Galactic enrichment history. By leveraging the inverse relationship between the metallicity range as a function of age and the time evolution of the stellar birth metallicity gradient ($d$[Fe/H]($R$, $\tau$)/$dR$), we can locate the birthplace ($R_b$) of any star given its age and metallicity. When applied to a high-precision dataset of Milky Way disk subgiants, our method reveals that the birth metallicity gradient steepened between 11 and 8 billion years ago, coinciding with the final major merger, Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE). This shift significantly influenced both the age-metallicity relation and the bimodality observed in the [$\alpha$/Fe]-[Fe/H] plane. By analyzing the disk as distinct mono-$R_b$ populations, we identified clumps within the low-[$\alpha$/Fe] sequence that are absent in aggregate samples and align temporally with known star-formation bursts. Our analysis estimates that the Sun formed approximately $4.5 \pm 0.4$ kpc from the Galactic center. These birth radius estimates supply the critical missing component for reconstructing the Milky Way's formation history, while the derived [Fe/H]($R$, $\tau$) relationship offers the previously missing prior required for chemical evolution models.

Traditional scheduling research has predominantly concentrated on a single resource category, such as computing nodes. Yet, contemporary scientific applications within modern High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments handle vast data volumes, creating varied demands across multiple resource types, including cores, cache, memory, and I/O. These diverse resources can all be leveraged by runtime schedulers to enhance application performance. This paper investigates multi-resource scheduling aimed at minimizing the makespan of computational workflows consisting of parallel jobs governed by precedence constraints. We assume the jobs are moldable, permitting the scheduler to dynamically allocate a variable set of resources prior to execution. We introduce a list-based, multi-resource scheduling algorithm and demonstrate that, for a system featuring $d$ schedulable resource types, the algorithm attains an approximation ratio of $1.619d+2.545\sqrt{d}+1$ for any $d$, improving to $d+O(\sqrt[3]{d^2})$ for large $d$. Additionally, we provide enhanced results for independent jobs and those with specific precedence structures, such as series-parallel graphs and trees. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $d$ for the approximation ratio of any list scheduling approach incorporating local priority considerations. To our knowledge, these constitute the inaugural approximation results for moldable workflows exhibiting multiple resource requirements.

We present an adaptive learning algorithm designed for the tomography of general quantum states. Built upon the simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation method, our approach is applicable to mixed qudit states. Key advantages of this algorithm include efficient post-processing with a complexity of $O(d^3)$ relative to the state dimension $d$, robustness against both measurement and channel noise, and superior infidelity performance compared to existing adaptive state learning techniques. The enhanced resilience to measurement noise renders this algorithm particularly suitable for noisy intermediate-scale quantum applications.

The superconducting ground state of the newly discovered ZrIrSi was investigated using resistivity measurements combined with the $\mu$SR technique. Resistivity data confirmed superconductivity emerging at $T_\mathrm{C}$ = 1.7 K. ZF-$\mu$SR analysis showed that no spontaneous magnetic field exists below $T_\mathrm{C}$, implying that time-reversal symmetry (TRS) remains intact in ZrIrSi. Furthermore, TF-$\mu$SR measurements allowed for the estimation of superfluid density across temperatures, which aligns with an isotropic $s$-wave model and a superconducting gap ratio of $2\Delta(0)/k_\mathrm{B}T_\mathrm{C}$ = 5.1, suggesting significant spin-orbit coupling. {\it Ab-initio} electronic structure calculations reveal four bands crossing the Fermi level, creating four Fermi surface pockets. These low-energy bands are primarily governed by the $4d$-orbitals of the transition metal Zr, with a notably smaller contribution from the $5d$-orbitals of Ir atoms.

Driven by the scarcity of hydrocarbon reserves and the high risks associated with exploration, there is a growing need for high-fidelity algorithms and computationally efficient methods in exploratory geophysics. While early methods focused on least-squares minimization, recent advancements prioritize robust formulations and the structured integration of prior information into inverse problems. However, this increased flexibility in optimization comes at the cost of greater computational complexity; whereas least-squares problems can be solved using standard techniques like steepest descent, Gauss-Newton, or L-BFGS, incorporating robust (non-smooth) penalties often requires custom modifications that are challenging to integrate into general seismic inversion workflows. This study introduces a generic, adaptable optimization framework designed to accommodate a wide variety of noise models, forward models, regularizers, and reparametrization transforms. The framework seamlessly supports robust noise models such as Huber and Student's $t$, along with sparse regularizers, projected constraints, and Total Variation regularization. Furthermore, the system is highly extensible, with clear guidelines provided for incorporating new formulations. Finally, we present several numerical examples to illustrate the framework's versatility.

This paper introduces a hybrid feedback strategy to address the navigation challenge of a point mass within an n-dimensional space populated by an arbitrary number of ellipsoidal obstacles. The proposed hybrid control algorithm ensures global asymptotic stabilization toward a reference point while simultaneously preventing collisions with obstacles. The core concept of this hybrid feedback involves toggling between two distinct control modes: stabilization and obstacle avoidance. By constructing the flow and jump sets of the hybrid controller using hysteresis regions, the method guarantees Zeno-free transitions between these modes. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid control approach in both 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional environments.

A method is introduced for combining two ergodic measure-preserving transformations to generate a third limiting transformation. This approach resolves a question about the rigidity of weak mixing transformations by demonstrating that for any given rigidity sequence associated with an ergodic measure-preserving transformation, one can find a weak mixing transformation that exhibits rigidity along that same sequence. Consequently, this result establishes a broad spectrum of rigidity sequences for weakly mixing dynamical systems.

Utilizing memristors in circuits presents avenues for developing new reconfigurable electronics, though research on device ensembles remains limited compared to large-scale arrays. This study introduces a vertically stacked memristor architecture featuring a shared central electrode. We investigate the resultant compound resistive states of these series-connected devices, manipulating them either through independent control of each unit or by adjusting the entire configuration via the selective use of the intermediate floating electrode. This shared middle electrode provides a unique perspective on the combined system that is typically inaccessible in standard vertical stacks. Our findings indicate that individually switching devices propagates effects to the full assembly (in a non-linear manner), thereby expanding the resistive state spectrum. This expansion yields a greater number of distinguishable states—exceeding signal-to-noise ratio variance limits—and consequently boosts memory capacity. Furthermore, applying stimuli to the external electrodes allows for the simultaneous switching of both devices, effectively turning the configuration into a voltage divider with distinct memristive elements. Leveraging this setup and the inherent voltage division enables surge protection for delicate components, while also demonstrating that resetting stacked devices simultaneously can drastically reduce the reset time required for large arrays.

We approximate sums involving functions of the negative eigenvalues for Schr\"odinger-type operators where the kinetic energy is zero on a codimension one submanifold. The primary technical instrument employed is the Stein-Tomas theorem along with several of its extensions.

This paper introduces the first investigation into leveraging large-scale pre-trained language models to automatically construct event-level temporal graphs from documents. Although neural pre-training has achieved remarkable success in NLP, its application to temporal reasoning within event graphs remains underexplored, largely due to the scarcity of large training corpora containing human-annotated events and temporal relationships. To overcome this obstacle, we employ existing Information Extraction/NLP tools to automatically generate a substantial dataset of 89,000 system-produced document-graph pairs and reframe the contextualized graph generation task as a sequence-to-sequence mapping problem. These approaches allow us to fine-tune pre-trained models on this synthetic data for graph generation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively produces graphs that are both structurally and semantically valid. Furthermore, evaluation on a difficult, out-of-domain, hand-labeled corpus reveals that our approach significantly outperforms the nearest existing methods across multiple metrics. The code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/madaan/temporal-graph-gen.

The Shapley value has recently emerged as a widely adopted method for explaining the predictions of both complex and simple machine learning models. This paper investigates the factors influencing Shapley values, specifically examining the relationship between a feature's distribution and its resulting Shapley value. Our analysis extends to the variations in Shapley explanations that arise for different predicted outcomes from the same model. We conclude that a Shapley value for a specific feature depends not only on its expected mean but also on other statistical moments, such as variance. Furthermore, we observe discrepancies regarding baseline predictions, the signs of feature contributions, and the identification of the most important feature across different outcomes—such as probability, log odds, and binary decisions—generated by the same linear probability model (logit/probit). These inconsistencies affect both local explainability and global feature importance. Ultimately, we find that there is no unique Shapley explanation for a given model; instead, it varies based on the model's outcome type (probability, log-odds, or binary decision) and its specific application.

The non-linear correlation between ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray luminosity in quasars has served as a basis for constructing a Hubble diagram up to redshifts of approximately $z\sim$ 7 and determining quasar distances, relying on the assumption that this relation remains independent of redshift and luminosity. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a detailed spectroscopic analysis of 130 high-redshift quasars ($z>$ 2.5) using high-quality X-ray and UV data. Our results confirm that the X-ray to UV correlation persists at these redshifts with an exceptionally low intrinsic dispersion of 0.12 dex, improving upon previous estimates of 0.20–0.22 dex. For a specific subset of quasars at $z\sim$ 3 with superior observation quality, the dispersion decreases further to 0.09 dex, a level fully explainable by intrinsic variability and source geometry. Additionally, composite spectra for both X-ray and UV bands show no deviations from the average spectra of lower-redshift quasars. The lack of spectral evolution combined with the tightness of the luminosity relation indicates that evolutionary effects are absent, allowing the relation to be safely used for distance measurements. Applying this method yields a luminosity distance at $z\sim$ 3 with 15% uncertainty, which presents a 4$\sigma$ tension with the concordance cosmological model.

This work examines both theoretically and numerically the impact of thermal noise on pulses within backward Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS). By integrating stochastic calculus with numerical techniques, we develop a theoretical framework capable of quantitatively forecasting noise measurements. We analyze how various optical pulse configurations—including pump and Stokes input powers, pulse durations, and interaction times—influence noise levels in the output Stokes field. Furthermore, we explore the effects of optical loss and waveguide length on noise, discovering that the signal-to-noise ratio can be substantially enhanced or diminished depending on specific combinations of waveguide characteristics and pulse parameters.

We establish a Poisson summation formula applicable to the zero set of a quadratic form involving an even number of variables, without imposing any restrictions on the support of the functions. A distinctive feature of this formula is that all resulting "boundary terms" are expressed either as constants or as sums over smaller quadrics associated with the original one. Furthermore, we explore the connection to the classical challenge of estimating the number of solutions for quadratic forms in an even-dimensional space. The proof of the summation formula relies on computing the (Arthur truncated) theta lift of the trivial representation of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{A}_F)$. As noted by Ginzburg, Rallis, and Soudry, this construction serves as an analogue for orthogonal groups on even-dimensional vector spaces of the global Schrödinger representation of the metaplectic group.

Fundamental theory investigations often necessitate detectors constrained by quantum mechanical laws. Specifically, in cavity-based searches for axionic dark matter, vacuum fluctuations within the two quadratures of the cavity's electromagnetic field cap the sensitivity to axion-induced fields. We present an experimental demonstration, using an apparatus that partially replicates current axion detectors, showing that these quantum limits can be surpassed by employing squeezed states. By preparing a microwave cavity in a squeezed state and measuring only the squeezed quadrature, we achieved a spectral scan rate enhancement of $2.12 \pm 0.08$. This result aligns precisely with a theoretical model that incorporates both imperfect squeezing and measurement effects.

Precision measurements of the Higgs boson heavily rely on its decay into $b$ and $c$ quarks. However, semileptonic decays within jets from these quarks introduce missing energy caused by undetectable neutrinos. By analyzing the decay kinematics, one can derive a correction for the missing neutrino momenta, though this yields a two-fold ambiguity. A kinematic fit resolves the correct solution by utilizing the well-defined initial state of an $e^{+}e^{-}$ collider to adjust measured values within their uncertainties so they satisfy kinematic constraints. The ParticleFlow approach, which reconstructs individual particles within jets, enables an unprecedented understanding of jet-level uncertainties. This discussion will examine the modeling of these jet uncertainties and the resulting fit performance using the ILD detector as an example. When applied to $H\rightarrow b\bar{b}/c\bar{c}$ events, combining the neutrino correction with the kinematic fit significantly enhances Higgs mass reconstruction, improving both the resolution and the peak position.

This study introduces the Sparse Multi-Family Deep Scattering Network (SMF-DSN), a new architecture designed to combine the interpretability of Deep Scattering Networks (DSN) with enhanced expressive capabilities. By cascading wavelet transforms, complex modulus operations, and translation-invariant operators, the DSN extracts salient and interpretable features from signals. First, we adopt a multi-family approach that utilizes highly specialized wavelet filters developed over recent decades. Specifically, our method applies multiple wavelet transforms across every network layer, which boosts feature diversity and eliminates the necessity for manual expert filter selection. Second, we devise an optimal thresholding strategy tailored to the DSN that regularizes the network and mitigates instabilities caused by signals, such as non-stationary noise. This systematic and principled method sparsifies the network's latent representation by functioning as a local mask that distinguishes between actual activity and noise. Ultimately, the SMF-DSN improves upon the standard DSN by (i) increasing the diversity of scattering coefficients and (ii) enhancing robustness against non-stationary noise.

Conventional LiDAR odometry (LO) relies primarily on geometric data from the environment to align scans and determine ego-motion, often struggling in dynamic or unstructured settings. This paper introduces InTEn-LOAM, a robust and low-drift odometry and mapping technique that comprehensively utilizes implicit data from laser sweeps, including geometry, intensity, and temporal attributes. By projecting scanned points onto cylindrical images, the method enables efficient and adaptive extraction of diverse features such as ground, beams, facades, and reflectors. A new intensity-based point registration algorithm is developed and integrated into the odometry framework, allowing the system to simultaneously estimate ego-motion using both geometric and intensity features. To mitigate interference from moving objects, a temporal-based dynamic removal strategy filters them out prior to map updates. Additionally, a time-related voxel grid filter organizes and downsamples the local map to preserve consistency between the current scan and the static map. Extensive evaluations on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach matches or exceeds the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods in standard driving conditions and significantly outperforms purely geometric-based LO systems in unstructured environments.

Wireless network performance is inherently constrained by aggregate interference, which is determined by the spatial arrangement of interferers, channel states, and user traffic dynamics (or queueing behavior). Since these elements typically display spatial and temporal correlations, network performance becomes environment-specific, relying on factors such as topology and blockage locations. These correlations can be leveraged in protocol design—through resource allocation strategies sensitive to spectrum, load, location, and energy—to deliver efficient wireless services. Consequently, accurate system-level evaluation that accounts for spatio-temporal correlations is essential. In this regard, stochastic geometry and random graph methods have been employed to create analytical frameworks capturing spatio-temporal interference in large-scale networks. This article serves as a tutorial on stochastic geometry analysis for large-scale wireless networks, focusing on modeling spatio-temporal interference and the resulting signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) correlations. The discussion begins by highlighting the significance of spatio-temporal performance analysis, detailing the parameters influencing SIR correlations, and identifying relevant performance metrics. Subsequently, methodologies for characterizing spatio-temporal SIR correlations across various network configurations are described, covering independent, attractive, and repulsive setups, as well as shadowing effects, user positioning, queueing dynamics, relaying, retransmission, and mobility. The piece concludes by proposing future research avenues within the context of spatio-temporal analysis for emerging wireless communication scenarios.

Recent self-supervised learning (SSL) models have demonstrated the ability to capture rich speech representations, making them highly effective for various downstream applications. While extensive research has examined how acoustic, phonetic, and semantic information is encoded within these models, the physical grounding derived from speech production has remained largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive analysis linking speech representations to articulatory trajectories captured via electromagnetic articulography (EMA). Using a linear probing method that evaluates the average correlation between linear mappings and EMA data, we assessed SSL models from the SUPERB benchmark leaderboard, with a detailed layer-wise investigation of the top-performing models, Wav2Vec 2.0 and HuBERT. Surprisingly, we found that representations from these modern SSL models exhibit strong correlations with EMA traces (peak correlation of r = 0.81), achieving high performance (r = 0.77) with just five minutes of training data. These results indicate that SSL models inherently align closely with continuous articulatory movements, offering new insights into the nature of speech SSL.

Although numerous quantum hardware platforms cannot execute fully fault-tolerant quantum computations, they remain viable as analogue quantum simulators for tackling many-body problems. Nevertheless, inherent errors obscure the degree to which these devices can surpass classical computers. This study investigates the application of noisy analogue quantum simulators in calculating physically significant properties of many-body systems, covering both equilibrium states and dynamic evolution. We initially establish a system-size-independent definition of stability against extensive errors, demonstrating its validity for Gaussian fermion models and a limited subset of spin systems. Notably, our analysis of Gaussian fermion models reveals the stability of critical, gapless models at zero temperature, even in the presence of long-range correlations. Additionally, we examine how this stability facilitates quantum advantage when computing the thermodynamic limits of many-body models under constant error rates, without relying on explicit error correction.

Addressing income disparity across social groups remains a worldwide issue. This research examines how female earnings influence household size and purchasing power. By employing statistical techniques including simple linear regression, maximum likelihood estimation, and hypothesis testing, I assessed the relationship between pre-tax female income and family size. The findings reveal that average purchasing power declines with each additional household member. Furthermore, Bayesian analysis suggests that the probability of an individual having a pre-tax income at least one and two standard deviations above the mean being female is roughly 1/3 and 1/4, respectively, underscoring persistent gender-based income gaps in Canada. In conclusion, while pre-tax female income alone does not significantly affect family size, pre-tax female income per person does exert a statistically significant impact on it.

We investigate the characteristics of lowest-energy states at non-zero total momentum (known as yrast states) within the Hubbard model for spin-1/2 fermions in a quantum ring featuring attractive on-site interactions at low density. For the one-dimensional (1D) scenario, we employ the Bethe ansatz to solve the model, whereas we utilize the Full-Configuration-Interaction Quantum Monte-Carlo (FCIQMC) method to determine yrast states for spin-balanced Fermi systems during the transition into the two-dimensional (2D) regime. Our findings illustrate the evolution of the yrast excitation spectrum from 1D to 2D and examine the influence of pairing on these spectra. Additionally, we identify indications of fragmented condensation in specific yrast states, a phenomenon typically linked to dark solitons.

Bravyi et al. recently demonstrated a separation between $\mathbf{QNC^0}$ and $\mathbf{NC^0}$—the classes of constant-depth, polynomial-size quantum and classical circuits with bounded fan-in gates—by analyzing two specific problems: the 2D hidden linear function problem and the 1D magic square problem. This paper introduces a third problem with the same distinguishing property, the magic pentagram problem, which is derived from the magic pentagram nonlocal game. Specifically, we establish that this problem can be solved deterministically by a $\mathbf{QNC^0}$ circuit but cannot be solved by any $\mathbf{NC^0}$ circuit.

Sentiment analysis remains a foundational and extensively researched task in natural language processing, which has seen significant advancements through the development of more sophisticated and scalable machine learning models. However, Brazilian Portuguese continues to suffer from a scarcity of linguistic resources, particularly datasets designed for sentiment classification that include standardized splits for training, testing, and validation to ensure fair algorithmic comparison. Driven by these gaps, this study evaluates the predictive performance of various document embedding strategies, using polarity as the target output. The research consolidates five Brazilian Portuguese sentiment datasets into a unified corpus and establishes a public reference partitioning for training, testing, and validation sets via a digital repository. Furthermore, a cross-evaluation is performed to assess how well dataset-specific models generalize across different contexts and to determine the viability of employing a single model for all scenarios.

To improve evacuation efficiency in scenarios characterized by asymmetric exits with partial observability under guidance, this study introduces a general framework for a dynamic guiding assistant system designed to examine the impact of density control. Within this framework, multiple evacuation assistants are deployed to monitor partial pedestrian location data and dynamically adjust guiding signals. A straightforward on-off density control algorithm is developed for these assistants, utilizing delayed observational data regarding pedestrian densities near specific exits. By employing a force-driven cellular automaton model, the paper offers strategic recommendations for configuring observed regions and target densities. Results indicate that the proposed algorithm effectively manages the global distribution of pedestrians and mitigates arching phenomena, even when relying on partial information subject to time delays. Furthermore, setting a moderate target density helps prevent collisions near exits and avoids inefficient pedestrian segregation. To further enhance efficiency, the study reveals that, without loss of generality, observing pedestrian locations in a small area near the exit is sufficient when observation delays are minimal. These numerical findings are anticipated to offer valuable insights for designing computer-aided guiding strategies in real-world evacuation scenarios.

This paper introduces Mutual Information Maximization Knowledge Distillation (MIMKD). The proposed approach employs a contrastive objective to jointly estimate and maximize a lower bound on the mutual information between local and global feature representations of teacher and student networks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIMKD enhances the performance of low-capacity models by transferring knowledge from larger, computationally intensive models, thereby enabling the creation of efficient models suitable for resource-constrained devices. The method is highly flexible, supporting knowledge distillation between teacher and student networks with arbitrary architectures. Empirical results indicate that MIMKD surpasses competing methods across diverse student-teacher pairs, varying architectures, and scenarios involving extremely low-capacity students. Specifically, on CIFAR100, a ShufflenetV2 student achieved 74.55% accuracy (up from a baseline of 69.8%) by learning from a ResNet-50 teacher. On ImageNet, a ResNet-18 student improved from 68.88% to 70.32% accuracy (+1.44%) when distilled from a ResNet-34 teacher.

This work investigates the spectral characteristics of $N=2$ supersymmetric lattice models in $D$ dimensions. We identify systematic deviations from the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) manifested as a degenerate collection of analytically constructed supersymmetric (SUSY) doublets, commonly known as many-body scars. These states demonstrate stability against any perturbation that preserves SUSY, even when inhomogeneous couplings are present. Specifically, for two-leg ladder systems, extensive numerical analysis reveals that these states are the exclusive ETH violators and evaluates their resilience to SUSY-breaking perturbations. Our findings propose a universal mechanism for stabilizing quantum many-body scars within lattice models across arbitrary dimensions.

Comprehending the genesis and long-term evolution of atmospheric plasmas generated by ultrashort, long-wavelength infrared (LWIR) pulses remains a critical yet partially unresolved challenge. A specific focus lies on plasmas formed in air at peak intensities around 10$^{12}$ W/cm$^2$, known as the clamping intensity in LWIR atmospheric guiding contexts, where tunneling and multi-photon ionization—effective at near-IR wavelengths or shorter—are non-functional. Our findings indicate that avalanche breakdown occurring on aerosol (dust) surfaces can initiate the air breakdown observed above the 200 GW/cm$^2$ threshold when utilizing a sequence of 3 ps, 10.6 $\mu$m laser pulses spaced by 18 ps. Initially manifesting at the focal point, the breakdown propagates backward toward the focusing optic as plasma density nears critical levels, thereby preventing forward propagation. This backward-moving breakdown can reach velocities up to 10$^9$ cm/s, roughly ten times faster than breakdown induced by nanosecond pulses, and is well-explained by the breakdown wave mechanism. Transverse plasma expansion, occurring at comparable speeds, is facilitated by UV photoionization and manifests as a secondary longitudinal breakdown mechanism in approximately 10% of shots. When a terawatt-class beam spanning centimeters is transmitted, aerosol interception is inevitable, generating multiple (40 cm$^{-3}$) breakdown sites that each initially create near-critical density plasma. Over a 10 ns to 1 $\mu$s timescale, shockwaves from these sites expand radially and merge to form a large, hot gas channel. The radial expansion velocity aligns closely with predictions from blast wave theory adapted for ultrafast atmospheric detonations.

Kondo breakdown represents a fascinating challenge within strongly correlated electron systems, stemming from various anomalous electronic phenomena observed in heavy-fermion materials. While this breakdown in Kondo lattice systems typically stems from strong magnetic frustration or critical fluctuations of collective modes, we identify a novel mechanism arising entirely from different origins in interacting topological Kondo insulators. Utilizing numerically exact quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that under open boundary conditions, interaction effects at the edges or corners inevitably dismantle Kondo screening. We propose that this breakdown is mandated by the system's symmetries, as the resulting ground states correspond to symmetry-protected Haldane phases.

We introduce two novel polynomial families that extend the concept of permanents, establishing upper and lower bounds on their determinantal complexities that align with existing results for permanents. The first family arises by substituting permutations with signed permutations, while the second is formed by replacing permutations with surjective functions that have preimages of specified sizes.

Classical density functional theory (DFT) at finite temperatures is typically developed within the grand-canonical ensemble, allowing for arbitrary fluctuations in local density. Nevertheless, many systems of interest are closed regarding mass, corresponding to canonical ensembles with fixed temperature and particle number. While grand-canonical tools are frequently applied ad hoc to these closed systems, a direct canonical formulation has previously been elusive. This study revisits the foundational theorems of classical DFT and compares them across both ensembles, revealing that the differences are merely formal and trivial. The viability of canonical DFT is demonstrated by deriving the exact Helmholtz functional for specific systems: an ideal gas, restricted geometries in various dimensions, and a pair of hard spheres (hard rods) in one dimension within a confined cavity. Notable parallels between the ensembles emerge even for small systems, with the canonical results reflecting the strong echoes of Percus's famous exact grand-canonical findings.

This study examines joint scheduling and power control for V2V multicast systems that support multihop communication, taking into account both co-channel and adjacent channel interference. Initially, the research addresses maximizing network throughput and connectivity. The framework is subsequently extended to minimize latency and Average Age of Information (AoI), defined as the freshness of the most recently received message. To ensure fairness, an additional formulation aims to maximize the worst-case throughput and connectivity. All these scenarios are modeled as Mixed Boolean Linear Programming problems to derive optimal solutions. The study also incorporates link failure error probabilities across all formulations, ensuring requirements for specific throughput, connectivity, latency, or AoI levels are met. To efficiently manage large-scale V2V networks, a clustering algorithm with scalable computational complexity is introduced. Additionally, a multihop distributed scheduling scheme is proposed to address scenarios where the scheduler lacks channel state information.

This study presents the interface of our developed crowdsourcing tool and provides a detailed explanation of the annotation process. The tool, titled "Parupalli Padajaalam" (meaning "web of words by Parupalli"), is designed to populate OntoSenseNet, a Telugu resource annotated with sentiment polarity. Building on recent findings that highlight the significance of word-level annotations for sentiment analysis, we investigate the value of sense-annotations derived from OntoSenseNet in enhancing sentiment analysis performance. We detail the features extracted from Telugu OntoSenseNet and analyze the distribution of adverbial classes associated with verbs within the same resource. This analysis supports word-sense disambiguation, thereby improving the effectiveness of word-sense disambiguation (WSD) tasks.

We investigate localization effects within a one-dimensional lattice subjected to a uniformly translating disordered potential. At low velocities, a sliding localized phase emerges, where the initially localized matter wave adiabatically tracks the moving potential without diffusion, thereby preserving initial state memory in the many-body dynamics. This distinctive localized phase differs from standard Anderson localization in two key ways: it is not robust against interactions but remains stable under slowly varying perturbations. This sliding localized phase arises from interference between wavepacket paths under moving quasi-periodic potentials with periods incommensurate with the lattice constant. Additionally, we discuss the experimental realization and detection of this phenomenon.

Efficient quantum error correction relies heavily on developing rapid, low-error methods for qubit readout. In this study, we evaluate neural networks designed to classify single-shot spin detection events, which serve as the readout signals for our qubit measurements. These signals feature a stochastic peak, for which a Bayesian inference filter incorporating Gaussian noise is theoretically optimal. Consequently, we benchmark neural networks trained using various strategies against this Bayesian approach. We find that training a network with $10^{6}$ experimentally recorded single-shot traces yields no improvement in post-processing performance. Conversely, a network trained on synthetically generated measurement traces achieves detection error rates and processing speeds comparable to the Bayesian filter. Furthermore, this neural network demonstrates greater robustness to variations in signal offset, duration, delay, and signal-to-noise ratio. Notably, combining a network trained on synthetic traces with the measured noise profile of our setup increases Rabi-oscillation visibility by 7%. Thus, our work highlights the potential benefits of implementing neural networks in both software and hardware for scalable spin qubit processor architectures.

This chapter examines the mechanisms responsible for X-ray emission across various classes of cataclysmic variables (CVs). These semi-detached binary systems involve mass transfer from a donor star (companion or secondary) to a white dwarf primary. CVs are categorized into sub-classes based on their optical and X-ray phenomenology, which is primarily dictated by the magnetic field strength of the accreting star. Non-magnetic systems display diverse behaviors dependent on accretion rates, including novae, dwarf novae, nova-like variables, symbiotic binaries, and supersoft sources. In contrast, magnetic systems—specifically polars (AM Her systems) and intermediate polars (DQ Her systems)—direct the accretion flow toward magnetic poles, resulting in distinct observational signatures. X-rays in CVs generally arise from high-energy processes, generated via shocks (in boundary layers, accretion columns, or through interactions within nova ejecta or between ejecta and stellar winds) or hydrogen fusion (steady-state or thermonuclear runaway). This discussion covers all types of accreting white dwarfs, analyzing both spectral and temporal variability across these populations.

By integrating the non-flat condition with Kaniadakis entropy within a cosmological extension of the standard holographic principle, we develop the non-flat Kaniadakis holographic dark energy (KHDE) model. This framework utilizes the Kaniadakis parameter $K$ and a parameter $c$ to derive a differential equation governing the KHDE density parameter, which characterizes the universe's evolution. This equation successfully describes both open and closed universe scenarios. An analysis of matter and dark energy dominated regimes indicates that the KHDE scenario can delineate the universe's thermal history and allows for a quintom phase. Expressions for the deceleration and equation of state (EoS) parameters are derived for both open and closed cases, and the model's classical stability is confirmed by varying its parameters. Specifically, assuming positive curvature, the universe exhibits quintom behavior at significantly lower $K$ values compared to the flat case, where only quintessence is achieved for those same $K$ values; a similar trend is observed under negative curvature. Consequently, incorporating slight spatial curvature into the KHDE model enhances its phenomenological capabilities while keeping $K$ values low. To constrain the model parameters, we employ recent $30\;H(z)$ measurements within the redshift range $0.07 \leq z \leq 1.965$, alongside distance modulus data from the Union 2.1 type Ia supernovae sample.
This paper presents a full classification of $n$-dimensional nilpotent non-Tortkara anticommutative algebras defined over $\mathbb{C}$ that possess an annihilator of dimension $(n-4)$.

This study examines the mean-field game (MFG) framework for price formation proposed by Gomes and Sa\'ude, where agents trade a commodity with either deterministic or stochastic supply. Agents seek to maximize profits by considering both current and anticipated prices, with market equilibrium prices established by the balance of supply and demand. We propose a potential function that transforms this MFG into a convex variational problem, a formulation well-suited for machine learning applications. Specifically, we employ a recurrent neural network to solve this problem and, in the final section, validate our findings by comparing them against established analytical solutions.

While MRI employing multiple protocols is standard for diagnosis, the lengthy acquisition times render images susceptible to motion artifacts. To mitigate this, various techniques have been developed to reconstruct full images from under-sampled k-space data; however, these methods face two critical limitations. First, the aliasing artifacts produced in the image domain are structural and non-local, meaning that restoration within the image domain alone is insufficient. Second, although MRI exams involve multiple protocols, most prior research relies solely on reconstructing individual protocols using highly distorted under-sampled inputs, largely neglecting the potential of fully-sampled short protocols (such as T1) as complementary information. This study addresses these gaps by introducing the Dual Domain Recurrent Network (DuDoRNet), which incorporates a deep T1 prior to simultaneously recover k-space and images, thereby accelerating long-protocol MRI acquisition. Specifically, we customized a Dilated Residual Dense Network (DRDNet) to perform dual-domain restoration on under-sampled MRI data. Extensive experiments across various sampling patterns and acceleration rates demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods in reconstructing high-quality MRI images.

Currently, developers of data-intensive deep neural networks (DNNs) extensively search the internet for training data, often depriving users of control and awareness regarding their data's appropriation. To help users resist unauthorized data usage, we have designed, implemented, and assessed a practical system that allows individuals to determine if their data contributed to a DNN's training. We demonstrate that users can generate unique data points, termed isotopes, which embed "spurious features" into DNNs during the training phase. By utilizing only query access to a trained model—without needing knowledge of the training process or control over data labels—users can employ statistical hypothesis testing to identify whether a model has learned these specific spurious features linked to their isotopes. This approach effectively leverages DNNs' susceptibility to memorization and false correlations as a mechanism for establishing data provenance. Our findings validate the system's effectiveness across various scenarios, accurately detecting and distinguishing among hundreds of isotopes. Additionally, we show that the system functions on public machine learning-as-a-service platforms and large-scale models like ImageNet, can utilize physical objects rather than digital markers, and maintains robustness against several adaptive countermeasures.

We introduce PNN-smoothing, a meta-method designed to initialize the $k$-means clustering algorithm. This approach involves partitioning a dataset into $J$ random subsets, performing individual clustering on each subset, and then integrating the results using the pairwise-nearest-neighbor (PNN) technique. As a meta-method, PNN-smoothing allows for the use of any seeding algorithm when processing the subsets. Provided that the underlying seeding algorithm scales linearly with the data size $N$ and the number of clusters $k$, PNN-smoothing achieves nearly linear complexity with a suitable selection of $J$, offering strong practical performance. Empirical evaluations across various synthetic and real datasets, utilizing multiple existing seeding strategies, demonstrate that this procedure consistently yields lower costs. Specifically, our enhancement of $k$-means++ seeding outperforms the widely used "greedy" $k$-means++ variant in both efficacy and speed. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/carlobaldassi/KMeansPNNSmoothing.jl.

Understanding and reasoning about narratives fundamentally relies on explaining the motivations behind characters' actions. Although Question Answering (QA) has seen recent advancements, it remains uncertain whether current models can address "why" questions that depend on commonsense knowledge outside the provided story. To address this, we present TellMeWhy, a new crowd-sourced dataset featuring over 30,000 questions and free-form responses regarding character motivations in short narratives. Notably, for one-third of this dataset, the correct answers are not contained within the narrative itself. Due to the challenges of automated assessment for this specific task, we also developed a structured human evaluation interface. Our testing of state-of-the-art models reveals that they significantly underperform humans, a gap that widens further when answers require external knowledge, thereby highlighting a critical area for future research in QA and narrative comprehension.

This study explores legal concepts and their expression in Portuguese, specifically focusing on the Bar exam administered by the Order of Attorneys of Brazil. By utilizing a corpus of multiple-choice questions, three norms from the Ethics section of the OAB exam, linguistic resources (Princeton WordNet and OpenWordNet-PT), and analytical tools (AntConc and Freeling), the research identifies gaps in the Portuguese lexicon within the OpenWordNet-PT knowledge base. These missing concepts and terms are subsequently integrated into OpenWordNet-PT, resulting in a lexical representation of the texts that is fully contained within the knowledge base.

Human-in-the-loop methodologies are crucial for robotic applications. This study implements a multimodal human-robot interaction (HRI) scenario where a simulated robot conveys its intentions via speech and confirms its chosen actions through pointing gestures. The human partner assesses whether the robot's verbal intention aligns with its corresponding gesture. When a mismatch occurs, we anticipate the generation of error-related potentials (ErrPs) in the human electroencephalogram (EEG). These real-time intrinsic evaluations were recorded, continuously segmented online, and classified asynchronously. To enhance feature selection, we propose a method that combines forward and backward sliding windows to train the classifier. Across nine subjects, this approach achieved an average classification accuracy of 91%, though notable inter-subject variability was observed. Future work will extend the feature selection method to enable customization, automatically identifying optimal sliding window combinations to address performance differences between individuals. Additionally, we plan to leverage the ErrP signals indicative of human error evaluation within interactive reinforcement learning to further improve multimodal HRI.

We explicitly determine the structural properties of $p$-adic special orthogonal groups in dimension three for every prime $p$, including a concurrent analysis of the two-dimensional case. Specifically, beginning with the unique definite quadratic form in three dimensions (up to linear equivalence and rescaling), we demonstrate that every element of $SO(3)_p$ constitutes a rotation around an axis. A critical component of this analysis involves classifying all definite forms in two dimensions, which provides a description of rotation subgroups around any fixed axis; these subgroups are all abelian and are naturally parametrized by the projective line. Additionally, we establish that for odd primes $p$, the full group $SO(3)_p$ allows a representation using Cardano angles of rotations about reference axes, mirroring the real orthogonal case. However, this representation is valid only for specific orderings of the product of rotations around coordinate axes, contingent upon the prime in question, and a general Euler angle decomposition does not exist. For $p=2$, neither Euler nor Cardano decompositions are possible.

The sensitivity of a string compression algorithm $C$ quantifies the potential increase in output size $C(T)$ resulting from a single character edit on an input string $T$. This study analyzes the worst-case multiplicative sensitivity, defined as $\max_{T \in \Sigma^n}\{C(T')/C(T) : ed(T, T') = 1\}$, where $ed(T, T')$ represents the edit distance between $T$ and $T'$. Specifically, we demonstrate that for standard Lempel-Ziv 77 compressors, this worst-case multiplicative sensitivity is bounded by a small constant. We reinforce these upper bounds with corresponding lower bounds and extend the findings to the smallest bidirectional scheme $b$. These results differ from prior knowledge, such as the finding that the Lempel-Ziv 78 factorization size $z_{\rm 78}$ can grow by a factor of $\Omega(n^{1/4})$ [Lagarde and Perifel, 2018] and the number of runs $r$ in the Burrows-Wheeler transform can increase by $\Omega(\log n)$ [Giuliani et al., 2021] upon prepending a character to a string of length $n$. Furthermore, we establish that the worst-case multiplicative sensitivity of $r$ is upper bounded by $O(\log r \log n)$. We also examine the worst-case sensitivity of various grammar-based compressors, including RePair, LongestMatch, Bisection, AVL-grammar, GCIS, and CDAWG. Additionally, we broaden the concept of worst-case sensitivity to string repetitiveness metrics like the smallest string attractor size $\gamma$ and substring complexity $\delta$, presenting non-trivial upper and lower bounds for $\gamma$ and matching bounds for $\delta$. Finally, we explore the worst-case additive sensitivity, defined as $\max_{T \in \Sigma^n}\{C(T') - C(T) : ed(T, T') = 1\}$.

This study examines how growth conditions and device architecture impact the performance of (GaIn)As/Ga(AsSb)/(GaIn)As "W"-quantum well lasers. To achieve this, the epitaxial process was expanded to full 2-inch substrates to enhance homogeneity, and the growth was executed in a single run to ensure superior quality. Additionally, the optical confinement factor was boosted by raising the aluminum concentration in the cladding layers to 65%. These procedures were applied to devices targeting emission wavelengths of 1.26 and 1.30 micrometers. At room temperature, the 1.26-micrometer devices demonstrated differential efficiencies up to 58% and threshold current densities as low as 0.16 kA/cm². These devices also showed excellent characteristic temperatures of T₀=(72 ± 5)K and T₁=(293 ± 16)K across a temperature range from 10°C to 100°C. In contrast, the 1.30-micrometer devices achieved differential efficiencies of 31% and threshold current densities of 0.50 kA/cm² at room temperature. The paper also briefly discusses strategies for further improving these properties and extending the wavelength range.

The subset sum problem is an NP-hard challenge in computer science, where the most efficient known algorithm operates with a time complexity of $O(2^{0.3113n})$. The perfect sum problem represents a further extension of this concept, introducing additional complexity that renders large-scale computations difficult. This paper introduces a probabilistic method that approximates solutions to the perfect sum problem by modeling the distribution of potential sums. Because the perfect sum problem builds upon the subset sum framework, this approach also offers probabilistic insights into solving the original subset sum problem. By utilizing distributional approximations to estimate the count of subsets summing to specific values, we employ two distinct strategies: applying bounds to validate normal approximations and estimating the empirical distribution through density analysis. These methods achieve $O(n)$ computational complexity and improve in accuracy as input size grows, making them suitable for large-scale combinatorial tasks. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/KristofPusztai/PerfectSum.

This study presents a convergence analysis of online stochastic gradient descent algorithms applied to functional linear models. By characterizing the regularity of the slope function, the capacity of the kernel space, and the covariance operator of the sampling process, the authors achieve notable improvements in convergence rates. The analysis covers both prediction and estimation tasks, demonstrating that capacity assumptions can mitigate the saturation of convergence rates as target function regularity increases. Specifically, for prediction problems, appropriately chosen kernels allow capacity assumptions to fully offset regularity requirements, a capability that does not extend to estimation problems. This distinction highlights the fundamental differences between prediction and estimation within functional data analysis.

Reduced order models (ROMs) offer computationally efficient means to characterize essential dynamical and statistical properties of natural systems. This paper introduces a systematic multiscale stochastic ROM framework tailored for complex systems exhibiting strong chaotic or turbulent behavior. Unlike traditional Galerkin ROMs (G-ROMs) or deterministic variants designed to minimize path-wise errors in laminar systems, this new approach prioritizes the recovery of large-scale dynamics. It employs cost-effective conditional linear functions as closure terms to capture statistical features of medium-scale variables and their feedback to large scales, while also integrating physics constraints. A distinctive advantage of this framework is its facilitation of an efficient and accurate nonlinear data assimilation scheme, solved via closed analytic formulae. This analytic solvability enhances computational speed and circumvents potential numerical and sampling issues associated with recovering unobserved states from partial data. Furthermore, the overall model calibration is both efficient and systematic, relying on explicit mathematical expressions. Applied to complex nonlinear systems where intrinsic turbulence arises from either external random forcing or deterministic nonlinearity, the proposed ROM demonstrates superior performance compared to G-ROMs in reproducing both dynamical and statistical features, as well as in recovering unobserved states through the associated data assimilation process.

We introduce Wi-Lo, a solution that transforms standard 802.11 (WiFi) access points into IoT gateways capable of supporting LoRa technology for downlink communications. The Wi-Lo system operates without requiring additional hardware, relying solely on a software update.
