It employs a signal emulation technique grounded in complementary code keying modulation derived from 802.11b to simulate LoRa long-range transmissions. This gateway enables standard WiFi-enabled smartphones to transmit packets to LoRa-compliant IoT devices, such as smart sensors. We developed a prototype using off-the-shelf WiFi hardware, and experimental results demonstrate that Wi-Lo allows regular WiFi nodes to communicate with LoRa devices over long distances, achieving performance comparable to systems utilizing dedicated LoRa transmitters and receivers.

The goal of lifelong reinforcement learning (RL) is to optimize agents capable of continuously adapting and interacting within evolving environments. Yet, existing RL methods struggle significantly when faced with non-stationary conditions and non-episodic interactions. To address this, we introduce Lifelong Skill Planning (LiSP), a framework for non-episodic lifelong RL that utilizes planning within an abstract space of higher-order skills. These skills are acquired unsupervised through intrinsic rewards, and subsequent planning occurs over these skills using a learned dynamics model. Additionally, our framework allows for skill discovery from offline data, minimizing the reliance on extensive real-world interactions. Empirical results demonstrate that LiSP effectively facilitates long-horizon planning and trains agents that can avert catastrophic failures, even in difficult non-stationary and non-episodic settings drawn from gridworld and MuJoCo benchmarks.

Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) directly derives semantic meaning from audio, offering the potential to minimize misunderstandings and error accumulation in end-user applications. Nevertheless, publicly accessible SLU resources remain scarce. This paper introduces SLURP, a novel SLU package comprising: (1) a challenging, English-language dataset covering 18 domains that is significantly larger and linguistically more varied than current options; (2) competitive baselines utilizing state-of-the-art NLU and ASR systems; and (3) a new, transparent metric for entity labeling designed to facilitate detailed error analysis and pinpoint areas for enhancement. SLURP can be accessed at https://github.com/pswietojanski/slurp.

Using a binned approach, we independently reconstruct the primordial black hole (PBH) mass function from GWTC-3 data, revealing it aligns with a broad, red-tilted power spectrum of curvature perturbations. While the GW190521 event, featuring component masses above the upper mass gap ($m>65M_\odot$), fits naturally within the PBH framework, events in the light mass range ($m<3M_\odot$)—specifically GW190814, GW190425, GW200105, and GW200115—are highly improbable as binary PBH mergers. This unlikelihood persists despite the absence of electromagnetic counterparts, as the predicted merger rates for such PBHs fall significantly below LIGO-Virgo observations. Moreover, we anticipate that future detections by ground-based and space-borne gravitational-wave detectors, as well as pulsar timing arrays, will confirm both the GW background from binary PBHs and the scalar-induced GWs arising from PBH formation.

For a weight function defined on the unit disk as the modulus of a finite product of Blaschke factor powers, we provide a canonical expression for the reproducing kernel of the associated weighted Bergman space, expressed through the kernel's values and derivatives at the origin. This approach results in a formula for the contractive zero divisor of a Bergman space with a finite set of zeros.

Machine learning relies heavily on data for model training and validation. Consequently, organizations frequently outsource data-related tasks—including data generation, annotation, and output evaluation—to crowdsourcing platforms and business process outsourcing (BPO) firms. This study examines outsourced machine learning data work within Latin America by analyzing three platforms in Venezuela and a BPO in Argentina. Drawing on Foucault's concept of the *dispositif*, we define the "data-production dispositif" as a strategic assemblage of discourses, actions, and objects designed to reproduce power-knowledge dynamics in data and labor. Our analysis utilizes 210 data work instructions, 55 interviews with workers, managers, and clients, and participant observation. The findings reveal that instruction-based discourses replicate and normalize the requesters' worldviews. Additionally, precarious employment conditions and economic dependence alienate workers, fostering obedience to directives. Furthermore, discourses and social contexts manifest in material artifacts like user interfaces and performance metrics, which restrict worker agency and enforce specific interpretations of data. The paper concludes by emphasizing the need to resist the data-production dispositif by combating alienation and precarity, thereby empowering data workers to become valuable assets in the pursuit of high-quality data.

Recent studies have shown that both a classical Schwarzschild black hole (BH) and a dense cluster of self-gravitating fermionic dark matter (DM) at the Galactic center can account for the precise astrometric data—specifically positions and radial velocities—of the 17 best-resolved S-stars orbiting SgrA*. This analysis incorporates tests of general relativistic effects, such as the gravitational redshift observed in the S2-star. Furthermore, the DM model presents a significant finding: the dense fermionic core represents the central region of a continuous density distribution, where the diluted halo successfully explains the Galactic rotation curve. In this paper, we extend these results by examining the relativistic periapsis precession of the S2-star within both frameworks. While the Schwarzschild BH scenario predicts a singular prograde precession for S2, the DM scenario allows for either retrograde or prograde precession, contingent on the mass of DM enclosed within the S2 orbit, which varies with the DM fermion mass. We demonstrate that current public data on S2 cannot distinguish between the two models; however, future astrometric observations of S2 near its next apocentre passage may eventually determine whether SgrA* is governed by a classical BH or a quantum DM system.

This study presents a comprehensive broadband X-ray analysis of NGC 4258, aiming to accurately determine the AGN's coronal luminosity and accretion flow characteristics while monitoring variations over a twenty-year period. By compiling archival spectroscopic data from XMM-Newton, Chandra, Swift/BAT, and NuSTAR spanning 15 years, we utilize advanced modeling, including a warped disk component to account for known X-ray obscuration, alongside existing literature results. Significant spectral variability across different epochs is evident. The obscuring column density exhibits potential periodic fluctuations on a decade-long timescale, whereas the intrinsic luminosity demonstrates a long-term decline by a factor of three over 15 years, dropping from approximately $10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ in the early 2000s to $3 \times 10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$ by 2016. Combining the average absorption-corrected X-ray luminosity ($L_{2-10~\text{keV}}$) with archival bolometric luminosity estimates yields a bolometric correction of $k_{\rm bol} \sim 20$, a value characteristic of Seyferts fueled by geometrically thin, radiatively efficient disks. Additionally, the X-ray photon index $\Gamma$ aligns with typical values for the general AGN population. However, the Eddington-normalized accretion rate remains very low, consistent with the RIAF regime. These findings indicate that NGC 4258 is a true low-luminosity Seyfert II, with no compelling evidence in its X-ray emission for a hot, RIAF-like accretion flow.

This work addresses Bayesian multiple statistical classification where unknown source distributions are inferred from labeled training data and subsequently utilized as nominal distributions within a robust hypothesis testing framework. Specifically, we implement the DGL test proposed by Devroye et al. and derive non-asymptotic, exponential upper bounds for the classification error probability. These bounds are straightforward to compute and illuminate the impact of training sequence length, alphabet size, and the number of hypotheses on the error exponent. Furthermore, the proposed approach remains effective for large alphabet sources provided the alphabet grows sub-quadratically relative to the test sequence length. Simulation results demonstrate that the method's performance converges toward that of optimal hypothesis testing as the training sequence length increases.

Deep generative models have the capacity to automatically produce content across various formats. Nevertheless, there is no assurance that this generated material will meet the standards required for end-user presentation or functionality; for instance, created game levels might be unsolvable or logically inconsistent. This paper examines this issue through a geometric lens, offering a technique for dependable interpolation and random walks within the latent spaces of Categorical VAEs by leveraging Riemannian geometry. We evaluate our approach using "Super Mario Bros" and "The Legend of Zelda" levels, comparing it against simpler baselines rooted in current practices. The findings indicate that the proposed geometry facilitates superior interpolation and sampling, consistently maintaining proximity to latent regions that decode into playable content.

Using density functional theory enhanced by dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to account for electronic correlations, we computed the magnetic Compton profiles (MCPs) of Nickel (Ni) and compared them with experimental data. These theoretical MCPs were derived via two distinct approaches: the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) method paired with a perturbative spin-polarized T-matrix fluctuation exchange DMFT solver, and the full potential linear augmented planewave method combined with a numerically exact continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo DMFT solver. Our findings indicate that the total magnetic moment diminishes as the intra-atomic Coulomb repulsion ($U$) increases, a trend clearly mirrored in the calculated MCPs. Furthermore, experimental measurements of the total magnetic moment align with intermediate $U$ values. Analysis of the spectral function demonstrates that, relative to density functional theory results, the minority X$_2$ Fermi surface pocket becomes both shallower and smaller.

Large-scale contrastive vision-language pre-training has made substantial strides in visual representation learning. Diverging from traditional systems reliant on fixed discrete labels, the paradigm introduced in \cite{radford2021learning} enables the direct alignment of images with raw text within an open-vocabulary framework. For downstream applications, zero-shot predictions are typically achieved using carefully crafted text prompts. To mitigate the need for complex prompt engineering, context optimization \cite{zhou2021coop} was developed to learn continuous, task-specific prompt vectors via few-shot training. However, this paper argues that superior vision-language models can be achieved through an alternative strategy beyond prompt tuning. While prompt tuning modifies textual inputs, we introduce CLIP-Adapter, which fine-tunes either the visual or language branch using feature adapters. Specifically, CLIP-Adapter incorporates an additional bottleneck layer to acquire new features and merges them with original pre-trained features through a residual-style blending mechanism. Consequently, CLIP-Adapter surpasses context optimization in performance while maintaining a straightforward design. Extensive experiments and ablation studies across various visual classification tasks validate the efficacy of our method.

This study establishes novel upper and lower bounds for multiple vertex- and edge-based topological indices, specifically the Albertson irregularity index, degree variance index, Mostar index, and the first Zagreb index. Additionally, we derive a new upper bound for graph energy utilizing the IRB-index. The majority of these findings are grounded in the established characterization of the Laplacian spectral radius.

Combining neural networks with orthogonal characteristics through a committee approach is a well-established method for reducing generalization errors. This study demonstrates that such ensembling is particularly effective for medical machine learning. First, ensembles support parallel and asynchronous learning, allowing for the efficient training of patient-specific neural networks. Second, by selecting uncorrelated, patient-specific models to minimize generalization error, we show that a small ensemble of these models can outperform a single model trained on significantly larger pooled datasets. Third, the non-iterative process of combining ensembles provides an optimal low-dimensional interface for applying output perturbation, thereby ensuring the privacy of patient-specific networks. We validate this framework of differentially private ensembles on the task of early sepsis prediction using real-world intensive care unit data annotated by clinical experts.

Accelerating the design of biological sequences can significantly advance medical progress. This challenge is formulated as a global optimization task involving an expensive black-box function, constrained by limited query rounds and batch sizes. While Bayesian Optimization offers a principled approach, the vast state space of biological sequences makes exhaustive search impossible. To address this, we introduce MetaRLBO, which employs Meta-Reinforcement Learning to train an autoregressive generative model that proposes candidate sequences for Bayesian Optimization. We frame this as learning an optimal policy across a distribution of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) derived from data subsets sampled in prior rounds. Our in-silico experiments demonstrate that meta-learning over these ensembles ensures robustness against reward misspecification and yields competitive performance against leading baselines.

The text outlines the development of elementary particle properties and interactions, starting from the Planck scale of $10^{19}$ GeV. This framework relies on the hypothesis that the high-temperature (high-energy) limit of the Standard Model arises through gauge group contraction. As the temperature approaches infinity, particle characteristics undergo a fundamental shift: all particles become massless, leaving only neutral $Z$ bosons, $u$ quarks, neutrinos, and photons. In this state, weak interactions transform into long-range forces mediated by neutral currents, and quarks retain a single color degree of freedom.

Despite recent progress in applying deep learning to chest x-ray analysis, we highlight three key hurdles in translating these algorithms to clinical practice. We evaluated the top 10 models from the CheXpert leaderboard across three specific tasks: tuberculosis detection, pathology identification on chest x-ray images, and pathology detection using data from an external institution. Our findings reveal that the top 10 models achieved an average AUC of 0.851 for TB detection on two public datasets without fine-tuning or TB labels in their training. Additionally, model performance on photographs of x-rays (AUC = 0.916) was comparable to their results on original x-ray images (AUC = 0.924). Finally, when tested on an external dataset, the models performed as well as or better than the average radiologist. We believe this study will facilitate the rapid development of safe and effective clinical decision support tools, enabling prospective validation through large-scale impact studies and clinical trials.

This review examines the mathematical and algorithmic underpinnings of non-reversible Markov chains within the framework of event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC), a continuous-time lifted Markov chain utilizing the factorized Metropolis algorithm. After analyzing various model applications, it assesses the formulation and performance of ECMC across key statistical physics models. The review concludes by detailing an ongoing effort to apply this method to the sampling challenges of molecular simulation, specifically targeting real-world systems involving peptides, proteins, and polymers in aqueous environments.

We investigate the nonclassical characteristics and thermal decoherence of photon-added squeezed vacuum (PASV) states, focusing on sub-Poissonian statistics and the negativity of the Wigner function (WF). By transforming the PASV into a squeezed Hermite polynomial excitation state, we obtain a concise formula for the normalization factor of m-PASV, which corresponds to an m-order Legendre polynomial of the squeezing parameter r. Additionally, we derive the explicit WF for m-PASV and identify its negative regions within phase space. Our analysis reveals an upper limit for r that allows for sub-Poissonian statistics, a bound that increases with m. Furthermore, we provide an explicit analytical expression for the time evolution of the m-PASV WF in a thermal environment and examine the degradation of nonclassicality based on WF negativity, specifically presenting the threshold decay time for single PASV states.

Establishing reliable machine learning and its applications requires significant research into adversarial attack and defense techniques. While many current approaches utilize Gaussian random variables to traverse the data space in search of the most adversarial points (for attacks) or the least adversarial points (for defense), the Gaussian distribution is not always the optimal choice when the exploration must adhere to the complex structures inherent in real-world data distributions. This paper examines how the statistics of random variables influence such random walk explorations. Specifically, we extend the Boundary Attack, a leading black-box decision-based strategy, by introducing the Lévy-Attack, which employs symmetric $\alpha$-stable random variables to drive the random walk. Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets demonstrate that the Lévy-Attack explores the image data space more efficiently and substantially enhances performance. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into recent discoveries in white-box attacking scenarios, highlighting that the selection of the norm used to measure the amplitude of adversarial patterns is crucial.

The relationship between matrix-valued Stieltjes functions and matrix-valued complete Bernstein functions is utilized to demonstrate that solutions to matricial convolution equations featuring extended LICM kernels fall within specific functional categories. Specifically, the paper examines solutions to the matricial Sonine equation and the viscoelastic duality relation, highlighting applications in anisotropic linear viscoelasticity and a broadened framework for fractional calculus. In the context of duality, it is established that for completely monotone relaxation functions and Bernstein creep functions to be dual, the relaxation function must incorporate a Newtonian viscosity term alongside the memory effects characterized by the completely monotone kernel. Furthermore, anisotropic generalized fractional derivatives (GFD) are introduced by substituting the Caputo derivative's kernel, $t^{-\alpha}/\Gamma(1-\alpha)$, with completely monotone matrix-valued kernels that exhibit weak singularity at zero.

The persistent gap between experimental measurements and theoretical predictions for the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, defined as $a_\mu = (g-2)/2$, stands as a compelling potential indicator of new physics within the field. Following a brief overview, this work details the current state of theoretical predictions for g-2, emphasizing the sources that contribute most significantly to uncertainties. It subsequently examines the comparison between these predictions and the latest experimental results.

Entanglement experiments are rarely analyzed using path integrals primarily due to the lack of a standard toolkit for translating arbitrary experimental setups into forms suitable for sum-over-history calculations. Once this missing component—a method for executing multi-particle measurements within an entangled basis—was finalized, researchers applied this alternative approach to examine several intriguing 4- and 6-particle experiments. Although the resulting joint probabilities align perfectly with conventional quantum mechanics, the distinct calculation methods yield valuable foundational insights regarding nonlocality, retrocausality, and the objective nature of entanglement.

Mean profiles serve as common indicators of customer electricity consumption patterns. At 'Electricit\'e De France (EDF), load profiles are currently estimated using point-wise mean functions; however, the mean is notoriously sensitive to outliers, such as consumers with abnormally high usage. This paper introduces a more robust alternative: the $L_1$-median profile. Given the challenges of handling large functional datasets (e.g., load curves), survey sampling methods offer an efficient way to estimate the median profile without retaining the entire dataset. We propose estimators for the median trajectory employing various sampling strategies and compare them using a test population. Furthermore, we demonstrate that stratification based on a linearized variable significantly enhances estimator accuracy compared to simple random sampling without replacement. Additionally, we suggest an improved estimator that incorporates auxiliary information and outline potential directions for future research.

How can we effectively identify and concisely summarize the concepts learned by a neural network? This capability is crucial for classification-based inference applications, such as medical diagnosis using fMRI or x-ray data. Our work introduces a framework that categorizes learned concepts by clustering input examples, grouping neurons based on their activation patterns, and mapping input features within a shared latent space. This unsupervised approach requires no labeled input features, relying solely on access to the network's internal activations for each example, which ensures broad applicability. Through extensive evaluation, we demonstrate that the method generates coherent, human-interpretable concepts regarding what a ResNet-18 has learned on the CIFAR-100 dataset.

Our Brownian dynamics simulations demonstrate that the Kirkwood-Riseman model accurately describes the motion of an isolated polymer coil in a shear field, whereas the Rouse model is qualitatively flawed. These two models yield fundamentally different predictions: while Kirkwood and Riseman predict that polymer coils undergo whole-body rotation in a shear field, the Rouse model fails to account for such rotation. Our results confirm that in shear flow, polymer coils do rotate, Rouse modes exhibit cross-correlations, and both the amplitudes and relaxation rates of these modes vary with the shear rate. Since the Rouse calculation was originally derived for a polymer coil in a quiescent fluid without viscous dissipation, its application to a coil subjected to shear flow is invalid.

Critical data for electricity access planning, specifically details on the locations and connectivity of transmission and distribution towers (the power grid), is frequently incomplete, obsolete, or entirely missing. Moreover, traditional methods for gathering this information are both expensive and restricted. To address this, we propose automatically mapping the grid using deep learning applied to overhead remote sensing imagery. In support of this objective, we have created and made publicly available a substantial dataset ($263km^2$) of overhead imagery with corresponding ground truth for the power grid; to our knowledge, this is the inaugural public dataset of its kind. Additionally, we introduce scoring metrics and baseline algorithms for two specific grid mapping tasks: (1) tower recognition and (2) power line interconnection (which involves estimating a graph representation of the grid). We anticipate that the release of this training data, evaluation metrics, and baselines will accelerate progress on this vital issue, enabling decision-makers to better meet the energy requirements of societies globally.

**Objective:** Causality mining represents a vibrant field of research that demands the deployment of advanced natural language processing methods. Within healthcare, medical professionals generate clinical narratives to address the constraints of rigid, schema-driven information systems. This study aims to develop a framework capable of transforming clinical text into structured causal knowledge.

**Methods:** We employed a practical methodology involving term expansion, phrase generation, BERT-based phrase embedding, semantic matching, enrichment, expert verification, and model evolution to build a comprehensive causality mining system. This active transfer learning framework, supported by auxiliary services, effectively extracts and enriches causal relationships and their associated entities from clinical records.

**Results:** Applying the multi-model transfer learning technique across multiple iterations yielded significant improvements in accuracy and recall while maintaining constant precision. A comparative analysis against common alternatives confirms the validity of our approach and demonstrates its superior ability to capture the majority of causal relationships.

**Conclusion:** The proposed framework delivers state-of-the-art results for the healthcare sector. Nevertheless, it can be adapted to perform causality detection in other domains as well.

**Significance:** The framework is sufficiently generic for application across various fields. Healthcare services, characterized by vast and diverse data volumes, can derive substantial benefits from it. This causal knowledge extraction tool can be utilized to summarize clinical text, generate personas, uncover medical insights, and support evidence-based clinical decision-making.

Analyses at both the ATLAS and CMS experiments prioritize the search for Top and Bottom Partners. These vector-like quarks, which are third-generation Standard Model partners, are attractive candidates for detection when singly produced due to their substantial cross-sections across various topologies. Although previous research has predominantly focused on the resonant single-production mode, recent investigations have uncovered a complex phenomenology driven by non-resonant diagrams, particularly at narrow widths. This letter systematically examines how these non-resonant diagrams affect diverse single-production topologies for Top and Bottom partners and their influence on inclusive cross-section estimates. Furthermore, we introduce a parameterization to compute the correction factor for single vector-like quark production cross-sections when accounting for these diagrams.

The fractional matching number of a graph $G$ is defined as the maximum size of a fractional matching within $G$. This paper establishes sharp lower bounds for a graph $G$ with order $n$ and characterizes all corresponding extremal graphs. Specifically: (1) For $n \geq 2$, the sum of the fractional matching number of $G$ and that of its complement is at least $n/2$. (2) When both $G$ and its complement are non-empty and $n \geq 28$, this sum is at least $(n+1)/2$. (3) If neither $G$ nor its complement contains isolated vertices and $n \geq 28$, the sum is at least $(n+4)/2$.

High-purity glass is valued for its minimal optical and mechanical losses, making it ideal for optical system components like inertial sensor oscillators. However, creating complex geometries often necessitates assembling multiple glass pieces via permanent bonding. A prevalent technique, hydroxide catalysis bonding, introduces an enclosed interlayer with distinct mechanical properties from the surrounding bulk glass. This layer's elevated mechanical loss increases susceptibility to displacement noise caused by energy conversion between oscillation and heat. Consequently, alternative bonding methods are required for glass assemblies. To address this, we conducted experiments measuring the mechanical losses of various bonding techniques common in fused silica production, including adhesive bonding, laser welding, hydroxide catalysis bonding, and plasma activated direct bonding. This paper outlines the experimental setup and presents preliminary results from the first test sample.

This study reports findings from deep Chandra observations of the young Type Ia supernova remnant (SNR) 0509-68.7, also identified as N103B, situated within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The remnant exhibits a brightness asymmetry, where the western hemisphere is markedly brighter than the eastern side. While earlier multi-wavelength data linked this disparity to a density gradient and proposed circumstellar material origins—drawing parallels to Kepler's SNR—this work employs a clustering technique alongside conventional imaging to pinpoint specific emission components. Our analysis reveals that oxygen and magnesium emission peaks along the blast wave, aligning with Spitzer dust data and optical signatures from non-radiative shocks. Furthermore, oxygen and magnesium abundances in these zones exceed average LMC levels and display a spatial pattern distinct from ejecta products, thereby reinforcing the circumstellar medium hypothesis. Additionally, chromium distribution matches that of iron within the remnant's interior but shows no correlation with the oxygen and magnesium emission.

The Petrov classification serves as a key algebraic categorization for the Weyl tensor within 4-dimensional space-times. This thesis extends that classification to manifolds of arbitrary dimension and signature by treating the Weyl tensor as a linear operator acting on the bundle of p-forms for any p, then determining its Jordan canonical form. The study assumes complexified spaces, where varying signatures represent distinct reality conditions, thereby offering a unified approach. Additionally, a higher-dimensional extension of self-dual manifolds is explored.

The Goldberg-Sachs theorem represents the most significant outcome associated with the Petrov classification. This work presents two partial generalizations of this theorem applicable to even-dimensional manifolds. The first generalization asserts that specific algebraic constraints on the Weyl operator necessitate an integrable maximally isotropic distribution. The second version posits that these same constraints lead to the existence of a null congruence whose optical scalars satisfy particular restrictions.

To achieve these findings, a spinorial formalism for 6 dimensions was developed from the outset using group representation theory. Given the profound geometric significance of spinors and their efficacy in handling isotropic structures, it is natural that they offer a powerful framework for the issues addressed in this thesis. Notably, the generalizations of the Goldberg-Sachs theorem take on an elegant form when expressed through pure spinors.

The formation and structural organization of planetary systems are heavily influenced by the physical mechanisms that drive the evolution and dispersal of protoplanetary disks. Since the publication of *Protostars and Planets VI*, both new observational data and theoretical developments have increasingly supported disk winds as a primary driver of this process. This chapter offers a thorough review of recent observations investigating outflowing gas across various disk radii and evolutionary phases, thereby fostering an empirical grasp of wind evolution. Simultaneously, we examine recent theoretical progress in magnetohydrodynamic and photoevaporative disk wind models, pinpointing predictions suitable for observational testing. By connecting theory with data, we critically evaluate the significance of disk winds in the lifecycle and dispersal of protoplanetary disks. Furthermore, we investigate how these winds affect planet formation and development, while emphasizing key theoretical studies, observational efforts, and critical tests needed for future advancements.

Let $G$ be a fixed graph with a list-assignment $L$, and let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be two valid $L$-colorings of $G$. An $L$-recoloring sequence begins with $\alpha$ and transforms it into $\beta$ by sequentially recoloring one vertex at a time, ensuring every intermediate coloring remains proper with respect to $L$. We establish that such a sequence exists where each vertex is recolored at most a constant number of times under three specific conditions: (i) $G$ is planar and triangle-free with a 7-list assignment, (ii) the maximum average degree of $G$ is less than $17/5$ with a 6-list assignment, or (iii) the maximum average degree of $G$ is less than $22/9$ with a 4-list assignment. These results for cases (i) and (ii) validate conjectures proposed by Dvo\v{r}\'{a}k and Feghali.

Current vision benchmarks primarily focus on tasks where humans can perform nearly flawlessly. However, humans often encounter visual information they cannot classify with absolute certainty, and standard models trained on these benchmarks struggle significantly when tested on such data. To resolve this, we present a method for generating datasets of ambiguous images, resulting in SQUID-E ("Squidy"), a collection of noisy frames extracted from videos. Every image in this dataset includes ground truth labels, while the test set is additionally annotated with human uncertainty assessments. We utilize this resource to analyze human uncertainty in visual tasks and to benchmark existing visual event classification models. Our experimental findings indicate that current vision models are ill-equipped to generate meaningful outputs for ambiguous inputs and that such datasets are valuable for evaluating and enhancing model calibration through direct assessment and retraining. These results underscore the need for large-scale creation of ambiguous datasets and further research dedicated to noisy visual data.

**Context.** Radiation-driven mass loss is essential for understanding the evolution of massive stars. However, low-luminosity O-type stars present a significant discrepancy between empirically measured and theoretically predicted mass-loss rates, a phenomenon known as the "weak-wind problem." **Aims.** Our objective is to model radiation-line-driven winds for a typical weak-wind star to analyze its temperature structure and its influence on ultraviolet (UV) line formation. **Methods.** We performed hydrodynamic simulations of the line-deshadowing instability (LDI) for a Galactic weak-wind star. These LDI models were then used as input for a short-characteristics radiative transfer code to generate synthetic UV line profiles. **Results.** We discovered that line-driven weak winds undergo significant shock heating, reaching high temperatures and failing to cool efficiently. This creates a complex thermal structure where over half the wind volume exists at temperatures far exceeding the star's effective temperature. Consequently, a large portion of the wind becomes more ionized, reducing UV line opacity and leading to weaker line profiles for a specific mass-loss rate. Quantitatively, we find that if high-temperature gas is ignored in spectroscopic analysis, mass-loss rates derived from unsaturated UV lines could be underestimated by a factor of 10 to 100. This provides a preliminary explanation for the weak-wind problem: line-driven weak winds are not inherently weaker than theory predicts; rather, a substantial fraction of their volume is significantly hotter than the stellar effective temperature.

We propose a model explaining the origins of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter. In this framework, dark energy and dark matter correspond to residual pre-inflation false vacuum zero-point energy ($w=-1$), characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressure, respectively. These represent the incoherent "zero point" component of a superfluid (or supersolid) ground state. Conversely, gravity emerges from second-order topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate," which constitutes the coherent component. Consequently, we predict that the LHC will fail to detect exotic real on-mass-shell particles capable of explaining dark matter. Furthermore, we argue that the future holographic dark energy de Sitter horizon acts as a total absorber, defined by retro-causal Wheeler-Feynman action-at-a-distance electrodynamics, because it serves as an infinite redshift surface for static detectors. Thus, the advanced Hawking-Unruh thermal radiation emanating from this future de Sitter horizon serves as a candidate for the negative pressure dark vacuum energy.

Although chiral quantum field theories (QFTs) encompass a broad spectrum of physical phenomena, ranging from the Standard Model to topological quantum matter, implementing them on a lattice has historically been hindered by the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem and potential quantum anomalies. This thesis addresses these challenges by leveraging the relationship between chiral matter phases and chiral QFTs to construct lattice-based definitions, thereby enabling the numerical simulation of a vast array of exotic field theories. Building upon the 'mirror fermion' methodology—which characterizes chiral theories as the edge modes of chiral phases—the work begins by examining the profound interplay among chiral phases, field theories, and anomalies. Subsequently, it establishes numerical frameworks for $SU(2)$ chiral field theories and offers a semiclassically solvable formulation for Abelian $2+1$ chiral topological orders. This progression yields an exactly solvable definition of chiral $U(1)$ SPT phases with zero correlation length, facilitating the precise extraction of their associated edge chiral field theories. Notably, these zero-correlation length models represent a significant simplification compared to earlier approaches for defining chiral field theories on the lattice.

Constraining the physical properties of dust in planet-forming disks through high-resolution observations is essential for understanding solid trapping within substructures and the conditions favoring accelerated dust growth. Utilizing ALMA dust continuum data from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales (MAPS) survey, we explore a broad parameter space to determine the radial distribution of solid mass and maximum grain size for each disk, analyzing both scenarios with and without dust scattering. In models excluding scattering, dust surface density and maximum grain size profiles decline from the inner to outer disks, exhibiting local peaks at bright ring locations consistent with dust trapping theories; inferred maximum grain sizes decrease from approximately 1 cm in inner disks to 1 mm in outer disks. For IM Lup, HD 163296, and MWC 480 under scattering models, two viable solutions exist for their inner disk emission: one implying maximum grain sizes of a few millimeters (comparable to the nonscattering case) and another suggesting sizes of a few hundred micrometers. Based on Toomre parameter estimates, only IM Lup, which displays a distinct spiral morphology in millimeter dust, is deemed gravitationally unstable. The estimated maximum Stokes numbers across all disks range from 0.01 to 0.3, while turbulence parameters in the rings of AS 209 and HD 163296 lie near the threshold where turbulent fragmentation limits dust growth. This work is included in the MAPS special issue of the Astrophysical Journal Supplement.

This paper addresses a multiobjective bilevel optimization problem characterized by vector-valued objectives at both the upper and lower levels, an area that has gained significant attention recently. While scalarization has traditionally been the primary method for handling the lower-level component, this study introduces the frontier map concept, which generalizes the optimal value function to parametric multiobjective lower-level problems. Leveraging this concept, we establish a tractable constraint qualification to derive necessary optimality conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these conditions constitute a natural generalization of the necessary optimality conditions found in standard optimistic bilevel programs with scalar objectives.

This paper introduces novel model-based techniques for generating channel charts. Using our proposed algorithms—the inverse of the root sum squares of channel coefficients (ISQ), linear regression (LR), and the MUSIC/MUSIC (MM) algorithm—we estimate the angle of arrival ($\theta$) and the distance between the base station and user equipment ($\rho$). These methods are benchmarked against training-based approaches, specifically principal component analysis (PCA), Samson's method (SM), and autoencoders (AE). Results indicate that ISQ, LR, and MM surpass all three training-based methods in performance. Among them, MM delivers superior accuracy compared to LR and ISQ but incurs higher complexity. ISQ and LR exhibit comparable performance, with ISQ offering lower complexity than LR. Additionally, we evaluate our MM algorithm against a literature-based method, the JM algorithm, which applies MUSIC jointly to both $\theta$ and $\rho$. While JM achieves marginally better performance than MM, it requires significantly greater complexity. Finally, we propose the rotate-and-sum (RS) algorithm, which matches the performance of both MM and JM while reducing complexity by eliminating eigenvector and eigenvalue analysis, facilitating a more efficient register transfer logic (RTL) implementation.
This article presents an algorithm designed for the automated creation and classification of theorems in triangle geometry.

Polysynthetic languages with rich morphology pose significant challenges for NLP systems, primarily due to data sparsity, making subword segmentation a common solution to address this problem. This study examines a broad range of supervised and unsupervised morphological segmentation techniques across four polysynthetic languages: Nahuatl, Raramuri, Shipibo-Konibo, and Wixarika. We then evaluate how morphologically inspired segmentation methods compare to Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) when serving as inputs for machine translation (MT) tasks involving Spanish, both as a source and target language. Our findings indicate that, with the exception of Nahuatl, unsupervised morphological segmentation algorithms consistently outperform BPEs. Furthermore, although supervised methods yield superior segmentation scores, they result in inferior performance on MT tasks. Additionally, we introduce two new morphological segmentation datasets for Raramuri and Shipibo-Konibo, along with a parallel corpus for Raramuri–Spanish.

Precise and robust quantum control is fundamental to the advancement of emerging quantum technologies. We reveal a critical correspondence between driven noisy quantum evolution and multiplex space curves, whose characteristics offer an explicit geometric description of the dynamics. Building on this insight, we formulate a theory to address generic quantum errors and establish its necessary and sufficient conditions. This analytic-numerical hybrid protocol facilitates the creation of universal, robust quantum gates using simple pulses for any specified duration. Numerical simulations confirm that gate fidelity remains above the fault-tolerance threshold across a wide range of noise strengths, utilizing realistic models of semiconductor spin qubits and superconducting transmons. Consequently, our theoretical framework is poised to accelerate progress in quantum information processing across diverse physical platforms.

This study rigorously addresses the diffraction of an electromagnetic plane wave by a perfectly conducting circular disk and its complementary scenario involving a circular aperture in an infinite conducting sheet using the Kobayashi potential method. The mathematical framework relies on a dual integral equation derived from the potential integral and the boundary conditions at the disk or hole's location. By leveraging the properties of Weber-Schafheitlin's discontinuous integral, the weighting function within the potential integral is established, yielding solutions in the form of a matrix equation. The matrix elements governing the expansion coefficients are defined by three distinct infinite integrals, for which series solutions are derived. To validate these series, numerical integrals are computed using Gaussian quadrature for confirmation. The resulting numerical data for the far-field diffraction pattern of the conducting disk are compared with those from the physical optics (PO) method, demonstrating a satisfactory degree of agreement.

We have developed, validated, and implemented massively parallel, distributed-memory algorithms for the Lagrangian particle hydrodynamic method, as detailed in Samulyak et al. (2018). Central to these parallel algorithms is a particle management module responsible for constructing octree databases in parallel, dynamically adapting and refining octrees, and migrating particles across subdomains; this module relies on the p4est (parallel forest of k-trees) library. Furthermore, the code has been utilized to solve diverse problems in fundamental science and applied research. This work includes a summary of applications ranging from impurity injection into thermonuclear fusion devices to simulating supersonic hydrogen jets for laser-plasma wakefield acceleration projects.

We introduce a novel splitting technique designed for the robust numerical resolution of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model. Applied across both deterministic and adaptive random meshes, we establish a uniform moment bound and demonstrate strong error convergence of order $1/4$ in both $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms, specifically within the parameter regime $\kappa\theta>\sigma^2$. Unlike the schemes examined by Hefter & Herzwurm (2018), which achieve a maximum convergence order of $1/4$ for a new class of Milstein-based methods across all parameter values, our approach requires a distinct convergence analysis. We subsequently extend this method to encompass the entire parameter range by incorporating a 'soft zero' region, where the deterministic flow governs the approximation, thereby creating a hybrid scheme to address the reflecting boundary. Numerical simulations indicate a convergence rate of order $1$ when $\kappa\theta>\sigma^2$, surpassing the theoretical $1/4$ bound. Asymptotically, under conditions of large noise, while convergence rates decline similarly to other methods, our proposed scheme exhibits notably smaller error constants. Furthermore, these findings provide numerical validation supporting the conjecture of Hefter & Jentzen (2019) regarding methods utilizing non-uniform Wiener increments.

Current state-of-the-art optical flow estimation techniques depend on deep learning, necessitating intricate sequential training protocols to achieve peak performance on real-world datasets. This study presents the COMBO deep network, which directly incorporates the brightness constancy (BC) model traditionally employed in non-deep methods. Acknowledging that BC is an imperfect physical model often violated in practice, we propose a hybrid architecture combining a physically-constrained network with a data-driven counterpart. We introduce a distinct and interpretable flow decomposition separating the physical prior from the data-driven complement, complete with uncertainty quantification for the BC model. Furthermore, we establish a unified training framework for learning the decomposed components, ensuring optimal synergy across both supervised and semi-supervised settings. Experimental results demonstrate that COMBO surpasses leading supervised networks, such as RAFT, achieving state-of-the-art outcomes on multiple benchmarks. We illustrate how COMBO effectively utilizes the BC model while adapting to its constraints. Additionally, our semi-supervised approach significantly streamlines the training process.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems translating English to SPARQL represent a significant advancement in query generation; however, existing models fail to incorporate knowledge base (KB) schemas and struggle with queries involving unseen resources, classes, or properties, limiting their utility beyond the training domain. Drawing inspiration from recent improvements in natural language processing, we suggest implementing a copy mechanism for neural SPARQL generation to address this limitation. Our approach involves integrating a copy layer and a dynamic KB vocabulary into two sequence-to-sequence architectures (CNNs and Transformers), enabling models to directly copy KB elements from input questions rather than generating them from scratch. We assess this method using state-of-the-art datasets that include unknown KB elements, measuring the accuracy of these copy-augmented systems. Our findings demonstrate a substantial performance improvement across all datasets compared to traditional non-copy architectures.

The newly introduced symbol-level precoding (SLP) technique offers a promising solution for multi-user wireless communication systems by transforming detrimental multi-user interference (MUI) into constructive signals, thereby boosting overall system performance. However, the immense computational complexity associated with traditional SLP designs significantly impedes their practical deployment. To address this challenge, we propose a novel deep learning (DL)-based method for the efficient design of symbol-level precoders. Specifically, this correspondence focuses on a multi-user multi-input single-output (MU-MISO) downlink scenario. We introduce an Efficient Precoding Neural Network (EPNN) to optimize symbol-level precoders, aiming to maximize the minimum quality-of-service (QoS) for all users while adhering to power constraints. Simulation results indicate that the proposed EPNN-based SLP design drastically reduces computation time, albeit with a minor sacrifice in performance, when compared to conventional convex optimization-based SLP approaches.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) utilizes a combination of labeled and unlabeled data to train machine learning (ML) models. Current state-of-the-art SSL techniques can match the performance of supervised learning while requiring significantly fewer labeled examples. However, most existing research prioritizes enhancing SSL performance rather than addressing training data privacy. This study shifts focus to investigate the privacy risks inherent in SSL, specifically by introducing the first membership inference attacks based on data augmentation against models trained via SSL. The objective of such an attack, given a data sample and black-box model access, is to ascertain whether the sample was part of the model's training set. Our evaluation demonstrates that this proposed attack consistently surpasses existing membership inference methods and yields superior results against SSL-trained models. Furthermore, we reveal that the mechanism behind membership leakage in SSL differs from the conventional understanding in supervised learning, which attributes leakage to overfitting (the disparity between training and testing accuracy). Instead, we find that SSL models generalize well to test data with negligible overfitting but "memorize" training samples by issuing highly confident predictions, regardless of their accuracy. Finally, we examine early stopping as a potential defense strategy. Results indicate that while early stopping can reduce the effectiveness of membership inference attacks, it does so at the expense of the model's utility.

We examine the derivatives of the iterated Minkowski question mark function, denoted as $f_n(x) = \underbrace{?(?(...?}_\text{n times}(x))$. While finding explicit irrational numbers $x$ where $f'_n(x)=0$ is non-trivial outside of obvious rational cases, this paper introduces a specific set of irrational numbers. For any element $x_0$ in this set and every positive integer $n$, it holds that $f'_n(x_0)=0$.

The textile and apparel sectors have expanded significantly in recent years, eliminating the need for customers to visit multiple physical stores, endure long lines, or try on clothes in fitting rooms, as millions of items are now accessible through online catalogs. Nevertheless, with such an overwhelming array of choices, robust recommendation systems are essential to effectively organize, sequence, and convey pertinent product details to users. Efficient fashion recommendation systems can substantially enhance the shopping experience for billions of consumers while boosting sales and revenue for providers.

This survey aims to review recommender systems specifically tailored to the garment and fashion domain. We have pinpointed the most critical challenges in fashion recommendation research and developed a taxonomy that classifies existing literature based on its objectives (such as item or outfit recommendation, size prediction, and explainability) and the types of side-information utilized (including user, item, and context data). Furthermore, we have identified key evaluation goals and perspectives—such as outfit generation, pairing recommendations, and fill-in-the-blank compatibility prediction—along with the most frequently employed datasets and assessment metrics.

Bowden, Hensel, and Webb recently introduced the fine curve graph for surfaces, broadening the concept of curve graphs to investigate the homeomorphism and diffeomorphism groups of surfaces. Subsequently, Long, Margalit, Pham, Verberne, and Yao demonstrated that for any closed surface with genus $g \geqslant 2$, the automorphism group of this fine graph is naturally isomorphic to the surface's homeomorphism group. We generalize this finding to include the torus case where $g=1$; notably, our approach applies to a broader class of surfaces, whether compact or non-compact, and orientable or non-orientable. Additionally, we examine the scenario involving a smooth variant of the fine graph.

This paper introduces a new framework called Statistical Compressed Sensing (SCS), designed to efficiently sample signals adhering to statistical distributions and achieve accurate average reconstruction. The study focuses deeply on SCS utilizing Gaussian models. For signals conforming to a single Gaussian model, the framework requires only O(k) measurements using Gaussian or Bernoulli sensing matrices—a substantial reduction from the O(k log(N/k)) needed by conventional Compressed Sensing (CS) based on sparse models, where N represents the signal dimension. When paired with an optimal decoder implemented through linear filtering, which is significantly faster than the pursuit decoders used in standard CS, the SCS error is tightly upper-bounded by a constant multiple of the best k-term approximation error with overwhelming probability. Furthermore, the failure probability is markedly lower than that of traditional sparsity-oriented CS. Additional robust yet simpler results demonstrate that for any sensing matrix, the error of Gaussian SCS is upper-bounded by a constant times the best k-term approximation with probability one, and this bound constant can be efficiently computed. Regarding Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), which assume multiple Gaussian distributions with unknown signal indices, a piecewise linear estimator is proposed for decoding SCS. The accuracy of model selection, central to this decoder, is analyzed based on Gaussian distribution properties and the number of measurements. Additionally, a maximum a posteriori expectation-maximization algorithm is presented to iteratively estimate GMM parameters, select signal models, and decode signals within GMM-based SCS. In practical image sensing applications, GMM-based SCS demonstrates improved results compared to conventional CS at a significantly reduced computational cost.

As the definition of the Metaverse evolves, its ability to trigger a new era of digital disruption and generate tangible real-world value becomes evident. Characterized by immersive experiences, simultaneous interactivity, and user agency, the Metaverse holds the power to revolutionize every aspect of life. However, the technologies that enable it—specifically digital twins, artificial intelligence, blockchain, and extended reality—are notoriously energy-intensive, sparking concerns regarding the sustainability of its widespread adoption. To address this, this article introduces the concept of Green Metaverse Networking for the first time, aiming to optimize energy efficiency across all network components to ensure sustainable development. We begin by examining the energy consumption, efficiency, and sustainability profiles of these energy-heavy technologies. Subsequently, we focus on computation and networking to highlight key advancements in energy efficiency and their integration within the Metaverse. A case study demonstrates energy conservation strategies through the use of semantic communication and stochastic resource allocation. Finally, we outline the critical challenges facing sustainable Metaverse development and suggest potential directions for future research toward a green Metaverse.

This paper examines the action of a countable group $\Gamma$ on the space of group orders, focusing specifically on invariant probability measures known as invariant random orders. We demonstrate that for any countable group, the space of such random invariant orders is sufficiently rich to encompass an isomorphic copy of any free ergodic action, and we identify the conditions under which non-free actions are realizable. Furthermore, we establish a Glasner-Weiss dichotomy concerning the simplex of invariant random orders. Additionally, we show that the invariant partial order on $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbf{Z})$ associated with the semigroup of positive matrices cannot be extended to an invariant random total order. Consequently, we present the first example of a partial order—whether deterministic or random—that resists random extension.

Time series classification stands as a prominent machine learning task. This study investigates the utilization of Hidden Markov Models (HMM) for this purpose, distinguishing between two application modes: constructing a single model per class versus building one model per time series. These strategies are subsequently adapted to the domain of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCM), resulting in four specific models: HMM NN (one per series), HMM 1C (one per class), FCM NN, and FCM 1C. Through a series of experiments, we evaluate the performance of these models and analyze how hyperparameters influence classification accuracy. Empirical results indicate a distinct advantage for the one-model-per-series approach, while demonstrating that the optimal choice between HMM and FCM depends on the specific dataset.

We introduce a new cutting plane algorithm designed to handle a separation oracle for a convex set $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that fits within a box of radius $R$. The objective is to either identify a point within $K$ or demonstrate that $K$ lacks a ball of radius $\epsilon$. Our approach requires $O(n \log (\kappa))$ oracle evaluations, where $\kappa = nR/\epsilon$, and incurs an additional $O(n^2)$ computational time per evaluation.

This method offers two key improvements over existing literature:
1.  It surpasses Vaidya's algorithm [Vaidya, FOCS 1989a], which has a time complexity of $O(\text{SO} \cdot n \log (\kappa) + n^{\omega+1} \log (\kappa))$, by reducing the polynomial dependence on the dimension $n$, where $\omega < 2.373$ represents the matrix multiplication exponent and $\text{SO}$ denotes the cost of a single oracle call.
2.  It outperforms the Lee-Sidford-Wong algorithm [Lee, Sidford and Wong, FOCS 2015], with a complexity of $O(\text{SO} \cdot n \log (\kappa) + n^3 \log^{O(1)} (\kappa))$, specifically by improving the dependence on $\kappa$.

In numerous critical economic applications, $\kappa$ scales as $\Omega(\exp(n))$, making the distinction between $\log(\kappa)$ and polynomial terms of $\log(\kappa)$ substantial. Furthermore, we present evidence that the $O(n^2)$ time requirement per evaluation is likely optimal, suggesting our total running time cannot be further improved.

A primary limitation in previous cutting plane techniques was the need to compute leverage scores, which quantify the relative significance of historical constraints. Our advancement relies on a novel multi-layered data structure for maintaining these scores. This structure synthesizes various advanced methods, including random projection, batched low-rank updates, inverse maintenance, polynomial interpolation, and fast rectangular matrix multiplication. Notably, our approach necessitates the integration of distinct fast rectangular matrix multiplication algorithms.

Hackathons and comparable time-constrained gatherings have emerged as a favored mode of collaboration, typically characterized by intense, short-term teamwork in physical spaces to develop projects of mutual interest. While existing research predominantly highlights the benefits of radical co-location in face-to-face settings, the 2020 global pandemic shifted many of these events online, thereby challenging established understandings of their operational dynamics. This study bridges that gap through a multiple-case study of ten teams across four hackathons on two continents. Our analysis reveals that teams successfully sustained shared understanding and task awareness by blending synchronous and asynchronous communication methods. Task allocation occurred organically based on individual skills and interests, whereas team leadership arose from diverse factors such as prior experience or the responsibility of team registration. Although some advantages of in-person collaboration, specifically radical co-location, were partially replicated via "radical virtual co-location" through the use of shared synchronous audio channels, other benefits diminished. Specifically, interactions with other teams, access to mentors, and networking opportunities suffered in the virtual environment. Furthermore, participants faced significant technical difficulties and felt overwhelmed by the limitations of various communication platforms and tools. Ultimately, this work enhances the understanding of how small teams collaborate virtually in online hackathons and illustrates how organizer-imposed technologies and structures influence these collaborative efforts.

Numerous studies have focused on developing privacy-preserving automatic speaker verification systems to enable user authentication without compromising voice privacy. However, existing methods assume that speaker embeddings are extracted locally by the user, which introduces two critical challenges. First, exposing the embedding extraction model creates security and robustness vulnerabilities, as attackers could exploit this knowledge to generate adversarial examples that deceive the system. Second, for service providers, this model represents a core asset; its disclosure is highly undesirable. This work demonstrates how Secure Multiparty Computation can be used to extract speaker embeddings while maintaining the privacy of both the user's voice and the service provider's model. Furthermore, we show that reasonable trade-offs between security and computational cost are achievable. Complementing existing research on private authentication, this approach advances the goal of fully private automatic speaker recognition.

The Standard Model of particle physics currently fails to explain the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry or the origin of flavour structure. This article presents recent efforts to connect these two unresolved issues within the framework of electroweak baryogenesis. We demonstrate that Standard Model fermion Yukawa couplings can generate the necessary CP-violation for electroweak baryogenesis, provided they vary simultaneously as the Higgs field acquires its vacuum expectation value. This approach offers a promising new pathway that avoids the stringent constraints typically imposed by Electric Dipole moments. These concepts are applicable if the mechanism driving flavour structure is linked to electroweak symmetry breaking, as suggested by models such as Randall-Sundrum or Composite Higgs theories. Furthermore, we calculate the resulting baryon asymmetry for various configurations of Yukawa coupling variation across the bubble wall, showing that the values can naturally fall within the required range.

Researchers have created hundreds of techniques to evaluate interactions between pairs of processes within complex systems. However, these computational approaches—ranging from correlation coefficients to causal inference—depend on separate quantitative theories that have remained largely isolated. This work introduces a library comprising 249 statistics for pairwise interactions and evaluates their performance across 1,053 multivariate time series drawn from diverse real-world and model-generated systems. Our analysis reveals new shared patterns among different mathematical formulations, offering a unified perspective on a rich, interdisciplinary body of literature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining methods from various scientific disciplines allows for the identification of those best suited for specific problems, resulting in both high accuracy and interpretable insights. This framework is available as extensible open-source software, facilitating comprehensive data-driven analysis by integrating decades of methodological progress.

Inspired by BICEP2 findings suggesting gravitational waves arise during an expansion energy of approximately $Mc^2 \approx 10^{14}$ GeV, and by the Standard Model's natural extension involving right-handed neutrinos at a mass scale of $m_{\nu_R}c^2 \approx 10^{14}$ GeV, I propose a See-Saw Inflation model within the "Wiggly Whipped Inflation" framework \cite{Hazra:2014WWI}. In plausible physical scenarios, the remaining heavy right-handed neutrinos serve as Dark Matter. The scalar boson that stabilizes the heavy neutrino mass functions as the Inflaton, with its potential determined by self-coupling and the coupling to the heavy right-handed neutrino. Following this phase of See-Saw Inflation, the seesaw mechanism generates an offset in the Inflaton potential near the GUT scale after electroweak symmetry breaking; this offset, governed by the lightest neutrino mass, yields a "Dark Energy" scale corresponding to the lightest left-handed neutrino mass ($m_{\nu_L} \sim 10^{-3}$ eV). Since these neutrinos are Majorana particles that violate lepton number conservation, they naturally mediate baryogenesis at the electroweak scale. Although the residual heavy right-handed neutrinos act as Dark Matter requiring some fine-tuning, this model elegantly connects the four remaining fundamental cosmological issues to the neutrino sector. Furthermore, the revived SO(10) Grand Unified Theory offers a framework for this scenario, enabling specific predictions for the Inflaton potential and providing a method to fit both neutrino and cosmological data.

This paper addresses secure machine learning inference in scenarios involving a malicious client and a semi-trusted server, ensuring the client receives only the inference result while the server learns nothing. Initially formulated by Lehmkuhl et al. (MUSE, Usenix Security'21), this problem was later significantly optimized by Chandran et al. (SIMC, USENIX Security'22). Despite these advances, a substantial gap remains regarding practicality, specifically concerning the reduction of overhead and the acceleration of secure inference. We introduce SIMC 2.0, which adheres to the core structure of SIMC but delivers major optimizations for both linear and non-linear model layers. First, we developed a novel coding method for homomorphic parallel computation between matrices and vectors, leveraging the complementarity of cryptographic primitives within SIMC. This approach minimizes costly rotation operations relative to other homomorphic tasks like addition and multiplication. Second, we reduced the size of garbled circuits (GCs)—used for non-linear activation functions such as ReLU—by approximately two-thirds, replacing them with a lightweight alternative protocol. Experimental results demonstrate that SIMC 2.0 achieves up to a $17.4\times$ speedup in linear layer computations compared to SIMC. Furthermore, it reduces computation and communication overheads by at least $1.3\times$ for non-linear layers across various data dimensions. Finally, SIMC 2.0 shows an encouraging runtime improvement of $2.3\sim 4.3\times$ over SIMC when evaluated on different state-of-the-art machine learning models.

This research introduces a Bayesian Optimization framework designed for optimizing area- and distance-based time-of-day pricing (TODP) within urban networks. The complexity of road pricing optimization varies significantly based on the specific pricing scheme, detailed network characteristics, and heterogeneous demand attributes. Our model incorporates travelers with unique trip attributes and departure-time preferences alongside a Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) to represent the urban network. We formulate the problem mathematically and develop an agent-based simulation to serve as the evaluation function for TODP optimization. Consequently, the problem becomes highly nonlinear with an objective function that is computationally expensive. To address this, we propose and evaluate a Bayesian Optimization method that determines various TODP schemes by maximizing social welfare. Our approach efficiently learns the price-welfare relationship across few iterations, successfully identifying robust solutions even in high-dimensional decision spaces, thereby offering a pathway to reduce complexity in realistic road pricing scenarios. Additionally, simulation results confirm, as anticipated, that implementing TODP enhances social welfare compared to a no-pricing baseline.

Recent interest has focused on tabletop experiments designed to reveal the quantum nature of gravity by showing its ability to induce entanglement. We contend that these experiments also yield insights into the interpretation of quantum mechanics: assuming specific conditions, $\psi$-complete interpretations generally forecast a positive outcome, $\psi$-nonphysical interpretations predict a negative one, and $\psi$-supplemented models allow for either result. We propose that a positive experimental outcome would exclude a category of quantum gravity theories termed $\psi$-incomplete quantum gravity (PIQG)—models where gravity interacts with non-quantum beables instead of quantum ones. Following a review of current PIQG models, we examine necessary improvements to enhance their appeal and conclude by discussing a cosmological phenomenon that could serve as evidence supporting PIQG models.

Characterizing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided communications under phase noise conditions remains a critical unresolved challenge. This letter leverages copula modeling to address the non-standard dependencies arising from discrete phase noise. Specifically, we analyze the outage probability of RIS systems operating in Rayleigh fading environments and derive joint distributions that reflect the correlations caused by finite-resolution phase shifters. Numerical results validate the derived closed-form outage probability expressions and support the application of bivariate copulas for future RIS research.

We report the mass and density of a sub-Neptune with a radius of $2.043\pm0.069 ~\rm{R}_{\oplus}$ orbiting the quiet K-dwarf Wolf 503 (HIP 67285) using radial velocity data from four instruments. By analyzing previously unused short-cadence $K2$ campaign 17 photometry, we derived improved orbital and transit parameters and performed a joint radial velocity-transit fit to constrain the eccentricity at $0.41\pm0.05$. The inclusion of a new $Spitzer$ transit observation further refines the orbital ephemeris for future follow-up. Combining our mass determination of $6.26^{+0.69}_{-0.70}~\rm{M}_{\odot}$ with updated radius measurements yields a bulk density of $\rho = 2.92\pm ^{+0.50}_{-0.44}$ $\rm{g}~\rm{cm}^{-3}$ for Wolf 503 b. Interior composition models indicate this density aligns with an Earth-like core containing either a significant $\rm{H}_2\rm{O}$ mass fraction ($45^{+19.12}_{-16.15}\%$) or a modest H/He envelope ($0.5\pm0.28\%$). Given the low H/He mass fraction and the system's old age ($11\pm2$ Gyrs), Wolf 503 b serves as an ideal candidate for testing XUV-driven mass loss theories, while the host star's brightness ($J=8.3$ mag) makes it a promising target for transmission spectroscopy.

By deriving a sharp Strichartz estimate for velocity and density, we establish the local well-posedness of solutions to the Cauchy problem for the two-dimensional compressible Euler equations, given initial conditions for velocity, density, and specific vorticity $(\bv_0, \rho_0, \varpi_0)$ in the spaces $H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^2)\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^2) \times H^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ with $s>\frac{7}{4}$. Our approach builds upon the work of Smith and Tataru \cite{ST} regarding quasi-linear wave equations.

This work examines the THDMa, a variant of the type II two Higgs doublet model augmented by an extra pseudoscalar that acts as a gateway to the dark matter sector, which includes a fermionic dark matter candidate. I provide a recent comprehensive scan of the model's parameter space, allowing all parameters to vary freely, and analyze the prospects for detecting this model at future $e^+e^-$ colliders, specifically focusing on scenarios that lie beyond the scope of standard THDM searches.

Smart cities function as urban environments equipped with sensor networks that gather data to facilitate efficient management. Acting as a source of ubiquitous data, these initiatives offer potential for improving residents' awareness of their urban surroundings. Nevertheless, interpreting smart city data remains difficult, creating a divide between available data and practical applications for end-users. Sonification presents itself as a viable solution for both decoding smart city data and generating new musical experiences. This paper begins by outlining the smart city paradigm, proceeds to discuss ubiquitous and mobile music alongside an overview of sonification research, and concludes by proposing an approach known as ubiquitous sonification. Furthermore, it introduces an initial design for a speculative use case involving musical smart city systems that utilize both user and urban data to guide behavior.

We examine neutral triple gauge boson production within the large extra dimensions (LED) framework, specifically considering Kaluza-Klein (KK) excited gravitons at future linear colliders like the ILC and CLIC. Our analysis covers the $\gamma\gamma\gamma$, $\gamma\gamma Z$, $\gamma Z Z$, and $ZZZ$ production channels, evaluating their influence on total cross sections and critical kinematic distributions. These processes are vital for new physics investigations at linear colliders. Our findings indicate that KK graviton exchange exerts the strongest impact on the $\gamma Z Z$ process for relatively low $M_S$, whereas it dominates the $\gamma\gamma\gamma$ process at higher $M_S$ values. Utilizing neutral triple gauge boson production allows us to establish a discovery reach for the fundamental Planck scale $M_S$ of approximately 6–9 TeV (assuming $\delta = 4$) at a 3 TeV CLIC.

As of July 24, 2021, the COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in 4.1 million deaths. Researchers have utilized various machine learning models to analyze related data for predicting key metrics such as infection rates and disease severity, yet the practical value of these findings is often diminished by a lack of interpretability. Recent advancements in model interpretability offer the potential to extract deeper insights using standard machine learning approaches. This study analyzes COVID-19 blood work data using popular machine learning algorithms, followed by the application of state-of-the-art post-hoc interpretability techniques—specifically global methods like symbolic metamodeling and local methods such as SHAP and LIME—to generate understandable conclusions from black-box models. Among machine learning algorithms, regression stands out as one of the most straightforward and explainable models due to its clear mathematical basis. We investigate symbolic metamodeling, a recent technique, to derive the mathematical expressions underlying machine learning models for predicting COVID-19 outcomes. Our analysis identifies Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), initial Albumin levels (ALBI), Aspartate aminotransferase (ASTI), initial Total Bilirubin (TBILI), and initial D-Dimer (DIMER) as critical prognostic indicators for disease severity. The primary contributions of this work are: (i) revealing the underlying mathematical formulas of black-box models in the context of COVID-19 severity prediction, (ii) being the first to apply symbolic metamodeling to this specific task, and (iii) uncovering significant features and their interactions.

The lattice Sommerfield model, which features a massive vector gauge field interacting with a light fermion in two dimensions, serves as an excellent framework for testing perturbative predictions. Unlike exact solutions in the continuum, we demonstrate that infinite field renormalization is absent, leading to a reduced degree of ultraviolet divergence, and that anomalies remain non-renormalized. These characteristics mirror the fundamental properties underlying the perturbative renormalizability of the Standard Model. Furthermore, these findings are non-perturbative, as the averages of gauge-invariant observables are formulated via convergent expansions that hold uniformly across lattice size and volume.

Interacting bosonic cold atomic gases, when subjected to rapid rotation and confined within anharmonic traps, can theoretically display analogues of the fractional quantum Hall effect typically observed in electrons under strong magnetic fields. In this context, the Coriolis force generated by rotation emulates the Lorentz force acting on charged particles, while artificial gauge fields can be created by coupling the atoms' internal states to light fields. The chapter explores the mathematical underpinnings of transitions between various strongly correlated phases that emerge as parameters within a model Hamiltonian are adjusted.

This study presents a fourth-order accurate finite element approach for simulating incompressible flows with variable density. Utilizing the Taylor series technique for implicit time integration and standard high-order Lagrange basis functions for spatial discretization, the method achieves high-order accuracy through time derivative correction terms. We detail specific algorithms for approximating the time derivatives within the variable density Navier-Stokes equations. Numerical experiments verify fourth-order accuracy for smooth scenarios, while also demonstrating that the Taylor series approach becomes unsuitable when regularity is lost, as shown by solving the 2D Rayleigh-Taylor instability problem.
