In the context of the optical Raman coherent effect, we utilize atomic coherent states—also known as angular momentum coherent states with varying angular momentum values—within the Schwinger bosonic framework. These states serve as the eigenvectors of the Hamiltonian that governs the Raman effect. Much as photon coherent states characterize laser light, atomic coherent states are intrinsically linked to the Raman process.

Linking the chemistry of planet-forming disks to the atmospheres of gas giant exoplanets, specifically via C/O ratios, represents a primary objective in disk chemistry. Small hydrocarbons such as $\rm C_2H$ and $\rm C_3H_2$ serve as effective tracers for C/O because they become abundant under high C/O conditions. This study presents resolved $\rm C_3H_2$ observations from the TW Hya Rosetta Stone Project, which aims to map the chemistry of ubiquitous molecules at $15-20$ au resolution within the TW Hya disk. Combined with archival data, these observations constitute the most comprehensive multi-line dataset for both ortho and para spin isomers across a broad energy range ($E_u=29-97$ K). We determine that the ortho-to-para ratio of $\rm C_3H_2$ remains consistent with 3 throughout the emission region, with a total abundance for both isomers of $(7.5-10)\times10^{-11}$ per H atom, representing $1-10$% of the previously reported $\rm C_2H$ abundance in this source. Furthermore, $\rm C_3H_2$ originates from a surface layer extending no deeper than $z/r=0.25$. Our findings support significant radial variations in gas-phase C/O in TW Hya, characterized by a sharp rise beyond $\sim30$ au. Even if planets do not directly accrete from the midplane, processes like meridional flows from the surface could imprint these changes onto forming planets. Notably, the HR 8799 system also exhibits an increasing gradient in the atmospheric C/O ratios of its giant planets. Although these stars differ significantly, hydrocarbon rings are common in disks, suggesting that the young planets of HR 8799 likely retain the chemical signature of their parent disk's volatiles.

Despite current image generation techniques achieving remarkable quality, they fail to create plausible and diverse images of handwritten text. In contrast, natural handwriting exhibits significant variation among different writers, as well as involuntary inconsistencies even within the work of a single individual. This study advances the creation of realistic and varied synthetic handwritten words through a novel approach that conditions the generative process on both textual content and calligraphic style features. Our method is guided by three complementary objectives: generating realistic images, emulating specific handwriting styles, and conveying precise textual information. Unlike previous models, our system is unconstrained by a fixed vocabulary, allowing it to render any input word. Furthermore, it can mimic the calligraphic traits of a specific writer in a few-shot learning scenario. We demonstrate significant improvements over prior art, supported by qualitative, quantitative, and human-based evaluations that confirm the realistic nature of the generated images.

This study examines kinematics and symmetry within projective geometry, focusing on $(\alpha,\beta)$ spacetime, a specific category of Finsler spacetime. Projectively flat $(\alpha,\beta)$ spacetime characterized by constant flag curvature is categorized into four distinct types. The symmetry properties of Type A (Riemannian spacetime with constant sectional curvature) correspond to those in de Sitter special relativity, while Type B (locally Minkowski spacetime) mirrors the symmetry found in very special relativity. Both Type C (Funk spacetime) and Type D (scaled Berwald's metric spacetime) exhibit the Lorentz group as their isometric group. The paper provides the geodesic equations, algebra, and dispersion relations for $(\alpha,\beta)$ spacetime. Furthermore, the invariant special relativity applicable to each of the four types involves two parameters: the speed of light and a geometrical parameter potentially linked to a new physical scale. When this geometrical parameter approaches zero, all four types reduce to Einstein's special relativity.

We introduce a technique for automatically assessing and structuring the quality of various Computer Science publishing venues. Because this approach relies solely on paper publication data, we applied it to a vast segment of the DBLP dataset covering 50 years, involving millions of authors and thousands of venues. By treating venue authorship as a regression problem focused on specific metrics, we calculated quality scores for every conference and journal included. These scores also generate a yearly model of conference quality, illustrating the evolution and shifts within the field over time. Furthermore, the scores facilitate the evaluation of individual researchers and academic institutions. We demonstrate that using these venue scores to assess authors and institutions yields quantitative results comparable to those derived from citation counts or peer reviews. Unlike many existing metrics, our method leverages large-scale, open data, ensuring the approach is both repeatable and transparent. To support further research, all associated code and data are accessible at https://github.com/leonidk/venue_scores.

This study establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for a refinable step function to generate an orthogonal multiresolution analysis (MRA) within the $L_2(\mathfrak G)$ spaces on Vilenkin groups $\mathfrak G$. Specifically, we examine a class of refinable step functions where the mask $m_0(\chi)$ remains constant on cosets $\mathfrak G_{-1}^\bot$ and its modulus $|m_0(\chi)|$ assumes only the values 0 and 1. We demonstrate that any refinable step function $\varphi$ from this class, which generates an orthogonal MRA on a $p$-adic Vilenkin group $\mathfrak G$, possesses a Fourier transform satisfying ${\rm supp} \hat \varphi(\chi)\subset \mathfrak G_{p-2}^\bot$. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of this finding.

This research investigates a variational framework for ferronematics within two-dimensional domains, specifically focusing on the "super-dilute" regime. The free energy functional comprises a reduced Landau-de Gennes term for the nematic order parameter, a Ginzburg-Landau term for spontaneous magnetization, and a coupling component that encourages the alignment of the nematic director with the magnetization. Under a specific asymptotic limit, we demonstrate that the nematic order parameter converges to a canonical harmonic map featuring non-orientable point defects, whereas the magnetization converges to a singular vector field. This field contains line defects that pair up the non-orientable point defects via a minimal connection.

An unidentified emission line near 3.5 keV has been observed in the spectra of dark matter-dominated systems. Recent research by Dessert et al. [1812.06976], which utilized 30 Msec of XMM-Newton blank-sky data to limit the permissible line flux, argued against a dark matter decay origin. However, we show that these constraints are overestimated by more than an order of magnitude resulting from flawed background modeling. Consequently, the hypothesis that the 3.5 keV signal arises from dark matter remains a viable explanation.

A March 2016 publication in EPJC by Faria demonstrates that quantum massive conformal gravity is renormalizable despite the presence of ghost states, and we provide commentary specifically on its renormalizability.

A standard procedure in constructing NLP datasets, particularly those relying on crowd-sourced labels, entails collecting multiple annotator assessments for the same items and collapsing them into a unified "ground truth" via majority voting, averaging, or adjudication. Although these methods suit specific annotation scenarios, they fail to account for the socially constructed nature of human perception, which is central to capturing relatively subjective tasks. Specifically, such aggregations often mask systematic disagreements stemming from annotators' socio-cultural backgrounds and lived experiences. This paper empirically shows that label aggregation can embed representational biases reflecting individual and group viewpoints. Consequently, we offer a series of recommendations to enhance the utility and transparency of these datasets for downstream applications.

This paper investigates the valuation of a multiple reset put option, granting the holder the right to reset the strike price multiple times to secure an at-the-money European put. We model this as a multiple optimal stopping problem, decomposing it into a series of single optimal stopping problems to analyze the corresponding free-boundary conditions. By applying induction based on the number of remaining resets and utilizing probabilistic techniques, including local time-space calculus along curves, we solve these sequential problems. Consequently, we identify each optimal reset boundary as the unique solution to a nonlinear integral equation and establish representations for the option's reset premium. Furthermore, we suggest that these multiple reset options serve as viable cryptocurrency derivatives and a compelling alternative to standard European options, given the extreme volatility inherent in crypto assets.

We utilize stochastic variational inference paired with natural gradient descent to approximate a variational distribution, thereby characterizing the full joint posterior for spatially varying basal traction and ice softness parameters within an ice sheet model based on surface speed observations. By employing a Gaussian process prior over the parameters and framing the problem using kernel eigenfunctions, we achieve significant control over prior assumptions regarding parameter smoothness and length scales while ensuring the inference remains computationally feasible. In a synthetic test case, the method successfully recovers known parameters and addresses mutual indeterminacy, both of which impact observed surface speeds. When applied to Helheim Glacier in Southeast Greenland, we demonstrate that the approach scales effectively to glacier-sized datasets. Furthermore, we observe that posterior uncertainty remains high in slow-flowing regions, irrespective of the chosen observational noise model.

Existing literature addresses the reliability analysis of one-shot devices within accelerated life testing frameworks involving multiple stress factors. This methodology is applicable to the biomedical sector, where disease emergence under varying stressors—such as environmental conditions, lifestyle choices, and co-morbidities—is frequently observed. This study applies one-shot device data analysis to a Murine model dataset for Melioidosis, assuming a two-parameter logistic exponential distribution for lifetime modeling. Robust parameter estimation is achieved using Weighted Minimum Density Power Divergence Estimators (WMDPDEs), alongside conventional Maximum Likelihood Estimators (MLEs). The research further examines the asymptotic properties of the WMDPDEs and conducts hypothesis testing based on them, with estimator performance validated through extensive simulations. These developments are subsequently applied to the Melioidosis Murine model data. Recognizing the critical need to determine precise inspection times for tested one-shot devices, the study performs an optimization search to identify ideal inspection intervals. This process minimizes a specific cost function that balances estimation precision against experimental expenses, utilizing a population-based heuristic approach known as the Genetic Algorithm.

This paper investigates the behavior of multifractal Hewitt-Stromberg dimension functions when projected into Euclidean space. As an application, we examine the multifractal analysis of projected measures. Specifically, we derive general results regarding the multifractal analysis of orthogonal projections onto $m$-dimensional linear subspaces for a measure $\mu$ that adheres to a multifractal formalism grounded in Hewitt-Stromberg measures.

Complex Networks serve as an effective method for uncovering internal relationships and modeling class structures within datasets to facilitate high-level classification. While prior research relies on K-Nearest Neighbors to construct these networks using the entire sample set, this study proposes an alternative approach that builds Complex Networks exclusively from samples belonging to a specific class. Furthermore, the paper employs a metric to evaluate network structure and introduces an optimization strategy to enhance performance. Experiments conducted via cross-validation, utilizing both grid search and Genetic Algorithms for the optimization process, demonstrate that this approach can yield performance improvements of up to 10%.

Let $\mathcal F$ denote a family of graphs that are free of odd cycles of length $2r+1$, with $r\geq 2$. Assuming every graph in $\mathcal F$ possesses a minimum degree that scales linearly with the number of vertices, Thomassen demonstrated that such a family exhibits a bounded chromatic number; equivalently, every graph within $\mathcal F$ admits a homomorphism to a complete graph of bounded order. However, by focusing on homomorphic images that are themselves $C_{2r+1}$-free, we have constructed a family of dense $C_{2r+1}$-free graphs that lack any $C_{2r+1}$-free homomorphic image of bounded size. This result establishes the first nontrivial lower bound for the homomorphism threshold of odd cycles with length $2r+1 \geq 5$, thereby resolving a query posed by Ebsen and Schacht. Our proof employs a novel method for characterizing the topological structure of graphs. We develop a graph-theoretic counterpart to homotopy equivalence, facilitating the analysis of the relative positioning of odd closed walks within a graph. This concept reveals surprising links to the neighborhood complex, prompting several intriguing inquiries.

Driven by the growing demand for robotics systems to automate repetitive tasks within smart factories, robotic grasping has emerged as a critical yet difficult challenge. This process involves using robotic arms to autonomously handle objects across diverse environments, relying on various computer vision techniques like object detection, segmentation, grasp prediction, and pick planning. Although deep learning has advanced the field significantly, a major hurdle remains the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality RGBD datasets capable of covering a wide range of scenarios. To address this data limitation, we draw inspiration from the metaverse concept, which bridges virtual and physical realities by enabling the creation of digital twins for real-world manufacturing. These digital twins allow for the virtual generation of numerous scenarios to produce vast training datasets. In this paper, we introduce MetaGraspNet, a large-scale benchmark for vision-driven robotic grasping synthesized through physics-based metaverse methods. The dataset comprises 100,000 images featuring 25 distinct object types and is categorized into five difficulty levels to assess model performance across varying grasping contexts. Additionally, we propose a novel layout-weighted performance metric designed to better evaluate detection and segmentation for robotic grasping than current general-purpose metrics. This open-source benchmark, available on Kaggle, includes detailed object detection, segmentation, and layout annotations, along with a script for the layout-weighted metric in its first phase.

The recent achievements of pre-trained language models (PLMs) have sparked interest in their numerical comprehension and manipulation capabilities. However, reasoning over measurements—a critical aspect—has not been formally investigated. This study demonstrates that PLMs currently lack the necessary capacity for measurement-based reasoning. Additionally, we observe that training a language model on a corpus rich in measurement data enhances its performance in understanding such concepts. Finally, we introduce a straightforward embedding strategy to more effectively differentiate between numerical values and units, resulting in significant improvements across various probing tasks.

The efficacy of language Transformers largely stems from the masked language modeling (MLM) pretext task, which relies on tokenizing text into semantically significant units. This paper investigates masked image modeling (MIM) to explore the benefits and hurdles associated with employing a semantically meaningful visual tokenizer. We introduce iBOT, a self-supervised framework capable of executing masked prediction using an online tokenizer. Our approach applies self-distillation to masked patch tokens, utilizing the teacher network as the online tokenizer, while also applying self-distillation to the class token to capture visual semantics. This online tokenizer is learned jointly with the MIM objective, eliminating the need for a multi-stage training pipeline that requires pre-training the tokenizer beforehand. We demonstrate iBOT's superiority by achieving 82.3% linear probing accuracy and 87.8% fine-tuning accuracy on ImageNet-1K. In addition to surpassing state-of-the-art image classification benchmarks, we highlight the emergence of local semantic patterns, which enhance the model's robustness against common corruptions and yield leading performance on dense downstream tasks such as object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation.

This paper introduces a new approach to model the NP-hard wireless channel assignment problem as a higher-order unconstrained binary optimization (HUBO) task, utilizing Grover adaptive search (GAS) to achieve a quadratic speedup. Unlike conventional methods that rely on one-hot encoding of channel indices—leading to a quadratic formulation—we develop ascending and descending binary encodings, design a tailored quantum circuit, and calculate the precise qubit and gate requirements for GAS. Our analysis demonstrates that this proposed HUBO formulation markedly decreases both the qubit count and query complexity compared to standard quadratic approaches. Although this efficiency comes with an initial increase in the number of quantum gates, we show that our descending binary encoding strategy effectively mitigates this overhead.

Under specific assumptions, particle motion in $1+3$ dimensional spherical spacetimes can be represented as curves on two-dimensional optical and Jacobi manifolds for null and timelike trajectories, respectively. This paper utilizes auxiliary two-dimensional metrics to investigate circular geodesics in generic, static, spherically symmetric, and asymptotically flat $1+3$ dimensional spacetimes with at least $C^2$ smooth functions. The analysis examines the Gaussian curvature of the corresponding bidimensional manifold and the geodesic curvature of circular paths on it, covering both null and timelike cases. By analyzing null geodesics via the optical manifold, the study recovers established results regarding the count of light rings outside black holes and horizonless compact objects. Similarly, an analogous procedure allows for the formulation of a theorem determining the number of marginally stable timelike circular orbits for spacetimes meeting the stated assumptions.

We introduce a novel search approach for higgsinos, focusing on the production of higgsino-like pairs in association with a $W$ or $Z$ boson within the missing energy and hadronically-tagged vector boson channel. Sensitivity limits are established for (HL-)LHC scenarios involving mass differences of $\mathcal{O}({1\mathrm{-}3.5}~\mathrm{GeV})$ between the lightest neutral and charged states. We highlight that leveraging the $E_T^\mathrm{miss}$ distribution markedly enhances the search's sensitivity. Our analysis shows that higgsinos with masses up to 110 (210) GeV can be excluded using $139~(300)~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of data. Furthermore, the complete dataset from the HL-LHC is projected to exclude (or discover) higgsinos reaching masses of up to 520 (280) GeV.

We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for attaining Heisenberg scaling in general adaptive multi-parameter estimation schemes under Markovian noise. For scenarios where this scaling is feasible, we present a semidefinite program to determine the optimal quantum error correction (QEC) protocol that maximizes estimation precision. To address technical challenges arising from the potential incompatibility of measurements designed to extract information on distinct parameters, we employ the Holevo Cramér-Rao (HCR) bound for pure states. Furthermore, we demonstrate examples highlighting the substantial benefits of our joint-QEC protocols, which estimate all parameters using a single error-corrected subspace, compared to separate-QEC protocols that isolate each parameter into its own subspace.

Persistent random walks represent a transport mechanism situated between uniform rectilinear motion and Brownian motion, characterized by successive steps of random finite lengths and directions taken at a constant speed. In one dimension, the isotropic and symmetric variant is described by the telegrapher's equation, also known as the hyperbolic heat conduction equation. These equations were developed to address the paradox of infinite propagation speed inherent in standard heat and diffusion models. The combination of finite speed and correlation length gives rise to various classes of random walks; specifically, one-dimensional persistent random walks can exhibit anomalies, such as anisotropy and asymmetry, that are impossible in Brownian motion. This study examines the scenario where the mean free path is anisotropic—the sole condition producing physical behavior distinct from the standard telegrapher's case. We derive exact expressions for the Green's function, scattering statistics, and the distribution of first-passage times at the origin. The analysis of these quantities reveals a transition in phenomena such as escape probability and residence time. (This is the second version, corrected for typos found in the first.)

Computed tomography (CT) is a prevalent technique for non-destructively analyzing internal structures. Achieving high-quality reconstructions typically necessitates densely sampled trajectories to prevent angular undersampling; however, many applications require sparse-view measurements, which, if unaddressed, result in streak artifacts. Existing methods often fail to leverage domain-specific information effectively, leading to unreliable reconstructions for highly undersampled data. We introduce a novel sparse-view tomography framework that separates the reconstruction process into two stages. Initially, a super-resolution network (SIN), trained on sparse projections, addresses the ill-posed nature of the problem. This intermediate output enables a closed-form tomographic reconstruction that maintains detail while significantly mitigating streak artifacts. Subsequently, a refinement network (PRN), trained on these reconstructions, eliminates any residual artifacts. Additionally, we propose a lightweight perceptual-loss variant that enhances domain-specific information to improve restoration accuracy. Experimental results indicate a performance gain of 4 dB compared to current solutions.

We illustrate how category theory yields specifications that can be efficiently realized through imperative algorithms, specifically within the domain of graph rewriting. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate that this software development paradigm facilitates the rapid creation of both correct and high-performance code. We present a modern implementation of graph rewriting techniques operating at the abstraction level of finitely-presented C-sets, while elucidating the relationship between C-sets and the typed graphs found in current rewriting tools. We highlight that our open-source library is extensible: by incorporating new categorical constructs—such as slice categories, structured cospans, and distributed graphs—and mapping their limits and colimits to those of their underlying categories, users gain access to efficient algorithms for pushout and (final) pullback complements. This capability enables double-, single-, and sesqui-pushout rewriting across a wide range of data structures.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are anticipated to be integral components of future communication networks. Traditionally, determining the optimal placement of UAVs acting as base stations requires either extensive field measurements or ray tracing simulations, provided a 3D model of the area exists. This paper introduces an alternative method to optimize UAV base station altitude using deep learning. Specifically, a 2D satellite image of the target region is fed into a deep neural network to forecast path loss distributions across various altitudes. These predicted distributions enable the calculation of regional coverage, allowing the identification of the altitude that maximizes this coverage. The neural network is engineered to generate multiple path loss distributions during a single inference, eliminating the need to train separate networks for each altitude.

Photospheric brightness fluctuations on cool, main-sequence stars can distort absorption line profiles, potentially masking or surpassing radial velocity (RV) shifts induced by exoplanets. Although next-generation precision RV spectrographs strive to detect velocity amplitudes of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$, they necessitate effective mitigation of stellar noise. Researchers are developing statistical methods to distinguish between Keplerian signals and activity-induced perturbations. However, two significant hurdles remain: ensuring the interpretability of stellar activity components as RV models advance, and preventing the inadvertent absorption of the smallest Keplerian signatures within flexible activity models. In the case of the K2V exoplanet host $\epsilon$ Eridani, we utilized ground-based photometry to constrain Gaussian processes for RV modeling and TESS photometry with a light-curve inversion algorithm to reconstruct the stellar surface. Models derived from TESS data reduced the rms scatter in EXPRES RV measurements from 4.72 m s$^{-1}$ to 1.98 m s$^{-1}$. We also conducted a pilot study using the CHARA Array and MIRC-X beam combiner to directly image starspots identified in the TESS data. While current spot detections remain marginal due to limited phase coverage, a dedicated future observing campaign should enable definitive imaging and the determination of the star's inclination and orientation relative to its debris disk. This study demonstrates that stellar surface maps generated from high-cadence time-series photometry and interferometric data offer the necessary constraints to accurately minimize RV scatter.

Matrix-based centrality metrics have become widely popular in network analysis, largely because their behavior can be rigorously examined as parameters change. Recent studies have explored the link between subgraph centrality, defined via the matrix exponential $f(x) = \exp(x)$, and a network's walk structure. In walk-regular graphs, the count of closed walks of any given length remains identical for all nodes, resulting in uniform $f$-subgraph centralities for any function $f$ (or maximum $f$-walk entropy). This study investigates conditions under which non-walk-regular graphs can achieve maximum entropy, defining such graphs as $\textit{entropic}$. For parameterized measures, we also identify which parameter values induce this uniformity. To date, only a single entropic graph has been found, featuring just two witnessing parameter values, which raises the question of the total number of such graphs and parameters. We address these issues by constructing infinite families of entropic graphs, alongside a family of witnessing parameters that converge to zero.

We present an investigation into spontaneous magnetization (spin-polarization) within TRS-breaking superconductors featuring unitary pairing potentials, specifically in the absence of external magnetic or Zeeman fields. In superconductors lacking inversion symmetry, spin-singlet ($\Delta_s$) and spin-triplet ($\Delta_t$) pairings can coexist; when a relative phase of $\pm\pi/2$ emerges, they form a TRS-breaking unitary state ($\Delta_s\pm i\Delta_t$). We show that this unitary pairing, assisted by spin-orbit coupling, induces spontaneous spin-polarization. This finding offers an alternative perspective on TRS breaking beyond the existing framework for noncentrosymmetric superconductors, and we discuss experimental data from Zr$_3$Ir and CaPtAs in light of our theoretical model.

On a homogeneous manifold $G/H$, a smooth curve is termed a Riemannian equigeodesic if it acts as a homogeneous geodesic under every $G$-invariant Riemannian metric. The manifold $G/H$ itself is defined as Riemannian equigeodesic if, for any point $x$ and nonzero tangent vector $y$ at $x$, there exists a Riemannian equigeodesic $c(t)$ starting at $x$ with initial velocity $y$. These concepts extend naturally to Finsler geometry, yielding the definitions of Finsler equigeodesics and Finsler equigeodesic spaces. This work establishes two classification theorems: one for Riemannian equigeodesic spaces and another for Finsler equigeodesic spaces. First, a homogeneous manifold $G/H$, where $G$ is a connected, simply connected, quasi-compact Lie group and $H$ is connected, is Riemannian equigeodesic if and only if it decomposes into a product of Euclidean factors and compact, strongly isotropy irreducible factors. Second, if $G$ is a compact semi-simple Lie group, a homogeneous manifold $G/H$ is Finsler equigeodesic if and only if it locally decomposes into a product where each factor is isometric to $Spin(7)/G_2$, $G_2/SU(3)$, or a compact-type symmetric space. These findings indicate that equigeodesic properties characterize both symmetric spaces and compact-type strongly isotropy irreducible spaces. Furthermore, as an application, we classify homogeneous manifolds $G/H$ with compact semi-simple $G$ such that all $G$-invariant Finsler metrics are of Berwald type. This result points toward a new research direction in homogeneous Finsler geometry: systematically investigating homogeneous manifolds where all $G$-invariant Finsler metrics satisfy specific geometric conditions.

This study examines the unweighted Stochastic Score Classification (SSClass) problem under arbitrary cost conditions. We present two constant-factor approximation algorithms, both achieving a 6-approximation ratio relative to the optimal adaptive algorithm and operating in a non-adaptive manner. The first algorithm adapts a modified round-robin strategy across three sequences, drawing inspiration from recent findings on the unit cost SSClass case. The second algorithm originates from the work of Gkenosis et al.; in our study, we enhance its approximation factor from 2(B-1) to 6. Our analysis relies significantly on the relationship between function computation and verification, a concept explored in information theory.

Existing lane detection research heavily depends on large, manually annotated datasets. We mitigate this reliance by utilizing vast amounts of inexpensive, unlabeled data. Our approach introduces a new loss function that incorporates geometric properties of lanes within Hough space, treating lanes as local maxima. By assigning lanes to distinct channels, we enable localization through straightforward global max-pooling. In this framework, the position of the maximum represents the lane's layout, while its intensity reflects the likelihood of the lane's presence. Maximizing the log-probability of these peak bins allows neural networks to detect lanes without supervision. Experiments on the CULane and TuSimple datasets demonstrate that our proposed Hough Transform loss significantly boosts performance by effectively learning from extensive collections of unlabeled images.

We examine rings where one-sided ideals closely resemble automorphism-invariant modules. Specifically, we investigate rings where every finitely generated right ideal is automorphism invariant, as well as those where each right ideal decomposes into a finite direct sum of automorphism invariant ideals. Furthermore, we explore the relationships between these ring classes and $q$-rings and $\Sigma$-$q$-rings.

Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) offers a thorough framework for understanding how humans make decisions from experience in dynamic settings. Since its introduction nearly twenty years ago, numerous computational models derived from IBLT (known as IBL models) have proven highly effective at explaining and forecasting human choices across various decision-making scenarios. However, as the theory has developed, the original formulation has lost some precision, leaving gaps in how it applies to increasingly complex, dynamic, and multi-agent environments. This paper introduces a refined and precise restatement of IBLT's core theoretical components. It also presents an advanced implementation called SpeedyIBL, which expands IBLT's capacity to address a broad spectrum of individual and multi-agent decision problems. SpeedyIBL specifically resolves a critical computational bottleneck in previous IBL models: the "curse of exponential growth" caused by memory-based tabular computations. As observations accumulate, the memory of instances expands exponentially, resulting in a corresponding exponential slowdown in processing time. To counter this, SpeedyIBL utilizes parallel computation and vectorization to significantly accelerate IBL model execution. We assessed the robustness of SpeedyIBL against existing IBLT implementations within increasingly complex decision games. The findings not only confirm the versatility of IBLT across diverse decision tasks but also underscore the superior performance of SpeedyIBL over prior versions as decision feature complexity and the number of agents rise. This library is open-sourced for the benefit of the wider research community.

Flow cytometry (FCM) is an analytical method used to detect and record light scattering and fluorescence emission from individual cells or particles, collectively referred to as "events" within a population. Standard FCM experiments generate vast datasets, rendering their analysis computationally demanding. Although existing platforms like FlowJo are valuable, they cannot support online interactive processing due to data volume constraints. This study introduces a more efficient solution: Freecyto, a free, user-friendly web application built on Python and Flask. It employs a weighted k-means clustering algorithm to enable interactive FCM data analysis. Since web browsers struggle to render massive datasets interactively, Freecyto overcomes this limitation by using k-means to quantize the data, allowing users to visualize complex datasets through a representative subset of points. Additionally, Freecyto maintains standard FCM visualization capabilities, including scatterplots, histograms, heatmaps, and boxplots, while offering SQL-based sub-population gating. The tool has been demonstrated to handle various experimental setups requiring FCM, and comparisons confirm that it preserves data accuracy relative to conventional FCM software.

This paper explores the relationship between d-orthogonal polynomials and the Toda lattice hierarchy. Specifically, we examine polynomial systems analogous to Hermite polynomials that obey a recurrence relation involving $d+2$ terms, where $d > 1$. Each such system generates a solution to the Toda lattice hierarchy; however, by additionally requiring these polynomials to be eigenfunctions of a differential operator—thereby addressing a bispectral problem—we derive a solution with unique characteristics. Notably, the associated tau-functions $\tau_m$ satisfy Virasoro constraints. A striking attribute of these functions is that they all represent partition functions of matrix models, including well-known examples such as the Kontsevich model, Kontsevich-Penner models, and $r$-spin models. A particularly significant observation is that the solution for $d=2$ encompasses two renowned tau-functions: those describing intersection numbers on moduli spaces of both compact and open Riemann surfaces.

Existing quantum annealers have demonstrated viability for initial practical applications within the noisy-intermediate-scale-quantum (NISQ) era. Nevertheless, fully leveraging their potential requires a thorough analysis of finite-time excitations. To achieve this, we construct a phase diagram for driven Ising chains, enabling the extraction of excess work scaling behavior as a function of process duration and system size. Specifically, "fast" processes align well with the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, "slow" processes follow effective Landau-Zener dynamics, and "very slow" processes can be modeled using adiabatic perturbation theory.

Although learning-based approaches offer promising solutions to enduring control challenges, the neural networks (NNs) prevalent in modern methods create significant obstacles for analyzing the safety of the resulting systems. Fortunately, emerging literature presents tractable strategies for verifying and analyzing these high-dimensional, highly nonlinear models. This tutorial introduces and unifies recent techniques—many drawn from computer vision and machine learning—to verify the robustness of NNs. These methods are subsequently extended to deliver formal guarantees for neural feedback loops, such as closed-loop systems utilizing NN control policies. The presented tools facilitate closed-loop reachability analysis and support robust deep reinforcement learning.

The COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, emerged abruptly in early 2020 in China and rapidly spread globally. This event precipitated a significant surge in research concerning the virus itself, as well as epidemics in general, across numerous scientific disciplines. This study examines the dynamics of epidemic propagation and investigates how individual differences in adhering to social norms—specifically, the adoption of health and hygiene practices by population members—influence these dynamics.

This study assesses how well established machine learning algorithms can classify social network documents as aggressive, gender-biased, or communally charged by utilizing both probabilistic and state-of-the-art vector space modeling (VSM) techniques. The process began with an exploratory phase designed to identify optimal configurations; this involved training various algorithms using multiple VSM and probabilistic approaches on training and development datasets, subsequently eliminating less informative setups. The resulting systems were then entered into the ComMA@ICON'21 Workshop on Multilingual Gender Biased and Communal Language Identification.

On social media, popularity and engagement function as key currencies that drive user retention through reinforcement. GitHub, a social coding platform, fulfills a dual role: it acts as a practical tool for asynchronous, distributed software development collaboration while also accommodating passive, social-media-style interactions. GitHub employs three distinct mechanisms to express approval or interest in content: forking repositories to duplicate their contents, watching repositories to receive update notifications, and starring to signal endorsement. This paper investigates popularity within the GitHub ecosystem, analyzing the interrelationships among these three quantitative metrics. Furthermore, we propose a Weighted Total Popularity Score (WTPS), derived from the historical trajectories of these various popularity indicators.

Recently, RobustBench (Croce et al. 2020) has emerged as a prominent benchmark for assessing the adversarial robustness of image classification networks. Its primary task involves ranking trained neural networks based on their performance on CIFAR10 under AutoAttack (Croce and Hein 2020b), utilizing l-infinity perturbations constrained to an epsilon of 8/255. Given that top-performing models currently achieve scores around 60% of the baseline, the benchmark is rightly considered quite challenging. Despite its widespread adoption in recent research, this paper seeks to stimulate debate regarding RobustBench's appropriateness as a definitive indicator of robustness applicable to real-world scenarios. Our critique rests on two main points, substantiated by extensive experiments: first, the AutoAttack procedure with l-infinity, epsilon = 8/255 perturbations imposes unrealistically strong adversarial examples, leading to near-perfect detection rates even by simple algorithms and human observers; second, we demonstrate that other attack methods can achieve comparable success rates while being significantly harder to detect. Furthermore, we argue that results derived from low-resolution datasets like CIFAR10 fail to generalize to higher-resolution images, as gradient-based attacks appear to become increasingly detectable as resolution increases.

We detail quantum circuits that produce four-qubit maximally entangled states, measuring entanglement via the absolute value of the Cayley hyperdeterminant as a monotone. Specifically, we demonstrate that these states can be generated by applying a specific family of CNOT circuits to particular states within the local unitary (LU) orbit of |0000>.

This study identifies multiple solutions within the Nonlinear Coupled Constitutive Relation (NCCR) model and proposes a method for selecting the physically accurate solution. Based on Eu's generalized hydrodynamic equations, the NCCR model developed by Myong is designed to characterize rarefied flows. However, as a complex nonlinear system, solving its equations typically relies on various assumptions that can lead to numerical instabilities and unphysical results. Furthermore, uncertainties in numerical discretization make it difficult to assess the model's stability and physical fidelity. To address these challenges, a novel numerical approach is introduced to analyze the NCCR equations by transforming the nonlinear system into a single-variable objective function. This formulation enables the detection of multiple solutions and establishes criteria for isolating the physical one, thereby constructing a robust numerical scheme. Finally, a series of flow problems across near-continuum and low-transition regimes with varying Mach numbers are simulated to validate both the proposed method's numerical performance and the physical accuracy of the NCCR model.

This article introduces a collaborative framework between deep neural networks and human-in-the-loop systems to rapidly generate precise segmentation maps for remote sensing imagery. Essentially, an agent engages in iterative exchanges with the network to refine its initially inaccurate predictions through semantic label annotations. Our methodological contribution consists of two parts: first, we develop two interactive learning schemes that incorporate user inputs, either by concatenating annotations with other network inputs or by utilizing them as sparse ground truth for network retraining. Second, we implement an active learning strategy to direct users toward the most critical areas requiring annotation. For this purpose, we evaluate several state-of-the-art acquisition functions, including ConfidNet, entropy, and ODIN, to assess neural network uncertainty. Experiments across three remote sensing datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. Notably, we find that uncertainty-based active learning effectively guides users to identify errors, making it highly relevant for steering user interventions.

Although various post hoc explanation techniques, such as feature attribution methods, have emerged in recent research, there remains a significant lack of systematic and transparent benchmarking frameworks. To address this, we present OpenXAI, an extensible, open-source platform designed for the evaluation and benchmarking of post hoc explanation methods. OpenXAI includes three core components: (i) a versatile synthetic data generator alongside a diverse array of real-world datasets, pre-trained models, and leading feature attribution methods; (ii) open-source implementations of twenty-two quantitative metrics to assess faithfulness, stability (robustness), and fairness; and (iii) the inaugural public XAI leaderboards for benchmarking explanations. The framework is highly extensible, allowing users to easily integrate custom explanation methods and update the leaderboards. Overall, OpenXAI offers an automated, end-to-end pipeline that streamlines and standardizes the evaluation process while enhancing transparency and reproducibility. All OpenXAI datasets, data loaders, state-of-the-art method implementations, evaluation metrics, and leaderboards are publicly accessible at https://open-xai.github.io/.

Dynamical systems, frequently represented by non-linear governing equations, are pervasive yet often computationally expensive to solve numerically due to their high-dimensional state spaces. Consequently, there is significant interest in deep learning-based reduced order models (ROMs), particularly those grounded in Koopman theory. This study extends a recent adversarial Koopman model to stochastic spaces, where the operator acts on the probability distribution of an encoder's latent representation. Specifically, the system's latent encoding is treated as a Gaussian, evolved over time by an auxiliary neural network that generates two Koopman matrices, $K_{\mu}$ and $K_{\sigma}$. The implementation of adversarial and gradient losses is shown to reduce prediction errors. Additionally, a reduced formulation is explored by assuming a tridiagonal structure for the Koopman matrices, achieving prediction accuracy comparable to the baseline model with full matrices. The model's effectiveness is validated across various test cases, including chaos, fluid dynamics, combustion, and reaction-diffusion systems. Furthermore, the approach is applied to generalize via input-conditioned Koopman matrices to simulate Lithium-ion battery states over time. The results indicate that these stochastic Koopman models hold great promise for addressing a broad spectrum of complex problems.

Perfect state transfer in uniformly coupled networks, defined by a graph structure, offers significant advantages over engineered chains, including substantially faster transfer times that do not depend on the distance between input and output nodes. This efficiency arises from multiple couplings operating in parallel. However, the trade-offs involve the necessity for higher qubit connectivity and a larger number of graph vertices. Since the size of current graph constructions grows exponentially with the transfer distance, these approaches are currently impractical for anything beyond very short distances. This leads to the question of minimizing the graph size required for a specific transfer distance. In this paper, we demonstrate reductions in the necessary vertex count, though the overall exponential scaling with distance persists. Additionally, we refine existing bounds on the minimum degree required for the graph's vertices.

Group-based sparse representation holds significant promise for image denoising; however, current approaches predominantly rely on the nonlocal self-similarity (NSS) prior found only within the noisy input. This reliance limits denoising quality to the characteristics of the degraded image, causing performance to deteriorate rapidly as noise levels rise. To address this, we introduce a novel prior model termed the group sparsity residual constraint (GSRC). Unlike traditional methods that utilize a single prior, GSRC leverages two distinct NSS priors: those derived from both the noisy and pre-filtered images. By integrating these priors through a sparsity residual mechanism, the denoising task is reframed as minimizing the group sparsity residual. Specifically, we first generate a robust estimate of the original image's group sparse coefficients via pre-filtering, then use the noisy image's coefficients to approximate this estimate. To enhance the accuracy of selecting nonlocal similar patches, an adaptive patch search scheme is implemented. Additionally, an effective iterative shrinkage algorithm is developed to solve the GSRC model and optimally fuse the dual priors. Experimental results indicate that the proposed GSRC model surpasses many state-of-the-art denoising techniques across both objective and perceptual metrics.

During a pandemic such as COVID-19, proactive testing and interventions remain the sole effective strategies for curbing transmission until widespread vaccination occurs. While recent academic studies provide strong support for this approach, a critical challenge persists: can we detect all daily new infections without the prohibitive cost of testing every individual daily? Although group testing reduces the number of required tests, it often overlooks infection time dynamics and assumes independent infections, ignoring the reality of community spread. Conversely, epidemiological models like the continuous-time SIR stochastic network account for temporal dynamics and community correlations but lack discrete-time testing and intervention mechanisms. This paper introduces a "discrete-time SIR stochastic block model" that integrates daily group testing and interventions. This model functions as a discrete counterpart to the continuous-time SIR network model, operating on a weighted graph that reflects underlying community structures. We analyze the minimum number of daily group tests required to identify all infections with vanishing error probability. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging community knowledge and the model enables nonadaptive group testing algorithms that are order-optimal, achieving performance comparable to complete testing with significantly fewer resources.

A well-known paradox in the formation of high-mass stars involves the idea that intense radiation pressure can stop accretion, thereby halting the growth of the central star. While disk accretion has been suggested as a solution, the nature of disks and accretion in this regime remains poorly understood. To investigate this, we conducted high-resolution ($R$=35,000-70,000) iSHELL spectroscopy in the $K$-band for eleven high-mass protostars. Br-$\gamma$ emission was detected in eight of these sources, and their line profiles largely resemble those of low-mass pre-main-sequence stars. By applying an empirical relation between Br-$\gamma$ and accretion luminosities, we tentatively estimated disk accretion rates spanning from $\lesssim$10$^{-8}$ to $\sim$10$^{-4}$ $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. These rates, comparable to those of low-mass systems, imply that high-mass protostars also accumulate mass through episodic accretion. Although CO overtone emission ($v$=2-0 and 3-1), likely originating from the inner disk ($r \ll 100$ au), was identified in only two sources, this low detection rate aligns with prior studies. Furthermore, absorption features at the $v$=0-2 ${\rm R(7)-R(14)}$ CO R-branch were observed in ten of the eleven sources. Most of these features are either blueshifted or redshifted, suggesting an association with outflows or inflows reaching velocities of up to $\sim50$ km s$^{-1}$. Our analysis indicates that this absorption layer is thermally equilibrated (requiring $n_{\mathrm H_2} \gtrsim 10^6$ cm$^{-3}$) at a uniform temperature of roughly 100-200 K and is situated within 200-600 au of the star.

MPLAPACK, previously known as MPACK, serves as a multiple-precision adaptation of LAPACK (https://www.netlib.org/lapack/). Version 2.0.1 builds upon LAPACK 3.9.1, having been converted from Fortran 90 to C++ via FABLE, a source-to-source translation tool (https://github.com/cctbx/cctbx_project/tree/master/fable/). This release includes both real and complex implementations of MPBLAS, with MPLAPACK supporting the full spectrum of LAPACK capabilities: solving systems of linear equations, least-squares problems, eigenvalue and singular value analyses, and associated matrix factorizations, excluding mixed-precision routines. The library defines a numerical linear algebra API analogous to LAPACK, facilitating the porting of legacy C/C++ numerical software. MPLAPACK accommodates various precision libraries, including binary64, binary128, FP80 (extended double), MPFR, GMP, and QD (double-double and quad-double). Users may select MPFR or GMP for arbitrary precision, while double-double and quad-double options cater to rapid 32 or 64-decimal computations. The binary64 variant effectively functions as a C++ counterpart to LAPACK. Additionally, the package features an OpenMP-accelerated MPBLAS for specific operations and CUDA support (compatible with A100 and V100 GPUs) for double-double versions of Rgemm and Rsyrk. The OpenMP implementation scales nearly linearly with core count, whereas the CUDA version delivers impressive performance, reaching approximately 400–600 GFlops. MPLAPACK is hosted on GitHub (https://github.com/nakatamaho/mplapack/) under the 2-clause BSD license.

We demonstrate that split Courant algebroids, defined on a Whitney sum $A \oplus A^*$, establish a bijective correspondence with multiplicative curved $L_\infty$-algebras. This bijection also applies to Nijenhuis morphisms and remains consistent under the twisting operation by a bivector.

We recently introduced a recursive method for calculating the matrix elements of a generic Gaussian transformation within the photon-number basis, designed to evolve quantum states by constructing the full transformation matrix and then performing a matrix-vector multiplication. In this work, we introduce a more efficient algorithm that directly computes the final state, bypassing the need to generate the complete transformation matrix. This approach reduces the time complexity for evolving an $N$-dimensional $M$-mode state under Gaussian dynamics from $O(MN^{2M})$ to $O(M(N^2/2)^M)$, representing an exponential improvement with respect to the number of modes. Furthermore, for scenarios involving high squeezing, the evolved state can be approximated with a complexity of $O(MN^{M})$. Since our new algorithm is differentiable, it can be integrated with gradient-based optimizers for circuit optimization. Benchmarks demonstrate its superiority over current methods, showing it is up to an order of magnitude faster when optimizing circuits to generate single photons, Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states, and NOON states.

While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) excel at producing high-quality images, explicitly defining the semantics of these synthesized outputs remains a challenge. This study seeks to clarify how GANs represent semantics to facilitate control over their generation process. We discovered that well-trained GANs encode image semantics in their internal feature maps in an unexpectedly straightforward manner: a simple linear transformation of these maps is sufficient to extract the underlying semantics. Extensive experiments across various GAN architectures and datasets confirm this simplicity, allowing us to train a semantic segmentation model for a pre-trained GAN using as few as eight labeled images. Building on this insight, we introduce two few-shot image editing methods, Semantic-Conditional Sampling and Semantic Image Editing. With a trained GAN and minimal semantic annotations (e.g., eight labels), users can generate diverse images adhering to a specific semantic layout and precisely control the synthesized content. The accompanying code is publicly available.

In topology optimization (TO), controlling the length scale is essential to ensure designs meet manufacturing constraints and functional needs. Generally, two approaches exist: \emph{exact} and \emph{approximate} control. Although exact methods are ideal, they are often difficult to implement and computationally intensive. Consequently, approximate methods are favored, particularly for early design phases. This paper introduces an approximate length scale control strategy for TO by adapting a recent neural network-based formulation (TOuNN). We achieve this by incorporating a Fourier space projection to regulate minimum and/or maximum length scales. Our approach avoids additional constraints and automates sensitivity calculations by utilizing end-to-end differentiability within the neural network library. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical experiments involving both single and multi-material designs.

Given the increasing intricacy of contemporary software architectures, formal models are increasingly employed to elucidate the underlying reasons for a system's behavior, rather than merely confirming that it functions as intended. This paper reviews methodologies for formally characterizing the observable behavior of reactive systems. We outline how Halpern and Pearl's concept of actual causation has inspired verification-focused investigations into cause-and-effect relationships within system evolution. A secondary emphasis is placed on the application of the Shapley value to attribute responsibility, specifically to quantify the impact of an event on an observable outcome. Furthermore, various formal approaches to probabilistic causation are synthesized and linked, with a discussion on their significance for comprehending probabilistic systems.

Recent advancements in sim-to-real learning for bipedal locomotion have achieved unprecedented robustness and agility across diverse terrains. Nevertheless, these studies, along with much prior research, have largely overlooked locomotion under varying external loads, which significantly alter system dynamics. In practical applications, robots must often maintain stable movement despite dynamic disturbances—such as pulling a cart or transporting a container of sloshing liquid—ideally without relying on explicit load-sensing hardware. This study investigates the potential of reinforcement learning (RL) and sim-to-real transfer for bipedal locomotion under such dynamic loads using solely proprioceptive feedback. We demonstrate that RL policies previously trained for unloaded conditions fail under certain loads, whereas training specifically within loaded contexts yields successful and enhanced policies. Furthermore, we compare the efficacy of training specialized policies for individual loads against a single unified policy, analyzing how resulting gaits adapt to different weight distributions. Finally, we validate sim-to-real transfer, noting that while successful, it exhibits a larger sim-to-real gap than previous unloaded studies, suggesting promising avenues for future research.

The swift evolution and widespread adoption of deep learning for image recognition have raised significant security concerns regarding their deployment in safety-critical applications. Because the accuracy and robustness of these models depend heavily on the purity of their training data, deep learning architectures are inherently vulnerable to adversarial attacks. These attacks involve introducing subtle, often imperceptible perturbations to standard images that can severely mislead even state-of-the-art machine learning systems. To address this, we introduce APuDAE, a framework that utilizes Denoising AutoEncoders (DAEs) to purify adversarial samples through an adaptive mechanism, thereby enhancing the classification performance of targeted networks under attack. Furthermore, we demonstrate that employing DAEs adaptively rather than directly yields superior classification accuracy and increased resilience against adaptive attacks designed to bypass the purification process. Our evaluation across the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet datasets shows that APuDAE achieves comparable or superior performance compared to baseline purification methods. Additionally, we developed a specialized adaptive attack to target our purification model, confirming that our defense remains robust against such threats.
This paper examines the graded Betti numbers of powers of edge ideals in hypergraphs through combinatorial invariants, thereby establishing combinatorial bounds for the regularity of these powers.

This paper addresses the optimal control of general nonlinear spatio-temporal systems governed by Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Control strategies for such systems are gaining significant attention within the automatic control community due to their inherent complexities. While recent approaches rely on finite-dimensional optimization applied to discretized Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) approximations of these infinite-dimensional systems, we propose a Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) framework tailored for distributed and boundary control in infinite dimensions. Our method generalizes both the spatio-temporal Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) solution and contemporary finite-dimensional DDP techniques. We investigate the convergence properties of the resulting continuous-time forward-backward equations, providing a proof of global convergence. Furthermore, we develop numerical strategies to manage implementation sensitivities and apply the proposed STDDP algorithm to both linear and nonlinear spatio-temporal PDE systems. Derived within infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, this framework offers a discretization-agnostic approach for controlling nonlinear spatio-temporal PDE systems.

We established a perturbative framework for entropy dynamics that accounts for sudden system-bath coupling and remains valid in general environments without relying on the Markovian approximation. Separate perturbative formulas were derived for both bosonic and fermionic environments. Our findings indicate that the Renyi entropy response depends solely on the spectral functions of the system and environment, mediated by a specific statistical kernel distribution function. We observed a $t^2$ growth or decay for second Renyi entropy at short times, transitioning to linear ($t$) behavior at longer scales. Furthermore, we identified a generally non-monotonic Renyi entropy behavior in fermionic systems when the environment is cold. When two systems have similar temperatures, heat transport adheres to Fourier's law. A consistency check using the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model coupled to free fermions revealed Page-curve-like dynamics corresponding to a process dual to black hole evaporation. Finally, we detected oscillations in entanglement entropy arising from a gapped environmental spectrum.

Explainable machine learning models are gaining significant traction, particularly for mission-critical real-world applications where bias detection and risk mitigation are essential. While inherent interpretability—designing models from the ground up for transparency—offers intuitive insights, this paper introduces CoLabel, a novel approach to constructing interpretable models grounded in ground truth. We demonstrate CoLabel within a vehicle feature extraction task for vehicle make-model recognition (VMMR). The system leverages a composite of interpretable features, including vehicle color, type, and make, all derived from interpretable ground truth annotations. The process begins with corroborative integration to merge multiple datasets containing subsets of these desired annotations. Subsequently, CoLabel employs decomposable branches to extract complementary features aligned with specific annotations. Finally, these features are fused for prediction, during which CoLabel harmonizes the branches to ensure compatibility and project VMMR features into a unified semantic space for classification. Thanks to its inherent interpretability, CoLabel outperforms state-of-the-art black-box models, achieving accuracies of 0.98, 0.95, and 0.94 on the CompCars, Cars196, and BoxCars116K datasets, respectively. By providing intuitive explanations through constructive interpretability, CoLabel delivers both high accuracy and usability in critical scenarios.

The Quantum-Electrodynamical Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (QED-TDDFT) framework is implemented by evolving the wave function across a tensor product grid combining real space and Fock space. Applications to molecules within cavities demonstrate the method's precision, illustrating its ability to model the dependence of energies, wave functions, optical absorption spectra, and Rabi splitting on coupling strength and light frequency. Additionally, the approach successfully describes high harmonic generation phenomena occurring inside cavities.

This study evaluates the contributions of $\pi^\pm$ and $K^\pm$ box diagrams to the hadronic light-by-light component of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$. We calculate the associated electromagnetic form factors (EFFs) using the Dyson-Schwinger equations (DSE) framework in quantum chromodynamics. The computation employs the rainbow-ladder (RL) truncation via two distinct methods, followed by a more refined approximation that includes meson cloud effects. The resulting EFFs are mutually consistent, demonstrating that within the range relevant for $a_\mu$, they are practically identical. Our analysis produces combined estimates of $a_\mu^{\pi^\pm\text{-box}}=-(15.6\pm 0.2)\times 10^{-11}$ and $a_\mu^{K^\pm\text{-box}}=-(0.48\pm 0.02)\times 10^{-11}$, which align perfectly with prior DSE-based results and other current estimates.

This study introduces a novel class of renormalizable simplified dark matter models for LHC investigations, grounded in two-Higgs-doublet frameworks augmented by an additional pseudoscalar mediator. Unlike the spin-0 simplified models utilized in Run I analyses, these new models are self-consistent and unitary, with Higgs physics bounds generally imposing no restrictions. We examine predictions for various missing transverse energy ($E_{T, \rm miss}$) searches and investigate the discovery potential of the 13 TeV LHC. Our findings indicate that these models generate a diverse array of complementary observables resulting in significant constraints. Specifically, we highlight the sensitivity of the $t\bar t + E_{T, \rm miss}$, mono-$Z$, and mono-Higgs channels, which impose tighter limits than mono-jet searches across substantial regions of the parameter space. Furthermore, we derive constraints from spin-0 resonance searches, electroweak precision measurements, and flavor observables, demonstrating their value as crucial tools for testing and restricting these dark matter scenarios.

The unitary group operating on the Hilbert space of three qubits contains a Lie subgroup isomorphic to the symmetric group, which permutes the qubits. Under this group's action, the Hilbert space decomposes into three invariant subspaces with dimensions 4, 2, and 2, each forming an irreducible representation of su(2). The four-dimensional subspace is uniquely defined and represents the symmetric sector, containing states invariant under the symmetric group. We analyze the entanglement properties, separability criteria, and dynamics of pure states within this symmetric sector. Furthermore, we parametrize all possible invariant two-dimensional subspaces and extend our analysis to include them. We propose a physical model involving a symmetric network of three spin-1/2 particles driven by a common electromagnetic field. Within this framework, we address a control problem aimed at transforming a separable state into one possessing maximal distributed entanglement.

Driven by recent CDF and LHCb data suggesting significant annihilation contributions in nonleptonic B meson decays, alongside improved experimental precision, this paper investigates the magnitude of such contributions within the QCD factorization (QCDF) framework. Utilizing measurements of two-body $B_{u,d,s} \to \pi\pi, \pi K, KK$ decays, we perform a comprehensive fit on the phenomenological parameters $X_A^{i,f}$ (or $\rho_A^{i,f}$ and $\phi_A^{i,f}$), which parameterize endpoint singularities in annihilation amplitudes, employing a statistical $\chi^2$ method. Our findings indicate that: (1) flavor symmetry breaking effects are difficult to distinguish between $X_{A,s}^i$ and $X_{A,d}^i$—parameters governing nonfactorization annihilation in $B_s$ and $B_{u,d}$ decays, respectively—due to substantial experimental errors and theoretical uncertainties; thus, assuming $X_{A,s}^i = X_{A,d}^i$ is currently a valid approximation. (2) Theoretically, the parameter $X_A^f$, associated with factorization annihilation contributions and independent of the initial state, can be treated as a universal variable for $B_{u,d,s}$ decays. (3) Numerically, two solutions emerge: the first yields $(\rho_A^i, \phi_A^i) = (2.98^{+1.12}_{-0.86}, -105^{+34}_{-24})$ and $(\rho_A^f, \phi_A^f) = (1.18^{+0.20}_{-0.23}, -40^{+11}_{-8})$, while the second gives $(\rho_A^i, \phi_A^i) = (2.97^{+1.19}_{-0.90}, -105^{+32}_{-24})$ and $(\rho_A^f, \phi_A^f) = (2.80^{+0.25}_{-0.21}, 165^{+4}_{-3})$. Notably, the nonfactorization parameter $X_A^i$ generally differs from the factorization parameter $X_A^f$, contrasting with traditional approaches. Using these fitted parameters, all calculated observables for $B_{u,d,s} \to \pi\pi, \pi K, KK$ decays align well with experimental data.

We present quantum Monte Carlo results for electromagnetic transitions in 8Be. Using realistic Argonne v18 two-nucleon and Illinois-7 three-nucleon potentials, we construct the ground state and nine excited states, achieving energies that closely match experimental data. We subsequently evaluate a dozen M1 and eight E2 transition matrix elements among these states. The E2 calculations are restricted to the impulse approximation, with specific adjustments made for transitions involving broad resonant states. For M1 matrix elements, we incorporate two-body meson-exchange currents derived from chiral effective field theory, which generally account for 20–30% of the total expectation value. Since many transitions occur between isospin-mixed states, we perform calculations on isospin-pure states and apply empirical mixing coefficients for comparison, while also investigating alternative mixing schemes. Overall, our findings indicate that transitions between states sharing the same dominant spatial symmetry align reasonably well with experiment, whereas transitions between states of different spatial symmetries are frequently underpredicted.

This work examines the convex hull of a set $S$ defined by quadratic inequalities. A straightforward method to derive inequalities valid for $S$ involves forming nonnegative linear combinations of the set's defining constraints, a process we term "aggregations." Certain special aggregations inherently contain the convex hull of $S$, and we provide sufficient conditions under which these aggregations exactly define the convex hull. We introduce the concept of hidden hyperplane convexity (HHC), which extends the classical notion of hidden convexity for quadratic maps. We demonstrate that if the quadratic map associated with $S$ satisfies HHC, then the convex hull of $S$ is characterized by special aggregations. To our knowledge, this finding generalizes all existing results concerning aggregations that define convex hulls. Leveraging this sufficient condition, we identify previously unknown classes of sets for which aggregations yield the convex hull. Furthermore, we show that the combination of positive definite linear combinations and hidden hyperplane convexity constitutes a sufficient condition for a finite number of aggregations to define the convex hull. All aforementioned results apply to sets described by open quadratic inequalities; however, for sets defined by closed quadratic inequalities, we establish a new result regarding aggregations and the convex hull, free from topological assumptions on $S$.

Randomized Ensemble Double Q-learning (REDQ) (Chen et al., 2021b) has recently set a new benchmark for sample efficiency in continuous-action reinforcement learning, a feat enabled by its large Q-function ensemble. However, this approach comes at a significant computational cost compared to non-ensemble methods like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) (Haarnoja et al., 2018a). To address this inefficiency, we introduce DroQ, a computationally optimized variant of REDQ that employs a compact ensemble of dropout Q-functions. These functions are straightforward implementations featuring dropout connections and layer normalization. Despite their simplicity, experimental results demonstrate that DroQ achieves dual efficiency: it matches REDQ's sample efficiency while offering superior computational performance over REDQ and parity with SAC.

In a general Lorentzian manifold M, the past lightcone of a point constitutes a proper subset of M and lacks the necessary information to define the remainder of M. However, when M represents a globally hyperbolic Cauchy development of vacuum initial data on a Cauchy surface S, and a specific point has a past lightcone that encompasses S, the data within that lightcone uniquely determines the entire manifold M (up to isometry). This discussion presents findings regarding the properties of M that ensure past lightcones either fully determine or significantly constrain the manifold, with null lines and observer horizons—characteristic features of de-Sitter spacetime—playing a central role.

Biometric data offers a wealth of information for identifying individuals and inferring private details, creating significant privacy risks. To address this, anonymization techniques apply transformations to raw data to obscure sensitive information while maintaining its utility. Despite promising claims, these methods are often lacking in rigorous evaluation. Consequently, we investigated the effectiveness of recent face anonymization techniques by assessing their reversibility. Our methodology is technique-agnostic, utilizing a machine learning model trained on both original and anonymized datasets. Our findings reveal that 10 out of 14 tested techniques are at least partially reversible, with six exhibiting a high degree of reversibility.

Network Representation Learning (NRL) extends traditional graph mining techniques by addressing social networks, knowledge graphs, and intricate information networks in fields like biomedicine and physics. Although dozens of NRL algorithms have been documented, most concentrate on generating node embeddings for homogeneous networks, varying primarily in their encoding strategies and the specific semantic types of nodes they capture. This survey examines the design principles and diverse node embedding techniques applicable to homogeneous networks. To enable systematic comparison, we propose a unified reference framework that categorizes the node embedding learning process into preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training stages, tailored for NRL tasks such as link prediction and node clustering. Utilizing this framework, we highlight representative methods and models employed across each phase of the learning process. Consequently, this survey offers researchers and practitioners a deep comprehension of various NRL techniques while delivering practical guidance for developing future-generation NRL algorithms and systems.

Let $F_q$ denote a field containing $q$ elements, where $q$ is a power of a prime $p \geq 5$. For any integer $m \geq 2$ and element $a \in F_q^*$ such that the polynomial $x^m - a$ is irreducible over $F_q[x]$, we synthesize two distinct approaches to explicitly construct elements of high order within the quotient field $F_q[x]/\langle x^m - a \rangle$. Specifically, we identify elements possessing a multiplicative order of at least $5^{\sqrt[3]{m/2}}$, which surpasses the previously established bounds for this class of extension fields.
I demonstrate that if a geodesic space possesses a local lower curvature bound in the Alexandrov sense, then its completion inherits this same lower curvature bound globally.

Decentralized stochastic control (DSC) addresses the optimal control challenge within multi-agent systems; however, it remains unsolvable except for specific instances due to the generally intractable nature of inter-agent estimation. This study introduces memory-limited DSC (ML-DSC), a framework where each agent condenses its observation history into finite-dimensional memory. By simplifying inter-agent estimation through this compression, ML-DSC becomes solvable in broader scenarios utilizing mean-field control theory. We apply ML-DSC to the general Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) problem. Since estimation and control are not distinctly separated in the general LQG context, we modify the standard Riccati equation into a decentralized Riccati equation, which enhances both estimation and control performance. Numerical experiments indicate that this decentralized Riccati equation outperforms the conventional version.

Learning from data relies on tuning parameters like penalization strength or step size, making it crucial to evaluate entire classes of estimators—defined by finite sets of these parameters—rather than isolated, finely tuned methods. This study examines such classes by assessing the relative performance of the best method within them, focusing on linear regression with random isotropic ground truth. We analyze the estimation capabilities of two core approaches: gradient descent and ridge regression. Our findings reveal two key phenomena. First, for general designs, constant-stepsize gradient descent surpasses ridge regression when the eigenvalues of the empirical covariance matrix decay slowly (as a power law with an exponent less than one); conversely, if eigenvalues decay rapidly (with an exponent greater than one or exponentially), ridge regression outperforms gradient descent. Second, for orthogonal designs, we determine the exact minimax optimal class of estimators, which achieves min-max-min optimality and corresponds to gradient descent with a decaying learning rate, while identifying that both ridge regression and constant-stepsize gradient descent are suboptimal. These results underscore how statistical performance heavily depends on tuning parameters. Specifically, although optimally tuned ridge regression is the superior estimator in our setting, it can be surpassed by gradient descent by an arbitrary or unbounded margin when both are restricted to finite sets of regularization parameters.

This paper establishes the foundational framework for a project initiated by Felix Rehren, which seeks to classify all 2-generated primitive axial algebras of Monster type $(\alpha, \beta)$. Initially, we revisit Rehren's construction of an initial object within the category of primitive $n$-generated axial algebras, formalizing it to address gaps and correct inaccuracies while validating his original findings. Subsequently, we examine 2-generated algebras, dividing them into three categories: two critical cases where $\alpha=2\beta$ and $\alpha=4\beta$, and a generic case comprising all other scenarios. While detailed analysis of these cases will appear in future publications, we currently provide dimension bounds (with the generic case already addressed by Rehren) and classify all such algebras over $\mathbb Q(\alpha, \beta)$ when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are algebraically independent indeterminates over $\mathbb Q$.
