Furthermore, these algebras exhibit robust congruence properties that can be reflected back onto the posets, and we highlight their relevance to specific non-classical logical systems.

Accurate segmentation of brain tumors (BTS) from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data is essential for diagnosis, treatment planning, and research. Despite the significant progress in the ten-year BraTS challenges and the advancements of CNN and Transformer architectures, numerous high-performing BTS models have struggled to address specific technical hurdles, particularly in the rational fusion of multi-modality images. To address this, we introduce CKD-TransBTS, a clinical knowledge-driven segmentation model that incorporates radiologists' diagnostic principles regarding multiple MRI modalities. Rather than simple concatenation, our approach reorganizes input data into two distinct groups based on MRI imaging principles. We employ a dual-branch hybrid encoder featuring a novel modality-correlated cross-attention (MCCA) block to extract multi-modal features. This model combines the long-range extraction capabilities of Transformers with the precise local feature representation of CNNs, which is vital for defining lesion boundaries in 3D volumetric images. Furthermore, to harmonize features between these two architectures, we implement a Trans&CNN Feature Calibration (TCFC) block within the decoder. Evaluated against five CNN-based and six Transformer-based models on the BraTS 2021 dataset, extensive experiments confirm that CKD-TransBTS achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming all competing methods.

This paper investigates the finite boundary regularity and estimates for asymptotically hyperbolic Einstein manifolds in even dimensions $n+1$. We demonstrate that if the initial compactification possesses $C^{n-1}$ regularity and its $(n-3)$-th scalar curvature derivative is H\"older continuous, the AHE metric becomes $C^{m,\alpha}$ conformally compact, assuming the boundary metric is $C^{m,\alpha}$. This result improves upon Helliwell's findings and includes an estimate for the Yamabe compactification metric within this new framework.
We offer an alternative derivation of a quantum-mechanical extension to the work penalty equation, originally introduced as Eq. (6) in Phys. Rev. Lett., 127, 190602 (2021).

We present a hybrid method for achieving Bose-Einstein condensation of metastable Helium-4 atoms, combining a magnetic quadrupole with a crossed optical dipole trap. This setup successfully crosses the phase transition with 2x10^6 atoms, yielding pure condensates of 5x10^5 atoms within the optical trap. This innovative cooling technique for Helium-4 offers superior cycle stability and excellent optical accessibility, producing a condensate every 6 seconds—three times faster than current state-of-the-art methods. This significant acceleration will substantially shorten the data acquisition time required for measuring many-body correlations, leveraging the capability of individual detection in metastable Helium.

The Epidemic Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model is a cornerstone for analyzing seismic sequences and serves as the foundation for Operational Earthquake Forecasting (OEF). Nevertheless, evaluating the reliability of inverted ETAS parameters is difficult due to several factors. Most standard algorithms provide only point estimates with minimal uncertainty quantification, while Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods are often computationally slow, lack scalability, and rarely incorporate spatial structures. This study introduces a novel ETAS modeling approach utilizing the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). We have developed a new R-package, ETAS.inlabru, which leverages R-INLA and inlabru; although this release focuses on the temporal component, the framework supports spatio-temporal modeling with various spatial covariates. Through synthetic case studies, we investigated the robustness of our inversion technique. Our results indicate that reliable parameter estimates necessitate catalog data containing both triggered sequences and periods of relative quiescence. We further demonstrated the method's resilience against stochastic uncertainty in training data and its insensitivity to a wide range of initial conditions. Additionally, we examined how incorporating historical earthquakes prior to the modeled period influences inversion quality. Finally, we found that rate-dependent incompleteness following major earthquakes significantly degrades ETAS posteriors. We contend that the computational efficiency of the inlabru inversion, combined with rigorous uncertainty estimation, will facilitate a more thorough investigation into the robust application of ETAS for seismicity modeling and operational earthquake forecasting.

Although pretrained language models have greatly enhanced downstream language understanding tasks, such as extractive question answering, through high-quality contextualized word embeddings, training these models still necessitates extensive annotated data for specific domains. This paper introduces RGX, a cooperative self-training framework designed to automatically produce non-trivial question-answer pairs and boost model performance. Built on a masked answer extraction task, RGX operates within an interactive learning environment comprising an answer entity Recognizer, a question Generator, and an answer eXtractor. When presented with a passage containing a masked entity, the Generator formulates a question centered on that entity, while the Extractor is trained to retrieve the masked entity using both the generated question and the original text. This framework enables the training of question generation and answering models on any text corpus without requiring annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that RGX surpasses state-of-the-art pretrained language models and transfer learning methods on standard question-answering benchmarks, achieving new state-of-the-art performance under specific model size and transfer learning configurations.

Using the resummed perturbation method within the Gribov-Zwanziger framework at finite temperature, the interaction potential between a heavy quark pair is evaluated. The inclusion of resummed loop corrections renders the potential complex. While the real component, as anticipated, exhibits screening and transitions to a short-range interaction in a hot medium, the magnitude of the imaginary component grows with temperature and becomes comparable to the real part, marking a significant departure from prior calculations using the HTL approach. Consequently, both color screening and Landau damping are crucial factors in the dissociation of heavy flavor hadrons within a hot environment.

To alleviate the burden on physicians, research into automatic medical report generation using deep learning has intensified. This field increasingly combines encoder-decoder frameworks with attention mechanisms and reinforcement learning to boost model performance. Nevertheless, current state-of-the-art approaches face two primary limitations: (i) their attention mechanisms fail to leverage high-order feature interactions, and (ii) reliance on TF-IDF-based reward functions makes them prone to generating repetitive terms. To address these issues, this study introduces ReMRG-XR, a reinforcement learning-based framework featuring x-linear attention and repetition penalty mechanisms. Specifically, the x-linear attention modules facilitate the exploration of high-order feature interactions and enable multi-modal reasoning, while the repetition penalty mechanism discourages the generation of repeated terms during training. Comprehensive experiments conducted on two public datasets demonstrate that ReMRG-XR significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines across all evaluation metrics.

Time series classification remains a significant area of study within machine learning. Although accuracy is typically the primary metric, certain applications necessitate rapid decision-making, requiring an optimization strategy that balances earliness with accuracy. This paper introduces a generic, end-to-end trainable framework designed for early time series classification. The proposed system incorporates a learnable decision mechanism compatible with a broad spectrum of existing models. Experimental results using deep neural networks across various time series tasks demonstrate that our approach performs competitively against state-of-the-art methods and is easily adaptable to any neural network architecture that assesses a hidden state at each time step.

Anderson localization represents the widespread suppression of transport for both classical and quantum waves within disordered environments. In one-dimensional systems, it is established that all states become localized; consequently, an initially narrow wave packet released into a disordered potential will exhibit an exponential decay at long times, governed by the localization length. Nevertheless, the precise form of the stationary localized distribution deviates from a simple exponential profile, a result originally calculated by Gogolin nearly half a century ago. Leveraging the atomic quantum kicked rotor as a quintessential quantum simulator for Anderson localization, we investigate this asymptotic distribution through two distinct methods. First, we explore the relationship between the statistical characteristics of the system's localized eigenfunctions and their exponential decay relative to the Gogolin localization length. Subsequently, utilizing our experimental setup to create an ideal Floquet disordered system, we measure the long-term probability distribution. Our results demonstrate excellent agreement with the analytical prediction, showing significant deviation from a purely exponential profile across three orders of magnitude.

In recent years, Deep Learning (DL) has gained immense popularity. Although initially celebrated for image classification and manipulation, DL applications in biomedical sciences have expanded significantly. However, the inherent complexity and prevalence of missing data in biomedical datasets pose substantial hurdles for DL methods. This work offers a formal approach to handling missing data within Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), a widely used unsupervised DL architecture for dimensionality reduction, imputation, and learning latent representations. We introduce NIMIWAE, a novel VAE architecture that is among the first to flexibly address both ignorable and non-ignorable missingness patterns during training. Post-training, samples drawn from the approximate posterior distribution of the missing data enable multiple imputation, supporting downstream analyses of high-dimensional incomplete datasets. Statistical simulations demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches in both unsupervised learning tasks and imputation accuracy. Finally, we present a case study involving an electronic health record dataset of 12,000 ICU patients, characterized by numerous partially observed diagnostic measurements and clinical outcomes.

This paper introduces a model for optimally training a rational agent who exhibits sluggishness. In this framework, a trainer commits to a discrete-time, finite-state Markov process that dictates the trajectory of training intensity. The agent then observes the current state and incrementally adjusts their capacity at each period, with changes restricted to single-unit steps. The trainer aims to maximize the agent's long-run capacity—specifically defined by the minimum capacity level reached under the invariant distribution—while adhering to a cap on average training intensity. We derive the trainer's optimal strategy and demonstrate that stochastic, time-varying training intensity can significantly enhance the long-term capacity of such an agent. Finally, we connect these theoretical results to periodization methods used in exercise physiology.

We calculate the third-order moments of a complex Wigner matrix by deriving a formula for $\alpha_{m_1,m_2,m_3}$ involving quotient graphs $T_{m_1,m_2,m_3}^{\pi}$, where $\pi$ represents the Kreweras complement of a non-crossing pairing on an annulus. By demonstrating that these graphs can be enumerated using partitioned permutations, we express the third-order moments in terms of high-order free cumulants, which admit a straightforward formulation.

How much do the assumptions underlying our models influence estimates of nonpharmaceutical intervention (NPI) effectiveness against COVID-19? To address this, we examined two leading NPI effectiveness models and developed six variants incorporating distinct structural assumptions. Specifically, we assessed how well these estimates generalize to countries not included in the training data and their sensitivity to unobserved factors. Models that incorporate noise in disease transmission demonstrated superior performance. We also evaluated the robustness of these estimates regarding varying epidemiological parameters and data choices. Focusing on models that account for transmission noise, we found that previously published results remain remarkably stable across these variables. Finally, we provided a mathematical foundation for interpreting NPI effectiveness estimates in scenarios where common assumptions fail.

This paper investigates the antenna selection (AS) problem within full-duplex (FD) cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks, where a multi-antenna FD relay facilitates communication between a multi-antenna base station and a NOMA far user. We propose two AS strategies, max-$\SUu$ and max-$\SUuu$, designed to maximize the end-to-end signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio for the near user, the far user, or both. Additionally, we introduce a two-stage QoS provisioning AS scheme that ensures a target rate for the far user while simultaneously boosting the near user's rate. To further optimize this QoS scheme, dynamic antenna clustering is employed at the relay to adaptively divide its antennas into transmit and receive groups. We derive exact expressions for the outage probability and achievable rates of the proposed schemes, and obtain closed-form asymptotic outage probability formulas for the max-$\SUu$ and max-$\SUuu$ approaches to offer deeper insights. Simulation results indicate that while the QoS provisioning scheme achieves near-optimal performance with a static relay antenna configuration, it yields up to a $12\%$ average sum rate improvement compared to optimal AS selection under a fixed antenna setup.

We adapt an established method for identifying ideal classes of any order and apply it to three distinct families of number fields. First, we demonstrate that within a family of cyclic sextic fields, there exist infinitely many instances containing a relative ideal class of order $r$, where $r$ is a positive integer coprime to the extension degree. Similarly, we establish that this property holds for a family of cyclic quartic fields. Although this technique is conventionally used for Galois extensions, we illustrate its adaptation to a family of non-Galois cubic fields, proving that this family also contains infinitely many fields with ideal classes of arbitrary order relatively prime to three.

The surge in deepfake media has sparked significant concern among both the public and relevant authorities, making the development of countermeasures against forged faces on social media a critical priority. This paper introduces a comprehensive study of two novel countermeasure tasks: multi-face forgery detection and segmentation in the wild. Identifying forged faces among multiple individuals in unrestricted natural scenes presents a far greater challenge than traditional deepfake recognition. To advance these emerging fields, we have established OpenForensics, the first large-scale dataset designed with face-wise rich annotations specifically for forgery detection and segmentation, offering a high level of difficulty. Beyond its utility in deepfake prevention, the extensive annotations in OpenForensics hold significant potential for research in general human face detection. Furthermore, we have developed a suite of benchmarks by rigorously evaluating state-of-the-art instance detection and segmentation methods across various scenarios using our new dataset. The dataset, benchmark results, code, and supplementary materials will be made publicly accessible at our project page: https://sites.google.com/view/ltnghia/research/openforensics.

Transformer-based pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success across most traditional NLP tasks, yet they frequently falter when numerical comprehension is required. This limitation may stem from tokenizers and pre-training objectives that are not explicitly crafted to acquire and maintain numeracy skills. This study examines the capacity of the text-to-text transfer learning model (T5)—which has surpassed its predecessors in standard NLP applications—to grasp numerical concepts. We evaluated T5 on four specific numeracy tasks: numeration, predicting magnitude order, identifying minimum and maximum values within a sequence, and sorting. Our findings indicate that while T5 models perform adequately in interpolation scenarios, they face significant difficulties in extrapolation settings across all four tasks.

This work investigates dynamical systems arising from skew products defined by $T(x,y)=(bx\mod1,\gamma y+\phi(x))$, where $b$ is an integer greater than or equal to 2, $0<\gamma<1$, and $\phi$ is a real analytic function with period 1. We establish a dichotomy regarding the SRB measure $\omega$ for $T$: either the support of $\omega$ constitutes the graph of a real analytic function, or its dimension equals $\min\{2,1+\frac{\log b}{\log(1/\gamma)}\}$. Additionally, for fixed $b$ and $\phi$, the first scenario occurs for only a finite number of $\gamma$ values unless $\phi$ is constant.

Multimodal conditional generation, encompassing text-to-image synthesis and image translation, is a rapidly evolving field. Recent advancements in manipulating images through linguistic prompts have introduced novel challenges in this domain. Nevertheless, existing conditional image generation models primarily prioritize producing high-quality, photorealistic visuals, often neglecting the alignment between the image and the specific partial details of the instruction. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Increment Reasoning Generative Adversarial Network (IR-GAN), designed to reconcile semantic increments in instructions with visual increments in images. Our approach begins by employing word-level and instruction-level encoders to extract user intent from contextually related historical instructions as semantic increments. Subsequently, we integrate the representation of these semantic increments into the source image embedding to facilitate target image generation, treating the source image as a referential aid. Finally, we develop a reasoning discriminator to evaluate the consistency between visual and semantic changes, thereby refining user intent and ensuring the logical coherence of the generated output. Comprehensive experiments and visualizations across two datasets demonstrate the efficacy of IR-GAN.

The standard Einstein relation, which links the ambipolar diffusion coefficient and the Dember field to carrier mobilities, is extended to account for an interacting electron-hole plasma. Calculations are provided for non-degenerate plasmas generated by light injection in silicon and germanium semiconductors, incorporating Debye-Hückel correlations and Wigner-Seitz exchange effects. The analysis also considers corrections to carrier mobilities arising from the discrepancy between average and effective electric fields within the plasma. This generalized relation significantly diverges from the conventional Einstein relation at low temperatures, offering a potential explanation for the recently observed experimental anomalies in the ambipolar diffusion coefficient.

This research investigates the superheavy dark matter (DM) scenario within an extended $B-L$ framework, where a single generation of right-handed neutrino ($\nu_R$) serves as the DM candidate. The presence of a lighter sterile neutrino that co-annihilates with the DM exponentially boosts the annihilation rate, enabling a DM mass significantly exceeding the Griest-Kamionkowski bound ($\sim10^5$ GeV). We demonstrate that DM masses of $M_{\nu_R}\gtrsim10^{13}$ GeV are achievable. Although this mass scale lies beyond the reach of conventional DM detection methods, the scenario remains testable through gravitational waves (GWs) generated by cosmic strings arising from the $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry breaking. Quantitative analyses indicate that future GW detectors can probe DM masses in the range of $\mathcal{O}(10^9-10^{13}~{\rm GeV})$.

Managing cattle across vast territories remains a significant challenge for the agricultural industry. As technology advances, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with consumer-grade digital cameras have emerged as a popular, safer, and more cost-effective alternative to manual livestock counts for estimation purposes. This study assessed and compared state-of-the-art object detection algorithms, including YOLOv7, RetinaNet with a ResNet50 backbone, RetinaNet with EfficientNet, and Mask R-CNN. The primary objective was to enhance the detection of occluded cattle within extensive drone-captured datasets using deep learning techniques for improved accuracy. Experimental findings indicated that YOLOv7 outperformed the other algorithms, achieving a precision of 0.612. The proposed approach demonstrated superiority over standard competing methods in detecting cow faces, particularly under difficult conditions.

This research extends the Pokrovski--Vinogradov model, originally describing flows of incompressible viscoelastic polymeric solutions and melts, to encompass nonisothermal conditions within an infinite planar channel subjected to a magnetic field. For the linearized scenario—where the base state mirrors classical Poiseuille flow for a Navier-Stokes viscous fluid—we derive a formal asymptotic representation for eigenvalues as their modulus increases. Furthermore, we establish a necessary condition ensuring the asymptotic stability of Poiseuille-type shear flows.

We introduce multiple findings within the CONGEST model regarding the round complexity of Replacement Paths (RPaths), Minimum Weight Cycles (MWC), and All Nodes Shortest Cycles (ANSC). These core problems are examined across both directed and undirected graphs, as well as weighted and unweighted variants. Our results are largely optimal up to a polylogarithmic factor: for an $n$-node graph $G$, we demonstrate near-linear lower and upper bounds for RPaths in directed weighted graphs, and for MWC and ANSC in weighted graphs regardless of directionality. Additionally, we establish bounds near $\sqrt{n}$ for undirected weighted RPaths and a $\Theta(D)$ bound for undirected unweighted RPaths. We further provide bounds for approximate versions of these challenges, including a $(2-(1/g))$-approximation algorithm for undirected unweighted MWC that executes in $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}+D)$ rounds, surpassing the prior best of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{ng}+D)$ rounds (where $g$ denotes MWC length). Moreover, we present algorithms for $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation of directed weighted RPaths and $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation of weighted undirected MWC for any constant $\epsilon > 0$, both of which achieve better round complexity than the lower bound for exact solutions.

Machine Learning (ML) routines are increasingly utilized by mobile applications for data analysis. Performing these tasks locally on user devices reduces the energy consumption associated with transmitting and processing large datasets on remote cloud servers. However, limited memory and computational power often prevent these devices from supporting resource-heavy ML routines, leading to inaccurate task execution. This study addresses edge-assisted analytics in resource-constrained environments by introducing and assessing a rigorous selective offloading framework. Under this framework, devices perform tasks locally and delegate them to cloudlet servers only when a substantial performance gain is anticipated. The research considers a realistic scenario where offloading benefits and resource costs fluctuate over time, proposing an online optimization algorithm that maximizes service performance without prior knowledge of these variables. Our method employs an approximate dual subgradient method integrated with a primal-averaging scheme, functioning under minimal assumptions regarding system stochasticity. We implemented the proposed algorithm in a wireless testbed and evaluated it using a state-of-the-art image recognition application, demonstrating significant improvements in performance and cost efficiency.

Integrating Josephson weak links made from semiconducting nanowires with circuit QED methods has allowed researchers to resolve fine structures arising from spin-orbit interactions, thereby paving the way for Andreev spin qubits. However, directly manipulating spins within a specific Andreev state is generally more difficult than performing inter-doublet manipulations when Zeeman effects are absent. Furthermore, noisy spin-flip mechanisms restrict coherent manipulation strategies to post-selection based on spin states. We propose a hybrid approach that combines a spin polarization protocol resembling sideband cooling with stimulated Raman adiabatic passage, specifically adapted for these systems. We demonstrate that this method remains robust across a wide range of design parameters, even under the currently stringent constraints of coherence times.

Light curves from fast-rotating, early-type stars hosting tidally locked hot Jupiters offer valuable insights into both the host star and the planet, particularly because full-phase coverage allows for detailed atmospheric analysis. While transit asymmetries caused by rotation-induced gravity darkening theoretically permit the calculation of the true spin-orbit angle $\Psi$—a notoriously difficult parameter to constrain—correlations among transit parameters have historically led to significant discrepancies in published values for certain systems. This study investigated these phenomena using the ultra-hot Jupiter MASCARA-1 b. By combining optical CHEOPS transit and occultation data with a full-phase Spitzer/IRAC 4.5 $\mu$m curve, we found that jointly fitting the transits significantly reduces degeneracies, yielding results consistent with prior Doppler tomography studies. Incorporating priors based on tomography further improved precision, resulting in a measured spin-orbit angle of $\Psi=72.1^{+2.5}_{-2.4}$ deg. Analysis of occultations and phase variations revealed dayside and nightside temperatures of $3062^{+66}_{-68}$ K and $1720\pm330$ K, respectively. Additionally, CHEOPS data enabled the separate derivation of geometric albedo ($A_g=0.171^{+0.066}_{-0.068}$) and spherical albedo ($A_s=0.266^{+0.097}_{-0.100}$), while the Spitzer phase curve yielded a Bond albedo of $A_B=0.057^{+0.083}_{-0.101}$. We conclude that using Doppler tomography-informed priors during transit fitting of fast-rotating stars is preferable where feasible, although multi-colour photometry may also facilitate accurate $\Psi$ measurements. Furthermore, our methodology for modeling phase variations across different wavelengths establishes a framework for disentangling thermal emission from reflected light in future spectrally resolved JWST phase curves.

Molecular cations are abundant in diverse astronomical settings, particularly in cometary atmospheres and tails, where solar radiation generates intense near-ultraviolet to visible emissions. These cations generally exhibit brighter electronic emissions at longer wavelengths compared to their neutral counterparts. A comprehensive grasp of their near-UV to visible characteristics would enable their use as probes for local plasma conditions or as tracers for neutral gas within cometary systems. However, constructing complete spectral models for small, oxygen-containing molecular cations remains unfeasible due to current limitations in available molecular data. While the five simplest species—H₂O⁺, CO₂⁺, CO⁺, OH⁺, and O₂⁺—are well-characterized in certain spectral regions, they lack robust reference data in others. These knowledge gaps impede the creation of fully quantitative models of cometary spectra, specifically hindering accurate assessments of physical-chemical processes derived from the most prevalent cometary molecules. This work compiles existing spectral data for these species and identifies critical areas requiring future research, particularly where data scarcity significantly limits our understanding of cometary evolution.

This work focuses on the practical execution of summing out, expanding, and reordering messages within Local Conditioning (LC) for undirected networks. Specifically, incoming messages, which may be conditioned on varying subsets of the receiving node's relevant set, must first be expanded to align with this set and then reordered to facilitate the fusion of corresponding matrix columns via element-wise multiplication. Subsequently, an outgoing message is reduced by summing out loop cutset nodes located upstream of the outgoing edge. The study's main contribution lies in its implementation focus, distinguishing it from the theoretical foundation of LC provided by Fay et al. However, it is noted that for grid networks, the complexity of Local Conditioning remains comparable to that of Clustering.

This research synthesizes three key areas of dissimilarity-based clustering into a unified, principled functorial framework. These sources include Jardine and Sibson's overlapping clustering, Carlsson and Mémoli's functorial treatment of partition-based clustering, and the Isbell/Dress tradition of studying injective envelopes. Building on Carlsson and Mémoli's concept of treating clustering methods as functors mapping metric spaces to clusters—where functoriality encapsulates numerous desirable traits—our initial results extend this theory to accommodate overlapping clusters, aligning with Jardine and Sibson's approach. This extension eliminates certain negative chaining effects seen in methods like single-linkage clustering. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between these general overlapping clustering functors and projections of weight spaces onto what we call clustering domains, grounded in the order structure defined by morphisms. As a concrete application, we demonstrate that no functorial projections exist to cut metrics or even to tree metrics. Finally, while our primary focus is on clustering domains rather than methods derived from injective envelopes, we present preliminary findings to illustrate the role of this third foundational element.

Interpersonal trust, defined as a mutual expression of confidence and vulnerability among individuals, plays a crucial role in the evolution of human societies. Safra, Chevallier, Grézes, and Baumard (2020) investigated the historical trajectory of this trust by employing a machine learning algorithm to assign trustworthiness scores to historical portraits based on facial characteristics. Their findings indicated that these scores rose between 1500 and 2000 CE, which they interpreted as evidence of a general increase in interpersonal trust aligned with various indicators of societal advancement. We contend that these conclusions are compromised by multiple methodological and analytical flaws and draw concerning parallels between Safra et al.'s algorithm and the discredited pseudoscience of physiognomy. We elaborate further on the implications and potential real-world ramifications of these shortcomings.

Three-dimensional space is defined as spherically symmetric when it admits the SO(3) group as its isometry group. Under this symmetry constraint, the vacuum Einstein Field Equations yield the Schwarzschild Metric as the unique solution, which effectively constitutes the well-known Birkhoff's Theorem. Geometrically, this theorem asserts that pseudo-Riemannian space-times possess more isometries than anticipated from the initial metric holonomy or ansatz. In this study, we employ Lie Symmetry Analysis to examine the vacuum Einstein Field Equations and derive the symmetry generators of the associated differential equations. Furthermore, by applying the Noether Point Symmetry method, we have determined the conserved quantities linked to the generators of the Schwarzschild Lagrangian, thereby opening a new pathway to reformulate Birkhoff's Theorem from an alternative perspective.

Estimating treatment effects from observational data remains a core challenge in causal inference. Existing approaches address this by leveraging inductive biases and heuristics to construct multi-head neural networks and regularizers. This study introduces neurosymbolic program synthesis—a technique valued for its data efficiency and interpretability—as a solution to treatment effect estimation. We provide theoretical proof that neurosymbolic programming can effectively resolve this problem. By developing a Domain Specific Language (DSL) grounded in the inductive biases prevalent in current literature, we contend that neurosymbolic programming offers a superior alternative to traditional methods. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that this approach, which embeds inductive biases directly into the DSL, outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets.

SciPy serves as an open-source scientific computing library designed for Python. Its 1.0 version launched in late 2017, marking roughly 16 years since the initial 0.1 release. Now recognized as the standard for applying scientific algorithms within Python, SciPy boasts over 600 unique contributors, thousands of dependent packages, more than 100,000 dependent repositories, and millions of annual downloads. Its adoption is widespread, covering nearly half of all machine learning projects on GitHub and supporting high-profile initiatives such as LIGO's gravitational wave analysis and the generation of the first image of a black hole (M87). The library offers a broad spectrum of tools, including statistics, signal processing, sparse matrix operations, computational geometry, linear algebra, integration, interpolation, Fourier transforms, clustering, image processing, orthogonal distance regression, minimization algorithms, and file I/O. This paper provides an overview of SciPy's capabilities and development methodologies, emphasizing recent technical advancements.

In a previous work, the authors established a flat projective connection on the bundle of nonabelian theta functions associated with the moduli space of semistable parabolic G-bundles over families of smooth projective curves marked with points, where G is a simple, simply connected complex algebraic group. This paper demonstrates that the identification linking the bundle of nonabelian theta functions to the bundle of WZNW conformal blocks remains flat under both this newly constructed connection and the one developed by Tsuchiya-Ueno-Yamada. Furthermore, as a practical application, we provide a geometric derivation of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov connection on a trivial bundle defined over the configuration space of points in the projective line, where the typical fiber corresponds to the space of invariants arising from a tensor product of representations.

Automating action recognition from video streams is a difficult endeavor, particularly when constrained by legacy hardware. This project pursues two primary objectives: first, to detect actions using the front-facing camera on Android devices, and second, to ensure compatibility across the widest possible range of Android versions and phone models. These constraints necessitate the use of compact models capable of running on mobile devices regardless of GPU presence, relying exclusively on camera input for recognition. The paper evaluates the performance of the YOLO architecture across various devices (both with and without dedicated GPUs) using models trained on a custom dataset. Furthermore, it examines the inherent limitations of recognizing facial expressions and actions on hardware with restricted capabilities.

Recent data from proton-proton collisions at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of \sqrt{s} = 7 TeV reveal two new bottom hadrons. The ATLAS experiment detected a novel state in radiative transitions to \Upsilon(1S) and \Upsilon(2S), identifying it as the first observation of \chi_b(3P) states. Meanwhile, the CMS experiment observed a new bottom baryon decaying into \Xi_b-\pi+ (and its charge conjugate), which is classified as a neutral J^P = 3/2^+ \Xi_b* baryon.

The compact semi-major axes of Hot Jupiters result in atmospheric temperatures reaching several thousand Kelvin. Under such extreme conditions, thermally ionized metals generate abundant charged particles, creating significant electrical conductivity. While electromagnetic phenomena like induced currents, Ohmic heating, magnetic drag, and the suppression of zonal winds have traditionally been analyzed using linear, steady-state induction models, the situation differs for Hot Jupiters with equilibrium temperatures exceeding 1500 K. In these cases, the induction of atmospheric magnetic fields becomes a runaway process that requires non-linear feedback mechanisms—such as the Lorentz force's back-reaction on fluid flow or magnetic instabilities—to halt. We also examine the potential for self-excited atmospheric dynamos. Our findings indicate that induced magnetic fields and currents decouple from electrical conductivity and internal fields, instead being constrained by the planet's rotation rate and wind velocity. Specifically, we analyze the induction process for KELT-9b, the hottest known exoplanet, by computing electrical conductivity along day- and nightside pressure-temperature profiles. Despite temperature fluctuations between 3000 K and 4500 K, conductivity remains consistently high at approximately 1 S/m. The resulting magnetic fields are primarily horizontal, potentially saturating at 400 mT, which is two orders of magnitude stronger than the internal magnetic field.

This study examines a quark-antiquark effective model within a toroidal topology at finite temperatures. The system is governed by a Schrödinger equation featuring a linear potential embedded in a torus. Four key areas are investigated: (i) the nonclassical structure via the Wigner function formalism; (ii) the impact of finite temperature and system size, analyzed through a phase-space generalization of Thermofield Dynamics; (iii) the inclusion of quark spin using a Pauli-like Schrödinger equation; and (iv) the analysis of size-induced fluctuations in the ground state. The findings indicate that the size effect vanishes at zero, finite, and high temperatures. Overall, the results underscore the critical role of spin within this quark-antiquark effective model.

This research details the development, numerical implementation, and validation of a theoretical framework grounded in variable-order mechanics, designed to simulate dynamic fracture in brittle and quasi-brittle materials. Specifically, recasting the elastodynamic problem using variable and fractional-order operators provides a highly effective method for modeling crack nucleation and propagation under dynamic loads. The resulting formulation is entirely evolutionary, allowing for the analysis of intricate crack patterns without prior assumptions regarding damage locations or growth trajectories, nor the need for algorithms to track the evolving crack surface. Furthermore, the evolutionary nature of this variable-order approach eliminates the requirement for additional partial differential equations to predict the damage field, significantly reducing computational costs. Notably, this formulation naturally captures fine-scale features of dynamic crack propagation, such as surface roughening and both single and multiple branching. The accuracy and robustness of the proposed variable-order method are confirmed by comparing direct numerical simulation results with experimental data from benchmark problems found in existing literature.

Using Keldysh Green functions, we derive exact analytical formulas for currents and current correlation functions within a Cooper pair splitter model consisting of a double quantum dot system coherently linked to a superconductor and two normal metallic electrodes. By restricting our analysis to the inter-dot singlet subspace, we demonstrate perfect entanglement of split electrons occurring through two separated crossed Andreev reflection processes. The investigation centers on the noise power spectrum across the entire bias voltage range. Specifically, in the large voltage limit, shot noise prevails, and its spectrum displays two distinctive side dips resulting from resonant inter-level current correlations driven by coherent electron-hole recombination accompanied by photon emission and absorption. In the linear response regime, we calculated the frequency-dependent admittance, revealing distinct interference patterns for both cross and auto current correlations.

String diagrams constitute a potent and intuitive graphical language rooted in symmetric monoidal categories. Over the past few years, they have been increasingly utilized to model diverse computational structures across disciplines ranging from Computer Science and Physics to Control Theory, Linguistics, and Biology. In numerous such frameworks, system transformations are represented as rewrite rules applied to diagrams; however, these advancements necessitate a rigorous mathematical basis for string diagram rewriting. While rewrite theory for terms is well-established, the two-dimensional nature of string diagrams introduces unique complexities.

This research organizes and extends recent conference work establishing such a foundation. Initially, the study focuses on rewrite systems for string diagrammatic theories incorporating Frobenius algebras. Such structures are ubiquitous: for example, in the algebraic semantics of linear dynamical systems, Frobenius structures represent circuit wiring, while in categorical quantum mechanics, they model interacting quantum observables.

The proposed work offers a combinatorial interpretation of string diagram rewriting modulo Frobenius structures using double-pushout hypergraph rewriting. We demonstrate that this interpretation is both sound and complete. Furthermore, the approach is generalized to handle rewriting modulo multiple Frobenius structures. As a proof of concept, we apply these findings to derive a termination strategy for Interacting Bialgebras, a critical rewrite theory within the analysis of quantum circuits and signal flow graphs.

Within the framework of the LHC Injector Upgrade (LIU) Project at CERN, a new beam dump has been designed, constructed, installed, and operated to safely handle the future proton beam extracted from the Proton Synchrotron Booster (PSB). Following upgrades scheduled for CERN's Long Shutdown 2 (2019-2020), this beam is expected to deliver up to 1E14 protons per pulse at 2 GeV. To efficiently dissipate the heat generated by the primary beam, the new dump was engineered as a cylindrical assembly of copper alloy, utilizing forced airflow for cooling. Monte Carlo simulations using the FLUKA code were conducted to determine the energy density distribution deposited by the beam, with subsequent thermo-mechanical analyses performed in ANSYS by importing these energy density values. Additionally, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of the airflow were executed to accurately estimate the heat transfer convection coefficient on the dump's surface. This paper outlines the design process, emphasizes the constraints and challenges involved in integrating a new dump for increased beam power into the existing facility, and presents operational data.

We introduce a framework designed to demonstrate the rapid convergence of shifted QR algorithms that utilize Ritz values as shifts within finite arithmetic. Our primary contribution is a dichotomy result that tackles the established forward-instability problems associated with the shifted QR iteration [Parlett and Le 1993]. This result provides a procedure that either reliably computes a set of approximate Ritz values for a Hessenberg matrix with strong forward stability, or achieves early decoupling of the matrix through a minimal number of QR steps. Leveraging this framework, we establish that the shifting strategy proposed in Part I of this series [Banks, Garza-Vargas, and Srivastava 2021] achieves rapid convergence in finite arithmetic, requiring only a polylogarithmic bound on the bits of precision needed, provided the matrices have controlled eigenvector condition numbers and sufficient minimum eigenvalue gaps.

To date, the absence of axion detections has necessitated a substantial separation between the Peccei-Quinn and electroweak symmetry breaking scales, which in turn imposes significant fine-tuning on the Standard Model Higgs via the unavoidable Higgs portal. However, if the Peccei-Quinn global symmetry possesses residual discrete symmetries, these combined symmetries can facilitate symmetry breaking at low energy scales, such as the accessible TeV range. This innovative mechanism allows for new phenomena, including a substantial coupling between the Standard Model Higgs boson and the axion.

We introduce a gravitational dual describing a local operator quench within a two-dimensional CFT featuring conformal boundaries. This system corresponds to a massive excitation in a three-dimensional AdS space containing an end-of-the-world (EOW) brane. Owing to gravitational backreaction, the EOW brane undergoes a nontrivial deformation. We demonstrate that the energy-momentum tensor and entanglement entropy, when calculated via both the gravity dual and the BCFT in the large $c$ limit, align precisely. Notably, this comparison elegantly circumvents the need to fold the EOW brane.

Stereo superpixel segmentation seeks to collaboratively and efficiently group pixels into perceptual regions by leveraging both left and right views. Most existing algorithms rely primarily on color and spatial features, which can overly constrain spatial information while processing disparity data from stereo pairs. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel stereo superpixel segmentation approach featuring a decoupling mechanism for spatial information. Our method temporarily removes spatial information before fusing features from stereo image pairs, employing a proposed Decoupled Stereo Fusion Module (DSFM) to manage stereo feature alignment and occlusion. Furthermore, recognizing the critical role of spatial information, we design a Dynamic Spatiality Embedding Module (DSEM) to reintegrate it, utilizing a Dynamic Fusion (DF) mechanism within DSEM to adaptively adjust spatial weights for finer segmentation. Extensive experiments on the KITTI2015 and Cityscapes datasets confirm our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, while its application to salient object detection on the NJU2K dataset demonstrates its efficiency. The source code will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.

By leveraging diffeomorphism invariance, we connect the finite size effects in massless theories to their Weyl anomaly. We demonstrate that the universal components of these finite size effects are fixed by specific coefficient functions within the heat kernel expansion of the associated wave operators. For massless scalars confined within a four-dimensional curved spacetime featuring a boundary, the pertinent coefficients are derived—validating the findings of Moss and Dowker, as well as Branson and Gilkey. Furthermore, we extend these general findings to theories defined on bounded regions in two- and four-dimensional flat spacetimes, calculating the variation of the effective action under arbitrary conformal deformations of those regions.

This study addresses multiple testing with false discovery rate (FDR) control, specifically when p-values exhibit discrete and heterogeneous null distributions. We introduce a novel estimator for the proportion of true null hypotheses, showing it exhibits less upward bias compared to Storey's estimator and two additional methods. This new estimator drives two adaptive procedures: an adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method and an adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg-Heyse (BHH) method. We establish that the adaptive BH procedure is conservatively valid without relying on asymptotic assumptions. Simulation results indicate that these adaptive approaches generally outperform their non-adaptive equivalents, with the adaptive BHH procedure typically surpassing both the adaptive BH procedure and a method utilizing randomized p-values. When applied to an HIV vaccine efficacy study, these adaptive procedures identified a greater number of differentially polymorphic positions than the standard BH procedure while maintaining the same FDR level.

We investigate the characteristics of marginal distribution sets within infinite translation-invariant systems on a 2D square lattice. When local variables are restricted to a small finite set of values $d$, we provide complete solutions to the membership problem for nearest-neighbor distributions ($d=2,3$) and for nearest plus next-to-nearest neighbor distributions ($d=2$). Notably, these sets constitute convex polytopes within probability space, enabling the exact calculation of the minimum energy per site for any translation-invariant Hamiltonian in these regimes. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward algorithm to approximate the minimum energy per site to any desired precision for cases outside these specific scenarios. For variables with higher, yet finite, dimensionality, we establish two impossibility results. First, determining the exact energy per site for arbitrary translation-invariant Hamiltonians with nearest-neighbor interactions is an undecidable problem. Second, when $d \geq 2947$, the boundary of the nearest-neighbor marginal distribution set features both flat and smoothly curved regions, rendering the set non-semi-algebraic; consequently, it cannot be characterized using semidefinite programming, even if polynomial inputs of nearest-neighbor probabilities are permitted.

This study introduces a novel model-free control (MFC) strategy designed to utilize photovoltaic (PV) generation locally at the distribution level by coordinating it with building loads, specifically distributed heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems. By consuming PV energy on-site, this approach mitigates the strain on the distribution grid, lowers the necessary battery storage capacity for high PV penetration, and facilitates greater integration of solar power. Unlike model-based methods, which struggle with the complexity of accurately modeling diverse building architectures, the proposed MFC framework relies on intelligent controllers that function without requiring precise building models. The primary goal is to maximize local PV consumption while ensuring occupant comfort and adhering to HVAC physical constraints. This is achieved through the intelligent temporal and spatial scheduling of responsive loads to align demand with production, thereby minimizing voltage fluctuations and bidirectional power flow. Computer simulations demonstrate promising outcomes, indicating that a substantial portion of PV generation can be effectively absorbed by building HVAC units through this intelligent control method.

This document explores simplicial categories—defined as simplicial objects within the category of categories—framing them as a two-fold categorical structure with significant homotopical implications. While double categories, the most recognized two-fold structures, are typically employed to organize bimodules across various contexts, a corresponding double category of spaces has historically been absent despite the conceptual viability of bimodules in that domain. We address this gap by constructing a meaningful simplicial category of spaces. Subsequently, we extend the analogy with double categories by introducing double colimits and postulating an equipment property, which holds true in our examples. As an application, we demonstrate that specific double colimits correspond naturally to homotopy colimits. Remarkably, this analogy reveals a fundamental principle: the relationship between simplicial categories and simplicially enriched categories mirrors that between double categories and 2-categories.

Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing and text mining have allowed researchers to automatically identify an author's identity and demographic traits, such as age and gender, by analyzing linguistic variations across various text genres. However, applying these techniques in real-world settings—specifically within regular online social media and cybercriminal forums—differs significantly from general applications because these environments are defined by both domain-specific and process-dependent characteristics. Consequently, this creates numerous challenges that current research has only barely begun to address. Specifically, text mining approaches applied to social media communications often lack control over dataset size, as the number of available messages varies per user; therefore, systems must be robust against limited data availability. Furthermore, data quality cannot be guaranteed, necessitating that the approach tolerate a degree of linguistic noise, including abbreviations, non-standard language, spelling errors, and variations. Finally, in the context of cybercriminal fora, the system must be resilient to deceptive or adversarial behaviors, such as obfuscation (hiding criminal intent) or imitation (adopting false digital personas), which may involve coded language. In this work, we present a comprehensive survey discussing problems already addressed in existing literature and reviewing potential solutions, while also highlighting areas requiring further attention.

We introduce a framework for quantum process tomography of two-ion interactions that utilizes modulations of the trapping potential and composite pulses derived from a global laser beam to enable individual-ion addressing. Analysis of identity and delay processes within this framework identifies laser decoherence and slow qubit frequency drift as the primary sources of error during the experiment. Applying this method to two co-trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions, we evaluate both an optimized and an overpowered M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate, comparing the findings against less informative Bell-state tomography measurements and predictions from a simplified noise model. These results demonstrate the technique's efficacy in characterizing two-ion quantum processes and extracting meaningful insights into system errors. Furthermore, the experimental convenience of this approach promises to facilitate broader adoption of process tomography for characterizing entangling gates in trapped-ion systems.

The ratio of sixth-order to second-order cumulants ($C_6/C_2$) for conserved quantities has been suggested as a sensitive indicator of the chiral crossover transition. Recent findings from both theoretical Lattice QCD and experiments at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV have reported negative values for this ratio. This study examines the net-proton $C_6/C_2$ behavior within a statistical Binomial distribution (BD) at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV in Au + Au collisions. Utilizing BD parameters derived from RHIC/STAR data, we demonstrate that $C_6/C_2$ can indeed be negative. Moreover, applying the same magnitude of experimental statistics and calculation methods to simulations yields a smaller $C_6/C_2$. In the 0-10% centrality range, a significant discrepancy exists between the simulated results and theoretical expectations. Based on the extracted parameters and experimentally gathered statistics, we establish a baseline for the net-proton $C_6/C_2$ in the BD framework.

5G wireless networks hold the potential to revolutionize future technologies. These networks are anticipated to meet the varied demands of multiple vertical applications, which include requirements for high traffic volumes, massive connectivity, superior quality of service, and low latency. To satisfy these needs in 5G and beyond, emerging technologies such as SDN, NFV, MEC, and CC are being implemented. However, these technologies introduce challenges related to transparency, decentralization, and reliability. Additionally, 5G networks are expected to interconnect numerous heterogeneous devices and machines, raising significant security concerns regarding user confidentiality, data privacy, and trustworthiness. To operate seamlessly and securely in such environments, future 5G networks must integrate smarter and more efficient security functions. Driven by these challenges, researchers have proposed blockchain as a solution to address 5G issues, leveraging its ability to ensure transparency, data reliability, trustworthiness, and immutability within a distributed setting. Consequently, blockchain has gained traction as an innovative technology that fosters a wide array of new decentralized solutions. This chapter explores the integration of blockchain with 5G networks and beyond, presenting how blockchain applications can facilitate various services at both the edge and the core.
Ron Aharoni and Vladimir Korman proposed that every hypergraph containing exclusively finite edges possesses a strongly minimal cover. We provide a counterexample to this conjecture.

This paper investigates recurrence and the associated $\mathscr P_\mathcal F$ property for linear operators acting on Banach spaces. We demonstrate that for specific families known as block families, any hypercyclic operator possessing the $\mathscr P_\mathcal F$ property is necessarily $\mathcal F$-hypercyclic. Conversely, we establish that if $b\mathcal F$ denotes the block family corresponding to a given family $\mathcal F$, then adjoint operators that are $b\mathcal F$-hypercyclic exhibit the $\mathscr P_\mathcal F$ property. As a direct result, we prove that reiteratively hypercyclic operators possess a perfect spectrum, thereby resolving an open question regarding their existence. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of backward shift operators that satisfy the $\mathscr P_\mathcal F$ property.

It is well established that the phase of an optical field within a linear amplifier undergoes diffusion, characterized by a coefficient inversely proportional to the photon number. This same phenomenon occurs in lasers, where it constrains the intrinsic linewidth and complicates the calculation of phase uncertainty. Typically, researchers employ the small-noise approximation, which assumes a narrow photon-number distribution for the optical field. For coherent light, this condition depends on the average photon number. This approximation rests on two pillars: (i) the input possesses a high signal-to-noise ratio, and (ii) this ratio is sustained throughout amplification. This study investigates the minimum number of photons required in a coherent input to a quantum linear amplifier so that the resulting output phase noise remains suitable for small-noise analysis. By deriving phase uncertainty without relying on the small-noise approximation, we demonstrate that even for an ideal linear amplifier—the type most conducive to this approximation—the small-noise assumption fails with only a few average photons. However, as the input strength rises to tens of photons, the approximation becomes significantly more accurate, allowing the phase diffusion process to be effectively analyzed using small-noise methods. This finding defines the boundary of the small-noise assumption in linear amplifiers, noting that the validity of this assumption diminishes further for nonideal amplifiers.

Let $i=1,\ldots,N$ denote indices for a simple random sample drawn from a large population. For each unit, we observe a regressor vector $X_{i}$, and for every ordered pair of units, we record an outcome $Y_{ij}$. These outcomes are independent only if their indices are disjoint; otherwise, they exhibit dyadic dependence. Defining $W_{ij}=\left(X_{i}',X_{j}'\right)'$, we aim to construct a nonparametric estimator of the mean regression function $g\left(W_{ij}\right)\overset{def}{=}\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{ij}|X_{i},X_{j}\right]$ using the observed data. We provide two sets of findings: first, we derive lower bounds on the minimax risk for estimating the regression function both at a specific point and under the infinity norm; second, we establish (i) pointwise and (ii) uniform convergence rates for a dyadic version of the standard Nadaraya-Watson kernel estimator. We demonstrate that the NW estimator attains the optimal rates indicated by these risk bounds when an appropriate bandwidth sequence is selected. This optimal rate diverges from that under independent and identically distributed (iid) data: the effective sample size is reduced, and the dimension $d_W=\mathrm{dim}(W_{ij})$ affects the rate differently.

We introduce a novel iterative framework designed to numerically resolve over-determined boundary value problems associated with general quasilinear elliptic partial differential equations. The core approach involves repeatedly solving the linearized form of the problem using the quasi-reversibility method, incorporating an appropriate Carleman weight function. This weight function facilitates the application of a Carleman estimate, which is used to demonstrate the convergence of the generated sequence toward the target solution. Notably, the iteration converges rapidly at an exponential rate, eliminating the necessity for a precise initial guess. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by computing solutions for various general quasilinear elliptic equations and a broad spectrum of first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations, accompanied by numerical results.

Experimental hints from LSND and MiniBooNE suggest the potential existence of an extra sterile neutrino at the eV scale. Incorporating this particle significantly alters the standard three-flavor neutrino oscillation model, specifically by introducing new sterile parameters that create additional degeneracies. This study investigates how the presence of such a sterile neutrino affects the ability to determine the octant of $\theta_{23}$ within the standard oscillation framework. We analytically compute oscillation probabilities in a 3+1 scenario using the approximation that the smallest mass-squared difference, $\Delta_{21}$, is zero. These calculations allow us to analytically examine degeneracies across various baselines. Specifically, we analyze the octant sensitivity of $\theta_{23}$ for the DUNE experiment within the 3+1 framework. Our results present the octant sensitivity derived from beam neutrinos detected by a liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) at the DUNE far detector. Furthermore, we determine octant sensitivity using atmospheric neutrinos at DUNE with a LArTPC that lacks charge identification capabilities. Additionally, we calculate octant sensitivity assuming the charge tagging capability provided by muon capture in argon, which distinguishes between neutrino and antineutrino events. We also delineate the combined sensitivity from both beam and atmospheric neutrinos at DUNE. Our findings indicate that by combining simulated data from beam and atmospheric neutrinos (including charge identification for muons), the sensitivity to the octant of $\theta_{23}$ for true values of $\theta_{23}=41^\circ(49^\circ)$ surpasses $4\sigma(3\sigma)$ for over 50% of the true $\delta_{13}$ values.

This study introduces an algorithm capable of generating any arbitrary cubic planar map via sequential edge insertion, concurrently producing a corresponding set of valid edge labels and Hamiltonian cycles for each configuration. We provide a publicly accessible Python implementation of this algorithm and examine both theoretical and numerical evidence supporting its correctness, specifically in relation to the Four Colour Theorem.

Graphene plasmons have garnered considerable interest owing to their tunability, potential for long propagation distances, and ultracompact wavelengths. However, the latter feature complicates light-plasmon coupling in real-world applications, typically necessitating complex coupling mechanisms, extremely high doping concentrations, and graphene nanostructuring that approaches the limits of current lithography. In this study, we propose and theoretically validate a solution to mitigate these technological hurdles by employing a practical substrate with a low, negative dielectric function that naturally extends the graphene polariton wavelength to more manageable scales. Specifically, we examine silicon carbide (SiC), which displays a real dielectric component between -1 and 0 and an imaginary component below 0.05 within the 951 to 970 cm$^{-1}$ mid-infrared range. Our calculations reveal that hybridization with the substrate's phonon polariton yields a polariton wavelength approximately ten times longer than that achieved on a silicon dioxide substrate, accompanied by a corresponding tenfold increase in propagation length.

A 3-Sasakian structure on a 7-manifold yields two distinct Einstein metrics: the 3-Sasakian metric and the squashed Einstein metric. Both are derived from nearly parallel $G_2$-structures, which can alternatively be described via the 3-Sasakian structure. Analogous to how Einstein metrics represent critical points of the Ricci flow (up to rescaling), nearly parallel $G_2$-structures serve as natural critical points for the Laplacian flow and Laplacian coflow—geometric flows defined on $G_2$-structures. We examine these flows within the 3-Sasakian context and observe significant differences in their dynamics, especially concerning the stability of the nearly parallel $G_2$-structures. Furthermore, we contrast the behavior of these $G_2$-structure flows with the (rescaled) Ricci flow.

Virtual Try-On (VTON) enhances e-retailing by allowing users to try on clothes from the comfort of their homes. However, most current VTON methods struggle to generate consistent results when a person assumes a pose with folded, bent, or crossed arms, a challenge that becomes particularly severe with long-sleeved garments due to potential overlaps between clothing parts. Existing approaches, particularly warping-based methods relying on Thin Plate Spline (TPS) transformations, fail to address these scenarios. To overcome this, we propose a solution that segments the source clothing into semantically meaningful parts, warping each independently to match the target person's shape. To handle bending, we utilize hand-crafted geometric features aligned with human body geometry. Additionally, we introduce two learning-based modules: a synthesizer network and a mask prediction network. Collectively, these components aim to deliver a photo-realistic and pose-robust VTON solution without the need for paired training data. Comparative analysis against benchmark methods demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

Chest X-Ray (CXR) images are routinely utilized for clinical diagnosis and screening. Automating the generation of reports for these images can significantly reduce radiologists' workload by summarizing descriptive findings and final impressions. However, the intricate structural relationships both between and within report sections present a significant challenge to automatic report generation. Specifically, the "Impression" section serves as a diagnostic summary of the "Findings" section, and normal findings typically dominate abnormal ones. Existing research seldom addresses this fundamental structural information. This study introduces a novel framework that leverages structural information between and within report sections to generate CXR reports. First, we propose a two-stage strategy that explicitly models the relationship between Findings and Impression. Second, we develop a cooperative multi-agent system that implicitly captures the imbalance between normal and abnormal findings. Experiments on two CXR report datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across various metrics. Our results indicate that the proposed approach successfully generates high-quality medical reports by integrating structural information.

The Lagrangian framework is a versatile tool for addressing numerous problems in undergraduate and graduate physics, yet many existing resources omit the foundational details that render it so effective. This paper elucidates the derivation of the principle of stationary action, the Euler-Lagrange equations, and the classical Lagrangian through three specific steps: first, we mathematically derive the Lagrange formalism from the problem of minimal distance between two points, introducing the variational principle and the Euler-Lagrange equation; second, we convert Newton's second law into an Euler-Lagrange equation to demonstrate that the Lagrangian equals kinetic energy minus potential energy; and third, we justify the reformulation of Newton's laws by proving that the Euler-Lagrange equation remains invariant across any coordinate system. This invariance simplifies and clarifies the role of coordinates in classical mechanics compared to the Newtonian approach, emphasizing that coordinates are arbitrary mathematical conveniences rather than reflections of physical reality.

MicroScope and microarchitectural replay attacks leverage speculative execution to trap victim applications in infinite loops, thereby allowing attackers to indefinitely amplify side-channel vulnerabilities. Because of this replay mechanism, these attacks can compromise security-critical trusted execution environments, such as secure enclaves, even in scenarios where traditional side-channel attacks would fail. Unlike standard speculative side-channel attacks, MicroScope can also amplify the correct execution path, which renders many existing defenses ineffective. In this paper, we extend the scope of microarchitectural replay attacks beyond MicroScope and propose an efficient countermeasure. We observe that these attacks depend on the repeated squashing of "replay handles" and that the instructions triggering the side-channel must exist within the same reorder buffer window as those handles. We introduce "Delay-on-Squash," a technique designed to track squashed instructions and prevent them from being replayed by speculative handles. Our evaluation demonstrates that full protection against microarchitectural replay attacks is achievable with minimal hardware overhead while preserving 97% of the performance of the insecure baseline.

Practitioners and regulators alike favor covariate adjustment in randomized clinical trials as it enhances the precision of treatment effect estimates, yet this approach poses specific challenges within time-to-event analyses. We introduce a covariate-adjusted pseudovalue regression method designed to estimate differences in restricted mean survival times (RMST) between treatment groups. By integrating a prognostic covariate, our approach boosts the precision of treatment effect estimation while rigorously maintaining type I error control and avoiding bias. Furthermore, the method allows for quantifying the precision gains, enabling these improvements to be factored into sample size calculations during the study design phase. Ultimately, this proposed technique facilitates the design of smaller randomized trials without compromising statistical power.

In Spring 2021, an instrumented baffle was installed around the suspended mirror within the input mode cleaner's triangular cavity at Virgo. This setup serves as a technology demonstrator for the baffles intended for the main arms in the near future. For the first time, we present results on the measured scattered light distribution inside the cavity, derived from data collected between May and July 2021 during Virgo's commissioning phase, with an input laser power of 28.5 W. The baffle's sensitivity is analyzed, and the findings are compared against scattered light simulations.

Phase-stabilized optical fiber networks offer a promising alternative to satellite-based methods for precision measurements and metrological frequency comparisons. However, the scarcity of dedicated channels in the standard C-band due to network constraints presents a challenge. In this work, we successfully distribute an SI-traceable ultrastable optical frequency within the L-band across a 456 km fiber ring network that is fully occupied by C-band data traffic. We analyzed the optical phase noise, finding a link instability of $4.7\cdot 10^{-16}$ at 1 second and $3.8\cdot 10^{-19}$ at 2000 seconds of integration, along with a link accuracy of $2\cdot 10^{-18}$, matching the performance of established C-band metrology networks. We validated the utility of this distributed frequency by establishing SI-traceability for a laser in a remote laboratory and confirmed that the metrological signal does not interfere with telecommunications data. By combining the unconventional use of the L-band spectrum with proven frequency-stabilization methods, our approach provides a novel, cost-effective solution for ultrastable frequency dissemination, potentially serving as a foundation for a global metrological network.

Since a model merely represents an abstraction of a real system, factors such as unmodeled dynamics, parameter fluctuations, and disturbances can degrade the performance of conventional controllers reliant on that model, making it difficult to maintain optimal tuning. To address this, the paper introduces an adaptive neuro-fuzzy controller integrated with a learning algorithm derived from sliding-mode control (SMC) theory for a spherical rolling robot. The proposed architecture combines a neuro-fuzzy network with a conventional controller to ensure the system's asymptotic stability within a compact region. Parameter updating rules for the neuro-fuzzy system are formulated using SMC theory, and the learning process's stability is validated through a Lyapunov function. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this control scheme, utilizing the SMC-based learning algorithm, successfully eliminates steady-state error and enhances transient response performance for the spherical rolling robot, even without prior knowledge of its dynamic equations.

When dark matter (DM) annihilation yields non-relativistic particles that couple directly to a light force mediator, non-perturbative phenomena such as final state bound state (FBS) formation and the final state Sommerfeld (FSS) effect must be accounted for. These effects become relevant when the final-state particles are non-relativistic, typically occurring due to a small mass splitting between the DM and its products. Consequently, we investigate these mechanisms within the degenerate mass regime—encompassing kinematically forbidden scenarios—using two specific models. Our analysis reveals that the FBS effect can substantially alter the DM relic abundance compared to standard perturbative calculations within certain mass-split ranges. Furthermore, we highlight that the FBS effect is comparable in magnitude to the FSS effect in these regimes. Considering the conservation of angular momentum during FBS formation is complex; in some instances, the process does not proceed via an $s$-wave. To address this, we employ two models that illustrate distinct partial wave contributions to the FBS effect. Additionally, we demonstrate that FBS formation accompanied by vector boson emission impacts the DM relic abundance and present the first calculation of the $p$-wave FSS effect within a specific model.

Capsule networks, as discussed by Hinton et al. (2018), are designed to encode information and reason about the relationships between objects and their constituent parts. This paper introduces a \emph{generative} model for such data and develops a variational algorithm to infer both the transformations of individual objects and the assignments of observed parts to them. We apply this framework to two datasets: (i) synthetic data composed of geometric shapes like squares and triangles forming "constellations," and (ii) data derived from a parts-based representation of faces. While Kosiorek et al. [2019] previously addressed this challenge using stacked capsule autoencoders (SCAEs) with amortized inference, our results demonstrate a significant performance advantage over their approach in comparable settings, specifically on the constellations data.

This paper provides a comprehensive survey of reinforcement learning (RL) methods within the field of social robotics. As a decision-making framework where an agent learns optimal behaviors through trial-and-error interactions with its environment, RL aligns well with social robotics, given that interaction is central to both domains. The study specifically targets research involving physical social robots and real-world human-robot interactions. Beyond a general overview, the authors categorize existing RL approaches based on their methodologies and reward mechanism designs. Furthermore, acknowledging the critical role of communication in social robots, the paper groups studies by the communication medium utilized for reward formulation. A significant portion of the analysis focuses on reward function design, classifying the literature into three primary themes: interactive reinforcement learning, intrinsically motivated methods, and task performance-driven approaches. Additionally, the article examines the advantages and challenges of applying RL in social robotics, evaluates the studies based on their use of subjective versus algorithmic metrics, discusses real-world implementation hurdles and proposed solutions, and highlights underexplored areas. Ultimately, this work aims to serve as a foundational resource for researchers seeking to apply RL techniques in social robotics.

Numerous organizations utilize compute clusters outfitted with accelerators like GPUs and TPUs to train deep learning models across distributed environments. However, this training process is highly resource-demanding, drawing heavily on compute power, memory, and network capacity. While previous research has sought to minimize the training resource footprint without sacrificing quality, these efforts often concentrate on specific bottlenecks, such as network usage, thereby restricting their capacity to enhance overall cluster efficiency. Addressing this limitation, our work leverages the distinct properties of deep learning workloads to introduce Structured Partial Backpropagation (SPB). SPB systematically regulates the volume of backpropagation performed by individual workers during distributed training, effectively lowering network bandwidth, compute consumption, and memory usage while maintaining model performance. To maximize cluster-wide benefits, we also present JigSaw, an SPB-aware scheduler that manages Deep Learning Training (DLT) jobs at the iteration level. Our findings indicate that JigSaw can boost large-scale cluster efficiency by up to 28%.
