Previous research by Azimifard, Samei, and Spronk (JFA 2009; arXiv 0805.3685) established that the ZL-amenability constant of a finite group is bounded below by 1, achieving this value precisely when the group is abelian. Furthermore, their work demonstrated that for any finite non-abelian group, this invariant is at least 301/300, a conclusion dependent on a significant theorem by D. A. Rider regarding the norms of central idempotents in group algebras. In this study, we prove that if G is a finite non-abelian group, its ZL-amenability constant is at least 7/4, a bound that is optimal. Our approach circumvents Rider's result by examining cases where G is merely non-abelian through calculations found in Alaghmandan, Choi, and Samei (CMB 2014; arXiv 1302.1929), while also deriving a novel estimate for groups possessing a trivial center.

The structure of real-world ecological and socio-economic networks diverges markedly from random networks. From the perspective of network science, these non-random patterns require explanation regarding their origins and their potential systemic impacts. This review examines one such pattern: nestedness. Defined within the context of interacting nodes, nestedness refers to the propensity for nodes to connect with subsets of the partners of more highly connected nodes. Recognized in biogeography for over eight decades, nestedness appears in diverse systems ranging from ecological mutualisms and global trade to inter-organizational dynamics. This article addresses three core areas: current methods for detecting nestedness, theoretical mechanisms explaining its emergence in both ecological and socio-economic contexts, and the implications of nested topologies for system stability and feasibility. By synthesizing findings from statistics, graph theory, ecology, and economics, we survey a broad interdisciplinary landscape. Furthermore, while nestedness has historically been studied in bipartite networks, recent research has identified it in unipartite networks as well; this review offers the first comprehensive unification of these previously separate streams. We posit that this truly interdisciplinary approach, grounded in complex systems theory, will foster new models and algorithms with applications extending far beyond current disciplinary boundaries.

This paper investigates the G-utility maximization problem of a representative investor using the G-martingale method within Peng's G-expectation space \cite{Pe19}. The financial market consists of a single bond and stock, where uncertainty is modeled by G-Brownian motions. Since the standard approach in \cite{Wxz} is ineffective due to the quadratic variation of a G-Brownian motion being a stochastic process, we employ an extended nonlinear expectation to address this challenge. We first establish a sufficient condition for G-utility maximization. Specifically for log-utility, we derive an explicit optimal strategy by constructing and solving a system of coupled G-FBSDEs, subsequently verifying that this strategy satisfies the sufficient condition. Furthermore, applying this methodology yields an explicit solution for a stochastic interest rate model. All economic interpretations of the resulting optimal strategies align with our initial intuitions.

Quantum computing offers potential computational benefits for machine learning, yet noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices present significant engineering hurdles to achieving quantum machine learning (QML) advantages. Recently, new QML models inspired by the brain's noise-tolerant dynamics have been developed to bypass these hardware constraints. This article introduces a quantum recurrent neural network (qRNN), adapting a well-established brain circuit model for quantum use. The qRNN leverages the natural Hamiltonian dynamics of interacting spin-1/2 particle ensembles for computation. When the Hamiltonian is diagonal, the qRNN mimics classical dynamics; beyond this limit, however, it exhibits distinct quantum computational features that enhance its processing capabilities. Specifically, we examine a qRNN constructed from Rydberg atom arrays, demonstrating that it can replicate learning in various cognitive tasks—including multitasking, decision-making, and long-term memory. This success relies on exploiting key platform attributes such as interatomic species interactions and quantum many-body scars.

Identifying rumors and fake news relies heavily on stance detection, which entails determining an author's position toward a specific textual claim. This study focuses on stance classification within the Russian language. It presents RuStance, a novel dataset comprising Russian tweets and news comments from various sources across multiple topics, alongside text classification methods used as benchmarks for stance detection in this language. By releasing this open-access dataset—the first of its kind for Russian—the paper also establishes a baseline for predicting stance in the language.

The challenge of expressing a totally positive element as a sum of squares has a long mathematical lineage, tracing back to Bachet and Lagrange. While established methods exist for decomposing elements into sums of squares in certain specific rings, such as the integers or polynomials over the rationals, the problem remains largely unsolved for many other significant rings and fields. This paper introduces an explicit algorithm capable of decomposing an element from any global field—whether a number field or a global function field—into a sum of squares with minimal length.

This paper characterizes nonhomogeneous wavelet bi-frames. We begin by introducing reducing subspaces of Sobolev spaces defined over local fields of prime characteristic, followed by the characterization of nonhomogeneous wavelet bi-frames within such fields.

Recently, end-to-end speech recognition systems utilizing joint Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)-Attention loss have become widely adopted. These architectures typically employ a non-autoregressive CTC decoder at inference to leverage its efficiency and straightforwardness. Nevertheless, personalizing these models proves challenging due to the conditional independence assumption inherent in CTC, which restricts predictions at the current time step from being influenced by prior outputs. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel two-stage method: first, the encoder is biased via attention mechanisms focused on a curated list of rare long-tail and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms; second, dynamic boosting and a phone alignment network are applied during decoding to further refine subword predictions. Our evaluation on the open-source VoxPopuli dataset and proprietary medical corpora demonstrates a 60% increase in F1 score for domain-specific rare words compared to a robust CTC baseline.

This paper introduces the design, implementation, and analysis of a free library for boundary element calculations, licensed under the GNU General Public Licence. Aimed at enabling users to address a broad spectrum of problems via the boundary element method, the library integrates a fast multipole method specifically adapted for higher-order boundary elements. This adaptation accounts for the finite size of elements when constructing the domain tree. Validation using a sphere and a cube demonstrates the method's capability to manage sharp edges, confirming that it is accurate, efficient, and convergent.

This study models and simulates a quantum key distribution (QKD) downlink from a low Earth orbit (LEO) small satellite to an optical ground station (OGS), serving as a core component of the preliminary design and concept phase for the QuantSat-PT mission. By rigorously modeling downlink transmission channel effects—specifically atmospheric turbulence and losses for both BB84 and E91 protocols—we establish a consistent performance envelope that clarifies ambiguities in previously reported mission experimental data. For the 4-state BB84 protocol at a 750 km zenith orbit, we calculate a sifted key rate of 32.1 kbit/s and a Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) of 4%. Regarding the E91 protocol, a Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) test was conducted, yielding a correlation factor of $S \in[-2.63\pm0.02,-1.91\pm0.03]$ for the mission. The paper further discusses the consistency of these findings with state-of-the-art simulators and their significance for experimental satellite-based QKD.

I demonstrate that the high-energy neutrino flux expected from AGN cores can account for the PeV neutrinos observed by Ice Cube, without violating the limits imposed by measured extragalactic cosmic ray and gamma-ray backgrounds.

We employed a novel spectral-fitting method to isolate 6 narrow-band giant pulses from a sample of 1578 within the Crab pulsar. These events were observed over a 77-minute window using the 46-m dish at the Algonquin Radio Observatory, operating in the 400-800 MHz band. The detected narrow-band giant pulses include both main- and interpulses, suggesting an intrinsic emission origin rather than a propagation effect. While Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) exhibit comparable narrow-band characteristics, such features are rarely seen in pulsar giant pulses. We report a fractional bandwidth ($\Delta \nu / \nu$) of approximately 0.1 for these pulses, which aligns closely with the 0.05 value observed in the repeater FRB 20190711A. Consequently, this finding further solidifies the link between FRBs and pulsar giant pulses.

Task-oriented dialogue systems depend critically on specialized dialogue state tracking (DST) modules to dynamically infer user intent during interactions. Current state-of-the-art DST models are generally trained via supervised learning using manually annotated turn-level data. However, acquiring these annotations is expensive, hindering the development of precise dialogue systems for emerging domains. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a reinforcement learning-based approach that enables DST models to transfer to new domains without requiring turn-level supervision. Experimental results across multiple domains demonstrate that this method rapidly adapts pre-trained models to new settings, achieving performance comparable to those trained with turn-level supervision. Furthermore, we show that our approach can enhance models initially trained with turn-level supervision through subsequent fine-tuning optimized for dialog-level rewards.

Tensor completion leverages low-rank structures to reconstruct missing entries in partially observed tensors, a technique widely used for visual data recovery. In sequential contexts like streaming video completion, these missing entries must be recovered dynamically. Conventional streaming methods treat the entire visual dataset as a single tensor, which often fails when significant subspace variations occur over time, such as those caused by strong motion between frames. To address this, we introduce a novel patch tracking-based streaming tensor ring completion framework for visual recovery. Upon receiving a new frame, the system tracks small patches from the preceding frame and constructs a patch tensor for each by stacking similar patches from the current frame. These patch tensors are then completed using a streaming tensor ring algorithm, enabling the recovery of the incoming frame. We also propose an improved patch tracking strategy capable of accurately and efficiently handling patches with missing data, alongside a new streaming tensor ring completion algorithm that precisely updates latent core tensors to fill missing entries. Extensive experiments confirm that our proposed methods outperform both batch and existing streaming state-of-the-art tensor completion techniques.

Although classical chaos is well-defined by consistent theories and intuitive methods like Lyapunov exponents, quantum chaos remains poorly understood, particularly regarding its connection to multi-partite entanglement and information scrambling. We examine the benchmark kicked top model, which exhibits chaotic dynamics in its classical form, to thoroughly analyze the temporal evolution of chaos and entanglement in the quantum regime. Introducing the quasi-probability distribution associated with the out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) as a new tool, we calculate its cumulative nonclassicality. This metric has been demonstrated to surpass the simple OTOC in distinguishing between integrable and nonintegrable Hamiltonians. In a comprehensive comparative analysis, we contrast this nonclassicality with entanglement measures, including tripartite mutual information and entanglement entropy. Our findings reveal that initial states residing in the classical "sea of chaos" develop characteristics indicative of chaotic behavior and entanglement generation within closed quantum systems as they evolve. We validate this observation by detecting these dynamics using our novel OTOC-based measure.

In reference [1], we introduced the concept of mechanical learning and outlined two corresponding approaches. This paper focuses on one of these methods to clearly define the objects and processes involved. We examine two types of patterns: objective and subjective, noting that the subjective pattern is fundamental to the learning machine. We demonstrate that for any given objective pattern, an appropriate subjective pattern can be constructed using the least number of base patterns to effectively represent the objective one. The X-form serves as the algebraic expression for the subjective pattern, and the collection of X-forms constitutes the internal representation space at the core of the learning machine. We analyze learning processes both with and without teaching, defining data sufficiency in terms of X-forms. Following this, we explore various learning strategies and prove that, given sufficient data and specific capabilities, the learning machine can acquire any pattern, thereby functioning as a universal learning machine. Finally, the appendix offers an alternative perspective on deep learning by examining its internal representation space and learning dynamics through the lens of the learning machine.

Using the topological particle (MTP) framework, we calculate the interaction energy between monopole pairs, which act as sources and sinks of a Coulombic field. These monopoles are modeled as finite-sized, massive topological solitons defined by a divergence-free field. By numerically fixing soliton centers at various separations, we observe deviations from the standard Coulomb potential at distances comparable to a few soliton radii, a result attributed to the solitons' finite extent. We then compare these numerical findings regarding such deviations with the behavior of the running coupling in perturbative QED.

We have introduced a novel spectroscopy method using photonic devices that performs spectral cross-correlation against a template entirely on the chip. By engineering photonic components with specifically modulated transmission spectra, this optical cross-correlation eliminates the need for dispersion, thereby streamlining the instrument design and lowering costs. The resulting correlation lag allows for the identification of atomic and molecular species as well as the measurement of radial velocities for specific astrophysical objects.

This overview details two emerging design strategies utilizing distinct photonic platforms: silicon and fibre-based systems. The silicon approach employs thermo-optically modulated ring resonators to execute the cross-correlation, whereas the fibre method relies on strain-modulated custom fibre Bragg gratings (FBGs) with tailored transmission spectra. Both techniques have successfully detected molecular gas in laboratory environments, and on-sky testing is currently underway.

Finally, we explore the future potential of these devices; their inherent simplicity paves the way for affordable, specialized multi-object or integral field spectrographs. Such instruments could significantly advance scientific initiatives focused on stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet detection.

Although non-Arrhenius temperature dependence in anomalous diffusion coefficients is observed in various metals, a definitive explanatory framework remains elusive. In this study, we employ first-principles calculations grounded in density functional theory to determine self-diffusion coefficients in bcc Mo and $\beta$-Ti. By integrating quasiharmonic transition state theory with large displacement phonon calculations, we demonstrate that anharmonicity arising from thermal expansion is the primary driver of the anomalous temperature dependence. Utilizing a modified Debye approach to quantify thermal expansion across the full temperature range, we also introduce a technique to relax vacancy structures within mechanically unstable crystals like $\beta$-Ti. Our findings indicate that while thermal expansion only weakly influences the activation enthalpy, it significantly impacts the diffusion coefficient's prefactor. This successfully reproduces the non-linear, non-Arrhenius "anomalous" self-diffusion in both bcc systems, yielding strong agreement with experimental data. The proposed methodology is both general and straightforward, making it applicable to other mechanically unstable crystals.

The closeness of metal nanoparticles intensifies plasmonic coupling and alters resonance frequencies. This article reports a numerical investigation into the photothermal effects within clusters of small gold nanorods, examining both ordered and random configurations. In ordered aggregates, lateral coupling induces blueshifts in the plasmonic resonance, whereas random aggregates exhibit redshifts. The plasmonic response of these random clusters can be tuned to cover the second infrared biological therapeutic window. Observations indicate that aggregates demonstrate superior absorption capabilities, resulting in greater temperature increases compared to individual or monodisperse gold nanorods. Furthermore, the position of the absorption resonance peak in random aggregates varies based on the incident light's angle and polarization. Since nanoparticle aggregation naturally occurs within biological environments, it significantly influences the photothermal process. This research elucidates the mechanisms of photothermal heating in nanoparticle clusters and aids in selecting optimal light sources that align with the absorption peaks of aggregate suspensions for therapeutic applications.

Uncertainty quantification in full-waveform inversion offers a probabilistic assessment of the problem's ill-conditioning, specifically addressing the solution's sensitivity to the initial model and data noise. This evaluation helps determine confidence in the resulting solution and its implications for subsequent imaging tasks, such as stratigraphic segmentation within reservoir characterization. Traditionally, uncertainty is represented as a probability distribution derived from Bayesian principles, from which samples are extracted, often via Monte Carlo methods. In contrast, this study proposes a method that trains a deep network to map Gaussian random inputs into model space (e.g., density or velocity), effectively generating samples as if drawn from the true posterior distribution. This network is trained to solve a variational optimization problem that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the network's output and the actual posterior. Grounded in recent advances in invertible networks, this approach leverages special architectures that are computationally efficient and allow for the analytic calculation of output density functions. Consequently, after training, these networks can serve as a new prior for related inversion problems, unlike Monte Carlo methods which yield only samples. The validity of this approach is demonstrated through an application to angle-versus-ray parameter analysis for reservoir characterization.

This paper introduces a mathematical formula to determine the maximum and minimum voltage ripples across the capacitors of sub-modules (SMs) in a modular multilevel converter (MMC). By utilizing the arm-averaged model of the MMC, instantaneous power for both upper and lower arms is derived, establishing the foundation for characterizing arm energy. To compute peak SM capacitor voltages, an analytical expression for the maximum and minimum energy levels must be established; however, the presence of terms with varying magnitudes, frequencies, and phases makes this difficult. To address this challenge, the instantaneous arm energy equation is refined through mathematical assumptions that consolidate disparate components into a single term capable of analytically identifying the maximum energy point. This modified expression is then applied to calculate the peak arm capacitor voltages. Applying the same methodology at the arm level yields the final analytical expressions for the SM capacitor voltage extremes. Finally, simulations are conducted to verify the accuracy of the proposed analysis under various power delivery scenarios.

Various imaging techniques, such as patch-based denoising, time series recovery, and convolutional neural networks, leverage the manifold structure of signals. Although these methods demonstrate strong empirical results, the theoretical understanding of recovering signals and functions residing on manifolds remains limited. This paper addresses the recovery of signals situated on a union of surfaces, specifically focusing on smooth, band-limited surfaces within high-dimensional spaces. We demonstrate that an exponential mapping converts this data into a union of low-dimensional subspaces. Leveraging this relationship, we propose a sampling-theoretic framework for reconstructing smooth surfaces from limited samples and for learning functions defined on these surfaces. Furthermore, we utilize the low-rank nature of the resulting features to estimate the requisite number of measurements for surface recovery. Additionally, this low-rank property enables an efficient, neural-network-like approach for the local representation of multidimensional functions on the surface.

Consider an exchangeable random vector $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ governed by the distribution function $F$, where $Y_1\leq \cdots\leq Y_n$ represent the associated order statistics. We demonstrate that the conditional distribution of $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ given $(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$ remains independent of $F$.

Achieving ignition in inertial confinement fusion (ICF) demands radiation-hydrodynamics simulations that rely on precise models of core material properties, including equation of state, opacity, and conductivity, all of which must be validated through experimentation. A feasibility study investigated the use of spatially-integrated, spectrally-resolved X-ray Thomson scattering (XRTS) to diagnose the temperature, density, and ionization states of the compressed DT shell and hot spot during a laser direct-drive implosion at two-thirds convergence. By generating synthetic scattering spectra using 1-D implosion simulations from the LILAC code, post-processed with the X-ray Scattering (XRS) model embedded in SPECT3D, researchers analyzed two extreme adiabat capsule scenarios. The results demonstrated that plasma conditions within both compressed DT shells could be successfully resolved.

An $m \times (n+1)$ multiplicity matrix is defined as a matrix $M = (\mu_{i,j})$ where rows are indexed by $i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$ and columns by $j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$. The entries are nonnegative integers subject to two conditions: (1) whenever $\mu_{i,j} \geq 1$, it must hold that $j \leq n-1$ and $\mu_{i,j+1} = \mu_{i,j} - 1$, and (2) for every column $j$, the sum of its entries satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^{m} \mu_{i,j} \leq n-j$. Consider a field $K$ of characteristic 0 and a polynomial $f(x) \in K[x]$ of degree $n$, where $f^{(j)}(x)$ denotes the $j$-th derivative of $f$. Let $\Lambda = (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_m)$ be a sequence of distinct elements in $K$. For each $i \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$ and $j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, let $\mu_{i,j}$ represent the multiplicity of $\lambda_i$ as a root of $f^{(j)}(x)$. The resulting $m \times (n+1)$ matrix $M_f(\Lambda) = (\mu_{i,j})$ is termed the multiplicity matrix of $f(x)$ relative to $\Lambda$. An unresolved issue is to categorize which matrices can be realized as multiplicity matrices of polynomials over $K[x]$ and to construct examples of matrices that cannot be so realized.

Robotic surgery has expanded the range of feasible procedures, with numerous instances of partial automation emerging over the last ten years. This analysis categorizes automation tasks by their necessary features and offers a checklist to guide the pursuit of advanced surgical automation. Additionally, we examine existing obstacles and the innovations needed to achieve this goal.

We investigate recent developments and unresolved issues regarding local minima and saddle points within the Cahn--Hilliard energy framework for dimensions $d\geq 2$, specifically focusing on the critical regime characterized by large system sizes and mean values near $-1$. Utilizing the String Method developed by E, Ren, and Vanden-Eijnden—a numerical technique for determining transition pathways in complex systems—we apply this approach in $d=2$ to further elucidate the characteristics of these minima and saddle points. Guided by these numerical findings, we modify the approach proposed by Caffarelli and Spruck to examine the convexity of level sets across dimensions $d\geq 2$.

This study extends the previously introduced concept of Energy Mover's Distance, demonstrating that the derived observables enable the identification of rare events in proton-proton collider experiments. We show that these observables cluster distinct processes in varied ways, offering potential enhancements to experimental analyses. Using $t\bar{t}Z$ production at the Large Hadron Collider as a benchmark, we illustrate the method's practical applicability. Additionally, we investigate the utility of these observables as novel features for training Deep Neural Networks.

Wave-particle duality represents a peculiar core concept in quantum mechanics, describing how quantum entities exhibit mutually exclusive wave and particle properties. The quantum eraser experiment highlights a counterintuitive dimension of this duality. This study demonstrates that the quantum eraser can be quantitatively explained through the recently formulated relation between duality and entanglement. Specifically, we establish that a triality involving wave, particle, and entanglement encompasses the entire physics of quantum erasure. Furthermore, we show that a controllable partial erasure of which-path information is achievable, allowing for the partial restoration of quantum interference and broadening the applicability of standard quantum eraser protocols.

While H$_3^+$ molecular ion emission serves as a key diagnostic for the upper atmospheres of Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus, it has never been detected at Neptune. To investigate this, we conducted near-infrared spectral observations of Neptune from 3.93 to 4.00 $\mu$m using the newly commissioned iSHELL instrument at the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility in Hawaii during August 17–20, 2017. Despite accumulating 15.4 hours of integration time across the planet's disk, we could not definitively identify any H$_3^+$ line emissions. Assuming a temperature of 550 K, we established an upper limit on the column-integrated density of $1.0^{+1.2}_{-0.8}\times10^{13}$ m$^{-2}$, representing a 30% improvement over the best prior observational constraint. This finding indicates that current models overestimate the density by at least a factor of five, underscoring the necessity for updated modeling. One potential resolution involves strong vertical mixing of polyatomic neutral species from Neptune's upper stratosphere into the thermosphere, where they react with H$_3^+$ to significantly lower its column density. Furthermore, this upper limit offers valuable constraints for future detection efforts using the James Webb Space Telescope.

This paper investigates the exact connection between the parameter $\alpha$ in the nonlinear term of the parabolic equation $$h_t+h_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}|h_x|^\alpha=f$$ and the Hausdorff dimension of the singular point set $\mathcal{S}$ associated with suitable weak solutions. It is demonstrated that for the range $5/3\leq\alpha<7/3$, the $\frac{3\alpha-5}{\alpha-1}$-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure of $\mathcal{S}$ vanishes. This finding extends recent results by Oz\'anski and Robinson [31,SIAM J. Math. Anal. 51: 228--255, 2019], which addressed the case where $\alpha=2$ and $f=0$. Furthermore, this result also applies to a 3D modified Navier-Stokes system.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted weaknesses in healthcare systems, underscoring the urgent need for innovative tools that enable rapid and affordable screening and diagnosis. Clinical evidence suggests that SARS-CoV-2 infection can lead to cardiac damage, positioning electrocardiograms (ECG) as a potential diagnostic biomarker. This study seeks to automatically detect COVID-19 using ECG signals. We introduce a new technique to extract ECG data from physical paper records, feeding these digitized signals into a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) for disease learning and diagnosis. To assess the quality of the digitization, R peaks in the original paper-based ECG images are manually labeled. Subsequently, RR intervals derived from each image are compared against those from the corresponding digitized signal. Experiments conducted on a dataset of COVID-19 ECG images show that the proposed digitization method accurately preserves original signals, achieving a mean absolute error of 28.11 ms. The 1D-CNN model, trained on these digitized signals, successfully identifies individuals with COVID-19 against various other groups, demonstrating classification accuracies of 98.42% (COVID-19 vs. Normal), 95.63% (COVID-19 vs. Abnormal Heartbeats), and 98.50% (COVID-19 vs. other classes). Additionally, the method performs well on multi-classification tasks. These results suggest that a deep learning system trained on digitized ECG signals holds significant promise as a tool for diagnosing COVID-19.

Our objective is to develop an efficient technique for distinguishing young, low-mass stars and brown dwarfs from low-resolution near-infrared spectra by analyzing gravity-sensitive features and their age-dependent evolution. We constructed a comprehensive dataset comprising approximately 2,800 publicly available near-infrared spectra of dwarfs ranging from spectral types M0 to L3. Initially, we explored methods for determining spectral type and extinction through comparisons with spectral templates and various spectral indices. Subsequently, we investigated gravity-sensitive indices and applied machine learning algorithms to effectively separate young objects (less than 10 Myr) from field populations. By utilizing a set of six spectral indices for typing—including two newly developed ones, TLI-J and TLI-K—we achieved a precision of better than one spectral subtype across the full range. We introduced a novel gravity-sensitive index (TLI-g) that consistently distinguishes young from field objects, outperforming existing literature indices. Furthermore, machine learning approaches utilizing the entire near-infrared spectrum yield even superior separation, demonstrating that the H- and K-bands alone are sufficient for this task. Finally, we assessed the relative importance of different spectral regions for gravity classification based on machine learning outputs, identifying the H-band broad-band shape as the most critical feature, followed by FeH absorption bands at 1.2 $\mu m$ and 1.24 $\mu m$, and the KI doublet at 1.24 $\mu m$.

This research investigates the optical characteristics of a hybrid system comprising a quantum dot (QD) resonantly coupled to an optical microcavity mode and a Majorana nanowire—a topological superconducting segment featuring Majorana bound states (MBSs) at its termini. Under conditions of strong light-matter coupling, the leakage of the Majorana mode into the QD facilitates new optical transitions between polaritonic states, which arise from the hybridization of material excitations with cavity photons. This interaction reshapes the Jaynes-Cummings ladder and can generate a robust single-peak emission at the cavity eigenfrequency. Furthermore, the study identifies weak satellite peaks in both low and high-frequency regions, corresponding to distinct scenarios: highly isolated MBSs, overlapped MBSs, and MBSs that are poorly localized at the nanowire ends.

This work introduces a novel resummation of the $S$-factor for a composite system consisting of two relativistic spin-1/2 particles with arbitrary masses, interacting through a Coulomb-like chromodynamical potential. The study utilizes a relativistic quasipotential approach grounded in the Hamiltonian formulation of covariant quantum field theory within the relativistic configuration representation. It examines pseudoscalar, vector, and pseudovector configurations, providing a detailed investigation into the $S$-factor's behavior near the threshold and in the relativistic limit. Furthermore, the spin dependence of these $S$-factors is analyzed. It is concluded that while spin contributions significantly mitigate the Sommerfeld effect at the threshold, their influence wanes at ultrarelativistic velocities, causing the $S$-factor to converge with that of spinless systems. Finally, the new results are linked to previously derived $S$-factors for spinless particles of arbitrary masses and for relativistic spinor particles with equal masses.

This study analyzes 20 years of magnetic field data from the Oersted, CHAMP, and Swarm satellite missions, enhanced by calibrated magnetometer readings from CryoSat2, to investigate temporal changes in the Earth's core field at both satellite altitude and the core-mantle boundary (CMB). By processing satellite data, we generated composite time series of the core field's secular variation (SV) at a 4-month interval across 300 globally distributed Geomagnetic Virtual Observatories (GVO). The GVO radial SV records exhibit regional fluctuations lasting 5 to 10 years with amplitudes up to 20 nT/yr, particularly evident at low latitudes over Indonesia (2014), South America and the South Atlantic (2007, 2011, 2014), and the central Pacific (2017). Utilizing the Subtractive Optimally Localized Averages (SOLA) technique, we mapped CMB SV as a set of locally averaged estimates. We demonstrate that 2-year CryoSat2 data windows allow for reliable estimation of both SV and secular acceleration (SA) at the CMB with a spatial resolution equivalent to spherical harmonic degree 10. Along the CMB equator, significant SA features were identified under Indonesia (2011–2014), Central America (2015–2019), and alternating-sign SA sequences across the Atlantic (2004–2019). CryoSat2 data provide a crucial contribution to understanding sub-decadal core field variations. Furthermore, Swarm satellite data over 1-year windows enable the study of SA changes at low latitudes on timescales as short as 1 year, also with degree 10 spatial resolution. In 2017, strong positive and negative SA features appeared simultaneously in the Pacific and subsequently drifted westward.

Although the biomedical field has released numerous "open data" initiatives over the past ten years, researchers continue to face significant logistical and technical hurdles when attempting to discover, query, and integrate diverse data and knowledge from various sources. To address these obstacles, the community has explored Semantic Web and linked data technologies to establish the Life Sciences Linked Open Data (LSLOD) cloud. In this study, we derive schemas from over 80 publicly accessible biomedical linked data graphs to construct an LSLOD schema graph and perform an empirical meta-analysis to assess the degree of semantic heterogeneity within the LSLOD ecosystem. Our findings reveal that many LSLOD sources operate in isolation without linking to others, rely on unpublished schemas with little reuse or mapping, and contain elements that lack utility for biomedical data integration. We anticipate that the resulting LSLOD schema graph and the insights gained from this research will support researchers aiming to query and integrate data and knowledge from multiple biomedical sources simultaneously on the Web.

Approximately two decades ago, Ghys proposed that any finite subgroup within the diffeomorphism group of a compact smooth manifold $M$ must contain an abelian normal subgroup with an index bounded by a constant $a(M)$ determined solely by $M$. We initially demonstrated a family of counterexamples to this original conjecture, notably including the product space $T^2\times S^2$. After our counterexamples were published on the arXiv, Ghys formulated a revised conjecture asserting the existence of a nilpotent normal subgroup of index at most $n(M)$. Our primary achievement is the proof of this updated conjecture. Furthermore, we establish that this result extends to homeomorphism groups of topological manifolds that are not necessarily compact, provided they possess finitely generated homology groups. Our methodology relies on finite group theory, offering a broad strategy for deriving analogous Jordan-type theorems.

We investigate a system of non-interacting spinless fermions subject to local dephasing and boundary driving, governed by a Lindblad master equation. This model exhibits a competition between bulk dephasing-induced thermalization at infinite temperature and a non-equilibrium steady state maintained by boundary dissipation and driving. We re-examine both linear and non-linear transport characteristics, observing a transition from ballistic to diffusive scaling, and calculate spectral and occupation properties via single-particle Green's functions derived exactly from the Lindblad equations of motion, despite the \emph{interacting} character of the dephasing mechanism. Our results demonstrate that the bulk distribution function flattens and becomes frequency-independent, aligning with infinite temperature thermalization, whereas the regions near the boundaries display pronounced non-equilibrium signatures resulting from the continuous injection and removal of particles.

This work reviews the mind-body problem through a non-technical lens of quantum information theory. It emphasizes the necessity of precisely defining "what is physical," as this clarification is essential for understanding "non-physical." Physicality is characterized by interaction, which is itself defined as a correlated exchange of information. This framework is posited as the foundation of any meaningful epistemology, leading to the conclusion that non-physical entities cannot possess knowledge of the world. The discussion further explores information transfer via quantum entanglement and offers an argument regarding our perception of time. Finally, it is argued that the concept of "mind" can be meaningfully examined within a quantum theoretic context.

The triplet or type-II seesaw mechanism offers the most straightforward method for generating neutrino mass within the Standard Model. This review covers the theoretical framework and phenomenological implications, including constraints imposed by the $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters, neutrino observations, charged lepton flavour violations, and collider searches. Additionally, we analyze limits arising from the consistency of electroweak symmetry breaking, specifically regarding perturbative unitarity and vacuum stability. We further explore novel effects mediated by the scalar responsible for neutrino mass, such as (i) rare processes like $l_\alpha \to l_\beta \gamma$ decays at the intensity frontier, and (ii) four-lepton signatures at high-energy colliders. These phenomena can significantly probe neutrino properties, offering tests for absolute neutrino mass, mass ordering, and the atmospheric octant, while potentially providing the first evidence of charged lepton flavour violation in nature. Conversely, non-standard neutrino interaction strengths are determined to be below current detection thresholds.

The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) has recently become an efficient alternative to traditional Navier-Stokes solvers, especially for hemodynamic simulations within complex geometries. However, its basic formulation using the single relaxation time (SRT) collision operator suffers from a limited stability domain in the Courant/Fourier space, which severely restricts the minimum time-step and grid size. The introduction of advanced collision models, such as the multiple relaxation time (MRT) operator in central moments space, has significantly expanded this stability domain and eliminated several documented artifacts, thereby enabling simulations across a broader range of grid and time-step resolutions. This study focuses on implementing and validating a specific collision operator—the central Hermite moments MRT model with a full expansion of the equilibrium distribution function—to simulate blood flow in intracranial aneurysms. The numerical model was validated through various test cases and compared against experimental data from stereoscopic particle image velocimetry (PIV) and phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (PC-MRI). Results for a patient-specific aneurysm showed fair agreement between the simulation and both PIV and PC-MRI measurements. Furthermore, low-resolution simulations were demonstrated to capture blood flow information with sufficient accuracy, as confirmed by qualitative and quantitative flow field analyses, while drastically reducing computation times. For example, in the patient-specific case, doubling the grid size reduced computation time by a factor of 14, maintaining high similarity indices between 0.83 and 0.88.

Lately, self-supervised pre-training has demonstrated significant promise in utilizing vast amounts of unlabeled data to enhance performance on downstream tasks. Nevertheless, expanding the volume of unlabeled data for pre-training in practical settings incurs prohibitive computational expenses and struggles with uncurated samples. To overcome these hurdles, we developed a task-specific self-supervised pre-training framework grounded in data selection, relying on the hypothesis that pre-training on unlabeled data with a distribution similar to the target task yields substantial improvements. Based on this premise, we introduce Scalable and Efficient visual Pre-Training (SEPT), a novel framework that incorporates a retrieval pipeline for data selection. First, SEPT utilizes a self-supervised pre-trained model to extract features from the entire unlabeled dataset to initialize the retrieval process. Subsequently, for a given target task, SEPT identifies and retrieves the most similar samples from the unlabeled pool based on feature similarity for every target instance to serve as pre-training data. Finally, the target model undergoes self-supervised pre-training using these selected samples before fine-tuning. By separating the scale of pre-training from the available upstream data for a specific task, SEPT achieves both high scalability regarding the upstream dataset and high pre-training efficiency, offering greater flexibility in model architecture. Experiments across various downstream tasks show that SEPT delivers competitive or superior performance compared to ImageNet pre-training, while reducing the training sample size by an order of magnitude without requiring any additional annotations.

This paper introduces a new numerical approach for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that maintains polynomial first integrals. By incorporating several quadratic auxiliary variables, the ODE is transformed into an equivalent, higher-dimensional system featuring solely quadratic integrals, upon which the midpoint rule is applied. Eliminating these auxiliary variables subsequently produces a midpoint-like method within the original phase space, which is demonstrated to be a novel discrete gradient method. Additionally, the averaged vector field method emerges as a specific instance of this proposed technique. The method supports extension to higher orders via composition and is validated through various numerical examples.

Fake news detection has evolved from a purely academic pursuit into a field with profound societal implications. While recent progress has largely centered on text-based methods, it is now evident that effectiveness requires integrating additional contextual data, such as news dissemination patterns and user interaction behaviors on social platforms. We propose building heterogeneous social context graphs centered on news articles and reframing the challenge as a graph classification problem. By investigating various information types to determine the optimal level of social context and employing different graph neural network architectures, our approach demonstrates high effectiveness and robust performance on standard benchmark datasets.

This paper establishes fine-grained hardness results for the Subgraph Isomorphism (SI) problem with respect to fixed-size induced patterns $H$, leveraging the $k$-Clique hypothesis which posits that current Clique algorithms are optimal. Our primary finding demonstrates that for any pattern graph $H$ classified as a {\em core}, the SI problem is at least as difficult as $t$-Clique, where $t$ represents the size of the largest clique minor in $H$. This advancement improves upon prior results by Dalirrooyfard and Vassilevska W. (STOC'20), which only established a lower bound based on the largest clique {\em subgraph} within $H$ or its chromatic number (assuming the Hadwiger conjecture). Furthermore, for detecting arbitrary graph patterns $H$, we eliminate the reliance on the Hadwiger conjecture found in the earlier work, albeit with a sub-polynomial reduction in the lower bound. These results regarding cores enable us to prove that detecting induced $k$-Paths and $k$-Cycles is more difficult than previously established. While Floderus et al. (Theor. CS 2015) showed these structures are at least as hard as detecting a $\lfloor k/2\rfloor$-Clique, we demonstrate they are actually at least as hard as a $3k/4-O(1)$-Clique, thereby improving the conditional lower bound exponent by a factor of $3/2$. Lastly, we introduce a new conditional lower bound for induced $4$-cycle detection, showing that $n^{2-o(1)}$ time is required even when searching within graphs containing $n$ nodes and $O(n^{1.5})$ edges.

Sleep plays a critical role in the well-being of infants, children, and adolescents, serving as the foundational step for diagnosing and treating potentially fatal conditions. However, pediatric sleep remains significantly under-researched compared to adult sleep within the realm of machine learning for health, and algorithms trained on adults often fail when applied to infants. This study presents the first automated sleep scoring results derived from a recent, large-scale pediatric dataset collected during routine clinical care. We introduce a transformer-based model capable of classifying five distinct sleep stages from millions of multi-channel EEG epochs, achieving an overall accuracy of 78%. Additionally, we perform a detailed analysis of model performance across various patient demographics and EEG channels. These findings underscore the increasing necessity for dedicated machine learning research focused on pediatric sleep.

We introduce a heuristic approach to derive an approximate groundstate for a qubit-based Hamiltonian utilizing the stabilizer formalism. These states are suitable candidates for initializing subsequent refined calculations. Evaluating the method's efficiency and scalability would be a valuable next step.

We establish the solvability and regularity of the Dirichlet problem for fully non-linear elliptic equations, which may feature a degenerate right-hand side, on Hermitian manifolds by proving a quantitative boundary estimate under a subsolution condition. Furthermore, we construct such a subsolution in cases where the underlying manifold is a product of a closed Hermitian manifold and a compact Riemann surface with a boundary.

By employing the on-shell recursion relations for string scattering amplitudes (SSA), we demonstrate that every n-point SSA within open bosonic string theory can be formulated using Lauricella functions. This finding generalizes the previously established exact SL(K+3,C) symmetry of the four-point Lauricella SSA (LSSA)—involving three tachyons and one arbitrary string state—to the entirety of tree-level open bosonic string theory. Additionally, we illustrate three applications of this SL(K+3,C) symmetry to SSA: the solvability of all SSAs via a single amplitude, the presence of iteration relations among the residues of a specific SSA that mitigate its hard scattering behavior, and the re-derivation of infinite linear relations among hard SSAs [12].

Interpretability is a paramount concern in critical decision-making domains like medical diagnosis, prompting research in eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to address this challenge. However, many XAI methods are typically evaluated only on generalist classifiers, failing to address realistic scenarios such as medical diagnostics. This paper presents a case study involving skin lesion images, where an existing XAI approach is adapted to explain a deep learning model designed for recognizing various skin lesions. The generated explanations utilize synthetic exemplar and counter-exemplar images to help practitioners identify the key features driving classification decisions. Surveys involving domain experts, novices, and unskilled individuals demonstrate that these explanations enhance trust and confidence in the automated system. Furthermore, an analysis of the explainer's latent space reveals that several common skin lesion classes are distinctly separated, a pattern likely stemming from intrinsic class characteristics. This separation may aid human experts in resolving frequent misclassifications.

Data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) enable the investigation of quark-gluon plasma properties. Accurately constraining these properties necessitates integrating measurements from various collision systems while rigorously addressing both theoretical and experimental uncertainties, a process that demands extensive and expensive numerical simulations. Although computationally cheap surrogate models, or "emulators," can efficiently approximate heavy-ion simulation outcomes across diverse parameter ranges, training a robust emulator is itself resource-intensive. This study employs transfer learning to project parameter dependencies from one emulator onto another by exploiting commonalities among different heavy-ion collision simulations. By restricting the need for extensive simulations to just a single emulator, this approach significantly lowers the computational burden of comprehensive uncertainty quantification when analyzing multiple collision systems and exploring various models.

Within human-robot interaction research, automatically estimating the mass of a container being manipulated by a human using solely visual data presents a significant challenge, primarily due to occlusions, varying fill materials, and fluctuating lighting. Accurate mass estimation is crucial for robots to adjust grasping forces appropriately. We introduce a method utilizing a single RGB-D camera to identify a manipulated container and estimate its empty mass, regardless of its contents. The approach begins by automatically selecting candidate containers based on their distance from a fixed frontal viewpoint, then averages mass predictions from a lightweight model to generate the final estimate. Experiments on the CORSMAL Containers Manipulation dataset demonstrate that our method achieves a 71.08% score in estimating empty container mass across diverse lighting and filling conditions.

This study presents the experimental nondemolition measurement of coherence, predictability, and concurrence within a two-qubit system. We implemented the quantum circuits suggested by De Melo et al. on both IBM Q (superconducting) and IonQ (trapped ion) platforms. To evaluate the performance of these machines, we analyzed three specific criteria: measurement accuracy, the preservation of the observable during nondemolition, and quantum state preparation. Our results indicate that the IonQ system maintains constant state fidelity throughout the nondemolition process, whereas fidelity on IBM Q systems declines post-measurement, thereby demonstrating IonQ's superior performance. Furthermore, our work contrasts the current capabilities of these two technologies across various stages of the nondemolition measurement of bipartite complementarity.

Addressing the cyber hunt problem at scale introduces significant technical hurdles. Analyzing the massive volume and complexity of data within large enterprise networks to detect and characterize cyber threats is difficult, especially as adversaries employ diverse and evolving tactics. Consequently, there is a critical need to automate every facet of the cyber hunting workflow, an area where AI provides substantial support. We have created the WILEE system, which automates threat hunting by converting high-level threat descriptions into numerous concrete implementations. Both these abstract and low-level implementations are encoded using a custom domain-specific language (DSL). Leveraging these implementations alongside additional DSL-based logic, WILEE automatically generates queries designed to verify or disprove hypotheses related to potential adversarial workflows across various layers of abstraction.

We experimentally achieve optical dipole trapping of a cold atom cloud using a dynamically coupled mode within a high-finesse cavity. Our results indicate that the trap relies on collective atomic behavior, as individual atoms cannot be trapped under identical laser conditions. The atoms shift the cavity mode's frequency toward resonance, enabling the requisite light intensity for trapping. Additionally, the atoms' back-action on the trapping light is evidenced by the trap's non-exponential collapse.

Affective behavior analysis has garnered significant research interest due to its extensive applications, yet acquiring precise annotations for vast collections of facial images remains a labor-intensive task. To address this, we propose leveraging prior facial knowledge through a Masked Auto-Encoder (MAE) pretrained on unlabeled face data. Additionally, we integrate an MAE-pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) with an AffectNet-pretrained CNN to execute multi-task emotion recognition. We observe that expression and Action Unit (AU) scores serve as pure and robust features for valence-arousal (VA) regression; consequently, we employ the AffectNet-pretrained CNN to extract expression scores, which are concatenated with expression and AU scores derived from the ViT to generate the final VA representations. Furthermore, we introduce a co-training framework utilizing two parallel MAE-pretrained ViTs for expression recognition. To ensure the independence of these two views, we randomly mask the majority of patches during training. Subsequently, we apply Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence to align the predictions of both views as closely as possible. Experimental results on the ABAW4 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

Searching for life outside our planet remains a critical scientific pursuit with far-reaching consequences. One specific strategy, the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), aims to identify engineered signals, or "technosignatures," that would confirm the presence of technologically advanced life elsewhere. In this report, we detail the discovery of a narrowband signal-of-interest at approximately 982 MHz, captured while observing Proxima Centauri using the Parkes Murriyang radio telescope. Designated "BLC1," this signal displays features broadly aligned with theoretical technosignatures and stands as one of the most significant candidates identified to date. Although we conclude that BLC1 is actually an unusual form of local interference (as detailed in a companion paper by Sheikh et al., 2021), our observations of Proxima Centauri represent the most sensitive radio technosignature search ever conducted on a specific star.

This paper details WAAW Csound, an implementation of WebAudio Csound based on WebAssembly Audio Worklets. It begins by outlining the history of Csound's initial web ports, which utilized Native Clients and asm.js, before introducing the relevant aspects of WebAssembly technology. The discussion then explores the Web Audio API's AudioWorklet interface and its specific application within WAAW Csound. Furthermore, the paper addresses the challenge of supporting multiple platforms with varying Web Audio implementations. Initial examples demonstrate the system's potential applications, and the text concludes by examining current fundamental issues affecting this project and other initiatives relying on robust WASM-based audio computing.

We examine the oscillation between axion-like particles (ALPs) and photons within the gamma-ray spectra of the blazars Markarian 421 (Mrk 421) and PG 1553+113, utilizing high-precision measurements from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT) and the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov Telescopes (MAGIC). By analyzing 15 distinct phases for Mrk 421 and 5 phases for PG 1553+113, we derive constraints on the ALP parameter space. Our results indicate that combining all 15 phases of the Mrk 421 data strengthens the exclusion limits. Specifically, the combined Mrk 421 analysis rules out an ALP parameter region where the ALP-photon coupling is $g_{a\gamma} \gtrsim 2 \times 10^{-11} \, \rm GeV^{-1}$ for ALP masses in the range of $\sim 8\times 10^{-9}\, {\rm eV} \lesssim m_a \lesssim 2\times 10^{-7}\rm \, eV$, at a 95% confidence level. Additionally, while the ALP hypothesis marginally improves the fit to PG 1553+113 data in certain parameter regions, it does not yield exclusion limits for this source.

In 1973, Neil Sloane introduced a compelling problem in a brief paper: select a decimal integer $n$, multiply its digits together, and repeat this operation until a single digit, $\Delta(n)$, remains. This final digit is known as the \textsl{multiplicative digital root} or \textsl{target} of $n$. The number of iterations required to reach $\Delta(n)$, denoted as $\Xi(n)$, is termed the \textsl{multiplicative persistence} or \textsl{height} of $n$, with a conjecture suggesting it never exceeds 11. Much like other straightforward number-theoretic conjectures, the mystery of multiplicative persistence has defied numerous attempts at resolution. This paper establishes that the conjecture is valid for all odd target values: specifically, if $\Delta(n) \in \{1, 3, 7, 9\}$, then $\Xi(n) \leq 1$, and if $\Delta(n) = 5$, then $\Xi(n) \leq 5$. Consequently, we outline the challenges currently hindering the extension of this method to nonzero even targets.

Accurately and efficiently estimating the Lipschitz constant of neural networks is a critical challenge in deep learning. Recent findings reveal an inherent trade-off between a network's smoothness and its accuracy; consequently, using a loose Lipschitz constant estimation acts as a strong regularizer that can severely degrade model performance. This paper introduces a unified theoretical framework based on a quantitative geometric approach to tackle Lipschitz constant estimation. Utilizing this framework allows for the immediate derivation of key theoretical insights, such as the computational complexity and approximability of the estimation problem. Additionally, this geometric perspective sheds light on recent empirical observations regarding why techniques for different norms often fail to transfer between one another. We have implemented algorithms derived from this approach in a tool called GeoLIP, which relies on semidefinite programming (SDP). Empirical results show that GeoLIP offers superior scalability and precision compared to existing tools for estimating Lipschitz constants under $\ell_\infty$-perturbations. We also explore its complex relationships with other recent SDP-based methods, supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence. Ultimately, we argue that this unified quantitative geometric perspective will provide novel theoretical tools and insights for investigating neural network smoothness and robustness.

In recent years, there has been a growing focus on creating interpretable models within Natural Language Processing (NLP). While most current approaches concentrate on pinpointing specific words or phrases crucial for predictions, NLP neural models frequently encode word semantics hierarchically. Consequently, text classification demands hierarchical modeling to aggregate local information, thereby handling topic and label shifts more effectively. Relying solely on word or phrase-level interpretation fails to accurately elucidate model decisions in this context. To address this, we introduce Hint, a novel Hierarchical INTerpretable neural text classifier. Hint automatically produces explanations for model predictions as hierarchically structured, label-associated topics, shifting the fundamental unit of interpretation from individual words to topics. Experiments conducted on both review and news datasets demonstrate that Hint achieves classification performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art classifiers while generating interpretations that are both more faithful to the model's logic and more comprehensible to humans than other interpretable neural text classifiers.

Although galaxy spin holds significant clues about the Universe's initial conditions, efficiently determining spin orientation for the vast numbers of galaxies targeted by current and future cosmological surveys remains difficult. We introduce a machine learning classifier designed to distinguish between Z-wise and S-wise spirals, aiding in the resolution of degeneracies inherent in spin direction measurements. The proposed Chirality Equivariant Residual Network (CE-ResNet) is explicitly equivariant under image reflection, ensuring no intrinsic asymmetry exists between the probability estimators for Z-wise and S-wise spirals. Trained on Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) images with labels from the Galaxy Zoo 1 (GZ1) project, the model incorporates various data augmentation techniques to enhance its robustness for application across other surveys. When applied to Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) images, which offer superior imaging quality, we observe an approximately 30% increase in the classification counts for both spiral types. We confirm that the previously observed ~7σ discrepancy between Z-wise and S-wise spiral numbers stems from human bias, as our CE-ResNet results reduce this difference to less than 1.8σ. Finally, we address potential systematics relevant to future cosmological applications.

This paper investigates the hydrodynamic limit of a stochastic process modeling the temporal evolution of membrane potentials within a spatially dependent neuronal network. Unlike mean-field models, we do not assume such interactions. The system comprises $\epsilon^{-2}$ neurons distributed in $[0,1)^2$, where membrane potentials change due to chemical and electrical synapses as well as leak currents. Each neuron fires randomly according to a point process with a rate determined by its current potential and location. Upon spiking, neuron $i$ resets its potential, while any influenced neuron $j$ experiences an increase of $\epsilon^2 a(i,j)$ in its potential. Between spikes, the system undergoes deterministic motion driven by leak currents and electrical synapses, which facilitate synchronization. The strength of this synchronization between any pair $(i,j)$ is scaled by $\epsilon^2 b(i,j)$, where $b(i,j)$ is a nonnegative symmetric function. Meanwhile, leak currents suppress neuronal activity by pulling all potentials toward a resting state. Our main result demonstrates that as $\epsilon$ approaches zero, the empirical distribution of membrane potentials converges to a probability density $\rho_t(u,r)$ that satisfies a nonlinear hyperbolic partial differential equation.

A primary objective of heliophysics is to comprehend the propagation of cosmic rays within the solar system's intricate and dynamic environment. One critical observable is solar modulation, which describes the alterations in cosmic ray flux and spectrum as they travel inward. By leveraging recent magnetic power spectral density measurements from the Parker Solar Probe, we have developed an enhanced force-field model to forecast solar modulation inside Earth's orbit. Our findings indicate that cosmic ray modulation between the Sun and Earth is relatively minor, particularly during solar minimum conditions and along the ecliptic plane. Furthermore, our results align significantly better with the sparse data regarding cosmic-ray radial gradients within Earth's orbit compared to previous force-field model applications. These predictions can be validated by upcoming direct cosmic-ray observations in the inner heliosphere conducted by the Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter. Additionally, these insights are crucial for interpreting solar gamma-ray emissions caused by the scattering of cosmic rays against solar matter and photons.

This study estimates the break point in large-dimensional factor models featuring a single structural break in factor loadings at an unknown common date. Initially, we introduce a quasi-maximum likelihood (QML) estimator for the change point, derived from the second moments of factors estimated via principal component analysis. We demonstrate that this QML estimator remains consistent even when the covariance matrix of the factor loadings before or after the break, or both, is singular. In scenarios where the loading matrix experiences a rotational shift while the number of factors stays constant, the QML estimator yields a stochastically bounded estimation error, allowing us to derive its asymptotic distribution. Simulation results confirm the estimator's viability in finite samples. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's practical utility through empirical applications to estimate break points in U.S. macroeconomic and stock return datasets.
This paper provides a concise overview of the rule-based programming system known as P$\rho$Log and demonstrates its capabilities.

By improving upon the volume estimate of Heintze and Karcher \cite{HK}, we derive a precise pinching condition for the genus of a surface within $\mathbb S^{3}$. This condition incorporates an integral of the norm of the surface's traceless second fundamental form. Specifically, we establish that for a closed orientable surface $\Sigma$ embedded in a $3$-dimensional orientable Riemannian manifold $M$ with sectional curvature bounded below by $1$, the inequality $4 \pi^{2} g(\Sigma) \le 2\left(2 \pi^{2}-|M|\right)+\int_{\Sigma} f(|\stackrel \circ A|)$ holds, where $\stackrel \circ A$ denotes the traceless second fundamental form and $f$ represents an explicitly defined function. Consequently, the collection of closed orientable embedded minimal surfaces $\Sigma$ possessing a uniformly bounded $\|A\|_{L^3(\Sigma)}$ forms a compact set in the $C^k$ topology for any $k\ge2$.

Since the 1980s, the *Einstein* observatory has revealed that Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) emit X-rays with luminosities, in the 0.3--8 keV range, reaching up to 1,000 to 10,000 times that of the Sun, and noted that this emission is highly variable. ROSAT confirmed the widespread nature of X-ray emission from YSOs, while ASCA provided evidence that Class I YSOs largely emit from optically thin plasma at temperatures between 1 and 50 $\times 10^6$ K. These unexpected intrinsic properties, combined with the transformative capabilities of the *Chandra* and *XMM-Newton* observatories, have established X-rays as a potent tool for tracing star formation processes out to distances of several kiloparsecs from the Sun. Building on the early evidence from the 1980s and the compelling questions it raised, I will summarize the resulting findings and their impact on our current understanding of the underlying physical processes, while also addressing remaining open questions and potential pathways that next-generation X-ray observatories may uncover.

Granger causality is a prominent data-driven method for analyzing causal relationships in time series data, finding extensive use in fields such as neuroscience, molecular biology, and economics. This methodology faces two primary hurdles: over-fitting due to short data spans and correlated process noise acting as a confounder, both of which compromise the accuracy of identifying causal links. While sparse estimation using LASSO effectively mitigates these issues during parameter estimation, traditional Granger causality tests rely on asymptotic analysis of ordinary least squares (OLS), which demands lengthy data durations and remains vulnerable to confounding factors. This study bridges that gap by proposing a LASSO-based statistic and examining its non-asymptotic behavior under the assumption that true models possess sparse autoregressive structures. We demonstrate that the conditions sufficient for LASSO also guarantee robust detection of Granger causal influences. Furthermore, we define the false positive error rate associated with a straightforward thresholding approach for identifying these effects. Simulation studies and real-world data applications compare the performance of OLS and LASSO in detecting Granger causality, providing empirical support for our theoretical findings.

This paper presents the first investigation into topological defects within nonlocal field theories, where Lagrangians incorporate infinite-order differential operators. Specifically, we examine domain walls. Despite the inherent complexity of solving non-linear infinite-order differential equations, we successfully derive an approximate analytic solution. Our approach begins by establishing the asymptotic behavior of the nonlocal domain wall near the vacua. Subsequently, we obtain a linearized nonlocal solution by perturbing around the standard local 'kink' and demonstrate its consistency with the previously determined asymptotic behavior. We also develop a formalism to analyze the solution near the origin, utilizing it to confirm the validity of the linearized approximation. Our findings indicate that nonlocality results in a narrower domain wall width and reduced energy per unit area compared to the local scenario. For the specific domain wall solution studied, we establish a theoretical constraint requiring the nonlocality energy scale to exceed the corresponding symmetry-breaking scale. Finally, we offer brief remarks on other topological defects, such as strings and monopoles.

During instrument commissioning, JWST NIRCam short-wavelength photometry was employed to record a transit lightcurve of the exoplanet HAT-P-14 b, evaluating the instrument's performance. After correcting for spatially correlated 1/f noise, the short-wavelength precision reached 152 ppm per 27-second integration against a theoretical limit of 107 ppm across the full time series. Charge trapping persistence effects were effectively modeled by an exponential function with short characteristic timescales, settling within 5 to 15 minutes. Additionally, this defocused short-wavelength photometry provides a unique capability for measuring real-time wavefront error. Analysis of images and reconstructed wavefront maps revealed that two distinct hexagonal primary mirror segments experienced rapid "tilt events," changing orientation in under approximately 1.4 seconds. In certain instances, telescope models could accurately predict the magnitude and timing of the resulting flux jumps. These events can be detected solely by simultaneous longer-wavelength NIRCam grism spectral images through point spread function changes diagnosed via FWHM, or alternatively by the FGS instrument using difference images. Anticipated during commissioning due to ground-based testing findings, these tilt events likely stem from sudden stress releases in the mirror backplane structure; while their frequency has decreased, they have not fully ceased. Detectors showed minor (under 1%) deviations from linearity in the initial groups of each integration, which may affect absolute fluxes and transit depths for bright targets with limited group counts. Overall, noise levels remained within 50% of theoretical photon and read noise, indicating strong prospects for high-precision time series measurements.

The terminal Wiener index is a widely utilized topological descriptor in mathematical chemistry. Compounds sharing the same terminal Wiener index typically exhibit analogous physico-chemical characteristics. This study introduces a novel approach for generating trees that are equiseparable with respect to the terminal Wiener index. Unlike current methods, which rely on the count of pendant vertices, the proposed technique utilizes distance parameters.

We introduce a framework for the end-to-end optimization of metasurface imaging systems that reconstruct targets using compressed sensing, a method for solving underdetermined imaging problems when the target exhibits sparsity (meaning the object can be described by a small number of non-zero values, though their locations are unknown). By embedding an iterative, unapproximated compressed sensing reconstruction algorithm into our optimization pipeline, we achieve an interpretable and data-efficient approach that maximizes the use of metaoptics to exploit object sparsity. We demonstrate this framework through super-resolution and high-resolution depth imaging using a phase-change material; in both cases, our end-to-end system computationally identifies optimal metasurface structures for compressed sensing recovery, automatically managing complex design constraints. The resulting optimized metasurface imaging systems prove robust against noise, significantly outperforming random scattering surfaces and nearing the ideal compressed sensing performance of a Gaussian matrix, thereby illustrating how physical metasurface systems can effectively approach the theoretical limits of compressed sensing.

We introduce KKhhFoam, a novel semi-analytical tool that offers a streamlined framework for verifying the amplitude-level exponentiation scheme (CEEX) within the full KKMChh program under semi-soft conditions. Furthermore, the architecture of the KKhhFoam integrand aids in clarifying the underlying structure of CEEX. Additionally, we examine the representation of Initial State Radiation (ISR) in KKMChh, comparing the ISR contributions added by KKMChh against those from switching to QED-corrected parton distribution functions (PDFs) at the individual quark level, and propose a new methodology for implementing KKMChh with QED-corrected PDFs.

A SAS-based approach utilizing multiple imputation and bootstrap techniques to address missing data in mediation analysis is presented and applied. Simulation results demonstrate the method's robust performance under both MCAR and MAR conditions, with or without auxiliary variables. Furthermore, the method proves equally effective for MNAR data when auxiliary variables linked to the missingness mechanism are incorporated. The utility of this approach is illustrated by analyzing a subset of data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth.

Protecting the privacy of machine learning models remains a significant obstacle to the widespread implementation of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This study addresses this issue specifically within image datasets featuring human faces. Given the critical role of such data in training autonomous vehicles and the extensive data collected by surveillance systems, anonymizing these datasets is becoming increasingly vital. While previous research has focused on de-identifying facial images by altering identity features directly in pixel space, our approach projects images into the latent space of a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). We identify features that maximize identity disentanglement and then manipulate them in the latent space, pixel space, or both. The primary contribution of this work is the development of StyleID, a feature-preserving anonymization framework designed to safeguard individual identities while retaining as many original facial characteristics as possible. Additionally, we introduce a novel disentanglement metric, three complementary disentanglement methods, and offer new insights into identity disentanglement. StyleID offers tunable privacy levels, maintains low computational complexity, and demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art solutions.

This report presents measurements of Higgs boson properties within the $H \to \gamma\gamma$ decay channel. The study utilizes data from the CMS experiment, gathered during the 2016 LHC run of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 35.6 fb$^{-1}$. With a floating Higgs mass, the analysis determines a signal strength relative to the Standard Model prediction of 1.18 $^{+0.17}_{-0.14}$, which decomposes into 1.18 $^{+0.12}_{-0.11}$ (stat) $^{+0.09}_{-0.07}$ (syst) $^{+0.07}_{-0.06}$ (theo); this result remains largely unaffected by the precise Higgs mass near 125 GeV. Additionally, signal strengths for various Higgs production mechanisms, boson and fermion couplings, and effective couplings to photons and gluons are determined.

We establish a solution theory for singular elliptic stochastic PDEs featuring fractional Laplacians, additive white noise, and cubic non-linearities. This approach encompasses the entire sub-critical regime and relies on Wilsonian renormalization group theory alongside the Polchinski flow equation.

This paper presents a novel family of intensional Martin-Löf type theory models utilizing constructive ordered algebra within toposes. Identity types in these models are defined through a concept of Moore paths. By examining a specific gros topos, we demonstrate the existence of a non-truncated model, meaning it retains non-trivial structure across all dimensions. Consequently, within this model, a type nested within a sequence of identity types can contain multiple elements regardless of the nesting depth. While inspired by prior non-truncated type theory models based on simplicial and cubical sets, this approach is distinguished by its avoidance of any Kan filling conditions in the semantic interpretation of types.

Recent years have seen the proposal of many machine learning models aimed at tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting drug-drug interactions, and designing combination therapies. In this work, we offer a unified theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of addressing these challenges. We establish core definitions, contrast current architectural approaches, and examine performance metrics, datasets, and evaluation protocols.
