Furthermore, we highlight potential high-impact applications and outline key directions for future research within this field.

This study analytically derives the path integral representation for conditional probabilities governing non-Markovian kinetic processes by utilizing the free energy of the underlying thermodynamic system. We further perform an analytical solution of time-fractional kinetic equations for these processes. Consequently, we provide a straightforward generalization of Markovian path integral solutions to the non-Markovian regime. We conclude that these pedagogical findings are applicable to various physical problems, including deformed ion channels, internet networks, and non-equilibrium phase transitions.

A newly developed tuning-dressed protocol adapts the Bell and Bloom magnetometer for sensing subtle radio-frequency (RF) magnetic field fluctuations. We propose employing this advanced detection method as either a supplement or alternative to existing RF atomic magnetometers within electromagnetic induction imaging systems.

This study introduces a computationally efficient workflow for deriving low-energy tight-binding Hamiltonians for twisted bilayer graphene that strictly adhere to both crystal and time-reversal symmetries. Hamiltonians at the first magic angle are constructed using the Slater-Koster method, with parameters fitted to ab-initio data from larger angles. Employing the Wannier90 software, we build low-energy symmetric four-band and twelve-band models. The primary benefit of this approach is that it yields purely real low-energy Hamiltonians through a maximum-localization procedure, which minimizes the spread of basis functions. Furthermore, we calculate extended Hubbard parameters for both models using the constrained random phase approximation (cRPA) for screening, ensuring symmetry compliance. All relevant data and results are accessible via an online repository, and the proposed workflow is easily adaptable to other twisted multi-layer materials.

Spectrum sensing techniques that utilize the limiting eigenvalue ratio of the covariance matrix provide enhanced detection capabilities and resolve issues related to noise uncertainty. Although an exact mathematical expression for this ratio exists, its complexity has led to the publication of several approximate solutions in existing literature. This work derives a refined, highly accurate integral solution for the probability density function of the ratio by applying order statistical analysis to eliminate the flawed assumption of independence. Consequently, this study advances the rigorous theoretical framework for eigenvalue-based spectrum sensing.

Image segmentation, defined as the process of distinguishing objects from their backgrounds, remains one of the most difficult challenges in digital image processing. Since achieving 100% accuracy with a single algorithm is practically unattainable, many different techniques have been developed, each possessing specific limitations. This paper introduces a novel region-based Falling-Ball algorithm, which serves as an alternative to the traditional watershed transform (grounded in the waterfall model). The method identifies catchment basins by simulating a ball descending from hilly terrain until it settles in a basin. Once these basins are located, multi-criterion fuzzy logic is employed to assign each pixel to a specific basin. Edges are formed by partitioning the image into these distinct basins using a membership function. Subsequently, a closed contour algorithm identifies enclosed regions, and objects within them are segmented based on intensity data. The algorithm's effectiveness was assessed through both objective and subjective evaluations. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method outperforms conventional Sobel edge detection and standard watershed segmentation. To demonstrate its superiority over existing techniques, various comparative analyses were conducted.

Transformer-based masked language models like BERT and RoBERTa, trained on general corpora, have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across numerous downstream applications. Consequently, researchers are increasingly "finetuning" these models to enhance their performance on domain-specific challenges. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation applying 14 transformer-based models to 11 scientific tasks to assess how downstream performance shifts in response to variations in dimensions such as training data, model scale, pretraining duration, and finetuning length. During this process, we developed ScholarBERT, the most extensive and diverse scientific language model to date, by training a 770M-parameter BERT architecture on a 221B-token dataset of scientific literature covering multiple disciplines. Surprisingly, our assessment of the 14 BERT-based models—which included seven versions of ScholarBERT, five existing science-specific large language models, BERT-Base, and BERT-Large—showed minimal performance variation across the 11 science-focused tasks, despite significant disparities in model size and training data. We contend that these findings establish the performance ceiling achievable with BERT-based architectures for tasks within the scientific domain.

Deriving road networks and optimal routes directly from remote sensing data is vital for numerous commercial and humanitarian endeavors. Although prior efforts have focused on identifying road pixels, estimating travel times from overhead imagery remains an innovative challenge, especially when dealing with off-nadir perspectives. To address this, we extract road networks alongside travel time estimates from the SpaceNet MVOI dataset. By employing the CRESIv2 framework, we demonstrate the capability to identify road networks across various observation angles and evaluate performance at 27 distinct nadir angles using the graph-theoretic APLS_length and APLS_time metrics. A minimal discrepancy of 0.03 between these scores suggests our method produces speed limits and travel times with exceptional accuracy. Furthermore, we investigated the benefits of training models using all available angles, achieving a peak APLS_time score of 0.56. This combined model shows significantly enhanced robustness compared to angle-specific models, effectively overcoming the substantial visual differences between road networks captured at extreme oblique angles versus those taken directly overhead.

Beginning in December 2020, global spread of COVID-19 variants, particularly Delta and Omicron, introduced new traits affecting transmission and mortality rates. To capture these evolving disease dynamics, we introduce a dynamical model incorporating two strains (native and mutant), mutation processes, and imperfect vaccination. The model assumes that individuals recovered from the native strain remain susceptible to the mutant strain via direct contact or exposure to contaminated surfaces and aerosols. We calculate the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) for each strain independently and define the system's threshold as the maximum of these values. Using center manifold theory, we demonstrate that backward bifurcation does not occur and establish the global stability of the disease-free equilibrium when $R_0 < 1$. An intermediate mutation rate ($\nu_1$) induces oscillatory behavior; however, once $\nu_1$ exceeds a specific threshold, the system stabilizes and displays a phenomenon termed the "endemic bubble." We also derive an analytical formula for vaccine-induced herd immunity. Parameterized with Indian data on cumulative confirmed cases and deaths from March 1 to September 27, 2021, and estimated via the MCMC method, our results indicate that increasing vaccine efficacy against both strains lowers cumulative cases and deaths. Specifically, a 90% efficacy against the native strain would reduce cumulative cases by 3.27% and deaths by 5.2%, whereas 90% efficacy against the mutant strain would yield reductions of 0.9% and 2.5%, respectively. Ultimately, our findings suggest that while certain mutation rates may exacerbate the pandemic through oscillations, higher mutation rates can improve outcomes by stabilizing the system at lower infection levels.

This work proposes a flexible and curtailable resource activation framework designed to address voltage and thermal congestion in distribution networks (DN). The approach uses the network state, calculated without considering flexible resources, as input to determine a Flexibility Activation Signal (FAS). Inspired by volt-Var and volt-watt inverter controls, the FAS functions similarly to optimal power flow duals or locational marginal prices, which typically activate only upon network violations; however, due to its drooping design, the FAS corrects issues before such limits are breached. To solve the nonlinear resource dispatch optimal power flow (RDOPF) problem, second-order cone (SOC) relaxations are employed for convexification. Three case studies, evaluated using newly proposed performance metrics, demonstrate the framework's capabilities. The first study illustrates the multi-objective nature of the SOC-relaxed RDOPF and offers a Pareto front tuning mechanism to simultaneously minimize DN losses and the optimality gap relative to RDOPF. The second study introduces a method for assessing temporal and locational flexibility needs, aiding distribution system operators (DSOs) in planning. The final study quantifies the effect of reactive power flexibility on DNs with varying load power factors, revealing that active power flexibility requirements can be reduced by up to 50% when the power factor is 0.8.

Introducing sufficient non-adsorbing polymer into a stable colloidal suspension triggers diverse phase behaviors and kinetic arrest driven by polymer-induced depletion attraction between colloids. This study examines these effects within a two-dimensional colloidal layer. While the three-dimensional crystal-fluid coexistence phenomenology is replicated, gelation manifests uniquely, featuring gel strands that are locally crystalline. Our results align substantially with prior simulations and theoretical models.

The increasing integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) creates dynamic operating conditions that distribution grid operators must manage effectively. The variability of DERs, such as solar photovoltaic systems, combined with inaccuracies in load forecasting, heightens grid uncertainty and introduces critical power quality issues, including voltage unbalance and magnitude violations. To mitigate the effects of this uncertainty, this study employs a chance-constrained optimization framework. We introduce the chance-constrained optimal power flow (CC-OPF) formulation for distribution networks and detail a reformulation technique based on constraint tightening that avoids approximations or relaxations of the three-phase AC power flow equations. Furthermore, we develop two iterative algorithms designed to solve this reformulation efficiently. Case studies utilizing real PV and load data from the IEEE 13-bus test feeder demonstrate that both algorithms successfully enforce chance constraints in both in-sample and out-of-sample evaluations.

Numerous municipalities and road authorities aim to adopt automated road damage assessment systems, yet they frequently lack the necessary funding, technical expertise, and advanced equipment for data collection and analysis. While nations like Japan have pioneered cost-effective, smartphone-based solutions for monitoring road conditions, other countries continue to struggle with finding efficient alternatives. This study addresses these challenges through four key contributions: first, it evaluates the applicability of the Japanese model to other nations; second, it introduces a large-scale, heterogeneous dataset of 26,620 road damage images gathered from various countries using smartphones; third, it develops generalized models capable of detecting and classifying road defects across multiple regions; and fourth, it offers strategic recommendations for local agencies and municipalities regarding the adoption of foreign data and models for automatic damage detection. The dataset is publicly accessible at (https://github.com/sekilab/RoadDamageDetector/).

We report 63 novel multi-site radial velocity observations of the K1III giant HD 76920, a star recently identified as hosting the most eccentric planet known to orbit an evolved star. Our observations concentrated on the anticipated periastron passage, securing near-continuous coverage of the radial velocity peak. By integrating our data from four instruments with prior publications, we reaffirm the system's high eccentricity, determining an updated value of $e=0.8782 \pm 0.0025$. Additionally, we derive an orbital period of $415.891^{+0.043}_{-0.039}\,\mathrm{d}$ and a minimum planet mass of $3.13^{+0.41}_{-0.43}\,\mathrm{M_J}$. These measurements significantly reduce uncertainties in the orbital elements, particularly for the period and eccentricity. A comprehensive spectroscopic analysis yielded atmospheric stellar parameters, enabling the calculation of fundamental properties ($M_*, R_*, L_*$) when combined with Gaia DR2 parallax; stellar mass and radius were also independently constrained via asteroseismology. Notably, at periastron, the planet approaches within 2.4 stellar radii of the host's surface. Despite this proximity, the planet shows no signs of significant orbital decay and will avoid engulfment by the stellar envelope for at least another $50-80$ Myr. Finally, although we computed a transit probability of $16\%$, no transit was observed in the TESS photometric data.

Recent studies have shown significant interest in graph clustering for data partitioning using graph information; however, a primary limitation of most existing graph-based approaches is their reliance on fixed and reliable graph structures. These methods often struggle with spurious edges—connections that hinder effective clustering. This paper introduces a novel dual graph embedding network (DGEN), the first to apply graph pooling techniques to node clustering. DGEN functions as a two-step graph encoder linked by a graph pooling layer to learn graph embeddings. The model operates on the premise that an edge is cluster-friendly if both a node and its nearest neighbor are proximate to the same clustering center, thereby identifying such nodes as informative. To leverage this, we propose the neighbor cluster pooling (NCPool) mechanism, which selects the most relevant nodes and edges based on their proximity to cluster centers, effectively mitigating the negative impact of spurious edges. Ultimately, a classifier is trained on the clustering results of these selected nodes to determine the final assignments for all nodes. Experiments across five benchmark datasets confirm that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.

Mining aligned pairs of natural language (NL) and programming language (PL) is essential for advancing NL-PL understanding. While current approaches rely on specialized hand-crafted features or models trained individually for each programming language, they often struggle with low transferability across multiple languages, particularly for niche languages lacking sufficient annotated data. Fortunately, Stack Overflow answer posts inherently consist of text and code blocks, where the global textual context offers language-agnostic supplementary information. This paper introduces a Sequence Labeling-based Question Answering (SLQA) method designed to mine NL-PL pairs in a language-agnostic fashion. Specifically, we utilize the BIO tagging scheme rather than the conventional binary scheme to extract code solutions that frequently comprise multiple blocks within a post. Experiments conducted on existing single-language, single-block benchmarks and a manually labeled cross-language, multi-block benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of SLQA. Additionally, we present Lang2Code, a parallel NL-PL corpus automatically mined using SLQA, which includes approximately 1.4 million pairs across six programming languages. Through statistical analysis and downstream evaluations, we show that Lang2Code serves as a large-scale, high-quality data resource for future NL-PL research.

This paper demonstrates that for any $m$-gonal form $F_m(\mathbf x)$ with $m \ge 12$ representing all positive integers up to $m-4$, one can construct a universal form by combining only unary $m$-gonal forms.

This paper introduces NNV, a software tool designed as a set-based verification framework for deep neural networks (DNNs) and learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS). At its core, NNV utilizes a suite of reachability algorithms that leverage diverse set representations, including polyhedra, star sets, zonotopes, and abstract-domain methods. The tool supports both exact (sound and complete) and over-approximate (sound) reachability algorithms to verify the safety and robustness of feed-forward neural networks (FFNNs) with various activation functions. For learning-enabled CPS, such as closed-loop control systems integrating neural networks, NNV offers exact and over-approximate reachability analysis for linear plant models paired with FFNN controllers featuring piecewise-linear activations like ReLUs. Regarding similar neural network control systems (NNCS) with nonlinear plant models, NNV provides over-approximate analysis by merging star set analysis for FFNN controllers with zonotope-based analysis for nonlinear plant dynamics, building upon CORA. The authors evaluate NNV through two real-world case studies: the safety verification of ACAS Xu networks and the safety verification of a deep learning-based adaptive cruise control system.

Building upon Papers I and II in this series, we have investigated the properties of the embedded Orion-S Molecular Cloud and the thin ionized layer situated between it and the observer at higher spatial resolution. These clouds are located within the ionized cavity of the Orion Nebula. Our analysis utilized both new and existing spectra of [NII] (658.3 nm) and [OIII] (500.7 nm) to map the central Huygens Region of the Orion Nebula. Despite the observational evidence indicating a necessary connection between the surface brightness of the Orion-S Cloud and a foreground Nearer Ionized Layer, the specific mechanism linking them remains uncertain. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the Cloud alters the outer regions of the Huygens Region, particularly in the direction of the extended hot X-ray gas.

This study examines the selection of optimal financial derivatives for completing a market under stochastic volatility (SV) models. We present a precise and efficient simulation-based technique, suitable for generalized diffusion models, to estimate the best derivative-driven portfolio strategy. Building on the double optimization framework (combining expected utility maximization with risk exposure minimization) introduced by Escobar-Anel et al. (2022), we demonstrate that strangle options are the superior instruments for market completion in equity options. Additionally, we analyze the advantages of employing volatility index derivatives, finding them to be more practical alternatives when only long-term equity options are accessible.

The point-to-set principle \cite{LutLut17} defines the Hausdorff dimension of a subset $E\subseteq\R^n$ in terms of the algorithmic dimension of its constituent points. This framework has facilitated proofs of various results in classical analysis and has recently been applied effectively to Marstrand's projection theorem, a cornerstone of fractal geometry. This paper introduces an extension of the point-to-set principle through the concept of \textit{optimal oracles} for subsets $E\subseteq\R^n$. A key motivation for this definition is that if a set $E$ possesses optimal oracles, Marstrand's projection theorem applies to it. We demonstrate that all analytic sets admit optimal oracles and prove that equality between the Hausdorff and packing dimensions of $E$ is also a sufficient condition. Furthermore, we establish that the presence of sufficiently regular outer measures on $E$ guarantees the existence of optimal Hausdorff oracles; specifically, the existence of exact gauge functions for $E$ ensures these oracles and, consequently, the validity of Marstrand's theorem. This finding broadens the known sufficient conditions under which Marstrand's theorem holds. While optimal oracles exist for every set under specific assumptions, we construct sets lacking such oracles by assuming the axiom of choice and the continuum hypothesis. This construction naturally yields a generalization of Davies' theorem on projections.

This study examines the impact of external noise on the Lorenz model, specifically near the onset of convection and the Hopf bifurcation. We demonstrate a diverging time scale in the vicinity of convection onset and a resonance phenomenon near the Hopf bifurcation. Furthermore, our calculations offer insight into the numerically observed noise-induced stabilization of the limit cycle.

We present high-resolution angular magnetoresistance (AMR) measurements on ReO$_3$ crystals characterized by high carrier mobility (90,000 cm$^2$/Vs at 2 K) and exceptionally low residual resistivity (5-8 n$\Omega$cm). The material's Fermi surface, consisting of intersecting cylinders, accommodates open orbits. Under a 9 T magnetic field, the longitudinal resistivity $\rho_{xx}$ exhibits a distinct pattern. When the electric field aligns with $\hat{x}$ and the magnetic field $\bf B$ starts parallel to $\hat{z}$, tilting $\bf B$ within the longitudinal $k_z$-$k_x$ plane causes $\rho_{xx}$ to drop sharply by a factor of 40. Conversely, tilting $\bf B$ in the transverse $k_y$-$k_z$ plane results in a steep rise in $\rho_{xx}$ by a factor of 8. Applying the Shockley tube integral method reveals that this singular behavior in ReO$_3$ stems from the swift transformation of closed orbits into open ones, producing opposing AMR signs in orthogonal planes. We associate the minimum $\rho_{xx}$ values in both scans with particular configurations of open and closed orbits. Furthermore, the observed "completion angle" $\gamma_c$ is identified as an intrinsic geometric property offering a novel method to determine the Fermi radius $k_F$. Nevertheless, additional sharp resonant features emerging at very small tilt angles in the longitudinal AMR scans remain unexplained by the tube integral approach.

We introduce a novel information-theoretic bound on generalization error that synthesizes Bu et al.'s error decomposition method with the conditional mutual information (CMI) framework developed by Steinke and Zakynthinou. While Haghifam et al. previously derived a distinct bound combining these same techniques—termed the conditional individual mutual information (CIMI) bound—we found that in simple Gaussian scenarios, both the CMI and CIMI bounds are inferior in order compared to Bu et al.'s original result. This finding prompted our development of the new bound, which addresses this limitation by minimizing the conditioning terms within the conditional mutual information. Furthermore, deriving this bound required establishing a conditional decoupling lemma, which simultaneously facilitates a significant comparison and dichotomy among various information-theoretic bounds.

This study investigates the rare decay of the Higgs boson into two light pseudoscalar particles, denoted as a$_1$, assuming one decays into an opposite-sign muon pair while the other decays into a b$\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ pair. These signatures are anticipated in various extensions of the Standard Model, such as next-to-minimal supersymmetry and two-Higgs-doublet models augmented with an extra scalar singlet. The analysis utilizes 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC in 2016, corresponding to a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. No significant excess over Standard Model backgrounds was found within the search region covering pseudoscalar masses from 20 GeV up to half the Higgs boson mass. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the product of the Higgs production cross-section and branching fraction, $\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}\mathcal{B}$(h $\to$ a$_1$ a$_1$ $\to$ $\mu^+\mu^-\mathrm{b}\bar{\mathrm{b}}$), are established between 5 and 33 fb, varying with the pseudoscalar mass. Assuming the Standard Model prediction for $\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}$, these results imply branching fraction limits of $(1$-$7)\times$ 10$^{-4}$.

This paper examines the random graph model $G(n,p)$, where every edge of a complete graph on $n$ vertices exists independently with probability $p$. We investigate the minimum number of edge modifications required to transform such a graph into an Eulerian one. Specifically, we derive deviation estimates for three distinct measures of these edit operations: those involving only additions, only deletions, or a mix of both. Our results demonstrate that, with high probability, approximately $n/4$ operations are sufficient to achieve an Eulerian graph under any of these three strategies.

Code retrieval involves aligning natural language queries with programming code. This study introduces an adversarial learning framework for code retrieval, constrained by question-description relevance. First, we modify a basic adversarial approach to produce challenging code snippets based on input questions, addressing the difficulties of handling bi-modal data and scarcity. Second, we utilize question-description relevance to regularize this adversarial process, ensuring that generated code snippets contribute more significantly to the training loss only when their associated natural language descriptions are deemed less relevant to the user's query. Experiments across large-scale datasets for two programming languages demonstrate that our adversarial method enhances the performance of state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, incorporating an additional duplicate question prediction model to further regularize the adversarial learning yields even better results, outperforming the use of duplicated questions within strong multi-task learning baselines.

The study investigates the spatiotemporal characteristics of two-dimensional (2D) Hall-magnetohydrodynamic turbulence at an intermediate plasma $\beta$ of 2 using Fast Iterative Filtering, a novel method for decomposing nonstationary nonlinear signals. Findings indicate that magnetic energy at sub-ion scales resides in perturbations with frequencies below the ion-cyclotron (IC) frequency and exhibits polarization inconsistent with both kinetic Alfvén waves (KAWs) and ion-cyclotron waves. While signatures of whistler waves and KAWs are distinctly observed at higher frequencies, their impact on the magnetic power spectrum is minimal. Consequently, the dynamics of 2D Hall-MHD turbulence at sub-ion scales are primarily governed by localized intermittent structures, with wavelike fluctuations playing an insignificant role.

Granular-fluid mixtures are ubiquitous in nature, yet their rheological behaviors remain poorly understood as solid fractions increase under varying conditions. The difficulty in predicting their dynamics stems from the ambiguous combined influence of fluid-solid and solid-solid interactions on macroscopic behavior. This study generalizes and unifies the frictional rheologies of both dense suspensions and dry granular media by employing a dimensionless number derived from the ratio of physically meaningful length scales. This approach spans a broad spectrum of flow regimes and consolidates existing theories for both dry and immersed granular flows. These findings corroborate recent reports of power-law scaling behaviors near the jamming state. Furthermore, the results establish a comprehensive constitutive framework for visco-inertial granular flows, enhancing our understanding of granular-fluid mixtures in both natural and engineering contexts, while offering a robust method for analyzing multi-phase, multi-scale flows under complex force fields.

This paper launches an investigation into demand-aware payment channel networks, which are off-chain cryptocurrency systems designed with topologies optimized for current transactional demand. Specifically, we introduce a model and optimization framework that determines the most effective locations to establish virtual payment channels. These channels facilitate direct routing by bypassing intermediaries, thereby lowering fees and latency; however, their creation incurs associated costs.

The notion of a tolerance relation, commonly referred to as a tolerance, has been investigated across diverse algebraic structures since the 1970s by B. Zelinka and the first author. Because tolerances are not required to be transitive, their equivalence classes can overlap, which generally prevents the set of all blocks from forming a quotient algebra in the manner possible with congruences. Nevertheless, G. Cz\'edli demonstrated that lattices admit a natural factorization via tolerances, and J. Grygiel and S. Radelecki established a variation of an Isomorphism Theorem specifically for tolerances on lattices. The objective of this paper is to generalize the concept of a lattice tolerance to partially ordered sets (posets), thereby enabling the derivation of results analogous to those achieved for lattices.
In this paper, we investigate generalized quantum operations and nearly sharp quantum effects, with our findings extending and refining key results presented in references [2] and [3].

Just-in-time (JIT) compilation and code caching are standard techniques for enhancing performance in dynamic programming languages; however, these caches and their associated profiling data for frequently executed code impose substantial memory overhead and additional compilation latency. On Android, the current JIT implementation and its caches operate independently per process, meaning each runtime instance maintains its own private cache and data. Since applications on the same platform often utilize shared libraries, pooling cached code across multiple processes and applications could significantly lower memory usage, reduce compilation time, and decrease the cumulative time spent interpreting code, thereby boosting overall runtime efficiency. This paper introduces ShareJIT, a global code cache designed for JIT compilers that enables code sharing across diverse applications and processes. Implemented within the Android Runtime (ART), ShareJIT increases sharing potential by restricting the context available to the JIT compiler for optimization, highlighting a core tradeoff where greater specialization for a single process reduces code shareability. To prioritize shareability, ShareJIT deliberately limits certain optimizations. Evaluation across 30 experiments involving eight popular Android applications demonstrates that ShareJIT achieves an average 9% performance improvement, reduces memory consumption by 16%, and cuts JIT compilation time by 37%.

Generating text that is perceived as creative has long been a primary objective for researchers. Recent studies increasingly focus on enhancing the creative writing capabilities of human authors through this approach. This paper investigates how exposure to automatically generated text impacts human writing, specifically examining the "sentence infilling" task, which requires completing a sentence from a given list of words. A key criterion for success is "storability," defined as the quality of sentences that inspire a reader's curiosity about a potential narrative. Both humans and a neural language model attempted this task. In one condition, participants wrote independently, while in another, they viewed model-generated examples while composing their own sentences. Subsequently, readers evaluated the output for storiability. Results indicate that human-authored sentences were rated as more storiable when writers had observed the model's examples, with higher storiability correlating to the degree of semantic content derived from those examples. These findings support an "inspiration through observation" framework for human-computer collaborative writing, demonstrating that text generation models can improve human writing without necessitating direct copying of their output.

Deriving the atomistic structure and dynamics of disordered condensed phase systems from first principles remains a leading challenge in chemical theory. This study leverages recent progress in periodic electronic structure to demonstrate that transfer learning, initiated from lower-tier electronic structure methods, enables the generation of machine-learned potential energy surfaces for liquid water using high-tier AFQMC, CCSD, and CCSD(T) approaches with $\le$200 energy calculations. Through classical and path integral molecular dynamics simulations on these surfaces, we reveal the interaction between dynamical electron correlation and nuclear quantum effects throughout the entire liquid range of water, while also establishing a general strategy for efficiently applying periodic correlated electronic structure methods to investigate disordered condensed phase systems.

Current computational approaches to learning spoken language through perceptual grounding typically rely on multimodal associations, mapping speech and visual inputs into a shared vector space. However, a significant challenge regarding ecological validity arises from the training data, which usually consists of images or videos paired with spoken descriptions of the scene. This pairing creates an artificially strong correlation between language and visuals. In reality, the connection between linguistic and visual modalities is much looser and frequently entangled with non-semantic features of the speech signal. To overcome this limitation, we utilize a dataset derived from the children's show *Peppa Pig*. We train a straightforward bi-modal architecture on dialogue segments between characters and assess performance on descriptive narration clips. Despite the training data offering a weak and confounded signal, our model successfully learns visual semantic aspects of spoken language.

The singlet majoron model, which explains neutrino mass via the seesaw mechanism, is extended by introducing a dark Majorana fermion singlet $\chi$ with lepton number $L=2$ and a dark complex scalar singlet $\zeta$ with $L=1$. This minimal framework enables $\chi$ to acquire a small radiative mass linked to the same heavy right-handed neutrinos, while the one-loop decay of the standard-model Higgs boson into $\chi \chi + \bar{\chi} \bar{\chi}$ establishes the freeze-in production mechanism, allowing $\chi$ to serve as the light dark matter candidate of the Universe.

In his study of $H_{3}\left(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Q}),\mathbb{Z}\left[\frac{1}{2}\right]\right)$, Hutchinson described its structure using $K_{3}^{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathbb{Q})\cong \mathbb{Z}/24$ and the scissor congruence group associated with the residue field $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for a prime $p$. This paper advances the properties of the refined scissors congruence group to generalize Hutchinson's findings to imaginary quadratic number fields where the ring of integers is Euclidean with respect to the norm.

Observations indicate a significant rise in the ion temperature of Jupiter's and Saturn's magnetospheres between approximately 10 and 30 planetary radii. Various heating mechanisms have been suggested to account for this, notably a Jupiter-specific model relying on MHD turbulence with flux-tube diffusion. More recently, an advection-based MHD turbulent heating model was demonstrated to explain the temperature increase in both planets. This study further advances the turbulent heating framework by integrating both diffusion and advection effects. The resulting combined model satisfies the physical consistency condition that diffusion must prevail when radial flow velocity is low, while advection dominates at higher velocities. Comparative analysis with observational data confirms that prior agreements achieved with the advection-only model remain valid at greater radial distances. Furthermore, the inclusion of additional diffusive heating improves alignment with temperature observations at smaller radial distances.

We introduce efficient and practical algorithms designed for large, distributed processor networks to perform secure and reliable computations. Specifically, we tackle the challenge of calculating a general function based on multiple private inputs spread across a network's processors, ensuring both result accuracy and input confidentiality even in the presence of accidental or malicious faults. Our algorithms are characterized by low local processing costs, achieve optimal fault-tolerance for the first time, and, most significantly, feature low communication complexity. Unlike previous state-of-the-art methods that demand numerous rounds even for simple tasks, our protocols utilize small messages and a constant number of rounds, independent of the function's complexity. By employing direct algebraic methods, we decouple the communication complexity of secure computing from the computational complexity of the target function. We evaluate security under both modern computational complexity-based cryptography and classical information-theoretic security, providing formal proofs to address a notable gap in existing literature and ensuring our protocols are provably secure. Within the realm of information-theoretic security, we identify the specific functions that two parties can jointly compute with absolute privacy and those that a weak processor can solve with the assistance of powerful processors without revealing the problem instances. Our approach incorporates a novel technique known as locally random reduction, which has not only yielded efficient solutions for many of the problems addressed here but also generated several significant new results in complexity theory.

Periodically-driven oscillators are typically modeled within a frame rotating with the drive, employing the rotating-wave approximation (RWA). However, this approach is recognized to produce inaccuracies under off-resonant conditions. We demonstrate that the standard quantum framework, which relies on creation and annihilation operators at the oscillator's natural frequency, yields incorrect results when paired with the RWA. Using the simple harmonic oscillator as a case study, we introduce an alternative operator basis that harmonizes the RWA with off-resonant driving. This methodology extends to more intricate models, addressing known inconsistencies. As an illustration, we highlight the benefits of this scheme by applying it to the driven quantum Duffing oscillator.

This work examines evolutionary models on quantum graphs formulated through linear and nonlinear partial differential equations. We investigate the existence and stability of standing waves localized on these graphs by employing variational theory, dynamical systems analysis on a phase plane, and Dirichlet-to-Neumann mappings.

Federated clustering represents an unsupervised learning challenge relevant to various real-world domains, such as personalized recommendation engines and healthcare platforms. The implementation of recent regulations guaranteeing the "right to be forgotten" has elevated the necessity for machine unlearning techniques specifically tailored to federated clustering. This study introduces the inaugural unlearning mechanism for federated clustering that incorporates privacy standards, enabling simple, provably secure, and efficient data deletion at both client and server levels. The core strategy involves merging specialized initialization protocols with quantization techniques to facilitate the secure aggregation of local cluster count estimates at the server. Within our proposed framework, we present Secure Compressed Multiset Aggregation (SCMA), a method of independent value for securely aggregating sparse models. To achieve low communication complexity while supporting secret sharing protocols, we incorporate Reed-Solomon encoding with specific evaluation points into the SCMA architecture and establish theoretical bounds on the time and communication overhead for various scheme components. In contrast to the computationally expensive process of fully retraining K-means++ locally and globally for every unlearning request, our approach delivers an average acceleration of approximately 84x across seven datasets, including two sets containing biological and medical data that frequently require unlearning.

Recent investigations into the planet-dominated regime of Type II migration revealed that massive planets can migrate outward, contradicting established beliefs. These studies, utilizing `fixed-planet' simulations, identified a correlation between the sign of the torques acting on a planet and the parameter $K'$, which quantifies the depth of the gap the planet creates in the disc. To validate and expand upon these findings, we conducted `live-planet' simulations across various $K'$ and disc mass values. A key distinction in live-planet simulations is the excitation of planet eccentricity, which disrupts the direct link between the imposed torques and the migration rate (the rate of change of the semi-major axis)—a factor absent in fixed-planet models. By separating the torque contributions arising from semi-major axis evolution from those due to eccentricity evolution, we re-established the relationship between the magnitude and sign of migration and $K'$. We further propose that this relationship is more accurately described using the related gap depth parameter $K$. Additionally, we introduced a toy model demonstrating that the sign of planetary migration reverses at a specific limiting value of $K$, allowing us to examine migration within viscously evolving discs. This torque reversal influences planetary system architecture by causing planets to accumulate either at a stalling radius or within a band surrounding it, determined by the interplay between migration and disc evolution. Consequently, planets tend to cluster in the 1–10 au region, thereby hindering the formation of hot Jupiters via Type II migration in the planet-dominated regime.

We extend and refine recent upper bounds concerning the additive energies of modular roots. Our approach integrates diverse methodologies, drawing from additive combinatorics, algebraic number theory, and the geometry of numbers. Furthermore, we apply these findings to establish novel bounds on correlations between Salié sums and to derive a fresh equidistribution estimate for the set of modular roots of primes.

Square relative non-zero sum Heffter arrays, denoted as $\mathrm{NH}_t(n;k)$, represent a variation of the traditional Heffter array concept. An $\mathrm{NH}_t(n;k)$ is defined as an $n\times n$ partially populated matrix containing elements from $\mathbb{Z}_v$ (where $v=2nk+t$), featuring exactly $k$ filled entries in each row and column. The design ensures that the sum of elements within any row or column is non-zero modulo $v$, and for every $x\in \mathbb{Z}_v$ outside the subgroup of order $t$, either $x$ or its additive inverse $-x$ is included. This paper presents direct constructions for fully populated square non-zero sum Heffter arrays, $\mathrm{NH}_t(n;n)$, for all odd $n$, specifically when $t$ divides $n$ or $t\in\{2,2n,n^2,2n^2\}$. These constructed arrays possess the restrictive characteristic of being "globally simple," which facilitates the derivation of novel orthogonal path decompositions and new biembeddings of complete multipartite graphs.

Scientific workflow applications have become mainstream, and their automated, efficient execution on large-scale computing platforms is a major focus of current research. To ensure success, researchers need a robust experimental methodology to evaluate workflow systems, which relies heavily on realistic workflow instances. Although public repositories offer dozens of instances for a limited number of scientific applications, they are insufficient because they do not cover all relevant application scales. To overcome this gap, prior work has created tools to generate synthetic yet representative workflow instances at arbitrary scales. While these tools are popular, building them manually is labor-intensive and requires deep expert knowledge, resulting in generators that cover only a few applications despite hundreds being used in production. This paper introduces WfChef, a framework that fully automates the creation of synthetic workflow generators for any scientific application. By taking a set of input workflow instances, WfChef automatically produces a corresponding generator. We define and evaluate specific metrics to quantify the realism of generated workflows and use them to compare WfChef's output against that of previously existing, hand-crafted generators. Our findings show that WfChef not only eliminates development effort through automation but also produces workflows that are more realistic than those created manually.

Boolean Skolem function synthesis, also referred to as Boolean functional synthesis, involves generating outputs as Boolean functions of inputs to satisfy a given relational specification. This field has significant applications, such as designing safe controllers for autonomous systems, solving certified Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF), and cryptanalysis. While theoretical research has established the complexity-theoretic hardness of this problem, various algorithms remain effective in practice. This gap between theoretical difficulty and practical success has driven investigations into specific input specification normal forms that enable efficient synthesis, potentially explaining the algorithms' performance.

This paper advances this line of inquiry by investigating whether a normal form can precisely define "efficient" synthesis. We introduce SAUNF, a normal form that exactly characterizes tractable synthesis: a specification is polynomial-time synthesizable if and only if it can be compiled into SAUNF in polynomial time. Furthermore, a specification has a polynomial-sized functional solution if and only if it possesses a semantically equivalent polynomial-sized SAUNF representation. SAUNF is exponentially more concise than established forms like Binary Decision Diagrams (BDDs) and Deterministic Negation Normal Forms (DNNFs) used in AI, and it strictly encompasses recently proposed forms such as SynNNF. Possessing compositional properties akin to DNNFs, SAUNF offers an optimal balance for knowledge representation in Boolean functional synthesis.

The dynamics and characteristics of magnetoacoustic (MA) waves are significantly influenced by the non-uniformity of the solar atmosphere and non-adiabatic processes, such as radiation cooling and unknown heating mechanisms. To examine how these factors jointly impact the dispersion properties of MA waves, we analyzed a single magnetic slab containing thermally active plasma. By applying perturbation theory, we derived a differential equation governing the dynamics of two-dimensional perturbations. Under the assumption of strong magnetic structuring, we established dispersion relations for both kink and sausage MA modes. Numerical solutions of these relations, calculated under coronal conditions, were used to explore the interaction between thermal misbalance and atmospheric non-uniformity. For the heating scenario considered, we found that the phase speeds of both slow kink and sausage MA waves are substantially altered by thermal misbalance in the long-wavelength limit. The characteristic dissipation timescales of these slow waves align with the periods of waves observed in the corona. Conversely, the phase speed of fast waves remains unaffected by thermal misbalance, as the geometry of the magnetic structure continues to serve as the primary dispersion mechanism. Our estimates indicate that, under coronal conditions, the dissipation of fast waves is weaker than that of slow waves. These findings highlight the importance of using magnetoacoustic waves not only for estimating plasma parameters but also for quantifying non-adiabatic processes.

Temperate rocky planets represent the most promising targets for identifying extraterrestrial life and habitable worlds beyond our Solar System. Over recent decades, the pursuit of these worlds has fueled the development of new instruments and extensive observational initiatives. To maximize the returns on these technological and observational investments, climate models capable of assessing the habitability of rocky planets are indispensable. In this regard, we introduce EOS-ESTM, a rapid and adaptable model designed to investigate how various climate factors—including those not yet constrained by observations—influence habitability. Built upon the ESTM framework, a seasonal-latitudinal energy balance model with sophisticated handling of meridional and vertical transport, EOS-ESTM introduces several innovations: (1) parameterizations that simulate the climatic effects of oceans, land, ice, and clouds based on temperature and stellar zenith angle; and (2) an EOS procedure for computing radiative transfer in atmospheres with both terrestrial and non-terrestrial compositions under illumination from solar and non-solar stars. By inputting Earth's specific stellar, orbital, and planetary data, we generate a reference model that aligns with numerous observational constraints of Earth's climate. Validation tests under non-terrestrial conditions produce results consistent with those from a hierarchy of comparable climate models. Furthermore, applying EOS-ESTM to planetary atmospheres in extreme greenhouse states reveals the ability to trace the snowball transition at the outer boundary of the Habitable Zone (HZ) across diverse planetary parameters, thereby enabling future multi-parametric studies of the HZ.

We present a comprehensive formulation of Poincaré gauge theory, progressing from the fibre bundle framework to the resulting Riemann-Cartan spacetime. Additionally, we explore various gravity theories derived from this foundation. Specifically, we investigate the cosmological implications of the simple scalar-torsion (0⁺) mode within Poincaré gauge theory. In this context, the geometric influence of torsion is treated as an effective quantity that mimics dark energy, allowing us to analyze the model's effective equation of state (EoS). Furthermore, we develop an extra-dimensional theory of teleparallel gravity utilizing differential forms. We specifically examine Kaluza-Klein and braneworld scenarios through direct dimensional reduction and by defining the geometry of the fibre. Finally, the FLRW cosmological model of braneworld teleparallel gravity demonstrates equivalence to General Relativity (GR) regarding their field equations, as both yield the identical Friedmann equation.

Recommender systems are integral to contemporary online platforms, yet they raise significant concerns about steering society toward harmful trajectories, such as filter bubbles. A primary difficulty in evaluating these systems lies in comparing user outcomes generated by the systems against a credible counterfactual scenario where no such systems exist. We address this challenge using a model-based approach that compares two distinct process models: first, a "recommender" model representing a generic item-matching process within a personalized system, and second, an "organic" model depicting a baseline counterfactual where users discover items without algorithmic mediation. Our central finding is that these two models yield vastly different outcomes at both individual and societal levels, a conclusion supported by theoretical proofs and simulation experiments using real-world data. Furthermore, the two models generate divergent trade-offs during inference; specifically, standard performance-enhancing techniques like regularization and shrinkage have opposite effects. While shrinkage reduces mean squared error in both contexts as anticipated, it leads to less diverse (less radical) item selections in the recommender model but more diverse (more radical) selections in the organic model. These results offer a formal framework for understanding how recommender systems fundamentally reshape how we search for and engage with content in an increasingly mediated world.

This study investigates pair-produced resonances that decay into three jets, utilizing 2016 proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis explores a mass spectrum ranging from 200 to 2000 GeV across four distinct regions. Observations align with Standard Model predictions. Within the context of $R$-parity violating supersymmetry, where gluinos pair-produce and decay into a six-quark final state, gluino masses under 1500 GeV are excluded at the 95% confidence level. Furthermore, an analysis incorporating multijet events reconstructed at the trigger level extends the search reach down to 200 GeV. Enhanced analysis methods have improved sensitivity, establishing the most stringent limits to date on gluino pair production.

This paper presents an application of Sobol's global sensitivity analysis to quantify the impact of evidence from specific nodes on a target variable within a Bayesian network. By leveraging the network's structure, we convert the task of estimating Sobol indices into a marginalization inference problem. This approach enables efficient index computation for networks where traditional brute-force or Monte Carlo variance-based estimators would necessitate millions of expensive samples. Furthermore, our method yields exact results when paired with exact inference and accommodates correlated inputs. Drawing inspiration from tensor networks, the proposed algorithm extends previous tensor-based sensitivity techniques from acyclic to cyclic structures. We validate the method using three medium-to-large Bayesian networks relevant to project risk management and reliability engineering.

The fact that chains of embedding-projection pairs (ep-pairs) are closed under bilimits in various categories of domains and predomains is a well-established result. For example, Scott's $D_\infty$ construction is recognized for generating directed bilimits of ep-pairs within the category of directed-complete partial orders (dcpos), and de Jong and Escardó have formalized this within the constructive domain theory of a topos. In contrast, explicitly constructing bilimits for categories involving predomains and partial maps remains problematic regarding constructivity; most treatments rely on the heuristic that every lift-algebra is free, thereby reducing the task to constructing bilimits in a category of pointed domains with strict maps. While Claire Jones's dissertation proposes an explicit construction for these bilimits, it lacks a formal proof, leaving open the question of whether the category of dcpos and partial maps is closed under directed bilimits of ep-pairs in a topos. This paper provides a proof valid in a (Grothendieck)-topos demonstrating that the category of dcpos and partial maps between them is indeed closed under bilimits, and it outlines several applications toward models of axiomatic and synthetic domain theory.

Ensuring creditor protection stands as a fundamental goal of financial regulation. In sectors with high protection needs, such as banking and insurance, solvency requirements serve as a tool to prevent creditors from suffering losses on their claims. While existing regulations based on Value at Risk (VaR) and Average Value at Risk (AVaR) successfully limit the probability of default for financial institutions, they do not adequately control the magnitude of recoveries on creditors' claims should a default occur. This study addresses that gap by introducing a new risk metric, Recovery Value at Risk (RVaR). Our conceptual framework is adaptable, enabling the creation of broad recovery risk measures suited for diverse risk management applications. By design, these measures govern recoveries on creditor claims and embed creditor protection incentives directly into management structures. We present detailed case studies and applications, examining how recovery risk metrics respond to the joint distributions of assets and liabilities on corporate balance sheets, and we compare the resulting capital requirements against current VaR and AVaR benchmarks. Furthermore, we outline methods for calibrating these recovery risk measures to historical regulatory standards. Finally, we demonstrate that recovery risk measures are applicable to performance-based management of business units and offer a manageable way to characterize optimal risk-return tradeoffs within investment management.

Imitation learning addresses the challenge of crafting effective reward functions for agent training by leveraging expert demonstrations. While most existing algorithms assume that both the expert and the agent operate within the same Markov Decision Process (MDP), this paper investigates the scenario where discrepancies exist between the expert's and agent's MDPs. These domain differences may involve variations in dynamics, viewpoints, or morphology. We introduce a novel framework designed to learn mappings between such disparate domains. Distinct from previous research, our method utilizes unpaired and unaligned trajectories containing solely states from the expert domain to establish these correspondences. This is achieved through a cycle-consistency constraint applied to both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space. Furthermore, we employ a normalized position estimator to ensure temporal alignment of states, thereby synchronizing the trajectories across the two domains. Once the correspondence is established, demonstrations can be directly transferred from one domain to the other for imitation tasks. Extensive experiments across diverse and challenging domains validate the effectiveness of our approach.

We investigate the low-energy collective behaviors of a one-dimensional spin-1 Bose gas by employing bosonization. Following a physical overview of this technique, we apply it to the $S=1$ Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian, identifying a new separation between quadrupole, spin, and charge sectors, a result validated by time-MPS numerical simulations. Furthermore, analysis of the single-particle spectrum reveals the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and the specific point where the system is governed by a Heisenberg-like Hamiltonian. We derive magnetic phase diagrams for both superfluid and insulating regimes; the latter is established by decomposing the full Heisenberg bilinear-biquadratic Hamiltonian—which characterizes the Mott insulator—into simpler effective forms. This approach ensures our methodology remains flexible and applicable to other intriguing interacting condensed matter systems.

Reconstructing images from compressive measurements necessitates a signal prior, and recent efforts have investigated deep generative models with low-dimensional latents for this purpose. However, their effectiveness is constrained by substantial representation errors. We propose a technique to minimize this error by employing generators as priors. Specifically, at inference time, we remove one or more initial blocks from a pre-trained generator and optimize within an expanded latent space to recover the target image. Experimental results indicate that this method yields significantly superior reconstruction quality across various network architectures. Furthermore, the approach performs robustly on images outside the training distribution and remains competitive with leading state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate that modifying network architectures during testing can substantially enhance the recovery capabilities of generator-based signal priors in compressed sensing.

Autonomous mobile robots frequently encounter difficult conditions when navigating complex settings, requiring them to identify static and dynamic obstacles, devise driving routes, and execute movements. To tackle challenges in perception and path planning, this paper presents OctoPath, a self-supervised encoder-decoder deep neural network designed to forecast the optimal local trajectory for the ego-vehicle. By leveraging a 3D octree environment model for discretization, the proposed method transforms trajectory prediction into a classification task with adjustable resolution. During training, OctoPath reduces the discrepancy between predicted and manually driven trajectories within a specific dataset, thereby circumventing the limitations of regression-based estimation, which suffers from an infinite output state space. Sensing is achieved through a 40-channel mechanical LiDAR sensor, combined with an inertial measurement unit and wheel odometry for state estimation. Experiments were conducted in both simulated and real-world environments using the custom GridSim simulator and RovisLab's Autonomous Mobile Test Unit platform. The study evaluates OctoPath across various indoor and outdoor driving scenarios, comparing its performance against a baseline hybrid A-Star algorithm, a regression-based supervised learning approach, and a CNN-based optimal path planning method.

This project investigates the correlation between temperature fluctuations and the blooming dates of cherry trees. By utilizing modeling techniques, we aim to predict future flowering times, thereby assisting the public in planning their travel and avoiding peak pollen seasons. Since determining the exact blossoming date can be framed as a multiclass classification task, we employed both a multi-class Support Vector Classifier (SVC) and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), specifically the Long Short-term Memory (LSTM) architecture. Finally, we assess and contrast the performance of these methods to identify the most practical approach for real-world application.

Most event-related potential (ERP) brain-computer interface (BCI) systems target single-trial P300 detection for spelling tasks. Although this is a key goal, current P300 BCIs still necessitate multiple repetitions to reach satisfactory classification accuracy. Recent advancements in signal processing and machine learning for P300 BCI have primarily focused on detection, often neglecting character classification. To minimize repetition counts while ensuring high accuracy, it is essential to address the complete classification challenge. We propose an end-to-end pipeline that begins with feature extraction and combines ERP-level classification via probabilistic Riemannian MDM with character-level classification through Bayesian accumulation of confidence across trials. Unlike existing methods that only boost a character's confidence upon its flashing, our proposed pipeline, termed ASAP (Bayesian accumulation of Riemannian probabilities), updates the confidence for every character after each flash. We present the rigorous derivation and theoretical reformulation of this Bayesian framework to ensure seamless information flow from raw signals to BCI characters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms standard methods on public P300 datasets.

Junctions offer extensive insights into the symmetry of superconducting order parameters. This study examines both normal-superconducting and Josephson junctions within twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) and analogous systems. Specifically, normal-superconducting junctions model the tip-sample interaction in scanning tunneling microscope (STM) setups, whereas Josephson junctions and SQUIDs are realized by applying non-uniform gate voltages to TBG. Since the TBFermi surface comprises at least two pockets—one per valley—the analysis focuses on distinguishing superconducting phases that are either even or odd under valley exchange, corresponding to s- and f-wave pairings. Both Andreev reflection in STM measurements and the critical current in Josephson junctions exhibit a pronounced sensitivity to the character of the superconducting electrons; additionally, STM results are influenced by short-range elastic scattering caused by the tip.

A Hermitian metric on a complex manifold $(M, I)$ of complex dimension $n$ is termed Bismut-Ricci flat or Calabi-Yau with torsion (CYT) when the restricted holonomy of its associated Bismut connection lies within $SU(n)$. It is referred to as pluriclosed or strong Kähler with torsion (SKT) if the corresponding fundamental form $F$ satisfies the $\partial \overline \partial$-closed condition. This paper investigates the existence of left-invariant SKT and CYT metrics on compact semi-simple Lie groups equipped with a Samelson complex structure $I$. Specifically, we demonstrate that if $I$ arises from a maximal torus $T$ and $g$ is a left-invariant Hermitian metric that remains invariant under the right action of $T$, and if $g$ is simultaneously SKT and CYT, then $g$ must be Bismut flat.

This study examines the institutional connections among a group of English schools, many of which are private and potentially fuel the 'old boy network.' The research utilizes a network of mutually determined rugby union matches between these schools. Since geographical proximity is a primary factor in scheduling these fixtures, it serves as a spatial benchmark for evaluating model performance. Results indicate that a Bayesian fitting of the latent position cluster model offers the strongest fit among those tested. This model facilitates a consistent and detailed interpretation of various methods regarding the factors driving community and edge formation within the network. Notably, the study identifies homophily based on fees and the ratio of boarders as significant influences. Evidence suggests that a specific community of schools, characterized by high boarder proportions and fees, drives this dynamic, pointing to the existence and structure of an 'old boy network' at an institutional level.

Image warping seeks to transform images originally defined on rectangular grids into arbitrary forms. While implicit neural functions have recently demonstrated exceptional capabilities in representing images continuously, a standalone multi-layer perceptron struggles to learn high-frequency Fourier coefficients. To address this, we introduce the Local Texture Estimator for Image Warping (LTEW), which precedes an implicit neural representation to facilitate the deformation of images into continuous shapes. By estimating local textures using a deep super-resolution (SR) backbone and multiplying them by the locally varying Jacobian matrices of a coordinate transformation, our method predicts the Fourier responses of the warped image. Our LTEW-based neural function surpasses existing warping techniques in asymmetric-scale super-resolution and homography transform tasks. Additionally, the algorithm demonstrates strong generalization to arbitrary coordinate transformations, including homography transforms with large magnification factors and equirectangular projection (ERP) perspective transforms, even when these were not present during training.

Historically, time-resolved investigations have depended on initiating photo-induced dynamics in chemical or biological species and subsequently interrogating them with a swift beam of photons or electrons traversing the sample briefly. Consequently, the signal's temporal resolution is primarily constrained by the pulse widths of both the pump and probe sources. This paper introduces an alternative strategy capable of consistently attaining time resolutions orders of magnitude superior to those achievable via laser technology or electron beam compression. Our method involves accelerating the sample to relativistic velocities to induce time dilation; probing this dilated sample would unlock previously unattainable regimes of temporal resolution.

A multi-relational graph encompasses two or more relations defined over a vertex set. This paper introduces an algebra for navigating these graphs, which integrates an $n$-ary relational algebra, a concatenative single-relational path algebra, and a tensor-based multi-relational algebra. The proposed algebra establishes a theoretical foundation rooted in monoids, automata, and formal language theory to facilitate the development of a multi-relational graph traversal engine.

Ultrasound imaging provides a cost-effective, compact, and widely available medical imaging option; however, it is plagued by significant speckle noise caused by random sub-wavelength interference, which degrades image quality and complicates interpretation. Unlike CT and MRI, these challenges necessitate advanced denoising techniques. This study introduces a novel unsupervised method for speckle reduction and denoising that employs maximum-a-posteriori estimation combined with deep generative priors derived from high-quality MRI scans. To capture generative tissue reflectivity, we utilize normalizing flows, a technique recently proven effective for modeling signal priors in diverse applications. To ensure broad applicability, we factorize the prior and train the flow model on patches from the NYU fastMRI (fully-sampled) dataset, subsequently applying this prior within an iterative denoising framework for inference. We first demonstrate the efficacy of our learned priors on noisy MRI data without domain shift, followed by an evaluation on both simulated and in-vivo ultrasound images from the PICMUS and CUBDL datasets. The findings indicate that this approach surpasses other unsupervised denoising methods, including NLM and OBNLM, in both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments.

Utilizing nano-fabrication to engineer metamaterials with specific band structures, topology, and chirality significantly transforms modern science and influences daily life; however, this study adopts a distinct methodology. We investigate a periodic sequence of dissipative optical solitons rotating within a single ring microresonator, treating it as a metacrystal that functions as an electromagnetic metamaterial across the radio to terahertz spectrum. Each unit cell comprises a bound pair of solitons, with the inter-soliton distance serving as a tunable control parameter. This work reports on the band structure and topological characteristics of the soliton metacrystal, the latter verified by $\pi$-step shifts in the geometrical (Zak) phase of the crystal's phonons. Additionally, we identified phononic edge states in defective metacrystals created by removing multiple solitons. Spectral butterfly patterns observed in optical frequency combs associated with these soliton metacrystals act as indicators of spatio-temporal chirality, visually echoing the natural occurrences of chirality found in butterfly wings.

It is demonstrated that, with the exception of three specific instances, conjugacy classes within the classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ belong to type ${\rm D}$. This finding establishes that Nichols algebras derived from irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$ (defined as $H_{n}\rtimes \mathbb{S}_{n}$) are infinite-dimensional, excluding only the types $(2, 3)$ and $(1^{2}, 3)$ found in $\mathbb S_{5}$, and the type $(1^{n-2}, 2)$ present in $\mathbb S_{n}$ for $n >5$.

This paper investigates two foundational frameworks for understanding multi-scale turbulence and energy organization in the logarithmic region of high-Reynolds number wall-bounded flows: the inner-outer interaction model (Marusic, Mathis & Hutchins, Science, vol. 329, 2010, 193-196) and the attached-eddy model (Townsend, Cambridge University Press, 1976). By integrating the additive description with the attached-eddy model, the study elucidates the generation mechanism of streamwise wall-shear fluctuations caused by wall-attached eddies. Subsequently, utilizing the inner-outer interaction model, it isolates the streamwise wall-shear stress fluctuations produced by these attached eddies within a turbulent channel flow. A direct statistical comparison reveals that the two models are mutually consistent and complementary. Furthermore, the validity of strong and extended self-similarity confirms that attached eddy superpositions strictly adhere to an additive process. Additionally, a Gaussian model is proposed to describe the instantaneous distribution of streamwise wall-shear stress arising from these superpositions. These insights hold significant value for the development of advanced reduced-order wall models.

Spin nutation resonance has been extensively studied in one-sublattice ferromagnets; in this work, we examine spin nutation in two-sublattice antiferromagnets and, for comparison, in ferrimagnets featuring both inter- and intra-sublattice nutation coupling. Specifically, we derive the susceptibility of two-sublattice magnetic systems under an external magnetic field, calculating the precession and nutation resonance frequencies for antiferromagnets and ferrimagnets in the sub-THz and THz regimes, respectively. Our findings indicate that in antiferromagnets, precession resonance frequencies and effective damping decrease with increasing intra-sublattice nutation coupling but increase with inter-sublattice nutation coupling. Conversely, THz nutation resonance frequencies decline with both types of coupling. In ferrimagnets, we identify two distinct nutation modes, a feature absent in antiferromagnets. Regarding ferrimagnetic precession, the exchange-like mode behaves similarly to antiferromagnets—decreasing with intra-sublattice coupling and increasing with inter-sublattice coupling—whereas the ferromagnetic-like mode remains largely unaffected by either coupling type.

We describe the emergence of low-energy features within the photoelectron momentum distribution of a hydrogen atom subjected to two-color, counter-rotating bi-circular laser fields. Originating from AC-Stark shifted resonances, these features disrupt the characteristic three-fold symmetry of $\omega-2\omega$ bi-circular configurations. We analyze the physical basis of this structure through partial-wave interference between direct ionization pathways and a resonant route involving the AC-Stark shifted state, while also demonstrating how the population of the underlying Rydberg states varies with field intensity and pulse length.

A recent study by Polterovich, Shalom, and Shem-Tov demonstrated that non-discrete, conjugation-invariant norms on higher-rank arithmetic Chevalley groups induce highly constrained topologies, specifically those possessing profinite norm-completions. This note outlines an argument extending this result to ${\rm SL}_2(R)$, where $R$ denotes a ring of algebraic integers containing infinitely many units.

Gamma rays, being the most energetic photons, transport data from distant extragalactic regions with minimal interaction or data loss, revealing insights into particle acceleration within environments too extreme for terrestrial replication. The synergy between gamma-ray astrophysics and collider research is so profound that particle and astroparticle physicists often overlap in their roles. Over the last decade, instruments like the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope have been instrumental in significant multi-messenger breakthroughs. Currently, there is substantial interest and expertise driving advancements in new technologies and the development of space-based, ground-based, and multi-messenger gamma-ray networks. Consequently, it is alarming that without sustained long-term planning for gamma-ray astrophysics support, much of this critical infrastructure could be lost before the community can regroup for future planning. Gamma rays spanning the MeV to EeV energy range are vital to multiwavelength and multi-messenger investigations, ranging from astroparticle physics involving compact objects to dark matter research using large-scale diffuse structures. These objectives and emerging discoveries have sparked a surge in proposals and programs for new gamma-ray facilities. This paper outlines these proposed technologies and facilities, which are tailored to address specific needs in measuring extreme astrophysical sources that tackle pressing fundamental physics questions for the coming decade. Furthermore, these proposed instruments align with the priorities established in the recent Astro2020 Decadal Survey, a complementary astrophysics study offering opportunities relevant to Snowmass.

The widespread use of mobile devices has caused location tracking systems—including satellites, cellular base stations, and wireless access points—to generate vast quantities of data regarding moving objects. There is a significant demand across various applications, such as intelligent transportation systems and location-based services, to identify groups of moving objects that travel together, known as traveling companions, by analyzing their trajectories. Current approaches generally fall into two categories: pattern mining methods that define specific companion patterns, or representation learning methods that derive similar representations for analogous trajectories. However, pattern mining struggles with the pairwise point-matching issue, while representation learning often neglects temporal proximity between trajectories. To address these challenges, we introduce ATTN-MEAN, a generic deep representation learning model utilizing autoencoders for discovering traveling companions. This model integrates spatial and temporal information into input embeddings via skip-gram and positional encoding techniques, respectively. Furthermore, it enhances learning by leveraging the Sort-Tile-Recursive algorithm, mean operations, and a global attention mechanism to allow trajectories to learn from their neighbors. Once the encoders generate trajectory representations, we apply DBSCAN clustering to identify traveling companions; trajectories within the same cluster are classified as companions. Experimental results demonstrate that ATTN-MEAN outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in detecting traveling companions.

This paper introduces a reduction method utilizing bilinearization and double Wronskians (alternatively, double Casoratians) to derive explicit multi-soliton solutions for the recently introduced integrable space-time shifted nonlocal equations by Ablowitz and Musslimani [Phys. Lett. A, 2021]. The approach applies to the space-time shifted nonlocal nonlinear Schrödinger and modified Korteweg-de Vries hierarchies, as well as the semi-discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation. We demonstrate that these nonlocal integrable systems, regardless of the presence of space-time shifts, exhibit identical eigenvalue distributions; however, the inclusion of space-time shifts imposes additional constraints on the phase components of the solutions.

Monitoring data drift is critical for machine learning, as statistical shifts in processed data often significantly degrade model performance. Existing detection methods generally fall into two categories: supervised approaches requiring true labels during inference, or unsupervised ones that ignore label information entirely. We introduce a novel semi-supervised, task-sensitive drift detection scheme that leverages label data during initial model training but operates without labels during inference.
