Implemented on Raspberry Pi hardware, LwHBench was executed over 100 days across 45 devices to create a comprehensive dataset designed to facilitate AI-driven device management. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the dataset's versatility through AI-enabled use cases exploring device identification and the impact of context on performance. Finally, the benchmark application was adapted and tested in an agriculture-focused scenario involving three RockPro64 devices.

Dataloaders, responsible for transferring data from storage to GPUs during machine learning model training, may be pivotal to significantly enhancing training performance. Recent developments have demonstrated potential by substantially reducing training durations and introducing capabilities such as accessing remote storage like S3. This paper is the first to identify the dataloader as a distinct component within the Deep Learning workflow, detailing its architecture and characteristics. Furthermore, we provide an exhaustive comparison of existing dataloading libraries, analyzing their trade-offs regarding functionality, usability, and performance, along with the insights gained from this evaluation.

Tensor product state (TPS) methods serve as highly effective instruments for simulating quantum many-body systems, both in equilibrium and out of equilibrium. Specifically, the one-dimensional matrix-product state (MPS) approach has become a standard technique within condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry. These lecture notes offer a concise overview of fundamental TPS principles alongside the presentation of TeNPy, a flexible Python tensor library [https://github.com/tenpy/tenpy]. We illustrate these concepts using concrete examples, namely time-evolving block decimation and the density matrix renormalization group algorithms based on MPS. Furthermore, the notes include a practical guide on implementing abelian symmetries, such as particle number conservation, to optimize tensor operations.

This letter introduces a novel Integrated Sensing and Wireless Power Transfer (ISWPT) concept, which combines radar sensing and wireless power transfer functions onto a single hardware platform. By integrating these operations, ISWPT offers advantages in reducing system size, hardware costs, power consumption, and spectrum usage, making it a promising enabler for future 6G wireless networks. As a foundational study, we investigate the fundamental trade-off between radar sensing and wireless power transfer by optimizing transmit beamforming vectors. We first develop a semi-definite relaxation-based method to achieve a globally optimal solution for the associated optimization problem, followed by a low-complexity sub-optimal approach. Finally, numerical results validate the efficacy of our proposed solutions and illustrate the inherent trade-off between sensing performance and power transfer capabilities.

Recent experimental and evaluated $\alpha$-decay half-lives for nuclei with $82 \leq Z \leq 118$ have been employed to refine two empirical models: the Horoi scaling law [J. Phys. G **30**, 945 (2004)] and the Sobiczewski formula [Acta Phys. Pol. B **36**, 3095 (2005)]. This refinement involved incorporating asymmetry-dependent terms ($I$ and $I^2$) and re-evaluating the coefficients. The updated versions demonstrate significant enhancements in accuracy compared to twenty-one other formulas, enabling more precise predictions of $\alpha$-decay half-lives in the unexplored superheavy region. Furthermore, the spontaneous fission (SF) half-life model proposed by Bao *et al.* [J. Phys. G **42**, 085101 (2015)] has been improved by integrating ground-state shell-plus-pairing corrections from FRDM-2012 and utilizing the latest experimental SF data for $82 \leq Z \leq 118$. Applying these enhanced formulas, the competition between $\alpha$-decay and SF was investigated for nuclei with $112 \leq Z \leq 118$, yielding estimates for probable half-lives and decay modes. Potential decay chains for $^{286-302}$Og and $^{287-303}$119 (within the $168 \leq N \leq 184$ island of stability) were analyzed and show excellent consistency with existing experimental data. Additionally, four machine learning algorithms—XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), Decision Trees (DTs), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) neural networks—were utilized to train predictors for $\alpha$-decay and SF half-lives. The predictions for decay modes generated by XGBoost and MLP align remarkably well with available experimental data, corroborating the results from the aforementioned modified formulas.

The Short Message Service (SMS), launched for mobile users a decade ago, constitutes the world's oldest large-scale network, boasting billions of users and consequently drawing significant fraud. As mobile networks converge with the internet, SMS-based scams pose a potential threat to the security of online services as well. This study introduces a novel SMS scam dataset comprising 153,551 messages, which will be made publicly available for research and represents the largest such collection to date. We evaluate and compare the performance of various established machine learning techniques on this new dataset, spanning from shallow learning methods and deep neural networks to syntactic and semantic feature models. Furthermore, we analyze existing models from an adversarial standpoint by testing their robustness against different degrees of adversarial manipulation. This perspective not only consolidates the current state of the art in SMS spam filtering but also identifies limitations and opportunities for enhancing existing approaches.

We derive both the $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ laws of the iterated logarithm (LIL) for the capacity of the range of a simple random walk in all dimensions $d \ge 3$. Although the growth order of this LIL for $d \ge 4$ aligns with that of the random walk range volume in dimension $d-2$, this correspondence unexpectedly fails for the capacity of the range at $d=3$. Additionally, we establish the LIL for the Brownian capacity of a 3-dimensional Brownian trajectory and provide new, sharp moderate deviation bounds for the capacity of the range of a 4-dimensional simple random walk.

The Lipschitz constant of neural networks is crucial in various deep learning domains, including robustness certification, regularization, and stability analysis for systems controlled by neural networks. Consequently, deriving tight bounds for this constant is essential. We present LipBaB, a branch-and-bound framework designed to calculate certified bounds of the local Lipschitz constant for deep neural networks with ReLU activations to any specified precision. This is accomplished by bounding the norms of Jacobians associated with different activation patterns induced within the input domain. Furthermore, our algorithm guarantees the exact computation of the Lipschitz constant for any p-norm.

This work demonstrates the equivalence between weak and viscosity solutions for non-homogeneous $p(x)$-Laplace equations featuring a right-hand side that varies with the spatial variable, the unknown function, and its gradient. By utilizing inf- and sup-convolution methods, we show that viscosity solutions satisfy the weak formulation, whereas comparison principles establish the reverse implication. Distinctive features of the $p(x)$-Laplacian relative to the constant exponent case include the emergence of $\log$-terms and the absence of translation invariance.

Stellar mergers represent a frequent yet short-lived stage in the lifecycle of binary star systems, with significant astrophysical consequences such as the formation of exotic stars (including magnetic stars, blue stragglers, and rapid rotators), insights into stellar populations, and the origins of compact object mergers detected by LIGO. Despite their prevalence, the direct observation of these events and the specifics of their evolution have remained difficult to achieve. While a few mergers have been directly witnessed recently, their central remnants are typically hidden behind opaque shells of dust and molecules, preventing astronomers from determining their ultimate fate—whether as a single merged star or a tighter binary. This study reports the detection of an unusual, ring-shaped ultraviolet nebula surrounding the central star TYC 2597-735-1. The nebula's dual opposing fronts indicate a bipolar outflow originating from the star. Although TYC 2597-735-1's spectrum and location above the Galactic plane suggest it is an old star, it displays abnormally low surface gravity and a measurable long-term decline in luminosity, characteristics inconsistent with its evolutionary phase. Furthermore, the star exhibits H-alpha emission, radial velocity shifts, enhanced ultraviolet output, and excess infrared radiation, all indicative of dusty circumstellar disks, stellar activity, and accretion. Integrating these observations with stellar evolution models implies that TYC 2597-735-1 merged with a lower-mass companion several thousand years ago. This system offers a rare, unobstructed view of a stellar merger at a transitional stage between its initial dynamic phase and the theorized final equilibrium, providing direct evidence of how two stars coalesce into one.

We demonstrate that the subset sum problem, the knapsack problem, and the rational subset membership problem for permutation groups are all NP-complete. Specifically regarding the knapsack problem, we establish NP-completeness for any fixed $n \geq 3$, where $n$ represents the count of permutations in the knapsack equation; equivalently, membership in products of three cyclic permutation groups is NP-complete. This refines Luks's earlier finding, which proved NP-completeness for the membership problem involving products of three abelian permutation groups. Additionally, we examine the context-free membership problem within permutation groups, proving it is PSPACE-complete, yet NP-complete when restricted to context-free grammars whose acyclic derivation trees possess a constant Horton-Strahler number. These upper bounds apply to black box groups. Furthermore, the findings on context-free membership in permutation groups provide novel complexity bounds for several non-emptiness intersection problems involving deterministic finite automata (DFAs) and a single context-free grammar.

We investigate the statistical properties of the product $G_1 G_2 \cdots G_r$ of $r$ independent Gaussian matrices of varying dimensions, where $G_i$ has size $d_{i-1} \times d_i$. Letting $p = d_0$ and $q = d_r$, we assume the constraint $d_1 = d_{r-1}$, with each matrix entry being a standard normal variable (mean 0, variance 1). These products are relevant in fields such as wireless communication, dynamical systems, and quantum transport. We demonstrate that if each dimension $d_i$ satisfies $d_i \geq C p \cdot q$ for a constant $C \geq C_0$ (where $C_0$ depends on $r$), the resulting product matrix is within a variation distance of at most $\delta$ from a $p \times q$ matrix of i.i.d. standard normals with mean 0 and variance $\prod_{i=1}^{r-1} d_i$. Here, $\delta$ approaches 0 as $C$ increases. Furthermore, for a fixed $r$, we establish a converse result: if $d_i < C' \max\{p,q\}^{1/2}\min\{p,q\}^{3/2}$ for some $i$, the total variation distance is at least $\delta'$, where $\delta'$ is an absolute constant depending on $C'$ and $r$. This lower bound is optimal when $p=\Theta(q)$.

Rust, a low-level language renowned for its distinctive memory-safe systems programming capabilities and challenging learning curve, presents specific hurdles for adoption. By analyzing top discussions on Reddit and Hacker News, we formulated three hypotheses regarding these barriers. Our findings indicate that several critical features, idioms, and integration patterns remain difficult for newcomers to access.
Building upon the findings of \cite{Dutra}, we demonstrate that any generating pair of a triangle group corresponds to a specific type of almost orbifold covering.

Our workflow relies on a suite of Python programs designed for numerically simulating liver perfusion. This includes an application capable of semi-automatically creating finite element meshes from computed tomography scans and reconstructing the liver's vascular architecture. In cases where real vascular trees cannot be extracted from CT data, we synthesize artificial ones using the constructive optimization method. These generated meshes and vascular structures are then imported into SfePy (Simple Finite Elements in Python) to conduct numerical simulations, yielding pressure distributions and perfusion flows within the liver tissue. Finally, during post-processing, we compute the transport of contrast fluid through the liver parenchyma.

This study introduces a general framework for developing interpretable multivariate discriminative models that facilitate efficient statistical inference in neuroimage analysis. Named the generative discriminative machine (GDM), this approach enhances discriminative models by incorporating a generative regularization term. We show that the proposed formulation can be optimized in both closed form and dual space, enabling efficient computation for high-dimensional neuroimaging data. Additionally, we offer an analytic estimation of the null distribution for model parameters, which supports efficient statistical inference and p-value calculation without relying on permutation testing. We evaluated the GDM against purely generative and discriminative learning methods using two large structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) datasets: one for Alzheimer's disease (n=415) and another for Schizophrenia (n=853). Analysis of the AD dataset highlighted GDM's capacity to robustly manage confounding variations, while the Schizophrenia dataset demonstrated its effectiveness in handling multi-site studies. Collectively, these findings underscore the promise of the proposed approach for neuroimaging analyses.

A phase diagram for a one-dimensional fiber bundle model is developed based on the continuous variation of two parameters that govern its dynamics: disorder strength and the range of stress relaxation. When the stress relaxation range is minimal, stress concentration dominates, leading to a nucleating failure process where a single crack propagates from a specific nucleus with high spatial correlation, unless disorder strength is substantial. Conversely, a high stress relaxation range corresponds to the model's mean-field limit, characterized by spatially random failure events. At intermediate levels of both disorder strength and stress release, the competition between these factors results in avalanches and precursor activities. Increasing the bundle size favors nucleating failure; in the thermodynamic limit, only nucleating failure is observed unless disorder strength is extremely high or the stress release range is sufficiently large to maintain the mean-field regime. A complex phase diagram is presented across the dimensions of disorder strength, stress release range, and system size, delineating three distinct failure modes—(I) nucleation, (II) avalanche, and (III) percolation—based on the observed spatial correlation during failure.

A pivotal element in power systems research is the accessibility of appropriate data, which is often restricted by privacy issues and the sensitive nature of energy infrastructure. This scarcity impedes progress in modern research areas like machine learning and stochastic modeling. To address this limitation, the paper introduces a systematic, data-driven framework designed to reconstruct high-fidelity time series using publicly available grid snapshots and historical records from transmission system operators. Applying this methodology—which ranges from geo-spatial data analysis and generation capacity reconstruction to time series disaggregation—to the French transmission grid results in the generation of synthetic yet highly realistic time series data. This output covers multiple years with a 5-minute resolution at the individual component level.

Distributed data processing platforms like Hadoop, Spark, and Flink are commonly utilized to spread data storage and computation across cloud computing nodes. The centralization of cloud resources has spurred the development of edge computing, which allows data processing to occur near its source rather than transmitting it to the cloud. However, due to limitations such as energy constraints, edge computing is not suitable for all applications; consequently, tasks are offloaded from edge devices to more capable cloud infrastructures. While prior studies have assessed the energy usage of these platforms in isolated cloud and edge settings, there is a significant lack of research evaluating their energy consumption in integrated edge-cloud environments where tasks move from resource-constrained to resource-rich devices. To address this gap, this paper introduces a framework for energy-aware evaluation of distributed data processing platforms. Using this framework, we assessed the energy consumption of Hadoop, Spark, and Flink within an integrated edge-cloud setup comprising Raspberry Pi devices, edge nodes, edge servers, private clouds, and public clouds. The evaluation findings indicate that (i) Flink is the most energy-efficient, followed by Spark, with Hadoop being the least efficient; (ii) offloading tasks from constrained to rich devices reduces energy consumption by 55.2%; and (iii) bandwidth and the distance between client and server are critical factors influencing energy usage.

This study calculates nuclear level densities and corresponding parameters ($a_{f}$ for fissioning nuclei at saddle points, and $a_{n}$, $a_{p}$, $a_{\alpha}$ for neutron, proton, and alpha-particle emission residues at ground states) across isotopic chains of superheavy nuclei with atomic numbers $Z$=112–120. Employing the superfluid formalism and single-particle energies derived from the diagonalization of a deformed Woods-Saxon potential, the analysis examines spectra at global minima of adiabatic potential energy surfaces and at saddle points. These critical points were identified using a multidimensional minimization method for minima and the "immersion water flow" technique for saddle points, both allowing for reflection and axial symmetry breaking. The research investigates how shell effects influence the excitation energy dependence of the ratios of level-density parameters for various decay residues relative to neutron emission. Results indicate that, unlike the $a_{f}/a_{n}$ ratio, the $a_{p}/a_{n}$ and $a_{\alpha}/a_{n}$ ratios do not exhibit characteristic maxima as a function of the compound nucleus excitation energy. Furthermore, in alpha decay, the collective enhancement arising from cluster degrees of freedom is found to be significant. The identified energetic evolution of level density parameters prior to reaching asymptotic values—a factor previously overlooked—is crucial for estimating de-excitation cascade probabilities involving light particle emission competing with fission. Consequently, this knowledge aids in determining survival probabilities and the total production cross-sections of superheavy nuclei in channels involving light particle participation.

Integrated nonlinear wavelength converters shift optical energy from lasers or quantum emitters to other wavelengths, yet chromatic dispersion restricts the extent of these shifts. Additionally, geometric dispersion causes fabrication variations to diminish the precision of achieving specific target wavelengths. In this work, we introduce nonlinear wavelength converters that do not rely on dispersion engineering but still achieve high-accuracy output wavelengths. Our approach utilizes coherent coupling between counter-propagating waves within a photonic crystal microresonator to generate a photonic bandgap, which isolates particular wavenumbers for nonlinear gain in dispersion space. We first validate the broad applicability of this method by simulating its role in third harmonic generation, dispersive wave formation in Kerr microcombs, and four-wave mixing Bragg scattering. Experimentally, we demonstrate Kerr optical parametric oscillators where this wavenumber-selective coherent coupling defines the signal mode, resulting in discrepancies between targeted and actual signal wavelengths of less than 0.3 percent. Furthermore, by exploiting the bandgap-protected wavenumber selectivity, we continuously tune output frequencies by nearly 300 GHz without sacrificing efficiency. These findings suggest a paradigm shift in the design of microresonators for nonlinear optics and advance the broader goal of constructing wavelength-accurate light sources via integrated photonics.

We examine fermion mixing within the context of field quantization in curved spacetime. By calculating the expectation value of the energy-momentum tensor for mixed fermions on the flavor vacuum, and focusing on spatially flat Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker metrics, we demonstrate that this tensor is both diagonal and conserved. Consequently, it can be interpreted as the effective energy-momentum tensor of a perfect fluid. Specifically, under a fixed De Sitter background, the fluid's equation of state aligns with that of dust and cold dark matter. These findings establish a novel connection between quantum phenomena and classical fluids, suggesting that the flavor vacuum of mixed fermions could constitute a new component of dark matter.

Rapid and dependable wireless connectivity is essential for modern life, yet traditional networks often fail to provide ubiquitous coverage during natural disasters. In such mission-critical situations, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks present a viable alternative, offering speed, flexibility, and reliability. Leveraging unique attributes like mobility, adaptable deployment, and swift reconfiguration, drones can dynamically reposition to deliver on-demand ground communication. Consequently, utilizing UAV Base Stations (UAV-BSs) is regarded as an effective strategy for establishing rapid connections in emergency scenarios. This paper examines the control of a UAV-BS within both static and dynamic settings, specifically addressing a scenario where a natural disaster destroys a macro Base Station, necessitating the deployment of a UAV-BS using Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB) technology to restore coverage. We introduce a data collection framework, signaling protocols, and machine learning applications tailored to this use case. Furthermore, we develop a deep reinforcement learning algorithm designed to jointly optimize the three-dimensional placement and the tilt angles of both access and backhaul antennas on the UAV-BS. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm enables the autonomous navigation and configuration of the UAV-BS, ensuring satisfactory service for mission-critical users on the ground.

We present a remarkable giant optical beam shift occurring in a tilted polarizer setup, which mirrors the Imbert-Fedorov shift observed during partial reflection near the Brewster angle. This phenomenon is elucidated through a generalized theoretical framework for beam shifts in tilted uniaxial anisotropic media, accounting for the three-dimensional orientation of the optic axis within the laboratory frame. Furthermore, we show that both the magnitude and direction of these shifts can be precisely regulated and tuned by adjusting the input polarization state and its associated orientation angles. These results suggest the potential for accurate micron-scale beam steering using a straightforward linear polarizer.

Although long-standing co-orbital asteroids have been hypothesized as the origin of the zodiacal dust ring surrounding Venus, the literature presents conflicting views regarding the orbital stability and existence of Venus Trojans. This study conducts a comprehensive survey of Venus Trojan stability, incorporating the dynamical effects of general relativity and the Yarkovsky effect. Through numerical simulations of thousands of fictitious Venus Trojans, we employ frequency analysis to detail their orbital stabilities and underlying dynamical mechanisms. By performing long-term simulations, we investigate the impacts of general relativity and the Yarkovsky effect, which were previously either ignored or oversimplified. Stability maps on the $(a_0,i_0)$ and $(a_0,e_0)$ planes are generated, revealing that the most stable Venus Trojans reside in low-inclination horseshoe orbits with low eccentricities. We identify the resonances responsible for the fine structures within these stability maps. While general relativity slightly reduces orbital stability, the Yarkovsky effect can eject nearly all Venus Trojans from the Trojan region within a relatively short timeframe. Consequently, Venus Trojans exhibit poor orbital stability and cannot survive the Solar System's age. Therefore, the zodiacal dust ring observed near Venus is more likely a sporadic phenomenon resulting from the temporary capture of dust particles—produced by passing comets or asteroids—into the 1:1 mean motion resonance, rather than being sourced from Venus Trojans.

Knowledge tracing (KT) involves modeling a student's evolving mastery using their past interaction history to forecast future performance. While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps are often proprietary and custom-tailored, hindering experimental standardization. Second, current DLKT studies frequently employ inconsistent evaluation protocols that lack alignment with real-world educational settings. To resolve these issues, we present \textsc{pyKT}, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform designed to ensure valid comparisons across DLKT methods through exhaustive evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library features standardized, integrated preprocessing procedures for seven popular datasets across various domains, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DLKT models to facilitate transparent experimentation. Our rigorous, fine-grained empirical studies reveal key insights for effective DLKT, such as how incorrect evaluation settings can cause label leakage and artificially inflate performance, and how many recent DLKT improvements are marginal compared to the initial model by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have open-sourced both \textsc{pyKT} and our experimental findings at https://pykt.org/, and we invite contributions from other research groups and practitioners.

An analysis of the $X(3872)$ lineshape by the LHCb collaboration reveals a significant negative effective range, which contradicts the hypothesis of a shallow $D\bar{D}^*$ bound state. Applying Weinberg's compositeness criterion alongside Smorodinsky's theorem indicates that the $X$ particle must possess a compact hidden-charm configuration, likely a tetraquark, that interacts with unbound $D\bar{D}^*$ pairs through short-range color forces. This finding is further supported by the broader trends recently observed among exotic mesons.

In the Relativistic Brueckner-Hartree-Fock (RBHF) framework, the single-particle potential for in-medium nucleons, specifically its momentum and isospin dependencies, serves as a fundamental quantity. This potential is determined by extracting the scalar and vector components within nuclear matter. Unlike traditional RBHF calculations restricted to positive-energy states (PESs) in Dirac space, incorporating negative-energy states (NESs) allows for a uniquely determined single-particle potential through a full Dirac space approach. Using realistic Bonn nucleon-nucleon potentials, the saturation properties of symmetric and asymmetric nuclear matter within this full Dirac space are systematically examined. To underscore the significance of this method, the study investigates neutron star properties, noting that the direct URCA cooling process occurs at densities of $\rho_{\rm{DURCA}}=0.43,~0.48,~0.52$ fm$^{-3}$ with corresponding proton fractions of $Y_{p,\rm{DURCA}}=0.13$. For a $1.4M_\odot$ neutron star, the predicted radii are $R_{1.4M_\odot}=11.97,~12.13,~12.27$ km, and the tidal deformabilities are $\Lambda_{1.4M_\odot}=376,~405,~433$ for Bonn potentials A, B, and C, respectively. Compared to PES-only Dirac space results, the full-Dirac-space RBHF calculations yield the softest symmetry energy, a finding more consistent with gravitational wave (GW) detections from GW170817. Additionally, these results align well with recent astronomical observations regarding massive neutron stars and simultaneous mass-radius measurements.

Reconstructing the kinematics of top quarks enables the definition of specific observables crucial for physics processes involving these particles and offers an extra method to suppress background events. Photon radiation accompanying top quarks modifies both the event's kinematics and topology, resulting in systematic effects in measurable quantities. This study presents an enhanced top quark kinematic reconstruction technique designed to account for such photon radiation. The findings are detailed for both top quark pair production and singly-produced top quarks.

Using the statistical hadronization model, we present predictions for the integrated yields of bottomonia in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Our study examines the centrality dependence of $\Upsilon$ production and offers forecasts for a broad range of unmeasured open-beauty hadrons.

Historically, period searches in event data have relied on the Rayleigh statistic ($R^2$), whereas X-ray pulsar analysis typically employs the $Z^2$ statistic, which aggregates multiple harmonics. For gamma-ray data, the $H$-test is frequently utilized to optimize the summation of harmonics. However, these traditional periodograms share a common limitation: artifacts resulting from correlations in Fourier components when testing frequencies that do not correspond to an integer number of cycles. This article addresses this issue by discussing the modified Rayleigh statistic and formulating its generalization to any harmonic, $\mathcal{R}^2_k$, from which the modified $Z^2$ statistic, $\mathcal{Z}^2$, is derived. Versions of these statistics for both binned data and point measurements are developed, demonstrating that variance in uncertainties can significantly impact the periodogram. The text further illustrates how to synthesize information across different harmonics to estimate signal frequency with maximum precision. Application to an *XMM-Newton* observation of the Crab pulsar reveals that the pulse profile's power is predominantly concentrated in the second, third, and fifth harmonics. Additionally, the study shows that the $\mathcal{R}^2_k$ statistic offers superior statistical detection power compared to the FFT and matches the performance of the Lomb-Scargle (LS) method. While assessing responses to data gaps, it is found that LS fails to mitigate distortions caused by such gaps. The primary conclusion is that classical $R^2$ and $Z^2$ should be replaced by $\mathcal{R}^2_k$ and $\mathcal{Z}^2$ in all event data applications, and LS should be superseded by $\mathcal{R}^2_k$ whenever measurement uncertainties vary across point observations.

This research investigates the viability of constructing a detector for Earth-skimming cosmic tau neutrinos, aiming to identify the ideal dimensions for a natural mountain-valley site and determine the optimal energy range (likely between 10^15 eV and 10^20 eV) to potentially locate a suitable facility in Algeria. Initially, a Monte Carlo simulation models neutrino-mountain interactions and subsequent tau lepton decays to establish the necessary mountain dimensions and the precise location of decays within the valley. Subsequently, a CORSIKA simulation utilizing the CONEX option tracks the development of nearly horizontal air showers generated by these tau leptons. The analysis of the spatial distribution of shower particles—including electrons, muons, gammas, and pions—allows for the determination of the valley's optimal width and the required distance for deploying the detection network.

The scarcity of water on terrestrial planets implies they originated inside the solar system's water snow line, making the accurate prediction of this boundary's temporal evolution crucial for understanding planetary formation. This study examines the migration of the snow line in protoplanetary disks governed by laminar magnetic accretion—a mechanism supported by various nonideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. Based on these simulations, which reveal that accretion heating is far less efficient in laminar disks than in turbulent ones, we develop an empirical temperature model to track the snow line's position over time. Our findings indicate that in magnetically accreting laminar disks, the snow line shifts inward past Earth's current orbit within 1 million years, a process that takes significantly longer in conventional turbulent disks. Consequently, this suggests that rocky protoplanets either formed during this early disk phase or migrated outward from near the protosun to their present locations.

Accurately measuring and predicting migration trends and their evolution is crucial for grasping wider demographic shifts, crafting effective policies, and distributing resources appropriately. Yet, migration data are frequently scarce or delayed. Social media presents a novel solution, offering timely demographic estimates that can supplement conventional data sources; for instance, Facebook functions like a continuously updated digital census. However, Facebook's user base does not reflect the general population. This paper introduces a statistical framework that merges social media data with traditional surveys to generate timely "nowcasts" of migrant populations by U.S. state. The model employs bias adjustment for Facebook data and a pooled principal component time series method to capture correlations across age, time, and geography. Using examples of migrants from Mexico, India, and Germany, the study demonstrates that this hybrid approach outperforms models relying exclusively on either social media or survey data.

Identifying new multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions serves as a critical indicator of disease progression, a process that could be efficiently automated through learning-based approaches. However, the scarcity of annotated longitudinal data featuring newly appearing lesions hinders the development of robust and generalizable models. This study presents a deep-learning pipeline designed to tackle the difficult challenges of detecting and segmenting new MS lesions. First, we leverage transfer learning by utilizing a model pre-trained on single-time-point segmentation tasks, thereby capitalizing on the abundance of annotated data available for this simpler task. Second, we introduce a data synthesis strategy that generates realistic longitudinal scans containing new lesions from single-time-point inputs, allowing us to pretrain our detection model on extensive synthetic datasets. Finally, we employ a specialized data augmentation technique to simulate MRI data diversity, effectively expanding the volume of available small longitudinal datasets. Our ablation study confirmed that each proposed contribution individually improved segmentation accuracy. Ultimately, the implemented pipeline achieved the highest scores for both detecting and segmenting new MS lesions in the MSSEG2 MICCAI challenge.

This work investigates the effective dynamics of ferromagnetic spin chains subject to long-range interactions. Specifically, we analyze the one-dimensional Heisenberg Hamiltonian where spins interact via power-law exchange couplings characterized by an exponent $\alpha$, alongside an added $z$-directional anisotropy. Employing a semiclassical framework and the Holstein-Primakoff transformation, we derive an effective discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation with long-range characteristics. By taking the continuum limit, we arrive at a fractional nonlinear Schrödinger-like equation. We subsequently examine the modulational instability of plane waves in this continuum regime, demonstrating that, unlike in short-range scenarios, plane waves exhibit modulational instability when $\alpha < 3$. Furthermore, we analyze how the growth rate and critical wave-number of this instability depend on the Hamiltonian parameters and the exponent $\alpha$.

This study examines the asymptotic properties of a 2-dimensional soft random geometric graph, $G(\lambda,s,\phi)$, constructed by distributing a Poisson($\lambda s^2$) number of vertices uniformly within a square of side length $s$. Edges connect any pair of vertices $x$ and $y$ with probability $\phi(\|x-y\|)$, where $\phi$ is a finite-range connection function mapping non-negative real numbers to $[0,1]$. The analysis focuses on the behavior of $G(\lambda,s,\phi)$ as $s$ approaches infinity, keeping $\lambda$ and $\phi$ constant. It is demonstrated that the fraction of vertices belonging to the largest connected component converges in probability to the percolation threshold of the associated random connection model, which is defined over a Poisson process on the entire plane. The analysis explicitly excludes the scenario where $\lambda$ matches the critical value $\lambda_c(\phi)$.

Emission substructures in gas and dust are frequently observed within protoplanetary disks, often serving as indicators of planet formation or existing planets. This study investigates gas substructures in AS 209 by combining high-spatial resolution data from the MAPS program with thermochemical modeling using RAC2D. Observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 emission reveal a pronounced depression at 88 au, which aligns with multiple gaps detected in millimeter dust continuum emission. Our results indicate that the observed CO column density could result from either gas surface-density perturbations or chemical processing, whereas C$_2$H column density reflects variations in the C/O ratio rather than H$_2$ gas surface density. However, explaining the extent of this gas depression would necessitate a massive planet (> 0.2 M$_{Jup}$), a scenario that contradicts constraints derived from dust emission and the pressure profile inferred from gas kinematics. Consequently, our models suggest that a localized reduction in CO abundance is essential to account for the observed CO structure, overshadowing any potential influence of a gap-carving planet on the H$_2$ surface density. This work is included in the MAPS special issue of the Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series.

Given the current integration process, it is natural to consider whether CAPADR economies could gain from adopting a single currency. This study evaluates the viability of an Optimum Currency Area (OCA) across seven CAPADR nations. Utilizing Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) models, we analyze demand and supply shocks occurring between January 2009 and January 2020 to assess their symmetry. Subsequently, we calculate two regional dispersion indicators and the potential costs of joining a hypothetical OCA for each nation. Our findings reveal that asymmetric shocks are dominant. Furthermore, while dispersion metrics indicate that business cycles have grown more synchronized over time, CAPADR countries remain sources of cyclical divergence. Consequently, these nations would face substantial costs regarding cycle correlation if they pursued monetary unification. Ultimately, we conclude that the region lacks the necessary symmetry and synchronicity to justify an OCA.

We introduce lattice QCD computations of the valence parton distribution function (PDF) for the pion, utilizing next-to-next-leading-order (NNLO) perturbative QCD matching. These computations rely on three gauge ensembles comprising 2+1 flavor highly improved staggered quarks alongside Wilson--Clover valence quarks, specifically targeting pion masses of $m_\pi=140$~MeV at a lattice spacing of $a=0.076$~fm and $m_\pi=300$~MeV at spacings of $a=0.04$ and $0.06$~fm. This setup allows us to provide, for the first time, continuum-extrapolated lattice QCD results for the NNLO valence PDF of the pion at the physical point. By applying a leading-twist expansion to renormalization group invariant (RGI) ratios of bi-local pion matrix elements with NNLO Wilson coefficients, we derive the $2^{\mathrm{nd}}$, $4^{\mathrm{th}}$, and $6^{\mathrm{th}}$ Mellin moments of the PDF. Furthermore, we reconstruct the Bjorken-$x$ dependence of the NNLO PDF from real-space RGI ratios using a deep neural network (DNN) and from momentum-space matrix elements renormalized via a hybrid-scheme. All findings align broadly with global fits to experimental data conducted by the xFitter and JAM collaborations.

This study investigates online gradient and proximal-gradient approaches in the presence of stochastic gradient noise. Specifically, we analyze the behavior of online gradient descent when the cost function adheres to the Polyak-\L ojasiewicz (PL) inequality, offering both expected and high-probability bounds that hold for each iteration; the latter utilizes a sub-Weibull framework to model gradient errors. Our convergence analysis demonstrates that instantaneous regret decreases linearly, converging toward a limit determined by the problem's variability and the statistical properties of the sub-Weibull gradient errors. We extend these findings to the online proximal-gradient method under the proximal-PL condition for composite costs. Furthermore, for static cost scenarios, we derive new regret bounds assuming sub-Weibull gradient errors, and we present simulation results to validate these theoretical outcomes.

This paper introduces a novel and challenging information extraction task within the materials science field. We propose an annotation framework for identifying key details regarding solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) experiments in scientific literature, specifically targeting materials and measurement conditions. In this work, we release our annotation guidelines alongside the SOFC-Exp corpus, which comprises 45 open-access scholarly articles annotated by domain experts. Through a combination of the corpus and an inter-annotator agreement study, we illustrate the complexity inherent in the proposed named entity recognition and slot filling tasks while confirming high annotation quality. Additionally, we introduce robust neural network-based models designed for various tasks utilizing this new dataset. Results indicate that employing BERT embeddings yields significant performance improvements across all tasks; however, as task complexity increases, augmenting the architecture with a recurrent neural network proves advantageous. These models are intended to serve as competitive baselines for future research, and an analysis of their performance sheds light on challenging modeling scenarios while pointing toward promising avenues for further investigation.

Large pre-trained language models like GPT-3 have demonstrated an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. For instance, to classify sentiment without training data, one can "prompt" the model with a review and the query "Does the user like this movie?", asking if the subsequent word is "yes" or "no." Nevertheless, the underlying next-word prediction objective remains misaligned with the goals of zero-shot learning. To resolve this, we introduce meta-tuning, a method that directly optimizes the zero-shot objective by fine-tuning pre-trained models on a diverse set of datasets. Focusing on classification, we built a meta-dataset by combining 43 existing datasets and creating 441 label descriptions in a question-answering format. On unseen tasks, our meta-tuned models surpassed both a similarly sized QA model and the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot system based on natural language inference. Furthermore, scaling parameters from 220M to 770M boosted AUC-ROC scores by 6.3%, suggesting that even larger models will yield better results. Consequently, evaluating zero-shot performance on models out-of-the-box may undervalue their true potential, and collaborative efforts to aggregate and standardize datasets could lead to models that respond more effectively to prompts.

Singular value decomposition (SVD) applied to principal component analysis (PCA) fails in high-dimensional settings with limited samples when the eigen-signal-to-noise ratio (eigen-SNR) drops below a critical threshold determined by system dimensionality and sample count. In this sub-critical regime, SVD estimates become asymptotically uncorrelated with the true latent principal components. This study examines a scenario where the left singular vector of a rank-one signal matrix is sparse and the right singular vector is equisigned (containing exclusively non-negative or non-positive entries). We evaluate six distinct algorithms for estimating the sparse principal component using various statistical criteria, demonstrating that leveraging sparsity enables consistent estimation even in the low eigen-SNR regime where standard SVD fails. Our analysis identifies conditions under which a coordinate selection scheme based on a \textit{sum-type decision statistic} outperforms methods relying on $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norm-based statistics. Furthermore, we establish lower bounds for the detectable size of coordinates within the principal left singular vector and use these bounds to determine lower limits on the worst-case risk. Finally, numerical simulations validate our theoretical findings, including an application to video data for object identification.

Planet formation typically begins within the relatively dense star-forming regions surrounding the host star, where external environmental factors significantly influence the process's outcome. Specifically, regions hosting massive stars generate intense far-ultraviolet (FUV) and extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) radiation, which can trigger photoevaporative mass loss from protoplanetary discs. This study presents a parameter-space analysis of anticipated FUV and EUV fields within N-body simulations of star-forming regions under various initial conditions. By applying recently published models, we quantify the resulting photoevaporative mass loss. Our investigation focuses on how variations in initial spatial structure, virial ratio, and stellar density affect these outcomes. We find that FUV fields in star-forming regions are substantially stronger than in the interstellar medium, even in cases with stellar densities comparable to the Galactic field, primarily due to the presence of intermediate-mass and massive stars (>5 solar masses). These intense radiation fields can strip the gas component of protoplanetary discs within 1 million years. Consequently, gas giant planets must either form extremely rapidly (in less than 1 Myr) or arise exclusively in star-forming regions devoid of massive or intermediate-mass stars, such as Taurus. This latter possibility conflicts with meteoritic evidence indicating that the Sun and its protoplanetary disc were born in close proximity to massive stars.

We introduce and computationally investigate a technique for simultaneously aligning the angular momentum of asymmetric top molecules along three specific directions: 1) a fixed laboratory axis, 2) the molecule's intermediate moment of inertia axis, and 3) the wavevector of the laser field. This approach employs a coherent control strategy where a customized optical centrifuge pulse populates rotational states characterized by well-defined projections of total angular momentum onto molecular axes. By precisely shaping these optical centrifuge pulses in time, we can create unique rotational coherences that result in strong three-dimensional transient alignment, causing an arbitrary molecular axis to point along the direction of laser propagation. As a demonstration, we show how to produce highly robust rotational quantum states in D2S molecules, where rotation occurs primarily around the intermediate inertia axis, thereby permanently aligning the electric dipole moment with the laser pulse's propagation direction. Potential applications of this method include retrieving clearer data in various photo-electron imaging experiments.

Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently become widely adopted for solving partial differential equations due to their ability to circumvent the curse of dimensionality. This paper introduces PINNs as an underdetermined point matching collocation method, elucidates the relationship between Galerkin Least Square (GALS) and PINNs, and derives an a priori error estimate for elliptic problems. Specifically, the error analysis employs techniques from least square finite elements alongside Rademacher complexity theory.

Let $Q$ denote a nonempty, closed, and convex subset within a real Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Consider a nonexpansive mapping $T:Q\rightarrow Q$ possessing at least one fixed point, alongside a Lipschitzian function $f:Q\rightarrow \mathcal{H}$ and a mapping $F:Q\rightarrow \mathcal{H}$ that is both Lipschitzian and strongly monotone. Under suitable conditions governing the sequences $\{\alpha _{n}\}$ and $\{\beta _{n}\}$, as well as the error term $\{e_{n}\}$, we demonstrate that for any initial point $x_{0} \in Q$, the sequence $\{x_{n}\}$ produced by the perturbed iterative scheme \[ x_{n+1}=\beta _{n}x_{n}+(1-\beta _{n})P_{Q}\left( \alpha _{n}f(x_{n})+(I-\alpha _{n}F)Tx_{n}+e_{n}\right) \] converges strongly to the unique solution of the variational inequality problem: \[ \text{Find }q\in C\text{ such that }\langle F(q)-f(q),x-q\rangle \geq 0\text{ for all }x\in C, \] where $C=F_{ix}(T)$ represents the set of fixed points of $T$. This primary finding unifies and broadens numerous established results found in prior literature.

This paper introduces a Markov Decision Process (MDP)-based algorithm designed as a safety compliance layer for human-in-the-loop systems within the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). While many sectors are advancing toward Industry 4.0 automation via robotics, human-in-the-loop configurations remain prevalent in developing nations such as India. Whenever human-machine interaction is required, there is an inherent risk of health hazards. Consequently, this study developed a system for a specific industry utilizing MDP. The proposed algorithm learns state transition probabilities from experience and adapts to new changes through transfer learning. The system was evaluated using data from 39 sensors attached to a Computer Numerically Controlled (CNC) machine, operating continuously in a 24/7 environment. State transitions are typically initiated by humans, which can lead to intentional or unintentional errors. The system triggers alarms to warn operators, who may acknowledge or ignore them based on their perception of the current system state. If an operator repeatedly ignores warnings for a specific state transition, the system retrains the model. Observations indicate that 95.61% of the alarms were addressed by the operator, 3.2% resulted from system changes that prompted model retraining, and 1.19% were false alarms. However, the error rate stemming from human operator mistakes could not be calculated due to the unavailability of ground truth data.

We introduce a normal graph algebra inspired by structures in genetics. While this algebra does not invariably specify its underlying graph, it frequently reveals distinctive characteristics. Following an exploration of the algebra's fundamental properties, we analyze specific minimal graphs and subsequently apply these findings to the Petersen graph to uncover interrelations among its various features. Notably, the outer automorphisms of Sym(6) arise naturally in this context, and the normal algebra associated with the Petersen graph stands as unique within the class of normal graph algebras.

This work extends the toric Bertini theorem, originally established by Fuchs, Mantova, and Zannier, to settings of positive characteristic. Central to this proof is the construction of a novel algebraically closed field that contains the rational function field \kk(t_1,\dots,t_d) over an algebraically closed base field \kk of prime characteristic. Consequently, we broaden the tropical Bertini theorem of Maclagan and Yu to apply to any characteristic, thereby eliminating the reliance on specific characteristic constraints regarding the $d$-connectivity of tropical varieties found in their original paper.

In 2006, Bonato and Tardif introduced the Tree Alternative Conjecture (TAC), which posits that the equivalence class of a tree under the embeddability relation is isomorphic to either a trivial or an infinite set. In 2022, LaFlamme et al. presented a rigorous exposition of a counterexample to TAC, originally developed by Tetano in his 2008 PhD thesis. That same year, the current author demonstrated a positive resolution to TAC regarding the topological minor relation. Alongside embeddability and the topological minor, the graph minor relation forms the trio of most extensively investigated graph relations. This paper offers a positive solution to TAC for the graph minor relation.

We present the notion of quasi-linearity, demonstrating its necessity for a monomial ideal to possess a linear resolution, and we characterize all quasi-linear quadratic monomial ideals. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of a strongly linear monomial within a monomial ideal $I$ and establish that if $\mathbf{u}$ is strongly linear over $I$, then $I$ has a linear resolution (respectively, is quasi-linear) if and only if $I+\mathbf{u}\mathfrak{p}$ has a linear resolution (respectively, is quasi-linear), where $\mathfrak{p}$ denotes an arbitrary monomial prime ideal.

The recent surge in the development of touchless gestural interfaces is driven by the widespread adoption of commercial midair gesture systems and public interactive screens. This study examines an application utilizing the Microsoft Kinect that enables students to navigate a university website displayed publicly using simple hand movements. We conducted two empirical evaluations to assess user reactions to this novel interaction method. Beyond confirming the current absence of established standards, our findings offer valuable insights for designing future touchless interaction systems.

Given the extensive consumption of reheated oil, particularly in South Asia, this practice poses significant global health risks. Although multispectral imaging systems (MISs) are widely used for rapid food quality screening, they have not yet been applied to analyze oil reheating. This study addresses that gap by utilizing a low-cost multispectral imaging (MSI) system to estimate the number of reheat cycles and identify critical points where substantial chemical changes occur in the oil. First, the reheat cycle count was estimated by calculating the Bhattacharyya distance between reheated samples and pure oil, with classification performed via a support vector machine achieving 83.34% accuracy. Subsequently, a modified spectral clustering algorithm was employed in an unsupervised manner to distinguish these critical classes. Laboratory experiments further validated these findings through chemical analysis of coconut oil samples, which showed statistically significant results (p < 0.05) aligning with the imaging data. Consequently, this research bridges the gap in applying multispectral imaging to oil reheating and introduces a novel algorithm for unsupervised detection of critical property changes. The work holds significant practical value for food image analysis and contributes to advancements in unsupervised classification mechanisms.

Acquiring and analyzing time-tagged events is a fundamental technique across both scientific and industrial sectors. However, as time resolution, input channels, and event volumes increase, the resulting data volume often overwhelms conventional processing methods. To address this, we created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), a robust, versatile, and user-friendly software solution designed for the efficient analysis and visualization of time-tagged data. Unlike traditional start-stop measurements, our tool enables flexible correlation extraction from time-tagged datasets of arbitrary complexity. By integrating state diagrams with straightforward code snippets, ETA maintains high computational efficiency while supporting sophisticated analytical workflows.

This research investigates a flat FRW cosmological model containing a perfect fluid coupled with a massless scalar field within a higher-order gravity framework. We derive two distinct universe scenarios: an accelerating phase characterized by power-law cosmology, and a transition phase defined by hyperbolic expansion. Various physical and kinematic parameters are computed and analyzed against observationally constrained values of $H_{0}$. The transition redshift is determined to be $z_{t}=0.414$, where the model exhibits signature flipping and aligns with recent observational data. Furthermore, in our proposed models, the equation of state parameter $\omega_{0}$ evolves across the cosmological constant value of $-1$, and the current age of the universe is also calculated.

We provide a survey of globular clusters (GCs) within the massive lensing cluster SMACS J0723.3-7327 ($z=0.39$), utilizing early JWST/NIRCam data. Analysis of the point source color-magnitude diagrams reveals a dense population of intracluster GCs distributed across a broad region of the cluster. Accounting for the cluster's redshift, these GCs have ages younger than 9.5 Gyr. Their F200W (AB) magnitudes, ranging from 26.5 to 29.5, translate to absolute magnitudes between -15.2 and -12.2, indicating they are among the brightest GCs (encompassing ultracompact dwarfs). Spatially, these clusters form a megaparsec-scale structure aligned with the major axis of the brightest cluster galaxy. Furthermore, numerous substructures are present, some correlating with diffuse intracluster light patterns. The GC number density map generally aligns with dark matter mass density maps derived from strong lensing studies. However, the radial number density profile in the outer regions is steeper than the dark matter profile from lensing models. These findings mirror results from deep HST observations of the massive cluster Abell 2744 ($z=0.308$) and simulated clusters. Consequently, intracluster GCs serve as a robust independent method for investigating dark matter distributions and uncovering cluster assembly histories during the JWST era.

Over recent years, Machine Learning has been extensively utilized across diverse applications, including image classification, autonomous driving, and natural language processing. The Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) has garnered significant attention recently due to its energy-based architecture for modeling data probability distributions. However, this technique remains vulnerable to adversarial manipulation, involving either minor or substantial alterations to data. As a solution to this adversarial vulnerability, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) offer an alternative by modeling data distributions and producing adversarial examples that mimic the originals. Consequently, this study proposes the artificial generation of RBMs through Adversarial Learning, utilizing pre-trained weight matrices as inputs for the GAN. Additionally, the approach involves sampling large quantities of matrices to form ensembles, thereby reducing the need to train numerous new models. Experimental findings confirm the efficacy of this method in image reconstruction and classification tasks, illustrating that artificial ensembles serve as a viable alternative to pre-training extensive collections of RBMs.

We investigate the impact of isovector and isoscalar proton-neutron pairing on the binding energies of even-even nuclei where $N-Z$ equals 0, 2, or 4 and the atomic mass $A$ ranges from 20 to 100. Binding energies are computed using a mean-field approach that combines a Skyrme-type functional with a zero-range isovector-isoscalar pairing force. This force is modeled within the quartet condensation model (QCM), which strictly conserves both particle number and isospin. To account for the interplay between pairing and deformation, we conduct self-consistent Skyrme-HF+QCM calculations in the intrinsic frame. Results indicate that enabling isoscalar pairing produces minimal changes in binding energies. This observation stems from the off-diagonal matrix elements of the pairing force, which are less attractive in the isoscalar channel, alongside the competition between isoscalar and isovector pairing mechanisms.

Recent advancements in differentiable deep learning have significantly boosted superpixel segmentation; however, processing high-resolution images remains difficult due to prohibitive memory and computational demands, causing current state-of-the-art networks to fail. To address this, we introduce Patch Calibration Networks (PCNet), designed to achieve efficient and accurate high-resolution superpixel segmentation. PCNet operates by generating high-resolution outputs from low-resolution inputs to conserve GPU memory and reduce computational costs. To recover fine details lost during down-sampling, we propose a novel Decoupled Patch Calibration (DPC) branch that collaborates with the main superpixel generation branch. Specifically, DPC extracts local patches from high-resolution images to dynamically create binary masks, guiding the network to concentrate on region boundaries. By sharing parameters between the DPC and main branches, fine-grained knowledge derived from high-resolution patches is transferred to calibrate and restore lost information. To our knowledge, this is the first application of deep learning for high-resolution superpixel generation. We also establish evaluation benchmarks using two public datasets and one newly constructed dataset, spanning diverse scenarios from fine-grained human parts to cityscapes. Extensive experiments show that PCNet outperforms existing methods quantitatively and raises the resolution upper limit from 3K to 5K on 1080Ti GPUs.

Rapid progress in artificial intelligence, sensor technology, and wireless communication has enabled ubiquitous sensing via distributed networks, fostering smart systems across healthcare, transportation, environmental monitoring, and other sectors. The collaborative interaction among these systems connects end-user devices to form a unified entity known as Smart Cities. This study presents a comprehensive survey of data analytics within Smart Cities, with a specific focus on Smart Mobility—a critical component that significantly enhances urban decision-making. Intelligent decision-making systems in this domain offer numerous benefits, including energy conservation, traffic optimization, and the reduction of air pollution through the provision of real-time, actionable insights. However, timely decision-making in smart cities remains challenging due to the complexity and high dimensionality of frequently uncollected factors and parameters. Consequently, this paper first examines current challenges and potential solutions, subsequently proposing a "Universal Smart Cities Decision Making" framework. This framework consists of three primary stages: data capturing, data analysis, and decision-making, all designed to optimize smart mobility. Finally, we explore the fundamental concepts of big data, machine learning, and deep learning algorithms applied to smart cities, discussing their specific roles in facilitating decision-making for smart mobility.

Assuming $K$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, when the Jacobian determinant $(\partial f/\partial x)(\partial g/\partial y) - (\partial g/\partial x)(\partial f/\partial y)$ remains constant for polynomials $f,g\in K[x,y]$, Magnus' formula (cited from *Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.* 5 (1954), 256–266) characterizes the relationships among the homogeneous components $f_i$ and $g_i$. This paper extends Magnus' result to a broader context and utilizes it to establish a specific instance of the two-dimensional Jacobian conjecture.

This paper details an active research initiative focused on enabling machines to execute basic actions through demonstrations via an interactive interface. Building on prior work where human-performed actions served as training data for neural network trajectory models designed for agents in new environments, we identified specific constraints in our initial framework. To address these, we aim to integrate communication between humans and computational agents, leveraging their interaction to refine the machine-learned model. We introduce a novel framework that employs multimodal human-computer interaction to impart action concepts to machines. This approach utilizes two distinct teaching modalities—live demonstrations and natural language communication—while minimizing the number of required training samples.

The swift advancement of modern science and technology has generated abundant research themes and a vast body of literature. Drawing a parallel to X-ray imaging in medicine, this study investigates whether the internal evolution patterns and developmental limits of scientific topics can be intuitively discerned from massive knowledge relationships. To address this, we gathered 71,431 seminal articles spanning 16 disciplines along with their citation data, extracting an "idea tree" for each topic to reconstruct 71,431 topic networks from the ground up. We introduce the Knowledge Entropy (KE) metric, defining the contribution of high-entropy nodes to deepening the idea tree as the fundamental driver of topic development. By analyzing these "X-ray images" of topics, we identified two key phenomena: (1) despite potentially unlimited growth in scale, topic development faces an insurmountable ceiling where the idea tree depth never exceeds six jumps, aligning with the classical "Six Degrees of Separation"; (2) a single article rarely contributes more than three jumps to topic depth, meaning that sustained increases in depth rely on the relay of influence from multiple high-entropy nodes. Through rigorous statistical analysis, we established a unified quantitative relationship linking the change in topic depth ${\Delta D}^t(v)$ to the change in knowledge entropy over time ${KE}^t\left(v\right)$ for an article $v$ driving depth expansion: ${\Delta D}^t(v) \approx \log \frac{KE^{t}(v)}{\left(t-t_{0}\right)^{1.8803}}$. This formula effectively characterizes topic evolution patterns and forecasts their development potential. The insights gained from this scientific "X-ray" approach offer a new paradigm for comprehending the evolution of science and technology.

Tsallis thermostatistics, specifically the non-extensive framework, serves as a prevalent paradigm for modeling large-scale gravitational systems. This study applies Tsallis Cosmology to investigate thermodynamic gravity and derive corresponding modified Friedmann equations. We demonstrate that non-extensive corrections influence the evolution of the Hubble function throughout the radiation-dominated era. Consequently, these effects introduce significant alterations to the Universe's mass density and pressure, offering a plausible mechanism for baryogenesis that remains viable even when the standard interaction between the Ricci scalar and baryon current is present. By enforcing consistency with current observational constraints on baryogenesis, we limit the Tsallis $\delta$ parameter to $|\delta-1| \simeq 10^{-3}$. Finally, leveraging the recently identified link between Tsallis thermostatistics and the quantum gravitational generalization of the uncertainty principle (GUP) at the Planck scale, we confirm that this bound aligns with GUP parameter estimates predicted by numerous quantum gravity models.

This study experimentally investigates the nonlinear fluid damping of a rigid, elastically mounted pitching wing in a quiescent environment. The elastic mount's dynamics are modeled via a cyber-physical system. By perturbing the wing, we measure the fluid damping coefficient from damped oscillations across a broad spectrum of pitching frequencies, amplitudes, pivot locations, and sweep angles. We propose a universal scaling law for fluid damping that integrates all these parameters. Furthermore, particle image velocimetry-derived flow fields are analyzed to elucidate the underlying nonlinear behaviors of the fluid damping.

This paper derives various classes of linear codes featuring $t$-weights ($t=3,5,7$) for any odd prime $p$ and integer $m\ge 3$, utilizing specific defining sets. The complete weight enumerators for these codes are explicitly calculated through the application of Gauss sums and quadratic character sums. Notably, when $m=3$, a class of MDS codes with parameters $[p,3,p-2]$ is identified. Additionally, several of these codes demonstrate potential utility in secret sharing schemes and $s$-sum sets for any odd integer $s>1$.

Incorporating acoustic waves into compressible flow models often complicates both analytical and numerical investigations. To address this, various techniques have been created to eliminate these waves, resulting in distinct "sound-proof" frameworks such as the Boussinesq, anelastic, and pseudo-incompressible approximations. This study evaluates the suitability of each of these models for representing magnetic buoyancy within the solar interior. We introduce a generalized sound-proof model and compare it against the fully compressible system across several asymptotic limits, covering both rotating and non-rotating scenarios. Our analysis derives specific conditions required for a model to accurately capture the leading-order dynamics of the fully compressible system. We then examine which existing sound-proof models meet these criteria and identify the relevant parameter regimes. Furthermore, we provide a variational derivation of the pseudo-incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model to highlight its inherent Hamiltonian structure.

This research examines anisotropic lattice strips under a magnetic field within the quantum Hall regime. At particular magnetic field strengths that induce resonant Umklapp scattering, the bulk of the system becomes gapped while supporting chiral edge states, mirroring the behavior of topological insulators. These gaps generate plateaus in Hall conductivity precisely at the established fillings of $n/m$ (where both $n$ and $m$ are integers, with $m$ being odd), applicable to both integer and fractional quantum Hall effects. In the case of double strips, we observe topological phase transitions involving phases that host midgap edge states with flat dispersion. The topological phenomena predicted in this study are amenable to direct experimental verification using optical lattices.

The concept of a black hole functioning as an elementary particle is an intriguing one. While standard black holes inevitably allow surrounding particles to fall into their interior due to the infinite potential well at the center, we demonstrate for the first time that an extreme dilatonic black hole with spherical symmetry behaves exactly like an atom. In this scenario, the surrounding cloud of particles remains completely stable, forming a spherical dilatonic black hole configuration. We derive the exact wave functions for this cloud across any value of the gravitational fine structure constant ($\mu M$) and elucidate the physical basis for this stability. By analyzing these exact wave functions, we determine the system's spectrum. Furthermore, we explore the significance of this discovery, particularly regarding entropy considerations and the potential to investigate the quantization of gravitational waves through future observations.

This study experimentally investigates the diverse nonlinear coherent structures that emerge within a turbulent superfluid light flow passing an obstacle in an all-optical setup. The observed hydrodynamic regimes are systematically arranged in a comprehensive phase diagram defined by flow velocity and obstacle diameter. We then examine the vortices formed in the obstacle's wake, analyzing their intensity profiles and the relationship between their core radius and the healing length. These findings open avenues for deeper research into photon superfluid turbulence and offer adaptable experimental tools for simulating quantum transport using nonlinear light.

This study examines powerspace constructions within topological spaces, specifically targeting the category of quasi-Polish spaces. We demonstrate that for all quasi-Polish spaces, the upper and lower powerspaces commute, and further establish that this commutativity corresponds generally to the topological property of consonance. Subsequently, we analyze powerspace constructions applied to the open set lattices of quasi-Polish spaces, offering a comprehensive characterization of how these upper and lower powerspaces distribute over the open set lattice formation.

This study investigates almost Ricci-Yamabe solitons within specific contact metric manifolds. First, we demonstrate that if a complete contact metric manifold possesses an almost $(\alpha, eta)$-Ricci-Yamabe soliton with $\alpha
eq 0$, where the potential vector field is collinear with the Reeb vector field $\xi$ and $\xi$ acts as an eigenvector of the Ricci operator, then the manifold must be a compact Einstein Sasakian space, and the potential vector field is a constant scalar multiple of $\xi$. Second, we show that any complete $K$-contact manifold admitting a gradient Ricci-Yamabe soliton with $\alpha
eq 0$ is necessarily a compact Sasakian manifold isometric to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}$. Finally, assuming the existence of a gradient almost Ricci-Yamabe soliton with $\alpha
eq 0$ in a non-Sasakian $(k,\mu)$-contact metric manifold, we establish that for dimension 3, the manifold is flat; for $n>1$, it is locally isometric to $E^{n+1}	imes S^n(4)$, with the soliton vector field being tangential to the Euclidean factor $E^{n+1}$. An illustrative example is provided to validate these findings.

We derive subelliptic estimates for the $\bar{\partial}$-problem on complex algebraic surfaces within $\mathbb{C}^n$ that possess isolated singularities. Specifically, we bound the $W^{\epsilon}$ Sobolev norms of a form $f$, where $0< \epsilon < 1$, using weighted $L^2$ norms of both $\bar{\partial} f$ and $\bar{\partial}^{\ast}f$ with weights that vanish at the singularities, alongside weighted $L^2$ norms of $f$ employing weights that diverge at the singularities.

Physically, disordered ensembles of non-homopolymeric polypeptides are anticipated to be heterogeneous, meaning they should differ from homogeneous homopolymer ensembles, which exhibit a nearly unique correlation between the average end-to-end distance ($R_{\rm EE}$) and radius of gyration ($R_{\rm g}$). However, recent proposals suggest that small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data regarding the conformational dimensions of disordered proteins can be explained almost entirely by homopolymer models. To assess this viewpoint, chain-model simulations were employed to test the ability of SAXS-derived molecular form factors (MFFs) to distinguish between homogeneous and heterogeneous ensembles. This general approach makes no assumptions about ensemble encodability, as the heterogeneous ensembles evaluated were not limited to those arising from simple interaction schemes. Analysis of MFFs for specific heterogeneous ensembles with more narrowly distributed $R_{\rm EE}$ and $R_{\rm g}$ revealed that, although they deviate from homogeneous ensemble MFFs, these differences can be minimal. Strikingly, certain heterogeneous ensembles possessing significantly different asphericity and $R_{\rm EE}$ values compared to homogeneous ones can still display practically identical MFFs. This demonstrates that SAXS MFFs do not provide unique characterizations of the fundamental properties of conformational ensembles; rather, the mapping from ensemble to MFF is effectively many-to-one and likely non-smooth. Furthermore, variations in the $R_{\rm EE}$--$R_{\rm g}$ relationship for heteropolymers were illustrated using a new analytical perturbation theory developed for flexible heteropolymers. The implications of these findings for interpreting experimental data are discussed.

We aim to develop methods for modeling, controlling, and analyzing robot teams engaged in long-term environmental monitoring within fixed regions. While standard bottom-up task assignment techniques fail to scale with increasing numbers of robots and locations due to computationally intensive replanning, top-down approaches have been limited by their focus on transition times rather than broader dynamics. This study investigates a class of nonlinear macroscopic models to control the time-varying distribution of robots executing diverse tasks. Our proposed ensemble model and control strategy maintains desired, time-evolving robot populations by utilizing natural interactions between agents. Validation across multiple fidelity levels, including experimental results, demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach for environmental monitoring.

Users frequently overtrust AI-driven decision support systems, accepting incorrect recommendations without scrutiny. Contrary to expectations, providing explanations for AI decisions fails to mitigate this overreliance and may even exacerbate it. Grounded in dual-process theory, we propose that individuals rarely analyze specific AI suggestions and their accompanying explanations analytically; instead, they form broad heuristics regarding when to trust the AI. Drawing on previous medical decision-making research, we developed three cognitive forcing interventions designed to compel more thoughtful engagement with AI-generated explanations. In an experiment involving 199 participants, we evaluated these three interventions against two standard explainable AI methods and a no-AI control group. The findings indicate that cognitive forcing significantly lowers overreliance compared to simple explainable AI approaches. However, this improvement came at a cost: participants rated the most effective interventions least favorably. To assess for intervention-induced inequalities, we examined whether the benefits varied based on participants' Need for Cognition (their motivation to engage in effortful thinking). Results showed that, on average, individuals with higher Need for Cognition benefited more from the cognitive forcing interventions. Consequently, our research indicates that human cognitive motivation acts as a moderating factor in the effectiveness of explainable AI solutions.

Investigating alterations in brain functional connectivity via resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) is essential for understanding Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). However, detecting these changes in individual MDD patients is challenging due to the limited data volume from single scans, as well as inherent data issues such as incompleteness, sparsity, variability, high dimensionality, and noise.
