Given the vast and unpredictable scope of applications for these models, this raises critical questions about defining sufficiently safe system behaviors. These findings contribute to an expanding discourse advocating for a redefinition of a "better" model—one that looks beyond mere accuracy in task-oriented metrics and instead prioritizes deployment-critical factors, such as specific use contexts and the people interacting with the system.

Let $IET(\mathbb{S}^{1})$ denote the group of interval exchange transformations on the circle, and let $\mathcal{AC}_{+}(\mathbb{S}^{1})$ represent the group of orientation-preserving bijections that are absolutely continuous with absolutely continuous inverses. We define $\mathcal{ACI}$ as the group generated by both $IET(\mathbb{S}^{1})$ and $\mathcal{AC}_{+}(\mathbb{S}^{1})$. By considering an appropriate metric on $\mathcal{ACI}$, we classify every continuous homomorphism $\rho: \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{ACI}$. Specifically, any such $\rho$ is conjugate to a continuous homomorphism $\hat{\rho}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{AC}_{+}(\uplus_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{1})_{i})$.

This study introduces a reinforcement learning approach for object goal navigation (ObjNav), enabling agents to traverse 3D indoor spaces toward specific targets by leveraging long-term observations of scenes and objects. Central to this proposal is the Object Memory Transformer (OMT), built upon two core concepts: 1) Object-Scene Memory (OSM), which retains long-term scene and object semantic information, and 2) a Transformer mechanism that focuses on salient objects within the historical sequence of stored scenes and objects. This architecture allows the agent to navigate indoor environments efficiently without relying on prior knowledge, such as topological maps or 3D meshes. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural work to apply long-term object semantic memory to goal-oriented navigation tasks. Empirical evaluations on the AI2-THOR dataset demonstrate that OMT surpasses prior methods in unknown environments, specifically highlighting that the incorporation of long-term object semantics enhances navigation efficiency.

Recent NICER observations of the neutron star PSR J0740+6620, particularly the minimal variation in its radius between 1.4 and 2.1 solar masses, illuminate critical aspects of the neutron star matter equation of state. These findings indicate that pressure increases sharply at baryon densities roughly 2 to 4 times the nuclear saturation density ($n_0$)—a range where hadronic matter is anticipated to transition into quark matter—and that pressure within the nuclear regime exceeds predictions from microscopic many-body variational models. To integrate these insights into a unified microscopic description spanning nuclear to quark matter, we developed the QHC21 equation of state using a quark-hadron crossover (QHC) framework. This model primarily relies on advanced chiral effective field theory for nuclear matter, while also considering results from variational calculations based on empirical nuclear forces. We limit explicit nuclear degrees of freedom to densities up to approximately $1.5n_0$ to investigate the emergence of additional physical degrees of freedom beyond nucleons. The resulting QHC21 exhibits a sound velocity peak around 2 to $4n_0$, is stiffer than the previous QHC19 model below $2n_0$, and predicts larger radii that align well with NICER data.

Device-to-Device (D2D) communication is a key component of the developing 5G architecture, offering enhancements in energy and spectral efficiency, system capacity, and data rates. These performance gains have spurred extensive research into D2D, revealing significant challenges that must be overcome to fully leverage its potential in emerging 5G networks. To address these issues, this paper proposes a distributed intelligent method for managing D2D network generation. Specifically, the approach employs Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) agents with extended capabilities (BDIx) to independently and autonomously control each D2D node without Base Station assistance. The study provides a detailed algorithmic framework for deciding transmission modes that maximize data rates, minimize power consumption, and account for computational load. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of BDI agents in jointly resolving D2D challenges.

We demonstrate a method to differentiate between circuits containing $\log k$ negations (equivalently, $k$-monotone functions) and uniformly random functions within $\exp\left(\tilde{O}\left(n^{1/3}k^{2/3}\right)\right)$ time by utilizing random samples. This represents an improvement over the prior best distinguisher by Blais, Cannone, Oliveira, Servedio, and Tan (RANDOM'15), which required $\exp\big(\tilde{O}(n^{1/2} k)\big)$ time. Our approach leverages Fourier analysis performed on specific slices of the Boolean cube. We establish that certain "middle" slices of circuits with limited negations exhibit strong low-degree Fourier concentration, allowing us to apply a modified version of the classic Linial, Mansour, and Nisan "Low-Degree algorithm" (JACM'93) to these slices. Furthermore, our methodology yields a marginally enhanced weak learner for negation-limited circuits under the uniform distribution.

It is unlikely that animals possess flawless inverse models of their limbs (such as calculating the exact muscle contractions needed for every joint to reach a specific spatial point). Conversely, robotic arm control—whether moving an end-effector to a target location or following a trajectory—demands precise forward and inverse models. This study demonstrates that by acquiring a transition (forward) model through interaction, one can leverage it to train an amortized policy. Consequently, we re-examine policy optimization within the deep active inference framework, introducing a modular neural network architecture that concurrently learns system dynamics via prediction errors and a stochastic policy capable of generating continuous control commands to achieve desired reference positions. The model's efficacy was assessed by comparing it to a linear quadratic regulator baseline, with the discussion concluding with further directions for achieving human-like motor control.

We present ALMA sub-arcsecond observations spanning 272–375 GHz directed at the Circumnuclear Disk (CND) surrounding Sgr A*. The dataset consists of 8 distinct pointings, revealing significant SiO (8(7)–7(6)) and SO (7–6) emission from 98 locations. Furthermore, H2CS (9(1,9)–8(1,8)), OCS (25–24), and CH3OH (2(1,1)–2(0,2)) were detected in a smaller subset of these positions. Utilizing peak line flux densities alongside Bayesian Inference guided by radiative transfer models, we systematically derived the physical conditions of the gas at each site. Our estimates indicate that most of the surveyed gas exhibits temperatures below 500 K and densities approximately $10^6$ cm$^{-3}$, aligning with prior studies of similar regions traced by HCN clumps. Notably, we identified an unusually hot (T $\approx$ 600 K) and dense (n $\approx$ $10^6$ cm$^{-3}$) source in the Northeastern Arm, which appears to be a gravitationally bound region dominated by turbulence. We also detected a nearby cold (T $\approx$ 60 K) yet extremely dense (n $\approx$ $10^7$ cm$^{-3}$) position that similarly suggests gravitational binding and turbulent dominance. The total gas mass within the CND is calculated to be roughly $4 \times 10^4$ $M_{\odot}$. Qualitatively, the large-scale chemical enrichment observed in the CND supports bulk grain processing, although multiple desorption mechanisms may contribute. Additional chemical modeling is necessary to pinpoint the physical origins of this grain processing and the localized emissions of H2CS and OCS.

Gaining insight into spin current transport at metal-semiconductor junctions over pico- and femtosecond durations is vital for advancing ultrafast spintronics, data storage, and processing. Nevertheless, directly observing spin current propagation at these speeds has been restricted by the concurrent absence of both ultrafast, element-specific magnetic probes and engineered metal-semiconductor interfaces. In this work, utilizing free-electron laser-based element-sensitive Kerr spectroscopy, we provide direct experimental confirmation of spin currents crossing a Ni/Si interface, evidenced by distinct magnetodynamics at the Ni M2,3 and Si L2,3 absorption edges. Furthermore, this approach enables the calculation of the spin current's propagation velocity within silicon, which is approximately 0.2 nm/fs.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) involves three core subtasks: identifying aspect terms, extracting opinion terms, and classifying sentiment polarity. While these are typically executed jointly to conserve resources and mitigate error propagation, most current joint models prioritize encoder sharing between subtasks while neglecting their distinct differences. To address this, we introduce a novel joint ABSA model that leverages encoder sharing advantages while specifically targeting these differences to enhance overall performance. Specifically, our approach employs a dual-encoder architecture where one pair encoder specializes in classifying candidate aspect-opinion pairs, while the original encoder remains focused on sequence labeling. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our model exhibits robustness and significantly surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods across four benchmark datasets.

This work examines the polarization of gravitational radiation using the standard framework of linearized general relativity. Motivated by recent experimental detections of gravitational waves, we revisit the consequences of spin-rotation-gravity coupling on polarized radiation, specifically analyzing how the helicity of gravitational waves interacts with an observer's rotation or the gravitomagnetic field of a rotating astronomical source. We also briefly investigate potential observational signatures of polarization-dependent effects for future gravitational wave detectors.

This paper introduces and examines the arithmetic properties of the ring of $\mathbb{U}$-operators associated with reductive $p$-adic groups. These operators extend the concept of "successor" operators found in trees with a designated endpoint. We demonstrate that these operators are integral over the spherical Hecke algebra. This integrality plays a pivotal role in constructing Euler systems derived from special cycles on general Shimura varieties and in generalizing the renowned Eichler-Shimura relation.

This study calculates the electric dipole polarizabilities ($\alpha_d$) for alkali-metal negative ions ranging from H$^-$ to Fr$^-$ using four-component relativistic many-body techniques. We examine variations in the outcomes by incorporating the Dirac-Coulomb (DC) Hamiltonian, the DC Hamiltonian augmented with the Breit interaction, and the DC Hamiltonian including lower-order quantum electrodynamics effects. These interactions are first treated self-consistently within the Dirac-Hartree-Fock (DHF) framework, after which electron correlation effects are integrated into the DHF wave functions via second-order many-body perturbation theory, the random phase approximation, and coupled-cluster (CC) theory. The influence of relativistic corrections and electron correlation is evaluated across these methods in relation to ion size. Finally, we provide precise $\alpha_d$ values for these negative ions by estimating uncertainties in the CC calculations and comparing them with existing literature where data is available.

This paper demonstrates that for a closed oriented surface, the length spectrum serves as a distinguishing feature between flat metrics arising from holomorphic quadratic differentials and other flat cone metrics.

This study derives box-counting estimates for pinned distance sets associated with (dense subsets of) planar discrete Ahlfors-regular sets where the exponent $s$ exceeds 1. As a direct consequence, we refine a recent finding by Orponen: if $A$ is an Ahlfors-regular set of dimension $s>1$, then the lower box-counting dimension of almost all its pinned distance sets equals 1. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for subsets $A$ and $B$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than 1, where $A$ is Ahlfors-regular, the set of distances between them possesses a modified lower box-counting dimension of 1. Setting $B=A$ in this context offers an alternative improvement to Orponen's result, reducing the packing dimension to the modified lower box-counting dimension. These proofs utilize ergodic-theoretic concepts, specifically drawing upon the theory of CP-processes and projections.

The RFX-mod2 project represents an upgrade to the RFX-mod nuclear fusion experiment, which was decommissioned in 2016. In addition to structural and diagnostic enhancements, the upgrade plans to incorporate a greater quantity of electromagnetic probes (EMs). This expansion aims to yield deeper insights into plasma instabilities and facilitate enhanced real-time plasma control. The proposed Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) architecture is designed to simultaneously support transient recording and real-time data streaming, while also enabling FPGA-based time integration of inputs. Transient recording ensures full-speed data acquisition (up to 1 MSample/s) by storing data locally for post-discharge retrieval, whereas real-time streaming delivers sub-sampled data necessary for active control systems. The selected technology relies on the XILINX Zynq architecture, which integrates a multi-core ARM processor and an FPGA within a single chip. FPGA units handle time-critical tasks such as managing circular data buffers, applying low-pass filters for subsampling, and performing digital integration. Conversely, the processor manages configuration settings received via TCP/IP or HTTP, retrieves acquired samples from transient recording buffers, and streams collected data over the network for real-time plasma control.

Dropout stands as a widely adopted regularization method in neural network training. Due to its effectiveness and conceptual simplicity, it has been the subject of extensive analysis, leading to numerous proposed variants. This paper examines various properties of dropout through a unified lens of information geometry. We demonstrate that dropout flattens the model manifold, with its regularization efficacy contingent upon the degree of curvature. Furthermore, we establish that dropout fundamentally corresponds to a regularization technique based on Fisher information, a claim supported by numerical experiments. Such a theoretical analysis from an alternative perspective is anticipated to significantly advance our understanding of neural networks, which remain in their early developmental stages.

Fiber breakage is a prevalent issue in Fiber Reinforced Composites (FRC) that leads to stress concentration. The stress transfer in the area surrounding a break is measured using the Stress Transfer Coefficient (STC). This study investigates how fiber volume fraction and spatial distribution influence both the STC and the ineffective length. Three scenarios were examined to alter the fiber volume fraction: varying the number of fibers, modifying the Representative Volume Element (RVE) dimensions, and adjusting the fiber radius. Analyses included periodic and semi-random fiber arrangements, with 200 RVEs evaluated for each volume fraction in both random and semi-random configurations. Results indicate that the STC distribution does not adhere to any standard distribution, even when the fiber arrangement itself is normally distributed. Furthermore, fiber cross-sectional dimensions are crucial for restoring strength in broken fibers. Finally, periodic fiber arrangements demonstrate superior stress transfer capabilities compared to random arrangements.

Electromagnetic metasurfaces allow for sophisticated control of surface-wave propagation through the spatial adjustment of local surface reactance. Notably, engineering the spatial distribution of surface resistance introduces novel, previously underutilized degrees of freedom. We demonstrate that appropriately modulating surface resistance between positive (loss) and negative (gain) values can generate unique dispersion phenomena that extend well beyond simple compensation. Drawing inspiration from parity-time symmetry in quantum mechanics, we introduce and investigate a category of non-Hermitian metasurfaces capable of displaying extreme anisotropy driven primarily by the interplay of gain and loss. Using both analytical modeling and comprehensive numerical simulations, we elucidate the phenomenon of surface-wave canalization, examine nonlocal effects and deviations from ideal conditions, and assess the practical feasibility of the necessary constitutive parameters. Our findings highlight promising avenues for the dynamic reconfiguration of surface-wave propagation, with significant potential applications in imaging, sensing, and communications.

The Cepheid period-luminosity (PL) relation, also known as the Leavitt law, forms the foundational step of the primary extragalactic distance ladder and is crucial for determining the local Hubble constant ($H_0$). This study examines how metallicity affects Cepheid brightness, a factor that substantially enhances the precision of the distance ladder and allows for a clearer understanding of its wavelength dependence. By analyzing PL relations from three distinct Cepheid samples with varying chemical compositions—drawn from the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds—while utilizing recent, high-quality data across a metallicity span of approximately 1 dex, we quantify the metallicity effect (denoted as $\gamma$). We evaluated $\gamma$ in 15 filters ranging from the mid-infrared to optical bands, including five Wesenheit indices. Our results reveal a significant metallicity term in all filters, aligning with recent empirical and theoretical models, which indicate that metal-rich Cepheids are intrinsically brighter than their metal-poor counterparts. We also detail the systematic effects influencing the determination of $\gamma$. Furthermore, we find no evidence that $\gamma$ varies across the $0.5-4.5 \, \rm \mu m$ wavelength range, suggesting that metallicity primarily impacts Cepheid luminosity rather than their color. Finally, we highlight factors that refine empirical constraints on the metallicity term compared to previous studies, such as correcting for the depth of the Magellanic Clouds, employing better-calibrated photometry, improving Milky Way extinction estimates, and incorporating revised, expanded metallicity measurements for the LMC.

This study investigates how near-miss clone detection can aid in characterizing domain models for smart contracts across various rapidly growing sectors. By utilizing code clone detection methods, we identify functional similarities within smart contracts deployed on the Ethereum blockchain. Furthermore, we examine the clusters of these code clones and the semantic meaning of the fragments within them to categorize them and uncover the structural patterns inherent in the cloned code.

This study examines the temperature-dependent characteristics of (GaIn)As/Ga(AsSb)/(GaIn)As W-quantum well heterostructures designed for lasers, combining theoretical models with experimental data. A microscopic theory is utilized to analyze band bending effects that cause the characteristic blue shift observed in type-II heterostructures as charge carrier density increases. Additionally, gain spectra for these W-quantum well structures are computed at high carrier densities, where the interaction among multiple type-II transitions produces broad, flat spectra with a width of roughly 160 nm. The research also investigates the temperature-dependent behavior of broad-area edge-emitting lasers through electroluminescence and laser characteristic measurements. Initial evidence supporting the predicted broad gain spectra is provided, alongside a discussion of how the temperature-induced red shift interacts with the carrier density-dependent blue shift. This interplay leads to a substantial reduction in the temperature-induced red shift of emission wavelengths, achieving negative shift rates of (-0.10 ± 0.04) nm/K.

This study addresses the challenge of adaptive sampling for uniformly estimating probability mass functions (pmfs), evaluating performance via worst-case mean squared error. We introduce a Bayesian adaptation of existing upper confidence bound (UCB) methods, demonstrating analytically that its performance is at least as good as traditional approaches. By leveraging the posterior distribution of pmfs within the Bayesian framework, we achieve tighter upper confidence bound calculations, resulting in substantial practical performance improvements. Applying this methodology, we propose adaptive sampling protocols to estimate SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence across diverse groups, including various locations and ethnicities. The efficacy of this strategy is illustrated using data from a seroprevalence survey conducted in Los Angeles County.

This study presents a measurement of the top quark mass within event topologies enriched by single top quarks generated through $t$-channel weak interactions. The analysis utilizes a dataset recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=8\,\mathrm{TeV}$, amounting to an integrated luminosity of $20.3\,\mathrm{fb^{-1}}$. The top quark mass is extracted using a template method that relies on the invariant mass distribution of the lepton and the $b$-tagged jet as the estimator. The final result is determined to be $m_{\mathrm{top}} = 172.2 \pm 0.7 {\mathrm{(stat.)}} \pm 2.0 {\mathrm{(syst.)}}\,\mathrm{GeV}$.

Column Generation (CG) serves as an iterative method for solving linear programs (LPs) characterized by an exceptionally high volume of variables (columns). It acts as the primary tool for addressing large-scale \textit{integer} linear programs, specifically by solving LP relaxations within branch-and-price frameworks. Two prominent applications include the Cutting Stock Problem (CSP) and the Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (VRPTW). In the VRPTW context, for instance, every binary variable dictates whether a specific \textit{route} is included or excluded, with the total number of potential routes being exponential; CG progressively expands the set of active columns until it converges on an optimal solution. We introduce RLCG, the inaugural Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for CG. Contrasting with conventional selection rules that myopically choose columns based solely on local iteration data, we frame CG as a sequential decision-making process where current selections influence future ones. This viewpoint aligns with a Deep Reinforcement Learning strategy utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the variable-constraint architecture of the target LP. Through extensive testing on the publicly available BPPLIB benchmark for CSP and the Solomon benchmark for VRPTW, RLCG demonstrates superior performance, converging faster and decreasing the average number of CG iterations by 22.4\% for CSP and 40.9\% for VRPTW relative to a standard greedy policy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/chichengmessi/reinforcement-learning-for-column-generation.git.

This work investigates the non-equilibrium thermodynamics of a heat engine functioning between two finite reservoirs with distinct temperatures. Under the linear response regime, we establish that the uniform temperature reached by both reservoirs at time $\tau$ has a lower bound determined by the entropy production, which scales as $\sigma_{\mathrm{min}}\propto1/\tau$. We identify a general trade-off between power and efficiency that depends on the ratio of the reservoirs' heat capacities ($\gamma$), and derive a universal efficiency at maximum average power applicable for any $\gamma$. Furthermore, we outline an operational protocol for an ideal gas heat engine to attain the optimal performance linked to $\sigma_{\mathrm{min}}$. These results provide a framework for optimizing thermodynamic cycles involving finite-sized reservoirs in practical applications.

Noor [9] introduced a Hardy space framework for the Nyman-Beurling and B\'aez-Duarte criteria concerning the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), asserting that RH is true if and only if the linear manifold $\mathcal{N}$, generated by the function sequence $(h_k)_{k\geq 2}$, is dense within the Hardy space $H^2$. This article examines three specific inquiries: $\mathbf{A.}$ What is the magnitude of the orthogonal complement to $\mathcal{N}$? $\mathbf{B.}$ Does the closure of $\mathcal{N}$ constitute a shift-invariant subspace of $H^2$? $\mathbf{C.}$ Can $\mathcal{N}$ be shown to be dense in $H^2$ under a weaker topology? To answer these questions, we employ techniques drawn from local Dirichlet spaces, de Branges-Rovnyak spaces, and the Smirnov class.

Controlling topological states within quantum materials represents a critical objective for advancing both fundamental physics and next-generation quantum technologies. In this study, we present the magnetic manipulation of Weyl fermions in the kagome spin-orbit semimetal Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$, utilizing high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy for observation. We show that suppressing magnetic order induces an exchange collapse, transforming spin-orbit-gapped ferromagnetic Weyl loops into paramagnetic Dirac loops. Furthermore, we detect the vanishing of topological Fermi arcs within the paramagnetic phase, indicating the annihilation of exchange-split Weyl points. These results suggest that the natural process of magnetic exchange collapse drives the annihilation of Weyl fermions, thereby creating new avenues for engineering topology through correlated order parameters.

This paper examines a modified van der Pol oscillator equation, which is prominent in various cardiac action models. We investigate its global dynamics and confirm several significant bifurcations, including Hopf, heteroclinic saddle connection, and homoclinic saddle connection bifurcations. The Conley index method is employed to identify some of these bifurcations. Furthermore, we illustrate how analyzing connection and transition matrices can guide the selection of meaningful parameter values for simulations.

We present an analytical model describing the dynamics of a cytoskeletal filament within a motility assay. This filament is treated as a rigid rod capable of sliding freely across a two-dimensional plane. The motor proteins are represented by polymeric tails anchored to the plane, modeled as linear springs, alongside motor heads that attach to the filament. Similar to related models involving rigid or soft two-state motors, the binding and unbinding kinetics of the motor heads, along with how transition rates depend on the load applied by the motor tails, are pivotal in governing the filament's behavior. Our findings indicate that over long time scales, the filament acts effectively as a self-propelled rod, albeit with non-Markovian noise resulting from its coupling to the motor binding and unbinding processes. We calculate the filament's effective propulsion force and the active renormalization of various friction and diffusion coefficients based on microscopic parameters of both the motors and the filament. These derived quantities are accessible for measurement via optical force microscopy.

We introduce a lattice spin model defined on a cubic grid that exhibits key characteristics of both the 3D toric code and the X-cube fracton model. Constructed from $\mathbb{Z}_3$ degrees of freedom located on the links, the model incorporates vertex, cube, and plaquette terms. As a stabilizer code, its ground states are exactly solvable. When restricted to only vertex and cube terms, the ground state degeneracy (GSD) is $3^{L^3+3L-1}$, where $L$ represents the linear size of the lattice. Beyond fractons, the system supports free vertex excitations termed "freeons." Adding plaquette terms drastically reduces the GSD to $3^3$, introducing fracton, fluxon, and freeon excitations; notably, only the freeons remain deconfined. This framework is designated the AB model when comprising solely vertex ($A_v$) and cube ($B_c$) terms, and the ABC model when plaquette terms ($C_p$) are also included. The AC model, formed by vertex and plaquette terms, corresponds to the $\mathbb{Z}_3$ 3D toric code. The extensive GSD of the AB model arises from both local and non-local logical operators linking distinct ground states, with the latter matching those of the $\mathbb{Z}_3$ X-cube model. Fractons in this system are immobile and always accompanied by fluxon creation—plaquettes with non-zero flux. In the ABC model, creating fluxons incurs an energy cost that confines the fractons. Distinct from previous fracton models, vertex excitations here move freely in all directions and acquire a non-trivial statistical phase upon passing through fluxons or fracton clusters.

The expansion of open access (OA) has rendered financial dynamics in scholarly journal publishing increasingly intricate, yet comprehensive data and transparency regarding these flows remain scarce. This opacity is particularly problematic in hybrid OA, where subscription journals allow individual articles to become OA upon payment of a fee. This research tackles the transparency deficit by utilizing Elsevier article metadata to deliver the inaugural publisher-level analysis of hybrid OA adoption and billing. Findings indicate that Elsevier's hybrid OA adoption has risen steadily but gradually between 2015 and 2019, doubling the annual count of hybrid OA articles and raising the proportion of OA content in hybrid journals from 2.6% to 3.7% of the total. Additionally, the study reveals that the majority of hybrid OA articles were billed directly to authors, with fewer invoiced via agreements with funders, institutions, or consortia; only a limited number of funding entities significantly drove hybrid OA uptake. Consequently, these results underscore the influence of publishing agreements and OA policies on hybrid OA practices. Furthermore, the study highlights the utility of publisher-provided metadata in enhancing transparency within scholarly publishing by connecting invoicing records with bibliometric data.

We introduce a formal moduli space of quasi-isogenies for isoclinic $p$-divisible groups, utilizing a non-reductive group as the structure group. Within this framework, we propose novel Arithmetic Fundamental Lemma conjectures concerning Bessel subgroups, situated under the broader context of the arithmetic Gan-Gross-Prasad conjectures. Finally, we present a small amount of supporting evidence.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) aims to bridge the gap between source and target domains by leveraging labeled source and unlabeled target data; however, in medical contexts, target data is often scarce and difficult to acquire, hindering UDA progress. This study investigates UDA within a more challenging yet realistic scenario where only a single unlabeled target patient sample is accessible, a setting we term Few-shot Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (FUDA). We first synthesize target-style images from source data and extract diverse target styles from the single patient using Random Adaptive Instance Normalization (RAIN). Subsequently, a segmentation network is trained in a supervised fashion using these generated images. Experimental results indicate that FUDA enhances segmentation performance by 0.33 Dice score points on the target domain compared to the baseline, achieving a 0.28 Dice score improvement in a stricter one-shot configuration. Our code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/MingxuanGu/Few-shot-UDA}.

Within the square root velocity framework, calculating shape space distances and registering curves necessitates solving a non-convex variational problem. This paper introduces a novel PDE-based numerical approach to address this issue. Derived from the numerical approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation associated with the variational problem, the method offers quadratic complexity and ensures global convergence for distance estimation. Additionally, we propose a backtracking scheme to approximate solutions for the registration problem, which also facilitates the computation of shape space geodesics. These techniques achieve linear numerical convergence and demonstrate enhanced efficiency relative to prior global solvers.

We introduce a vector dark matter framework based on a hidden $SU(2)_D$ gauge symmetry operating at the TeV scale. This symmetry is spontaneously broken by a scalar septuplet, which simultaneously acts as a portal connecting the Standard Model to the dark sector. Our analysis reveals two distinct vacuum configurations dependent on the sign of the quartic coupling $\lambda_3$, resulting in different gauge boson mass spectra: for $\lambda_3 < 0$, the masses are split, whereas for $\lambda_3 \geq 0$, they remain degenerate. Additionally, we examine the renormalization group evolution of the couplings, determining that requirements for perturbativity and vacuum stability impose strict limits on the parameter space. Phenomenologically, we evaluate experimental constraints from dark matter direct and indirect detection, relic density calculations, and Higgs coupling measurements. We identify viable regions of the parameter space that satisfy all these constraints and suggest they are testable in future direct and indirect dark matter experiments.

We introduce a framework to characterize the behavior of effectful higher-order recursive programs. Effects, such as execution cost, nondeterminism, global store, and user interaction, are modeled via effect operations. The program's denotational semantics is represented as a coinductive tree within a monad, aggregating potential return values alongside effect operations. Leveraging a straightforward test logic, we define two types of predicate liftings that elevate predicates on result types to predicates on computations yielding those results, each capturing a distinct aspect of program behavior. First, we examine inductive predicate liftings for describing effectful total correctness, followed by coinductive predicate liftings for effectful partial correctness. These two constructions are dual, allowing one to refute the other. These predicate liftings form the foundation of an endogenous logic for behavioral properties in higher-order programs. This program logic features a derivable negation based on the duality of the liftings and induces a program equivalence that encompasses bisimilarity. We provide specific definitions for both inductive and coinductive predicate liftings across a wide range of effect examples. The entire development has been fully formalized using the Agda proof assistant.

This paper introduces the TerraByte Client, a software tool designed to retrieve user-specified plant datasets from a Compute Canada-hosted data portal. The client provides two primary features: (1) It enables users to browse available data and visually inspect samples by processing database queries to display matching image counts, allowing for rapid downloads to verify suitability. (2) It facilitates the download of selected data to local storage, where the server splits the data into chunks that are transmitted and automatically unpacked into individual files on the user's system, with initial chunks typically ready within a minute or less, depending on bandwidth and data type. Featuring a user-friendly graphical interface and end-to-end encryption, the TerraByte Client operates on a low-level architecture. Its open-source nature allows users to build custom interfaces or utilize the core functionality directly, such as integrating on-demand data downloads into larger applications like machine learning model training.

We present both numerical and experimental analyses of the steady states generated by tapping a two-dimensional granular layer. Contrary to conventional assumptions, we demonstrate that the reversible branch of the density–acceleration curve is nonmonotonic. Consequently, steady states sharing the same mean volume can be achieved through tapping with vastly different intensities. Simulations involving dissipative frictional disks reveal that these equal-volume steady states possess distinct force moment tensor values. Furthermore, we observe that varying the duration of taps can yield steady states with identical stress levels, yet these states exhibit different mean volumes. These findings corroborate earlier hypotheses that both volume and the force moment tensor are essential for uniquely characterizing equilibrium states in static granular assemblies.

This paper establishes a criterion for complexity within the $g$-ary expansions of rational fractions $a/b < 1$, where $\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$. We demonstrate that for any purely periodic proper fraction $a/b$ and every $j \geq 1$, every sequence of $j$ digits appears in the $g$-ary repetend of $a/b^k$ with a relative frequency converging to $1/g^j$ as $k$ increases. These absolute frequencies are determined using a straightforward transition matrix. Furthermore, for a sequence $(a_k)$ of positive integers coprime to $b$, we show that each $j$-digit sequence occurs in the $g$-ary repetend of $a_k/b^k$ with a relative frequency approaching $1/g^j$ as $k$ grows, provided that not all prime factors of $b$ divide the base $g \geq 2$.

While 3D die stacking is frequently suggested for constructing large-scale DRAM caches, the inherent power and performance penalties of DRAM restrict the efficiency of high-bandwidth memory solutions. Additionally, DRAM encounters significant scalability hurdles, making alternative technologies increasingly attractive. This study introduces Monarch, a resistive 3D stacked memory architecture utilizing a new reconfigurable crosspoint array known as XAM. The XAM array can toggle between random access and content-addressable modes, allowing Monarch to (i) maximize in-package bandwidth usage and (ii) meet the diverse needs of applications requiring both random access memory and associative search capabilities. Furthermore, the Monarch controller guarantees a specific target lifespan for the resistive stack. Simulation results across various parallel, memory-intensive applications demonstrate that Monarch exceeds the performance of ideal DRAM caching by an average of 1.21x. Specifically, for in-memory hash table and string matching tasks, Monarch achieves performance gains of up to 12x compared to conventional high-bandwidth memories.

We introduce a novel global embedding of curved spacetimes into higher-dimensional flat spaces, offering a unified framework for describing both the Hawking and Unruh effects. Our analysis not only simplifies but also extends the conventional embedding methodology.

Smart contracts have faced significant security breaches, leading to considerable financial damage. Despite extensive research aimed at mitigating these risks, it remains unclear how software practitioners integrate security into smart contracts in real-world scenarios. To address this, we conducted a mixed-method study involving 13 interviews and 156 surveys from respondents across 35 countries on six continents to examine practitioner perceptions and practices. Our findings reveal the motivations and deterrents influencing smart contract security, as well as how security strategies align with the development lifecycle. Additionally, we discovered that blockchain platforms exert a statistically significant influence on practitioners' security attitudes and behaviors. Based on these insights, we offer recommendations for practitioners and suggest avenues for future research.

The breaking of charge symmetry within the strong interaction arises from the mass disparity between up and down quarks. Currently, the Standard Model fails to account for the observed hierarchy and patterns among particle masses, such as those of neutrons, protons, and the individual quarks. This limitation prevents us from determining the source of isotopic effects. Furthermore, the fundamental origin of matter's mass remains unresolved until the mechanism of chiral symmetry breaking in QCD is fully understood.

Data derived from electrohysterography (EHG) recordings may serve as a valuable supplementary tool for assessing preterm birth risk. While numerous recent studies have claimed near-perfect accuracy in distinguishing between term and preterm deliveries using the public Term/Preterm Electrohysterogram database, we contend that these findings are overly optimistic due to a specific methodological error: applying over-sampling before splitting the data into separate training and testing sets. This paper investigates this flaw by demonstrating how it biases results using artificial datasets and by replicating findings from studies where the issue was previously noted. Furthermore, we assess the genuine impact of pre-partitioning over-sampling on predictive performance, employing the same methodologies as related research to offer a realistic evaluation of generalization capabilities. To ensure reproducibility, we have released all associated code under an open license.

The emergence of Moiré materials has intensified interest in understanding charge carriers within topological bands. Unlike conventional materials where carriers are typically electron-like quasiparticles, topological bands permit exotic states where charge is transported by nontrivial topological textures, such as skyrmions. However, describing skyrmions in real space is inadequate for analyzing small or "baby" skyrmions, which comprise an electron and a minimal number of spin flips. This study investigates the formation of the smallest skyrmions—spin polarons, defined as bound states of an electron and a single spin flip—within Chern ferromagnets. We demonstrate that, in general, a purely topological attraction of $p$-wave symmetry exists between an electron and a spin flip, thereby facilitating spin polaron formation. Applying these findings to the topological bands of twisted bilayer graphene, we identify parameter ranges where spin polarons are energetically favored over free electrons. Specifically, spin polarons are found to be more stable when correlated insulators at integer fillings are doped toward charge neutrality, aligning with the observed absence of quantum oscillations and the rapid emergence of flavor polarization (cascade) transitions in this regime. Our work lays the groundwork for exploring spin polaron pairing, effectively bridging skyrmion pairing models with momentum-space approaches to superconductivity.

This work provides an introduction and overview of quantum annealing and analog computation. We examine how quantum fluctuations, specifically tunneling, operate within random systems characterized by rugged free energy landscapes and macroscopic barriers, highlighting the quantum advantage in locating ground state(s) via annealing. Additionally, the discussion covers quantum annealing as a physical, analog method for identifying optimal solutions to computationally challenging problems.

This study evaluates the achievable multiplexing gain (MG) in Wyner's symmetric network under conditions of random user activity and mixed-delay traffic arrivals. This traffic comprises both delay-tolerant and delay-sensitive data; however, only the delay-tolerant portion can leverage cooperation between transmitters and receivers due to the strict latency constraints imposed on the latter. With a constraint limiting the total number of cooperation rounds at both ends to $\D$, we establish both inner and outer bounds for the MG region. As $\D$ approaches infinity, these bounds converge, demonstrating that transmitting delay-sensitive messages incurs no penalty on the sum MG. Furthermore, for finite $\D$, the bounds remain tight, confirming that the penalty associated with delay-sensitive transmissions is negligible.

Semantic parsing is a critical challenge in natural language processing, especially for voice assistants like Alexa and Google Assistant. Current state-of-the-art parsers rely on sequence-to-sequence architectures built upon large language models pretrained on extensive text corpora. To maximize the utility of this pretraining, recent research has reframed semantic parsing so that outputs are natural language sentences within a controlled subset. This strategy yields strong performance, particularly in few-shot scenarios, which is practically vital and the primary focus of our study. We advance this approach by presenting an automated framework that achieves substantial gains by leveraging small amounts of unannotated data, which is readily available. Our technique integrates four novel methods: joint training with auxiliary unsupervised tasks, constrained decoding, self-training, and paraphrasing. We demonstrate that this approach establishes new state-of-the-art few-shot performance on the Overnight dataset, especially in extremely low-resource conditions, and delivers highly promising results on a newly created semantic parsing dataset.

Magnetic adatoms on surfaces experience exchange coupling with their surroundings, leading to rapid relaxation of excited spin states and decoherence. These effects can be mitigated by placing decoupling layers between the magnetic adsorbates and the metallic substrate. Utilizing low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, we examined the magnetic characteristics of individual Fe atoms on an Au(111) surface covered by a monolayer of MoS$_2$, focusing on how the moir\'e structure affects spin excitation spectra. Fe adatoms situated at moir\'e minima display nearly pure inelastic spin excitations. Conversely, Kondo correlations emerge for adsorption sites away from the moir\'e minimum, evolving into fully developed Kondo resonances at moir\'e maxima. This rise in Kondo correlations corresponds to a reduction in single-ion anisotropy, a trend we explain using poor-person's scaling. Furthermore, local variations in the tunneling spectra reveal significant interference between tunneling paths involving the spin-carrying orbitals and a hybrid Fe-S orbital, which forms even though the terminating sulfur layer is nominally inert.

This paper investigates the averaging principle for distribution-dependent stochastic differential equations featuring drift in localized $L^p$ spaces. By employing Zvonkin's transformation and deriving estimates for solutions to Kolmogorov equations, we demonstrate that as the time scale $\eps$ approaches zero, the solutions of the original system converge strongly and weakly to those of the averaged system. Furthermore, we establish rates for both strong and weak convergence that are contingent upon $p$.

We present a probabilistic forecasting framework consisting of two sequential machine-learning stages. The first stage involves dimensionality reduction, learning a mapping from predictor data to a low-dimensional space that retains information critical for forecast variables. The second stage employs normalizing flows for density estimation to calculate the joint probability density of these reduced predictors and the forecast quantities, which is subsequently renormalized to yield the conditional forecast distribution. In this approach, probabilistic calibration testing acts as a regularization mechanism to curb overfitting during the second stage, while the initial dimensionality reduction ensures forecast sharpness. The method's efficacy is validated using a 22-year, hourly time series of surface wind data from Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations on a grid.

The rigidity component of the spacetime positive mass theorem asserts that an initial data set $(M,g,k)$ meeting the dominant energy condition and possessing zero mass admits an isometric embedding into Minkowski space. While Beig-Chru\'sciel and Huang-Lee previously confirmed this result under supplementary decay conditions for the energy density $\mu$ and momentum density $J$, this note presents a novel and elementary proof in three dimensions that eliminates the need for these extra assumptions. The primary approach relies on spacetime harmonic functions and Liouville's theorem, supplemented by an alternative demonstration utilizing the Killing development of $(M,g,k)$.

The Born cross section for the $e^{+}e^{-} \rightarrow \Lambda_{c}^{+}\bar{\Lambda}_{c}^{-}$ reaction has been measured with exceptional precision using data from the BESIII detector at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=4574.5$, $4558.0$, $4590.0$, and $4599.5$ MeV. A non-zero cross section near the production threshold for $\Lambda_{c}^{+}\bar{\Lambda}_{c}^{-}$ was identified. With higher statistics available at $\sqrt{s}=4574.5$ and $4599.5$ MeV, the polar angle distributions of the $\Lambda_{c}$ were determined, allowing for the first-ever measurement of the ratio between the $\Lambda_{c}$ electric and magnetic form factors ($|G_{E}/G_{M}|$). The resulting values are $1.14\pm0.14\pm0.07$ and $1.23\pm0.05\pm0.03$, where the initial uncertainties represent statistical errors and the subsequent ones denote systematic uncertainties.

We experimentally investigate a quantum metamaterial realized on a superconducting chip featuring 25 frequency-tunable transmon qubits linked to a shared coplanar resonator. The collective bright and dark modes are examined through microwave response, specifically by measuring the transmission amplitude of an external microwave signal. Each qubit possesses dedicated control and readout lines. The tunability of their frequencies enables adjustments to the number $N$ of resonantly coupled qubits and the introduction of disorder in their excitation frequencies according to predetermined distributions. As $N$ increases, we confirm the anticipated $N^{1/2}$ scaling law for the energy gap (Rabi splitting) between bright modes near the cavity frequency. By incorporating controllable disorder and averaging the transmission amplitude across numerous realizations, we observe a decay in mesoscopic fluctuations that resembles convergence toward the thermodynamic limit. Furthermore, collective bright states persist despite disorder provided that the strength of individual qubit coupling to the cavity exceeds the disorder strength.

A promising strategy for addressing difficult long-horizon tasks involves deriving behavior priors, or skills, by fitting generative models to extensive offline datasets of demonstrations. However, these generative models often inherit biases from the source data, leading to ineffective and unusable skills when trained on imperfect demonstrations. To better align skill extraction with human intent, we introduce Skill Preferences (SkiP), an algorithm that learns a model based on human preferences to extract skills from offline data that align with human goals. Following the extraction of these human-preferred skills, SkiP leverages human feedback to solve downstream tasks using reinforcement learning. We demonstrate that SkiP enables a simulated kitchen robot to successfully complete complex multi-step manipulation tasks, significantly outperforming previous leading RL algorithms that rely on human preferences as well as top-tier skill extraction methods that do not incorporate human preferences.

The initial version of the proof format adopted by the SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed in various applications, and other solvers also produce proofs using this standard. To inform future enhancements, we seek community feedback. In this process, we examine the format's history, outline our pragmatic development strategy, and address potential issues that may emerge when other solvers utilize the format.

This paper examines the calibration of control-bounded analog-to-digital converters, showing that variations in the analog frontend can be mitigated by adjusting the digital estimation filter. Simulations conducted at both behavioral and transistor levels for a leapfrog analog frontend demonstrate that the proposed calibration technique effectively restores nominal performance. Furthermore, by focusing on digital-filter calibration, the study reformulates the design challenge for control-bounded converters, thereby illuminating the functions of sampling, target filter shape, and baseline conversion error.

Unsupervised learning techniques for monocular camera motion and 3D scene reconstruction have become increasingly popular, surpassing traditional methods that depend on epipolar geometry or non-linear optimization. Deep learning specifically addresses common challenges in monocular vision, including perceptual aliasing, low-textured regions, scale drift, and degenerate motions. Furthermore, unlike supervised approaches, unsupervised learning allows for the full utilization of video stream data without requiring depth or motion annotations. However, this work highlights that rotational motion poses a greater limitation to the accuracy of unsupervised pose networks than translational motion. To address this, we introduce RAUM-VO, a method leveraging model-free epipolar constraints for frame-to-frame motion estimation (F2F) to refine rotation during both training and online inference. This approach matches 2D keypoints across consecutive frames using pre-trained deep networks, Superpoint and Superglue, while training a separate network for depth and pose estimation via an unsupervised protocol. The predicted rotation is then corrected using F2F-derived motion estimates, initialized by the pose network's output. Ultimately, RAUM-VO demonstrates significant accuracy gains over other unsupervised pose networks on the KITTI dataset, reduces the complexity associated with hybrid or traditional methods, and achieves performance comparable to the state-of-the-art.

We introduce a low-energy continuum framework for phonons in twisted moir\'e bilayers utilizing a configuration-space method. By deriving interatomic force constants from density functional theory (DFT) calculations on untwisted bilayers with diverse in-plane shifts, we enable efficient computation of phonon characteristics for arbitrary small twist angles without sacrificing DFT accuracy. Using this model, we analyze the evolution of low-energy phonon modes—specifically interlayer shearing and layer-breathing modes—as a function of twist angle. We observe that decreasing the twist angle leads to a reordering of low-energy mode frequencies and causes the atomic displacement fields of phonon eigenmodes to lose translational symmetry, instead exhibiting periodicity on the moir\'e length scale. Finally, we validate our approach by computing phonon properties for three distinct systems: bilayer graphene, bilayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS$_2$), and the heterobilayer molybdenum diselenide-tungsten diselenide (MoSe$_2$-WSe$_2$).

While Differential Privacy (DP) establishes tight upper limits on optimal adversaries, these adversaries are seldom found in real-world scenarios. Adopting a hypothesis testing or membership inference perspective, we analyze the Gaussian mechanism by replacing the standard Neyman-Pearson-Optimal (NPO) adversary with a Generalized Likelihood Ratio Test (GLRT) adversary. This slight relaxation yields enhanced privacy guarantees, articulated through the frameworks of Gaussian DP and $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, complete with findings on composition and sub-sampling. Our numerical evaluation confirms that these results align closely with theoretical upper bounds.

While the parity of reflection amplitude under mirror operations is known to be either even or odd, all previously observed cases within the one-mode energy regime exhibited even parity. This paper presents a counterexample featuring odd parity in Andreev reflection (AR) within a three-terminal graphene-superconductor hybrid system. Specifically, we demonstrate that Andreev retroreflection (ARR) retains even parity, whereas specular Andreev reflection (SAR) displays odd parity. This phenomenon arises from graphene's unique band structure topology and the fact that SAR involves two energy bands with distinct parity symmetries. Consequently, due to the odd parity of SAR, the probability of SAR in a four-terminal system containing two superconducting leads (and thus two reflection interfaces) can vanish, even in asymmetric configurations, as a result of quantum interference between the two AR processes.

This study evaluates the viability of integrating an intelligent reflective surface (IRS) into a cell-free wireless communication framework. The received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for this IRS-empowered configuration is maximized by tuning the phase shifts of the passive reflecting elements. Subsequently, precise approximations for the probability density function and cumulative distribution function of this optimized SNR are established under Rayleigh fading conditions. To assess the system's performance, closed-form tight bounds and approximations for the achievable data rate and outage probability are derived. The model incorporates the effects of discrete phase shifts, and the resulting performance degradation due to phase-shift quantization errors is analyzed through an upper bound on the achievable rate. Monte-Carlo simulations are employed to verify the statistical characterization of the optimal SNR, while the analytical results are utilized to examine the performance improvements offered by the proposed system. The findings demonstrate that IRS-assisted communications significantly enhance the efficacy of cell-free wireless architectures.

Scalability of quantum dot spin qubit architectures necessitates long-distance quantum information transfer, which can be achieved by shuttling electrons between two quantum registers. This process relies on adiabatically adjusting interdot energy detunings to control electron movement through a chain of tunnel-coupled dots, yet deterministic transfer is compromised by coupling to thermal reservoirs, including electric field fluctuations and lattice vibrations. The study theoretically examines how electron-phonon scattering and interactions with $1/f$ and Johnson charge noise (affecting both detuning and tunnel coupling) influence electron transfer. In silicon quantum dots, electron-phonon scattering is negligible; instead, a competition between charge noise and the Landau-Zener effect dictates an optimal detuning sweep rate that minimizes the probability of electron loss. Conversely, in gallium arsenide (GaAs) quantum dots, strong phonon coupling causes phonon-assisted transfer to dominate over charge noise effects. Here, the probability of electron loss varies monotonically with the sweep rate, and sufficiently slow sweeps can yield much lower loss probabilities than in silicon. However, when accounting for spin coherence preservation constraints on transfer time, the minimal residual error probabilities for both GaAs and silicon double quantum dots are comparable. Achieving error rates below $10^{-3}$ requires temperatures of 100 mK or lower and tunnel couplings exceeding 20 $\mu$eV.

We compute the hydrodynamic force acting on a small, unsteady squirmer moving with time-varying velocity through a stationary fluid, incorporating both convective and unsteady fluid-inertia effects within a perturbation framework. This study extends the findings of Lovalenti and Brady (1993) from passive to active spherical particles. We observe that convective inertia modifies the history component of the hydrodynamic force, consistent with its effect on passive particles. Furthermore, we analyze how the hydrodynamic force varies with the swimming gait of the unsteady squirmer. Because swimming disrupts spherical symmetry, the force cannot be fully derived from the outer solution of the asymptotic-matching problem as it is for passive spheres; instead, additional contributions arise from the inhomogeneous solution of the inner problem. Additionally, we calculate the disturbance flow to illustrate convective and unsteady fluid-inertia effects during a sudden start of center-of-mass motion and during periodic swimming. Finally, we examine the implications of these results for small motile organisms in marine settings.

The discovery, made approximately three decades ago in Leiden, that optical vortex beams possess orbital angular momentum (OAM) has catalyzed a rapidly growing field of research and applications. This paper begins with a brief personal narrative on the origin of these concepts before detailing recent developments involving the interaction of transverse orbital and spin angular momentum (SAM) within tightly focused laser beams, which yields novel phenomena. Specifically, the deflection of a focused beam by an atom at the focal point mirrors the Magnus effect observed in aerodynamics. Conservation of momentum requires a corresponding transverse force on the atom relative to the optical axis. Consequently, an atom confined in an optical tweezer becomes trapped at a slight distance of up to $\lambda/2\pi$ from the axis, a position determined by the atom's spin state and the orientation of the magnetic field. This mechanism offers fresh pathways for controlling atomic motion in optical tweezers and holds promise for applications in quantum gates and interferometry.

We present the rank similarity filter (RSF), a new, computationally efficient artificial neural network capable of transforming and classifying high-dimensional, nonlinearly separable datasets. RSF weights are determined by the rank orders of features within data points, or alternatively by "confusion" adjusted ranks derived from feature distributions. A filter's activation strength reflects its similarity to other dataset points, a metric akin to cosine similarity. Activating multiple RSFs projects samples into a new nonlinear space conducive to linear classification, known as the rank similarity transform (RST). We further developed the nonlinear rank similarity classifier (RSC) for fast, accurate multiclass tasks and the nonlinear rank similarity probabilistic classifier (RSPC) for multilabel scenarios. Evaluations across various datasets show that RSC competes well with existing methods while offering superior computational efficiency. Open-source Python implementations of RST, RSC, and RSPC are available via the scikit-learn framework for easy access. Future developments aim to deploy the algorithm on specialized parallel hardware, such as GPUs and neuromorphic chips for Spiking Neural Networks, to further enhance performance. Consequently, RSF emerges as a promising solution for efficiently analyzing nonlinearly separable data.

Machine learning has become a standard practice in chemistry, yet its effectiveness is often constrained by data scarcity. Transfer learning offers a solution to this limitation by leveraging models trained on abundant data that capture general structural features of chemical compounds; these features can then be applied to datasets with limited samples to significantly enhance new model performance. This study implements such a transfer learning approach using graph convolutional neural networks for small organic molecules. The results demonstrate a marked improvement in predicting target properties when data is scarce, while also analyzing how dataset composition influences model quality and defining the applicability domain of the developed models.

Recently, there has been growing interest in representing data with hierarchical structures within hyperbolic space. Because of its constant negative curvature, hyperbolic space naturally mimics tree metrics, allowing hyperbolic embeddings to outperform traditional Euclidean models. However, many real-world hierarchically structured datasets, such as taxonomies and multitree networks, possess varying local structures and are not strictly trees, meaning they do not universally align with the constant curvature of hyperbolic space. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the complex hyperbolic space, which features variable negative curvature, for representation learning. Specifically, we propose learning embeddings for hierarchically structured data using the unit ball model of the complex hyperbolic space. These embeddings, based on the unit ball model, offer enhanced representational capacity to capture diverse hierarchical structures. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing hyperbolic embedding models. Furthermore, we examine the efficacy of complex hyperbolic geometry on multitree and 1-N structures.
We derive a sufficient condition under which a Fano threefold possessing terminal singularities admits a conic bundle structure.

This paper examines the thermodynamics of a system of collinear black holes undergoing acceleration. We establish a generalized First Law that accounts for changes in the tensions of strings used to link and accelerate these black holes. We explore the consequences of this law in several instructive scenarios, including the C-metric, and connect our results to existing thermodynamic descriptions of slowly accelerating black holes in anti-de Sitter spacetime. Our analysis confirms the robustness of the concept of thermodynamic length and derives a Christoudoulou-Ruffini formula for the C-metric.

Deployments of WiFi-based indoor localization in large public venues remain rare because most advanced solutions necessitate modifications to either client devices or the infrastructure, rendering them impractical due to costs and low adoption rates. The majority of these venues rely on commercial controller-managed WLAN systems (such as those from Aruba or Cisco), which prohibit such changes. Consequently, we have observed a highly heterogeneous mix of devices with very low rates of client-side app usage. This paper details our experience deploying a scalable location system tailored for these constrained environments. We demonstrate that server-side localization is non-trivial, highlighting two unique challenges: Cardinality Mismatch and High Client Scan Latency. The "Mismatch" issue creates a significant discrepancy between the access points (APs) reporting a client during offline and online phases, while the "Latency" issue results in few APs reporting data for any given client. To substantiate the scope and impact of these problems, we gathered three weeks of detailed ground truth data (approximately 200 landmarks) from a WiFi setup operational for over four years. Our analysis of real-world client devices indicates a current trend toward reduced scanning, which negatively affects localization accuracy. We examine the effects of minimal scanning and propose heuristics to mitigate accuracy loss despite fewer scans. Additionally, we summarize other challenges and pitfalls inherent in real-world deployments that hinder localization precision.

This study examines the statistical characteristics of an ensemble of disordered one-dimensional steric spin-chains (SSCs) with varying lengths. By employing a classical Hamiltonian of the 1D spin-glass type, we derive recurrent trigonometric equations for stationary points and establish the necessary conditions for constructing stable 1D SSCs. An analysis of the ideal spin-chain ensemble reveals latent connections between random angles and interaction constants within every triplet of nearest-neighbor spins. Analytical proof and numerical calculations demonstrate that the interaction constant follows L\'{e}vy's alpha-stable distribution law. Furthermore, the energy distribution across the ensemble is computed under various polarization conditions. Specifically, dimensional effects manifest as a set of local maxima in the energy distribution when the number of spin-chains $M$ is significantly less than $N_x^2$ (where $N_x$ represents the number of spins per chain). Conversely, when $M \sim N_x^2$, the energy distribution exhibits a single global maximum, and the ensemble satisfies Birkhoff's ergodic theorem. Finally, an effective algorithm for parallel simulation is developed, capable of calculating various statistical parameters of the 1D SSC ensemble.

This study examines the group inverse within unital rings concerning the products and differences of idempotents, thereby broadening certain findings from \cite{DENG} to more general frameworks. We demonstrate that the majority of the results in \cite{DENG} can be readily adapted to unital rings, although significant challenges arise when attempting to generalize statements involving complementary idempotents.

The Sum-of-Squares (SoS) hierarchy, a robust framework of semidefinite programs, delivers cutting-edge algorithmic guarantees across numerous problems. While SoS lower bounds in the average-case setting strongly suggest algorithmic hardness or information-computation gaps, they have historically been limited to "dense" input regimes involving independent Rademacher or Gaussian variables, leaving the "sparse" regime unexplored. This work marks the first advancement in this area by establishing robust SoS lower bounds for the Independent Set problem on sparse random graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that for an Erdos-Renyi random graph $G\sim G_{n,\frac{d}{n}}$ with average degree $d>\log^2 n$, a degree-$D_{SoS}$ SoS relaxation fails to disprove the existence of an independent set of size $k = \Omega\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}(\log n)(D_{SoS})^{c_0}} \right)$ with high probability (where $c_0$ is an absolute constant), despite the true maximum independent set size being $O\left(\frac{n\log d}{d}\right)$.

Our approach extends several techniques previously used for dense SoS lower bounds. Earlier results relied on the pseudo-calibration heuristic introduced by Barak et al. [FOCS 2016], which generates a candidate SoS solution indistinguishable from the input distribution via low-degree tests when using a planted distribution. However, in sparse settings, the natural planted distribution allows for low-degree distinguishers; we show how to adapt the pseudo-calibration heuristic to surmount this obstacle. Furthermore, addressing the significant technical challenge of matrix norm bounds in the sparse regime, we derive new norm bounds for graph matrices specific to this setting.

Machine learning models face membership inference attacks, where adversaries attempt to determine if specific data points were part of the training set. Current approaches typically rely exclusively on output information, such as losses, from the target model; however, when both member and non-member samples produce similarly low losses, these methods fail to distinguish between them. To overcome this constraint, we introduce \system, a novel attack strategy that leverages membership signals from the entire training process of the target model to enhance performance. Designed for common black-box environments, our method utilizes knowledge distillation to capture membership information via a \emph{distilled loss trajectory}—representing losses from intermediate models across various distillation epochs—combined with the loss from the target model itself. Experiments across diverse datasets and architectures demonstrate significant improvements in attack metrics. For instance, on the CINIC-10 dataset, our approach achieves at least a 6$\times$ higher true-positive rate at a 0.1\% false-positive rate compared to existing techniques. Additional analyses confirm the method's robustness even in stricter scenarios.

Although recently introduced to the medical field, checklists have gained significant traction in daily clinical practice because of their high effectiveness and interpretability. Typically crafted by expert clinicians through the manual collection and analysis of existing evidence, these tools are now facing challenges due to the exponential growth of medical data, necessitating a shift toward partially automated design. While recent studies have begun learning predictive checklists from categorical data, this work proposes extending that methodology to derive checklists from continuous medical data using mixed-integer programming. We demonstrate that this approach surpasses various explainable machine learning baselines when predicting sepsis from intensive care clinical trajectories.

Surface phonon polaritons on 6H-SiC offer significant optical field enhancement, thereby amplifying light-matter interactions. This study experimentally demonstrates an increase in mid-infrared second-harmonic generation (SHG) utilizing grating-coupled surface phonon polaritons. By varying the excitation beam's incidence angle, we mapped SHG intensity along the polariton dispersion curve. Our results reveal hybridization between propagating surface phonon polaritons and localized plasmon resonances within the gold grating, indicated by shifts in the polariton dispersion dependent on the substrate-to-grating area ratio. We outline strategies for engineering this plasmon-phonon polariton coupling. However, compared to prism-coupling and nanostructures, the overall yield of polariton-enhanced SHG in this configuration is relatively low, and we analyze potential reasons for this outcome.

We introduce a conjecture regarding the reduced Hilbert series of the coordinate ring for a simple polyomino, expressed through specific configurations of non-attacking rooks on the polyomino. Employing a computational method, we verify that this conjecture is valid for all simple polyominoes with a rank of 11 or less. Furthermore, we demonstrate the conjecture's validity for parallelogram polyominoes by analyzing them as simple planar distributive lattices. Finally, we provide a combinatorial interpretation of the Gorenstein property within the class of parallelogram polyominoes.

This paper examines the optimal control of a weighted mean-field system, characterized by coefficients that depend on the state process, its weighted measure, and the control variable. Utilizing variational methods, we derive a stochastic maximum principle. As an application, we analyze the optimal premium strategy for an insurance company within the context of asset-liability management.

Two-tint Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR) analysis of FeRh during its first-order antiferromagnetic (AF) to ferromagnetic (FM) transition reveals that the transient reflectance, $\Delta$R(t)/R, is highly sensitive to the sample's magnetic ordering. At a probe wavelength of roughly 783 nm, the AF phase demonstrates a significant negative response, whereas the FM phase shows a positive one. This magnetic phase sensitivity enables the investigation of transient responses in both pure AF and FM states, as well as the mixed phase. Notably, the AF phase displays a robust transient signal absent in the FM phase. Linear system modeling successfully characterized the behavior of the system across each phase. Furthermore, electron thermalization in the AF phase occurs on a timescale at least double that of the FM phase. These findings confirm that two-tint TDTR is an effective method for probing the transient properties of the AF, FM, and mixed phases of FeRh.

We construct hairy static black holes within higher-dimensional Einstein-Skyrme theories featuring a non-zero scalar potential and a non-positive cosmological constant, where the scalar multiplets adhere to the $O(d+1)$ model constraint with $d$ representing the spatial dimension ($d \ge 3$). The study examines physical characteristics of these solutions near the boundaries, specifically at the event horizon and in the asymptotic region. Furthermore, we demonstrate the global existence of these black hole solutions, which may possess finite energy under a non-positive cosmological constant. Finally, employing a perturbative approach for linear dynamical stability analysis, we establish the presence of both stable and unstable solutions within this framework.

Given the prevalence of downlink traffic in Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), numerous prior studies have focused on improving transmission from Access Points (APs) to Stations (STAs). The downlink Multi-User Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MU-MIMO) technology, enabled by the IEEE 802.11ac standard, is a pivotal advancement driving WLANs toward Gigabit speeds. However, the rising popularity of cloud uploading, Peer-to-Peer (P2P), and telepresence applications has made increased uplink capacity essential. This paper introduces Uni-MUMAC, a unified MAC protocol designed to boost IEEE 802.11ac WLAN performance by leveraging multi-user spatial multiplexing. Specifically, the downlink utilizes an IEEE 802.11ac-compliant MU-MIMO scheme allowing the AP to transmit frames simultaneously to multiple STAs, while the uplink extends traditional single-round contention to a two-round process that coordinates simultaneous frame transmission from multiple STAs to the AP. A new parameter, the 2nd-round Contention Window (CW2nd), is introduced to make the duration of the second contention round adaptive based on traffic conditions. Uni-MUMAC is assessed via simulations under saturated and non-saturated conditions with mixed uplink and downlink traffic, supported by an analytical saturation model that validates the simulation data. When key parameters like CW2nd are optimized, Uni-MUMAC is compared against a leading multi-user transmission scheme from existing literature. The findings demonstrate that Uni-MUMAC excels in downlink-dominant environments while effectively balancing throughput for both uplink and downlink in scenarios demanding higher uplink bandwidth.

Extending H. Tran's research on Loewner hulls driven by complex-valued functions—which demonstrated the presence of a phase transition—we investigate whether this transition aligns with that observed in real-driven hulls. This inquiry is addressed through an in-depth analysis of hulls generated by the driving functions $c\sqrt{1-t}$ and $c\sqrt{\tau + t}$, where $c \in \mathbb{C}$ and $\tau \geq 0$. Furthermore, this specific family of functions yields instances of novel geometric behaviors achievable by complex-driven hulls but forbidden in the real-driven case.

Radial basis functions (RBFs) are commonly employed when discretization schemes necessitate inhomogeneous node distributions. Although originally intended for interpolating functions on random node sets, they have proven effective in solving various differential equations. However, there is a distinct difference between the weights used in the linear superposition of basis functions to interpolate a solution and the solution's actual values. These weights essentially combine the solution values with the geometric locations of the discretization nodes. In this study, we utilize nodal radial basis functions, defined as interpolants of the impulse function at every node within the domain. This transformation enables the solution of linear hyperbolic partial differential equations through series expansion, avoiding the explicit calculation of a matrix inverse. Consequently, this approach acts as an implicit solver that relies solely on vector-matrix multiplications.
