By eliminating the need for matrix inversion or matrix-matrix products, the method achieves superior numerical stability and reduces error by at least two orders of magnitude compared to direct RBF solvers. Additionally, boundary conditions are incorporated directly into the solver without additional computational cost. The resulting method is inherently conservative, maintaining virtually constant error levels throughout the computation.

Open-domain code generation presents significant challenges due to the frequent evolution and expansion of functions and classes within programming communities. This paper addresses the difficulty of generating code for unknown libraries without additional training by proposing a framework that allows models to consult relevant API documentation, mimicking how human programmers operate. As an initial step, we developed a model capable of extracting pertinent code signatures from API documentation based on natural language intent and utilizing primitives from these signatures. To assess our framework and code generation for unknown libraries, we expanded an existing open-domain dataset and re-partitioned it so that the evaluation set exclusively contains examples involving libraries absent from the training data. Experimental results on this new split demonstrate that standard encoder-decoder baselines fail to generate code using primitives from unknown libraries as anticipated. Conversely, our model surpasses baseline performance on this split and successfully generates unknown primitives when the extracted code signatures are accurate.

This paper addresses user association, defined as determining the optimal mapping of user equipment to base stations to meet specific network performance goals. We concentrate on the transferability of these association policies. Conventional, non-trivial association methods are typically tied to specific scenarios or deployments, necessitating policy re-design or re-learning whenever user count or location shifts. Conversely, transferability enables the application of a single policy, originally developed for a particular scenario, to different user deployments without significant re-learning or re-design, thereby substantially lowering computational and management overhead. To realize this transferability, we formulate user association as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem. Subsequently, utilizing a neural attention mechanism specifically designed for this context, we introduce a novel distributed policy network architecture. This architecture supports transferability across users with zero-shot generalization capabilities, meaning it operates without additional training. Numerical evaluations demonstrate the solution's efficacy regarding total network communication rates, surpassing centralized benchmarks even when the user count doubles compared to the initial training conditions.

This study explores the implementation of a space mission utilizing nanosatellites propelled by an external laser directed at an optimized lightsail, offering a promising method to deploy spacecraft swarms throughout the Solar System. When equipped with appropriate sensors, these laser-driven nanosatellites can facilitate heliospheric exploration and planetary observation, or support network establishment in specific orbital configurations. By adjusting the area-to-mass ratio and laser power, it becomes possible to place nanosatellites into various hyperbolic trajectories relative to Earth, enabling controlled, rapid travel to target destinations. The research envisions a mission featuring approximately 1 kg nanosatellites, detailing all on-board subsystems while adhering to strict power and mass constraints. Significant focus is given to the telecommunication subsystem, ensuring it meets all necessary functional requirements. The lightsail fabrication utilizes thin-film technology, with thermal stability during the thrust phase verified. Additionally, the mechanical stability of the lightsail is addressed, highlighting the critical influence of the distance between the sail structure and the payload. Finally, potential applications of this technology, including heliospheric environment mapping, are discussed.

Surgical Site Infection (SSI) represents a key national priority within healthcare research, prompting significant efforts to enhance risk prediction models. While most current models rely on static risk factors like comorbidities and operative details, this study explores the potential of dynamic wound data for SSI forecasting. With the rise of mobile health (mHealth) tools capable of continuously monitoring patients and capturing evolving clinical and wound-related variables, there is a need to better leverage this dynamic information. To address the limitations of existing models in utilizing such data, we propose a solution that integrates multiple machine learning algorithms to handle the analytical complexities of spatial-temporal data. Our approach exploits the low-rank characteristics of this data through a bilinear formulation, further improving accuracy with automatic missing data imputation using matrix completion techniques. We developed efficient optimization algorithms to execute these models and validated our new predictive framework on a real-world SSI dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to various state-of-the-art methods.

The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aims to investigate the internal structures of nucleons and nuclei, as well as matter formation processes, by conducting high-luminosity, high-energy collisions between electrons and protons ($e+p$) or nuclei ($e+A$). Precise measurements of heavy flavor hadrons and jets at the EIC are critical for determining parton distribution functions in nucleons and nuclei, as well as understanding heavy quark hadronization in poorly constrained kinematic regions. To achieve this, a Forward Silicon Tracker (FST) with high granularity and minimal material budget is being designed to enable precise forward heavy flavor measurements, offering enhanced sensitivity to these extreme kinematic conditions. Currently under development for the EIC, the FST is evaluating two advanced silicon technologies: the Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (DMAPS) and the AC-coupled Low Gain Avalanche Diode (AC-LGAD), both of which offer superior spatial and timing resolution. This presentation will outline progress and results regarding the FST's conceptual design and ongoing R&D for DMAPS and LGAD detectors, while also discussing the path toward an integrated EIC detector system.

Interactions between isolated atoms and molecular clusters (dimers or trimers) in cold quantum gases subjected to electromagnetic fields present a significant area of study. In this work, we utilize microwave photoassociation within a degenerate $^{87}$Rb gas to generate weakly-bound dimers in their electronic ground state. By analyzing the density-induced shift of the photoassociation resonance, we quantify the atom-dimer scattering length for the two lowest-lying states of the molecular potential. Furthermore, we map out the full energy spectrum of a specific hyperfine manifold within the least-bound state, achieving accurate results using a straightforward theoretical model.

Amid the serene corners of cs.CV, cs.LG, and stat.ML, a vast array of novel learning architectures is arising from a foundational mix of mathematics-based, unsupervised systems. Currently, there is scant analysis regarding the origins of these self-supervised models or the underlying principles driving their ongoing diversification. Following a phase of rigorous, objective examination—during which authors humorously assigned themselves distinct Galapagos islands as virtual backgrounds—we are now convinced that each of these learning systems is a direct descendant of older, largely extinct species. Our contributions are fivefold: (1) We compile and catalog row-major arrays of machine learning specimens, each displaying heritable discriminative traits; (2) We describe a mutation mechanism where subtle genotype alterations result in dramatic phenotypic shifts, evidenced by "birdsong" (tweets) and vestigial features (press releases); (3) We introduce a unifying theory of self-supervised machine evolution, benchmarking it against other unifying theories to establish a new state of the art; (4) We examine the significance of digital biodiversity, contextualized by the optimistic spirit of the Paris Agreement.

Designing numerical approximations for the Cahn-Hilliard model that uphold the maximum principle is a difficult task, particularly when additional transport terms are involved. This study introduces a novel upwind Discontinuous Galerkin scheme tailored for the convective Cahn-Hilliard model with degenerate mobility, ensuring both the preservation of the maximum principle and the suppression of non-physical spurious oscillations. We provide numerical experiments that align with these theoretical findings and conduct comparative analyses against other existing schemes found in the literature.

Although human evaluation remains the most dependable method for assessing speech generation systems, it is typically expensive and labor-intensive. Previous research on automatic speech quality assessment attempts to solve this by using machine learning models to predict human scores; however, these approaches depend on supervised learning, leading to high annotation expenses and issues with domain shift. We introduce SpeechLMScore, an unsupervised metric that evaluates generated speech by leveraging a speech-language model. This metric calculates the average log-probability of a speech signal by converting it into discrete tokens and measuring the likelihood of generating the resulting token sequence. Consequently, SpeechLMScore eliminates the need for human annotation and offers a highly scalable framework. Experimental results indicate that the proposed metric exhibits a strong correlation with human evaluation scores across various speech generation tasks, including voice conversion, text-to-speech, and speech enhancement.

Recent advances in self-supervised contrastive learning have significantly leveraged Siamese architectures designed to minimize distances between positive pairs. Achieving high performance in Siamese representation learning critically depends on constructing effective contrastive pairs. While previous approaches typically rely on random sampling to create diverse crops from the same image, this strategy often neglects semantic information, potentially degrading view quality. To address this, we introduce ContrastiveCrop, a method that generates superior crops for Siamese representation learning. First, we propose a fully unsupervised, semantic-aware object localization strategy during training, which guides the generation of contrastive views to avoid common false positives, such as distinguishing objects from backgrounds. Furthermore, our empirical findings indicate that views with highly similar appearances offer little benefit to Siamese model training; consequently, we implement center-suppressed sampling to increase the variance of the crops. Notably, our approach carefully optimizes positive pairs for contrastive learning with minimal additional training overhead. As a plug-and-play, framework-agnostic module, ContrastiveCrop consistently boosts the classification accuracy of SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, and SimSiam by 0.4% to 2.0% across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet, and STL-10. Additionally, superior performance is observed in downstream detection and segmentation tasks when models are pre-trained on ImageNet-1K.

Contemporary A/B testing faces significant challenges due to its expansive scale across multiple dimensions, necessitating flexible sequential testing protocols. Current best practices typically summarize observed data streams into always-valid p-values before applying standard multiple testing thresholds. In contrast, we introduce AMSET (adaptive multistage empirical Bayes test), a novel approach that integrates historical data to enhance efficiency without compromising marginal false discovery rate (mFDR) control against peeking. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that AMSET's fully data-driven estimation maintains robust performance across diverse simulation scenarios and real-world applications within a large-scale mobile app social network company.

Utilizing the spectral lag catalog of 46 short gamma-ray bursts from Xiao et al. (2022), we conducted an independent investigation into Lorentz Invariance violation (LIV) by analyzing fixed energy intervals in the source frame. We modeled intrinsic astrophysical spectral lags using a power-law function of energy and derived the universe's expansion history via a non-parametric approach employing cosmic chronometers. Through Bayesian model comparison, we assessed whether the observed lags provide evidence for LIV beyond purely astrophysical effects. Our analysis yielded no evidence for LIV; consequently, we established 95% confidence level lower limits for the LIV energy scale at $4 \times 10^{15}$ GeV for the linear model and $6.8 \times 10^{9}$ GeV for the quadratic model.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a leading technique for image representation, allowing models to learn rich features from vast amounts of unlabeled data without relying on labels. This pre-trained encoder can subsequently be used to train downstream classifiers with minimal labeled data. While SSL has demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, its security vulnerabilities, particularly regarding Trojan attacks within SSL encoders, remain underexplored. This paper introduces ESTAS, a novel Trojan Attack method designed to achieve effective and stable attacks on SSL encoders using only a single target unlabeled sample. ESTAS employs consistent trigger poisoning and cascade optimization to enhance attack efficacy and model accuracy while avoiding the costly extraction of target-class data from large, disordered unlabeled datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets confirm that ESTAS achieves a stable attack success rate (ASR) exceeding 99% with just one target-class sample. Compared to previous approaches, ESTAS improves the average ASR by over 30% and increases model accuracy by more than 8.3%.

We offer a unified explanation for the experimentally observed minimal direct current conductivity in weakly disordered graphene. First, utilizing linear response theory, we demonstrate that inherent disorder inevitably introduces momentum-dependent corrections to the electron self-energy, naturally resulting in a conductivity that varies between samples. By examining long-ranged Gaussian and Coulomb potentials as cases, we derive the momentum-dependent self-energy within the Born approximation and confirm these findings through numerical simulations employing the large-scale Lanczos algorithm. We explicitly analyze how the self-energy depends on the potential's intensity, concentration, and range. Consequently, our findings provide a plausible rationale for the sample-specific minimal conductivity detected in graphene.

Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is frequently employed for path planning in both aerial and ground vehicles; however, the requirement for linear objectives and constraints in such formulations restricts the precision of vehicle state tracking, particularly regarding battery state of charge (SOC). Since accurate SOC estimation relies on solving nonlinear differential equations, these cannot be directly integrated into MILP-based planning frameworks. This limitation poses a significant risk: a path deemed feasible by an inaccurate estimation model might actually deplete the battery to critical levels during execution. To address this, we introduce a straightforward linear battery model capable of predicting SOC changes based on power consumption and duration, while also accounting for voltage shifts caused by electrical loads and SOC variations. We evaluate this model through numerical and experimental tests against alternative approaches and assess its impact on solving times for resource-constrained shortest path problems across two distinct algorithms. Results demonstrate that the proposed linear model offers high estimation accuracy while remaining compatible with MILPs and Linear Programs, with negligible impact on computational efficiency.

Identifying the fundamental laws that dictate physical and chemical behaviors is essential for comprehending and mastering systems within science and engineering. We present Discovery of Dynamical Systems via Moving Horizon Optimization (DySMHO), a scalable machine learning framework designed to extract governing laws expressed as differential equations from extensive, noisy experimental datasets. DySMHO employs an innovative moving horizon dynamic optimization approach that iteratively learns these underlying equations from a comprehensive library of basis functions. This sequential methodology enables the use of statistical reasoning to filter out superfluous basis functions, thereby preventing overfitting and ensuring the recovery of accurate, parsimonious equation forms. Demonstrations using canonical nonlinear dynamical systems illustrate that DySMHO can precisely reconstruct governing laws, maintain robustness against significant measurement noise, and effectively address complex challenges such as multi-scale temporal dynamics.

We present a topological protection mechanism for highly-twisted two-dimensional Skyrmions in systems featuring Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) coupling. In these systems, a non-zero DM energy density, termed "twisting energy density," functions as a real-space band gap, thereby generating an N invariant for such highly twisted Skyrmions. By applying contact topology and extending the system into a fictitious third dimension, we demonstrate this result and further confirm the structural stability of these Skyrmions against arbitrary chirality-preserving distortions. These findings are applicable to all two-dimensional systems supporting Skyrmion excitations, including those with spin-orbit coupling that exhibit quantum Hall ferromagnetism.

We examine three adjustments to disk size estimates derived from accretion models at specific frequencies: color correction, disk truncation where the inner radius exceeds the innermost stable circular orbit, and disk winds. These modifications are integrated into the standard disk model and subsequently applied to microlensing-based size estimates. Our findings suggest that the combination of these three effects resolves the persistent discrepancy where microlensing-derived disk sizes are significantly larger than those predicted by the standard model alone. Notably, an increase in color correction with rising temperature can substantially expand the half-light radius, even if the correction factor remains near unity at the temperature corresponding to the observed frequency. Furthermore, our proposed methodology for calculating the half-light radius also addresses the longstanding inconsistency between disk size estimates based on accretion rates versus observed flux.

CERN developed and constructed the 750 MHz PIXE-RFQ, a one-meter-long accelerator that delivers 2 MeV protons for analyzing cultural heritage artifacts via proton-induced X-ray emission. This paper details low-power radio-frequency measurements and tuning efforts finalized in mid-2020. By employing a novel algorithm derived from direct response matrix measurements, field and frequency were simultaneously adjusted to the required precision within just two steps. The report also covers single-module measurements, quality factors, and coupling strength; in every instance, the RF measurements showed excellent agreement with design specifications.

This article summarizes recent experimental findings from heavy-ion collisions at ultra-relativistic energies. Electroweak probe measurements help constrain initial collision geometries and nuclear parton distribution functions. Data on soft particle production indicates that the abundance of light-flavor hadrons, ranging from pions to hypertriton and $^4$He, follows a universal temperature and participates in collective system motion; similar effects observed in small systems are expected to be further studied to reveal underlying mechanisms. Hard probe investigations, including those of heavy quarks and jets, highlight the significance of parton energy loss in these collisions. Differential analyses of J/$\psi$ mesons clarify their production mechanisms, such as regeneration, and provide evidence for deconfinement in full-energy Pb–Pb collisions at the LHC. The extensive datasets available at the LHC facilitate the study of rare probes like $\chi_{\rm c1}$(3872) and top–anti-top production. Additionally, measurements of antinuclei cross sections offer valuable input for dark matter searches.

The rapid global spread of the deadly COVID-19 pandemic has prompted the use of various artificial intelligence methods for detection, yet these often rely on sharing public data with cloud datacenters, raising significant privacy issues. To address this, this paper introduces FedGAN, a novel federated learning scheme designed to generate realistic COVID-19 images for privacy-preserving detection using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) within an edge cloud computing environment. Specifically, we first develop a GAN where discriminators and generators, built upon Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) at each edge-based medical facility, are alternately trained to replicate the distribution of real COVID-19 data. Subsequently, we propose a federated learning solution enabling local GANs to collaborate and exchange parameters with a cloud server, thereby enriching the global GAN model to produce realistic images without transferring actual patient data. To further bolster privacy in federated analytics, we incorporate differential privacy at each hospital. Additionally, we present a blockchain-based FedGAN framework that secures COVID-19 data analytics by decentralizing the federated learning process through a new mining solution optimized for low latency. Simulation results confirm that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art schemes in COVID-19 detection.

Building upon the study by Romain Ruzziconi and C\'eline Zwikel \cite{Ruzziconi:2020wrb}, this paper extends the analysis of conservation, integrability, and renormalization in Bondi gauge and General Relativity to Topological Massive Gravity (TMG). We construct the phase space and eliminate divergences within the symplectic structure using a holographic renormalization approach. Our results demonstrate that charge expressions are generally finite and conserved, and can be rendered integrable through a field-dependent redefinition of the asymptotic symmetry parameters.

This paper investigates the symbolic calculus of pseudo-differential operators linked to the weighted symbol class $M_{\rho, \Lambda}^m(\mathbb{ T}\times \mathbb{Z})$, where $\Lambda$ is an appropriate weight function on $\mathbb{Z}$. We derive explicit formulae for asymptotic sums, as well as for composition, adjoints, and transposes. Additionally, we construct a parametrix for $M$-elliptic pseudo-differential operators defined on $\mathbb{T}$. We also establish a version of Gohberg's lemma for operators within the weighted class $M_{\rho, \Lambda}^0(\mathbb{ T}\times \mathbb{Z})$, and utilize this result to provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the compactness of the corresponding operator on $L^2(\mathbb{T})$. Finally, we derive Gårding's and Sharp Gårding's inequalities for $M$-elliptic operators on $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{T}$, respectively, and demonstrate an application regarding strong solutions to the pseudo-differential equation $T_{\sigma} u=f$ in $L^{2}\left(\mathbb{T}\right)$.

The robustness principle, originally formulated by Jon Postel in early TCP implementations, advocates that communicating entities should be liberal in what they accept. While many Internet entities adhere to this principle, this study demonstrates that numerous popular web servers are particularly generous, waiting extended periods for the completion of incomplete requests. This leniency inadvertently exposes them to Slow Rate Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks. Although HTTP/2 has recently been identified as susceptible to these threats, the real-world impact of Slow HTTP/2 DoS attacks on actual web servers remains unexamined. Furthermore, no existing defense mechanism can detect Slow Rate DoS attacks against HTTP/2 in real-time. To address these gaps, we first evaluate the vulnerability of HTTP/2-supporting web servers to such attacks and subsequently propose a real-time detection scheme. Our results indicate that the proposed method effectively identifies attacks with high accuracy and minimal computational overhead.

Recent research indicates that instruction-tuning—fine-tuning large pre-trained language models on instruction-based tasks—enhances their ability to generalize in zero and few-shot scenarios to unseen tasks. Nevertheless, the performance trade-offs associated with various decisions within the instruction-tuning process remain poorly understood. These decisions encompass the scale and diversity of the benchmark, task sampling strategies, the inclusion or exclusion of demonstrations during fine-tuning, the use of specialized datasets for reasoning and dialogue, and the specific fine-tuning objectives. This paper investigates how these instructional decisions impact downstream performance as both model and benchmark sizes scale. To facilitate this, we introduce OPT-IML Bench, a comprehensive dataset comprising 2,000 NLP tasks from eight existing benchmarks, organized into task categories. We also develop an evaluation framework to assess three distinct types of generalization: to entirely held-out categories, to held-out tasks within seen categories, and to held-out instances within seen tasks. Using this framework, we analyze the impact of instruction-tuning decisions on OPT-30B and subsequently leverage these insights to train OPT-IML 30B and 175B, instruction-tuned variants of OPT. OPT-IML exhibits all three generalization capabilities at both scales across four diverse evaluation benchmarks—PromptSource, FLAN, Super-NaturalInstructions, and UnifiedSKG—significantly outperforming the original OPT and remaining highly competitive with models fine-tuned on individual benchmarks. We make both OPT-IML scales and the OPT-IML Bench evaluation framework publicly available.

High-Level Synthesis (HLS) has brought reconfigurable logic into the realm of software development, with recent tools showing great promise. However, the question remains whether HLS is the ultimate solution for FPGA acceleration and capable of enabling non-experts to program FPGAs effectively, particularly when handling challenging data structures and intricate control flows common in graph algorithms. This work examines the current adoption of HLS within the software community, with a specific focus on graph analysis, to generalize insights regarding \textit{FPGA-unfriendly} problems. We highlight existing deficiencies in HLS development workflows that impede adoption and outline our vision for future improvements, suggesting how higher-level tooling could address these challenges.

The Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) framework serves as the foundation of epidemiological modeling; however, its reliance on only two parameters limits its flexibility and hinders the replication of the volatile reproduction numbers seen in reality. By incorporating nonlinear stochastic transmission, we extend the classic SIR model into a stochastic version. We derive its exact solution and examine the conditions required for herd immunity. While this stochastic SIR model assumes an infinite population, finite populations introduce additional sampling uncertainty. Consequently, we propose a state-space framework to evaluate the relative magnitudes of observational and stochastic epidemiological uncertainties throughout an epidemic's progression. Furthermore, we highlight the lack of robustness regarding herd immunity when the SIR model is subjected to time discretization.

This work examines a variant of the Student-Project Allocation problem, denoted as SPA-ST, which incorporates lecturer preferences over students and permits ties in the preference lists of both students and lecturers. We analyze the notion of strong stability within this framework. Informally, a matching is considered strongly stable if no student and lecturer $l$ can form a mutually beneficial private arrangement outside the current matching; specifically, such an arrangement would leave neither party worse off while strictly improving the situation for at least one. We present the first polynomial-time algorithm capable of identifying a strongly stable matching or determining that none exists for any given SPA-ST instance. This algorithm operates with a time complexity of $O(m^2)$, where $m$ represents the aggregate length of the students' preference lists.

Over the past few years, electrifying Canada's Remote Communities (RCs) has gained considerable focus due to the high costs and environmental pollution associated with their existing diesel-based energy systems. Furthermore, the unique geographic constraints of these communities present specific challenges for electricity supply planning. Consequently, this paper introduces an optimization model designed for the long-term planning of RC microgrids that incorporate Renewable Energy Sources (RESs) and Energy Storage Systems (ESSs), aiming to minimize both expenses and emissions. The model evaluates lithium-ion batteries and hydrogen systems as viable ESS technologies. It is applied to assess the feasibility of integrating RESs and ESSs in the Sanikiluaq microgrid, located in Nunavut, Northern Canada. The findings indicate that a combination of wind, solar, and storage technologies can effectively meet electricity demand while substantially lowering costs and greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, the study offers insights into policies that promote sustainable and affordable microgrid solutions for remote communities.

We propose a framework for designing linear precoders in massive MIMO downlink systems affected by nonlinear power amplifiers (PAs). By analyzing the spatial properties of distortion, we reveal that standard linear precoding methods inadvertently direct nonlinear distortions toward users. Conversely, by explicitly accounting for PA nonlinearity, we can design linear precoders that mitigate, and in single-user cases, entirely eliminate the distortion directed at users, albeit with a trade-off in reduced array gain. To balance this, we introduce optimization algorithms that jointly consider array gain, distortion, multiuser interference, and receiver noise. Specifically, we derive a sum rate expression and develop an iterative algorithm to identify the precoding matrix that maximizes it. Additionally, utilizing a PA power consumption model, we propose an algorithm to minimize power usage while maintaining a target minimum sum rate. Numerical results indicate that these distortion-aware precoding strategies yield substantial gains in both spectral and energy efficiency compared to conventional linear precoders.

This research addresses a new challenge involving sensor scanning in 3D, uncertain settings using heterogeneous multi-robot systems. Our motivation is twofold: first, 3D environments are intricate, and heterogeneous multi-robot systems can intuitively enhance sensor scanning by fully leveraging sensors with varying capabilities. Second, in uncertain scenarios (such as rescue operations), time is critical. Since learning processes typically require time to train and adapt to new environments, we must discover an effective method for rapid exploration and adaptation. To achieve this, we propose a meta-learning approach designed to boost exploration and adaptation capabilities. Experimental results show that our method outperforms other approaches by approximately 15%-27% in success rate and 70%-75% in adaptation speed.

We present a formula for the $n^{th}$ term of the $k$-generalized Fibonacci-like sequence based on the $k$-nacci number. Using this newly derived formula, we demonstrate that the ratio of successive terms in the sequence converges to a root of the equation $x + x^{-k} = 2$. Furthermore, we extend these findings to $k$-generalized Horadam ($k$GH) and $k$-generalized Horadam-like ($k$GHL) numbers. To analyze the limit of the ratio of successive terms for $k$GH and $k$GHL sequences, we apply a lemma by Z. Wu and H. Zhang [8]. Finally, we note that a similar result can be established for the $k$-periodic $k$-nary Fibonacci sequence.

Fock and Goncharov defined a class of cluster algebras linked to the moduli of SL(k)-local systems on a marked surface, incorporating additional decorations at marked points. This work examines the family through algebraic and combinatorial lenses, with a specific focus on configurations arising when the surface contains punctures. In the case where k equals 2, these configurations correspond to the tagged arcs and tagged triangulations established by Fomin, Shapiro, and Thurston. For values of k greater than 2, the concept of arc tagging is superseded by a Weyl group action at punctures, as identified by Goncharov and Shen. We develop a higher-dimensional analogue of tagged triangulations using tensor diagrams, building upon prior research by Fomin and the second author, and we introduce skein-algebraic methods for computations within these cluster algebras. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of examples that exhibit finite mutation types.

The sinkless orientation problem is central to the foundations of distributed computing, serving to distinguish between the LOCAL and SLOCAL models of distributed graph algorithms. Specifically, the locality required for sinkless orientation is $\Omega(\log n)$ within the deterministic LOCAL model and $O(\log \log n)$ within the deterministic SLOCAL model. Although these findings were previously established, this work presents new, straightforward, and self-contained proofs for both results.

Recently, Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD) has garnered significant attention as a metric for distinguishing probability distributions. This study examines the properties of its associated Wasserstein gradient flow to approximate a target distribution $\pi$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, which is known only up to a normalization constant. This investigation yields a straightforward, deterministic, score-based sampling method called KSD Descent, which employs a set of particles to represent $\pi$. Notably, due to its tractable loss function, KSD Descent can utilize robust, parameter-free optimization techniques like L-BFGS, distinguishing it from other particle-based approaches such as Stein Variational Gradient Descent. We analyze the convergence characteristics of KSD Descent and confirm its practical utility, while also identifying failure modes where the algorithm may become trapped in spurious local minima.

We introduce a category-theoretic framework for retrodiction to demonstrate a time-reversal symmetry inherent in all quantum channels. This approach relies on retrodiction families and functors, constructs that are sufficiently broad to cover both classical and quantum theories while embodying the intuitive requirements of retrodiction. Within this framework, classical Bayesian inversion and various rotated and averaged Petz recovery maps qualify as retrodiction families. Nevertheless, averaged rotated Petz recovery maps—including the universal recovery map by Junge, Sutter, Renner, Wilde, and Winter—do not constitute retrodiction functors because they violate specific compositionality rules. Among the identified retrodiction families, only the original Petz recovery map successfully defines a retrodiction functor. Furthermore, these functors reveal an inferential time-reversal symmetry that aligns with standard quantum theory, appearing to contradict numerous no-go theorems regarding time-reversal symmetry for quantum channels. This discrepancy arises because previous studies restricted their definition of time-reversal symmetry to the category of quantum channels, whereas our definition encompasses both quantum states and channels, thereby highlighting the critical role of a prior in establishing such symmetry.

In 1939, H. Weyl introduced intrinsic volumes $V_i(M^n)$, also referred to as Lipschitz-Killing curvatures, for any closed smooth Riemannian manifold $M^n$. Consider a Riemannian submersion between compact smooth Riemannian manifolds $M \to B$, where $B$ is connected. For $\varepsilon > 0$, define a new metric on $M$ by scaling the original metric by $\varepsilon$ in vertical directions while leaving the orthogonal horizontal directions unchanged; denote the resulting manifold as $M_\varepsilon$. The principal finding states that $\lim_{\varepsilon\to +0} V_i(M_\varepsilon) = \chi(Z) V_i(B)$, where $\chi(Z)$ represents the Euler characteristic of a fiber within the submersion. This outcome aligns with broader open conjectures regarding the convergence of intrinsic volumes previously proposed by the author.
Inspired by the generalized Bloch conjecture, we propose a conjecture regarding the Chow groups of Pl\"ucker hypersurfaces within Grassmannians and establish weak forms of this conjecture.

This study addresses the coupled challenges of dynamically estimating algebraic variables (voltage and phase angle) alongside generator states (rotor angle and frequency) within nonlinear differential algebraic equation (NDAE) power network models subject to uncertainty. Conventionally, these tasks are separated due to the complexity of NDAE handling. In contrast, this paper presents the inaugural coupled methodology that simultaneously computes estimates for both algebraic and generator states. The proposed algorithm features four key attributes: (i) it is straightforward to implement and relies on established Lyapunov theory; (ii) it accounts for diverse uncertainty sources, including generator control inputs, loads, renewables, and process and measurement noise; (iii) it accommodates phasor measurement units installed at arbitrary buses; and (iv) it requires less computational effort than traditional decoupled approaches found in existing literature.

Hackathons and comparable time-constrained events have evolved into a worldwide phenomenon. Their widespread adoption across diverse fields and their utility for various objectives have spawned numerous distinct formats. Although many guidelines exist for organizing these events, most concentrate on formats tailored to specific purposes, domains, and participant types, making it challenging for novice organizers to design an event that suits their specific requirements. To bridge this gap, we have developed a planning kit centered on twelve critical decisions organizers must make, along with the underlying tradeoffs that influence those choices. The primary planning kit is accessible online, whereas this report serves as a downloadable, citable resource.

Let $A$ be an algebra over a field $F$ where the characteristic is not 2. If $A$ is generated as an algebra by its derived subalgebra $[[A,A],[A,A]]$, then for any skew-symmetric bilinear map $\Phi: A \times A \to X$ (with $X$ being an arbitrary vector space over $F$), the condition $\Phi(x^2, x) = 0$ for all $x \in A$ implies that $\Phi(xy, z) + \Phi(zx, y) + \Phi(yz, x) = 0$ for all $x, y, z \in A$. This result addresses the problem of whether $A$ is zero Lie product determined and is also utilized to demonstrate that a Jordan homomorphism from $A$ onto a semiprime algebra $B$ decomposes into the sum of a homomorphism and an antihomomorphism.

Thomas-Whitehead (TW) gravity has recently been formulated as a projective gauge theory of gravity on a d-dimensional manifold. This framework incorporates reparameterization invariance into the gravitational action via the Thomas-Whitehead connection. Within this d-dimensional theory, projective invariance shares a profound connection with the Virasoro coadjoint elements found in string theory, as the connection component $\mathcal{D}_{ab}$ is directly linked to these algebraic elements. By utilizing projective Gauss-Bonnet terms in its action, TW gravity reduces to Einstein's General Relativity when $\mathcal{D}_{ab}$ approaches zero. This note presents the graded extension of TW gravity, termed Super TW Gravity, within the context of a DeWitt supermanifold. We derive the Lagrangian for Super TW Gravity, provide a comprehensive derivation of the classical field equations, and examine the graded extension of the projective connection. This analysis serves as a foundation for future insights into fully manifestly supersymmetric TW-Supergravity and its interplay with the Super-Virasoro algebra.

This resource consists primarily of pen-and-paper machine learning exercises covering topics such as linear algebra, optimization, both directed and undirected graphical models, the expressive capacity of these models, factor graphs and message passing, hidden Markov model inference, model-based learning (encompassing ICA and unnormalized models), sampling and Monte-Carlo integration, and variational inference.

Consider a graph $G=(V,E)$ and positive integers $t$ and $r$. A tower vertex $T$ with signal strength $t$ transmits a signal to a vertex $v$ defined by $sig(T,v)=max(t-dist(T,v),0)$, where $dist(T,v)$ represents the distance between $v$ and $T$. In 2015, Blessing, Insko, Johnson, and Mauretour introduced the concept of a \emph{$(t,r)$ broadcast dominating set}, or simply a \emph{$(t,r)$ broadcast}, on $G$ as a subset $\mathbb{T}\subseteq V$ where the aggregate signal received at every vertex $v \in V$ from the towers in $\mathbb{T}$ meets or exceeds $r$. The $(t,r)$ broadcast domination number of a finite graph $G$, denoted $\gamma_{t,r}(G)$, represents the minimum size of such a set.

Recent studies have aimed to establish bounds for $\gamma_{t,r}(G)$ on the $m \times n$ grid graph $G_{m,n}$. In 2014, Grez and Farina determined bounds for the $k$-distance domination number on grid graphs, which corresponds to $\gamma_{t,1}(G_{m,n})$. Subsequently, in 2015, Blessing and colleagues derived bounds for $\gamma_{2,2}(G_{m,n})$, $\gamma_{3,2}(G_{m,n})$, and $\gamma_{3,3}(G_{m,n})$. This paper advances that work by providing a tight upper bound for $\gamma_{t,2}(G_{m,n})$ for all $t>2$. Furthermore, we confirm the conjecture proposed by Blessing et al. that their bound for $\gamma_{3,2}(G_{m,n})$ is tight when $m$ and $n$ are sufficiently large.

Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) establishes a synergy between the demand for connectivity and the drive for enhanced productivity by utilizing communication networks to gather environmental data. Given that multiple existing sensory modalities already facilitate environmental perception, it is essential to investigate the specific benefits of ISAC relative to these approaches. Consequently, we present MaxRay, an ISAC framework designed to jointly simulate communication, sensing, and supplementary sensory inputs. Addressing the challenges inherent in building such networks, we define the necessary propagation characteristics for sensing and explain their application. To assess various sensing techniques, we evaluate four widely used metrics across different domains, analyzing their respective pros and cons. Our findings indicate that a prominence-based metric is well-suited to accommodate most algorithms. Furthermore, we underscore the necessity of clutter removal algorithms by applying two standard methods to detect targets within a typical industrial setting. Overall, the study demonstrates a versatile framework capable of automatically generating labeled datasets to explore a broad spectrum of tasks.

This work investigates rational solutions to the Abel equation $x'=A(t)x^3+B(t)x^2$ with coefficients $A, B$ belonging to $C[t]$. We establish that when $\deg(A)$ is even or $\deg(B) > (\deg(A)-1)/2$, the equation possesses at most two rational solutions. In all other scenarios, an upper bound for the count of rational solutions is derived. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if the number of rational solutions exceeds $(\deg(A)+1)/2$, the equation admits a Darboux first integral.

We identify the connected bipartite regular graphs possessing exactly four distinct adjacency eigenvalues that result in periodic Grover walks, demonstrating that the only such graph is $C_6$. Furthermore, we establish that there are precisely three types of second-largest eigenvalues for bipartite regular periodic graphs with five distinct eigenvalues, and we utilize walk-regularity to list the feasible spectra for these graphs.

We explore a model featuring multiple doubly charged particles, initially proposed to naturally account for minute neutrino masses via a three-loop mechanism, as a potential explanation for the recent 750\,GeV diphoton excess observed by ATLAS and CMS at the CERN LHC. In this framework, the enhanced radiatively generated effective coupling between a new singlet scalar $S$ and diphotons, mediated by multiple charged particles within the loop, significantly boosts both the production rate of $S$ through photon fusion ($pp\to S+X$) and its decay width into diphotons ($\Gamma(S\to \gamma\gamma)$), all without relying on a tree-level production mechanism. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive analysis covering scenarios both with and without mixing between $S$ and the Standard Model Higgs doublet.

We introduce FinText, a cutting-edge financial word embedding derived from the Dow Jones Newswires Text News Feed Database. Integrating this embedding into a machine learning model significantly boosts volatility forecasting accuracy, particularly during volatility jump days, for 23 NASDAQ stocks spanning from July 27, 2007, to November 18, 2016. Furthermore, a straightforward ensemble approach that merges our word embedding with a separate model utilizing limit order book data achieves superior forecasting results for both standard and jump volatility periods. Lastly, we employ Integrated Gradients and SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) to enhance the explainability of our findings and ensure greater transparency in model comparisons.

Current monocular depth research primarily relies on unsupervised training using large datasets, driven by photometric consistency from warped images. However, these methods lack robustness and fail to generalize to difficult scenarios like nighttime or adverse weather, where photometric assumptions no longer hold. We introduce DeFeat-Net (Depth & Feature network), which simultaneously learns a cross-domain dense feature representation and a robust depth-estimation framework based on warped feature consistency. This feature representation is acquired unsupervisedly without requiring explicit ground-truth correspondences. Our results demonstrate that within a single domain, our method matches the state-of-the-art in both monocular depth estimation and supervised feature learning. Furthermore, by jointly learning features, depth, and motion, our approach successfully generalizes to challenging domains; specifically, DeFeat-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by achieving approximately a 10% reduction in error metrics on difficult sequences, such as nighttime driving.

This study examines parameter estimation in imbalanced datasets using nonuniform negative sampling. We first demonstrate that in imbalanced scenarios, information regarding unknown parameters relies almost exclusively on the limited set of positive instances, thereby validating the necessity of negative sampling. However, we show that subsampling negatives to match the frequency of positives leads to information loss. To preserve more data utility, we derive the asymptotic distribution of a general inverse probability weighted (IPW) estimator and determine the optimal sampling probability that minimizes its variance. Furthermore, to enhance estimation efficiency beyond the IPW approach, we introduce a likelihood-based estimator that corrects log odds for the sampled data; we prove that this method achieves the smallest asymptotic variance within a broad class of estimators and exhibits greater robustness to pilot model misspecification. Our approach is validated through simulations and a real-world click-through rate dataset comprising over 0.3 trillion instances collected over one month. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results confirm the method's effectiveness.

We demonstrate that short-range resonating-valence-bond (RVB) correlations and long-range order can simultaneously exist within the ground state (GS) of a frustrated spin system. This conclusion stems from a thorough examination of quantum magnetism in the structurally pristine single crystal Cu$_2$(OH)$_3$NO$_3$, which hosts the $s$ = 1/2 Heisenberg model on a spatially anisotropic triangular lattice. Fitting magnetization data collected up to 55 T reveals competing exchange interactions that produce an unusual GS wavefunction characterized by dominant short-range RVB correlations alongside weak long-range stripe order (with an ordered moment $M_0$ = $|\langle s_i^z\rangle|$ $\sim$ 0.02). At low temperatures, a first-order spin-flop transition occurs at approximately 1-3 T. As the magnetic field increases further, two additional field-induced quantum phase transitions are detected at roughly 14-19 T and 46-52 T. Simulations of the Heisenberg exchange model exhibit semi-quantitative agreement with the magnetic-field modulation of these unconventional phases and the lack of observable magnetic reflections in neutron diffraction, supporting the notion that the GS of Cu$_2$(OH)$_3$NO$_3$ approximates a quantum spin liquid. Consequently, our work identifies structurally disorder-free materials with spatially anisotropic exchange interactions as viable platforms for studying spin liquids.

Scientific research is experiencing a surge in raw data volume and variety, fueled by data-intensive computational techniques like machine learning. However, the dominance of proprietary and ill-fitting data formats slows down computations and complicates research reproducibility and cross-platform portability. To address these challenges, we introduce RawArray: a straightforward, rapid, and extensible format designed for storing multidimensional numeric arrays on disk.

The RawArray structure consists of a simple concatenation of a header and a data array. The header contains seven or more 64-bit unsigned integers, while the data portion can hold any content. Users may optionally append arbitrary metadata to the file, such as measurement specifics, color palettes, or geolocation information.

Our benchmarks demonstrate a 2 to 3 times speedup over HDF5 across various array sizes, with reading speeds for common deep learning datasets like MNIST and CIFAR10 improving by up to 20 times.

Using data from $pp$ collisions recorded by the LHCb detector with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$, time-dependent CP violation is analyzed in the $B^0\rightarrow J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$ decay for various resonant $\pi^+\pi^-$ final states. The most frequent mode, $J/\psi\rho^0(770)$, yields a measurement of the effective CP-violating angle $2\beta^{\rm eff}$ as $(41.7\pm 9.6_{-6.3}^{+2.8})^{\circ}$. This value helps constrain penguin amplitude contributions to CP violation in decays such as $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$. Under the assumptions of approximate SU(3) flavour symmetry and the neglect of higher-order diagrams, the shift in the CP-violating phase $\phi_s$ is restricted to the range [$-1.05^\circ$, +$1.18^\circ$] at a 95% confidence level, with potential adjustments arising from SU(3) symmetry breaking also examined.

The article "integer divisibility properties and related prime factors natural number representation concepts" extends definitions of natural number representation across the entire infinite hyperoperation hierarchy, encompassing operations from addition through multiplication, exponentiation, tetration, and beyond. This framework allows familiar concepts such as "prime factor," "multiplier," and "divider" to be consistently applied within each specific operation. Drawing an analogy to the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic based on multiplication, the article formulates an exponentiation-based theorem stating that any natural number $M$ can be uniquely expressed as a tower of exponentiations: $M=a_n\uparrow(a_{n-1}\uparrow (\ldots (a_2\uparrow a_1)\ldots ))$, where each $a_i\neq 1$ (for $i=1,\ldots,n$) acts as a primitive exponentiation component arranged in a unique sequence, termed "biprimes" in the text.

Bearing-based distributed formation control is appealing because it enables the realization of desired formations using vision-based measurements. Gradient-descent controllers utilizing bearing data offer several advantages, including global convergence, compatibility with various graph topologies and arbitrary-dimensional workspaces, and flexibility in cost function selection. However, in practical applications, these controllers often generate convoluted trajectories from initial states to final formation positions. This paper introduces a novel method to optimize gradient-descent-based bearing controllers for shorter paths. Our strategy involves parameterizing both the cost function and the controller, then solving a nonlinear optimization problem where the objective is to minimize the sum of agent trajectory lengths, subject to maintaining original equilibrium points and global convergence requirements. Simulations demonstrate that optimizing these parameters using a minimal set of training samples (1 to 7) can straighten trajectories by approximately 16% across numerous random initial conditions for bearing-only formations. Nevertheless, without range information, the formation's scale remains unfixed, potentially causing undesired compression during optimization. Incorporating range measurements resolves this issue and achieves an additional 66% reduction in trajectory length.

We show that two-time correlation functions, which extend the concept of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs), can produce "false-flags" of chaos by displaying random matrix theory predictions even within systems governed by classically regular dynamics. Specifically, we examine a system of bosons confined in a double-well potential and interrogated by a dispersively coupled quantum dot; this setup constitutes an integrable system whether viewed in isolation or as a whole. Although the system evolves continuously under its actual Hamiltonian, the $n$-fold two-time correlation function of the probe reveals an effective stroboscopic or Floquet dynamics. In this regime, the bosons behave as if alternately driven by two non-commuting Hamiltonians, mimicking the Trotterized time evolution seen in digital quantum simulations. While the classical limit of this effective dynamics can exhibit a nonzero Lyapunov exponent, and the effective level statistics and return probabilities display conventional chaotic signatures, this work underscores the need for cautious interpretation of OTOCs and their generalizations, consistent with recent studies.

This paper introduces Linkage Measurement Minimization (LMM), a variable grouping technique rooted in cooperative coevolution designed for large-scale multi-objective problems (LSMOPs). For the sub-problem optimization phase, we present a hybrid NSGA-II algorithm incorporating a Gaussian sampling operator centered on an estimated convergence point. In the variable grouping stage, building on prior work, we formulate the grouping task as a combinatorial optimization problem and design a linkage measurement function using linkage identification via nonlinearity checks on real-coded representations (LINC-R), extending this approach to LSMOPs. During optimization, we assume that superior solutions are more likely to exist near the Pareto Front (PF); consequently, we estimate a convergence point at each generation and apply Gaussian sampling around it. Solutions exhibiting favorable objective values are selected as elites to drive further optimization. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our variable grouping method outperforms several popular alternatives, while the hybrid NSGA-II shows significant potential for multi-objective optimization.

Graphs provide an intuitive framework for addressing Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) and Multiple Object Tracking and Segmentation (MOTS) within the tracking-by-detection paradigm. However, learning on this structured domain poses significant challenges due to the difficulty of designing compatible models. This work leverages the classical network flow formulation of MOT to construct a fully differentiable framework utilizing Message Passing Networks (MPNs). By functioning directly on graphs, our approach enables global reasoning across all detections and utilizes contextual information. Consequently, it simultaneously predicts optimal data association solutions and segmentation masks for every object, capitalizing on the interdependencies between these tasks. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on various public datasets for both tracking and segmentation. The source code can be accessed at github.com/ocetintas/MPNTrackSeg.

Under the $SP(2,R)$ symmetry, the Two-time (2T) model features a six-dimensional spacetime comprising two time dimensions and a dilaton field, which can serve as the inflaton in a warm inflation scenario with a potential scaling as $\sim\phi^4$. Based on this framework, we determine the parameter range for the Higgs-Dilaton potential, finding that the Higgs-Dilaton coupling constant ($\alpha$) must exceed $0.0053$, while the dilaton mass remains below $10^{-7}$ GeV. Consequently, the 2T-model implies that extra dimensions could also act as a source of inflation.

Achieving efficient photon-photon interactions is a fundamental requirement for quantum information processing. Because photons are bosons, these interactions typically require mediation through an atomic medium, where the interaction duration—and consequently the efficiency—is governed by the characteristics of the atom-photon coupling. Although electromagnetically induced transparency enables photonic quantum memory, it does not extend interaction times because it completely transfers the photonic state to an atomic state. In contrast, the stationary light pulse (SLP) effect traps the photonic state within an atomic medium at zero group velocity, thereby facilitating significantly longer interaction times. This study presents the first experimental realization of trapping a free-propagating single photon into a cold atomic ensemble using the quantum SLP (QSLP) mechanism. We demonstrate that the quantum properties of the single-photon state remain intact throughout the QSLP process. These findings establish a foundation for developing novel strategies for efficient photon-photon interactions, generating exotic photonic states, and conducting many-body simulations in photonic systems.

This paper details an ATLAS experiment search at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for diphoton resonances within a mass range of 10 to 70 GeV. The study utilizes $pp$ collision data with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$ collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV between 2015 and 2018. While prior LHC searches had investigated masses down to 65 GeV without detecting new particles, this analysis leverages the specific kinematics of closely spaced photon pairs to probe invariant masses as low as 10 GeV. This approach examines a previously inaccessible region at hadron colliders, overcoming the experimental difficulties associated with low-energy photon detection and background estimation. No significant excess was found, and the resulting limits establish the most stringent constraints to date on promptly decaying axion-like particles coupling to gluons and photons in the 10–70 GeV mass range.

This study presents an attention-driven fusion approach for outfit recommendation that integrates product image and description data to isolate critical, fine-grained features within item representations. By evaluating various attention mechanisms, we show that this fusion strategy enhances item comprehension, ultimately surpassing state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets.

The Theory of Functional Connections (TFC) serves as a functional interpolation framework built on the concept of constrained expressions, which define a family of functions satisfying specific linear constraints. These expressions allow constrained problems to be converted into unconstrained ones, offering benefits such as accelerated solution times, improved accuracy, and more robust convergence. This dissertation provides a comprehensive and self-contained exposition of TFC theory, progressing from simple univariate point constraints to general linear constraints in $n$-dimensions, supported by relevant theorems and illustrative examples to enhance reader comprehension. Additionally, the work details TFC's primary application to estimating solutions for differential equations and includes comparisons with other state-of-the-art algorithms to highlight the method's strengths and limitations. Finally, the dissertation applies these concepts to estimate solutions within the domain of flexible body dynamics.

This note demonstrates that specific dual canonical basis elements of $\mathbb{C}[SL_m]$ yield positive values when evaluated on $k$-positive matrices—defined as matrices with positive minors of size $k \times k$ or smaller. Building on Skandera's finding that all such basis elements can be expressed via Kazhdan-Lusztig immanants (introduced by Rhoades and Skandera), we concentrate on those indexed by 1324- and 2143-avoiding permutations. This work extends the authors' prior research on Kazhdan-Lusztig immanants by employing analogous methods, specifically Lewis Carroll's identity (the Desnanot-Jacobi identity).

This study presents optical imaging and low-resolution spectroscopic monitoring of the supernova (SN) 2017iro, which occurred in the nearby galaxy NGC 5480 at a distance of approximately 31 Mpc. The presence of the \ion{He}{1} 5876 \AA\ feature in the earliest spectrum (observed at -7 days) classified the event as a Type Ib supernova. Observations covered the period from -7 to +266 days relative to the $B$-band peak. SN 2017iro exhibited a peak absolute magnitude in the $V$-band of ($M_{V}$)\,=\,$-17.76\pm0.15$ mag and a bolometric luminosity of log$_{10}$\,L)\,=\,42.39\,$\pm$\, 0.09 erg s$^{-1}$, identifying it as a moderately luminous Type Ib SN. Its light curve evolution closely mirrors that of SN 2012au in the early phase (up to ~100 days) and SN 2009jf in the late phase (>150 days). Near the peak, line velocities for both \ion{Fe}{2} 5169 \AA\ and \ion{He}{1} 5876 \AA\ were approximately 9000 km s$^{-1}$. Nebular phase spectral analysis (~+209 days) revealed an oxygen mass of roughly 0.35 M$_{\odot}$. A low [\ion{O}{1}]/[\ion{Ca}{2}] flux ratio of ~1 suggests a progenitor with a zero-age main-sequence mass between ~13 and 15 M$_{\odot}$, likely within a binary system, akin to iPTF13bvn. Explosion parameters derived from various analytical models applied to the quasi-bolometric light curve indicate a synthesized $^{56}$Ni mass of ~0.05--0.10 M$_{\odot}$, an ejecta mass of ~1.4--4.3 M$_{\odot}$, and a kinetic energy of ~0.8--1.9 $\times$ 10$^{51}$ erg.

Given a dataset comprising input states, measurements, and probabilities, can measurement probabilities for a quantum circuit be efficiently predicted? While Caro and Datta (2020) examined PAC learning quantum circuits from an information-theoretic perspective, they left computational efficiency unresolved. Specifically, Clifford circuits were considered a promising candidate for efficient learning because their generated stabilizer states are known to be efficiently PAC learnable (Rocchetto 2018). In this work, we present a negative result demonstrating that properly learning CNOT circuits is intractable for classical learners unless $\textsf{RP} = \textsf{NP}$. Since CNOT circuits form a classical subset and analogue of Clifford circuits, this implies hardness for Clifford circuits as well. Furthermore, we establish that if $\textsf{RP} = \textsf{NP}$, efficient proper learning algorithms would exist for both CNOT and Clifford circuits. Similarly, an efficient proper quantum learner for these circuits exists if and only if $\textsf{NP} \subseteq \textsf{RQP}$.

Synchronous updates can hinder the efficiency of cross-device federated learning as the number of active clients grows. The \textit{FedBuff} algorithm (Nguyen et al., 2022) mitigates this issue by enabling asynchronous updates that tolerate staleness, thereby improving training scalability while maintaining privacy through secure aggregation. This paper revisits the \textit{FedBuff} algorithm for asynchronous federated learning, extending prior analysis by eliminating boundedness constraints on the gradient norm. It provides a theoretical examination of the algorithm's convergence rate under conditions of data heterogeneity, varying batch sizes, and communication delays.

K. Borsuk introduced the concepts of capacity and depth for compacta during the 1979 Topological Conference in Moscow. This paper calculates these values for compact surfaces, demonstrating that for any compact orientable surface of genus $g\geq 0$, both capacity and depth equal $g+2$. Furthermore, we establish that for a compact non-orientable surface of genus $g>0$, the capacity and depth are given by $[\frac{g}{2}]+2$.

This short review outlines recent advancements in the functional determinant approach (FDA), an exact numerical technique used to study heavy quantum impurities within Fermi gases subjected to radio-frequency pulses. Previously, FDA successfully analyzed the universal dynamical responses of heavy impurities in ultracold ideal Fermi gases across both time and frequency domains, facilitating the investigation of Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe (OC). In these systems, OC arises from numerous particle-hole excitations in the Fermi sea—a phenomenon that defies simple perturbation theory and results in the non-existence of quasiparticles known as polarons. More recently, two new applications of FDA have emerged. The first extends the method to strongly correlated BCS superfluid backgrounds; here, the superfluid gap suppresses multiple particle-hole excitations, thereby prohibiting Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe and allowing for the formation of genuine polarons. The second direction generalizes FDA to multiple radio-frequency pulse schemes, adapting established one-dimensional Ramsey spectroscopy in ultracold atoms into a multidimensional framework similar to multidimensional nuclear magnetic resonance and optical coherent spectroscopy. This multidimensional Ramsey spectroscopy enables the examination of correlations between spectral peaks in impurity-medium systems that remain inaccessible through conventional one-dimensional spectra.

Razavi and Gupta have introduced the Variogram Analysis of Response Surfaces (VARS) as a novel, comprehensive approach to sensitivity analysis. They claim that VARS offers a more intuitive understanding of sensitivity and achieves significantly greater computational efficiency compared to Sobol' indices. This paper reviews those claims and critically evaluates the performance of VARS-TO, which calculates total-order indices, against the Jansen estimator. We contend that, unlike traditional variance-based methods, VARS fails to provide a precise definition of an "important" factor and demonstrate that its purported computational advantages do not hold up under examination. Ultimately, we conclude that although VARS expands the toolkit for sensitivity analysis—particularly for diagnosing mathematical models—it serves best as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, classic variance-based estimators.

Despite the widespread growth of informal online learning communities over the past twenty years, a core question persists: what specific learning outcomes are users expected to achieve? Drawing on Etienne Wenger's theory of communities of practice, this study identifies three primary learning objectives prevalent in these settings: acquiring domain-specific skills, cultivating an identity as a community member, and internalizing community-specific values and practices. To determine the most effective support mechanisms for these goals, the research examines how various forms of legitimate peripheral participation—such as contributing to core tasks, interacting with practice proxies, forming social bonds, and exchanging feedback—relate to these objectives. By analyzing quantitative data from the Scratch online community, the study investigates these relationships. Ultimately, the work offers both theoretical understanding and empirical evidence regarding how diverse learning processes unfold within informal digital environments.

Recognizing entities within document images is a foundational challenge. Conventional sequence labeling methods classify entities using fixed IDs, necessitating vast amounts of data and costly, high-quality annotations to grasp semantics. This paper introduces an entity recognition model designed for few-shot learning with minimal annotated images. To address data scarcity, we propose utilizing explicit label surface names to clarify entity type semantics and embedding these labels into a spatial embedding space to model the relationship between regions and labels. Moving beyond standard sequence labeling, we present LASER, a novel label-aware seq2seq framework. LASER employs a unique labeling scheme that explicitly generates label surface names word-by-word following entity generation. During training, the model refines semantic understanding by updating label surface name representations and enhances the correlation between labels and regions, enabling entity recognition based on both semantic and layout cues. Extensive experiments across two benchmark datasets confirm LASER's superior performance in few-shot scenarios.

The effectiveness of multi-head self-attention mechanisms (MSAs) in computer vision is now undeniable, yet their underlying functioning remains poorly understood. To address this, we offer fundamental insights into the nature of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs). Specifically, we identify three key properties: (1) MSAs enhance both accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes; this benefit stems mainly from their data specificity rather than long-range dependencies. Conversely, ViTs encounter non-convex losses, which can be mitigated through large datasets and loss landscape smoothing techniques. (2) MSAs and Convolutional Networks (Convs) display opposing behaviors; for instance, MSAs act as low-pass filters while Convs function as high-pass filters, making them complementary components. (3) Multi-stage neural networks operate similarly to a series of small individual models, with MSAs at the conclusion of a stage playing a pivotal role in final predictions. Leveraging these findings, we introduce AlterNet, a model that substitutes Conv blocks at the end of each stage with MSA blocks. AlterNet surpasses CNNs in performance across both large and small data regimes. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/xxxnell/how-do-vits-work.

Although deep learning methods excel at identifying objects in medical imagery, they often produce false positives that can compromise diagnostic accuracy. To mitigate this, researchers have utilized neural network output uncertainty to flag erroneous predictions. This study investigates how features derived from neural network uncertainty estimates and shape-based features from binary predictions can reduce false positives in liver lesion detection, specifically through a classification-based post-processing framework tailored for various uncertainty estimation techniques. Results indicate that this approach enhances the neural network's lesion detection performance (measured by F1-score) across two datasets containing abdominal MR and CT images, regardless of the uncertainty method used. Furthermore, the findings reveal that uncertainty-derived features offer limited utility in reducing false positives. Instead, the study demonstrates that class imbalance (the ratio of true to false positives) and shape-based features extracted from uncertainty maps are critical for distinguishing between true and false positive predictions. The associated code is available at https://github.com/ishaanb92/FPCPipeline.
This paper reviews existing findings concerning the fundamental groups of open manifolds characterized by nonnegative Ricci curvature and introduces several unresolved questions in this area.

Private Information Retrieval (PIR) was initially introduced by B. Chor, O. Goldreich, E. Kushilevitz, and M. Sudan in their 1995 FOCS publication. Subsequent work addressed PIR within MDS coded distributed storage systems, analyzing the capacity of such schemes. Furthermore, star product PIR schemes were constructed for general coded distributed storage systems involving colluding servers over arbitrary finite fields; these schemes impose no constraints on field sizes and are applicable across large server networks. This paper first establishes and proves a Singleton-type upper bound regarding the storage rate, the ratio of colluding servers, and the retrieval rate for star product PIR schemes. Additionally, it examines star product PIR schemes derived from algebraic geometry (AG) codes for coded distributed storage. The analysis demonstrates that as the number of servers approaches infinity, star product PIR schemes with colluding servers utilizing AG codes for distributed storage achieve parameters near the Singleton-type upper bound when operating over large fields. A comparison with star product PIR schemes based on Reed-Solomon and Reed-Muller codes reveals that AG-coded schemes with colluding servers offer superior performance. The discussion also covers AG-code based star product PIR schemes resilient to colluding, Byzantine, and unresponsive servers, as well as $q$-ary cyclic code based star product PIR schemes for replicated data storage. Finally, it is shown that when the storage code is Reed-Muller, the optimal retrieval code is not necessarily the Reed-Muller code itself.

**Objective:** To deliver a closed-form solution for the sinusoidal coil sensitivity model introduced by Kern et al., enabling the precise calculation of diverse simulated bias fields that can be directly overlaid onto raw intensity data.

**Approach:** By applying Fourier distribution theory and standard integration methods, the Fourier transform of magnetic fields generated by line segment sources was computed.

**Outcomes:** A function belonging to the space $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ has been derived in full generality to accommodate arbitrary line segment geometries. The discussion includes sampling requirements and verification of equivalence to the original sinusoidal model. Additionally, a CUDA-accelerated tool named $\texttt{biasgen}$ is introduced for on-demand generation of sensitivity and bias data.

**Implications:** Due to the flexibility of this simulation procedure, practitioners can now utilize a broader range of simulated datasets, facilitating quantitative comparisons of various prospective debiasing techniques.

Attacks involving False Data Injection (FDI) targeting power system state estimation have become an increasingly significant concern for operators. While prior research on FDI attacks largely assumed the adversary possessed complete knowledge of the system without providing clear justification, this paper introduces a topology-learning-aided FDI attack. This approach enables stealthy cyber-attacks against AC power system state estimation without requiring prior knowledge of system information. By combining topology learning techniques—which rely solely on branch and bus power flows—with attacker-side pseudo-residual assessment, the proposed method executes stealthy FDI attacks with high confidence. Furthermore, this study is the first to demonstrate how rapidly an attacker can acquire full knowledge of grid topology and parameters, thereby validating the full-knowledge assumptions made in previous works.

This work examines systems of String Equations, where block variables must be assigned strings that concatenate to form a specific target string. Analyzing the problem within a multivariate complexity framework, we identify tractable scenarios, particularly those involving a limited number of block variables or equations. Our primary findings include a polynomial-time solution for systems with two equations, whereas systems with three equations and systems of two equations with strict block variable constraints are proven to be computationally hard. Additionally, we explore a variant permitting a small number of deletions in the target string, for which we develop XP algorithms when the count of block variables remains constant.

Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) serves as a combinatorial optimization heuristic that begins with an initial variable assignment and iteratively refines it by exploring a broad neighborhood of solutions. This paper introduces a learning-enhanced LNS strategy tailored for mixed-integer programs (MIPs). We employ a Neural Diving model to approximate a probability distribution over assignments, collaborating with a standard MIP solver to produce an initial solution. By framing subsequent search steps as a Markov Decision Process, we train a Neural Neighborhood Selection policy to choose the optimal search neighborhood at each iteration, with the MIP solver determining the next assignment. This policy network is developed through imitation learning. We define a target policy for this imitation process that, provided sufficient computational resources, guarantees the selection of the neighborhood containing the optimal next assignment among all feasible options of a given size. Experimental results on five real-world MIP datasets featuring large-scale instances from various domains, including two Google production applications, demonstrate that our approach matches or exceeds all baselines. Notably, at extended runtime durations, it achieves a 2x to 37.8x improvement in average primal gap compared to the strongest baseline on three datasets.

Reference-free evaluation offers significant promise for enhancing the scalability of machine translation assessment, enabling swift adaptation to new languages and domains. Recent findings indicate that a large, multilingual model's probabilities can serve as a reference-free metric achieving state-of-the-art results. Through experiments involving various modifications and scaling up this model, we demonstrate that its performance can rival that of BLEU. Furthermore, our analysis of potential weaknesses reveals that the approach is unexpectedly robust and likely to deliver reasonable performance across diverse domains and varying system qualities.
