The emergence of the Black Lives Matter movement triggered a massive wave of user-generated content online. This paper introduces TweetBLM, a dataset of 9,165 manually annotated tweets specifically targeting the Black Lives Matter movement. The tweets are classified into two categories: HATE and NONHATE, based on whether they exhibit racism related to the movement's impact on the Black community. Additionally, this study provides statistical insights and conducts a systematic evaluation of multiple machine learning models—including Random Forest, CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, Fasttext, BERTbase, and BERTlarge—for classification tasks on the dataset. Our goal is to support the research community's broader efforts in identifying and mitigating online hate speech. The dataset is freely accessible to the public.

First-principles calculations demonstrate that in infinite-layer nickelates ($R$NiO$_2$), the extensively investigated tetragonal $P4/mmm$ phase remains dynamically stable only for early lanthanides ($R$ = La–Sm). Conversely, for late lanthanides ($R$ = Eu–Lu), an imaginary phonon frequency emerges at the $A=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$ point. In these latter cases, condensing this phonon mode into the $P4/mmm$ framework yields a more energetically favorable $I4/mcm$ structure, defined by an out-of-phase rotation of the "NiO$_4$ square." Particular focus is placed on the borderline cases of PmNiO$_2$ and SmNiO$_2$, where both $P4/mmm$ and $I4/mcm$ configurations act as local minima, with their relative energy difference adjustable via epitaxial strain. Relative to the $P4/mmm$ phase, the $I4/mcm$ structure exhibits a significantly narrowed Ni $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bandwidth, reduced Ni $d$ occupancy, a cleaner Fermi surface featuring a suppressed lanthanide-$d$-derived electron pocket at the $\Gamma$ point, and a lower critical $U_{\textrm{Ni}}$ required for long-range antiferromagnetic order. These characteristics indicate stronger correlation effects and support Mott physics. This study underscores the critical structure-property relationship in infinite-layer nickelates, specifically showing that the spontaneous "NiO$_4$ square" rotation serves as a tuning mechanism to make $R$NiO$_2$ in the $I4/mcm$ phase a closer analog to superconducting infinite-layer cuprates.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of bounded solutions for difference equations defined as $x(n+1)=Bx(n) + y(n)$ within a Banach space $\X$, where $n=1,2,...$, $B$ represents a linear continuous operator in $\X$, and the sequence $(y(n))$ approaches 0 as $n\to\infty$. An elementary proof establishes that if the spectrum of $B$ intersects the unit circle only at $\{1\}$, then every bounded solution $x(n)$ satisfies $\lim_{n\to\infty} (x(n+1)-x(n)) =0$. This finding generalizes a theorem by Katznelson-Tzafriri. Additionally, the proof techniques are applied to investigate the individual stability of solutions in the discrete system, accompanied by a discussion on potential further extensions.

We introduce an iterative variable selection approach designed for high-dimensional datasets featuring binary outcomes. This method employs a structured screen-and-select framework that integrates non-local prior-based Bayesian model selection. The screening phase relies on the association between independent variables and the outcome, quantified via the maximum marginal likelihood estimator. Comparative performance against several established methods, evaluated by true positive rate and false discovery rate, demonstrates that our proposed approach serves as a competitive alternative for sparse variable selection in high-dimensional binary outcome scenarios. The method is available in the R package GWASinlps.

While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in 2D computer vision, their irregular architecture complicates direct application to meshes. Subdivision surfaces offer a hierarchical multi-resolution framework where every face in a closed 2-manifold triangle mesh is precisely adjacent to three others. Drawing on these insights, this paper introduces SubdivNet, a flexible CNN framework designed for 3D triangle meshes using Loop subdivision connectivity. By treating mesh faces as analogous to pixels in a 2D image, we develop a convolution operator that aggregates local features from neighboring faces. This approach leverages face neighborhoods to accommodate standard 2D CNN concepts, including variable kernel sizes, strides, and dilation. Utilizing the multi-resolution hierarchy, the model employs pooling layers that merge four faces into one and upsampling techniques that split one face into four, enabling the adaptation of many popular 2D CNN architectures for 3D mesh processing. Furthermore, meshes with arbitrary connectivity can be remeshed to match Loop subdivision requirements through self-parameterization, establishing SubdivNet as a universal solution. Comprehensive evaluations and diverse applications confirm the method's effectiveness and efficiency.

The spined cube $SQ_n$, proposed by Zhou et al. in [Information Processing Letters 111 (2011) 561-567], serves as a variant of the hypercube $Q_n$ designed for parallel computing interconnections. A graph $\G$ is defined as a $m$-Cayley graph if its automorphism group $\Aut(\G)$ contains a semiregular subgroup with $m$ orbits on the vertex set, while a standard Cayley graph is a 1-Cayley graph. Since $Q_n$ is a well-established Cayley graph of the elementary abelian 2-group $\mz_2^n$ (order $2^n$), this paper establishes that $SQ_n$ is a 4-Cayley graph of $\mz_2^{n-2}$ for $n\geq6$, and a $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$-Cayley graph for $n\leq 5$. This structural symmetry implies that for $n\geq6$, an $n$-dimensional spined cube can be decomposed into eight vertex-disjoint $(n-3)$-dimensional hypercubes. As a consequence, it is demonstrated that $SQ_n$ contains two edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles when $n\geq4$. Furthermore, the study determines the vertex-transitivity of $SQ_n$, proving that the graph is not vertex-transitive except when $n\leq3$.

Total variation (TV) minimization stands as a pivotal technique in contemporary signal and image processing, boasting extensive practical applications. Although recent literature extensively addresses the restoration guarantees of TV minimization within compressed sensing, there remains a scarcity of research concerning restoration guarantees derived from partial observations. This study analyzes the error associated with TV-based restoration using random entrywise samples. Specifically, we quantify the discrepancy between the original underlying data and the approximate solution that interpolates (or approximates with a noise-dependent error bound) the provided data while possessing the minimal TV seminorm among all feasible solutions. Furthermore, we link the error estimates for the discrete model to sparse gradient restoration problems and to the approximation of the underlying function from which the true data originates.

High-throughput sequencing enables the parallel detection of tens of thousands of genes, offering potential to enhance diagnostic precision for various conditions, particularly sepsis—a rapid, inflammatory reaction to infection that may lead to organ failure and mortality. Although early sepsis screening is critical in clinical settings, effective diagnostic biomarkers remain unavailable. This study introduces Recurrent Logistic Regression as a novel approach to identify sepsis biomarkers within blood transcriptome data. The analysis identified a five-gene panel comprising LRRN3, IL2RB, FCER1A, TLR5, and S100A12 (collectively termed LIFTS) as diagnostic markers for sepsis. Across nine validation cohorts spanning three independent platforms, LIFTS demonstrated superior performance over existing markers, achieving high accuracy in distinguishing sepsis patients from healthy controls (average AUROC = 0.9959; IC = [0.9722–1.0]). These findings establish a reliable prediction model and reproducible transcriptome biomarkers that serve as a foundation for future clinical diagnostics and investigations into biological mechanisms.

Recent observations in contested online environments reveal an ideological asymmetry where conservative voices appear more prominent, despite liberals holding a population advantage on digital platforms. While previous studies largely examined either a single platform or a single political issue, they have not investigated whether specific ideological groups garner more attention across various platforms and topics, nor how these attention dynamics shift over time. This study presents a quantitative analysis linking collective attention across YouTube and Twitter, focusing on three controversial topics—abortion, gun control, and Black Lives Matter—over a 16-month period. We introduce several video-centric metrics to characterize how attention accumulates for different ideological groups. Our findings indicate that neither side maintains a consistent advantage: left-leaning videos generally receive more views and engagement but are shared less frequently on Twitter compared to right-leaning videos. Additionally, attention time series for left-leaning content develop more rapidly, whereas right-leaning content sustains attention over a longer duration. Network analysis of early adopters and tweet cascades reveals that left-leaning video diffusion relies more on centralized actors, while right-leaning video diffusion initiates earlier in the attention lifecycle. In summary, these results move beyond the static depiction of ideological asymmetries in digital spaces and offer new methods for quantifying attention dynamics across different social platforms.

We utilize flow equations to characterize quantum systems under a time-periodic drive featuring a time-varying envelope. The driven Hamiltonian is formulated using its constituent Fourier harmonics, whose amplitudes evolve over time. System dynamics are captured through a phase-independent effective Hamiltonian and a complementary micromotion operator, derived by solving flow equations. These equations, evolving with respect to an auxiliary flow parameter, progressively transform the quasienergy matrix (the Kamiltonian) into a block-diagonal structure within an extended space. We develop a flow generator that avoids introducing new Fourier harmonics during the process, allowing the method to be executed within a computer algebra system. Consequently, the automated derivation of otherwise complex high-frequency expansions for both the effective Hamiltonian and micromotion to any desired order becomes feasible for driven Hamiltonians defined by a finite algebra of Hermitian operators. We present several illustrative examples and explore the potential for extending this framework to handle rapid envelope modulations.

This work integrates concepts from category theory, K-theory, and geometric group theory by introducing a new class of groups known as $k$-cube groups. These groups act freely and transitively on the product of $k$ trees for any arbitrary $k$. The quotient of this action on the tree product yields a $k$-dimensional cube complex, which in turn generates a higher-rank graph. We analyze the K-theory of the associated $k$-rank graph C*-algebras and provide concrete examples of $k$-cube groups along with their K-theory. Furthermore, we present explicit K-theory computations for an infinite family of $k$-rank graphs where $k\geq 3$, results that do not follow directly from the K\"unneth Theorem regarding tensor products.

This work investigates the quantum metrological capabilities of superpositions of spin coherent states and establishes the criteria required to achieve Heisenberg-limit precision. It is shown that selecting different parameter-generating operators can result in distinct physical estimation outcomes. Specifically, closed-form analytical expressions are derived to describe the performance of spin cat states. These results outline the pathways for precise parameter control needed to attain Heisenberg-limit accuracy and offer valuable insights into the geometric structure of these specific coherent state superpositions and their impact on parameter estimation performance.

Causal loops, such as those found in time travel scenarios, present two primary challenges. The most prominent is the grandfather paradox, which highlights a logical inconsistency where an action creates a potential impossibility. The second, less recognized issue is the information paradox, which is essentially a variation of the first: rather than having too few consistent solutions (none), there are too many. Although the information paradox may initially appear less troubling than the grandfather paradox due to the absence of an obvious logical contradiction, this work demonstrates that both issues are equivalent under intervention. Specifically, if agents can intervene to trigger the information paradox, they can also intervene to create a logical contradiction, and conversely.

Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) viewers have frequently criticized the quality of captions in online videos produced by independent creators on platforms like YouTube. Despite these complaints, there has been a lack of research examining the practices, challenges, and perceptions of captions from the viewpoints of both creators and DHH audiences. This study addresses this gap by first interviewing 13 DHH individuals to understand their feedback, reactions, and experiences with captions, revealing that manually added tags can enhance confidence in caption quality. Subsequently, we analyzed 189 caption-related videos and surveyed 62 individual creators to uncover their specific practices, difficulties (such as back-captioning issues), and perceptions regarding captioning. Collectively, these findings offer a comprehensive understanding of captions generated by independent creators and help bridge the mutual knowledge gap between content creators and DHH audiences.

This work addresses the minimization of supplied energy in infinite-dimensional linear port-Hamiltonian systems and demonstrates that optimal trajectories display the turnpike phenomenon, converging toward specific subspaces determined by the system's dissipation.

Recent economic crises have demonstrated that understanding firm-level input-output network structures is essential for analyzing economic resilience from a microscopic perspective, particularly regarding how firms rewire connections in response to supply and demand shocks. However, empirical data on inter-firm networks is scarce due to confidentiality restrictions. Existing methods for reconstructing networks from partial information, originally designed for financial exposures, are unsuitable for inter-firm relationships because they assume all node pairs could interact, leading to an overestimation of the system's rewiring potential. This study utilizes two large transaction datasets from the Netherlands to map a significant portion of the Dutch inter-firm network, documenting the characteristics of one of the few such networks analyzed. We introduce a generalized maximum-entropy reconstruction method that maintains each firm's production function—specifically, the input and output flows for every product type. Our results confirm that this new method gains reliability with finer product resolution, establishing it as a robust generative model for inter-firm networks constrained by detailed production data. Furthermore, the model's likelihood, which is linked to entropy, serves as a proxy for the system's rewiring capability given a fixed input-output configuration.

This work examines probability measure preserving discrete groupoids, group actions, and equivalence relations within the framework of general probability spaces. It investigates concepts such as cost, the $\beta$-invariant, and their higher-dimensional counterparts for these structures. Furthermore, the paper presents several convergence theorems regarding $\ell^2$-Betti numbers and rank gradients for sequences of actions, groupoids, or equivalence relations, subject to weak finiteness conditions. Specifically, it establishes a connection between combinatorial cost and the cost of ultralimit equivalence relations. Additionally, a relative formulation of the Stuck-Zimmer property is explored.

This study addresses minimization problems involving $\ell_q$ ($0 < q < 1$)-norm regularization with a twice continuously differentiable loss function. While numerous first-order algorithms exist for these nonconvex, nonsmooth composite problems, we introduce HpgSRN, a hybrid approach combining the proximal gradient method with subspace regularized Newton methods. Distinct from existing global convergence results for regularized Newton methods, we prove that the entire sequence of iterates generated by HpgSRN has finite length and converges to an $L$-type stationary point, provided a mild curve-ratio condition and the Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz property of the cost function hold. If the cost function additionally satisfies a Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz property with an exponent of $1/2$, convergence becomes linear. Furthermore, under an extra local error bound condition, the algorithm achieves a superlinear convergence rate. Notably, our convergence guarantees do not depend on the isolatedness or strict local minimality of the $L$-stationary point. Numerical experiments on real data, comparing HpgSRN with ZeroFPR (a hybrid of proximal gradient and quasi-Newton methods for the forward-backward envelope of the cost function) in the context of $\ell_q$-norm regularized linear and logistic regression, demonstrate that HpgSRN requires significantly less computation time while producing comparable or superior sparsity and objective values.

Graph matching is a critical area of study, particularly within computer vision, where recent advancements increasingly integrate deep learning techniques. Despite this progress, the specific function of graph matching algorithms within these models remains unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce a method that incorporates an exact Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation of the graph matching problem, which serves as an optimal inherent baseline. Furthermore, we derive comparable approaches by relaxing the solver's optimality constraints and introducing a quality control parameter that regulates solution fidelity. We also evaluate various relaxations of the graph matching problem. Our experimental analysis yields key theoretical insights and informs the future trajectory of deep graph matching methodologies.

A machine learning-enhanced SPH approach based on PCA is introduced. In this framework, the smoothing tensor's eigenvalues are derived from the principal components of the covariance, utilizing a modified octree structure to rapidly estimate anisotropic, self-regulating kNN. Every SPH particle serves as the center of an optimal kNN cluster, defined as the group whose covariance tensor enables identification via the Mahalanobis metric. This machine learning process functions as a fixed-point problem. The resulting definitive, self-regulating kNN cluster determines the smoothing volume—specifically, an ellipsoid—necessary for anisotropic interpolation. Consequently, the smoothing kernel adopts an ellipsoidal shape, altering the calculation of kernel gradients. As a practical application, the collapse and fragmentation of a non-magnetic, rotating gaseous sphere were simulated. Notably, protostars formed through disc fragmentation proved significantly more persistent and abundant in the anisotropic simulation compared to the isotropic case.

This paper establishes a novel strong convergence theorem for the Riesz logarithmic means of one-dimensional Vilenkin-Fourier (Walsh-Fourier) series. We present the associated inequality and demonstrate that it is essentially sharp, particularly in the context of Walsh-Fourier series.

Integrating electricity into the transportation sector demands meticulous planning and synchronization with the power grid. Without management, the surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption could lead to uncoordinated charging that exacerbates peak demand, potentially exceeding the grid's ability to supply power reliably. This paper presents results from the OptimizEV Project, a pilot program in Upstate New York investigating a new method for coordinating residential EV charging. The proposed strategy leverages the inherent flexibility of EV charging by providing financial incentives to owners who delay charging. When initiating a charge, owners select from various time deadlines; in exchange for accepting these deadlines, they receive lower electricity rates, with prices dropping further as they agree to wait longer. A smart charging system then dynamically manages power distribution in real-time based on active requests, optimizing usage to reduce grid strain while guaranteeing that every vehicle is fully charged by its specified deadline. Our findings indicate that participants are often willing to engage in this optimized approach, with average charging completion times delayed by over eight hours. Utilizing this customer flexibility, the system successfully shifted most EV loads from peak times to fill nighttime valleys in the aggregate load curve. Throughout the study, customer opt-in rates remained consistent, offering empirical support for this coordination mechanism as a viable "non-wires alternative" to handle the rising electricity demand associated with growing EV adoption.

This study provides an initial light curve analysis of the contact binary SW Lac based on B and V band photometry collected over a two-year period (2009–2010). To model stellar spots, we incorporated data from Doppler maps generated using high-resolution, phase-dependent spectra acquired in 2009 with the 2.1 m Otto Struve Telescope at McDonald Observatory. Our findings indicate that the spot models derived from the light curve analysis align with the Doppler maps; however, employing a non-circular spot modeling technique is essential to achieve more accurate and reliable results.

We investigate the dissipative Fermi-Hubbard model under conditions of weak tunneling and strong repulsive interactions, with each lattice site coupled to a Markovian fermionic reservoir. For cold baths at intermediate chemical potentials, the Mott insulator state remains stable, exhibiting rapid relaxation of the particle number toward half-filling. However, on longer time scales, the anti-ferromagnetic order of the Mott-N\'eel ground state on bi-partite lattices decays, even at zero temperature. We quantify these distinct relaxation time scales at both zero and non-zero temperatures using waiting time distributions derived from an effective (non-Hermitian) Hamiltonian, yielding fully analytic expressions for the Fermi-Hubbard model on a tetramer ring.

The paper investigates the asymptotic expansion of Kr"atzel's integral, defined as $F_{p,
u}(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{
u-1} e^{-t^p-x/t}\,dt$ for $|\arg\,x|<\pi/2$, as $|x|$ grows large within the sector $|\arg\,x|<\pi/2$, utilizing the method of steepest descents. Additionally, an alternative derivation is presented via the Mellin-Barnes integral technique. The analysis extends to scenarios where $p<0$, $\Re (
u)<0$, or when both $x$ and $
u$ are large (with $p>0$). A subsequent section examines the asymptotic expansion of an integral containing a modified Bessel function, recently proposed as a generalization of the Whittaker function $M_{\kappa,\mu}(z)$. Numerical examples are included to demonstrate the precision of the derived expansions.

This study examined the individual mathematical work of 15 pre-service teachers in their first year at a Chilean public university, focusing on two complex number tasks. The tasks were designed within a Computer-Assisted Assessment environment (Moodle - Wiris) and required students to solve them using various Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), including GeoGebra, Symbolab, Photomath, and Wolfram Alpha. The research identified both challenges and strengths in the students' mathematical processes. Regarding difficulties, students struggled to interpret CAS outputs and feedback from the assessment system due to insufficient prior mathematical knowledge. Conversely, the study found that specific task characteristics and the integration of two or more artifacts enabled students to construct meaningful interpretations of the mathematical objects involved.
We introduce several issues concerning the conjugacy classes within $\mathsf{Aut}(\mathbb{N}^*)$.

This paper introduces a rapid block direct solver designed for the unified dynamic simulation of power systems. By employing a novel Q-learning approach for task scheduling, the solver effectively handles unified dynamic simulations, which seamlessly integrate electric-mechanical transients with medium-term and long-term dynamic behaviors. Given the high dimensionality and scale of the equations involved, efficient resolution is critical for accelerating simulations. The solver leverages the complex nested block structures inherent in sparse simulation systems to enhance performance. Specifically, within a Markov Decision Process framework, a learning-based task-tree scheduling technique optimizes the scheduling of blocks and frontals. This method allows for the acquisition of optimal scheduling strategies through offline training on numerous sample matrices, enabling the solver to automatically determine optimal task partitioning and scheduling for any given system based on the learned model. Numerical experiments confirm that this learning-based algorithm improves the performance of sparse solvers, with simulations on large power systems demonstrating a speedup of 2 to 6 times compared to KLU, the current state-of-the-art sparse solver for circuit simulation.

This study examines Lie groups encompassing Heintze groups and Sol-type groups, which extend the three-dimensional SOL group. We demonstrate that every left-invariant Riemannian metric on these groups is roughly similar under the identity map. Consequently, we unify previous findings by Le Donne-Xie, Eskin-Fisher-Whyte, Carrasco Piaggio, as well as recent work by Ferragut and Kleiner-M\"uller-Xie regarding quasiisometries of these solvable groups, within a single theoretical framework.

We propose that the enigmatic $f_X(1500)$ state, first detected by Belle and BaBar over ten years ago and previously interpreted as either a scalar or a mixture of even-spin resonances, corresponds to the recently identified vector $\rho^0(1450)$ reported by LHCb. Utilizing the perturbative QCD framework, we derive the di-kaon distribution amplitudes associated with the $\rho^0(1450)$ based on LHCb data concerning the quasi-two-body decays $B^{\pm}\to \pi^{\pm}\rho^0(1450)\to\pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$. Our analysis demonstrates that the $B^+ \to K^+K^+K^-$ decay spectrum near the invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5~\rm GeV$ observed by BaBar is accurately reproduced by the resonant contribution of $\rho^0(1450)$. Furthermore, the broad structure seen in the $B^{+}\to K^{+} K_SK_S$ spectrum around $1.5~\rm GeV$—a region inaccessible to $\rho^0(1450)$ due to Bose-Einstein statistics—is explained solely by a nonresonant $S$-wave component. We predict the branching fractions and direct $CP$ asymmetries for the $B^{\pm}\to \pi^{\pm}\rho^0(1450)\to\pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$, $B^{+}\to K^{+}\rho^0(1450)\to K^+K^+K^-$, and $B^{0}\to K^{0}\rho^0(1450)\to K^0K^+K^-$ modes, which can be verified by current and upcoming LHCb and Belle-II experiments. We invite experimentalists to rigorously test this hypothesis through high-precision analyses of relevant data.

Recent proposals suggest that integrating the Swampland program with the observed smallness of dark energy and experimental constraints predicts a single extra dimension, termed the "dark dimension," characterized by a length scale in the micrometer range. We demonstrate that the Hawking radiation rate for black holes sensitive to this dark dimension is reduced, and we examine the implications of this finding for estimating the proportion of dark matter that could consist of primordial black holes (PBHs). We find that for a species scale of ${\cal O}(10^{10}~{\rm GeV})$, it is viable for PBHs with masses between $10^{14}$ and $10^{21}$ grams to account for all dark matter. This mass range extends three orders of magnitude into the lower mass regime compared to predictions within 4D theory. Additionally, we show that PBHs with a mass of approximately $10^{12}$ grams could potentially explain the well-documented Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, provided they constitute a minor fraction of the total dark matter density.

We investigate the stellar evolution of AM CVn binary systems containing two white dwarfs (WDs) with orbital periods ranging from approximately 5 to 70 minutes. Our analysis specifically targets scenarios where the donor star is a helium WD with an initial mass $M_{\mathrm{He}} < 0.2 \, M_{\odot}$, while the accretor is a WD with a mass $M_{\mathrm{WD}} > 0.6 \, M_{\odot}$. Employing the Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics (MESA) code, we simultaneously evolve both components under assumptions of conservative mass transfer and angular momentum loss driven by gravitational radiation. This self-consistent approach highlights the feedback loop between the donor's properties and the mass transfer rate ($\dot{M}$), as well as the thermal history of the accreting WD. Aligning with previous studies, we observe that high initial $\dot{M}$ values induce adiabatic evolution in donors with $P_{\mathrm{orb}} < 30$ minutes, making their mass-radius relation largely dependent on initial entropy. As the donor's mass decreases to roughly $0.02-0.03 \, M_{\odot}$ at an orbital period of about 30 minutes, it transitions to a fully convective state, potentially losing entropy and expanding less than standard mass loss models would predict. However, the absence of reliable surface opacity data for the donor prevents a definitive prediction regarding this cooling process. Our simulations successfully model the core heating occurring during the initial $\approx 10^7$ years of accretion and extend into the subsequent WD cooling phase. Furthermore, comparing our results with observational data for accreting WDs (such as those from Cheng et al. for isolated systems), we find that these accreting WDs remain hotter than expected given their cooling timescales.

The finite cell method offers a highly adaptable discretization approach for performing numerical analysis on domains with intricate geometries. By employing a non-boundary-conforming computational domain that facilitates easy meshing, this technique allows for the automation of computations across a broad spectrum of geometrical models. However, the application of the finite cell method, along with other immersed methods, to substantial real-world and industrial challenges is frequently constrained by conditioning issues inherent to these approaches. These conditioning difficulties have led researchers to rely on direct solution methods, which significantly restrict the maximum size of systems that can be solved. In contrast, iterative solvers are more appropriate for large-scale computations than direct methods, owing to their reduced memory demands and compatibility with parallel processing. Nevertheless, these advantages can only be fully realized when systems are adequately conditioned. This contribution introduces an Additive-Schwarz type preconditioner that facilitates efficient, parallel, and scalable iterative solutions for large-scale multi-level hp-refined finite cell analyses.

This observational study, utilizing the Submillimeter Array, focuses on the young high-mass star-forming region G23.44-0.18. We detected two massive, radio-quiet dusty cores, MM1 and MM2, through 1.3 mm continuum emission and various dense gas tracers, including thermal CH$_3$OH, CH$_3$CN, HNCO, SO, and OCS lines. The $^{12}$CO (2--1) transition indicates a powerful bipolar outflow emanating from MM2, characterized by a low-velocity, wide-angle quasi-parabolic component alongside a more compact, collimated high-velocity component. This overall geometry mirrors outflow systems in low-mass protostars, featuring a jet-driven fast flow surrounded by an entrained gas shell. The outflow's dynamical age is estimated at $6\times10^3$ years, with a mass ejection rate of approximately $10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ year$^{-1}$. Prominent shock signatures are evident in SO and OCS, and also detected in CH$_3$OH and HNCO. We examined the chemistry within MM1, MM2, and the shocked region, finding that the dense core MM2 exhibits molecular abundances 3 to 4 times greater than those in MM1. We propose this abundance excess results from the combined effects of stellar evolution and embedded shocks in MM2, warranting further investigation.

We investigate continuous-time Markovian random walk models describing Lévy flights and demonstrate a case where convergence to stable densities fails when jumps adhere to a bi-modal power-law distribution that vanishes at zero. This finding holds dual significance: first, concerning the probabilistic derivation of the fractional diffusion equation, and second, regarding the notion of site fidelity within the context of Lévy-like movement patterns in wild animals.

Let $\A$ be a unital operator algebra and $\alpha$ an automorphism of $\A$ that extends to a *-automorphism of its $\ca$-envelope $\cenv (\A)$. This paper introduces the isometric semicrossed product $\A \times_{\alpha}^{\is} \bbZ^+ $ and demonstrates that $\cenv(\A \times_{\alpha}^{\is} \bbZ^+) \simeq \cenv (\A) \times_{\alpha} \bbZ$. Conversely, the $\ca$-envelope of the standard contractive semicrossed product $\A \times_{\alpha} \bbZ^+ $ does not necessarily equal $\cenv (\A) \times_{\alpha} \bbZ$. The primary method used to compute $\ca$-envelopes for semicrossed products is the notion of a relative semicrossed product of an operator algebra, which is investigated within the broader setting of injective endomorphisms. As an application, we generalize a recent finding by Davidson and Katsoulis to the tensor algebras of $\ca$-correspondences. Specifically, if $\T_{\X}^{+}$ is the tensor algebra of a $\ca$-correspondence $(\X, \fA)$ and $\alpha$ is a completely isometric automorphism of $\T_{\X}^{+}$ that fixes the diagonal elementwise, then the contractive semicrossed product satisfies $ \cenv(\T_{\X}^{+} \times_{\alpha} \bbZ^+)\simeq \O_{\X} \times_{\alpha} \bbZ$, where $\O_{\X}$ represents the Cuntz-Pimsner algebra of $(\X, \fA)$.

Multivariate matched proportions (MMP) data arises in diverse settings, such as pharmaceutical post-market surveillance for adverse events, disease classification, and assessing agreement among care providers. This data type involves multiple sets of paired binary measurements collected from the same subject. Although recent non-Bayesian methods have attempted to handle the complexities of MMP data, they fail to address the issue of sparse responses—situations where one or more sets contain no or very few "yes" outcomes. The presence of such sparse sets leads to variance underestimation, reduced coverage, and diminished statistical power in current approaches. While Bayesian methods have not previously been applied to MMP data, they offer a robust framework for handling sparse responses, with the Bayesian probit model specifically providing an elegant solution to variance underestimation. This study evaluates three approaches based on that model: a naive analysis with flat priors, a penalized analysis utilizing half-Cauchy priors for mean model variances, and a multivariate analysis incorporating Bayesian functional principal component analysis (FPCA) to model latent covariance. Results demonstrate that the multivariate approach excels with MMP data featuring sparse responses and surpasses existing non-Bayesian techniques. Furthermore, a re-analysis of data from a study on the System of Care (SOC) framework for children with mental and behavioral disorders yields a more comprehensive understanding of data relationships. This analysis offers new insights into SOC functioning that were overlooked by prior univariate analyses.

We experimentally verify electromagnetically induced absorption (EIA) within a vee + ladder configuration using the low-energy states of $^{87}$Rb. A corresponding theoretical model is developed to replicate these experimental findings. Furthermore, we investigate how EIA resonance properties vary with different combinations of control powers and examine the impact of various incoherent phenomena on the EIA signal.

Subsurface hydrogeological flow and transport are heavily influenced by the connectivity of geological properties. Because uncertainty regarding the subsurface arises from limited field data and prior knowledge, it is necessary to assess alternative geological conceptual models. To minimize the computational expenses of inversions (parameter estimation for specific models), it is advantageous to filter out unlikely conceptual models before proceeding with inversion. This study presents an approach that quantitatively compares ground-penetrating radar (GPR) data collected from the field with simulation results generated from various geological scenarios. This comparison utilizes three global distance metrics—related to wavelet decomposition, multiple-point histograms, and connectivity—to capture the geometrical features of geophysical reflection images. Using field data from the Tagliamento braided river system in Italy, we show that seven of the nine evaluated geological scenarios can be eliminated because their simulated GPR sections do not match observed field data. The remaining scenarios successfully replicate key characteristics, such as cross-stratified deposits and irregular property boundaries. Among the tested metrics, the one based on wavelet decomposition proves most effective. Furthermore, directly analyzing these distances offers the most intuitive and efficient method for comparing scenarios.

This study examines a status updating system that employs variable-length coding to send messages to a receiver across a noisy channel, with the objective of optimizing codeword lengths to minimize the Age-of-Information (AoI) and ensure timely delivery. A Hybrid ARQ (HARQ) protocol is utilized, wherein variable-length incremental redundancy (IR) bits are appended to the initial codeword until successful decoding is achieved. Notably, each decoding attempt introduces a non-zero processing delay. The optimal codeword lengths are analytically determined using a Sequential Differential Optimization (SDO) framework, which is broadly applicable as it relies solely on an analytical expression for the positive feedback (ACK) probability as a function of codeword length.

This paper establishes a lower bound for Bergman kernels associated with sequences of almost Kähler-Einstein Fano manifolds, extending the scope to Fano manifolds possessing almost Kähler-Ricci solitons. This work generalizes findings by Donaldson-Sun and Tian regarding sequences of Kähler-Einstein manifolds with positive scalar curvature. Furthermore, applying our main result, we demonstrate that the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of such a sequence is homomorphic to a log terminal $Q$-Fano variety that supports a Kähler-Ricci soliton on its smooth locus.

This paper investigates Algorithmic High-Frequency Financial Markets by modeling them as dynamical networks. Following an individual examination of 24 US stocks over a year of fully automated trading using ordinal pattern series, we introduce an information-theoretic metric for pairwise synchronization in time series. This metric enables us to analyze a subset of the US market as a dynamical network. We then apply multiple clustering algorithms to this network to identify collective market states, defined by their levels of centralized or decentralized synchronicity. This collective approach successfully reproduces, classifies, and explains anomalous behaviors previously noted at the individual level. Furthermore, we identify two distinct seasonal periods characterized by highly centralized and decentralized synchronicity, respectively. Finally, we model the dynamics of these states using a simple Markov framework.

Electrical conductance alone offers limited utility for identifying Andreev edge states (AESs), which are fundamental to generating topological excitations in quantum Hall (QH)-superconductor (SC) junctions. To unambiguously detect these states, we simultaneously measured shot noise and electrical conductance in a graphene-based QH-SC junction at an integer filling factor of ν=2. Remarkably, we observed that the shot noise Fano factor approaches 0.5 when the bias energy falls below the superconducting gap, while dropping close to zero above it. This finding is particularly striking because the electrical conductance remains quantized at 2e²/h both within and above the gap. Although quantized conductance typically implies dissipationless flow and zero shot noise, at a QH-SC interface, AESs transport current near zero bias; the resulting equal mixing of electron-like and hole-like states generates half of the Poissonian shot noise despite the quantized conductance. These experimental results align with detailed theoretical calculations of conductance and shot noise using the non-equilibrium Green's function method, which accounts for disorder. Consequently, our findings establish shot noise as a viable detection tool for searching for exotic topological excitations in QH-SC hybrid systems.

In the non-equilibrium statistical operator method (Zubarev's approach), the exponential multiplier is interpreted as the probability density for the system's past lifetime and may be substituted with an arbitrary distribution function. To define this distribution, the maximum entropy principle is applied, following the methodology of [Sch\"onfeldt J-H, Jiminez N, Plastino A R, Plastino A, Casas M 2007 \textit{Physica A} \textbf{374} 573], which yields a distribution closely resembling the exponential form. Alternatively, applying the maximum entropy principle as demonstrated in [Van der Straeten E and Beck C 2008 Phys. Rev. E \textbf{78} 051101] generates power-law, log-normal, and other types of distributions, along with transitions between them, rather than strictly exponential ones.

Federated Learning (FL) allows for the distributed training of machine learning models while ensuring personal data remains private on user devices. Although FL is increasingly applied in mobile sensing domains like human activity recognition (HAR), it has yet to be thoroughly examined within multi-device environments (MDEs), where individual users possess multiple data-generating devices. As mobile and wearable technology proliferates, MDEs are becoming ubiquitous in computing settings, creating a need to adapt FL for this context. FL in MDEs is defined by statistical non-IID distributions across clients and further complicated by dual heterogeneities involving both users and devices. Additionally, efficiently utilizing system resources on FL clients within an MDE remains a significant challenge. To address these issues, we introduce FLAME, a user-centric FL training framework designed to mitigate statistical and system heterogeneity in MDEs and ensure consistent inference performance across devices. FLAME incorporates three key features: (i) user-centered FL training that leverages temporal alignment among devices belonging to the same user; (ii) device selection strategies that balance accuracy and efficiency; and (iii) device-specific model personalization. We also developed an FL evaluation testbed featuring realistic energy consumption and network bandwidth profiles, alongside a novel class-based data partitioning method to adapt existing HAR datasets for federated learning. Experimental results across three multi-device HAR datasets demonstrate that FLAME surpasses various baselines, achieving 4.3% to 25.8% higher F1 scores, 1.02 to 2.86 times greater energy efficiency, and up to 2.06 times faster convergence to target accuracy through an equitable distribution of the FL workload.

Null-torsion holomorphic curves in the round 6-sphere serve as fundamental instances of minimal surfaces. This category is particularly extensive; according to a theorem by Bryant, later expanded upon by Rowland, any closed Riemann surface can be conformally embedded into the round 6-sphere as a null-torsion holomorphic curve. This study investigates the second variation of area for compact null-torsion holomorphic curves $\Sigma$ with genus $g$ and area $4\pi d$, specifically examining the spectrum of the Jacobi operator. We demonstrate that for genera $g \leq 6$, the multiplicity of the lowest eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = -2$ is precisely $4d$. Furthermore, we establish that for any genus, the nullity is at least $2d + 2 - 2g$. These findings are expected to influence the deformation theory of asymptotically conical associative 3-folds in $\mathbb{R}^7$, as explored by Lotay.

Contemporary computing architectures are increasingly adopting hybrid memory systems that integrate DRAM and non-volatile memory (NVM) to leverage the strengths of both, delivering low latency, high reliability, and increased density. A defining feature of these DRAM-NVM hybrids is the disparity in access speeds, where NVM exhibits significantly higher latency than DRAM, a phenomenon termed inter-memory asymmetry. We identify that parasitic elements within long bitlines are primary contributors to elevated latency in both memory types and a key driver of high-voltage operations in NVM, thereby affecting reliability. To address this, we introduce an architectural modification that splits each long bitline into two segments using an isolation transistor, allowing one segment to operate with reduced latency and voltage compared to the other. This tiered structure enables non-uniform access within individual memory types, creating intra-memory asymmetry that facilitates performance and reliability trade-offs in hybrid systems. We extend current NVM-DRAM operating systems through three key enhancements: first, by utilizing both inter- and intra-memory asymmetries to manage page allocation and migration between DRAM and NVM tiers; second, by refining page allocation strategies to predict the access intensity of new pages and assign them to appropriate tiers upon initial access, thus reducing migration overhead during execution; and third, by implementing a mechanism to migrate pages between tiers within the same memory type without traversing the memory channel, which lowers channel contention and boosts performance. Our proposed framework, MNEME, harnesses these asymmetries in tiered DRAM-NVM hybrid memory to simultaneously enhance performance and reliability across single-core and multi-programmed workloads.

We present an investigation into applying biaffine models for neural discourse dependency parsing, demonstrating substantial performance gains over baseline parsers. Our comparison between the Eisner and Chu-Liu-Edmonds algorithms reveals that the latter produces deeper trees and yields superior results. Additionally, by evaluating parser output structure through metrics like average maximum path length and average leaf node proportion, we confirm that the generated dependency trees closely resemble gold standard trees. Given the corpus permits non-projective structures, our analysis of non-projectivity complexity indicates that the dependency structures exhibit a maximum gap degree and edge degree of one.

To comprehend the microscopic roots of collective reorientational dynamics in aqueous environments, methods must transcend conventional chemical intuition. This study elucidates a mechanism via unsupervised learning, revealing that significant angular displacements in liquid water stem from highly cooperative, orchestrated movements. Our automated analysis of angular fluctuations uncovers heterogeneity among these concerted jumps. We demonstrate that substantial orientational shifts necessitate a highly collective dynamic process involving the correlated motion of up to 10% of water molecules within spatially connected clusters of the hydrogen-bond network. This phenomenon originates from collective fluctuations in network topology, generating defects on the terahertz timescale. The proposed mechanism involves a cascade of hydrogen-bond fluctuations driving angular jumps, offering fresh perspectives on the prevailing localized model of such events. These insights enhance the interpretation of various spectroscopies and deepen our understanding of reorientational dynamics in water near both biological and inorganic systems.

Initial JWST data has revealed a larger-than-anticipated number of bright galaxy candidates with redshifts $z\gtrsim 10$, allowing for the construction of rest-frame UV luminosity functions (LFs). These LFs provide critical insights into stellar populations, star formation rates, and galaxy assembly history in the early universe. By applying an upper limit to the total baryonic mass inflow rate into galaxies from their host halos—derived from abundance matching—we establish a lower bound on the product of star formation and UV-photon production efficiency at various redshifts. This constraint implies a high conversion efficiency of gas into stars ($\gtrsim 10-30\%$) if we assume a standard stellar population with a Salpeter-like initial mass function. Such efficiencies are significantly higher than those observed in typical local galaxies but align with values found in nearby starburst galaxies and super star clusters. Alternatively, if the stellar population is metal-free and follows a top-heavy mass distribution that generates intense UV radiation, the star formation efficiency could be as low as a few percent, matching the average for galaxies at $z\simeq 6$. We also examine other potential scenarios, such as energetic radiation from compact stellar remnants or quasars, and suggest observational strategies to differentiate between these possibilities.

Although synchronization is vital for many biological and physical systems, current optimization theories rely on global information and fail to adequately investigate local mechanisms that enhance synchrony. Consequently, our understanding of self-organized, collective processes designed to optimize or repair synchronous systems—such as paracrine signaling dynamics in cardiac cells—remains limited. This study introduces "grass-roots" synchronization optimization, a multiscale approach where local optimizations of smaller subsystems collaborate to optimize the entire system. Using models of cardiac tissue and power grids, we demonstrate that systems optimized through this grass-roots method perform comparably to globally optimized ones while offering the distinct advantage of robustness against targeted attacks or subsystem isolation. These findings encourage further research into the physics of local mechanisms that facilitate self-optimization in complex systems.

This paper presents a transversality theorem based on Hausdorff measures, enhancing notable results derived from Lebesgue measures, including Rene Thom's foundational theorem and John Mather's 1973 strengthening. Leveraging this improved theorem, we derive two new results concerning generic linear perturbations and their applications. Additionally, we apply these findings to multiobjective optimization through the lenses of differential topology and singularity theory.

We examine the development of hydrodynamic fluctuations during a heavy ion collision as the system approaches the QCD critical point. To describe this evolution, we define two small dimensionless parameters, $\lambda$ and $\Delta_s$. The parameter $\lambda$ represents the ratio of the microscopic relaxation time (in the non-critical regime) to the expansion rate, $\lambda \equiv \tau_0/\tau_Q$, while $\Delta_s$ quantifies the deviation of the baryon-to-entropy ratio, $n/s$, from its critical value, $\Delta_s\equiv (n/s - n_c/s_c)/(n_c/s_c)$. We establish the parametric dependence of critical hydrodynamic fluctuations on these two parameters. Subsequently, we apply this parametric framework to estimate the magnitude of critical fluctuations and the correlation length in heavy ion collisions, thereby providing direction for experimental efforts to locate the QCD critical point.

This paper substitutes real numbers with a topological R-module to introduce R-metric spaces $(X,d)$, subsequently establishing several common fixed point theorems within R-module metric spaces. As a specific instance, we derive Perov's theorem.

Ultracompact objects possessing photon spheres can replicate numerous observational characteristics of black holes. Previous hypotheses posited that anomalous tidal heating or specific resonances in gravitational wave signals would serve as definitive evidence for a surface or the lack of an event horizon. However, these assertions and related studies relied exclusively on frequency-domain analyses under the assumption of stationarity. We demonstrate that such objects must first undergo a "fueling" phase to attain a stationary state. Consequently, the existence of a stable light ring and extended light-travel durations within the object can significantly postpone this equilibration process, effectively obscuring structural differences. Essentially, black hole mimickers mimic black holes more effectively than earlier research indicated. These findings carry implications for other resonant systems exhibiting sharp resonances, such as "floating orbits" near rotating black holes. Consequently, accurately accounting for the self-force in these systems is essential and holds significant relevance for testing horizon physics.

This thesis presents two-level type theory, an extension of Martin-L\"of type theory that incorporates strict equality as an internal primitive. While Voevodsky initially proposed a system combining this strict equality with conventional equality—a feature central to homotopy type theory (HoTT)—known as HTS, this work generalizes and expands upon that concept. We develop a semantic framework offering a systematic treatment of type formers for two-level systems and establish a conservativity result linking them back to conventional type theories like HoTT. Furthermore, we demonstrate how two-level theories can offer partial solutions to unresolved issues in HoTT, specifically by constructing semi-simplicial types and establishing the foundations for an internal theory of $(\infty, 1)$-categories.

Executing complex autonomous maneuvers like drifting demands highly precise and frequent pose data to guarantee safety and accuracy, a challenge that is particularly acute when relying solely on onboard sensors. This paper introduces a drift controller featuring dual feedback loops: a sideslip controller that regulates the sideslip angle by adjusting the front wheel steering, and a circle controller that sustains a consistent trajectory radius and center point by modulating wheel rotational speed. We employ an extended Kalman filter for state estimation and propose a robustified KASA algorithm to accurately determine the circle parameters (center and radius) that best fit the current path. Based on the assumption of uniform circular motion during stable drift, the vehicle's dynamics are characterized using angular information rather than acceleration. The proposed method was validated on a 1/10 scale race car, which demonstrated stable drifting with a fixed center and radius, confirming the approach's effectiveness.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for data segmentation, addressing the multiple change point problem within a broad framework. This framework encompasses classic mean shifts, alterations in linear regression, and structural changes in time series, such as variations in Poisson-autoregressive parameters. Specifically, we establish a general theory grounded in estimating equations, demonstrating consistency for the estimated number of change points and deriving convergence rates for the estimators of their locations. Our approach considers two distinct types of MOSUM (moving sum) statistics: a MOSUM-Wald statistic derived from differences in local estimators, and a MOSUM-score statistic based on a global estimator. The latter is typically computationally more efficient, especially in non-linear contexts where closed-form solutions are unavailable and numerical methods are necessary. Finally, we assess the proposed methodology using both simulated datasets and real-world geophysical well-log data.

This paper introduces equivalent formulations for concepts involving set families where any subfamily with an empty intersection contains a bounded sub-collection that also has an empty intersection, and it reviews the progress made regarding the maximum size of such families. In this study, we resolve a boundary case of Tuza's problem for non-trivial $q$-Helly families by utilizing Karamata's inequality and calculating the minimum size of a $2$-self-centered graph such that the common neighborhood of every pair of vertices includes a clique of size $q-2$.

A critical phase in seismic data processing involves eliminating noise, such as interference caused by simultaneous or blended sources, from recorded data. Conventional techniques are often labor-intensive, frequently necessitating manual parameter selection to achieve satisfactory outcomes. In contrast, this study employs deep learning, specifically a U-net model integrated with a ResNet architecture pretrained on ImageNet and subsequently trained on synthetic seismic data, to address this challenge. The method is applied to common offset gathers, utilizing adjacent offset gathers as additional input channels for the denoising process. Results demonstrate that this approach effectively removes noise from multiple datasets acquired across various global regions, though with moderate success. We observe that incorporating three adjacent offset gathers on either side of the target gather yields the most effective denoising. Furthermore, since this method eliminates the need for manual parameter tuning, it offers a higher degree of automation compared to traditional approaches.

A precise investigation of electroweak symmetry breaking compellingly advocates for building a lepton collider capable of a center-of-mass energy of at least 240 GeV. Beyond measuring Higgsstrahlung ($e^+e^- \to hZ$), such a facility would determine weak boson pair production ($e^+e^- \to WW$) with remarkable accuracy. Furthermore, the weak-boson-fusion channel ($e^+e^- \to \nu \bar{\nu} h$) offers a progressively more potent probe as center-of-mass energies rise. Elevated energies also enhance the prospects for associated top-Higgs production ($e^+e^-\to t\bar th$), which is essential for directly constraining the top Yukawa coupling. This study examines the impact and complementarity of differential measurements across various center-of-mass energies and beam polarization setups within a global effective-field-theory framework. We introduce a "global determinant parameter" (GDP) to quantify the overall tightening of constraints regardless of the selected operator basis, and we evaluate the potential reach of the CEPC, CLIC, FCC-ee, and ILC designs.

Driven by oceanographic observational data, we introduce a probabilistic neural network (PNN) designed to estimate turbulent energy dissipation rates from vertical profiles of velocity and density gradients within density-stratified turbulent flows. The model was trained and evaluated using high-resolution simulations of decaying turbulence engineered to mimic geophysical conditions akin to those in the ocean. Our PNN surpasses a widely used baseline theoretical model for computing dissipation rates from vertical shear observed in the ocean, demonstrating superior robustness in capturing the tails of output distributions across various stages of turbulent decay. Differential sensitivity analysis suggests this enhanced performance stems from the network's capacity to encode additional underlying physics related to density gradients in the flow.

The perception system in autonomous vehicles handles the detection and tracking of surrounding objects, a task typically enhanced by combining multiple sensing modalities to boost robustness and accuracy, thereby making sensor fusion essential. This paper addresses radar and camera fusion, introducing a middle-fusion strategy designed for 3D object detection that leverages data from both sources. Our method, named CenterFusion, initially employs a center point detection network to locate objects by pinpointing their centers within the image. It then tackles the critical data association challenge through a novel frustum-based technique, linking radar detections to their corresponding image center points. These associated radar detections are utilized to create radar-derived feature maps that augment image features, enabling the regression of object attributes such as depth, orientation, and velocity. Evaluated on the demanding nuScenes dataset, CenterFusion enhances the nuScenes Detection Score (NDS) of current state-of-the-art camera-only methods by over 12%. Additionally, we demonstrate that CenterFusion markedly improves velocity estimation precision without relying on any extra temporal data. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/mrnabati/CenterFusion.

The theoretical prediction of a novel perturbation mode, termed the self-gravito-acoustic mode (SGAM), arises within cold self-gravitating degenerate quantum plasmas (SGDQPs). In these perturbed systems, compression is primarily driven by the self-gravitational pressure of heavy particles, while rarefaction is chiefly caused by the degenerate pressure of light particles. This SGAM represents a distinct mode because it vanishes entirely if the degenerate pressure of the light particle species is ignored. The application of this new SGAM prediction is demonstrated in the context of a white dwarf SGDQP.

This work investigates the mass of the $Y(2175)$ state with quantum numbers $J^{PC} = 1^{--}$ using QCD sum rules. We formulate both diquark-antidiquark currents, specifically $(ss)(\bar{s}\bar{s})$, and meson-meson currents, $(\bar{s}s)(\bar{s}s)$. Our analysis reveals two independent currents for each configuration and establishes the relationships connecting them. The Operator Product Expansion (OPE) for these currents converges rapidly, facilitating a robust sum rule analysis. Both the SVZ and finite energy sum rule approaches yield a mass of approximately $2.3 \pm 0.4$ GeV, which aligns with the experimentally observed mass within the uncertainties inherent to current QCD sum rule calculations. Furthermore, the coupling strength of these four-quark currents to lower-lying states, such as the $\phi(1020)$, is found to be notably small. Finally, we explore the potential decay characteristics of $Y(2175)$ under the assumption that it is a tetraquark.

Federated Learning (FL) is an emerging approach that enables the joint training of a global model while keeping data local, thereby addressing data privacy concerns through encryption mechanisms. In this framework, clients train their respective local models, and a server aggregates these models until convergence. To enhance the global model, the server employs incentive mechanisms to motivate clients to contribute high-quality, large-scale data. While FL has been applied to various sectors such as the Internet of Things (IoT), healthcare, and manufacturing, the technology remains in its early stages with numerous challenges to overcome. Enhancing the quality of FL models is currently a critical research focus and a demanding task. This paper offers a systematic and objective analysis of methods aimed at improving FL model quality. Additionally, we examine current research and application trends in FL and compare FL with non-FL approaches, addressing practitioners' concerns that privacy protection might compromise learning performance. Utilizing a systematic review methodology, we analyze 147 recent articles on FL. This review provides valuable insights for both academic researchers and industry practitioners by investigating trends in academic and industrial applications, identifying key factors influencing FL model quality, and comparing the learning efficacy of FL versus non-FL algorithms. Based on our findings, we offer recommendations for improving FL model quality and propose a practical application framework for industry users.

Contextual commonsense inference involves generating diverse explanations for events within dyadic dialogues, such as causes, motivations, and emotional responses. Crafting coherent and meaningful explanations demands an understanding of the dialogue's structure and the grounding of events within that context. This paper introduces CICEROv2, a dataset comprising 8,351 instances drawn from 2,379 dialogues, featuring multiple human-annotated answers for each inference question covering causes, subsequent events, motivations, and emotional reactions. We demonstrate that the inferences in CICEROv2 exhibit greater semantic diversity compared to other datasets in this domain. To address this task, we propose a set of pre-training objectives, including concept denoising and utterance sorting, to optimize pre-trained models for downstream contextual commonsense inference. Our findings indicate that these objectives effectively adapt the T5-Large model for this specific task.

Let $K_n$ represent the count of unique values within the initial $n$ terms of an infinite exchangeable sequence of random variables $(X_1, X_2, \ldots)$. We establish that for $n=3$, the extreme points of the convex set comprising all feasible distributions of $K_3$ correspond to i.i.d. sampling from discrete uniform distributions and the limiting scenario where $P(K_3=3)=1$, while proposing a conjecture for general $n$. Additionally, we examine related problems involving finite exchangeable sequences and exchangeable random partitions.

We present a comparison between unresolved reflectance spectroscopy of Solar System small bodies and laboratory measurements of reference surfaces. Specifically, we measured the bidirectional reflectance spectroscopy of howardite powder and a sublimation residue resembling Ceres. These spectra were inverted using both the Hapke semi-empirical physical model and the MRTLS parametric model to simulate surface reflectance under any required geometric configuration. While both models accurately render the reflectance spectroscopy, the MRTLS model introduces less noise than the Hapke model. Utilizing the inversion parameters, we simulated two spherical bodies: (1) Ceres and (4) Vesta, whose surfaces are uniformly covered with the Ceres analogue and howardite powder, respectively. We modeled various illumination and observation scenarios, including spot-pointing and fly-bys, for phase angles ranging from 6° to 135°. Reflectance spectroscopy was retrieved from the resulting images of these simulated bodies and compared to the reference surface data. Our findings indicate that the photometric phase curves of the simulated bodies differ from those of the reference surfaces due to variations in local incidence and emergence angles caused by surface shape and topography. Maximum discrepancies were observed at wide phase angles in various simulated observations of (4) Vesta, attributed to its high surface topography. Finally, we emphasize the differences in spectral parameters derived from unresolved observations at 30° compared to laboratory measurements taken under a single geometric configuration.

The dynamics driving the "tragedy of the commons"—where a shared resource is exploited to depletion—can be modeled as a prisoner's dilemma. In this scenario, although conserving the resource benefits the collective, individual self-interest at any specific moment favors over-consumption. To mitigate this tragedy, strategies involving punishment for excessive use and incentives for restraint can be employed to favor non-exploitative behaviors. This study evaluates the efficacy of various punishment mechanisms within an evolving consumer-resource system, utilizing a framework of parametrically heterogeneous ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Analytical methods based on adaptive dynamics identify conditions under which sustainable coexistence with the resource is possible for specific cases, while the impact of punishment on heterogeneous populations with varying initial compositions is assessed using the reduction theorem for replicator equations. The findings indicate that rewarding under-consumers alone is insufficient to avert the tragedy of the commons; instead, a punitive measure is necessary. This punishment must increase non-linearly with the degree of over-consumption and may need to vary according to the initial distribution of clones within the population.

In multiuser communication systems, user scheduling and beamforming (US-BF) design are typically treated as separate issues in current research. This study addresses the joint optimization of US and BF to maximize the number of scheduled users, a task that is computationally difficult due to non-convex objectives and constraints involving both discrete and continuous variables. To overcome these challenges, we first introduce a successive convex approximation-based algorithm (SCA-USBF). Subsequently, drawing inspiration from intelligent wireless communication, we develop a graph neural network-based approach (J-USBF) that integrates a joint user scheduling and power allocation network model with an analytical beamforming solution. Numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of both methods, showing that J-USBF achieves performance comparable to SCA-USBF with superior computational efficiency. Additionally, the proposed J-USBF exhibits strong generalizability in dynamic wireless network environments.

Although numerous explainability techniques have emerged recently, a unified framework for evaluating them remains elusive. While automated metrics facilitate rapid benchmarking, they often fail to capture how humans actually interact with explanations. Human assessment is critical, yet existing protocols neglect belief biases that can distort human performance and yield misleading results. This work outlines belief bias, its impact on human evaluation, and strategies for NLP practitioners to address it. Through a case study on gradient-based explainability using two experimental paradigms—models of varying quality and adversarial examples—we demonstrate straightforward methods to control for human prior beliefs. Our findings reveal that conclusions regarding top-performing methods shift when these controls are applied, underscoring the necessity of accounting for belief bias in evaluation.

The task of sequentially maximizing the expected value of a function aims to optimize the mean of a target function without direct control over its input features. Instead, these features are indirectly determined by an agent's actions within a specific context, distinguishing this approach from Bayesian optimization where inputs are directly controllable. If the full conditional distribution of the features must be incorporated into the optimization, one must account for the entire distribution rather than just its expectation. Additionally, the function itself is unknown, accessible only through noisy observations, which may involve mismatched datasets. We introduce a novel algorithm designed for this scenario that addresses uncertainty arising from both the estimated conditional distribution of the features and the unknown function. This is achieved by modeling the feature distribution as a Bayesian conditional mean embedding and the function as a Gaussian process. Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study presents a precise force control algorithm for series elastic actuators (SEAs) utilizing a new force estimation approach known as the transmission force observer (TFOB). Designed to address poor force measurements in SEAs resulting from elastic transmission nonlinearities, sensor noise, and deformation measurement errors, the paper first examines the limitations of traditional SEA force sensing methods and analyzes their stochastic properties, laying the groundwork for accurate force control via TFOB. Notably, a tuning parameter is derived from holistic closed-loop frequency domain analyses, offering a framework to achieve optimal performance in force-controlled SEA systems. The efficacy of the proposed algorithm is validated through experiments on a physical SEA hardware platform.

This work details our most recent advancements in integrating vector boson scattering (VBS) measurements into global SMEFT analyses of LHC data. We provide updates to our initial investigation (arXiv:2101.03180) and discuss a potential roadmap for incorporating higher-order terms beyond dimension 6 in the SMEFT, along with considerations for interpreting VBS data within alternative EFT frameworks.

A particle raft suspended on an expanding liquid surface serves as a macroscopic model for investigating material failure. The system's temporal scales enable the observation of both particle relaxation and rift formation. In our experiments, the raft—a collection of particles—is uniaxially stretched by the widening air-liquid interface beneath it. The resulting failure patterns evolve continuously with the stretching speed. This behavior arises from a competition between two velocity scales: the rate of re-aggregation, where particles relax toward a low-energy state governed by viscous and capillary forces, and the relative velocity differences between adjacent particles induced by the fluid's expansion. This interplay determines the cluster length, or the spacing between neighboring rifts. A model derived from this competition aligns with the observed experimental failure patterns.

Although neural forecasting has greatly enhanced the accuracy of large-scale systems, predicting over extended horizons remains difficult. We tackled the issues of prediction volatility and computational complexity by integrating smoothness regularization and mixed data sampling into a robust multi-layer perceptron architecture (NBEATS). Our proposed method, DMIDAS, was validated using high-frequency healthcare and electricity price datasets with long forecasting horizons (approximately 1,000 timestamps). This approach achieved a 5% improvement in prediction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models while reducing the NBEATS parameter count by nearly 70%.

Dynamic algorithms are categorized into three primary types: $\mathit{incremental}$ (handling only insertions), $\mathit{decremental}$ (handling only deletions), and $\mathit{fully}$ $\mathit{dynamic}$ (handling both). While fully dynamic algorithms represent the ultimate goal due to their generality, the question remains whether they are inherently more difficult to solve. Previous research has achieved reductions from fully dynamic to incremental or decremental models by exploiting either the specific structural properties of the latter two models (e.g., [HK99, HLT01, BKS12, ADKKP16, BS80, OL81, OvL81]) or the specific sequence of operations (e.g., [AW14, HKNS15, KPP16]). This work aims to establish a general, black-box reduction from fully dynamic to incremental settings. We identify two necessary conditions for such a reduction:
*   The incremental algorithm must provide worst-case running time guarantees rather than amortized ones.
*   The reduction must operate within a $\mathit{deletions}$-$\mathit{look}$-$\mathit{ahead}$ $\mathit{model}$, where the sequence of deletions among existing elements is known beforehand; a common practical instance is the "sliding window" (FIFO) update order.

Given these conditions, we propose:
*   A practical, simple reduction converting amortized fully dynamic algorithms to worst-case incremental ones, incurring a $\log(T)$ overhead factor on running time, where $T$ represents the total number of updates.
*   A theoretical reduction transforming worst-case fully dynamic algorithms to worst-case incremental ones, with a $\mathsf{polylog}(T)$ overhead factor on running time.

Tensors exhibiting low border rank—specifically those where the border rank matches or nearly equals the tensor's size—serve as a fundamental component in all existing asymptotically efficient matrix multiplication algorithms. Consequently, advancing the development of new, faster algorithms requires a deeper understanding of tensors with the smallest possible border rank, known as minimal border rank tensors. This study explores the relationship between the degenerations of associative algebras and the degenerations of their structure tensors, following Strassen's framework. This investigation enables the characterization of an open subset of $n \times n \times n$ minimal border rank tensors through the lens of commutative algebra smoothability. Furthermore, we identify the smoothable algebra linked to the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor and establish a lower bound for the border rank of the tensor utilized in the "easy construction" proposed by Coppersmith and Winograd.

Simulating the microstructural evolution of a device-embedded material frequently requires integral boundary conditions. This study introduces an adapted Nitsche's method to address the Poisson equation subject to such conditions, which are coupled with phase-field equations describing the microstructure evolution of strongly correlated materials experiencing metal-insulator transitions. Numerical results indicate that the proposed approach attains an optimal convergence rate, whereas the standard Lagrange multiplier method does not. Additionally, the linear system generated by this modified Nitsche's method can be efficiently resolved using an iterative solver equipped with algebraic multigrid preconditioning. Moreover, this technique is applicable to other physical boundary conditions that are mathematically analogous to the electric integral boundary condition discussed.

A real hypersurface in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is defined as Reinhardt if it remains invariant under the standard $\mathbb{T}^2$-action on $\mathbb{C}^2$. Its CR geometry is characterized by the curvature function of its "generating curve," which corresponds to the logarithmic projection of the hypersurface onto the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. We establish a sharp upper limit for the first positive eigenvalue of the Kohn Laplacian, corresponding to a natural pseudohermitian structure on a compact, strictly pseudoconvex Reinhardt real hypersurface with a closed generating curve (implying the $\mathbb{T}^2$-action is free). This bound is formulated using the $L^2$-norm of the generating curve's curvature function and is achieved if and only if the curve is circular.

It is demonstrated that the operator connecting the one-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$-Dunkl operator with the derivative can be realized using oscillator operators. This finding relies on the property that the Dunkl intertwining operator transforms Hermite polynomials into generalized Hermite polynomials.
