This technique enables the precise, efficient, and systematic calculation of electronic structures for key technological materials, including nanotubes of any chirality, nanowires, nanoribbons, chiral nanoassemblies, nanosprings, and nanocoils. Inspired by the success of plane-wave methods—spectral techniques relying on eigenfunction expansion for bulk crystalline systems—our approach sidesteps the computationally expensive approximations of periodic supercells common in standard plane-wave treatments of quasi-1D materials. Furthermore, it addresses limitations inherent in other discretization schemes, such as finite differences and atomic orbital bases. Our methodology involves establishing fast transforms to discretize governing equations using a specific basis set and employing matrix-free iterative diagonalization to derive electronic eigenstates. We detail various computational aspects, including eigensolver selection, preconditioning strategies, the evaluation of oscillatory radial integrals, and kinetic energy cutoffs. These strategies are integrated into a software package named HelicES (Helical Electronic Structure). Through numerous examples involving nanotubes, nanoribbons, and nanowires, we demonstrate the method's utility for systematic electronic structure analysis. Additionally, we examine the method's convergence behavior and accuracy, anticipating broad applications in computational nanomechanics and materials science.

A primary objective in task-oriented dialogue research is achieving flexible adaptation of dialogue models across new domains. To advance this area, we present DialoGLUE (Dialogue Language Understanding Evaluation), a public benchmark comprising seven task-oriented dialogue datasets that address four distinct natural language understanding tasks. This resource aims to foster research in representation-based transfer, domain adaptation, and sample-efficient task learning. We provide several robust baseline models that utilize pre-training on a large open-domain dialogue corpus combined with task-adaptive self-supervised training. These baselines outperform a standard BERT architecture and achieve state-of-the-art results on five of the seven tasks. By releasing the DialoGLUE benchmark, these baseline methods, and our evaluation scripts, we aim to accelerate progress toward developing more generalizable task-oriented dialogue models.

The Chen-Teo gravitational instanton constitutes an asymptotically flat, toric, Ricci-flat family of metrics defined on $\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^2\setminus S^1$, serving as a counterexample to the classical Euclidean Black Hole Uniqueness conjecture. This paper demonstrates that the Chen-Teo instanton is both Hermitian and non-Kähler, thereby implying that all currently known gravitational instanton examples possess Hermitian properties.

AI-driven code generation has emerged as a method for automatically creating programs from natural language descriptions using deep neural networks, such as Neural Machine Translation (NMT). These tools are notably utilized in ethical hacking and offensive security testing to produce proof-of-concept attacks. Despite their utility, evaluating code generators remains problematic. Current practices rely on automatic metrics that measure textual similarity between generated code and ground-truth references, yet it remains ambiguous which metric is most appropriate for specific contexts. This practical experience report examines a wide array of output similarity metrics applied to offensive code generators. Specifically, we evaluate two state-of-the-art NMT models against two datasets comprising offensive assembly and Python code paired with English descriptions. By comparing automatic metric estimates with human evaluations, we offer practical insights into the strengths and limitations of these metrics.

This study presents the development and demonstration of the occ-RI-K algorithm, designed to calculate the exact exchange component in density functional theory (DFT) for solids near the basis set limit. Implemented within Gaussian and Plane Wave (GPW) density fitting, our method delivers a 1-2 order-of-magnitude acceleration over standard GPW approaches. Leveraging its efficiency with large basis sets, we evaluated 12 hybrid functionals using pseudopotentials and extensive uncontracted basis sets on the band gaps of 25 simple solids. The most demanding calculation in this work involved 16 electrons and 350 basis functions per unit cell with a 6x6x6 k-mesh. Among global hybrid functionals, B3LYP, PBE0, revPBE0, B97-3, and SCAN0 (containing 20-27% exact exchange) exhibited comparable performance with root-mean-square deviations (RMSD) ranging from 0.61 to 0.77 eV; however, M06-2X and MN15 displayed higher RMSD values due to their greater exact exchange fractions. While the short-range hybrid HSE achieved a similar RMSD (0.76 eV), it significantly underestimated band gaps because it lacks long-range exchange entirely. Conversely, range-separated hybrids with high fractions of long-range exact exchange—specifically $\omega$B97X-rV, $\omega$B97M-rV, CAM-B3LYP, and CAM-QTP01—consistently overestimated band gaps. Despite these findings, no single functional has yet been identified that performs consistently for both molecules and solids, particularly following the poor results of $\omega$B97X-rV and $\omega$B97M-rV. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundation for creating more accurate hybrid functionals and expanding their utility to practical applications.

MAGRATHEA is an open-source code designed to model planet structures with fully differentiated, spherically symmetric interiors. By inputting the mass of individual layers and surface temperature, the code applies the shooting method to iterate hydrostatic boundary conditions until reaching a fitting point, thereby determining the planet's radius. The initial version supports up to four distinct layers composed of iron, silicates, water, and ideal gas. Temperature profiles can generally be selected as isothermal, isentropic, or user-defined functions. Users have extensive flexibility in choosing phase diagrams and equations of state for each layer, with documentation provided for adding new equations of state. This work outlines MAGRATHEA's capabilities and discusses its applications, while inviting the community to contribute to its development via https://github.com/Huang-CL/Magrathea.

Numerous quantum algorithms function as a shift from a specific initial quantum state within a complex system to an unknown target state, representing an eigenvalue of either a Hamiltonian or a transition operator. Frequently, this target state signifies the lowest energy within a specific band. Consequently, approximate quantum calculations involve transitioning not to the solitary minimum-energy state, but to a cluster of states near that minimum. This study examines the dynamics and outcomes of two scenarios for such a process: the migration of population from a single, initially isolated level to the quantum states bordering a band of levels. The first scenario involves a time-independent Hamiltonian, whereas the second involves a moving isolated level. We show that the energy width of the population distribution across the band is primarily governed by the time-energy uncertainty principle, even though the distribution's specific shape varies based on the configuration. Additionally, we analyze the impact of the statistical properties of coupling matrix elements between the isolated level and the band levels. While we utilize multiphoton Raman absorption by an ensemble of Rydberg atoms as our analytical model, the findings are applicable to other quantum computing architectures as well.

High angular resolution observations of Class 0 protostars have generated detailed maps of polarized dust emission within the envelopes of these young, embedded objects. Notably, ALMA's enhanced sensitivity has uncovered a wide range of polarization fractions, highlighting specific regions with unexpectedly high levels of polarized dust. Our objective is to determine the grain alignment conditions and dust properties driving this emission in the inner envelopes (approximately 1000 au) of Class 0 protostars. By analyzing ALMA-derived polarized dust maps alongside molecular line maps of specific tracers, primarily CCH, we investigated a critical component of dust grain alignment theories: the irradiation field. Our results demonstrate that CCH peaks coincide with outflow cavity walls, where polarized dust emission is similarly intensified. Our analysis reveals a tentative correlation between the morphology of polarized intensity and CCH emission, indicating that the radiation field striking cavity walls promotes both grain alignment and warm carbon chain chemistry in these areas. We hypothesize that shocks occurring along outflow cavity walls may serve as an additional photon source contributing to dust grain alignment. However, certain core regions, such as equatorial planes, display enhanced polarized flux despite a lack of radiation-driven chemistry, in areas where radiative torques are theoretically insufficient. This implies that other physical factors, including source geometry and dust grain evolution, likely influence grain alignment.

This paper introduces the Intra- and Inter-Human Relation Networks (I^2R-Net) for multi-person pose estimation, which relies on two fundamental components. The first is the Intra-Human Relation Module, which processes individual subjects to capture internal human dependencies. The second is the Inter-Human Relation Module, which analyzes relationships across multiple instances to focus on inter-personal interactions. Although the Inter-Human Relation Module can be designed to be lightweight by downscaling feature map resolution, it still learns valuable relational information that significantly enhances the performance of the Intra-Human Relation Module. Without any complex additions, our approach can rival or exceed the performance of current competition leaders. We performed extensive experiments on the COCO, CrowdPose, and OCHuman datasets, demonstrating that the proposed model outperforms all state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, it achieves 77.4% AP on the CrowdPose dataset and 67.8% AP on the OCHuman dataset, surpassing existing methods by a substantial margin. Furthermore, ablation studies and visualization analyses confirm the model's effectiveness.

Semi-supervised learning serves as a powerful method for utilizing vast amounts of unlabeled data. This paper introduces a new training approach called Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning (SsCL), which integrates contrastive loss from self-supervised learning with cross-entropy loss from semi-supervised learning, optimizing both objectives end-to-end. Unlike self-training methods that rely on prediction and retraining using identical model weights, SsCL exchanges predictions between two branches for unlabeled data, creating a co-calibration process that improves prediction quality and prevents convergence in local minima. In this framework, the contrastive loss branch captures pairwise sample similarities using neighborhoods derived from the cross-entropy branch, while simultaneously calibrating the cross-entropy branch's prediction distribution based on contrastive similarities. We demonstrate that SsCL generates more discriminative representations and enhances few-shot learning capabilities. Specifically, on the ImageNet dataset with a ResNet50 backbone, SsCL achieves 60.2% and 72.1% top-1 accuracy using only 1% and 10% labeled data, respectively, significantly surpassing baseline models and outperforming existing semi-supervised and self-supervised techniques.

This study presents a search for the decays of heavy, exotic long-lived particles (LLPs) generated in 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the CERN LHC, which subsequently come to rest within the CMS detector. These decays would occur in time intervals distinct from the collision events. The analysis examines two specific decay modes for stopped LLPs: hadronic decays observed in the calorimeter and muonic decays detected in the muon system. The calorimeter search utilized 721 hours of sensitivity across 38.6 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected in 2015 and 2016, while the muon system search covered 744 hours over 39.0 fb$^{-1}$. Results are interpreted within various LLP prediction frameworks, establishing production cross-section limits as a function of the LLP's mass and mean proper lifetime for lifetimes ranging from 100 ns to 10 days. These findings represent the most stringent constraints to date on the mass of hadronically decaying stopped LLPs and constitute the first LHC search for stopped LLPs decaying into muons.

Let $(M,
abla,\langle\;,\;angle)$ denote a manifold equipped with a flat, torsion-free connection $
abla$ and a Riemannian metric $\langle\;,\;angle$, along with the sequence of iterated tangent bundles $(T^kM)_{k\geq1}$ defined by $T^kM = T(T^{k-1}M)$ and $T^1M = TM$. We demonstrate that for every $k\geq1$, the bundle $T^kM$ admits a Hermitian structure $(J_k,g_k)$ and a flat, torsion-free connection $
abla^k$. Furthermore, if $M$ is a Lie group where both $(
abla,\langle\;,\;angle)$ are left-invariant, then each $T^kM$ inherits a Lie group structure such that the triple $(J_k,g_k,
abla^k)$ remains left-invariant.

It is established that the first iteration $(TM,J_1,g_1)$ forms a Kähler manifold if and only if the metric $\langle\;,\;angle$ is Hessian, meaning that in any affine coordinate system $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, the metric components satisfy $\langle\partial_{x_i},\partial_{x_j}angle= rac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_j}}$. Motivated by recent extensions of the Kähler condition, we derive the necessary conditions on $(
abla,\langle\;,\;angle)$ for $(TM,J_1,g_1)$ to be balanced, locally conformally balanced, locally conformally Kähler, pluriclosed, Gauduchon, Vaismann, or Calabi-Yau with torsion. Additionally, we establish criteria at the level of $(
abla,\langle\;,\;angle)$ that ensure specific or all higher-order bundles $(T^kM,J_k,g_k)$ satisfy generalized Kähler conditions.

Specifically, we identify classes of $(M,
abla,\langle\;,\;angle)$ for which $(T^kM,J_k,g_k)$ is both balanced and non-Kähler, yet Calabi-Yau with torsion, for all $k\geq1$. Through a detailed analysis of the geometry of $(M,
abla,\langle\;,\;angle)$, we develop a robust framework to construct extensive families of generalized Kähler manifolds.

Network data, widely utilized across physical, social, and biological disciplines, are characterized by nodes representing individuals and edges signifying their interactions. A primary method for capturing the intricate, high-dimensional nature of such data involves embedding the graph into a lower-dimensional geometric space. Specifically, the curvature of this space offers valuable insights into graph structure, including tendencies toward triangle formation or tree-like configurations. This work derives an estimating function for curvature that relies solely on a distance matrix, utilizing triangle side lengths and midpoints, while also proving its asymptotic normality. Furthermore, we present a new estimator for latent distance matrices in networks and an efficient algorithm to compute it by solving iterative quadratic programs. Application of this approach to the Los Alamos National Laboratory Unified Network and Host dataset demonstrates that curvature estimates can identify red-team attacks more rapidly than basic methods and reveal non-constant latent curvature within physics coauthorship networks.

This paper demonstrates that the spectral theorem—characterizing every self-adjoint matrix as admitting a specific canonical form under unitary similarity—extends to $*$-algebras beyond the complex numbers. When these algebras contain nilpotents, numerous classic matrix decompositions, including the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Takagi decomposition, skew-Takagi decomposition, and Jordan decomposition, emerge naturally as direct consequences of these generalized forms. Consequently, if computing the canonical form of a self-adjoint matrix were a subroutine, generating these classic decompositions would require merely a single function call without extra steps. Furthermore, we propose that operator overloading in programming languages could allow a numerical algorithm for unitary diagonalization of complex self-adjoint matrices to immediately generalize to solving problems like SVD or Takagi decomposition. While algebras without nilpotents (such as the quaternions) exhibit similar unifying properties, the resulting classic decompositions are not as readily derived. In developing this theory, we also establish some spectral results for Clifford algebras of the forms $\cl_{p,q,0}(\mathbb R)$ and $\cl_{p,q,1}(\mathbb R)$, noting that the former is relatively straightforward. The work concludes with a conjecture regarding spectral theorems.

Although lattice vibrations in solids can possess angular momentum, they typically do not behave rotationally like electron spin. Generating such momentum usually requires materials capable of supporting twisted normal modes, orthogonal mode pairs, or magnon excitations. However, these approaches are limited because excessive excitation can breach the Lindemann limit, causing the material to melt. To address this, we propose a theoretical method for inducing phonon angular momentum in the molecular crystal $\rm C_{60}$. Our findings demonstrate that a single laser pulse can transfer substantial angular momentum to $\rm C_{60}$ in a helicity-dependent manner; specifically, switching between right- and left-circularly polarized light reverses the direction of the phonon angular momentum. On ultrafast timescales, the evolution of orbital angular momentum mirrors the displacive excitation of coherent phonons, following a cosine time dependence that contrasts with spin dynamics. Notably, even under intense laser conditions, atomic displacements remain well below the Lindemann criterion. Furthermore, thermal excitation reveals that spinning $\rm C_{60}$ at room temperature generates significant angular momentum, approaching several hundred $\hbar$. These results suggest that similar angular momentum generation via light or heat is feasible across a broad range of fullerenes, including $\rm C_{70}$ and their endohedral derivatives. This discovery establishes a foundation for controlling electronic spins through phononic mechanisms and harvesting thermal energy via phonon angular momentum.

This paper introduces a novel method for developing transferable soft sensors, a critical data-driven application for industrial plant condition monitoring. Although hard sensors are versatile across different facilities, soft sensors are typically restricted to the specific plant and operating conditions for which they were originally designed. To overcome this limitation in data-driven monitoring systems, we propose a solution based on transfer learning. A primary challenge in data-driven modeling is the distribution mismatch between the training data and the target application data, which often degrades model accuracy. To address this, we developed Domain Adversarial Neural Network Regression (DANN-R), a transfer learning-based regression technique tailored for creating transferable soft sensors. Using data from the SCADA system of an industrial power plant, we thoroughly evaluated the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the developed transferable soft sensor effectively adapts to new plants.

Nanoscale heat engines experience significant fluctuations that limit their precision. The Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR) establishes a fundamental trade-off among output power, fluctuations, and entropic cost, a constraint that quantum-coherent systems can potentially surpass. This letter investigates the TUR within a prototypical quantum heat engine, the Scovil & Schulz-DuBois maser, using a classical reference system to isolate the impact of quantum coherence on performance. We analytically identify regions where coherence reduces fluctuations, offering a quantum advantage, alongside regions where it amplifies them. Notably, these fluctuation dynamics cannot be predicted solely from the off-diagonal elements of the density matrix; because fluctuations are not fully captured by the steady state, TUR violations stem from coherence effects that extend beyond steady-state properties. Although the system breaches the conventional TUR, it complies with a recently proposed quantum TUR formulation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that parameters driving the engine near the conventional limit are common, making TUR violations in this quantum model a frequent occurrence.

This study examines the unique determination of impenetrable obstacles or diffraction grating profiles within polyhedral domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ based on a single far-field measurement, with a specific focus on impedance-type scattering objects. We establish two new results regarding the unique identifiability of the inverse scattering problem in these complex settings. The core technical approach leverages specific quantitative geometric characteristics of Laplacian eigenfunctions, building upon our previous work [8,9]. In this paper, we develop novel geometric properties that extend and generalize findings from [9], thereby facilitating the derivation of these new identifiability results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that alongside recovering the shape of the obstacle or grating profile, it is possible to simultaneously retrieve the boundary impedance parameters.

Current coding curricula frequently require students to create interactive programs with complex dynamics, such as mouse-controlled games. Although these assignments are educationally valuable, existing autonomous feedback mechanisms are insufficient, as traditional unit tests cannot evaluate interactive code. This paper addresses the challenge of grading such programs by framing it as a classification task for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Specifically, each student's submission defines an MDP in which an agent must operate; the system then generalizes to determine if the underlying dynamics and reward model are correct or flawed. By establishing a cooperative objective between an agent and an autoregressive model, we enable the agent to sample differential trajectories from the input MDP, allowing a classifier to assess its validity through a method we call "Play to Grade." This approach facilitates an automated feedback system for interactive coding tasks. Additionally, we provide a dataset comprising 711,274 anonymized submissions for a single assignment, annotated with hand-coded bug labels to aid future research.

We introduce a method to precisely learn the dynamics of slow collective variables from atomistic data derived from ab-initio quantum mechanics, utilizing generalized Langevin equations (GLE). Within the Mori-Zwanzig formalism and adhering to the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, we construct the force fields, memory kernel, and noise generator. When integrated with Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics (DeePMD) and density functional theory, this GLE framework enables first-principles multi-scale modeling across diverse systems. We validate this capability by examining the dynamics of twin domain walls in ferroelectric lead titanate. Our results highlight the significance of memory effects, showing that while ab-initio GLE aligns closely with molecular dynamics near equilibrium, Markovian Langevin dynamics underestimates rare event rates by multiple orders of magnitude.

Mobile applications are now essential for both individuals and organizations providing digital services. Due to the inherent mobility of devices, these apps can be used in any location or condition, including areas without internet access. Consequently, an "offline-first" approach is a critical quality attribute for mobile apps. However, failing to properly manage connectivity changes or neglecting established best practices often results in bugs and crashes, which erode user confidence in app quality. This paper introduces the first study on Eventual Connectivity (ECn) issues in Android applications, based on a manual inspection of 971 scenarios across 50 open-source apps. We identified 304 ECn instances (averaging six per app) and categorized them into a taxonomy of 10 groups. Our analysis reveals that most ECn issues stem from messages that fail to accurately inform users about connectivity status or from the improper delegation of connectivity checks to external libraries and apps. Drawing on these findings, we provide a set of lessons learned for practitioners and researchers, outlining potential directions for future research.

Dynamic adaptation has emerged as a critical method for speeding up distributed machine learning (ML) training. Recent research indicates that dynamically modifying model architecture (such as applying the lottery ticket hypothesis) or hyperparameters (like batch size) can substantially accelerate training without compromising accuracy. However, current ML cluster schedulers are not equipped to manage this dynamic nature. We demonstrate that existing approaches struggle to maintain fairness and suffer reduced system efficiency when training throughput fluctuates under dynamic adaptation. To address this, we introduce Shockwave, a scheduler incorporating future planning based on two core principles: first, it adapts classic market theory from static to dynamic environments to jointly optimize efficiency and fairness; second, it employs stochastic dynamic programming to manage dynamic variations. We implemented a system for Shockwave and evaluated it using trace-driven simulations and real cluster experiments. The results indicate that for ML job traces involving dynamic adaptation, Shockwave achieves a 1.3X reduction in makespan and a 2X improvement in fairness compared to existing fair scheduling schemes.

This study tackles the challenge of generating background music for videos. While prior research has successfully produced effective music, it often fails to create melodious tracks specifically tailored to a video's content and neglects rhythmic synchronization between the video and music. To address this, we first define the rhythmic relationships between the two media by aligning video timing, motion speed, and motion saliency with corresponding musical features: beat, simulated note density, and simulated note strength. We then introduce CMT, a Controllable Music Transformer, which facilitates local adjustments to these rhythmic attributes while allowing global control over music genre and instrumentation. Both objective and subjective evaluations confirm that the generated music exhibits high compatibility with the input videos and maintains excellent audio quality. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/wzk1015/video-bgm-generation.

Although applying Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) to identify nonlinear systems has shown great promise, significant practical and theoretical challenges persist despite extensive recent research. The most critical unresolved issues involve noise management, model consistency, and achieving reliable estimation while minimizing prediction error. The latter problem introduces several practical hurdles, including a surge in computational costs regarding data sample volume and optimization instabilities. This study addresses these challenges by introducing a method that combines a truncated prediction loss with a subspace encoder for state estimation. The truncated prediction loss is calculated by averaging losses across multiple truncated segments of the time series. To ensure computational efficiency while minimizing this loss, we employ a subspace encoder modeled by an ANN, designed to approximate the state reconstructability map of the estimated model. This provides an initial state for each segment based on historical inputs and outputs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that, under mild conditions, this approach is locally consistent, enhances optimization stability, and improves data efficiency through overlapping subsections. Finally, we offer practical insights and user guidelines supported by a numerical example and comparisons with state-of-the-art benchmarks.

Current state-of-the-art methods for Sanskrit Dependency Parsing (SDP) are hybrid, utilizing lexicon-driven shallow parsers for linguistically motivated feature engineering; however, they struggle with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, restricting their practical utility. Conversely, purely data-driven models underperform compared to hybrid systems due to data sparsity. This study investigates the limits of a purely data-driven approach in low-resource settings by employing five strategies: data augmentation, sequential transfer learning, cross-lingual/mono-lingual pretraining, multi-task learning, and self-training. Our proposed ensemble system surpasses the best existing purely data-driven method by an absolute gain of 2.8/3.9 points in Unlabelled/Labelled Attachment Score (UAS/LAS). Notably, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art hybrid system by 1.2 points in UAS while achieving comparable LAS results. The code and data will be made publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/Jivnesh/SanDP}.

The primary barrier to developing integrated gallium nitride (GaN) electronics stems from its low hole mobility. This study investigates enhancing GaN's hole mobility through epitaxial matching with recently synthesized II-IV nitrides, specifically ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$. Utilizing advanced *ab initio* Boltzmann transport equation calculations, we demonstrate that applying effective uniaxial compressive strain to GaN along the $[1\bar{1}00]$ direction via lattice matching to these materials causes an inversion between the heavy hole and split-off hole bands. This inversion reduces the effective hole mass in the direction of compression. Our findings indicate that lattice matching to ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ boosts room-temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, compared to unstrained GaN. Furthermore, analysis of strain-dependent trends reveals a highly nonlinear mobility variation; notably, a hypothetical solid solution of Zn$_{0.75}$Ge$_{0.75}$Mg$_{0.25}$Si$_{0.25}$N$_2$ could achieve a 160% increase in hole mobility.

We conducted a systematic search for broad-velocity-width molecular features (BVFs) within the Galactic disk using CO J = 1-0 survey data collected by the Nobeyama Radio Observatory 45 m telescope. This investigation identified 58 BVFs. When compared against infrared and radio continuum images, 36 BVFs were found to have counterparts in both wavelengths; of these, 15 are documented in the literature as molecular outflows from young stellar objects. Additionally, 21 BVFs possess only infrared counterparts, with eight of them also described as molecular outflows in existing literature. A single BVF (CO 16.134-0.553) lacks any luminous counterpart in other wavelengths, suggesting it may be analogous to high-velocity compact clouds found in the Galactic center.

This paper examines the equivariant homotopy type of a connected sum of linear actions on complex projective planes, as defined by Hambleton and Tanase for cyclic groups of odd order. By employing spheres within unitary representations, we establish cellular filtrations on these connected sums. A carefully selected filtration yields a splitting in equivariant homology for all cyclic groups of prime power order, and for general cyclic groups provided a specific divisibility condition holds.

Although Reinforcement Learning (RL) has achieved significant results in various complex virtual settings, substantial obstacles remain when addressing problems where natural language is central. Interactive Fiction Games (also known as Text Games) represent such a challenge, presenting partially observable environments that necessitate the use of natural language within RL solutions. Consequently, this survey aims to facilitate the creation of novel Text Game problem settings and RL solutions driven by natural language. Specifically, it provides a systematic review by: 1) outlining the unique challenges inherent to Text Game RL, 2) detailing tools for generating and evaluating Text Games and their resulting environments, and 3) comparing existing agent architectures to highlight benchmark methodologies and future research opportunities.

E. Breuillard established that for any finite subset $F$ of matrices within $GL_d(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ that generates a non-virtually solvable group, the normalized height $\widehat{h}(F)$ satisfies $\widehat{h}(F) \ge \epsilon_d$ for some $\epsilon_d > 0$. This normalized height quantifies the arithmetic magnitude of $F$, framing the result as a non-abelian counterpart to Lehmer's Mahler measure problem. We present a more concise proof of this theorem, leveraging the existence of specific word maps in compact Lie groups (referred to as almost laws) whose images remain proximate to the identity element.

We introduce a Temporal Difference (TD) learning approach designed to tackle key challenges in robot navigation within marine environments. To enhance data efficiency, the method integrates TD updates with Gaussian Process regression. To facilitate online predictions, we propose a sparse approximation that offers superior quality compared to existing rejection-based techniques. By deriving the predictive value function posterior and utilizing its moments, we develop SPGP-SARSA, a novel algorithm for model-free policy evaluation. We further demonstrate that SPGP-SARSA can be easily adapted into its model-based equivalent, SPGP-TD. Through extensive simulations and physical trials with an underwater robot, our results indicate that SPGP-SARSA surpasses current state-of-the-art sparse methods, matches the prediction accuracy of its exact counterpart, and effectively solves underwater navigation tasks.

We introduce the first period-luminosity (PL) and period-Wesenheit (PW) relations for fundamental-mode anomalous Cepheids in the gri bands. These relations are based on a combined sample of five anomalous Cepheids from the globular cluster M92 and the Large Magellanic Cloud, both of which have distances known to approximately 1% accuracy from existing literature. Our g-band PL relation aligns with previous B-band PL findings. Applying these relations to anomalous Cepheids in the dwarf galaxy Crater II yields a distance modulus that is larger yet consistent with recent RR Lyrae-based measurements. Although our gri-band PL and PW calibrations are less precise due to the limited sample size of anomalous Cepheids, they will prove valuable for determining distances to dwarf galaxies.

Inspired by research into stochastic systems modeling the non-equilibrium behavior of real-valued spins within an infinite particle system in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we examine a row-finite system of stochastic differential equations featuring dissipative drift. The existence and uniqueness of solutions over infinite time intervals are established through finite volume approximation and an application of the Ovsjannikov method.

Numerous compelling theories extending beyond the Standard Model forecast signals characterized by atypical charged particle paths. Events where these unusual tracks are the most prominent feature present substantial hurdles for Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments, especially concerning trigger systems. This paper investigates track-based triggers for a selection of representative long-lived and non-standard signatures anticipated at the High Luminosity LHC, alongside providing recommendations for the target parameters of a hardware tracking system. The examined scenarios encompass large multiplicities of low-momentum tracks generated by a soft-unclustered-energy-pattern model, displaced leptons and anomalous prompt tracks arising from a Supersymmetry model featuring long-lived staus, and displaced hadrons predicted within a Higgs portal scenario involving long-lived scalars.

Coherence distillation represents a fundamental task within the resource theory of coherence. This paper establishes a framework for approximate coherence distillation utilizing strictly incoherent operations. The proposed protocol addresses scenarios where deterministic conversion from an initial state $\rho$ to a target state $\psi$ is impossible; instead, the objective is to deterministically transform $\rho$ into an intermediate state $\phi$ that maximizes fidelity with respect to $\psi$. Additionally, we provide an explicit strategy for this approximate coherence distillation process.

As society becomes increasingly reliant on communication technologies, ensuring resilience against network attacks is crucial for safeguarding digital sovereignty. While new network developments address resilience through in-network computing at higher protocol layers, the physical layer remains an unresolved challenge, especially in wireless systems where the open medium inherently invites adversarial attacks. In denial-of-service (DoS) scenarios, active adversaries can fully disrupt communication; it has been demonstrated that Turing machines cannot detect such attacks. Since Turing machines define the fundamental limits of digital information processing—and thus of digital twins—this means that even the most powerful digital twins capable of error-free information preservation cannot identify these attacks. This limitation raises the question of the computational power required to detect DoS attacks. Consequently, this paper advocates for neuromorphic twins and presents a first implementation using Blum-Shub-Smale machines that enables DoS detection, a result valid whether or not the adversary's input and jamming sequences are constrained.

This paper investigates non-Gaussianity within multiple-field inflation models by employing the field equation approach. We begin by reviewing the background and perturbation framework of such models, followed by the derivation of the second-order Klein-Gordon equation for perturbations. Subsequently, we compute the tree-level bispectrum of field perturbations and determine the corresponding non-linearity parameter $f_{NL}$ for the curvature perturbation $\zeta$ using the $\delta N$ formalism. Our results are compared with those derived from the Lagrangian formalism, showing consistency between the two methods. This study aims to deepen our understanding of inflationary perturbation theory.

We describe the helicity-sensitive terahertz photovoltaic response observed in a carbon nanotube configured as a field-effect transistor. Our findings indicate that the rectified voltage magnitude varies depending on whether the incident radiation is clockwise or anticlockwise circularly polarized. We demonstrate that this phenomenon serves as a signature of plasma wave interference within the transistor channel. Furthermore, we establish that this helicity- and phase-sensitive component of the photovoltaic response is a universal effect, occurring across systems with varying dimensionalities and single-particle spectra. The magnitude of this effect characterizes the plasma wave decay length, thereby opening new possibilities for applications in plasmonic interferometry.

This article offers a concise historical overview and evaluates our present knowledge of jets in radio galaxies and quasars through an observational lens, focusing primarily on radio wavelength data. It summarizes recent findings regarding the Fanaroff-Riley classification system, detailing the characteristics of radio structures and jets within both FR classes and high- versus low-excitation radio galaxies. The discussion covers the collimation and propagation of jets from nuclear sub-parsec scales out to hundreds of kiloparsecs, drawing on both observational and theoretical research. Evidence indicates that jets interact with a clumpy interstellar medium, particularly in young sources, potentially triggering or suppressing star formation based on specific physical conditions. The article presents observational data on these interactions and jet feedback mechanisms, which significantly impact our understanding of galaxy evolution. Additionally, it addresses recurrent jet activity observed across various projected linear sizes and time scales. The review concludes by briefly exploring unresolved questions about jets that future telescopes may help clarify.

This study explores the application of a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to estimate the maximum launch range of the Weapon Engagement Zone (WEZ). The WEZ defines an airspace around an aircraft where an adversary faces a high probability of being hit by a specific missile. We present a methodology that determines the WEZ for a given missile by training a DNN on 50,000 simulated launches conducted under varied conditions. This model achieves a coefficient of determination of 0.99, enabling accurate predictions of the WEZ across different firing scenarios. Unlike prior research, this approach utilizes a non-discretized model that simultaneously accounts for all directions within the WEZ. Furthermore, the proposed method employs an experimental design that reduces the number of required simulation runs, thereby accelerating the training process.

Owen and Hoyt recently demonstrated that effective dimensionality provides crucial structural insights into the input-output mappings of artificial neural networks. Building on this research, the present study introduces an estimation method to compute mean dimensionality from a dataset without requiring resampling from external distributions. This approach generates total indices for independent features and a corresponding variant for correlated features, which exhibits the zero independence property. Using synthetic data, we examine the layer-by-layer evolution of mean dimensionality and the influence of activation functions on interaction magnitudes. We subsequently apply mean dimensionality to analyze prominent convolutional architectures for image recognition, including LeNet, ResNet, and DenseNet. To address pixel correlations, we propose calculating mean dimensionality after an inverse PCA layer, enabling analysis on uncorrelated, PCA-transformed features without retraining the network. We utilize generalized total indices to create heatmaps for post-hoc explanations and apply mean dimensionality to PCA-transformed features for cross-architectural comparisons. The results offer valuable insights into the varying magnitudes of interactions across different architectures and reveal how mean dimensionality changes during training.

The idea of digital twins—interconnected digital replicas of physical systems—is attracting growing interest for modeling and simulating entire cities. Foundational to this concept is the creation of a 3D city model, typically represented as a mesh. However, constructing and updating these models is a labor-intensive task requiring significant manual effort, particularly when defining building geometries. This paper introduces a new algorithm and implementation designed to automatically, efficiently, and robustly generate meshes for large-scale urban modeling and simulation. The method utilizes standard, publicly accessible data, specifically 2D cadastral maps (building footprints) and 3D point clouds derived from aerial scans. It produces Level of Detail 1.2 city models in two formats: triangular surface meshes optimized for visualization and high-quality tetrahedral volume meshes suitable for simulation. Experimental results show strong performance and scalability, with potential for further optimization through parallelization. The ultimate objective is to develop a generic volume mesh generator for city digital twins capable of providing nearly real-time mesh manipulation at Level of Detail 2.x.

The Bohr atomic model relies on the premise that electrons occupying permitted, quantized orbits do not emit radiation. Key outcomes of this model are the determination of the radii for circular quantized paths and the energy levels of the hydrogen atom. The text provides quantum mechanical foundations for both Bohr's hypothesis and the established formula for orbital radii, which is essential for calculating energy levels.

Understanding the transition between chaotic and integrable regimes in spectral statistics is crucial for investigating Many Body Localization (MBL) in physical systems. The $\beta$-ensemble serves as a key example due to its structural simplicity; however, while its energy level correlations have been extensively analyzed, its eigenvector properties have remained largely unexamined. This study numerically investigates these eigenvector characteristics, revealing that the Anderson transition occurs at $\gamma = 1$ and ergodicity breaks down at $\gamma = 0$, given the repulsion parameter is defined as $\beta = N^{-\gamma}$. Consequently, alongside the Rosenzweig-Porter ensemble (RPE), the $\beta$-ensemble demonstrates the presence of Non-Ergodic Extended (NEE) states across a finite parameter range ($0 < \gamma < 1$). We observe that the chaotic-integrable transition aligns with the breakdown of ergodicity in the $\beta$-ensemble, whereas in the RPE or the 1-D disordered spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, this alignment occurs at the localization transition. Therefore, the dynamical time-scales within the NEE regime of the $\beta$-ensemble differ from those in the latter models.

Gravitationally bound neutrons have emerged as a vital instrument for experimental investigations into new physics, including potential modifications to Newtonian gravity and dark matter candidates. In this work, we incorporate relativistic effects arising from mass-energy equivalence into the framework of gravitationally bound neutrons. Specifically, we analyze a correction to the Hamiltonian of such a neutron caused by an external magnetic field. We demonstrate that the additional weight resulting from mass-energy equivalence induces minor shifts in the neutron's eigenenergies and eigenstates, and we assess the implications of this relativistic correction for experiments involving trapped neutrons. Furthermore, we evaluate the ultimate precision achievable in estimating the relativistic contribution to the precession frequency, revealing that at short time intervals, a joint measurement of both spin and motional degrees of freedom offers a metrological advantage over measuring the spin alone.

Most proposals for physics beyond the standard model suggest that neutrinos possess new interactions, some of which, despite currently appearing theoretical, will likely need to be considered in future neutrino experiments. This study demonstrates that such new interactions could lead to the misidentification of neutrino flavors and impact the experimental capability to distinguish between neutrinos and antineutrinos.

We present Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) findings for the itinerant ferromagnets LaCrGe3, CeCrGe3, and PrCrGe3. In the paramagnetic temperature range, these materials exhibit well-defined and highly similar spectra associated with itinerant Cr 3d spins. However, as the temperature drops below approximately 90 K, marking the onset of Cr ferromagnetic ordering, distinct spectral structures emerge that evolve differently across the three compounds. Specifically, resonance signals are detectable only in the paramagnetic region for the Ce- and Pr-based compounds, whereas in the La-compound, the resonance persists well below the ferromagnetic ordering temperature. We analyze this divergence by examining the unique interplay between 4f and 3d magnetism, a phenomenon particularly notable given that CeCrGe3 exhibits heavy fermion behavior even within its magnetically ordered state.

We demonstrate the local asymptotic normality (LAN) property for estimating a multidimensional parameter within the drift of a system of $N$ interacting particles, observed over a fixed time horizon under a mean-field regime as $N \rightarrow \infty$. Utilizing the classical framework of Ibragimov and Hasminski, we derive precise results for the maximum likelihood estimator that extend beyond standard asymptotic normality. Leveraging Hájek's convolution theorem and robust control of the likelihood process, we establish asymptotic minimax optimality (up to constants). These structural findings provide insight into the associated nonlinear McKean-Vlasov experiment and allow us to formulate simple, explicit criteria ensuring the identifiability and non-degeneracy of the Fisher information matrix. Such conditions are also valuable for recent research concerning parametric inference in interacting diffusions.

Although current state-of-the-art adaptive optics (AO) enables ground-based, diffraction-limited imaging with high Strehl ratios (SR), fully leveraging these datasets necessitates a precise understanding of the point spread function (PSF). This requirement becomes even more critical for next-generation AO systems on 30-meter class telescopes, where PSF characterization is essential to meet scientific goals. Consequently, there is increasing demand for tools capable of accurately reconstructing the observed PSF of AO systems, known as PSF reconstruction. In this context, the MICADO@ELT instrument has designated a PSF-R service as a key deliverable, a development led by our group. For MICADO, a "blind" PSF-R strategy is being adopted to maximize applicability across diverse science cases; this approach reconstructs the PSF using only telemetry and calibration data, without extracting information from the science images themselves. While our PSF-R algorithm is still under development, its implementation is sufficiently mature to evaluate performance using real observations. This presentation will address the reliability of our reconstructed PSFs and the uncertainties they introduce in measuring scientific quantities, specifically for bright, on-axis observations captured with the LBT's SOUL+LUCI instrument. This marks the first application of our algorithm to actual data, demonstrating its readiness and establishing a foundation for future testing. Our algorithm successfully reconstructs the SR and full-width at half maximum (FWHM) of observed PSFs with errors under 2% and 4.5%, respectively. Furthermore, we conducted a scientific evaluation of these reconstructed PSFs using a specialized set of simulated observations for an ideal science scenario.

This study introduces methodologies to measure the significance of agent interactions and their effect on global performance metrics within networks modeled as linear time-invariant systems. By utilizing Gramian-based metrics, we introduce a new concept of edge centrality that represents the first-order change in the metric resulting from alterations to edge weights, even for non-existent edges. The resulting Edge Centrality Matrix (ECM) is additive across inputs, meaning it isolates the specific contribution of individual actuators to each edge's centrality. We fully characterize the ECM structure for directed stem-bud networks, demonstrating that non-zero values occur only at specific sub/super-diagonals dictated by network dimensions and bud length. Furthermore, we establish bounds on the trace, trace inverse, and log-det of the Gramian before and after single-edge changes, as well as limits on modification weights to maintain network stability. Finally, simulations demonstrate the practical value of this edge centrality framework and confirm our theoretical findings.

A graph is defined as 1-plane if it can be embedded in a plane such that every edge is crossed by at most one other edge. In such graphs, a crossing is termed an $\times$-crossing if the edges involved form a matching at their endpoints. This paper presents a linear-time algorithm for computing the vertex connectivity of 1-plane graphs that lack $\times$-crossings. The approach relies on the observation that for any two vertices within a minimum separating set $S$, their distance in an auxiliary planar graph $\Lambda(G)$ is limited. The graph $\Lambda(G)$ is constructed by planarizing $G$ and adding a new vertex to each face, connected to all vertices on that face. Consequently, the problem reduces to finding a minimum separating set within specific subgraphs $\Lambda_i$ of $\Lambda(G)$, which possess small diameters. Because $\Lambda(G)$ is planar, these subgraphs have low treewidth. Furthermore, every minimum separating set $S$ induces a partition of $\Lambda_i$ into three distinct vertex sets with particular characteristics; such a partition can be identified in linear time using Courcelle's theorem.

This paper examines the expressive capabilities of successor-invariant first-order logic, an extension that permits the use of a successor relation provided that formula validity remains unaffected by the specific successor choice on finite structures. We demonstrate that under bounded degree constraints, this logic possesses no greater expressive power than standard first-order logic.

Predicting the dynamics of an underlying system using only scalar or partial time series data is a frequent challenge in time series analysis. While Takens' theorem establishes that time-delayed embeddings of partial states on smooth compact manifolds are diffeomorphic to the attractor, learning these delay mappings remains difficult for chaotic and highly nonlinear systems. To address this, we employ deep artificial neural networks (ANNs) to learn both discrete time maps and continuous time flows derived from partial state observations. Additionally, given training data for the full state, we train a reconstruction map. This approach enables time series predictions based on the current state and several prior observations, with embedding parameters derived from time series analysis. The resulting state space for time evolution has a dimension comparable to reduced-order manifold models, offering distinct advantages over recurrent neural networks, which typically demand high-dimensional internal states, extra memory terms, or numerous hyperparameters. We demonstrate the efficacy of deep ANNs in predicting chaotic behavior from scalar observations on a three-dimensional manifold using the Lorenz system. Furthermore, we examine multivariate observations within the context of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, noting that the observation dimension necessary for accurate dynamic reproduction increases with the manifold's dimension due to the system's spatial extent.

An expression for the two-particle relaxation time of collective excitations on a distorted Fermi surface is derived within the diffusion framework of kinetic theory, addressing the general case of momentum-dependent diffusion and drift coefficients, and the temperature dependence of this expression is determined.

Taking electrocardiograms as a case study, we illustrate the inherent issues that emerge when standard convolutional networks attempt to model one-dimensional signals with imprecise, repeating patterns. We demonstrate that these challenges are systemic, stemming from the way convolutional networks process composite objects where components possess significant mobility rather than being rigidly fixed. Furthermore, we highlight several counterintuitive phenomena concerning generalization within deep networks.

The IceCube experiment has detected PeV-energy neutrinos arriving from beyond our Galaxy, exhibiting an energy flux comparable to that of TeV gamma rays and EeV cosmic rays. Because neutrinos offer an unobstructed perspective, they are the only means to study the cosmic accelerators responsible for the highest-energy radiation reaching Earth. This review outlines the rationale behind constructing kilometer-scale neutrino detectors, detailing how the IceCube project converted a cubic kilometer of deep, transparent Antarctic ice into a massive neutrino telescope. It summarizes findings from the first decade of operations, including the current status of cosmic neutrino observations and the identification of the first source, the supermassive black hole TXS 0506+056. The text subsequently provides a detailed look at the phenomenology of cosmic accelerators. Beyond searching for the origins of Galactic and extragalactic cosmic rays, the scientific missions of IceCube and similar instruments being built in the Mediterranean Sea and Lake Baikal also encompass observing Galactic supernovae, searching for dark matter, and studying neutrinos themselves. Derived from notes for summer school lectures, this review is designed to be accessible to nonexperts.

Retrieving high-quality bitexts for low-resource languages presents significant challenges. This study demonstrates that sentence representations from language models fine-tuned using a contrastive objective with multiple negatives ranking loss effectively identify clean bitexts. Experimental results indicate that parallel data extracted via this approach significantly surpasses the previous state-of-the-art method when applied to the low-resource languages Khmer and Pashto.

G\"{o}del-type metrics that exhibit homogeneity across both space and time remain consistent within Chern-Simons modified gravity, similar to the Schwarzschild metric, regardless of whether the framework is non-dynamical or dynamical. Both frameworks involve an additional pseudoscalar field coupled to the Pontryagin density. This study examines stationary first-order perturbations to these metrics specifically within the non-dynamical framework. Under specific assumptions, we derive analytical solutions for the perturbed field equations. These solutions demonstrate that the translational and cylindrical symmetries of the original metrics are broken. Furthermore, the perturbation parameter influences the effective potential governing planar geodesic orbits, thereby altering the equilibrium radii for both massive particles and massless photons.

We examine simply connected isothermic surfaces where the Hopf differential decomposes into a real function and a meromorphic quadratic differential. This differential is holomorphic and non-vanishing everywhere except at a specific point where it possesses a zero or a pole. When restricted to a simply connected region excluding this exceptional point, both Darboux and Calapso transformations generate new isothermic surfaces. We analyze the limiting behavior of these transformed regions as the zero or pole of the meromorphic quadratic differential is approached, specifically investigating the continuity of these surfaces at that point.

Rastall gravity represents a significant modification of General Relativity (GR), and this study investigates the polarization modes of Gravitational Waves (GWs) within this framework. Our findings indicate that at vast distances from the source, Rastall gravity converges with GR, yielding only two massless tensor polarization modes for GWs. We subsequently expanded our analysis to examine the quasinormal modes of black holes in Rastall gravity under non-linear electrodynamic conditions. Specifically, we assessed the effects of various surrounding fields—cosmological, dust, phantom, quintessence, and radiation—on these modes in the presence of electrodynamic sources. Additionally, we evaluated the sensitivity of quasinormal modes to the Rastall parameter ($\lambda$), the black hole structural constant ($N_s$), and the black hole charge ($Q$). The results demonstrate that black holes with non-linear electrodynamic sources exhibit notable deviations from standard charged black holes in Rastall gravity under specific conditions, and that both the black hole behavior and its quasinormal modes are contingent upon the type of surrounding field involved.

In the fuzzy dark matter (FDM) framework, dark matter consists of ultra-light particles possessing a de Broglie wavelength of approximately kpc; beyond this scale, the behavior resembles that of cold dark matter (CDM). Consequently, FDM inhibits structure formation on small scales, thereby postponing the cosmic dawn (CD) and the subsequent epoch of reionization (EoR). This delay potentially leaves observable imprints in both the sky-averaged global 21-cm signal and 21-cm fluctuations, which can be investigated using current and upcoming global and intensity mapping surveys. Reliable detection requires incorporating key physical effects, such as dark-matter/baryon relative velocities and Lyman-Werner star-formation feedback, both of which further delay the signal, alongside CMB and \lya heating mechanisms that can substantially alter the signal's amplitude and timing based on the intensity of X-ray heating from the first stellar remnants. In this study, we simulate the 21-cm signal within FDM cosmologies spanning the CD and EoR phases using an enhanced version of the public code 21cmFAST. This modified code integrates all aforementioned effects and couples directly with the Boltzmann solver CLASS to comprehensively explore degeneracies between cosmological and astrophysical parameters. We assess the feasibility of distinguishing FDM from CDM and forecast the joint constraints on FDM, astrophysical, and cosmological parameters attainable by intensity mapping projects like HERA and global signal experiments such as EDGES. Our results indicate that HERA could detect FDM particle masses ranging from $10^{-19}\,{\rm eV}$ to $10^{-18}\,{\rm eV}$, contingent upon foreground assumptions, even when accounting for the delaying and heating mechanisms present in our analysis.

The ontological models framework differentiates between $\psi$-ontic and $\psi$-epistemic wavefunctions. While it is generally easy to classify the wavefunction of a specific quantum theory, a debate persists regarding the ontological status of the wavefunction within the statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics: is it $\psi$-epistemic and incomplete, or $\psi$-ontic and complete? I will argue that within this interpretation, the wavefunction is best understood as $\psi$-ontic yet incomplete.

Contemporary civil, mechanical, and aeronautical infrastructure is shifting toward continuous, automated, and online maintenance protocols to enhance safety and reliability. Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) is central to this transition, with active sensing acousto-ultrasound guided-wave techniques showing significant promise due to their sensitivity to minor structural changes. However, the robustness and diagnostic effectiveness of these methods are often compromised by environmental and operational fluctuations, such as temperature variations. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel stochastic time-series framework designed to model guided wave propagation across varying thermal conditions. It proposes specific stochastic time-varying models, including Recursive Maximum Likelihood Time-varying Auto-Regressive (RML-TAR) and Recursive Maximum Likelihood Time-varying Auto-Regressive with Exogenous Excitation (RML-TARX), to capture the underlying dynamics of wave propagation under thermal stress. The identification procedure's steps and components are detailed and clarified. Subsequently, these identified models are utilized for one-step-ahead predictions and the "simulation" of guided wave signals. From a physics-based perspective, high-fidelity finite element (FE) models were also developed to simulate the impact of temperature changes on guided wave propagation. Finally, surrogate models were constructed using stochastic time-dependent RML-TARX models and evaluated against the FE models under varying temperature scenarios.

The Scaled Relative Graph (SRG) extends the Nyquist diagram to nonlinear operators, enabling the graphical definition of nonlinear robustness margins. This abstract investigates methods for shaping an operator's SRG to optimize these margins.

In 1937, Ivan Vinogradov demonstrated that every sufficiently large odd natural number can be expressed as the sum of three primes, a result known as the weak Goldbach Conjecture. This work utilizes tools such as Dirichlet's Theorem and modular arithmetic to extend Vinogradov's findings, proving that every sufficiently large natural number—whether even or odd—is representable as a sum of three primes. We examine specific configurations of primes for particular three-prime sum cases, thereby establishing Vinogradov's Theorem as a subset of this broader result. Furthermore, we illustrate the bidirectional relationship between Vinogradov's Theorem and the Goldbach Conjecture, showing how one implies the other and vice versa. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the threshold of "sufficiently large" numbers and conclude by exploring the connections between the partition functions of Vinogradov integers $w(v)$ and Goldbach integers $w(m)$.

To accelerate reactive transport (RT) simulations, we substituted the geochemical solver in the RT code with surrogate models—specifically, trained deep neural networks (DNNs) or k-nearest neighbor (kNN) regressors. Our study examines the 2D leaching of hardened cement paste under both diffusive and advective-dispersive conditions, utilizing a solid solution model for calcium silicate hydrates with either 4 or 7 chemical components, while benchmarking against the HPx (coupled Hydrus-PHREEQC) baseline code. Results indicate that both the HPx-DNN and HPx-kNN emulators deliver satisfactorily accurate to highly precise predictions, offering speedups of 3 to 9 times compared to HPx running parallelized geochemical calculations across 4 cores. When benchmarked against single-threaded HPx, these speedups range from 8 to 33. Notably, when DNN regression and kNN searches are executed on a GPU, both emulators achieve near-optimal performance. Crucially, for the more intricate 7-component cement system, no globally accurate emulator could be constructed for the entire range of possible geochemical conditions. Instead, we developed "local" emulators valid only within a relevant subset of the input parameter space, identified by running a computationally inexpensive coarse full RT simulation and subsequently exploring the region via kernel density sampling. Future research will aim to enhance accuracy for these complex cement systems.

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center ensembles function as sensors for detecting NMR signals from micron-scale samples at room temperature. The high magnetic field regime is particularly valuable because it generates significant nuclear thermal polarization, ensuring a robust sensor response even in low-concentration samples, while simultaneously making chemical shifts and J-couplings more accessible. However, this regime has remained largely unexplored due to the challenges of coupling NV-based sensors with high-frequency nuclear signals. In this study, we overcome this obstacle using a technique that maps relevant energy shifts onto the amplitude of an induced nuclear spin signal, which is then transferred to the sensor. This process includes free-precession intervals for the sample's nuclear spins during which the sensor remains inactive. Consequently, our approach achieves high spectral resolution, ultimately constrained only by the coherence of the nuclear spin signal.

The stochastic sandpile model (SSM) extends the standard Abelian sandpile model (ASM) by introducing randomness into the toppling process of unstable vertices. Specifically, when a vertex becomes unstable, it distributes one grain to each neighbor independently with a probability $p \in (0,1)$. This study focuses on the SSM applied to complete graphs, presenting a stochastic adaptation of Dhar's burning algorithm to determine the recurrence of specific stable configurations. We demonstrate that the recurrent states of the SSM can be expressed as convex combinations of the recurrent states found in the ASM. This insight enables the recovery of a established theorem stating that the count of integer lattice points within the $n$-dimensional permutation polytope equals the number of labeled spanning forests on $n$ vertices. Furthermore, we examine a class of "partial" SSMs where certain vertices topple stochastically while others behave deterministically, similar to the ASM. We establish that this distinction is significant, resulting in recurrent state sets that generally differ from those of both the pure ASM and SSM. Additionally, we prove that generating all recurrent states of the SSM is possible by allowing up to two vertices to topple deterministically.

In the preliminary design of space missions, it is beneficial to identify dynamic regions that govern system behavior or distinguish between qualitatively different dynamics. While Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCS) are extensively utilized in dynamical systems analysis by extending the concepts of stable and unstable manifolds to time-dependent systems, their application in three-dimensional astrodynamics has remained limited. This paper applies the authors' novel numerical method, DA-LCS, to astrodynamics using the Elliptic-Restricted Three-Body Problem (ER3BP) as a case study. We demonstrate the ability to construct full three-dimensional LCS for the Sun-Mars ER3BP directly from variational LCS theory, even under numerically difficult initial conditions. The analysis details how the LCS separates regions of distinct behavior without prior knowledge. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of integration duration and initial condition parameterization on the resulting LCS. Finally, we address round-off errors stemming from floating-point arithmetic limits in the most challenging scenarios and offer practical strategies to mitigate these issues.

We establish the regularity of solutions to the strain tensor equation on a region $S$ where the Gauss curvature changes sign. Additionally, we demonstrate that smooth infinitesimal isometries are dense within the set of $W^{2,2}(S,\mathbb{R}^3)$ infinitesimal isometries and prove the matching property. These findings serve as essential tools for deriving recovery sequences, specifically the $\Gamma$-lim sup inequality, in the context of dimensionally-reduced shell theories in elasticity.

Visible thermal person re-identification (VT-ReID) is hindered by inter-modality discrepancies and intra-identity variations. While distribution alignment is a common approach for VT-ReID, it typically only addresses intra-identity variations. To mitigate the impact of these variations during alignment, this paper introduces the Cross-Modality Earth Mover's Distance (CM-EMD). CM-EMD employs an optimal transport strategy that assigns higher weights to feature pairs with lower intra-identity variation, allowing the model to prioritize reducing inter-modality discrepancies while minimizing focus on intra-identity differences, thereby enhancing modality alignment. Additionally, two techniques are introduced to further leverage CM-EMD. First, Cross-Modality Discrimination Learning (CM-DL) is developed to counteract the degradation in discriminative power caused by alignment; by lowering the ratio of intra- to inter-identity variance, CM-DL encourages the learning of more distinct representations. Second, a Multi-Granularity Structure (MGS) is constructed to facilitate alignment at both coarse and fine levels using CM-EMD. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of CM-EMD and its supporting techniques, achieving state-of-the-art results on two VT-ReID benchmarks.

We demonstrate that for any two continuous minimal (topologically free) actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space, continuous orbit equivalence implies conjugacy. Furthermore, we establish that this result does not hold when the infinite dihedral group is substituted with specific other virtually cyclic groups, such as the direct product of the integers and any non-abelian finite simple group.

This master thesis outlines an algorithm for the automated classification of scientific documents using deep learning, benchmarking its performance against established classification methods. Additionally, the work aims to develop a reusable API to facilitate the automation of classification tasks within existing software environments. The proposed design features a convolutional neural network serving as the classifier, integrated into a REST-based API, which forms the foundation for a proof-of-concept implementation presented in this thesis. The study demonstrates that the deep learning classifier yields highly effective results for multi-class document categorization and validates the feasibility of incorporating such classifiers into broader ecosystems through REST services.

Semiflexible filament networks are prevalent biological scaffolds, exemplified by the fibrous matrices in blood clots and bacterial biofilms, as well as fundamental elements of plant, animal, and fungal tissues. Despite their widespread presence in biomaterials, the link between their structural characteristics and their highly strain-sensitive mechanical properties remains poorly understood. This study employs simulations of three-dimensional networks generated through the irreversible crosslinking of linker-adorned semiflexible filaments. We analyze the architecture of networks assembled via a simple diffusion-driven process and evaluate their steady-state rheological properties at finite temperatures across a spectrum of prestrains that include the strain-stiffening transition. Furthermore, we quantify how network connectivity varies with crosslinker abundance and examine the resulting impacts on both linear elasticity and nonlinear strain stiffening, contrasting these findings with previous experimental data on the crosslinker-concentration-dependent elasticity of actin gels.

Verifying the soundness of cyclic induction reasoning within first-order logic featuring inductive definitions (FOLID) is a decidable task, though traditional approaches rely on an exponential complement operation for B\"uchi automata. We previously presented a polynomial-time verification method, where the most computationally intensive steps resemble comparisons using multiset path orderings. This approach has been implemented in the Cyclist prover under the name E-Cyclist, which successfully validated all proofs present in Cyclist's original distribution. Furthermore, we developed heuristics capable of automatically determining the trace-based ordering measures required for soundness by analyzing proof derivations.

Representational learning serves as the foundation for the majority of deep learning applications, where the worth of a learned representation is directly linked to its information regarding various factors of variation. The quality of these representations hinges on the type of supervision available and the learning algorithm employed. We introduce a new algorithm that leverages weak supervision by partitioning data into sets based on specific inactive (common) factors of variation that remain invariant within each set. Our central insight is that by establishing correspondences between elements of different sets, we can derive strong representations that filter out inactive factors and isolate the active factors that vary across all sets. Consequently, our approach can effectively utilize a combination of set-supervised and completely unsupervised data, even when sourced from different domains. We address the difficult challenge of transferring synthetic-to-real object poses without any pose annotations by isolating pose information that generalizes to the category level and bridges the synthetic/real domain gap. Furthermore, the method can enhance performance in supervised contexts by reinforcing intermediate representations and function in practical scenarios involving set-supervised natural images where data quantity is scarce and nuisance variations are prevalent.

We offer an in-depth analysis of the existence and uniqueness of Lu's momentum map. Specifically, we define the infinitesimal momentum map and examine its characteristics. This framework enables us to outline the theory for reconstructing the momentum map from its infinitesimal counterpart. Furthermore, we establish the conditions required for the uniqueness of the momentum map.

When non-linearly realized, exact discrete symmetries can shield a theory from ultraviolet sensitivities by ensuring the precise cancellation of quadratic divergences. This allows the lightest scalars arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking to acquire mass without violating the symmetry, distinguishing them from pseudo-Goldstone bosons associated with non-linearly realized continuous symmetries, whose masses necessitate explicit breaking. The symmetry-protected masses and potentials of these discrete Goldstone bosons present significant theoretical opportunities and align with current experimental efforts to detect Axion-Like Particles (ALPs). Utilizing invariant theory and analyzing natural potential minima, we demonstrate that a subgroup of the ultraviolet discrete symmetry typically persists explicitly in the spectrum, realized "à la Wigner," whether abelian or non-abelian. This implies distinct experimental signatures for identifying such low-energy symmetries: simultaneous production of at least two scalars for abelian cases or three for non-abelian ones, with specific multi-scalar amplitude ratios revealing the underlying full ultraviolet discrete symmetry. We provide an in-depth examination of exact ultraviolet $A_4$ and $A_5$ symmetries within this framework.

Although recent theoretical and observational progress has improved our ability to map magnetic fields in molecular clouds, their three-dimensional (3D) structures remain unclear. Comprehensive multi-wavelength and multi-scale observations are essential for fully characterizing the magnetic environments of star-forming regions. This study reconstructs the 3D magnetic morphology of the Perseus molecular cloud and compares it with cloud-formation models, which predict that magnetic fields bend along filamentary clouds. By integrating prior line-of-sight and plane-of-sky observations with Galactic magnetic field models, we derived complete 3D magnetic vectors for Perseus. The resulting morphology approximates a concave arc oriented toward decreasing longitude in the plane of the sky, reflecting a memory of the Galactic magnetic field. Assuming the cloud retains a record of its most recent interaction, and incorporating velocity data, we determined that the line-of-sight magnetic observations align with shock-cloud-interaction models. To our knowledge, this represents the first reconstruction of 3D magnetic fields for a molecular cloud. Our findings indicate that the Perseus cloud's 3D magnetic morphology is consistent with shock-cloud-interaction models, which describe the formation mechanism of filamentary molecular clouds.

Over the last few years, AI agents have transitioned from simple utilities to socially intelligent partners collaborating with humans toward shared objectives. In these collaborative contexts, an AI agent's capacity to anticipate future actions by analyzing the historical behavior of its human counterparts is increasingly valuable. Human goal-directed behavior is inherently complex, hierarchical, and operates across various timescales; however, research utilizing multi-timescale features to model such dynamics remains limited.
