This paper introduces an LSTM network architecture designed to process behavioral data across multiple timescales to forecast future actions. We show that modeling behavior across these varied timescales significantly enhances prediction accuracy compared to methods lacking this capability. Our architecture is evaluated using data from a virtual Minecraft-based testbed simulating an urban search and rescue mission, with performance benchmarked against several established baselines and alternative methods that do not account for multi-timescale inputs.

In addition to spirals caused by Lindblad resonances, planets can create tightly wound spiral structures via buoyancy resonances, a process dependent on the gas's thermal relaxation timescale. By calculating the timescales for radiation, diffusion, and gas-dust collisions, we demonstrate that in the surface layers ($Z/R\gtrsim0.1$) and outer regions ($R\gtrsim100$ au) of protoplanetary disks, thermal relaxation is constrained by rare gas-dust collisions. Consequently, the assumption of an isothermal equation of state or rapid cooling frequently used in simulations is unjustified. Three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations reveal that this collision-limited, slow thermal relaxation creates favorable conditions for buoyancy resonances. These resonances primarily drive vertical motions, reaching speeds of approximately $100~{\rm m~s}^{-1}$ at the $^{12}$CO emission layer for Jovian-mass planets, a magnitude detectable via molecular line observations with ALMA. We present synthetic observations and outline the distinctive signatures of buoyancy resonances in Keplerian-subtracted moment and velocity channel maps. Given the perturbation's morphology and strength, we suggest that the tightly wound spirals seen in TW Hya may result from a (sub-)Jovian-mass planet at 90 au. Furthermore, we discuss methods to distinguish non-Keplerian motions driven by buoyancy resonances from other causes, arguing that high-resolution, high-sensitivity observations of multiple lines tracing different disk heights will be essential to separate near-side and far-side emission and constrain the origin of these motions.

This research investigates a specific class of second-order degenerate linear parabolic equations defined in divergence form over the domain $(-\infty, T) \times \mathbb R^d_+$, subject to homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on $(-\infty, T) \times \partial \mathbb R^d_+$. In this setting, $\mathbb R^d_+$ denotes the half-space $\{x \in \mathbb R^d\,:\, x_d>0\}$, and $T$ is a given value in $(-\infty, \infty]$. The coefficient matrices are constructed as the product of a function $\mu(x_d)$ and bounded uniformly elliptic matrices, where $\mu(x_d)$ scales as $x_d^\alpha$ for a specified $\alpha \in (0,2)$, resulting in degeneracy at the boundary $\{x_d=0\}$. Assuming the coefficients satisfy a partially VMO condition, we establish the wellposedness and regularity of solutions within weighted Sobolev spaces. Furthermore, these findings are easily extendable to systems.

We present a family of three-parameter 2-dimensional algebras that represent elements within the Brauer group $BQ(k,H_4)$ of the Sweedler Hopf algebra $H_4$ over a field $k$. These algebras facilitate the description of the mutual intersection of subgroups derived from quasitriangular or coquasitriangular structures. Additionally, we define a novel subgroup of $BQ(k,H_4)$ consisting of elements represented by algebras where the two natural $\mathbb{Z}_2$-gradings are identical. We further construct an exact sequence linking this subgroup to the Brauer group of the 8-dimensional Nichols Hopf algebra $E(2)$, specifically regarding the quasitriangular structure associated with the $2 \times 2$ matrix $N$ (which contains a 1 in the $(1,2)$-entry and zeros elsewhere).

Marc Rieffel introduced the concept of quantum Gromov-Hausdorff distance on compact quantum metric spaces, identifying a sequence of matrix algebras that converges to the space of continuous functions on the 2-sphere—a result appearing frequently in theoretical physics literature. Over the past twenty years, numerous mathematicians have investigated compact quantum metric spaces and convergence within this distance. In this paper, we define a compact quantum metric space structure on a sequence of Toeplitz algebras associated with generalized Bergman spaces and demonstrate that this sequence converges to the space of continuous functions on odd spheres under the quantum Gromov-Hausdorff distance.

We offer a general, homotopy-theoretic definition of string group models within an $\infty$-category of smooth spaces and introduce novel smooth models for the string group. In this context, a smooth space is defined as a presheaf of $\infty$-groupoids on the category of cartesian spaces. Central to our definition and construction is a specific variant of the singular complex functor, which maps a smooth space to an underlying ordinary space. Building on the research of Nikolaus, Schreiber, and Stevenson, we provide fresh characterizations of principal $\infty$-bundles and group extensions in $\infty$-topoi. These insights enable the transfer of the definition of string group extensions from the $\infty$-category of spaces to the $\infty$-category of smooth spaces. Furthermore, we examine smooth higher-categorical group extensions that emerge as obstructions to the existence of equivariant structures on gerbes. We demonstrate that these extensions yield new smooth models for the string group, a result recently conjectured in our joint work with M\"uller and Szabo.

We examine the Hamiltonian formulation of the Nappi-Witten model, which utilizes a WZW action grounded in a non-semi-simple gauge group, and identify time-dependent non-commutativity through canonical quantization. Our methodology involves a two-stage constraint analysis: first, a first-class analysis is employed to fix the gauge of the original model, followed by a second-class analysis where boundary conditions are treated as Dirac constraints. Finally, we derive the reduced phase space by applying these second-class constraints to the variables within an extended Fourier space.

We investigate an online two-stage problem inspired by a university assignment scenario. Initially, students apply, necessitating the computation of a first stable matching, $M_1$. Subsequently, some students may exit the system due to changes in plans or enrollment elsewhere. Following these departures, a second stable matching, $M_2$, must be established for the remaining participants. Since altering assignments is undesirable, the objective is to minimize the number of changes between $M_1$ and $M_2$. We demonstrate that an optimal online algorithm exists for determining both matchings. Specifically, leveraging a dominance property, we prove that $M_1$ can be optimally computed without prior knowledge of which students will withdraw. This finding is extended to other potential input modifications, such as changes in available positions. Furthermore, we address scenarios involving more than two stages, establishing that no competitive online algorithm is feasible once the process involves three or more stages.

Rank minimization plays a crucial role in machine learning tasks like recommender systems and robust principal component analysis. Although minimizing the nuclear norm—a convex relaxation of the rank problem—offers strong performance guarantees, nonconvex relaxations provide superior results by reducing estimation bias and more effectively mitigating noise. This work introduces efficient algorithms that combine iteratively reweighted nuclear norm schemes with the low-rank factorization technique for semidefinite programs proposed by Burer and Monteiro. We demonstrate the algorithm's convergence and empirically validate its advantages over both convex relaxations and alternating minimization methods. Furthermore, each iteration maintains computational complexity comparable to leading state-of-the-art methods, enabling the rapid solution of rank minimization problems for large-scale matrices.

We investigate both the integer and fractional quantum Hall effects within the Hofstadter model featuring short-range fermionic interactions using a unified framework. An effective field, incorporating these interactions, is defined by its amplitude and phase; the amplitude scales with interaction strength, while the phase aligns with minimum energy. This problem reduces to a modified Harper equation governed by two distinct scales: the magnetic scale (representing unit quantum flux per cell) and a second scale that dictates the inhomogeneity of the effective field. This second scale generates the fine structure of the Hofstadter spectrum, enabling fractional quantum Hall states. In finite samples with open boundaries, this fine structure also encompasses edge chiral modes. Subbands within this refined Hofstadter band are separated by extremely narrow quasigaps, and the Chern number of a topological band remains conserved throughout the formation of this fine structure. Edge modes organize into the Hofstadter band, linking adjacent subbands and governing fractional conductance at fractional fillings, specifically at Fermi energies associated with these quasigaps.

We examine the electronic properties of cubic $\mathcal{T}$-symmetric Weyl semimetals under the influence of atomic-scale vacancy defects. The analysis reveals that isolated vacancies create nodal bound states characterized by $r^{{\scriptscriptstyle -2}}$ asymptotic tails, persisting even within a weakly disordered setting. As defect concentration rises, these states manifest as a markedly increased nodal density of states that evolves into a broadened nodal peak. This transformation results from inter-vacancy hybridization, which generates a series of satellite resonances at finite energies resembling a comb. Consequently, our findings identify point defects as a vital source of elastic scattering responsible for significant alterations in the electronic structure of Weyl semimetals.

Unlike the well-studied challenge of guiding macroscopic agents, such as aircraft or lunar landers, to a target, the quest for "optimal microswimming"—the ideal navigation strategy for microswimmers—remains unresolved. This study systematically investigates this issue, demonstrating that the specific flow fields generated by microswimmers are critical in determining the most efficient path to a destination. The resulting optimal trajectories often exhibit surprising and counterintuitive geometries that differ qualitatively from those of dry active particles or moving macroscopic agents. These findings offer general insights into how hydrodynamics and fluctuations affect optimal navigation at the microscale and suggest that microorganisms may gain survival benefits by strategically managing their distance from distant walls. Specifically, when fluctuations are present, adopting an optimal strategy that accounts for hydrodynamic effects can reduce the time required to reach a target by half compared to a direct approach.

We investigate the set of points $\mathcal{D}_{n,m}$ where two independent Brownian motions complete at least $n$ (respectively $m$) windings. We demonstrate that its area is asymptotically equivalent, both in $L^p$ and almost surely, to $\frac{\ell(\mathbb{R}^2)}{4\pi^2 n m}$, with $\ell$ denoting the intersection measure of the two paths. Furthermore, we establish that the appropriately scaled Lebesgue measure supported on $\mathcal{D}_{n,m}$ converges almost surely in the weak sense toward $\ell$.

This research investigates hallucinations in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), representing a severe form of NMT pathology. First, we link hallucinations caused by source perturbation to Feldman's (2020) Long-Tail theory, proposing and empirically validating a hypothesis that explains this phenomenon. Second, we examine hallucinations arising from corpus-level noise without source perturbation, showing that two major types of natural hallucinations—detached and oscillatory outputs—can be produced and explained by distinct noise patterns within the corpus. Finally, we clarify how hallucination amplification occurs in common data-generation techniques like backtranslation and sequence-level knowledge distillation.

This research was undertaken as part of Professor Fabrizio Granelli's "Advanced Network Modeling and Design" course at UniTn, focusing on drones serving as mobile base stations. The proliferation of fifth-generation (5G) radio access networks (RANs) necessitates handling a surge in diverse devices, placing heightened pressure on existing telecom infrastructures and operators. Current solutions may be inadequate to ensure reliable service under this escalating demand, particularly during emergencies where terrestrial networks are often unusable due to various constraints. These challenges highlight the potential of leveraging unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as mobile base stations to overcome such limitations. The study evaluates the current state of the art to identify the optimal approach that meets all requirements, while also considering business implications. This proposal serves as a roadmap for future research and potential startup development. The structure of this research is as follows: 1) An overview of the current state of the art, distinguishing between existing solutions and areas requiring further development. 2) A detailed research proposal suggesting a viable solution that addresses the shortcomings of current technologies. 3) An analysis of the potential business impacts and outcomes resulting from the further development and implementation of this research.

The planned late 2021 launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) heralds a new era for investigating galaxy formation at high redshifts (z > ~6) within the Cosmic Reionization epoch. By capturing sensitive, high-resolution infrared images and conducting multi-object spectroscopy, JWST will revolutionize our understanding of galaxy evolution during the universe's first billion years. This review synthesizes existing knowledge regarding the contribution of galaxies to intergalactic hydrogen reionization, derived from prior observations using the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based instruments such as Keck, the Very Large Telescope, Subaru, and the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array. Furthermore, we highlight key unresolved questions that JWST is poised to answer throughout its mission, including those targeted by the upcoming Cycle 1 programs. (Abridged)

This paper explores the connections between tiling, weak tiling, and spectral sets within finite abelian groups. Specifically, focusing on elementary $p$-groups $(\mathbb{Z}_p)^d$, we present an averaging method that yields a significant object of study: a 4-tuple of functions serving as a unified generalization of both tiles and spectral sets. We provide a complete characterization of these 4-tuples for dimensions $d=1$ and $d=2$, alongside several partial findings for the case $d=3$.

This paper explores specific characteristics of operator-valued semicircular random variables, specifically addressing the representation of the Cauchy transform for compactly supported probability measures via their operator-valued counterparts and demonstrating the presence of a nonzero discrete component in their associated distributions.

Let $G$ be a group, and let $H$ be a $G$-group defined via an embedding map $G \rightarrow H$. In reference [12], a topology was established on a specific subset of normal subgroups of $H$, known as prime ideals. This study extends that topology to broader classes of groups. We anticipate that these topological structures will serve as effective new instruments for addressing longstanding problems in group theory. Furthermore, we examine the properties of the topology introduced in [12], including the definition of the functor of points, dimension, and the formulation of a Galois theory.

User behavior targeting plays a critical role in online advertising. Unlike sponsored search keyword targeting or contextual page content targeting, which rely on specific search terms or webpage context, user behavior targeting constructs individual interest profiles by monitoring online activities. This approach delivers ads aligned with each user's specific interests, resulting in greater targeting precision and enhanced advertising performance. Existing profiling techniques typically involve creating keyword or topic tags or mapping users into a hierarchical taxonomy. However, to our knowledge, no prior research has explicitly examined the similarity of users' online visits and integrated this similarity into ad response prediction. This study introduces a general framework that derives user profiles from online browsing behavior and applies this learned knowledge to predict ad responses. Specifically, we develop a transfer learning model grounded in probabilistic latent factor graphical models, where ad response profiles are generated from online browsing profiles. Extensive experiments using real-world data confirm that our solution significantly outperforms several strong baselines.

Quantum key distribution (QKD), a technology facilitating perfectly secure communication, has advanced to a point where numerous protocols are now deployed in practical applications. While each protocol offers unique benefits, allowing users to select the optimal fit for their specific needs, they typically demand distinct hardware setups. This requirement complicates multi-user networks, particularly when multiple transmitters are needed for inter-communication. In this work, we present a direct-modulation transmitter capable of supporting most weak coherent pulse-based QKD protocols through minor adjustments to driving signals. Furthermore, this technology holds promise for classical communications by offering a low-chirp transmitter with straightforward driving needs that integrates both phase and amplitude shift keying. We successfully conducted QKD experiments utilizing concurrent time-bin and phase modulation alongside phase randomization. Analysis of the collected data assessed secure key rates for time-bin encoded BB84 with decoy states and finite key-size considerations, achieving megabit-per-second secure key rates that are 1.60 times higher than those obtained using purely phase-encoded BB84.

Precisely forecasting item-user relevance is vital for the prosperity of numerous social platforms. Traditional methods rely on training models using logged historical data; however, recommendation systems, media services, and online marketplaces constantly receive new content, turning relevance into a shifting target that standard predictive models struggle to handle robustly. This paper introduces a learning framework for relevance prediction designed to withstand shifts in data distribution. Our central insight is that robustness can be achieved by considering how users causally interpret their environment. We conceptualize users as boundedly-rational decision-makers whose causal beliefs are represented by a causal graph, demonstrating how minimal information about this graph can effectively address distributional changes. Experiments across various settings validate the efficacy of our proposed approach.

We characterize tropical curves within projective space and establish the definition of tropical Gromov-Witten invariants. Furthermore, we introduce amplitudes for higher topological quantum mechanics featuring a circle action on graphs, demonstrating that these amplitudes correspond exactly to the tropical Gromov-Witten invariants. Leveraging the state-operator correspondence in graph-based topological quantum mechanics, we express the sum of amplitudes in A-type quantum mechanics as an amplitude within deformed quantum mechanics, which naturally aligns with B-type quantum mechanics. Finally, by utilizing the equivalence of amplitudes for three specific observables, we prove the mirror symmetry applicable to cohomology rings.

It is established that isomorphisms between graph Jacobians result in cyclic bijections on the corresponding graphs. We identify the conditions under which these cyclic bijections can be upgraded to graph isomorphisms, using a readily calculable divisor. This finding enhances the tools employed in algebraic geometry for analyzing the fibers of the compactified Torelli map.

This paper investigates spacelike hypersurfaces embedded in twisted product spacetimes $I\times_f F$ where the fiber is complete. It outlines various conditions guaranteeing global hyperbolicity and establishes a necessary relation for a spacelike hypersurface in $I\times_f F$ to constitute a simple warped product. Assuming the fiber is closed (compact and boundary-free) and the ambient spacetime exhibits appropriate expansion, the study derives non-existence theorems for constant mean curvature hypersurfaces. Under identical assumptions, it provides characterizations of compact maximal hypersurfaces and those that are totally umbilic, subject to specific constraints on mean curvature. Additionally, the work describes maximal hypersurfaces within twisted product spacetimes featuring a one-dimensional Lorentzian fiber. Furthermore, the mean curvature equation for a spacelike graph on the fiber is calculated, leading to the proof of several Calabi-Bernstein-type results. An Appendix is also included, presenting established conformal geometry findings regarding the transformation of key tensors and operators under conformal mappings in a pseudo-Riemannian setting.

This study explores a method for universal quantum computation utilizing the modulation of longitudinal qubit-oscillator interactions. We demonstrate that a controlled-phase gate can be achieved by concurrently modulating the longitudinal coupling of two qubits to a shared oscillator mode. Unlike conventional transversal qubit-oscillator coupling, where the effective qubit-qubit interaction depends on a small perturbative parameter, our approach generates a strong effective interaction independent of such limitations. This results in significantly faster gate operations and enhanced fidelity. Furthermore, we illustrate how gate infidelity can be exponentially reduced through the use of squeezing and how the entangling gate can be extended to scenarios where qubits are coupled to distinct oscillators. This proposal is compatible with various physical quantum computing architectures, such as those based on superconducting and spin qubits.

We revisit the cosmological constant problem within a finite temperature framework and suggest a novel approach to perturbative analysis. This method utilizes a renormalization scheme where the renormalized Higgs mass (specifically the resummed mass) is set to be comparable to the CMB temperature. Our proposal relies on the principle that while the physical value of the cosmological constant remains invariant across renormalization schemes, the necessity of fine-tuning is scheme-dependent. Consequently, the cosmological constant problem is effectively resolved because the renormalization procedure no longer demands fine-tuning. This outcome is achieved through the renormalization scheme-independence of physical quantities, guaranteed by bare perturbation theory. However, this shift relocates the cosmological constant problem to an unusual characteristic of the resulting perturbation series for the Higgs mass and other massive Standard Model sectors; analyzing the expected mathematical structure of this series allows this peculiarity to serve as a signal for new physics. Additionally, we observe the finite-temperature-induced complexification of the effective potential and provide an interpretation for it, along with suggesting a consistency check within a cosmological context.

Extensive research confirms that hybrid synapses, comprising both electrical and chemical connections, are prevalent across most organisms and brain regions. While the individual roles of these connection types in generating neural activity diversity have been explored in networks of various complexities, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of how hybrid synapses influence self-organization and robustness within diverse dynamical states remains elusive. This study introduces a neural network model featuring hybrid synapses to examine the emergence of global and collective dynamics. The network comprises interacting excitatory and inhibitory populations; the excitatory group connects via excitatory synapses in a small-world topology alongside gap junctions to adjacent neurons, whereas the inhibitory group relies solely on chemical inhibitory synapses with all-to-all connectivity. Numerical simulations indicate that in balanced networks lacking electrical coupling, synchrony is primarily governed by neuronal heterogeneity and the balance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs. Conversely, in balanced networks with strong electrical coupling, multiple dynamical states emerge from varying combinations of excitatory and inhibitory weights. Crucially, we observe that states such as synchronous firing, cluster synchrony, and diverse ripple events arise through minor adjustments to chemical coupling weights. Furthermore, sufficiently large electrical synapse coupling leads to full network synchronization. These findings advance the investigation into the dynamical mechanisms and computational significance of mixed synapses in neural function.

We examined the field-angle dependence of magnetic excitations in Kitaev-like systems subjected to an in-plane magnetic field. Utilizing a combination of exact diagonalization and linear spin wave theory, we established that the magnetic excitation gap within the polarized phase originates from magnons at the $M$ points and exhibits significant anisotropy relative to the field direction near the critical field limit. The specific heat arising from this magnon mode displays qualitatively identical anisotropic characteristics to those anticipated for the non-Abelian spin liquid phase in the Kitaev model and those observed experimentally in the intermediate phases of $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$.

This study introduces second-order subdifferentials for functions that are Gâteaux differentiable on an open set with a locally Lipschitz Gâteaux derivative mapping. Utilizing the properties of these subdifferentials alongside variational analysis techniques, we establish second-order necessary conditions for weak Pareto efficient solutions in constrained multiobjective programming problems.

Simulating quantum systems numerically is essential for advancing our comprehension of natural phenomena. However, many pivotal systems in fields like superconductivity and quantum chemistry are modeled by equations that classical computers—whether analytically or numerically—cannot solve with adequate precision. Since the field's inception in the 1980s, leveraging quantum computers to simulate such quantum systems has been regarded as a foundational application of quantum computation. Furthermore, it is anticipated that meaningful results unattainable by classical methods could be achieved with fewer than one hundred qubits, positioning quantum simulation as a potentially early practical utility for these machines. This paper reviews the theoretical and experimental progress in quantum simulation using quantum computers, tracing the evolution from initial concepts to the vigorous research currently in progress.

We introduce a comprehensive dataset featuring industrial metal objects characterized by symmetry, lack of texture, and high reflectivity, presenting challenges absent in current datasets. This collection comprises both real-world and synthetic multi-view RGB images annotated with 6D pose labels. The real-world data, gathered by capturing images across diverse object shapes, materials, supports, compositions, and lighting scenarios, consists of over 30,000 images precisely labeled via a novel public tool. Synthetic data was generated by realistically simulating and systematically varying real-world conditions, yielding more than 500,000 images. The strong alignment between synthetic and real data, coupled with controlled variations, supports sim-to-real research. Furthermore, the dataset's scale and difficulty will advance computer vision studies involving reflective surfaces. All resources are accessible on the project website at https://pderoovere.github.io/dimo.

We investigate integrable non-diagonal open boundary conditions for spin chains that emerge from holographic gauge theories. These systems correspond dually to open strings connecting giant gravitons that intersect at various angles within spheres or projective spaces. By analyzing the ground and low-lying states, we successfully reproduce the anticipated spectrum near these intersections. In contrast to intersecting D-branes in flat space, giant gravitons related by $SU(N)$ rotations do not necessarily maintain additional supersymmetry. We measure this absence of enhancement by determining whether a simple ferromagnetic ground state exists for the associated open spin chain.

Deceptive systems offer a novel solution to escalating security challenges within cloud-based virtual networks, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. These systems aim to establish a layer of defensive nodes in publicly accessible cloud environments to mislead and distract malicious actors. Although various approaches exist for developing such systems, misery digraphs emerge as a particularly effective model for deterring powerful remote intrusions by delaying access to deep network targets. A primary obstacle in the theory of misery digraphs involves validating their applicability across major cloud platforms and assessing the efficiency of networks that integrate them. Consequently, there is a need for architectural support that leverages long-term technologies and can scale to large networks. This study introduces and evaluates a high-throughput architecture for misery digraphs, detailing implementation specifics and performance metrics. When fully deployed on Amazon Web Services, the architecture introduces minimal delays in normal request processing while significantly hindering stealthy intrusions.

In recent years, numerous studies have focused on exploring degenerate variants of specific polynomials and numbers, a field initiated by Carlitz through his introduction of degenerate Bernoulli and degenerate Euler polynomials. This paper aims to investigate the properties, recurrence relations, and identities associated with degenerate r-Bell polynomials, two-variable degenerate Fubini polynomials, and degenerate r-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

We examine the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator $[Pf](x) := \mathbb{E}[ f(Y) \mid X = x ]$, defined by the joint distribution of random variables $X$ and $Y$ on a second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space, under minimal assumptions. By adjusting the operator's domain, we demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated with arbitrary precision in the operator norm by Hilbert–Schmidt operators within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This capability enables the uniform estimation of $P$ by finite-rank operators on a dense subspace, even when $P$ lacks compactness. Regarding convergence modes, these findings highlight the advantage of kernel-based methods over traditional parametric projection techniques like Galerkin methods. Furthermore, they offer a fresh perspective on the limiting object toward which nonparametric estimates of $P$ converge. As an application, we illustrate that these results are crucial for a broad class of spectral analysis techniques used for Markov transition operators. Additionally, our study provides a novel asymptotic viewpoint on the kernel conditional mean embedding, which serves as the theoretical basis for numerous kernel-based nonparametric inference methods.

This paper focuses on constructing a novel generating function of (q-) Bernstein type polynomials and establishing its fundamental properties. Utilizing this function, we derive the recurrence relations and derivatives associated with these polynomials. Additionally, we explore connections between (q-) Bernstein type polynomials and Hermite polynomials, higher-order Bernoulli polynomials, and second kind Stirling numbers. By applying the Mellin transformation to the generating function, we define an interpolation scheme for these polynomials. Finally, the study presents various applications and open questions regarding the approximation capabilities of (q-) Bernstein type polynomials and the moments of specific statistical distributions.

To offer a physical illustration of quantum scars, we investigate many-body scars in the spin-1 Kitaev chain, noting that the PXP Hamiltonian is precisely embedded within its energy spectrum. Concerning conserved quantities, the Hilbert space decomposes into disconnected subspaces, allowing us to examine the resulting constrained dynamics. The continuous revivals observed in fidelity and entanglement entropy—when the initial state is set to $\vert\mathbb{Z}_k\rangle$ ($k=2,3$)—demonstrate the core physics of the PXP model. Furthermore, we analyze quantum phase transitions in the one-dimensional spin-1 Kitaev-Heisenberg model using the density-matrix renormalization group and Lanczos exact diagonalization techniques to map out the phase diagram. In this Hamiltonian, the two terms are parametrized by an angle $\phi$, with the Kitaev term defined as $K\equiv\sin(\phi)$ competing against the Heisenberg term $J\equiv\cos(\phi)$. This yields a rich ground state phase diagram dependent on $\phi$. Specifically, based on the ratio $K/J\equiv\tan(\phi)$, the system either transitions into a distinct symmetry-broken phase or remains in a quantum spin liquid phase characterized by frustrated interactions while preserving symmetry. Finally, we determine that scarred states remain stable under perturbations respecting $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry but become unstable when subjected to Heisenberg-type perturbations. \textit{Accepted for publication in Physical Review Research}

This paper addresses time-inhomogeneous nonlinear time series regression within a broad class of locally stationary time series. First, we introduce sieve nonparametric estimators for time-varying regression functions that attain the min-max optimal convergence rate. Second, we construct a unified framework for simultaneous inference, enabling both structural and exact form hypothesis testing on these functions. Our statistics demonstrate high power even when alternatives are locally weak. Additionally, we propose a multiplier bootstrap procedure to facilitate practical application. Notably, our methodology and theoretical framework impose no structural constraints on the regression functions and accommodate support over unbounded domains. Furthermore, we establish sieve approximation theory for two-dimensional functions on unbounded domains and derive a Gaussian approximation result for affine and quadratic forms in high-dimensional locally stationary settings, findings which hold independent interest. The validity of our results is supported by numerical simulations and an analysis of real financial data.

We conducted a comparative analysis of four physical dust models alongside two single-temperature modified blackbody models by fitting them to resolved WISE, Spitzer, and Herschel photometry of M101 (NGC 5457). Employing identical datasets and a grid-based fitting approach, we evaluated the resulting dust and radiation field properties. Our findings indicate that while the quality of the fits remains comparable, the dust masses derived from different models can differ by up to a factor of 3 (or 1.4 when considering only physical models). Despite varying definitions regarding the carriers of mid-IR aromatic features, all physical models exhibit consistent spatial variations in the abundance of this grain population. Leveraging M101's well-established metallicity gradient and resolved gas maps, we computed an approximate upper limit for dust mass as a function of radius. We discovered that all physical dust models exceed this maximum estimate across certain galactocentric ranges. However, we demonstrate that renormalizing the models to align with Milky Way high-latitude cirrus spectrum and abundance constraints can reduce inter-model dust mass discrepancies and ensure the total dust mass remains below the calculated upper limit at all radii.

This paper introduces a method for restoring the classical order of explicit exponential Runge-Kutta schemes when applied to reaction-diffusion problems. While high stiff-order methods exist for problems with vanishing boundary conditions, they often require additional stages, leading to higher computational costs compared to the proposed technique, which simply incorporates boundary information via extra terms. Furthermore, the approach directly addresses time-dependent boundary conditions.

The 2015 direct detection of gravitational waves from a merging black hole pair is celebrated as one of the most pivotal breakthroughs in 21st-century physics and astronomy. Driven by the vast scientific potential unlocked by gravitational-wave observatories and acknowledging that fully harnessing this new field demands facilities requiring 15 to 20 years from conception to operation, the Gravitational Wave International Committee (GWIC) established a subcommittee. This group was tasked with outlining the strategy to construct and manage a future network of ground-based observatories capable of extending the gravitational wave detection horizon far beyond the limits of current detectors. This document serves as the initial entry in a six-part series produced by the GWIC 3G Subcommittee, covering: i) Expanding the Reach of Gravitational Wave Observatories to the Edge of the Universe, ii) The Next Generation Global Gravitational Wave Observatory: The Science Book, iii) 3G R&D: Research and Development for Future Ground-based Detectors, iv) Gravitational Wave Data Analysis: Computing Challenges in the 3G Era, v) Future Ground-based Observatories: Synergies with Other Scientific Communities, and vi) An Exploration of Possible Governance Models for the Future Global Gravitational-Wave Observatory Network.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous computer vision applications. Nevertheless, the multi-head self-attention (MSA) layers used to model global correlations suffer from two significant drawbacks: excessive computational resource usage and a lack of inherent inductive bias for capturing local visual patterns. To address these challenges, we introduce Single-Path Vision Transformer pruning (SPViT), a straightforward yet powerful approach that efficiently and automatically compresses pre-trained ViTs into compact models while incorporating appropriate locality. Specifically, we propose a novel weight-sharing mechanism between MSA and convolutional operations, creating a unified single-path space to represent all candidate operations. This strategy reframes the operation search problem as selecting a subset of parameters for each MSA layer, which substantially lowers computational costs and optimization complexity, while allowing convolution kernels to be effectively initialized from pre-trained MSA parameters. Leveraging this single-path space, we further integrate learnable binary gates to encode operation selections, which are jointly optimized with network parameters to automatically determine the configuration of every layer. Extensive experiments on two representative ViTs demonstrate that SPViT establishes a new state-of-the-art for pruning on ImageNet-1k. For instance, SPViT reduces DeiT-B's FLOPs by 52.0% while simultaneously achieving an impressive 0.6% improvement in top-1 accuracy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ziplab/SPViT.

Cosmological data suggest that the Einstein equations might not fully capture the nature of gravity. Yet, many proposed modifications leave the theoretical foundations intact. This paper examines two critical issues necessitating a major revision: 1. The role of the relativity of space-time geometry concerning measuring devices within gravitational theory, and 2. The gauge transformations of field variables in a corrected framework of gravitation.

We highlight observational data suggesting that a significant portion of the known cosmic diffuse ultraviolet background radiation does not originate from dust-scattered starlight. Instead, based on its spectral properties across most of the sky, this radiation appears to stem from an unidentified physical source. This conclusion arises from a re-analysis of spectra from the diffuse ultraviolet background, originally collected decades ago using the ultraviolet spectrometers on the two Voyager spacecraft, which operated from distant and varied locations within our solar system. Since neither a conventional nor an unconventional astrophysical source adequately explains this newly identified fraction of the radiation, we speculate that the observed photons result from the extremely slow decay of particles constituting the ubiquitous dark matter that surrounds our Galaxy. Regardless of whether dark matter decay is indeed the source, this new radiation field extends slightly below 912 Å, meaning we have finally identified the radiation responsible for the universe's re-ionization.

We introduce a highly efficient strategy for managing a wide spectrum of non-integrable, one-dimensional quantum many-body systems, compatible with advanced tensor network techniques such as the Density Matrix Renormalization Group. To illustrate its effectiveness, we address a significant challenge in optical-lattice physics involving ultra-cold atoms: our approach reduces the time required to transition a superfluid gas into a Mott insulator state by approximately two orders of magnitude and decreases defect formation by over one order of magnitude compared to existing experimental methods [1]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal control pulse remains robust against fluctuations in atom number.

Workflow nets represent a mature mathematical framework used to analyze business processes derived from modeling tools or process mining. The primary decision problems associated with workflow nets include $k$-soundness, generalised soundness, and structural soundness, though most current tools prioritize $k$-soundness. This paper introduces new, scalable semi-procedures for assessing generalised and structural soundness by utilizing integral and continuous Petri net reachability relaxations. We demonstrate that our method performs competitively compared to state-of-the-art tools.

We derive a Bourgain-Br\'ezis-Mironescu formula describing the limiting behavior of a modified fractional Sobolev seminorm as $s\nearrow 1$, applicable to any bounded domain. For extension domains, this approach yields the classical result.

Solar filaments often remain stable for long durations before becoming the core of a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME). This study analyzes a filament eruption occurring on May 29–30, 2017, utilizing high-resolution He I 10830 Å and Hα spectra from the Dunn Solar Telescope, full-disk Dopplergrams of He I 10830 Å from the Chromospheric Telescope, and EUV and coronagraph observations from SDO and STEREO. Pre-eruption line-of-sight velocities, derived via He I inversion using the HAZEL code, reveal coherent 5 Mm patches indicating counter-streaming and/or buoyancy. As the eruption began, individual, aligned threads emerged in the He I velocity maps, and the velocity distribution shifted from Gaussian to strongly asymmetric. The maximum optical depth of He I 10830 Å dropped from 1.75 to 0.25, while temperature rose by 13 kK; simultaneously, the filament's average speed and width increased from 0 to 25 km s⁻¹ and from 10 to 20 Mm, respectively. Consistent across all datasets, the filament accelerated exponentially at a rate of 7.4 m s⁻², reaching a final velocity of 430 km s⁻¹ at 22:24 UT, coinciding with an associated CME. These eruptive characteristics support a kink/torus instability mechanism, implying the presence of a flux rope. We conclude that full-disk chromospheric Dopplergrams are effective for tracing the initial phase of on-disk filament eruptions in real-time, potentially aiding in the modeling of subsequent CME sources.

Recent studies indicate that pre-trained language models absorb social biases from their extensive training data, prompting efforts to develop mitigation strategies. This research provides an empirical evaluation of five recent approaches: Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), Dropout, Iterative Nullspace Projection, Self-Debias, and SentenceDebias. We assessed each method's efficacy using three intrinsic bias benchmarks, alongside measuring their influence on language modeling capabilities and performance in downstream NLU tasks. Our experiments reveal that: (1) Self-Debias emerges as the most effective debiasing method, achieving higher scores across all bias benchmarks; (2) Existing techniques demonstrate less consistency when addressing non-gender biases; and (3) enhancements on benchmarks like StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs via debiasing often coincide with reduced language modeling proficiency, complicating the assessment of whether the mitigation was truly successful.

We start by examining a basic model of phase synchronization within an open classical nonlinear system, described using angular momentum variables. Subsequently, we introduce the corresponding quantum version of this system. By applying the appropriate Lindblad master equation to the density matrix of a two-qubit realization, we demonstrate that the stationary state of this composite system is both pure and entangled, exhibiting minimal phase observable dispersion. We posit that this intriguing link between the entangled stationary states of a quantum composite system and the phase synchronization among its subsystems may be a characteristic feature of a broad class of similar nonlinear open systems.

We treat a static wormhole as a waveguide to identify the criteria for complete transmission of a quantum particle possessing zero angular momentum. Our findings indicate that the waveguide becomes transparent when the particle's de Broglie wavelength equals an integer multiple of twice the wormhole's throat diameter. This phenomenon could potentially be realized within graphene, plasmonic, or optical wormhole systems.

This work introduces entropy concepts applicable to the incremental practical stability and incremental stability of deterministic nonlinear systems subjected to disturbances. These entropy notions are derived from specific state space points, termed an approximating set, which guarantee the requisite stability characteristics. We establish system conditions that ensure this approximating set remains finite and calculate both lower and upper bounds for the resulting estimation entropies. Furthermore, the development of these finite approximating sets facilitates a robust state estimation algorithm for disturbed systems, utilizing quantized and time-discrete measurements.

This research investigates an $SO(2)^4$ truncation of four-dimensional $N=4$ gauged supergravity involving six vector multiplets with an $SO(4)\times SO(4)$ gauge group, yielding a novel class of holographic RG flows and supersymmetric Janus configurations. Within this framework, a unique $N=4$ supersymmetric $AdS_4$ vacuum emerges, dual to an $N=4$ three-dimensional SCFT. While the inclusion of an axion typically restricts the RG flows to $N=2$ supersymmetry, the symmetry is restored to $N=4$ when the axion vanishes. We identify solutions bridging the $AdS_4$ vacuum and singular geometries characterized by varying residual symmetries, demonstrating that all such singularities are physically consistent within the four-dimensional gauged supergravity context. Consequently, these solutions correspond holographically to RG flows originating from the $N=4$ SCFT and terminating in various non-conformal infrared phases. Furthermore, we discover $N=4$ and $N=2$ Janus solutions possessing $SO(4)\times SO(4)$ and $SO(2)\times SO(2)\times SO(3)\times SO(2)$ symmetries, respectively. The former arises from truncating all scalars in the vector multiplets, representing a solution to pure $N=4$ gauged supergravity, whereas the latter constitutes a genuine solution of the complete matter-coupled theory. These configurations represent conformal interfaces within the $N=4$ SCFT, exhibiting $N=(4,0)$ and $N=(2,0)$ supersymmetries.

This study examines the magnetotransport characteristics of massless Dirac fermions within a gapless HgTe quantum well. Experiments on samples featuring narrow channels reveal a substantial negative magnetoresistance exhibiting a Lorentzian shape, which is attributed to electron viscosity resulting from electron-electron interactions. By comparing experimental data with theoretical models, the shear stress relaxation time of these Dirac fermions, induced by electron-electron scattering, is determined.

This study investigates the weak Galerkin mixed finite element method (WG-MFEM) applied to second-order elliptic equations on two-dimensional domains featuring curved boundaries, where the Neumann condition serves as the essential boundary constraint. It is established that the geometric mismatch between a curved physical domain and its polygonal approximation typically degrades accuracy for polynomial degrees $\alpha > 1$. This paper addresses two primary objectives. First, it provides a comprehensive error analysis of the standard WG-MFEM on curved domains, revealing an $O(h^{1/2})$ convergence rate for all $\alpha \ge 1$. Notably, even the lowest-order scheme ($\alpha=1$) suffers accuracy loss, a phenomenon distinct from standard finite element or mixed finite element results and attributed to the interaction between the WG-MFEM formulation and the discrepancy in outward normal vectors between the polygonal and curved domains. Second, the authors propose a corrective strategy to restore optimal convergence rates by integrating two approaches: a specialized boundary correction technique and an exploitation of the WG-MFEM's capability to operate on polygonal meshes. This latter approach allows for a more precise representation of curved boundaries using multiple short edges without expanding the total element count. Rigorous theoretical analysis confirms that combining these methods achieves optimal convergence for all $\alpha$, a finding further supported by numerical experiments.

Non-native speech often degrades the performance of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. While previous approaches have utilized model adaptation, accent classification for model selection, or alternative pronunciation lexicons, this study employs a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with a Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss function trained on multi-accent English data, specifically covering US (native), Indian, and Hispanic accents. We leverage dark knowledge from a teacher model trained on this diverse dataset to guide student models using both the teacher's output and the CTC cost of the target transcription. Our results demonstrate that transferring knowledge from a single RNN-CTC model to a student model outperforms the standalone teacher. However, because outputs from different CTC models may not be temporally aligned, a simple ensemble of teacher models is ineffective. To resolve this, we train accent-specific models under the supervision of a single multi-accent teacher, ensuring the resulting multiple CTC models are aligned. Furthermore, training a student model under the guidance of these accent-specific teachers yields an even more robust model, achieving a 20.1% relative reduction in Character Error Rate (CER) compared to a baseline trained without any teacher guidance. With this effective multi-accent framework, we can further enhance performance by adapting the model to each specific accent. By using the accent-specific model's outputs to regularize the adaptation process—specifically through a knowledge distillation approach utilizing Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence—we achieve superior results compared to conventional methods using general teacher models.

We introduce a new 3D mapping framework that combines geometric and photometric techniques to enable precise, real-time scene reconstruction from single-view images. This approach integrates recent breakthroughs in dense monocular SLAM with real-time hierarchical volumetric neural radiance fields. Our core hypothesis is that dense monocular SLAM effectively supports real-time neural radiance field fitting by delivering precise pose estimations and depth maps complete with uncertainty metrics. By implementing an uncertainty-driven depth loss function, we attain superior performance in both photometric and geometric fidelity. Specifically, our pipeline outperforms existing methods in accuracy—demonstrating up to 179% higher PSNR and 86% better L1 depth—while maintaining real-time operation using only monocular input.

We formulate photo cropping as a deep learning-based cascade combining attention box regression and aesthetic quality classification. The proposed neural network features two distinct branches: one for predicting an attention bounding box and another for analyzing aesthetic appeal. This predicted box serves as an initial crop window, from which a set of cropping candidates is generated to ensure no critical information is lost. Aesthetic assessment is then applied to identify the final crop based on superior quality. By sharing features across full-image convolutional maps for all cropping candidates, our network avoids redundant computations, significantly enhancing efficiency. Leveraging abundant data for both attention prediction and aesthetic evaluation, the method achieves high-quality results even when training data for photo cropping is scarce. Experimental outcomes confirm competitive performance and rapid processing speeds, achieving 5 frames per second across all steps.

This study examines specific partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms featuring centers of any dimension, establishing the continuity of topological entropy under $C^1$ perturbations. The analyzed systems exhibit subexponential growth within the center direction and uniform exponential growth along the unstable foliation. Our findings are applicable to Lyapunov stable partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms in the center direction, as well as to a significant class of systems with subexponential center growth, for which we devised a method leveraging exponential mixing to achieve uniform distribution of unstable manifolds. A key example includes translations on homogeneous spaces, which can possess centers of arbitrary dimension and polynomial orbit growth.

Since internet search shapes human perception of reality, eliminating biases in search outcomes and developing equitable models are essential for societal benefit. This research examines a distinct gender bias within image search, where images retrieved for gender-neutral natural language queries are frequently skewed by gender. We evaluated two common image search architectures: a specialized model trained on domain-specific data and a generalized representation model pre-trained on vast internet-wide image and text corpora. Both exhibited significant gender bias. Consequently, we proposed two innovative debiasing techniques: an in-processing fair sampling strategy to correct gender imbalances during model training, and a post-processing feature clipping approach grounded in mutual information to mitigate bias in the multimodal representations of pre-trained models. Comprehensive experiments on the MS-COCO and Flickr30K benchmarks demonstrate that our methods substantially decrease gender bias in image search systems.

Timing data from the Nanshan 26-m radio telescope, collected between 2000 and 2014 for nine pulsars with a coverage ranging from 11.6 to 14.2 years, was utilized to detect glitches. Out of 114 years of rotational history, this analysis identified 16 new glitches across the nine pulsars by fitting timing residuals to measure glitch parameters. All detected glitches exhibited small fractional magnitudes. Notably, six new glitches were found in PSR J1833-0827, reinforcing its status as a frequent glitcher. While some glitches show exponential or linear recovery patterns, the significant gaps in the dataset preclude further detailed analysis. Additionally, glitch rates derived from Nanshan observations are higher than those reported by Jodrell Bank Observatory, potentially due to the small glitch sizes and high cadence of the observations.

Monitoring foot plantar pressure is a crucial instrument for biomechanical evaluation of posture, foot issues such as calluses and wounds, and sports performance. The high expense of commercial systems and the rigidity of their data analysis capabilities motivated the creation of a cost-effective, versatile alternative. This study details the development of such a system, featuring high-speed data acquisition and analysis tools specifically designed to assess plantar pressure variations in diabetic patients with calloused feet. The new system achieves a frame rate of 155 Hz, making it suitable for monitoring pressure during both standing and walking activities. Validation was conducted using 10 healthy subjects and 5 diabetic subjects with foot calluses. The results reveal significantly elevated mechanical stress on the skin beneath calluses and postural abnormalities during standing in these diabetic subjects.

Although the current Martian climate precludes large bodies of liquid water, small-scale, temporary brines may still form. This process, known as deliquescence, occurs when hygroscopic salts absorb atmospheric water vapor to dissolve. Since direct experiments on this phenomenon have not yet been conducted on Mars, atmospheric modeling remains the most dependable method for prediction, yet the specific times and locations for potential liquid emergence remain uncertain. This study presents our findings regarding probable brine formation, including seasonal windows and geographic locations, alongside identified limiting factors. Utilizing data from the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique Mars General Circulation Model (version 5), we determined that calcium perchlorate deliquescence is highly probable between solar longitudes (L$_s$) 35° and 160° above 30° N, specifically between 9 PM and 11 PM. Within this northern zone, optimal conditions concentrate in Acidalia Planitia and Utopia Planitia during the early morning hours of 1 AM to 3 AM. In the Southern Hemisphere, a weaker band of potential deliquescence exists between L$_s$ 195° and 320° near 60° S, with Argyre Planitia and Hellas Planitia also showing some likelihood of brine formation. Statistical analysis indicates that relative humidity is the primary limiting factor in most scenarios. Our results suggest that during summer and early fall, deliquescence could occur in specific regions of both hemispheres from late evening until early morning. Given the scarcity of existing research on the geological and temporal distribution of these brines, this work serves as a valuable guide for future landing site selection and targeted research locations.

We introduce the Infrared Database of Extragalactic Observables from Spitzer (IDEOS), a publicly accessible and homogeneous repository containing 77 fitted mid-infrared observables spanning 5.4–36 µm. This database includes data for 3,335 galaxies observed using the low-resolution staring mode of the Infrared Spectrometer on the Spitzer Space Telescope. The dataset encompasses PAH fluxes and equivalent widths, the 9.8 µm silicate feature strength, emission line fluxes, solid-state features, rest-frame continuum fluxes, synthetic photometry, and mid-infrared spectral classifications. The spectra were drawn from the Cornell Atlas of Spitzer-IRS Sources. Notably, we detected crystalline silicates at a confidence level exceeding 95% in 786 of these galaxies, with detections ranging from single bands to all fitted crystalline bands (16, 19, 23, 28, and 33 µm). Our analysis reveals a correlation between crystalline silicate band strength and amorphous silicate strength, and indicates that the transition from emission to absorption features occurs at higher obscuration levels as the crystalline band wavelength increases. These findings align with an origin for both amorphous and crystalline silicates in a centrally heated dust geometry, such as an edge-on disk or a cocoon. Furthermore, the 23 and 33 µm crystalline bands prove effective for classifying galactic nuclear obscuration, even amidst strong circumnuclear star formation. Based on our detection statistics, we conclude that crystalline silicates are a prevalent component of the interstellar medium within galactic nuclei.

Angular moments of the $Z$ boson serve as analyzers for the production dynamics in $t\bar t Z$ and $t Zj$ processes. In this work, we calculate these moments at both leading and next-to-leading order in QCD within the context of the LHC. We demonstrate that these observables function as powerful tools for detecting Beyond the Standard Model effects under the Standard Model Effective Field theory framework. Notably, we find that these probes reveal blind directions for CP-odd operators, achieving significant new physics sensitivity at the 14 TeV LHC using 3 ab$^{-1}$ of data.

This paper utilizes the Mackaay-Vaz approach to universal $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-homology to construct a family of transverse braid invariants known as $\beta_3$-invariants, a set that encompasses Wu's $\psi_{3}$-invariant. We examine the vanishing of the homology classes associated with these $\beta_3$-invariants and connect this phenomenon to the vanishing of both Plamenevskaya's and Wu's invariants. Additionally, we apply the $\beta_3$-invariants to derive certain Bennequin-type inequalities.

Answer Selection (AS) is a critical component of natural language processing, aimed at identifying the most probable response to a query from a set of candidate sentences. A prevalent strategy involves generating embeddings for both the query and each candidate sentence, then selecting the sentence whose vector is nearest to the query's representation. However, the primary limitation of this method is the suboptimal quality of embeddings, which has historically hindered performance on AS benchmarks. This paper introduces ASBERT, a framework leveraging the BERT architecture and utilizing Siamese and Triplet neural networks to learn an encoding function that maps text into fixed-size vectors within an embedding space. In this space, the distance between points reflects the semantic similarity between texts. Experiments on the WikiQA and TrecQA datasets show that our approach surpasses numerous state-of-the-art baseline methods.

This review begins with a general overview of the effective string theory (EST) framework describing confinement in pure gauge theories before examining how EST evolves with rising temperature. We demonstrate that as the system approaches the deconfinement point from the confined phase, the effective string accurately predicts several universal characteristics of confining gauge theories, including the ratio $T_c/\sqrt{\sigma_0}$, the linear growth of the squared flux tube width with interquark separation, and the temperature dependence of the interquark potential. Furthermore, near the deconfinement transition, EST behavior aligns well with predictions derived from conformal invariance or dimensional reduction, thereby reinforcing the validity of the EST approach to confinement.

Anisotropic outgassing from comets generates torques strong enough to rapidly alter the angular momentum of their nuclei, potentially causing rotational instability. In this study, we utilize empirical measurements of spin evolution across a comet sample to characterize these torques and contrast them with predictions from a simplified model. Both the observational data and the model indicate that the characteristic spin-up timescale, $\tau_s$, depends heavily on the nucleus radius, $r_n$. Empirically, for comets with perihelion distances between 1 and 2 AU and eccentricities around 0.5, the timescale scales as $\tau_s \sim 100 r_n^{2}$ (with $r_n$ in kilometers and $\tau_s$ in years). Additionally, the fraction of the active surface area follows the relation $f_A \sim 0.1 r_n^{-2}$. We determined that the median dimensionless moment arm of the torque is $k_T$ = 0.007, representing approximately 0.7% of the escaping momentum; there is weak ($<$3$\sigma$) evidence suggesting a size dependence of $k_T \sim 10^{-3} r_n^2$. For sub-kilometer nuclei, spin-up timescales are comparable to orbital periods, confirming that outgassing torques can swiftly drive small bodies toward rotational disruption. This mechanism likely explains the scarcity of sub-kilometer short-period cometary nuclei and the pre-perihelion destruction of sungrazing comets. Furthermore, sustained outgassing torques on small active asteroids can match or exceed YORP torques, even at very low mass loss rates ($\lesssim$1 g s$^{-1}$). Finally, we emphasize the significant impact of observational biases on the measured distributions of $\tau_s$, $f_A$, and $k_T$.

Various cognitive functions are linked to the synchronization of distinct $\gamma$-rhythms originating in different brain regions. This study investigates how widespread neuronal heterogeneity influences the synchronization of PING (pyramidal-interneuronal network gamma) and ING (interneuronal network gamma) rhythms. Since rhythm synchronization relies on how a network's collective phase responds to external inputs, we calculated the macroscopic finite-amplitude phase-response curve (fmPRC) through numerical simulations of fully connected integrate-and-fire (IF) neuron networks generating either PING or ING oscillations. We demonstrate that intrinsic neuronal heterogeneity can qualitatively alter the fmPRC. Specifically, while the phase-response curve for individual IF neurons is strictly positive (Type I), the fmPRC can become biphasic, displaying both positive and negative phases (Type II). Consequently, for PING rhythms, external excitation applied to excitatory cells can paradoxically delay the network's collective oscillation, even though the same stimulus would advance the phase in isolated neurons. This delay occurs because the external input triggers additional inhibitory spikes, and the resulting internal inhibitory delay surpasses the immediate phase advance from the excitation. These findings illustrate how intrinsic heterogeneity enables PING rhythms to synchronize with periodic forcing or other PING rhythms across a broader frequency mismatch. A comparable mechanism facilitates ING rhythm synchronization. Ultimately, our results highlight a potential role for neuronal heterogeneity in synchronizing coupled $\gamma$-rhythms, which may underlie neural information transfer through communication via coherence.

The general position problem in graph theory seeks the maximum subset $S$ of vertices in a graph $G$ such that no shortest path includes more than two vertices from $S$. This paper introduces a variation known as the \emph{monophonic position problem}, which substitutes "shortest path" with "induced path." We establish fundamental properties and bounds for the monophonic position number of graphs and calculate this value for specific graph families, including unicyclic graphs, complements of bipartite graphs, and split graphs. Additionally, we demonstrate that the monophonic position number of triangle-free graphs does not exceed the independence number. The study also includes realization results for the general position number, monophonic position number, and monophonic hull number, concluding with an analysis of the computational complexity associated with the monophonic position problem.

The ALICE Collaboration has determined the energy dependence of exclusive $J/\psi$ vector meson photoproduction off protons during ultra-peripheral p-Pb collisions at a nucleon pair centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. By utilizing the e$^+$e$^-$ and $\mu^+\mu^-$ decay modes, the cross section was measured across the $J/\psi$ rapidity range of $-2.5 < y < 2.7$, which corresponds to a $\gamma$p centre-of-mass energy interval of $40 < W_{\gamma\mathrm{p}}<550$ GeV. These results, which align with a power law dependence for the exclusive $J/\psi$ photoproduction cross section, were compared against prior data from HERA and the LHC, as well as various theoretical models, and were found to be consistent with previous measurements.

We present a new clean-label targeted poisoning attack that exclusively relies on data omission, distinguishing it from traditional attacks that typically involve adding, modifying, or removing data. This approach successfully misclassifies a specific target test sample without altering the sample itself. We validated the efficacy of this omission-based strategy across diverse learners—such as deep neural networks, SVMs, and decision trees—using datasets like MNIST, IMDB, and CIFAR. The restriction to data omission offers practical advantages, making the attack simpler to implement and analyze. Results indicate that with a minimal attack budget, the success rate exceeds 80% and reaches 100% in certain white-box scenarios, while consistently outperforming benchmarks in black-box settings. Crucially, model accuracy remains negligibly affected regardless of the learner type or dataset used. Furthermore, within a simplified agnostic PAC learning framework, we provide theoretical proof that our attack succeeds with high probability against any effective PAC learner, contingent upon dataset size and distribution.

Semantic communications aim to convey meaning more effectively than simply transferring precise symbols. This paper introduces an end-to-end deep neural network architecture for image transmission, validating its feasibility in real-time wireless channels through an FPGA-based prototype. Results indicate that this system surpasses conventional 256-quadrature amplitude modulation approaches in low signal-to-noise ratio conditions when using the CIFAR-10 dataset. To our knowledge, this study represents the first implementation and investigation of real-time semantic communications utilizing a vision transformer.

This study investigates the anisotropic Lorentz-Zygmund space $L_{\overline{p}, \overline\alpha, \overline{\tau}}^{*}(\mathbb{T}^{m})$, which consists of $2\pi$-periodic functions in $m$ variables, alongside the Nikol'skii–Besov class $S_{\overline{p}, \overline\alpha, \overline{\tau}, \bar{\theta}}^{\bar r}B$. We derive order-sharp estimates for the best approximation of functions from this Nikol'skii–Besov class by trigonometric polynomials featuring harmonic numbers from a step hyperbolic cross, measured within the norm of the anisotropic Lorentz-Zygmund space.

We present a new class of controlled Loewner-Kufarev equations and examine their algebraic properties. By lifting the solutions of these equations to the (Sato)-Segal-Wilson Grassmannian, we explore their connection to the tau-function. Additionally, we briefly outline the links between the Grunsky matrix, integrable systems, and conformal field theory. Our primary contribution is an explicit formula that represents the solution of the controlled equation via the signature of the driving function, utilizing the action of words formed from Witt algebra generators.

We demonstrate that limitations on scalar field potentials and sequences of light massive states within the asymptotic regions of scalar field space—specifically those predicted by the de Sitter Conjecture and the Swampland Distance Conjecture—are intrinsically linked to the feasibility of defining asymptotic observables in expanding Friedmann-Robertson-Walker cosmologies. Furthermore, the observational perspective of a "census taker" in an eternally inflating universe connects to inquiries regarding whether specific domain walls adhere to a variant of the Weak Gravity Conjecture. This interplay indicates that resolving fundamental questions about cosmological asymptotic observables could illuminate the Swampland program, while progress in the Swampland program could similarly advance our understanding of cosmological observables.

This paper investigates sorting networks built using comparators with an arity $k > 2$. In this framework, the comparator arity—representing the number of inputs sorted per unit cost—is treated as a variable parameter. We analyze its interplay with two other key metrics: $n$, the total number of inputs, and $d$, the network depth. This model has garnered significant interest, partly to elucidate the architecture of sorting networks, particularly how high-arity networks relate to recursive methods for standard sorting. Furthermore, research in this area parallels recent efforts in constructing majority circuits using majority gates with lower fan-in. Driven by these inquiries, we establish the first lower bounds for the arity of constant-depth sorting networks. Specifically, we examine networks with depths $d$ ranging from 1 to 4 to identify the minimum $k$ required for such structures. Our findings show that for depths $d=1$ and $d=2$, $k$ must equal $n$. At $d=3$, we prove $k = \lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil$. By contrast, at $d=4$, the minimal arity drops to a sublinear value of $k = \Theta(n^{2/3})$. This result differs from the context of majority circuits, where an arity of $O(n^{2/3})$ is attainable even at depth $d=3$.

We demonstrate that a Boolean function of degree $d$ defined on the slice $\binom{[n]}{k}$ is a junta whenever $k \geq 2d$, establishing that this threshold is tight. Furthermore, we prove an analogous result for functions taking values in an arbitrary finite set $A$ with degree $d$, as well as for functions on an infinite counterpart to the slice.

This study offers an exploratory analysis of the parity-odd $\Delta I = 1$ pion-nucleon coupling, denoted as $h_\pi^1$, utilizing lattice QCD. Leveraging the PCAC relation, we examine the parity-conserving effective Hamiltonian and derive the coupling by calculating the nucleon mass splitting induced by effective 4-quark interactions via the Feynman-Hellmann theorem. We provide initial findings for the mass shift on a $32^3 \times 64$ ensemble employing $N_f = 2 + 1 + 1$ twisted mass fermions, with a pion mass of 260 MeV and a lattice spacing of 0.097 fm.

Aligning two similar graphs from different domains is a well-established challenge. In many practical scenarios, vertices and edges lack reliable labels, leaving structural similarity as the sole basis for matching. Consequently, existing methods often assume a small set of pre-aligned vertices, known as seeds. Current state-of-the-art scalable seeded alignment techniques rely on percolation, where aligned vertices propagate to their neighbors in parallel across both graphs. However, these percolation-based approaches struggle with scale-free degree distributions. We introduce "IRMA" (Iterative Repair for graph MAtching) to demonstrate that the accuracy of percolation-based algorithms can be enhanced in real-world graphs with minimal additional computational cost and reduced runtime when implemented in parallel. IRMA initiates by generating a primary alignment via an existing percolation algorithm and then iteratively corrects errors from previous steps. We prove that IRMA outperforms single-iteration algorithms and numerically demonstrate that it significantly surpasses all current state-of-the-art seeded graph alignment methods on their respective test graphs. In scale-free networks, vertices with very low degrees are prone to erroneous alignments. We show that combining iterations characterized by high recall but low precision ultimately yields higher overall recall and precision for the complete alignment.

Investigating Ethereum within a multi-pool mining environment presents a complex and arduous challenge. Primary obstacles include modeling a generalized tree structure featuring multiple block branches or sub-chains associated with various pools, as well as analyzing a multi-dimensional stochastic system driven by competition among these pools. This paper addresses these issues by first establishing a mathematical framework for trees with multiple block branches. Subsequently, we introduce a classification of Ethereum blocks into five categories: regular blocks (main chain), orphan blocks, uncle blocks, stale blocks, and nephew blocks. Utilizing the law of large numbers, we derive key probabilities for generating each block type. Building on this foundation, we examine the blockchain's growth rate and the distribution of rewards among competing pools by applying the renewal reward theorem. Furthermore, simulation experiments validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating that the proposed approximate computational methods for key probabilities, long-term growth rates, and reward allocation rates converge more rapidly. Consequently, we offer a robust tool for analyzing how selfish mining attacks impact Ethereum's performance in multi-pool scenarios. We posit that the methodologies and results presented herein will illuminate the study of Ethereum with multiple mining pools, potentially inspiring a wave of future research.

We derive scattering angles for probes within Kerr metrics, specifically focusing on equatorial plane motion around the black hole. Our approach naturally resums all orders of the black hole's spin, enabling direct comparison with scattering-angle results from Post-Minkowskian expansions derived via scattering amplitudes or worldline calculations. Furthermore, we extend these findings to include spinning black-hole probes up to second order in probe spin (for spins aligned with the Kerr spin) at any Post-Minkowskian order. Upon truncation to third Post-Minkowskian order, our results align perfectly with those obtained using amplitude and worldline methods.

This paper introduces two main Euclidean embeddings for the quotient space formed by matrices identified under arbitrary row permutations, originally intended for node-relabeling invariant tasks in graph-based deep learning. The proposed methods include a sorting-based approach and one utilizing multivariate polynomial algebras. Although both schemes entail exponential computational complexity relative to the problem size, the sorting-based embedding offers a globally bi-Lipschitz property and maps to a low-dimensional space. Furthermore, an implementation of an almost everywhere injective scheme is possible with minimal redundancy and low computational overhead, demonstrating that nearly any classifier can be realized with negligible performance loss. Numerical evaluations were conducted on the QM9 chemical compound dataset and the PROTEINS protein dataset.

Inspired by a seminal theorem of Bourgain and Tzafriri, we investigate continuous matrix functions $A:\mathbb{R}\to M_{n\times n}$ and derive lower $\ell_2$-norm bounds for their restrictions to specific subspaces.
