This equation can be interpreted as a wave equation incorporating a source term that accounts for the tube's nonlinear geometry. In this work, we derive the equation using a simplified fluid model of an ideal gas. By applying a straightforward change of variables, we transform it into a Schrödinger equation and employ established variational and perturbative techniques to obtain perturbative solutions. As a specific application, we utilize these methods to analyze Gabriel's Horn, calculating the first-order corrections to the linear frequency. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm capable of determining harmonic modes to any order for a general horn geometry.

Long-form question answering (LFQA) focuses on producing paragraph-length responses to specific queries. Although existing LFQA approaches utilizing large pre-trained models succeed in generating fluent and partially relevant text, a significant hurdle remains in ensuring the output is faithful and minimizes hallucinations. We introduce a novel end-to-end framework that simultaneously handles answer generation and machine reading. Our core strategy involves enriching the generation model with fine-grained, answer-centric salient information, effectively prioritizing factual accuracy. Experiments on two LFQA benchmarks, ELI5 and MS MARCO, show that our method outperforms strong baselines across both automatic and human evaluation metrics. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis confirms our approach's ability to produce answers that are fluent, relevant, and notably more faithful.

By employing a straightforward and affordable water jet fabrication technique, we bypass silicon etching constraints to create a $6\,$mm deep atomic vapor cell. Although the initial generation of these cells was restricted to a minimum silicon feature width of $1.5\,$mm, we have successfully implemented a two-chamber design by incorporating a $\sim$25~mm meandering channel connecting the alkali pill chamber to the primary interrogation chamber. This work assesses how channel conductance influences alkali vapor density during the pill activation phase and addresses issues regarding glass damage and pill contamination near the main chamber. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the $6\,$mm silicon cell yields a superior signal compared to conventional $2\,$mm path length silicon vapor cells.

Rascal is a high-level transformation language designed to streamline software language engineering tasks, such as specifying program syntax, analyzing and transforming code, and generating programs. It offers key capabilities like built-in collections (lists, sets, maps), algebraic data types, advanced pattern matching with backtracking, and high-level traversals that support various strategies. However, understanding the interplay between these semantically rich features can be challenging. This report establishes a well-defined formal semantics for a significant subset of Rascal, known as Rascal Light, which is ideal for developing formal techniques like type systems and static analyses. Furthermore, the report defines and proves several notable properties of this semantics, including the purity of backtracking, strong typing, partial progress, and the existence of a terminating subset.

Current Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) methods primarily rely on cross-modal reasoning over discrete views, a strategy that often impedes an agent's spatial and numerical reasoning due to incomplete object visibility within single views and redundant observations across multiple views. A promising alternative involves projecting these discrete views into a unified bird's-eye view to consolidate fragmented and duplicate data. Although existing metric maps can facilitate this unification, they are constrained by limited semantic expressiveness (often relying on predefined labels) and restricted map dimensions, which ultimately degrade an agent's language grounding and long-term planning capabilities. Drawing inspiration from robotics, we propose integrating hybrid topo-metric maps into VLN, leveraging topological maps for long-term planning and metric maps for short-term reasoning. Beyond utilizing deep features for more expressive mapping, we introduce a pre-training framework that employs the hybrid map to learn language-informed representations, thereby strengthening cross-modal grounding and improving language-guided navigation. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of this map-based routing approach for VLN, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance across three benchmarks.

The general relativistic (GR) equation of motion for a planet and its solution are derived exclusively using special relativity (SR) techniques. Within the SR framework, the relative motions of the planet with respect to the sun and the sun with respect to the planet are solved independently via perturbation theory in celestial mechanics. This approach elucidates the structure of spacetime under the sun's gravity and subsequently analyzes its impact on the planet's trajectory. When these results are compared to the GR solution within the post-Newtonian (PN) approximation, the two differ regarding the mean motion and orbital radius, yet they yield identical outcomes for the perihelion precession.

Heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) arise from various extensions of the Standard Model and introduce modifications to the lepton mixing matrix, specifically adding new Dirac and Majorana CP-violating phases. Recent studies indicate that these phases significantly influence lepton number and flavor-violating processes, profoundly affecting predicted observable rates. This study investigates the impact of HNLs and the associated new CP-violating phases on lepton flavor-violating decays and CP asymmetries involving Higgs and Z bosons ($H, Z \to \ell_\alpha^\pm\ell_\beta^\mp$). To facilitate a detailed analysis, we derive complete analytical expressions for these observables, incorporating the effects of final-state charged lepton masses. Our comprehensive examination of $Z$ and Higgs flavor-violating decays reveals high sensitivity to the presence of additional heavy neutral leptons. Furthermore, the new CP-violating phases distinctly alter decay rates through both constructive and destructive interferences. Notably, in the $\mu\tau$ sector, the rates for $Z \to \ell_\alpha^\pm\ell_\beta^\mp$ decays fall within the reach of the FCC-ee, with potential CP asymmetries reaching up to 20–30%.

This study examines the fine-structure [C${\rm \scriptsize II}$] line at $158\,\mu$m as a tracer for molecular gas by exploring the correlation between molecular gas mass ($M_{\rm mol}$) and [C${\rm \scriptsize II}$] luminosity ($L_{\rm [CII]}$) in 11,125 main-sequence, star-forming galaxies at $z\simeq 6$ from the SIMBA simulations, utilizing the S\'IGAME model for line emission. Although approximately $50-100\,\%$ of the simulated gas mass is ionized, more than $50\,\%$ of the [C${\rm \scriptsize II}$] emission originates from the molecular phase. We identify a sub-linear relationship with a slope of $0.78\pm 0.01$ between $\log L_{\rm [CII]}$ and $\log M_{\rm mol}$, which contrasts with the linear relation observed in more massive, metal-rich galaxies at $z \lesssim 6$. The median conversion factor from [C${\rm \scriptsize II}$] to $M_{\rm mol}$ is derived as $\alpha_{\rm [CII]} \simeq 18\,{\rm M_{\rm \odot}/L_{\rm \odot}}$, lower than the observational average of $\simeq 30\,{\rm M_{\rm \odot}/L_{\rm \odot}}$; this discrepancy is attributed to reduced gas-phase metallicities in our simulations. Consequently, a luminosity-dependent, lower conversion factor is required when estimating molecular gas masses from [C${\rm \scriptsize II}$] observations of low-mass galaxies. Within our simulations, [C${\rm \scriptsize II}$] proves to be a superior tracer of molecular gas compared to CO $J=1-0$, particularly at low metallicities where significant amounts of gas are "CO-dark." Furthermore, $L_{\rm [CII]}$ exhibits a tighter correlation with $M_{\rm mol}$ than with star-formation rate (SFR), and both the $\log L_{\rm [CII]}-\log M_{\rm mol}$ and $\log L_{\rm [CII]}-\log {\rm SFR}$ relations stem from the Kennicutt-Schmidt law. These results indicate that $L_{\rm [CII]}$ is a promising indicator of molecular gas at the earliest cosmic times.

This paper investigates the dynamics of template iterations, which involve arbitrary compositions of functions selected from a finite set of polynomials. Specifically, we concentrate on templates utilizing complex unicritical maps within the family $\{ z^d + c, c \in \mathbb{C}, d \ge 2 \}$. We analyze how the connectedness locus for a given template varies with respect to its parameters, demonstrating that for the majority of templates, this locus exhibits upper semicontinuity. Conversely, lower semicontinuous dependence does not generally hold, a fact illustrated by a specific counterexample.

This brief note presents a novel bias-corrected maximum likelihood estimator for the shape parameter of the Weibull distribution, applicable to both complete and type I censored datasets. The proposed estimator demonstrates significantly reduced bias and enhanced efficiency compared to the standard maximum likelihood estimate, yet remains straightforward to calculate using current maximum likelihood software tools.

This is the second installment of our series on KAM theory. We begin by defining functorial analysis before focusing specifically on Kolmogorov spaces. We then construct a functional calculus grounded in local operators, which enables the definition of the exponential map and establishes the relationship between Lie algebra and Lie group actions within an infinite-dimensional setting. Subsequently, we introduce the concept of finite-dimensional reduction and apply it to demonstrate a fixed point theorem for Kolmogorov spaces. Finally, we conclude by proving general normal theorems.

A standard method for enhancing OCR accuracy involves a post-processing stage where models rectify misidentified characters and tokens. Typically, these models are trained using aligned datasets comprising raw OCR output and their manually verified versions. This paper demonstrates that the need for manually corrected training data can be reduced by inferring OCR errors from recurring text spans within extensive corpora of OCR-generated text and creating synthetic training examples that mirror this error distribution. We employed this generated data to train a character-level neural sequence-to-sequence model and assessed its performance on a manually corrected collection of 19th-century Finnish newspapers. The findings indicate that the proposed model achieves significant improvements over both the base OCR system and earlier models that utilized uniformly generated noise.

Let $f\colon X\rightarrow X$ be a surjective endomorphism of a normal projective variety defined over a number field. The dynamics of $f$ can be investigated by examining the linear action induced on $Pic(X)_\mathbb{R}$ by $f^*$, a process regulated by the spectral theory of $f^*$. Denoting $\lambda_1(f)$ as the spectral radius of $f^*$, we investigate $\mathbb{Q}$-divisors $D$ satisfying $f^*D=\lambda_1(f) D$ and possessing an Iitaka dimension $\kappa(D)=0$. We examine the base loci of these divisors and interpret the collection of small eigenvalues via the canonical heights of Jordan blocks, as outlined by Kawaguchi and Silverman. Furthermore, we establish a linear algebraic criterion applicable to surjective morphisms that could aid in proving specific cases of the Kawaguchi-Silverman conjecture.

This work establishes a Law of Iterated Logarithm for random walks on a specific family of diagonal products introduced by Brieussel and Zheng (2021). This result generates numerous novel instances of Law of Iterated Logarithm behaviors for random walks on groups. Specifically, it demonstrates that for any $\frac{1}{2}\leq \beta\leq 1$, there exists a group $G$ and a random walk $W_n$ on $G$ with $\mathbb{E}|W_n|\simeq n^\beta$ satisfying $$0<\limsup \frac{|W_n|}{n^\beta(\log\log n)^{1-\beta}}<\infty$$ and $$0<\liminf \frac{|W_n|(\log\log n)^{1-\beta}}{n^\beta}<\infty.$$

We construct an analytic sphaleron-like solution within a 5D $SU(2)$ gauge theory framework applied to 4D space-time. This solution is defined as a static, finite-energy configuration with a Chern-Simons number of $N_\text{CS}=\frac{1}{2}$. Focusing on the low-energy effective theory, we restrict our analysis to the 4D gauge fields $(A_{i}, A_{y})$ and retain only their Kaluza-Klein zero modes. Notably, the self-duality condition in this 4D space corresponds to the BPS condition for the 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole when the extra-dimensional component $A_y$ is treated as the requisite adjoint scalar. Consequently, the sphaleron-like solution arises from a BPS monopole embedded in higher-dimensional space-time, interpretable as a self-dual gauge field. Leveraging insights from standard 4D instantons, we derive the sphaleron-like configuration for $A_{i}$ carrying $N_\text{CS} = \frac{1}{2}$. A distinctive feature of this higher-dimensional approach, contrasting with ordinary BPS monopoles, is that the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the adjoint scalar is topologically fixed, leading to a sphaleron mass of $M_\text{sp} = \frac{4\pi}{g_{4}^{2}}\frac{1}{R}$ (where $g_{4}$ is the 4D gauge coupling and $R$ is the extra-dimensional radius). Furthermore, we contend that this sphaleron-like solution represents a saddle point within the energy landscape of static field configurations.

An algebra $A$ is defined as two-sided zero product determined if every bilinear functional $\varphi:A\times A\to F$ that vanishes whenever $xy=yx=0$ can be expressed as $\varphi(x,y)=\tau_1(xy) + \tau_2(yx)$ for certain linear functionals $\tau_1,\tau_2$ on $A$. This work outlines fundamental properties and equivalent characterizations, explores relationships with derivation properties, and establishes the primary result: a finite-dimensional simple algebra that is not a division algebra is two-sided zero product determined if and only if it is separable.

Accurate waveform models are essential for detecting and optimizing the scientific return of gravitational wave observations from compact binary systems. This work offers a non-expert overview of inspiral waveforms utilized in the data analysis of compact binary coalescence. It begins by outlining the fundamental principles of gravitational radiation using simple Newtonian orbital dynamics and linearized gravity, focusing on the adiabatic approximation that serves as the cornerstone for constructing theoretical waveforms. Next, it details waveforms within the post-Newtonian framework of General Relativity, emphasizing the core components for inspiral templates of slowly evolving, spinning, nonprecessing, quasicircular binary black holes: post-Newtonian energy and fluxes alongside the balance equation corrected for absorption. These post-Newtonian inspiral templates are then displayed in both time and frequency domains. Finally, the text briefly examines the two primary families of full waveform models currently used in the LSC Algorithm Library Simulation for compact binary mergers, which encompass the merger and ringdown phases: the effective-one-body approach and the phenomenological frequency domain model.

This paper investigates a recent proposal by Bodendorfer, Mele, and M\"unch and Garc\'\i{}a-Quismondo and Marug\'an, where the two polymerization parameters in spherically symmetric black hole spacetimes serve as Dirac observables within four-dimensional Ashtekar's variables. This framework naturally delineates the spacetime into internal and external regions via black and white hole horizons. By appropriately selecting the dependence of these polymerization parameters on Ashtekar variables, the external region can be rendered asymptotically flat. We demonstrate that the spacetime's asymptotic behavior is universal; to the leading order, curvature invariants are independent of the mass parameter $m$. Specifically, the Kretschmann scalar vanishes asymptotically as $K \simeq A_0r^{-4}$, where $A_0$ is a non-zero constant unrelated to $m$, and $r$ denotes the geometric radius of the two-spheres. Inside the internal region, all physical quantities remain finite, effectively replacing the Schwarzschild singularity with a transition surface of finite, non-zero radius. While quantum gravitational effects are negligible near the horizon of very massive black holes, the spacetime's behavior across the transition surface differs markedly from previously studied loop quantum black holes. Notably, the location and maximum amplitude of curvature scalars shift away from the transition surface and vary with $m$. Furthermore, the white hole radius is significantly smaller than that of the black hole and also exhibits a sensitive dependence on $m$.

This article reviews functional $f(R)$ approximations within the asymptotic safety framework for quantum gravity, with a primary focus on a formulation employing a non-adaptive cutoff that yields a second-order differential equation. This approach serves as a case study to illustrate how asymptotic and Sturm-Liouville analyses reveal key properties of the system. Specifically, when properly defined across the entire range $-\infty<R<\infty$, these techniques demonstrate that fixed points are at most discrete, support only a finite number of relevant operators, and exhibit universal scaling dimensions for high-dimensional operators, modulo parametric dependencies arising from the single-metric approximation. The review also examines formulations utilizing adaptive cutoffs, highlighting the principal distinctions between them.

We present Housekeep, a benchmark designed to assess commonsense reasoning in domestic settings for embodied AI. In this task, an agent must organize a home by repositioning misplaced items without receiving explicit directives on what to move; instead, success is measured by how well the agent aligns with human preferences regarding object placement in tidy versus untidy environments. To support this, we compiled a dataset featuring 1799 objects across 268 categories, capturing 585 placements within 105 rooms. Additionally, we developed a modular baseline approach combining planning, exploration, and navigation, which utilizes a large language model (LLM) fine-tuned on internet text to drive effective planning. Our results demonstrate that this baseline agent can generalize to rearrange unseen objects in unfamiliar environments. For further information, please visit our webpage: https://yashkant.github.io/housekeep/

Numerical analysts and scientists frequently encounter a phenomenon where enhancing accuracy inadvertently introduces instability. This paper demonstrates that for a broad range of numerical methods, a fundamental trade-off between error and stability is inescapable. While the framework focuses on reconstructing functions from data, it also encompasses solving differential equations by treating them as constrained function recovery problems involving differential operators and boundary conditions. Specifically, the study reveals that Kansa's Unsymmetric Collocation Method compromises accuracy to gain stability when contrasted with symmetric collocation approaches.

Astronomical imaging frequently suffers from various artifacts stemming from imperfect optics, defective sensors, cosmic ray impacts, and objects like aircraft or satellites. Among these, spurious reflections (or "ghosts") and light scattering from camera and telescope surfaces are especially challenging to eliminate. Identifying these phenomena efficiently within massive cosmological surveys generating petabytes of data presents a significant hurdle. This study utilizes Dark Energy Survey data to design, train, and validate a convolutional neural network for detecting ghosts and scattered light. We detail the model's architecture and training methodology, presenting performance metrics on training and validation sets. Furthermore, we evaluate the approach using independent test data and compare the results against a ray-tracing algorithm. As a proof of concept, our findings suggest that this method holds promise for the Rubin Observatory and future missions.

Recent interest in feature-based out-of-distribution (OOD) detection has largely focused on image classification, yet their application to object detection remains constrained by a poor understanding of the feature space in that domain. We introduce SAFE (Sensitivity-Aware FEatures), a method that exploits the inherent sensitivity of residual networks to flag OOD samples. Building on established image classification theory, we pinpoint shortcut convolutional layers immediately followed by batch normalization as particularly effective for OOD detection. SAFE eliminates the necessity for realistic OOD training data, costly generative models, or retraining the base detector by training a three-layer MLP on a surrogate task: distinguishing between noise-perturbed and clean in-distribution detections using only features from these sensitive layers. Our results demonstrate that this MLP identifies OOD object detections more reliably than prior methods, setting a new state-of-the-art across multiple benchmarks; for instance, on the OpenImages dataset, we reduced the FPR95 by an absolute 30%, dropping from 48.3% to 18.4%. Furthermore, our ablation studies provide empirical support for our findings, showing that this specific subset of layers is disproportionately effective at detecting OOD samples compared to the remainder of the network.

This study applies the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm to manage the longitudinal and lateral control of a simulated vehicle for path-following objectives. The DDPG agent, built with PyTorch, was trained and assessed within a custom Python-based kinematic bicycle simulation. Performance metrics included cross-track and velocity errors relative to the target trajectory. The findings demonstrate that the agent successfully learns a policy capable of maintaining minimal cross-track deviation while adjusting acceleration to reduce velocity discrepancies.

This article introduces a method to implement a "delayed choice experiment" using ultra-cold atoms, aiming to investigate "welcher-Weg" information without collapsing the atom's wavefunction. By integrating established techniques into a novel arrangement, the experiment maintains system coherence throughout the measurement process. Ramsey interference confirms the atom's wave nature, while its particle nature is examined through nondemolition detection of its internal state within an ultra-high finesse cavity. Finally, atomic coherence is preserved by tuning the atom-cavity interaction time so that the atom's state remains unaltered upon exiting the cavity.

This study introduces a data-driven modeling framework for switched dynamical systems operating under time-dependent switching, utilizing the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) as the core learning technique. The process begins with a method to identify switching events within training data derived from system traces, allowing the data to be segmented at these specific instants. Subsequently, ELM is employed to model the dynamics of individual subsystems through a learning process that involves merging segmented trace data and modeling subsystem behavior. Leveraging ELM's unique structure, this modeling task is formulated as an iterative Least-Squares (LS) optimization problem. Ultimately, the switching sequence is reconstructed using the outcomes from the switching detection and trace merging steps. The efficacy of this proposed approach is demonstrated through a case study on the data-driven modeling of a DC-DC converter.

Current artificial intelligence research on fairness often seeks to reduce discrimination through constrained optimization to ensure parity in specific fairness metrics. However, most of these approaches assume that class labels are available, an assumption that is often impractical in real-world scenarios like precision medicine, actuarial analysis, and recidivism prediction. This study addresses fairness within longitudinal right-censored environments where event times may be unknown, leading to censored class labels that render existing fairness frameworks inapplicable. We introduce applicable fairness measures and a debiasing algorithm, supported by theoretical constructs that connect fairness concepts with and without censorship, specifically for these socially sensitive tasks. Experimental results on four censored datasets validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Assessing wildlife abundance across space and time is crucial for understanding population dynamics and guiding effective management. Acoustic recording units offer a promising solution for efficiently monitoring bird populations and communities. We introduce an integrated modeling framework that merges high-quality yet temporally sparse bird point count survey data with acoustic recordings. Through simulations, we evaluated the accuracy and precision of abundance estimates derived from varying quantities of acoustic vocalizations identified by a clustering algorithm, traditional point count data, and a subset of manually validated vocalizations. Additionally, we applied this framework to a case study estimating the abundance of the Eastern Wood-Pewee (*Contopus virens*) in Vermont, U.S.A. The simulation results demonstrate that integrating acoustic and point count data through a unified model enhances the accuracy and precision of abundance estimates compared to models relying on either data source individually. Furthermore, combining acoustic data with a limited number of point count surveys allows for abundance estimation without requiring the validation of any identified acoustic vocalizations. In the case study, the integrated models provided moderate evidence of a decline in the Eastern Wood-Pewee population in the region. Our proposed approach combines dense acoustic data with few point count surveys to generate reliable species abundance estimates, eliminating the need for manual vocalization identification or prohibitively expensive, large-scale repeated surveys. This method offers an efficient monitoring alternative for extensive spatio-temporal areas, particularly when point count data are difficult to acquire or when monitoring rare species with low detection probabilities.

Ho2Ir3Si5 is part of the three-dimensional (3D) R2Ir3Si5 family (where R = Lu, Er, and Ho), characterized by a colossal first-order charge density wave (CDW) transition. This transition involves a significant orthorhombic-to-triclinic lattice distortion accompanied by superlattice reflections. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SXRD) analysis indicates that Ir-Ir zigzag chains along the c-axis drive the CDW formation across all three compounds. Substituting the non-magnetic Lu with magnetic Er or Ho reduces the CDW transition temperature, shifting from TCDWLu = 200 K to TCDWEr = 150 K and TCDWHo = 90 K. Among the three, Ho2Ir3Si5 is unique in displaying second-order superlattice reflections, suggesting an anharmonic modulation wave. The CDW transition manifests as anomalies in specific heat, electrical conductivity, and magnetic susceptibility, all exhibiting a substantial hysteresis of 90–130 K, which supports the SXRD findings. Similar to Er2Ir3Si5, there is a coupling between the CDW and magnetism; the Ho3+ moments are affected by the CDW transition even in the paramagnetic state. While earlier studies on polycrystalline samples reported antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering at TN = 5.1 K, this AFM order is suppressed in the highly ordered single crystals studied here, leaving only the CDW. First-principles calculations predict Ho2Ir3Si5 to be a metal with coexisting electron and hole pockets at the Fermi level, featuring spherically symmetric metallic charge densities on Ho and Ir atoms that are susceptible to CDW distortion. Phonon calculations confirm that Ir atoms are primarily responsible for the distortion, aligning with experimental results.

Estimating dense depth maps solely from sparse LiDAR measurements is a difficult challenge. Although depth-only techniques have seen extensive development, they still lag significantly behind RGB-guided approaches that leverage additional color imagery. Our analysis reveals that current depth-only methods perform well in "normal areas," where measurements are accurate and evenly distributed, but struggle in "overlap areas" (where foreground and background points intersect due to occlusion) and "blank areas" (lacking nearby measurements) due to insufficient input data. Addressing these limitations, we introduce the Coupled U-Net (CU-Net) architecture. Rather than relying on a single large regression network, our approach uses a local U-Net to refine values in normal areas and supplies the global U-Net with robust initial estimates for overlap and blank regions. The final output is generated by fusing predictions from both coupled U-Nets using learned confidence maps. Additionally, we incorporate a confidence-based outlier removal module that filters anomalies using straightforward criteria. This method enhances performance with reduced parameters, achieving state-of-the-art results on the KITTI benchmark. Furthermore, it demonstrates strong generalization across varying depth densities, lighting conditions, and weather scenarios.

This work addresses the best-arm identification challenge in multi-armed bandits featuring stochastic, potentially private rewards, specifically aiming to locate the arm with the highest quantile at a predetermined level. Initially, we introduce a (non-private) successive elimination algorithm designed for strictly optimal identification. We demonstrate that this method is $\delta$-PAC and analyze its sample complexity. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the expected number of pulls, proving that the proposed algorithm is essentially optimal up to logarithmic factors. Both the upper and lower complexity bounds rely on a specialized definition of the suboptimality gap tailored to the quantile bandit setting; notably, we show that as this gap vanishes, identification becomes impossible. Second, driven by the need for privacy in reward data, we develop a differentially private successive elimination algorithm. This approach guarantees finite sample complexity even for distributions with infinite support, and we characterize its complexity accordingly. Crucially, our algorithms operate without requiring prior knowledge of the suboptimality gap or other statistical parameters of the specific bandit problem.

This paper examines the diagonalization of the Nijenhuis tensor within a specific class of Poisson-Nijenhuis structures on compact hermitian symmetric spaces, focusing on its effect on the ring of invariant polynomials associated with a Thimm chain of subalgebras. We demonstrate that $\phi$-minimal representations provide an appropriate basis of invariant polynomials that fully resolves the diagonalization problem. Our results establish that such representations are present in the classical cases AIII, BDI, DIII, and CI, but are absent in the exceptional cases EIII and EVII. Furthermore, we explore an alternative general construction that, for these two exceptional cases, yields a partial computation of the spectrum and suggests a distinct behavior compared to the classical scenarios.

Rikudo is a number-placement puzzle requiring players to construct a Hamiltonian path on a hexagonal grid using provided clues, such as pre-filled numbers and path edges. We demonstrate that the game is NP-complete, even in instances without holes. While the problem becomes solvable in polynomial time when all odd numbers are given, it remains NP-hard if all numbers of the form $3k+1$ are placed.

Traditional model-independent frameworks describe the power spectrum of primordial perturbations using free parameters like the spectral index, its running, the running of running, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. However, this study demonstrates that for straightforward inflationary potentials, the exact primordial scalar and tensor power spectra can be derived by resumming all running terms. By expanding these spectra around the pivot scale in terms of the e-folding number for specific single-field inflation models, we generate a series of functions. Notably, for the viable models examined, summing these terms yields the precise form of the power spectra, resulting in a more accurate parametrization for these specific scenarios. Finally, a comparison with recent cosmic microwave background observations confirms that our newly derived power spectra align well with the data.

Limited training data and significant speaker variability in dysarthric speech result in low accuracy and poor generalization for spoken language understanding systems. By focusing on speech feature engineering, we aim to enhance model generalization despite scarce dysarthric data. Unsupervised Factorized Hierarchical Variational Auto-Encoders (FHVAE) have demonstrated effectiveness in separating content from speaker representations, with prior research indicating that dysarthria manifests within these feature vectors. To bridge the domain gap between control and dysarthric speech, we introduce adversarial training. Using weak supervision, we extract features that are invariant to both dysarthria and speaker identity. Evaluation on a Spoken Language Understanding task reveals that these extracted features achieve higher accuracy on unseen speakers with severe dysarthria compared to those derived from the standard FHVAE model or plain filterbanks.

Robustly estimating 3D hand meshes from RGB images is a highly sought-after task, yet it remains difficult due to the high number of degrees of freedom and challenges like self-similarity and occlusion. Existing methods typically rely on either parametric 3D models or model-free approaches; while parametric models offer greater robustness against occlusions, they lack expressiveness. We introduce a hybrid method that combines a deep neural network with differential rendering-based optimization to effectively merge the strengths of both paradigms. Furthermore, we investigate Virtual Reality (VR) applications, leveraging the multiple cameras found in modern headsets by extending our technique to the egocentric stereo domain, which demonstrates enhanced resilience to the aforementioned issues. Finally, as a practical application, we demonstrate that the improved alignment between images and models enables the acquisition of hand textures, resulting in more realistic virtual hand representations.

Approaches to enhancing the training and predictive performance of weakly supervised machine learning models differ significantly in their degree of specialization to specific tasks or integration with particular model architectures. In this study, we present Knodle, a software framework that decouples weak data annotations, deep learning models, and techniques for refining weakly supervised training into distinct, modular components. This modular design allows the training process to leverage fine-grained details, such as dataset attributes, heuristic rule matches, and specific elements of the deep learning model employed for prediction. Consequently, the framework accommodates a broad spectrum of training strategies for weak supervision, spanning from methods that analyze correlations between rules and output classes independently of the trained machine learning model, to those that exploit the interaction between neural networks and weakly labeled data. We demonstrate the framework's benchmarking capabilities by comparing the performance of various reference implementations across several datasets currently included in Knodle. The framework is released as an open-source Python package named `knodle` and can be accessed at https://github.com/knodle/knodle.

Achieving high-visibility on-chip quantum interference between indistinguishable single photons from multiple sources is essential for integrated linear optical quantum computing. Micro-ring resonators facilitate the generation of brighter, purer, and more indistinguishable single photons through resonant enhancement, eliminating the need for stringent spectral filtering. However, the indistinguishability of heralded single photons originating from multiple micro-ring resonators has never been measured within any photonic platform. This study presents on-chip indistinguishability measurements for heralded single photons produced by independent micro-ring resonators, utilizing an on-chip Mach-Zehnder interferometer and a spectral demultiplexer. We observed a raw two-photon interference fringe visibility of 72 ± 3% for the heralded photons, a result consistent with our theoretical model that accounts for device imperfections, spectral impurities, and multi-pair emissions. We determined that multi-pair emissions are the primary constraint on nonclassical interference visibility and demonstrated a pathway to achieving near-unity visibility in future experiments.

To alleviate the computational burden on edge devices running Deep Neural Network (DNN) applications within the race to deploy AI at the edge, collaborative intelligence has become a viable solution. This approach typically involves partitioning a deep model into edge and cloud components at a specific layer; the edge sub-model generates a deep feature tensor that is sent to the cloud for the cloud sub-model to complete the computationally heavy tasks. However, imperfections in the communication link often cause data loss in the received tensor. This study evaluates the efficacy of four low-rank tensor completion techniques for restoring missing data in these tensors. The research covers both sparse tensors, exemplified by outputs from the VGG16 model, and non-sparse tensors, such as those from the ResNet34 model, assessing performance under both complexity-constrained and unconstrained scenarios.
This paper adapts Masson's (2011) approach to create a user-friendly formula for conducting Bayesian hypothesis tests using only basic ANOVA summary data.

This research investigates the Universality and Membership Problems for gate sets composed of a finite number of quantum gates, utilizing techniques from compact Lie group theory. We introduce an auxiliary challenge known as the Subgroup Universality Problem, which aids in resolving specific cases of the Membership Problem and holds independent significance. The derived theorems are primarily expressed through centralizers and adjoint representations of a specified set of quantum gates.

In 1993, Csima and Sawyer demonstrated that any non-pencil configuration of $n$ pseudolines contains a minimum of $\frac{6}{13}n$ simple intersection points. Given that pseudoline arrangements correspond to the topological representations of reorientation classes of oriented matroids with rank $3$, this paper employs that finding to establish, via induction, that an oriented paving matroid of rank $r \ge 3$ with $n$ elements (where $n \geq 5+ r$) possesses at least $\frac{12}{13(r-1)} \binom{n}{r-2}$ independent hyperplanes. This result provides a novel necessary condition for the orientability of a paving matroid.

This paper examines a group of Bayesian agents sharing a common prior over a finite state space, where each agent receives specific information regarding that state. We determine which distributions over the empirical distribution of posterior beliefs within the population are achievable and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for feasibility. We apply this finding across multiple domains: first, by analyzing the maximization of belief polarization; second, by characterizing feasible agent-symmetric product distributions of posteriors; and finally, by addressing a specific instance of private Bayesian persuasion to derive a concise formula for the sender's optimal value.

Achieving long-term autonomy in robotic systems inherently depends on robust platforms capable of naturally managing hardware and software failures, behavioral issues, or knowledge gaps. Model-based dependable platforms further necessitate rigorous development methodologies, specifically employing correct-by-construction techniques to implement robot behaviors. As robotic autonomy advances, the cost of guaranteeing system dependability rises accordingly. We argue that certifiable dependability for autonomous robots can be enhanced through formal models integrating multiple cognitive functions, knowledge processing, reasoning, and meta-reasoning. This paper advocates for a generative model of cognitive architectures for autonomous robotic agents that aligns with the principles of model-based engineering, certifiable dependability, autonomic computing, and knowledge-enabled robotics.

In transportation systems, users often select routes independently to minimize personal travel costs, a behavior that frequently leads to suboptimal societal outcomes. Consequently, there is increasing focus on implementing road tolling strategies to mitigate these inefficiencies and guide traffic toward a system-optimal state. However, the effectiveness of such tolling mechanisms typically depends on comprehensive data regarding user trip characteristics, such as origin-destination pairs and values of time, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios.

Addressing this practical challenge, we introduce an online learning framework for setting tolls in traffic networks to encourage heterogeneous users with varying time values to adopt system-efficient patterns. Specifically, we present a straightforward yet robust algorithm that updates tolls at each time step based exclusively on observed aggregate road flows, eliminating the need for detailed user trip data and thus safeguarding privacy. Under the assumption that users' origin-destination pairs and values of time are independently and identically distributed across periods, we demonstrate that our method achieves an expected regret and road capacity violation of $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ represents the number of update periods. This regret metric is benchmarked against an offline oracle possessing full knowledge of user attributes. Furthermore, we prove a $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ lower bound on regret for any algorithm, confirming that our approach is optimal up to constant factors. Finally, empirical evaluations on a real-world transportation network show that our method outperforms several benchmarks, underscoring its practical viability.

Observations of filamentary molecular clouds reveal that their characteristics diverge from the isothermal equation of state, prompting theoretical models to suggest that logatropic and polytropic equations of state with negative indices offer superior descriptions. This study compares the impact of these softer, non-isothermal equations of state against their isothermal equivalents regarding the global gravitational instability of such filaments. Utilizing a non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics framework that incorporates ambipolar diffusion, we analyze a filament threaded by a uniform axial magnetic field. By perturbing the fluid and deriving the dispersion relation for both the logatropic and polytropic cases—while accounting for magnetic and diffusive effects—we find that without a magnetic field, a softer equation of state increases susceptibility to gravitational instability. Additionally, a moderate magnetic field enhances stability in a manner sensitive to the specific equation of state, though this effect diminishes under strong magnetic fields, where all equations of state yield similar stability outcomes. Finally, we determine that ambipolar diffusion consistently exerts a destabilizing influence across all considered equations of state.

Excited state energies for the nucleon, Delta, and Omega baryons have been calculated using lattice QCD with anisotropic lattices containing two light and one strange quark. These computations were conducted at three distinct pion masses: 392(4), 438(3), and 521(3) MeV. Utilizing a variational approach with a basis set of approximately ten interpolating operators, we successfully resolved six energy levels within each irreducible representation of the octahedral group. Our results for nucleon excited states are compared against the low-lying experimental spectrum, revealing a reasonable correspondence in the state patterns.

Deep semi-supervised learning is an expanding domain with numerous practical uses. This paper offers a thorough survey of its fundamentals and recent advancements, focusing on model design and unsupervised loss functions. We begin by establishing a taxonomy that classifies current approaches into deep generative methods, consistency regularization, graph-based techniques, pseudo-labeling, and hybrid strategies. Subsequently, we review 52 representative methods and present a detailed comparison based on their loss types, contributions, and architectural distinctions. Beyond highlighting recent progress, we also examine existing limitations and propose tentative heuristic solutions to address these open challenges.

Collider testable low-scale seesaw models forecast pseudo-Dirac heavy neutrinos capable of generating an oscillating sequence of lepton number conserving and violating events. We investigate whether these heavy neutrino-antineutrino oscillations can be detected at the HL-LHC. To this purpose, we conduct the inaugural comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation of these oscillations across multiple benchmark scenarios to determine the conditions under which the CMS experiment could achieve discovery. Our methodology utilizes a FeynRules model file for the phenomenological symmetry protected seesaw scenario (pSPSS) alongside a modified MadGraph version configured to simulate heavy neutrino-antineutrino oscillations. Employing the Delphes fast detector simulation, we implement a statistical analysis framework designed to deduce the significance of oscillations within the simulated datasets.

This research seeks to examine the topological arrangement of cortical thickness and functional networks organized by cortical lobes. Initially, I established the modular structure of these networks based on the frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions of the cortical surface. Subsequently, I identified overlapping edges between cortical thickness and functional networks corresponding to both positive and negative correlations. Ultimately, I demonstrated that overlapping edges with positive correlations correspond to interactions within lobes, whereas those with negative correlations correspond to interactions between lobes.

Canonical ensemble molecular dynamics simulations have examined a binary colloidal mixture with disparate particle sizes under an external potential barrier. Attractive depletion forces between the barrier and the larger colloids induce phase separation. At elevated volume fractions, a concentrated pure phase of larger particles accumulates near the barrier, eventually forming a face-centered cubic crystalline domain. This crystalline phase exhibits diffusion perpendicular to the potential barrier. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of the larger particles' diffusivity follows a non-Arrhenius trend, shifting from sub-Arrhenius to super-Arrhenius behavior as volume fraction increases. This transition in diffusion dynamics aligns precisely with the emergence of the crystalline phase near the barrier.

Building on Matthew Baker's prior research into an elegant, infinite-length game used to analyze subsets of real numbers, we offer two clear examples demonstrating how techniques from set theory or infinite game theory can address Baker's inquiry regarding whether this game precisely characterizes countable subsets of real numbers. Furthermore, we link this game to the extensively studied Banach-Mazur game within topology.

This paper examines the spectral properties of random feature kernel matrices defined as ${\bf K} = \mathbb{E}_{{\bf w}}\left[\sigma\left({\bf w}^{\sf T}{\bf x}_i\right)\sigma\left({\bf w}^{\sf T}{\bf x}_j\right)\right]_{i,j=1}^n$, where $\sigma(\cdot)$ is a nonlinear function, data points ${\bf x}_1, \ldots, {\bf x}_n$ reside in $\mathbb{R}^p$, and the random projection vector ${\bf w} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ consists of i.i.d. entries. In a high-dimensional regime where the sample size $n$ and dimension $p$ are large and comparable, we demonstrate under a Gaussian mixture data model that the eigenspectrum of ${\bf K}$ remains invariant to the distribution of the i.i.d. (zero-mean, unit-variance) components of ${\bf w}$. Instead, it depends solely on $\sigma(\cdot)$ through its generalized Gaussian moments: $\mathbb{E}_{z\sim \mathcal N(0,1)}[\sigma'(z)]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{z\sim \mathcal N(0,1)}[\sigma''(z)]$. Consequently, we introduce a new random feature approach termed Ternary Random Feature (TRF). This method (i) asymptotically reproduces the limiting kernel of the original ${\bf K}$ spectrally and (ii) offers significantly enhanced computational and storage efficiency by optimally tuning both $\sigma$ and ${\bf w}$ to take values in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. The proposed TRF eliminates the need for multiplication operations and reduces storage requirements by a factor of $b$ compared to classical random features like random Fourier features, where $b$ represents the bits needed for full-precision values. Furthermore, experiments on real-world datasets indicate that these substantial improvements in efficiency are accompanied by slightly better performance than existing state-of-the-art random feature compression and quantization techniques.

Detecting multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields presents significant challenges due to complex interference patterns inherent in practical scenarios. While measurements using Rydberg atoms show great promise for MW radar and communications, these atoms are susceptible not only to MW signals but also to environmental noise and atomic collisions. Consequently, solving the governing Lindblad master equation for light-atom interactions becomes complicated when accounting for these noise factors and high-order terms. This study addresses these issues by integrating Rydberg atoms with a deep learning model, demonstrating that this approach leverages atomic sensitivity while mitigating noise effects without the need to solve the master equation. As a proof-of-concept, the deep learning-enhanced Rydberg receiver successfully decoded frequency-division multiplexed (FDM) signals directly. This sensing technology is anticipated to advance Rydberg-based MW field detection and communication systems.

We have established spin-resolved resonant electron energy-loss spectroscopy (SR-rEELS) operating at primary energies between 0.3 and 1.5 keV. This range targets core excitations associated with $2p$-$3d$ transitions in transition metals and $3d$-$4f$ transitions in rare-earth elements, achieving an energy resolution of approximately 100 meV via a spin-polarized electron source based on a GaAs/GaAsP strained superlattice photocathode. By leveraging resonance enhancement from core absorptions alongside electron spin polarization, the technique enables the observation of element- and spin-selective carrier and valence plasmons. Additionally, because the selected primary energy aligns with an inelastic mean free path of 1–10 nm, the method yields bulk-sensitive EELS spectra. This approach is anticipated to offer new insights into elementary excitations comparable to those provided by resonant inelastic x-ray scattering and resonant photoelectron spectroscopy.

Recent evidence indicates that galaxies likely contain a molecular component within their multiphase circumgalactic medium (CGM), yet the theoretical structure and observational constraints of this molecular CGM remain poorly understood. Although recent studies suggest that molecular gas clouds capable of efficient cooling can survive acceleration in hot winds similarly to atomic clouds, the pressure-driven fragmentation of these clouds under external shocks or cooling conditions has not been investigated. To address this, we conducted radiative, inviscid hydrodynamics simulations of clouds disturbed from pressure equilibrium to examine hydrodynamic fragmentation down to molecular temperatures. Our results demonstrate that molecular clouds exceeding a specific critical size can fragment into a fine mist of tiny droplets, with this critical size differing markedly from that of atomic clouds. Furthermore, we observe that cold clouds only fragment when the sound crossing time surpasses the local peak of the cooling time at approximately 8000 K. Additionally, we identify evidence for a universal mechanism termed "splintering," wherein rotational fragmentation causes cold clouds to shatter into a mist of minute droplets. These findings have significant implications for interpreting the molecular phase of the CGM in both observational data and cosmological simulations.

This paper introduces a memory-enhanced method for conditioning an autoregressive language model using a knowledge graph. By representing the graph as a set of relation triples, the system retrieves pertinent relations within a specific context to boost text generation performance. Evaluations on the WikiText-103, WMT19, and enwik8 English datasets reveal that this approach yields a superior language model, achieving lower perplexity and fewer bits per character. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that relational memory enhances coherence, complements token-based memory, and facilitates causal interventions. Ultimately, our model offers a straightforward and effective mechanism for integrating knowledge graphs with autoregressive language models to achieve more coherent and logical output.

While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can rival transformer-based approaches in high-level computer vision tasks by leveraging large kernel decomposition and attention mechanisms, transformers retain dominance in low-level vision, such as super-resolution (SR), due to their superior long-range modeling capabilities. To address this, we introduce a CNN-based Multi-scale Attention Network (MAN) designed to enhance convolutional SR performance. This network comprises two key components: Multi-scale Large Kernel Attention (MLKA) and a Gated Spatial Attention Unit (GSAU). Our MLKA module refines large kernel attention through multi-scale and gating strategies to generate rich attention maps across various granularities, effectively combining global and local information while mitigating blocking artifacts. The GSAU integrates gating with spatial attention to eliminate redundant linear layers and capture informative spatial context. We validate our approach by testing MAN configurations with varying complexities, achieved by stacking different counts of MLKA and GSAU modules. Experimental results demonstrate that MAN offers flexible trade-offs between state-of-the-art performance and computational cost. The code is accessible at https://github.com/icandle/MAN.

Large pre-trained language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced numerous NLP tasks, inspiring researchers to probe their limitations and assess the gap toward human-level natural language understanding. This paper introduces the novel challenge of Ethical Quandary Generative Question Answering to test LLM capabilities. Unlike single-answer queries, ethical quandaries often admit multiple conflicting responses. We present AiSocrates, a system that emulates Socratic philosophy by offering deliberative exchanges of diverse perspectives rather than delivering definitive oracle-like answers. AiSocrates identifies applicable ethical principles and generates responses conditioned on these principles using prompt-based few-shot learning. To ensure safety, the system allows human users to select specific ethical principles. Our results indicate that AiSocrates produces multi-perspective answers promisingly well, outperforming human philosophers by 6.92% on one metric, though it still lags in fully matching human coherence. We argue that AiSocrates represents a significant step toward NLP systems that explicitly integrate human values via prompt instructions, and we are making the code available for research.
Horadam sequences and their partial sums are derived using generating functions, yielding results that are as straightforward as possible.

As autonomous systems increasingly depend on Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for navigation, estimating confidence in their predictions has become critical. While Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) provides a principled framework for modeling DNN uncertainties, current implementations often fail to capture system-wide uncertainty or account for how uncertainty propagates to downstream tasks. This paper introduces a method to quantify overall system uncertainty within UAV navigation. Specifically, we investigate how uncertainty in perception representations influences downstream control predictions. Furthermore, we utilize the system's output uncertainty to refine control decisions, thereby enhancing the UAV's overall task performance.

Recently, multiport interferometers utilizing integrated beamsplitter meshes have gained significant attention as a foundation for various emerging technologies. This paper introduces a new architecture for such interferometers, grounded in the Sine-Cosine fractal decomposition of unitary matrices. Our design is distinctively self-similar, which facilitates the creation of modular multi-chiplet systems. This modularity grants the architecture enhanced resilience against hardware imperfections compared to traditional multiport interferometers. Furthermore, the circuit's structure allows for systematic truncation, a critical feature for minimizing the chip's physical footprint and the computational time required for training optical neural networks, all while preserving full connectivity. Numerical simulations demonstrate that truncating these meshes yields robust performance even when subjected to substantial fabrication errors. Consequently, this design advances the development of large-scale programmable photonics, eliminating a significant barrier to scaling up practical applications in machine learning and quantum computing.

This work introduces kernel ridge regression estimators designed for long-term causal inference by integrating a short-term randomized dataset—featuring treatments and surrogates—with a long-term observational dataset comprising surrogates and ultimate outcomes. The proposed methods yield closed-form solutions for estimating treatment effects, dose-response relationships, and counterfactual distributions through kernel matrix operations. These estimators accommodate discrete or continuous covariates, treatments, and surrogates, regardless of whether they are low, high, or infinite dimensional. Regarding long-term treatment effects, the study establishes $\sqrt{n}$ consistency, Gaussian approximation, and semiparametric efficiency. For long-term dose responses, uniform consistency with finite sample rates is demonstrated, while convergence in distribution is proven for long-term counterfactual distributions.

The optimal transport (OT) problem, traditionally structured as a linear programming task, presents significant computational hurdles when applied to machine learning. Specifically, OT establishes a distance metric between real-world entities—such as images, videos, and texts—by modeling them as probability distributions. However, the high dimensionality of the resulting optimization problem renders classical techniques like network simplex or interior-point methods infeasible. This obstacle was addressed through the introduction of entropic regularization, which enables the use of the efficient Sinkhorn algorithm to solve the regularized variant. An adaptable alternative is the accelerated primal-dual gradient method, capable of utilizing any strongly-convex regularization scheme. This discussion covers these algorithms alongside related challenges, such as approximating the Wasserstein barycenter, and outlines efficient solution strategies, including decentralized distributed approaches.

This study reports a search for the pair production of heavy scalar leptoquarks (LQs), where each LQ decays into a top quark and a tau lepton. The analysis targets final states containing an electron or muon, one or two hadronically decaying tau leptons, and extra jets. Data collected in 2016 from proton-proton collisions at the LHC with the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV correspond to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. No evidence for LQ pair production was observed. Under the assumption of a 100% branching fraction for the LQ$ \to $t$\tau$ decay, upper limits on the production cross section were established as a function of LQ mass, ruling out masses below 900 GeV at the 95% confidence level. These findings currently represent the tightest constraints on the production of scalar leptoquarks decaying to a top quark and a tau lepton.

This study details measurements of slice energy spread at the injector of the European X-Ray Free Electron Laser (XFEL) for a 250 pC electron bunch. Two techniques, both utilizing a transverse deflecting structure (TDS) in the dispersive section, are evaluated. The initial method involves varying beam energies; when the TDS voltage is appropriately scaled to the energy, the rms error remains under 0.3 keV for a 6 keV energy spread. The second method maintains a constant beam energy while modifying the optics, which simplifies the process and lowers the rms error to below 0.1 keV. Numerical modeling that accounts for beam transport and collective dynamics validates these results. Furthermore, the measured slice energy spread at the European XFEL for the 250 pC charge is approximately three times lower than the recent SwissFEL report for the same cathode material and a 200 pC charge.

By employing appropriate convex functions, we define a novel class of flat Minkowski planes featuring automorphism groups of dimension no less than $3$. Specifically, these planes support automorphism groups that are isomorphic to the direct product of $\mathbb{R}$ and the connected component of the affine group acting on $\mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, we identify the isomorphism classes, automorphisms, and potential Klein-Kroll types associated with these examples.

The propagation of infections, contagions, memes, emotions, messages, and other spreadable entities has been explored in numerous studies. Specifically, burning and firefighting have been analyzed on static graphs. Graph burning models the dissemination of "fire" across a network (with one unburned node igniting at each time-step), while graph firefighting models the protection of nodes by deploying firefighters on unburned nodes to halt the spread initiated by a single source.

This article examines a hybrid of firefighting and burning within a graph class that generalizes temporal graphs. In this model, nodes can be infected from external sources. We introduce concepts for both upgrading (applying to unburned nodes, akin to firefighting) and repairing (applying to infected nodes). The selection of nodes for burning, firefighting, or repairing is probabilistic, allowing a variable number of nodes to undergo these states in each time-step.

In the proposed system, burning and firefighting occur concurrently to allow the study of how infection spread interacts with upgrade and repair mechanisms. The specific graph class utilized is a variation of temporal graphs where communication occurs probabilistically at each time-step if an edge exists. Furthermore, nodes can become "worn out" and be removed from the network, while new healthy nodes can be introduced. This graph class facilitates the simulation and analysis of highly complex systems.

The magnetic behavior of Fe$_3$O$_4$ nanoparticle assemblies was thoroughly examined using vibrating sample magnetometry and muon spin relaxation ($\mu$SR) techniques. Two distinct samples, with average diameters of 5 nm and 20 nm, were analyzed. In both cases, measurements revealed clear indicators of a superparamagnetic state at elevated temperatures and a magnetically blocked state at lower temperatures. The $\mu$SR findings indicate that the shift from superparamagnetism to blocking happens gradually across the entire sample volume over a wide temperature span, a phenomenon attributed to the finite size distribution within each sample. Specifically, this transition occurs between roughly 3 K and 45 K for the 5 nm particles, whereas for the 20 nm particles, it spans from approximately 150 K to 300 K. By further analyzing the magnetometry and $\mu$SR data, researchers estimated key microscopic magnetic parameters, including the nanoparticle spin-flip activation energy ($E_A$), magnetic anisotropy ($K$), and the intrinsic spin reversal attempt time ($\tau_0$). These outcomes underscore the complementary insights into magnetic nanoparticles that can be derived by combining bulk magnetic probes like magnetometry with local probes such as $\mu$SR.

We evaluate the precision of a newly proposed nonlinear interference model designed for general dual-polarization 4D formats. In contrast to earlier models used for polarization-multiplexed 2D formats, this approach achieves an average deviation of less than 0.1 dB when compared against split-step Fourier simulations.

This paper introduces a diffusion probabilistic model designed for generating handwriting. Unlike other generative approaches, diffusion models begin with Gaussian noise and progressively denoise it to create output. Our handwriting generation approach avoids the need for text-recognition or writer-style based losses, adversarial losses, or auxiliary network training. By directly incorporating writer stylistic features from image data, our model eliminates the requirement for user interaction during the sampling phase. Experimental results demonstrate that the model can produce realistic, high-quality images of handwritten text that mimic a specific writer's style. The project's implementation is available at https://github.com/tcl9876/Diffusion-Handwriting-Generation.

The recursive expansion of tree-level multitrace Einstein-Yang-Mills (EYM) amplitudes generates a refined graphic expansion, enabling the representation of any tree-level EYM amplitude as a sum over all feasible refined graphs. Each graph provides a distinct coefficient alongside a specific combination of color-ordered Yang-Mills (YM) amplitudes, which possess simpler structures in four dimensions compared to EYM amplitudes, thereby allowing the latter to be evaluated via the former. This study categorizes these refined graphs for EYM amplitude expansions into $\text{N}^{\,k}$MHV sectors. In four dimensions, amplitudes involving $k+2$ negative-helicity particles receive non-zero contributions exclusively from graphs within $\text{N}^{\,k'(k'\leq k)}$MHV sectors. Utilizing this classification, we compute non-vanishing amplitudes featuring two negative-helicity particles in four dimensions. We also identify a correspondence between refined graphs for single-trace amplitudes with $(g^-_i,g^-_j)$ or $(h^-_i,g^-_j)$ configurations and the spanning forests associated with the established Hodges determinant form. Building on this link, we propose a symmetric formula for double-trace amplitudes with $(g^-_i,g^-_j)$ configurations. Finally, by examining the cancellation mechanisms among refined graphs in four dimensions, we demonstrate that all other tree-level amplitudes containing two negative-helicity particles must vanish.

A core obstacle in artificial intelligence involves acquiring data representations that enhance downstream task performance without becoming overly reliant on irrelevant, spurious features. Deriving such predictive, task-specific information is especially challenging when dealing with real-world datasets. To address this, we introduce Contrastive Input Morphing (CIM), a representation learning framework that learns transformations within the input space to reduce the impact of non-essential features on downstream outcomes. Our approach utilizes a triplet loss function grounded in a perceptual similarity metric to guarantee that these transformations retain critical task-related information. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of CIM on tasks prone to spurious correlations, including classification with nuisance data, out-of-distribution generalization, and maintaining accuracy across subgroups. Furthermore, we show that CIM complements other mutual information-based methods, specifically enhancing the performance of the Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) when combined.

For any specific prediction task, several models often achieve nearly identical performance. This study investigates how predictions vary among such competing models, specifically focusing on predictive multiplicity within probabilistic classification. We formally establish metrics tailored to this context and create optimization-based techniques to calculate these metrics for convex empirical risk minimization problems. By applying our approach, we provide insights into the origins of predictive multiplicity and illustrate its frequency and widespread occurrence in real-world risk assessment scenarios. Our findings underscore the critical importance of broadly reporting multiplicity.

Although active matter driven by interacting molecular motors exhibits a non-potential structure locally, we demonstrate the existence of a quasi-potential that effectively characterizes the collective self-organization of motors propelling a cell at the continuum active gel level. This framework enables the interpretation of cell motility as an active phase transition between static and motile steady-state configurations that minimize this quasi-potential. Specifically, both states can coexist metastably, where even minor stochastic disorder within the gel can induce intermittent cell dynamics; in such scenarios, the probability of occupying either the static or motile phase depends on which state represents the global minimum of the quasi-potential.

Coulomb interactions significantly influence quantum spin Hall edge states by diminishing topological protection through two-particle scattering and altering the velocity and charge of collective plasmon modes relative to free electrons. Although these effects complicate the quantification of interactions, we introduce simple and robust edge resonator geometries designed to measure Coulomb interaction using high-frequency techniques. These methods employ a transmission line framework, leveraging the impedance mismatch between the edge states and the surrounding microwave environment.

A longstanding and heavily investigated issue in X-ray astronomy involves the mismatch between advanced theories and observations regarding the intensity ratio of two critical Fe XVII transitions, known as 3C and 3D, which are essential for plasma diagnostics. At the PETRA III synchrotron facility, we resolved this dilemma by enhancing the resolving power by a factor of 2.5 and improving the signal-to-noise ratio by a thousand times compared to our prior research. Previously, the Lorentzian wings could not be distinguished from the background and were therefore omitted from modeling, leading to biased estimates of line strength. Our new experimental oscillator-strength ratio, $R_\mathrm{exp}=f_{\mathrm{3C}}/f_{\mathrm{3D}}=3.51(2)_{\mathrm{stat}}(7)_{\mathrm{sys}}$, aligns with our current theoretical calculation of $R_\mathrm{th}=3.55(2)$ as well as several earlier theoretical predictions. To further eliminate uncertainties related to this measured ratio, we also calculated the individual natural linewidths and oscillator strengths for the 3C and 3D transitions, which also show strong agreement with theory. This successfully resolves the decades-old enigma surrounding Fe XVII oscillator strengths.

We demonstrate that in the context of compact metric spaces, the condition of possessing a finite covering dimension is equivalent to the presence of a total ordering characterized by a finite snake number.

For a driven, dissipative system modeled by a prototype quadratic Hamiltonian, the exact matrix elements of the reduced density matrix are derived from a generating function expressed through normal characteristic functions. This method relies on the Heisenberg equations of motion and operator calculus, with specific limiting cases examined.

Maritime autonomous transport has significantly contributed to global economic integration, with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) increasingly utilized for automatic path planning to simulate vessel collision avoidance in open waters. However, end-to-end methods that learn direct input mappings often struggle with generalization when encountering different environments. To address this, we introduce a novel strategy termed "state-action rotation," which enhances agent performance in unseen scenarios by rotating and storing state-action-state experiences within a replay buffer. Our architecture, built upon Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, incorporates a local view maker and planner, utilizing two deep Convolutional Neural Networks to estimate both policy and action-value functions. Extensive training and testing were conducted in maritime settings using real maps from cities like Montreal and Halifax. Experimental findings demonstrate that integrating state-action rotation into the CVN framework consistently boosts the rate of arrival to destination (RATD) by up to 11.96% compared to the Vessel Navigator with Planner and Local View (VNPLV), while achieving up to 30.82% superior performance in unseen mappings. These results highlight the approach's robustness in new environments, validating that state-action rotation effectively facilitates generalization.

Transmission measurements conducted on three-port microwave networks utilize a symmetric configuration, drawing parallels to three-terminal voltage-drop devices characterized by orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic symmetries. In this setup, a probe terminal is positioned symmetrically between two chaotic graphs, where each graph connects to one port: the input and the output. The analysis of the experimental results clearly reveals weak localization and antilocalization phenomena. We observe strong agreement with theoretical predictions, contingent upon accounting for dissipation effects and imperfect port coupling.

This paper presents a technique for transforming implicit equations into standard functional forms locally, even in the absence of differentiability. For systems of implicit equations involving continuous functions, if unique analytic implicit functions exist within a specific rectangle, each function can be expressed as a power series that serves as the weak-star limit of partial sums within the space of essentially bounded functions. Additionally, we offer numerical examples to illustrate the practical application of our theoretical findings and to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods.

S-boxes are utilized within block ciphers to introduce confusion, typically functioning as mappings over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{n}}$. To effectively counter differential, linear, and higher-order differential attacks, these functions must exhibit low differential uniformity, high nonlinearity, and a high algebraic degree, respectively. This paper presents new classes of permutations that are differentially 4- and 6-uniform by altering the image of the Dobbertin APN function $x^{d}$, where $d=2^{4k}+2^{3k}+2^{2k}+2^{k}-1$, restricted to a subfield of $\mathbb{F}_{2^{n}}$. Additionally, the study provides the algebraic degree and the lower bound for the nonlinearity of these newly constructed functions.

The recurring nature of pandemics, including SARS, H1N1, Ebola, Zika, and COVID-19, demonstrates that such global health crises are unavoidable. These events have frequently resulted in severe global shortages of medical supplies, largely due to inadequate stockpiles and a failure to coordinate the deployment of existing resources to areas of highest demand. This study examines contingency planning and resource allocation through a risk management lens, contrasting with the traditional supply chain approach. Its central premise is that competition for scarce critical resources occurs not only across different geographic regions but also throughout various stages of a pandemic. Drawing an analogy between financial risk aggregation and capital allocation, the paper applies similar principles to pandemic resource planning for healthcare systems. The primary contribution lies in proposing new strategies for optimal stockpiling and allocation that address the spatio-temporal competition between medical supply and demand.

Currently, the world faces an unprecedented pandemic of COVID-19, comparable in scale to the one a century ago. Among the most vital and efficient strategies for halting infection chains, particularly for respiratory illnesses like COVID-19, is contact tracing. Advances in technology have enabled digital solutions, such as the Corona-Warn-App, to facilitate this process. However, given the intrusive nature of contact tracing, safeguarding user privacy is paramount. Ensuring privacy is essential to fostering trust in the application and encouraging its adoption among privacy-conscious individuals. This paper introduces a visual simulation of the Corona-Warn-App's operations to illustrate how it protects user data, notifies individuals of potential infectious contacts, and contributes to curbing the spread of the virus.

Comparing and aligning related datasets situated in heterogeneous spaces is becoming increasingly vital for machine learning. The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) framework addresses this by seeking a coupling matrix to map points between otherwise incompatible datasets. As a non-convex, quadratic extension of optimal transport (OT), GW is NP-hard. Although heuristics perform well in practice—most notably by solving a sequence of nested regularized OT problems—they remain computationally expensive, exhibiting cubic complexity relative to the sample size $n$. This paper demonstrates how a recent Sinkhorn algorithm variant can significantly accelerate GW resolution. By restricting admissible couplings to those with a low-rank factorization into two sub-couplings and updating them alternately, our method computes a stationary point in quadratic time with respect to $n$. Furthermore, if the cost matrices are also low-rank, the algorithm achieves linear time complexity, $\mathcal{O}(n)$. We validate the efficiency of this approach using both simulated and real-world data.

A bipartite network consists of a graph structure containing nodes from two separate domains, with edges existing solely between these domains. Numerous network embedding techniques are available for deriving vector representations from general graphs, accommodating both homogeneous and heterogeneous node and edge types, some of which are tailored for specific bipartite properties.
