By evaluating two distinct approaches against standard segmentation methods using various accuracy metrics and Betti number error—a measure directly linked to topological correctness—we found that integrating topological data into a classical UNet architecture yields significantly superior results. These findings were validated through experiments conducted on the ISBI EM segmentation dataset.

This study establishes global sharp decay rates, serving as both upper and lower bounds, for the spin $\pm \mathfrak{s}$ components—solutions to the Teukolsky equation—within the exterior region and on the event horizon of a slowly rotating Kerr spacetime. These findings are extended to any subextreme Kerr background provided an integrated local energy decay estimate holds. The results encompass the scalar field ($\mathfrak{s}=0$), Maxwell field ($\mathfrak{s}=1$), and linearized gravity ($\mathfrak{s}=2$), thereby confirming the conjectured sharpness of Price's law decay. Our methodology depends on a new global conservation law for the Teukolsky equation, a technique adaptable for deriving precise asymptotics in solutions to semilinear wave equations.

Our research examined scientists participating in two-day workshops focused on fundamental software competencies to identify the most beneficial tools and methods. Survey data collected before and after the sessions indicated a rise in self-reported familiarity, whereas interviews revealed that participants deemed Python instruction more valuable than Unix shell training. Additionally, attendees found supplementary resource links and explanatory background material regarding the rationale behind specific skills to be highly valuable.

Accurate day-ahead electricity price forecasts are crucial for participants in the power sector. However, within the framework of European trade liberalization and market harmonization, obtaining reliable predictions has become increasingly challenging due to the expanding complexity of coupled markets. This study presents a methodology to examine how market coupling influences electricity price forecasting. We employ advanced Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) deep neural networks integrated with feature selection algorithms to predict prices while accounting for these couplings. LSTM models are particularly effective at managing nonlinear, complex issues and processing time-series data. Empirical analysis of the Nordic market demonstrates that the proposed models yield highly accurate results. Our findings indicate that feature selection is vital for precise prediction and that data from integrated markets significantly affects forecasting outcomes. Furthermore, feature importance analysis reveals that the German market plays a prominent role in determining Nord Pool price generation.

This study examines the effects of socioeconomic bias in screening procedures on access to top-tier firms and evaluates policies that could mitigate such bias. Leveraging administrative data from an elite Indian institution, the research reveals significant caste-based earnings gaps. These disparities stem mainly from the final screening stage, which consists of personal interviews focused on non-technical traits linked to socioeconomic status. No significant disparities are found in earlier stages of the job search, including applications, resume reviews, written aptitude tests, group debates assessing socio-emotional skills, or job selection decisions. Using a new model of the job placement process, the paper demonstrates that employers' willingness to pay for candidates from advantaged castes is comparable to the premium paid for a full standard deviation increase in college GPA. Furthermore, implementing a hiring subsidy to remove the caste penalty proves to be a more cost-effective strategy for diversifying elite recruitment compared to alternative policies, such as equalizing pre-college test score distributions or enforcing hiring quotas.

Mask-based annotation of medical images, particularly for 3D data, represents a significant bottleneck in creating dependable machine learning models. While utilizing minimal-effort user interactions (UIs) to steer the annotation process offers promise, challenges persist in effectively aligning mask predictions with these UIs. To overcome this, we introduce the User-Guided Domain Adaptation (UGDA) framework, which employs prediction-based adversarial domain adaptation (PADA) to model the joint distribution of UIs and mask predictions. Subsequently, the UIs serve as anchors to direct and align the mask predictions. Notably, UGDA is capable of learning from unlabeled data and capturing the high-level semantic intent behind various UIs. We evaluated UGDA on the task of annotating pathological livers using a clinically comprehensive dataset comprising 927 patient studies. By relying solely on extreme-point UIs, UGDA achieved a mean (worst-case) performance of 96.1% (94.9%), surpassing the 93.0% (87.0%) obtained by Deep Extreme Points (DEXTR). Moreover, we demonstrated that UGDA maintains this state-of-the-art performance even when provided with only a fraction of available UIs, highlighting its capacity for robust and reliable UI-guided segmentation with extremely minimal labor requirements.

Although the fundamental nature of dark matter is still unidentified, future observations of the high-redshift universe could offer crucial insights. When dark matter interacts with baryons via scattering, it is anticipated to alter the cosmic dawn and reionization processes by suppressing the matter power spectrum and cooling the average gas temperature. Nevertheless, the effects of these interactions on temperature perturbations in both dark matter and baryons have been overlooked until now. This study derives those missing contributions, evolves cosmological perturbations through the end of the dark ages, and demonstrates their potential significance during the onset of the cosmic dawn. Specifically, we observe that the amplitude of the temperature power spectrum on large scales can vary by up to one or two orders of magnitude, while the matter power spectrum experiences an additional suppression of 5–10% at $k\sim 200\, {\rm Mpc^{-1}}$ relative to $\Lambda$CDM predictions that ignore these scattering effects at current CMB sensitivity limits. Furthermore, using the HI power spectrum from the dark ages as a test case, we identify substantial discrepancies arising from altered temperature and ionization fraction power spectra. We conclude that these newly identified contributions must be incorporated into any research concerning this dark matter model that relies on cosmic dawn and reionization data.

We investigate light reshaping within the Schrödinger optics framework using optimal control theory. In technological contexts, Schrödinger optics typically models the slowly varying amplitude of a para-axially propagating electric field, treating the square of the waveguide's refractive index as the potential. The goal of this optimal control problem is to determine a controlling potential that, alongside the governing Schrödinger dynamics, optimally transforms the intensity distribution of Schrödinger eigenfunctions from one waveguide end to the other. This study examines reshaping challenges previously identified by Kunkel and Leger and meets computational demands by leveraging tools from quantum control literature. The efficacy of this optimal control strategy is validated through numerical simulations.

We establish a sufficient condition for the continuous extension of isometries concerning the Kobayashi distance on bounded convex domains within complex Euclidean spaces, provided their boundaries possess regularity slightly exceeding $\mathcal{C}^1$. This result extends a recent finding by A. Zimmer.

Driven by the goal of restricting microscopic models, we compute the precise one-loop corrected de Sitter entropy (defined as the logarithm of the sphere partition function) across all effective field theories of quantum gravity, accommodating particles with arbitrary spin. This approach establishes a universal connection between the sphere partition function and the ratio of a quasi-canonical bulk partition function to a Euclidean edge partition function, where both are expressed as integrals of characters representing the bulk and edge spectra of the observable universe. By expanding the bulk character, the bulk (entanglement) entropy is decomposed into contributions from quasinormal modes, termed quasiqubits. Specifically, for 3D higher-spin gravity described as an sl($n$) Chern-Simons theory, we derive exact results valid to all orders in the loop expansion. Additionally, we demonstrate that this theory possesses an exponentially vast landscape of de Sitter vacua, with their quantum entropy determined by the absolute square of a topological string partition function. For generic higher-spin gravity, the framework elegantly links results across de Sitter, AdS$^\pm$, and conformal contexts, while holography emerges through a quasi-exact cancellation between bulk and edge terms.

Extreme value geostatistics enables the modeling of asymptotic behaviors in random phenomena that vary with space or time. This paper introduces novel models for the extremal coefficient within spatially stationary fields governed by multivariate copulas. Furthermore, we construct extensions of the extremogram and cross-extremogram within a spatial context. Both of these geostatistical tools are represented using the extremal variogram, which captures the asymptotic stochastic behavior of the phenomena.

We explore enjoyable problems loosely connected to concepts and theorems from a differential geometry course. This paper serves as a weekend "treasure chest" to complement the weekday lecture notes. Although the problems and solutions are not original, their connection to the course may be.

Developing state-of-the-art speech translation models is often hindered by the substantial computational resources required, stemming from extensive training datasets and model complexity. Consequently, leveraging pre-trained models offers a promising avenue for constructing robust speech translation systems efficiently. Initially, we explored efficient methodologies for developing both cascaded and end-to-end speech translation architectures using pre-trained models, enabling training and deployment on a single GPU. Although end-to-end models demonstrate superior translation performance compared to cascaded ones, their practical application is constrained by the necessity for additional end-to-end training data. To address this, we introduced a supplementary similarity loss designed to incentivize the model to produce analogous hidden representations for both speech and transcript inputs. This approach enhances data efficiency and boosts translation quality by 6 BLEU points in scenarios characterized by limited end-to-end training data.

The Gomory-Hu tree, or cut tree (Gomory and Hu, 1961), is a foundational data structure designed to report $(s,t)$ mincuts (and, via duality, maxflow values) for every pair of vertices $s$ and $t$ in an undirected graph. Gomory and Hu demonstrated that this structure can be constructed using exactly $n-1$ maxflow computations. Remarkably, despite over 50 years of research, this approach remained the most efficient method for Gomory-Hu trees, even when approximations were permitted. In this work, we overcome this long-standing limitation by presenting an algorithm that computes a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate Gomory-Hu tree using only $\text{polylog}(n)$ maxflow computations.

First, we introduce a randomized (Monte Carlo) algorithm for undirected, weighted graphs that operates in $\tilde O(m + n^{3/2})$ time to return a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate Gomory-Hu tree with high probability. This surpasses the previous best running time of $\tilde O(n^{5/2})$, which was achieved by applying Gomory and Hu's original algorithm to a cut sparsifier of the graph.

Second, we propose a randomized (Monte Carlo) algorithm for undirected, unweighted graphs that runs in $m^{4/3+o(1)}$ time to produce a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate Gomory-Hu tree with high probability. This result improves upon our initial finding for sparse graphs (where $m = o(n^{9/8})$). Previously, the fastest known time for an exact Gomory-Hu tree in unweighted graphs was $\tilde O(mn)$ (Bhalgat et al., STOC 2007), and no superior bounds existed for approximate versions.

Consequently, our Gomory-Hu tree algorithms also resolve the $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate all-pairs and single-source mincut problems within the same time complexities. While these problems are simpler as they require only the mincut values rather than the cuts themselves, this achievement improves upon the recent $\tilde O(n^2)$ time algorithm by Abboud et al. (FOCS 2020).

This paper addresses the challenge of optimally bundling input symbols into transmit packets at the entry point of a wireless sensor network to minimize link delay, accommodating arbitrary arrival rates and a specific channel error rate. The suggested strategy leverages the variable packet length capability of modern communication protocols through packet length regularization to achieve this reduction. This approach relies on a precise analysis of end-to-end link delay for systems with zero error tolerance, utilizing a First Come First Serve (FCFS) queuing discipline and Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) retransmission mechanisms. Derivations are presented for both uncoded systems and coded systems with a defined bit error rate. The resulting packetization policy identifies an optimal interval that minimizes end-to-end delay for channels with a specific bit error probability. Furthermore, this algorithm supports near-optimal bundling of input symbols under dynamic channel conditions, provided these conditions change slowly relative to the symbol arrival rate. It enhances existing network-based delay-optimal routing and scheduling algorithms to further decrease end-to-end delivery times. Additionally, the proposed method is applied to maximize energy efficiency under an average delay constraint by reformulating the issue as a convex optimization problem.

Melanoma is recognized as the most aggressive type of skin cancer. Because malignant and benign lesions often share similar appearances, physicians require significantly more time to differentiate between them. Currently, determining malignancy relies mainly on invasive histological analysis of suspicious areas. Creating an accurate classifier for early and efficient detection could reduce the adverse impacts of skin cancer and improve patient survival outcomes. This study introduces a multi-class classification approach utilizing the CoAtNet architecture, a hybrid model that merges depthwise convolution operations from traditional CNNs with the capabilities of Transformer models and self-attention mechanisms to enhance generalization and capacity. The proposed classifier demonstrates high performance compared to other state-of-the-art networks, achieving an overall precision of 0.901, recall of 0.895, and an AP of 0.923.

We statistically analyzed the conversion efficiency of energy released during active-region transient brightenings into Doppler motion, as well as thermal and non-thermal forms. This analysis utilized two distinct datasets: spectroscopic images of Fe xiv, Fe xv, and Fe xvi lines captured by Hinode's EUV Imaging Spectrometer, and imagery from the 211 \AA channel of the Solar Dynamics Observatory/AIA. The study focused on active region NOAA 11890 during November 09, 2013, and the following day. Our findings indicate that the energy associated with Doppler motion and non-thermal processes accounts for roughly 0.1\--1\% and 10\--100\% of the thermal energy increase, respectively, in each enhancement. Based on these conversion rates, we determined that the total energy flux from AIA transient brightenings contributes no more than 2\% to the heating of the active region relative to conductive and radiative losses.

This paper introduces a new method for few-shot semantic segmentation using sparsely labeled images, specifically tailored for medical applications where sparse labeling and few-shot techniques can significantly reduce the expense of creating new annotated datasets. Our approach leverages the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) algorithm, utilizing sparse labels during meta-training and dense labels during meta-testing to enable the model to predict dense annotations from sparse inputs. We evaluated the method across four Chest X-Ray datasets using two annotation types (grid and points). The findings demonstrate that our approach is particularly effective when the target domain differs significantly from the source domain, achieving Jaccard scores comparable to those obtained with dense labels while utilizing less than 2% of labeled pixels in few-shot scenarios.

The exponential increase in network traffic has resulted in vast datasets, making the manual labeling required for intrusion identification both tedious and prone to errors. Moreover, this data exhibits complex, non-linear, time-varying relationships. Current state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems typically combine multiple supervised methods with fused feature subsets derived from traffic correlations; however, these approaches often incur high computational costs, demand manual model fine-tuning, and rely heavily on labeled data, thereby hindering real-time processing. While unsupervised methods lower computational complexity and eliminate the need for manual labeling, existing solutions fail to account for spatio-temporal correlations. To overcome these limitations, we propose a unified Autoencoder architecture integrating multi-scale convolutional neural networks and long short-term memory (MSCNN-LSTM-AE) for network traffic anomaly detection. The model first utilizes a Multiscale Convolutional Neural Network Autoencoder (MSCNN-AE) to extract spatial features, followed by an LSTM-based Autoencoder that processes temporal features using the latent space representations from the MSCNN-AE. Additionally, two Isolation Forest algorithms are employed as error correction mechanisms to mitigate false positives and negatives, enhancing detection accuracy. Our proposed method was evaluated on the NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and CICDDoS2019 datasets, demonstrating significant performance improvements over conventional unsupervised methods and other existing studies.

For upcoming MeV-scale neutrino experiments, Cherenkov scintillation detectors (CSDs) are highly promising due to their ability to reconstruct both the energy and direction of charged particles. One viable option involves using a novel target material called slow liquid scintillator (SlowLS), which enables the separation of Cherenkov and scintillation light signals. This study employs a Geant4-based Monte Carlo simulation to model a multi-hundred-ton spherical CSD, capturing the micro-processes of MeV particles and optical photons, as well as the functionalities of photomultipliers (PMTs) and readout electronics. Twelve distinct SlowLS samples were simulated to span a broad range of scintillation light yields and emission time constants. Leveraging a deep understanding of the underlying signal mechanisms, simplified functions were developed to predict PMT charge and time signals, thereby facilitating efficient reconstruction of particle energy, direction, and position. The study presents the reconstruction performance—including energy, angular, and position resolutions, as well as particle identification capabilities—for these samples and elucidates how performance varies with scintillation light yield and emission time constants. Ultimately, this research serves as a guide for the future design of MeV-scale neutrino CSDs and the development of SlowLS to meet specific physics objectives.

This paper presents a method for predicting sea surface salinity (SSS) in the Arctic Ocean using satellite data. Since SSS is a vital indicator of Arctic changes and climate dynamics, we specifically target areas where water is erroneously classified as ice by satellite algorithms. Traditional approaches rely on conservative ice masks to eliminate retrieval bias near sea ice, which significantly reduces available data. Our goal is to generate realistic SSS estimates for these regions to create a more comprehensive picture of the Arctic salinity surface and to support future applications requiring data near ice edges or coastlines. We introduce a scalable class of nonstationary processes capable of managing extensive satellite datasets and the Arctic's complex geometry. The proposed Barrier Overlap-Removal Acyclic directed graph GP (BORA-GP) builds sparse directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) where neighbors respect physical barriers and boundaries, effectively modeling dependence in constrained domains. Simulation studies demonstrate that BORA-GP yields more reasonable SSS values in data-sparse regions and outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives across various constrained environments. The R package is accessible at https://github.com/jinbora0720/boraGP.

Paleo-detectors represent a proposed experimental method for searching for dark matter (DM), differing from the standard approach of using tonne-scale real-time detectors to observe nuclear recoils. Instead, this technique leverages small samples of naturally occurring, deep underground rocks ($\gtrsim 5$ km) that have accumulated nuclear damage tracks from recoiling nuclei over geological timescales ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr). Advances in modern microscopy now enable the reading of these nanometer-resolution tracks within macroscopic samples. Benefiting from integration times on the order of a billion years, paleo-detectors could function as nuclear recoil detectors with keV energy thresholds and exposures reaching 100 kilotonne-years. This capability would allow them to probe DM-nucleon cross sections orders of magnitude lower than current limits from conventional direct detection experiments. In this work, we refine the sensitivity forecast for paleo-detectors by incorporating improved background modeling and a novel spectral analysis technique. We demonstrate that the forecast remains robust against uncertainties regarding sample age, background parameters, systematic mismodeling of background spectral shapes, and mineral radiopurity. Specifically, we show that even if uranium concentrations reach $10^{-8}$ (by weight)—far exceeding levels expected in the most radiopure ultra-basic or marine evaporite samples—paleo-detectors could still surpass existing cross-section limits. For DM masses below $\sim 10$ GeV/$c^2$, their sensitivity could extend down to the conventional neutrino floor in xenon-based direct detection experiments.

This paper introduces a novel and underexplored approach to event detection (ED) by reframing it as a question-answering (QA) task capable of handling multiple answers and leveraging entity support. Consequently, identifying event triggers becomes a matter of locating answer spans within a context while simultaneously attending to surrounding entities. The proposed architecture utilizes a pre-trained language model that has been fine-tuned, with the input context enhanced by entities annotated at various levels, including their positions, types, and argument roles. Experiments conducted on the ACE~2005 corpus show that this paradigm is an effective solution for ED, significantly surpassing current state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method can successfully extract event types that were not present during training.

The emergence of transformer architectures like BERT has catalyzed the development of neural ranking models, which have significantly outperformed traditional lexical matching approaches such as BM25 in retrieval effectiveness. While monolingual retrieval has advanced through large-scale datasets like MS MARCO and architectural innovations, cross-language retrieval (CLIR) has lagged behind. This paper presents ColBERT-X, an extension of the ColBERT multi-representation dense retrieval framework that leverages the XLM-RoBERTa encoder to enable CLIR. ColBERT-X supports two training paradigms: zero-shot training, where the model learns on English MS MARCO data while relying on the XLM-R encoder for cross-lingual alignment, and translate-train, where the system is trained using English queries paired with machine-translated versions of the corresponding passages. Experimental results on ad hoc document ranking across multiple languages demonstrate that these dense retrieval models achieve substantial and statistically significant gains over conventional lexical CLIR baselines.

A key component of General Relativity involves analyzing geodesic properties, for which the geodesic deviation equation serves as an effective instrument by linking tidal characteristics of massive bodies to spacetime curvature. This work examines the axially symmetric Taub-NUT metric by applying the geodesic deviation equation to investigate tidal phenomena, specifically focusing on radial geodesics aligned with the spacetime's symmetry axis. We demonstrate that every spatial component of tidal forces undergoes a sign reversal upon crossing the event horizon. Furthermore, we derive solutions for all components of the geodesic deviation vector, enabling a quantification of how the NUT-charge influences the tidal nature of the Taub-NUT metric. A significant finding is that all tidal force components exhibit regular behavior throughout the entire spacetime.

To determine the primary energy of cosmic rays via fluorescence detection, one must add the invisible energy to the measured calorimetric energy. This invisible energy represents the portion carried away by particles that fail to deposit their full energy within the atmosphere. Traditionally, this value is derived from Monte Carlo simulations, which rely on assumptions regarding the primary particle's mass and theoretical models for neutrino and muon production. In this study, however, the invisible energy is derived directly from events recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory. The approach utilizes the correlation between ground-level muon counts and the showers' invisible energy. By employing this method, systematic uncertainties stemming from the unknown mass composition and high-energy hadronic interaction models are substantially minimized, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the Observatory's energy scale estimation.

Since the 2000s, there has been a significant rise in the number of nanosatellites entering space. However, research indicates that a considerable portion of these missions fail. These failure rates are linked to inadequate verification and validation (V&V) practices among hobbyist developers, whereas major space agencies maintain high success rates for their small/nano satellite missions due to their stringent V&V protocols. To enhance payload integration testing for the NanosatC-BR-2, a 2-U Cubesat currently being developed by INPE, the fault injection technique was employed. This method is highly effective for testing system prototypes. This paper presents the design and implementation of a Failure Emulator Mechanism (FEM) on the I2C communication bus to test the interaction between NCBR2 subsystems, thereby verifying interoperability and robustness requirements. The FEM is configured to emulate faults within communicating subsystems by altering exchanged messages on the communication bus. Utilizing an Arduino board for the FEM and the NI LabView environment allows for the programming of various faults to be injected into the I2C bus across different operational modes. Based on a serial architecture, the FEM can intercept all messages and implement diverse faults, including service and timing faults. The FEM's interface with the tester is developed within the LabView environment, providing control and observation capabilities to generate and upload fault injection scripts to the FEM's Arduino board. The proposed FEM architecture and its implementation were validated using two subsystem prototypes: the On-Board Data Handling Computer and the Langmuir Probe payload for NCBR2. For this analysis, the prototypes simulated the expected behavior of each subsystem in communication using two separate Arduino boards.

Memes are ubiquitous on the internet and continuously evolve with our culture; understanding their spread can reveal public sentiment and cultural attitudes. This paper presents team BLUE's solution for the second edition of the MEMOTION shared task. We demonstrate two classification approaches for meme attributes (including sentiment, humor, offensiveness, sarcasm, and motivation): one using text-only BERT, and another employing a Multi-Modal-Multi-Task transformer that analyzes both the image and caption. Both methods utilize state-of-the-art pretrained models for text (BERT, Sentence Transformer) and image processing (EfficientNetV4, CLIP). Our results secured first place in Task A, second in Task B, and third in Task C, while achieving the highest average score across all three tasks.

We demonstrate that for any non-trivial hereditary graph family ${\cal P}$ and a fixed $p \in (0,1)$, the largest number of edges in a ${\cal P}$-subgraph of the random graph $G(n,p)$ is, with high probability, equal to $\left(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1)\right)p{n \choose 2}$. In this expression, $k$ denotes the smallest chromatic number among all graphs excluded from ${\cal P}$.

As quantum many-body simulators advance, Hamiltonian tomography has emerged as a vital technique for verifying quantum devices. This study explores the recovery of Hamiltonians for two spin chain models featuring 2-local and 3-local interactions through measurements of local observables. We demonstrate that once the chain length surpasses a specific critical threshold, the local Hamiltonian can be reconstructed from a single steady state by solving the homogeneous operator equation (HOE), as outlined in Ref. [1]. To elucidate the origin of this critical length, we introduce an alternative approach based on solving energy eigenvalue equations (EEE). Utilizing the EEE method, we successfully replicated the numerical outcomes achieved by the HOE method. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical proof establishing the equivalence between the HOE and EEE approaches. Specifically, we derive an analytical expression for the rank of the constraint matrix within the HOE framework using the EEE method, enabling the determination of the correct critical chain length across all scenarios.

Although the Attentive Neural Process (ANP) enhances the fitting capability and prediction accuracy of Neural Processes (NPs), its increased time complexity restricts the length of input sequences. Drawing inspiration from architectures like the Vision Transformer (ViT) and Masked Auto-Encoder (MAE), we introduce the Patch Attentive Neural Process (PANP), which utilizes image patches as inputs and refines the deterministic path structure of ANP. This approach enables more accurate and efficient extraction of image features for reconstruction.

This study extends and partially summarizes our earlier investigation into pairing phenomena at a quantum-critical point (QCP) within metals, focusing on systems where low-energy physics is governed by an effective model featuring a dynamical electron-electron interaction defined as $V(\Omega_m) = ({\bar g}/|\Omega_m|)^\gamma$, known as the $\gamma$-model. Representative cases include pairing at the emergence of spin and charge density-wave orders, nematic orders, and within SYK-type models. While previous work addressed the regime where $\gamma < 2$, demonstrating that the pairing onset temperature $T_p$ remains finite and scales with ${\bar g}$ despite an infinite set of zero-temperature gap solutions sharing the same spatial symmetry, this paper examines the specific case of $\gamma = 2$. Previously, the $\gamma=2$ model was notable for describing pairing via Einstein phonons in the limit of vanishing dressed phonon mass $\omega_D$. We demonstrate that for $\gamma = 2$, the condensation energy $E_c$ spectrum transitions from discrete to continuous. Consequently, associated gapless "longitudinal" fluctuations disrupt superconducting phase coherence at a finite temperature, resulting in pseudogap behavior for $0 < T < T_p$, where preformed pairs exist. Furthermore, for every gap function in the continuous spectrum, an infinite array of dynamical vortices exists in the upper half-plane of frequency. Regarding the electron-phonon interaction, our findings confirm that $T_p = 0.1827 {\bar g}$, a value derived in prior studies, signifies the onset of pseudogap behavior due to preformed pairs, whereas the true superconducting transition temperature $T_c$ vanishes as $\omega_D \to 0$.

This paper addresses the strong structural controllability of structured networks, which consist of interconnected node systems governed by a structured interconnection law, all defined via pattern matrices. The study establishes that a structured network is strongly structurally controllable if and only if its associated structured system is. However, because this associated system typically possesses a very large state space dimension, existing verification methods are computationally intractable. The primary contribution of this work circumvents this limitation by demonstrating that controllability can be assessed by substituting the original network with a new one where every original node system is replaced by an auxiliary system with a state space dimension of either 1 or 2. Consequently, the controllability of the original network can be verified by testing a structured system whose state space dimension is at most twice the number of node systems, independent of the dimensions of the original node systems.

Detecting the signature of non-thermal (or "hot") electrons in illuminated plasmonic nanostructures demands a thorough comprehension of the resulting non-equilibrium electron distribution and a meticulous experimental setup to differentiate them from thermal electrons. In this work, we present a theoretical framework for utilizing plasmonic molecular junctions to meet these requirements. We demonstrate methods for directly measuring non-thermal electrons independently from the inevitable thermal background and examine the applicability of our theory to recent experimental findings.

In everyday scenarios, handling multiple tasks driven by visual input necessitates the transmission of task-relevant data through the visual system. When a bottleneck prevents all potentially useful information from reaching higher processing layers, it becomes essential to modulate early visual processing based on the specific task. This study investigates how the efficacy of modulating the initial processing stage in an artificial neural network varies with the constraints imposed by an information bottleneck. We quantify this bottleneck using the number of tasks the network must execute and the capacity of its downstream neural layers. Effectiveness is measured by performance across various object detection tasks, utilizing a contemporary multi-task optimization framework. By linking neural modulations to task-driven state transitions within the network and identifying when these switches benefit early processing, our findings offer a functional explanation for why task-based modulation of early neural processes is observed in the primate visual cortex.

Explaining outliers involves pinpointing the specific features that make a sample distinct from normal data, a critical step for downstream human decision-making. Current techniques rely on beam search across feature subsets but quickly become computationally prohibitive because they must re-run an outlier detection algorithm from scratch for every subset. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithm for outlier explanation utilizing Sum-Product Networks (SPNs), a type of probabilistic circuit. Our method exploits the efficiency of marginal inference in SPNs to calculate outlier scores within feature subsets. This allows us to employ backward elimination rather than the conventional forward beam search, reducing the risk of omitting relevant features, particularly in high-dimensional settings. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing both recent search-based and deep learning-based explanation methods.

Dense environments like star clusters and active galactic nucleus disks are predicted to host intense dynamical interactions between stars and compact objects. Utilizing 3D hydrodynamics simulations with the moving-mesh code {\small AREPO}, this study examines the outcomes of close encounters between an equal-mass circular binary (with component masses of $2M_{\odot}$ or $20M_{\odot}$) and a solitary $20M_{\odot}$ black hole, specifically analyzing the resulting transient phenomena. During three-body interactions, the black hole can disrupt stars, generating electromagnetic transients. Encounters with impact parameters smaller than the binary's semimajor axis often produce unique transients distinct from standard two-body tidal disruption events; these range from the simultaneous or sequential full disruption of both stars to the complete disruption of one star followed by partial disruptions of the other. Conversely, when the impact parameter exceeds the semimajor axis, the binary is either merely tidally perturbed or dissociated into bound and unbound single stars via the ``micro-Hills'' mechanism. Our findings indicate that dissociating binaries with $10M_{\odot}$ stars can yield a runaway star and an active, isolated black hole receding from it. Furthermore, unbound stars resulting from dissociation may either form interacting binaries with the black hole or non-interacting, hard binaries that could shrink over time through weak encounters; both scenarios present potential candidates for high- and low-mass X-ray binaries exhibiting periodic luminosity variations.

Deep neural models currently yield top-tier results in semantic role labeling. Drawing inspiration from instance-based learning, which leverages nearest neighbors to manage low-frequency, context-specific training data, this study explores memory adaptation techniques within deep neural architectures. We introduce the Parameterized Neighborhood Memory Adaptive (PNMA) method, which employs a parameterized representation of token nearest neighbors stored in an activation memory to generate predictions based on the most similar training samples. Empirical results demonstrate that PNMA consistently enhances the semantic role labeling performance of baseline models, regardless of the word embedding type used. When combined with contextualized BERT embeddings, PNMA surpasses existing models on both span and dependency semantic parsing datasets, particularly for out-of-domain text, achieving F1 scores of 80.2 and 84.97 on the CoNLL2005 and CoNLL2009 datasets, respectively.

This paper introduces a new maximum entropy formulation of the Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) algorithm, deriving two variants based on unimodal and multimodal value function parameterizations. By integrating maximum entropy Bellman equations with a specific cost function approximation, we achieve a revised DDP formulation capable of escaping local minima through exploration enabled by a multimodal policy. To validate the algorithm's effectiveness, we present experimental results across four systems tackling tasks defined by cost functions with multiple local minima, comparing performance against standard DDP. Additionally, we examine connections to prior research on the linearly solvable stochastic control framework and its extensions regarding compositionality.

This study employs the Finite Element Method to computationally analyze how microstructure influences the saturation magnetostriction of Terfenol-D (Tb$_{0.27}$Dy$_{0.73}$Fe$_{2}$). Based on the equilibrium magnetoelastic strain tensor at magnetic saturation, the model indicates that crystal orientation exerts a greater influence on saturation magnetostriction than grain morphology. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between saturation magnetostriction and the dispersion angle of grains within oriented growth directions $<011>$ and $<111>$. Our findings reveal that distributions with low orientation significantly diminish saturation magnetostriction. These results underscore the necessity of rigorous grain orientation control during the synthesis of grain-aligned polycrystalline Terfenol-D and offer a quantitative assessment of the acceptable dispersion angle ranges for oriented grains.

Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities address the integration of products between convex functions and symmetric functions. This article aims to explore matrix extensions of these inequalities. Specifically, it establishes Fejér-type majorization results applicable to both convex and log-convex functions. Additionally, it offers more rigorous findings for the matrix Levin-Stečkin case, utilizing partial Loewner ordering within the context of Hermitian matrices.

To replicate the mechanical behavior of passive biological cilia within complex fluids, we investigate the bending dynamics of an anchored elastic fiber subjected to a dilute granular suspension under shear. Our findings indicate that the fiber's bending fluctuations precisely capture minute changes in the granular suspension's concentration. Specifically, beyond the steady bending caused by the continuous phase flow, the transit of individual particles generates an additional deflection. We establish that the primary particle-fiber interaction stems from direct contacts and propose a straightforward elastohydrodynamics model to forecast their amplitude. Consequently, our results illuminate the exceptional mechanical sensitivity of biological cilia in detecting nearby solid particles and provide a physical framework for describing their dynamics in particulate flows.

"Ultra-low" Q value $\beta$ decays are defined by their decay energies, which remain below approximately 1 keV. This phenomenon occurs when a parent nucleus transitions to an excited state in the daughter nucleus with an energy level nearly matching the Q value. These decays are significant for two primary reasons: they offer promising candidates for experiments aimed at determining neutrino mass, and they serve as a platform for investigating atomic interference effects within nuclear decay processes. This paper presents an updated assessment of atomic mass and nuclear energy level data to pinpoint potential candidates for ultra-low Q value $\beta$ decay. For numerous identified candidates, higher precision and accuracy in atomic mass data are required to confirm whether the Q value of the potential ultra-low decay branch is energetically feasible and genuinely ultra-low. Such precise measurements can be obtained through Penning trap mass spectrometry.

We introduce a protocol for heralded, dissipative generation of maximal entanglement. This configuration relies on incoherent coupling to two thermal baths at distinct temperatures, eliminating the need for work sources or external control. Initially, a pair of $(d+1)$-dimensional quantum systems is steered into an entangled steady state by the temperature difference; subsequently, maximal entanglement within dimension $d$ can be signaled through local filtering operations. Finally, we examine experimental feasibility, specifically focusing on superconducting implementations.

We introduce EpIC, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for exclusive processes that probe generalised parton distributions. Built upon the PARTONS framework, EpIC offers a versatile software architecture with diverse modelling choices for describing the nucleon's partonic structure. The tool includes a comprehensive feature set, such as multi-channel functionality and radiative corrections, making it suitable for both experimental data analysis and impact studies, particularly for future electron-ion colliders.

This paper introduces a general Bayesian framework designed for the simultaneous estimation of motion and the recovery of missing data within a damaged video sequence. By applying standard maximum a posteriori principles to a variational formulation, we derive generic minimum energy models for both reconstructing the video sequence and recovering motion. These energy formulations are then instantiated, and based on their corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations, we propose a comprehensive multiresolution algorithm. This algorithm computes effective local minimizers for the defined energies, with a specific focus on the numerical implementation of the inpainting component. We present experimental results using both synthetic and real video sequences. Additional image sequences and supplementary materials can be accessed at http://image.diku.dk/francois/seqinp.php.

Machine learning models trained on uncurated datasets can often produce adverse outcomes for inputs from underrepresented groups. To mitigate this, we address the challenge of adaptively constructing training sets to learn classifiers that achieve fairness in a minimax sense. We first introduce an adaptive sampling algorithm grounded in the principle of optimism and establish theoretical performance bounds for it. Additionally, we propose heuristic extensions of this algorithm tailored for large-scale, practical applications. Subsequently, by deriving algorithm-independent lower bounds for a specific problem class, we demonstrate that our adaptive scheme achieves optimal performance that cannot be generally improved. Finally, we validate the advantages of adaptively constructing training sets through experiments on synthetic tasks using logistic regression classifiers, as well as on various real-world tasks employing convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

This study examines the spin and cavity field dynamics within the Tavis-Cummings model by employing quasi-probability distribution functions and the second-order coherence function, respectively. It investigates the impact of both Markovian and non-Markovian noise. Furthermore, it analyzes how the evolution of atomic inversion, spin excitation, and cavity photon number varies across different quantum channels. The equal-time second-order coherence function is utilized to explore the sub-Poissonian nature of light, and this is contrasted with the two-time second-order coherence function to emphasize the (anti)-bunching characteristics of the cavity radiation.

This work addresses a regular Sturm-Liouville problem defined by $-y'' + q(x)y = \lambda y$, where the potential $q(x)$ is unknown. We demonstrate that, given a finite set of eigenvalues, it is possible to calculate additional eigenvalues without requiring further details about $q(x)$. Furthermore, for a Sturm-Liouville problem with boundary conditions $y'(0) - hy(0) = 0$ and $y'(\pi) + Hy(\pi) = 0$ (where $h$ and $H$ are constants), we show how to fully determine the spectrum without any additional information regarding the potential or the boundary constants. These eigenvalues are computed with uniform absolute accuracy. Building on this finding, we introduce a novel numerical approach to solve the inverse Sturm-Liouville problem, which involves recovering the potential from two spectra. This method consists of two stages: first, completing the spectra, and second, reducing the problem to a system of linear algebraic equations, from which the potential $q(x)$ is derived using the first component of the solution vector. The underlying theory relies on special Neumann series representations of Bessel functions for solutions to Sturm-Liouville equations, offering remarkable properties that result in an efficient algorithm for tackling inverse Sturm-Liouville problems.

This research investigates non-linear structure formation in cosmology by incorporating the quantum properties of dark matter (DM) particles within initial conditions at decoupling and regarding the relaxation and stability of DM halos. Unlike standard cosmological N-body simulations, our method employs a thermodynamic framework for collisionless, self-gravitating fermion systems under General Relativity, where halos attain a steady state by maximizing coarse-grained entropy. We demonstrate that this approach offers solutions to pivotal unresolved issues in cosmology, including the mass and identity of DM particles, the origins and characteristics of supermassive black holes in the early Universe, the nature of intermediate mass black holes in small halos, and the core-cusp problem.

Conducting wide-frequency radio observations of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) is essential for understanding the radiative processes shaping observed emissions and linking them to fundamental accretion physics. This study reports high-sensitivity, wide-band (5–45 GHz) (sub)-kpc resolution observations using the JVLA for a sample of 30 nearby AGN (0.003 < z < 0.3) identified by INTEGRAL/IBIS in hard X-rays. We observe a high detection rate across all frequencies, exceeding 95% at 5, 10, and 15 GHz, and remaining above 80% at 22 and 45 GHz, with only two of the thirty sources undetected. The nuclear radio structures are mostly compact, though some display extended jet-like features or more intricate morphologies. The spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the cores generally follow single or broken power laws, with a minority showing peaked components; spectral indices range from flat or inverted to steep, either across the full band or up to a break/peak. The average SED for the sample exhibits a flat slope until 15 GHz, steepens between 15 and 22 GHz, and flattens again beyond 22 GHz. Strong correlations between radio and X-ray emissions are found at every frequency. Approximately half of the sources reveal extended emission resolved by the JVLA, suggestive of low-power jets or large-scale outflows. The unresolved cores, which frequently dominate the radio luminosity, likely originate from jets, outflows, or coronal processes, varying by observed frequency.

We investigate the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the orthogonal-dimer lattice (Shastry-Sutherland model) using the Lanczos diagonalization technique. The system's behavior is governed by the interaction ratio $r=J_2/J_1$, where $J_1$ represents the coupling strength within orthogonal dimers and $J_2$ corresponds to interactions forming the square lattice. Our analysis specifically targets the phase boundary where the dimer state serves as the exact ground state. Through extensive large-scale diagonalization calculations on finite clusters containing 44 and 48 spins, we successfully identified this critical edge. Our findings indicate that the ratio at this boundary is $r= 0.6754(2)$. This theoretical estimate is subsequently compared against experimental data obtained from electron spin resonance measurements.

This work examines phase retrieval within group frames derived from permutation representations, specifically targeting the affine group acting over a finite field. We explore multiple formulations of the phase retrieval problem, such as conjugate phase retrieval, sign retrieval, and matrix recovery. Our primary finding demonstrates that the canonical irreducible representation of the affine group $\mathbb{Z}_p \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_p^\ast$ (where $p$ is prime), when acting on zero-sum vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{p}$, possesses the most robust retrieval capability. This allows for the reconstruction of matrices from scalar products involving a group orbit of rank-one projections. We explicitly identify the generating vectors that guarantee this property, present a linear algorithm for matrix recovery, and offer concrete examples of vectors enabling such recovery. Additionally, we discuss broader implications for general permutation representations.

Recent findings indicate that when X-ray pulsars transition to a low-luminosity state ($L\lesssim10^{35}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$), they undergo a significant spectral transformation. Specifically, the standard power-law spectrum with a high-energy cutoff evolves into a two-component profile, potentially featuring a cyclotron absorption line. This phenomenon has been theoretically attributed to cyclotron photon emission within the neutron star's atmosphere, driven by collisional electron excitation to higher Landau levels and subsequent Comptonization by an overheated electron layer in a thin atmospheric top section. This study employs Monte Carlo simulations to model radiative transfer in an accreting neutron star atmosphere, incorporating resonant scattering of polarized X-ray photons by thermally distributed electrons. The simulations reveal that the spectral shape exhibits strong polarization dependence in soft X-rays ($\lesssim 10\,{\rm keV}$) and near the cyclotron feature. By comparing these numerical results with observational data from the low-luminosity X-ray pulsar A 0535+262, we demonstrate that the proposed model successfully reproduces the pulsar's spectral characteristics. Finally, the implications of this discovery for the observational study of accreting neutron stars are explored.

Accurate numerical characterization remains a critical challenge in composite material analysis. To enhance the precision of image tomography, researchers have developed memory-efficient numerical methods, notably the FFT-based solver introduced by Moulinec and Suquet (1994, 1998), which reduced computational complexity to match that of the FFT. However, advancements in tomography sensors have pushed memory demands and computation times to new heights, creating a significant bottleneck. To address this, the paper explores the integration of recent quantum computing breakthroughs by applying the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) as a substitute for the FFT within the Moulinec and Suquet framework. The study primarily focuses on extracting Fourier coefficients encoded in a quantum state. First, it employs a modified Hadamard test algorithm combined with Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLQAE) to identify these quantum coefficients. Second, it introduces an optimization that eliminates the need for the Hadamard test when characterizing materials on mirrored domains. Finally, this optimized algorithm is applied to material homogenization to calculate the effective stiffness of fundamental geometries.

Numerical solutions to the wave equation dominate the computational expenses in fields such as seismic imaging and full waveform inversion. An alternative strategy involves solving the frequency-domain Helmholtz equation, which reduces dimensionality by addressing each frequency separately. However, classical Helmholtz solvers face significant hurdles, including the necessity of inverting large stiffness matrices, rendering them impractical for large 3D models or high-frequency simulations. Furthermore, these traditional methods lack a mechanism to transfer information between successive problems, creating a bottleneck for applications requiring repeated modeling, such as full waveform inversion. To address these issues, a new approach utilizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) has recently been introduced to solve the Helmholtz equation. This method demonstrates potential in overcoming limitations of conventional algorithms, offering flexibility to incorporate additional physics and leveraging transfer learning to accelerate computations. Despite this promise, the approach requires further refinement to become fully viable, with slow convergence rates and diminished accuracy in the presence of sharp velocity heterogeneities being primary concerns. Consequently, this study investigates various activation functions common in PINN literature, alongside the swish function—a ReLU variant known for improved performance in data science—to enhance convergence. Comparative analysis reveals that the swish activation function delivers superior performance compared to other standard options.

We introduce two stochastic models addressing the Coronavirus pandemic, calculating their statistical properties, including correlation functions and probability density functions. These models, which extend a prior publication in a specialized journal, incorporate both lockdown protocols and the critical functions of hospitals and health care institutes. Our analysis evaluates two scenarios: the standard SIS model (Susceptible-Infectious-Susceptible) under lockdown conditions, and an enhanced SIS model that integrates hospital interventions alongside lockdowns. We demonstrate that while a pure SIS model predicts a resurgence of the virus once lockdowns are lifted, the second scenario shows that exceeding a specific hospital capacity threshold can not only contain the outbreak but also reduce its transmission potential over time. Consequently, the synergy between lockdown measures and hospital capabilities effectively dampens the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, offering a viable strategy before mass vaccination becomes feasible. As an illustrative case, we applied these models to data from the USA and France, estimating noise intensities using Statistical Mechanics. For the USA, we examined two hypotheses regarding whether the country was experiencing its first or a subsequent wave of infection. The strong alignment between our theoretical predictions and actual data validates our methodology.

Hypothetical bosons proposed in theories extending beyond the standard model of particle physics could generate exotic spin-dependent interactions aimed at resolving certain physical mysteries. These interactions can be investigated through tabletop experiments employing high-precision measurement techniques. In this study, we describe an experiment utilizing a magnetic force microscope to probe parity-odd interactions between moving polarized electrons and unpolarized nucleons. The polarized electrons originate from a magnetic tip at the end of a silicon cantilever, with their polarization aligned within the plane of the tip's magnetic coating. The unpolarized nucleons are arranged in a periodic structure featuring alternating stripes of gold and silicon dioxide, creating a modulation in their number density. We anticipate that any exotic forces would alter the cantilever's oscillation amplitude, which is detected via a fiber laser interferometer. By scanning the tip over the nucleon source structure at a fixed separation, data were collected; however, no signal correlated with the density modulation was observed. Consequently, this experiment establishes an upper limit on the electron-nucleon coupling constant of $g_A^eg_V^N\leq 9\times 10^{-15}$ for wavelengths ranging from 15 $\mu$m to 180 $\mu$m, utilizing a direct force measurement approach.

Although pre-trained language models have significantly improved performance across many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, they struggle with high-quality generation requirements, such as producing commonsense or ad keywords. To address this, we introduce KFCNet, a novel framework that leverages external knowledge to enhance generation quality. Our approach utilizes a BERT-based filter to eliminate low-quality candidates and implements contrastive learning independently for both the encoder and decoder within a standard encoder-decoder structure. The encoder's contrastive component facilitates the capture of global target semantics, while the decoder's module improves the effectiveness of retrieved prototypes and general feature learning. Comprehensive experiments on the CommonGen benchmark demonstrate that our model substantially surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving +6.6 points for BLEU-4 (42.5 vs. 35.9), +3.7 points for SPICE (33.3 vs. 29.6), and +1.3 points for CIDEr (18.3 vs. 17.0). Additionally, we validate the proposed contrastive module on ad keyword generation, indicating its potential for commercial applications.

Accurately assessing the spatial spread of extreme rainfall is crucial for evaluating flood hazards and engineering resilient infrastructure, such as stormwater systems. Although environmental extremes often display a decaying spatial correlation as intensity increases, standard max-stable process models for block maxima rely on rigid dependence structures that fail to represent this phenomenon. To address this, we introduce a flexible Bayesian model derived from a wider class of (conditionally) max-infinitely divisible processes. This framework accommodates weakening spatial dependence at higher extremes and, through a hierarchical random effects formulation, ensures scalability to large datasets. Consequently, the model offers a flexible dependence structure alongside efficient, fully Bayesian inference, prediction, and high-dimensional conditional simulation. Built upon flexible random basis functions estimated directly from data, the approach facilitates clear identification of dominant spatial patterns. Furthermore, because (conditional) max-stability is included as a special case, the model enables inference regarding tail dependence classes. Applied to extreme precipitation in North-Eastern America, the model successfully reproduces the observed extremal behavior. Notably, the primary modes of spatial variation identified align with real-world patterns, such as localized tropical cyclones and convective storms along coastlines, as well as variations near mountain ranges. Given its adaptability to other environmental datasets, this model serves as a valuable tool for detecting extreme weather patterns and pinpointing vulnerable regions.

Twisted bilayer graphene (TBLG) systems, situated near a specific critical angle, display isolated flat electronic bands that result in pronounced electron localization. Consequently, these materials serve as excellent systems for investigating reduced-dimensional phenomena such as superconductivity, correlated insulators, magnetism, and quantized anomalous Hall states. When the twist angle drops below a threshold of approximately $1.1^\circ$, the TBLG superlattice reconstructs, forming a periodic moiré pattern with significant atomic corrugation. Utilizing a tight-binding model, this study reveals that such reconstruction substantially alters the electronic structure of small-angle TBLGs. The first magic angle at $\sim 1.1^\circ$ represents a critical point of globally maximized electron localization, effectively dividing reconstructed TBLGs into two distinct classes with unique electronic characteristics. Although low-energy Dirac fermions persist at larger twist angles ($> 1.1^\circ$), systems with smaller angles ($\lesssim 1.1^\circ$) exhibit shared traits, including strong electron localization and large spatial variations characteristic of unfavorable AA stacking regions. However, for twist angles below $1.1^\circ$, the relative influence of local AA regions diminishes progressively, thereby preventing the appearance of additional magic angles, a finding that aligns closely with current experimental data.

This note clarifies that the limit shape of the Jarník polygonal curve [1] is a circle, contradicting the claim in the main result of [2] (Section 2) that it consists of parabolic arcs. The accurate result has already been established and proven in [4].

It is demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of the fast escaping set for a quasiregular self-map on ${\mathbb R}^3$ can assume any value within the range $[1,3]$. Furthermore, the Hausdorff dimension of the Julia set for such maps is estimated under specific growth conditions.

Most comprehensive case studies on malicious code concentrate on botnets (recently resurging with IoT), prominent malware, Advanced Persistent Threats, exploit kits, and ransomware, whereas adware rarely receives comparable attention. Prior research on "unwanted" Windows applications, including adware, prioritized broad analysis to reveal connections between various actors and distribution channels. This paper, however, investigates the capabilities, privacy and security risks, and prevalence of a highly successful and active adware operation known as Wajam by tracing its evolution over nearly six years. We begin by examining its multi-layered antivirus evasion strategies, which combine established and novel techniques to maintain low detection rates for its daily variants, alongside key features such as traffic interception and browser process injection. Subsequently, we analyze the privacy and security consequences for infected users, including plaintext exposure of browser histories and search queries on major websites, arbitrary content injection into HTTPS pages, and remote code execution vulnerabilities. Finally, we assess Wajam's prevalence by analyzing the popularity of its associated domains. Although adware is now often dismissed as "not-a-virus," "optional," or "unwanted" despite its growing negative impact, we argue that it has been neglected for too long. The adware problem can rival or exceed the complexity and impact of traditional malware, posing significant privacy and security risks to users that surpass those of many well-known, thoroughly analyzed malware families.

This study examines continuous-time networked Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) disease propagation across a population, where each agent signifies a sub-population characterized by distinct infection and healing rates, with its state representing the infected fraction at any given moment. By incorporating real-time adjustments in agent behaviors based on infection rates, we aim to develop a feedback strategy that strictly maintains infection levels below a predefined threshold for every agent. Additionally, we seek to ensure the closed-loop system converges to either a disease-free equilibrium or an endemic equilibrium, if applicable. Implementing this strategy enables health authorities to guarantee adequate healthcare capacity for treating the most severe cases. We validate the efficacy of our proposed controller through numerical simulations.

While most influence maximization research assumes one-shot propagation—where influence spreads from seed users exactly once according to a probabilistic diffusion model, determining activation through a single cascade—real-world scenarios often require cumulative impact. Users typically need to receive a sufficient volume of information before making a final purchase decision. This paper models such cumulative activation by first propagating multiple independent pieces of information via the classical independent cascade model; a user then adopts the product if the total number of received messages meets their specific cumulative activation threshold. We examine two optimization problems within this framework: Seed Minimization with Cumulative Activation (SM-CA), which seeks the smallest seed set to activate at least $\eta$ nodes cumulatively, and Influence Maximization with Cumulative Activation (IM-CA), which aims to maximize the number of cumulatively active nodes given a fixed seed budget. For SM-CA where $\eta=n$, we present a greedy algorithm achieving a bicriteria $O(\ln n)$-approximation. However, we demonstrate strong inapproximability results for both SM-CA (when $\eta<n$) and IM-CA. To address this computational hardness, we develop two efficient heuristics for SM-CA and IM-CA based on the reverse reachable set method. Experiments on various real-world social networks indicate that our proposed algorithms significantly surpass existing baseline approaches.

This chapter explores Information Geometry through a non-parametric or functional lens, focusing on probability subsets defined by regularity conditions, such as mutual absolute continuity or specific smoothness levels of densities. We establish a manifold structure by defining an atlas of charts that map probabilities to a Banach space. Notably, these charts are unique because the transition mappings are restricted to being affine. Furthermore, we select a specific formulation for the tangent and cotangent bundles within this affine framework.

Digital agricultural services frequently depend on farmers or advisors manually submitting field boundary records, a process that is both time-consuming and prone to errors. Automating the extraction of these boundaries from satellite imagery could alleviate this manual burden, thereby supporting the delivery of remote services. Current scarcity of field boundary datasets likely reflects the limited adoption of existing methods, which are hindered by costly image preprocessing and the need for local, arbitrary parameter tuning. This paper addresses field boundary extraction as a multitask semantic segmentation challenge. We employed ResUNet-a, a deep convolutional neural network with a fully connected UNet backbone that utilizes dilated convolutions and conditioned inference. This model assigns three labels to every pixel: the probability of belonging to a field, the probability of being part of a boundary, and the distance to the nearest boundary. Combining these labels allows for the generation of closed field boundaries. When tested on a single Sentinel-2 composite image, the model demonstrated high accuracy in mapping field extent, boundaries, and individual fields. Accuracy decreased only marginally when using a single-date image close to the compositing period instead of a monthly composite. Furthermore, experiments confirmed that the model generalizes effectively across different resolutions, sensors, and spatiotemporal conditions without requiring recalibration. Averaging predictions from at least four images captured throughout the season is essential for managing temporal accuracy variations. By reducing preprocessing needs and substituting local, arbitrary choices with data-driven approaches, this method is poised to enable the large-scale extraction of individual crop fields.

Information retrieval serves as a critical element within numerous natural language processing frameworks, including open-domain question answering. Although early approaches relied on manually engineered features, neural networks utilizing continuous representations have recently achieved comparable performance. However, a significant hurdle in adopting these methods is the need for supervised training data consisting of query-document pairs. This paper introduces a novel technique for training retriever models for downstream applications, drawing inspiration from knowledge distillation, that eliminates the requirement for such annotated pairs. By utilizing attention scores from a reader model—which processes retrieved documents to complete the task—we generate synthetic labels for the retriever. Evaluations on question answering tasks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

O. Forster's theorem establishes that for a noetherian ring $R$ with Krull dimension $d$, any projective $R$-module of rank $n$ can be generated by at most $d+n$ elements. This bound was later proven to be sharp by S. Chase and R. Swan, who demonstrated the existence of modules requiring exactly $d+n$ generators. We interpret projective $R$-modules as $R$-forms of the non-unital $R$-algebra defined by zero multiplication. While the first two authors extended Forster's result to forms of various algebras (regardless of commutativity, associativity, or unitality), A. Shukla and the third author subsequently confirmed that this generalized bound is tight specifically for étale algebras. In this work, we derive new upper and lower bounds for the number of generators of an $R$-form of a $k$-algebra, where $k$ is an infinite field and $R$ possesses a finite transcendence degree $d$ over $k$. Contrary to prior assumptions, we demonstrate that for the majority of algebra types, the generalized Forster bound is significantly non-optimal, with our findings being especially comprehensive regarding Azumaya algebras. Our methodology relies on reframing the problem as an inquiry into approximating the classifying stack $BG$—where $G$ represents the automorphism group of the specific algebra—using algebraic spaces of a particular structure.

The paper presents findings from $H\to\tau\tau$ analyses conducted by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations using proton-proton collision data from the LHC at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=$7 and 8 TeV. These results encompass an examination of CP invariance within the vector-boson-fusion (VBF) production mechanism of the Higgs boson, along with a review of the experimental difficulties associated with testing CP invariance in $H\to\tau\tau$ decays.

This paper examines an initial value problem concerning a nonlinear time-fractional Schrödinger equation featuring a singular logarithmic potential. The analysis employs the left/forward Hadamard-Caputo fractional derivative with respect to time. By applying the test function method with a carefully selected test function, we establish sufficient conditions under which global weak solutions do not exist.

This study explores uncertainty estimation within image-guided depth completion. We enhance Deep Basis Fitting (DBF) by integrating it into a Bayesian evidence framework to generate calibrated per-pixel variance. The DBF methodology models depth completion through a network generating low-dimensional depth bases and a differentiable least squares module that calculates basis weights from sparse depth inputs. By applying a Bayesian approach, our proposed Bayesian Deep Basis Fitting (BDBF) method achieves two key objectives: 1) forecasting high-quality uncertainty estimates, and 2) facilitating depth completion even with minimal or no sparse measurements. Through controlled experiments comparing BDBF to standard uncertainty estimation techniques across diverse scenarios, our results demonstrate that the proposed method yields superior uncertainty predictions alongside accurate depth reconstruction.

Large-scale vision-language pre-trained (VLP) models frequently generate text describing visual objects that do not actually exist. This paper comprehensively investigates the issue of object hallucination across three dimensions. First, we analyzed multiple state-of-the-art VLP models and discovered that those scoring higher on standard metrics like BLEU-4 and CIDEr tend to hallucinate more often. Second, we explored the impact of different visual feature representations—specifically region-based, grid-based, and patch-based—on hallucination rates. Contrary to expectations, we found that patch-based features are most effective, with smaller patch resolutions significantly reducing object hallucination. Third, we disentangled various VLP objectives to assess their role in mitigating hallucinations, leading to the proposal of a new pre-training loss called object masked language modeling to further suppress this phenomenon. Our models were evaluated on the COCO (in-domain) and NoCaps (out-of-domain) datasets using an enhanced CHAIR metric. Additionally, we examined how different text decoding strategies and image augmentation techniques influence object hallucination.

Research into quantum communication between distant superconducting platforms is intensifying, aiming to expand the scale of integrated qubits and achieve distributed quantum computing. Because optical photons are necessary for transmission beyond the dilution refrigerator, converting microwave photons directly to optical photons has been extensively explored. However, this direct conversion method is hindered by increased photon noise, thermal effects from intense optical pumping, and the need for high cooperativity. As an alternative for linking superconducting qubits, we propose an entanglement distribution protocol utilizing a solid-state spin quantum memory that interfaces both microwave and optical domains. This quantum memory facilitates communication without the significant internal heating associated with high-power optical pumps used in direct conversion schemes. Furthermore, incorporating quantum memory inherently allows for entanglement heralding and parallel processing through the use of multiple memories.

The environment contains numerous articulated objects whose operation cannot be easily deduced from visual input alone, such as determining whether a door swings inward or outward. Humans navigate this uncertainty through strategic trial-and-error, for instance, by pushing a door first and pulling if that fails. We replicate these capabilities in autonomous agents through H-SAUR (Hypothesize, Simulate, Act, Update, and Repeat), a probabilistic generative framework. This system simultaneously produces a distribution of hypotheses regarding object articulation based on visual observations, tracks confidence in these hypotheses over time, and infers plausible actions for both exploratory and goal-directed manipulation. Evaluated on the PartNet-Mobility dataset after a few exploration steps, our model is compared against existing approaches. Additionally, we introduce a new PuzzleBoxes benchmark featuring locked containers that necessitate multi-step solutions. Our results demonstrate that H-SAUR significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art articulated object manipulation frameworks, even without any training data. Furthermore, we enhance the test-time efficiency of H-SAUR by incorporating a learned prior from vision models trained via learning-based methods.

We demonstrate that the group $\mathrm{QI}^{+}(\mathbb{R})$, consisting of orientation-preserving quasi-isometries of the real line, is a non-simple, left-orderable group that admits no effective action on $\mathbb{R}.$

Delay-differential equations are a subset of functional differential equations characterized by shifts and derivatives relative to one independent variable. Researchers have identified several potential integrable cases within this category. This study examines the elliptic and soliton-like solutions for three specific equations. By applying Hirota's bilinear method, we demonstrate that two of these equations admit three-soliton-type solutions.

MRI-based brain tumor imaging has long been a standard clinical tool for non-invasive tumor detection and grading. Segmenting these tumors is vital for managing primary brain cases, as it enables volumetric analysis to track tumor growth or regression over time, thereby monitoring disease progression and therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, segmentation supports advanced quantitative techniques like radiomics. In medical image analysis, particularly for brain tumor segmentation, deep learning models—specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)—are the preferred methodology. This study examined key design parameters of CNNs tailored for MRI-based brain tumor segmentation. We evaluated two prevalent architectures, DeepMedic and U-Net, by varying essential training parameters including learning rate, batch size, loss function, and optimizer. Using the BraTS 2018 dataset, we assessed different configurations to identify the most effective model, followed by a generalization test on an in-house dataset. Across all experiments, U-Net demonstrated a higher Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) than DeepMedic, though this difference reached statistical significance only for whole tumor segmentation with FLAIR data and tumor core segmentation with T1w data.
