Regarding optimizers, Adam with an initial learning rate of 0.001 yielded the highest DSC for U-Net, while SGD with the same learning rate was optimal for DeepMedic. No significant performance variation was noted among different normalization methods. In terms of loss functions, a weighted combination of soft Dice and cross-entropy with a weight of 0.5 enhanced both segmentation performance and training stability for both architectures.

Threshold queries represent a critical category of operations that compute or count results only up to a predefined limit. Despite their widespread practical application, these queries have surprisingly been overlooked in academic research. This paper offers a comprehensive theoretical examination of evaluating threshold queries, demonstrating that leveraging thresholds can substantially enhance the asymptotic performance of leading query evaluation algorithms. Furthermore, empirical evidence confirms their practical significance. Contrary to established beliefs, we identified key scenarios in real-world datasets where users require query results capped at a specific threshold, regardless of any ranking function used to order outcomes by importance.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have proven effective for analyzing non-grid data, a domain where classical Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are not directly applicable. However, like CNNs, GCNs require vast amounts of labeled data for training. Additionally, GCNs necessitate an adjacency matrix to define relationships among non-grid data points, meaning that training, validation, and test sets typically constitute a single graph structure. Since adjacency matrices are often pre-defined and static, standard data augmentation techniques cannot be applied to these graph structures to expand the training dataset. To enhance learning capacity and model performance despite limited labeled data, this paper introduces two self-supervised learning strategies designed to leverage inherent information within the input graph structure. We evaluate these strategies on two prominent GCN models across three public citation network datasets: Citeseer, Cora, and Pubmed. Experimental findings confirm the generalization and portability of our proposed methods, demonstrating that self-supervised learning significantly boosts GCN performance by improving feature extraction.

Although recent progress has been made, achieving high-performance single-shot 3D microscopy remains a significant challenge. By integrating custom diffractive optical elements (DOEs), a microscope can be transformed into a 3D "kaleidoscope," where a single snapshot captures an array of tiles, each focusing on a distinct depth. However, the resulting multifocal microscopic (MFM) images are hindered by various degradation factors that limit their practical utility. We introduce a unified computational framework that streamlines the imaging setup and enables 3D reconstruction through computation. Our optical design eliminates the chromatic correction grating and reconfigures the multifocal grating to expand the tracking range, requiring only a single grating alongside a standard microscope. Our fully automated, deconvolution-based algorithm incorporates aberration correction, as well as Poisson and background noise reduction, without the need for manual parameter tuning. Experimental results demonstrate spatial resolutions of 0.35 μm laterally and 0.5 μm axially, matching the performance of confocal deconvolution microscopy. Furthermore, we successfully recorded a 3D video of moving bacteria at 25 frames per second using this computational multifocal microscopy approach.

We demonstrate that the linear perturbations of any spin field in the near-zone limit of a Kerr black hole are exactly equivalent to those of an AdS$_2$ black hole sharing the Kerr's fundamental properties. Leveraging this correspondence, we compute the quasinormal mode spectrum and Love numbers for Kerr black holes by employing an AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ duality and a group-theoretical method.

We detail the design, fabrication, and preliminary validation of the variable-delay polarization modulator (VPM) developed for the PIPER cosmic microwave background polarimeter. This device switches between linear and circular polarization by applying a variable phase shift to orthogonal linear components. With a 39 cm diameter, each VPM is built to function in a cryogenic setting at 1.5 K. Our description covers the mechanical architecture and performance of the kinematic double-blade flexure and drive system, as well as the assembly of the high-precision wire grid polarizers.

The solar atmosphere is characterized by a rich presence of magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) wave modes, prompting extensive research into their propagation and energy deposition within the plasma. This journey is complicated by the vertical stratification of plasma properties throughout the atmosphere. Beyond this large-scale inhomogeneity, high-resolution observations from recent decades have revealed intricate fine-scale structures in the chromosphere and corona, which represent variations perpendicular to the local magnetic fields. While the specific impacts of this transverse inhomogeneity on wave propagation are still being elucidated, it is established that it fundamentally alters the characteristics of MHD modes and facilitates complex phenomena such as resonances, turbulence, and instabilities. This review examines key insights regarding how inhomogeneities, both parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field, affect the propagation of Alfvénic waves through the Sun's atmosphere.

Josephson junctions (JJs) form the core of contemporary quantum technologies and metrology. This study elucidates the quantum characteristics of an atomic soliton Josephson junction (SJJ), comprising two weakly coupled condensates with negative scattering lengths trapped in a one-dimensionally elongated double-well potential. By initiating with classical field theory, we uniquely map a two-soliton problem onto an effective two-mode Hamiltonian and apply second quantization. Unlike conventional Bosonic Josephson junctions (BJJs), the quantum SJJ model displays distinct features arising from an effective nonlinearity proportional to the square of the total particle number ($N^2$). We also identify a novel self-tuning mechanism for the effective tunneling parameter, which scales with particle number and decays rapidly as the population imbalance grows. The model predicts the emergence of entangled Fock state superpositions, highlighting dominant $N00N$-state components at the boundaries ($n=0, N$). Furthermore, we demonstrate that this quantum state exhibits enhanced resilience against few-particle losses when minor entangled Fock state components exist near the primary $N00N$-state component. This unique behavior distinguishes the quantum SJJ model from its semiclassical counterpart derived via the Hartree approach.

This study outlines three key findings regarding NP-complete sets. First, if an NP problem necessitates exponential time for almost all input lengths, then every many-one NP-complete set remains complete under length-increasing reductions computable by polynomial-size circuits. Second, if a coNP problem resists solution by polynomial-size nondeterministic circuits, then every many-one complete set is also complete under such reductions. Third, the existence of a one-way permutation secure against subexponential-size circuits, combined with a hard tally language within NP $\cap$ coNP, implies the existence of an NP language that is Turing complete but not many-one complete. Notably, the first two results rely on worst-case hardness assumptions, contrasting with prior work that depended on average-case or almost-everywhere hardness. The third result uniquely integrates both average-case and worst-case hypotheses, whereas earlier studies reaching the same conclusion relied solely on almost-everywhere hardness.

The Federated Distillation (FD) paradigm has emerged as a promising alternative to Federated Learning (FL), particularly for wireless sensor networks constrained by limited communication resources. However, existing state-of-the-art FD algorithms focus exclusively on classification tasks, with regression applications receiving little attention. This work introduces an FD framework specifically designed for regression learning problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate a practical application through an indoor localization system that achieves a favorable balance between communication overhead and accuracy compared to FL-based approaches. Our proposed framework reduces transmitted bit volume by up to 98% and exhibits significantly greater scalability than FL, making it better suited to accommodate the growth of wireless networks.

Facial age estimation involves predicting an individual's age from their images and is applicable across numerous real-world scenarios. While end-to-end deep learning models have delivered impressive results on benchmark datasets, their performance in uncontrolled environments remains limited due to significant variations in head pose, facial expressions, and occlusions. To overcome these challenges, we propose a straightforward yet effective approach that explicitly integrates facial semantics into the age estimation process. This enables the model to accurately identify and focus on the most informative facial regions within unaligned images, irrespective of head orientation or non-rigid deformations. Specifically, we develop a face parsing-based network to capture semantic information at multiple scales and introduce a novel face parsing attention module to utilize these features for age prediction. To facilitate evaluation on real-world data, we present IMDB-Clean, a new large-scale benchmark constructed by semi-automatically refining the noisy IMDB-WIKI dataset using constrained clustering. Extensive experiments on IMDB-Clean and other standard benchmarks, conducted under both intra-dataset and cross-dataset protocols, demonstrate that our method consistently surpasses existing age estimation techniques, establishing a new state-of-the-art. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of face parsing attention for semantic-aware age estimation, offering potential inspiration for other high-level facial analysis tasks. The code and dataset are accessible at \url{https://github.com/ibug-group/fpage}.

Video frame interpolation focuses on generating one or more intermediate frames between two successive video frames, a technique widely utilized for slow-motion creation, frame-rate upscaling, and video codec development. While earlier approaches relied on the assumption of linear per-pixel motion, real-world objects often exhibit non-linear movement, prompting recent methods to employ non-linear models, such as quadratic functions. However, quadratic models can still yield inaccuracies during motion discontinuities (sudden jerks) and occlusions, where flow data may be unreliable. Our paper introduces an approach that approximates per-pixel motion using a space-time convolution network capable of adaptively selecting the appropriate motion model. Specifically, our method enables a soft transition between linear and quadratic models. To achieve this, we utilize an end-to-end 3D CNN encoder-decoder architecture that processes bidirectional optical flows and occlusion maps to estimate the non-linear motion for each pixel. Additionally, a motion refinement module improves the accuracy of the non-linear motion estimates, with final interpolated frames generated by warping neighboring frames using the derived per-pixel motion. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the model's effectiveness, showing that our method surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms across four datasets: Vimeo, DAVIS, HD, and GoPro.

Given the prevalence of long texts in real-world Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, benchmarks have increasingly focused on measuring model accuracy for extended input sequences. However, these evaluations often overlook the balance between accuracy, speed, and power consumption as inputs and model dimensions change. This study systematically examines the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for two prominent long-sequence architectures, Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED) and Big Bird, during fine-tuning and inference across four datasets within the SCROLLS benchmark. By analyzing performance across four sequence lengths (1024, 2048, 3072, and 4096) and two model scales (base and large) under a fixed resource constraint, we explore how hyperparameter settings influence these trade-offs. Our findings indicate that LED consistently outperforms Big Bird by achieving superior accuracy with lower energy expenditure. In summarization tasks, increasing model size proves more energy-efficient than extending sequence length for gains in accuracy, though this results in a significant reduction in inference speed. Conversely, for question answering, smaller models demonstrate both higher efficiency and accuracy, attributed to the ability to utilize larger training batch sizes within the fixed resource budget.

This paper introduces a novel leakage vulnerability in modern encrypted databases known as update pattern leakage. We formally define the security model and concept of DP-Sync in the context of differentially private (DP) update patterns. Furthermore, we propose the DP-Sync framework, which enhances existing encrypted database schemes to support DP-Sync with DP update patterns. DP-Sync ensures that the complete history of data updates on the outsourced structure remains protected by differential privacy, accomplished through the application of differentially private strategies that govern how data owners synchronize their local data.

We introduce a straightforward category of mechanical models featuring an interaction between a standard degree of freedom and one possessing a negative kinetic term, known as a ghost. Analytical proofs demonstrate that the system's classical motion remains entirely stable across all initial conditions, despite the conserved Hamiltonian being unbounded both above and below; this finding is corroborated by numerical simulations. Although systems with negative kinetic terms frequently arise in high-energy physics, quantum gravity, and modern cosmology and are typically considered unstable, our results indicate that this conventional wisdom may be overly simplistic for mechanical systems. We show that mechanical systems containing ghosts can indeed maintain stability.

The production of double-strangeness $\Xi^{-}$ particles in Au+Au collisions at incident beam energies of 2, 4, and 6 GeV/nucleon is analyzed using a multi-phase transport model based on a pure hadron cascade. Results indicate that, driven by increased nuclear compression, the model employing a soft equation of state (EoS) predicts higher yields for both single-strangeness particles ($K^{+}$ and $\Lambda+\Sigma^{0}$) and double-strangeness $\Xi^{-}$. The $\Xi^{-}$ yield demonstrates a significantly greater sensitivity to the EoS than single-strangeness particles, as the phase-space distribution of $\Xi^{-}$ is notably more compact. Furthermore, the heightened sensitivity of the $\Xi^{-}$ to single-strangeness yield ratio with respect to the EoS, when comparing heavy and light systems, is maintained. Investigating $\Xi^{-}$ production in relativistic heavy-ion collisions offers an alternative avenue for the global heavy-ion program to determine the EoS at high densities, a critical factor for exploring the phase boundary and the onset of deconfinement in dense nuclear matter.

Kaur, Prabhakar, and Vesnin introduced F-polynomials for virtual knots in 2018, deriving them from flat virtual knot invariants. These polynomials extend Kauffman's affine index polynomial and utilize smoothing operations at classical crossings within a virtual knot diagram. This paper presents weight functions tailored for ordered orientable and flat virtual links. A flat virtual link is defined as an equivalence class of virtual links under a local symmetry that alters the type of classical crossing in a diagram. By examining three distinct smoothing types at classical crossings in virtual link diagrams and applying appropriate weight functions, we establish a recursive method for constructing new invariants. Through explicit examples, we demonstrate that the newly defined polynomial invariants are more powerful than F-polynomials.

The optimal receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which plots the maximum detection probability against the probability of false alarm, serves as a fundamental information-theoretic measure of the difficulty inherent in binary hypothesis testing (BHT). While the optimal ROC curve for a specific BHT, derived from the likelihood ratio test, is theoretically defined by the probability distributions of the observed data under both hypotheses, these distributions are often unknown or computationally unmanageable. In such scenarios, where only independent samples of the likelihood ratio are available, the challenge arises of estimating the optimal ROC curve from these samples. This study derives the maximum likelihood estimator for the optimal ROC curve, demonstrating that it converges to the true optimal curve in the Lévy metric as the number of observations approaches infinity. Additionally, a classical empirical estimator, which calculates error probabilities from two distinct sample sets, is examined. Simulation results indicate that the maximum likelihood estimator achieves significantly higher accuracy than the empirical estimator, particularly when sample sizes under one hypothesis are limited. Furthermore, the area under the maximum likelihood estimator is derived, establishing it as a consistent estimator for the true area under the optimal ROC curve.

The effective implementation of time-series classifiers in practical settings depends on identifying data that deviates from the training distribution, a process known as out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. This work addresses the emerging challenge of OOD detection specifically within the time-series domain, highlighting unique obstacles that render existing image-based methods ineffective. To tackle these issues, we introduce a new approach called Seasonal Ratio Scoring (SRS), which involves three core steps. Initially, inputs are broken down into class-specific semantic components and residuals. Next, deep generative models are used to calculate the conditional likelihoods for both the components and residuals, from which the seasonal ratio score is derived. Finally, a threshold range is established using in-distribution data to flag OOD samples. Empirical evaluations across various real-world benchmarks show that SRS outperforms baseline techniques for time-series OOD detection. The open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/tahabelkhouja/SRS.

Oxide heterostructures facilitate the investigation of two-dimensional electronic transport phenomena. This work examines various aspects of magnetotransport in specific spin-orbit-coupled systems, distinguishing between their single-band and multiband characteristics. Experimental data from the single-band system BaPbO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$, collected via temperature- and magnetic field-dependent measurements, demonstrate a significant interaction between weak antilocalization (WAL) and electron-electron interaction (EEI). By modeling both mechanisms equally, the study identifies a substantial EEI contribution at low temperatures, indicating the formation of a strongly correlated ground state. Additionally, theoretical analyses of multiband effects, as observed in the model system LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$, forecast a profound influence of carrier filling on the topological Hall effect in systems with overlapping bands. Even minimal band coupling leads to notable deviations from standard Hall conductivity, a phenomenon explainable through a fully quantum mechanical framework based on the hybridization of intersecting Hofstadter bands.

This study presents a search for strongly interacting massive particles (SIMPs), a form of dark matter, utilizing the CMS detector at the LHC. SIMPs are hypothesized to be produced in pairs, appearing experimentally as jet pairs devoid of associated tracks. To effectively suppress the substantial multijet background, the analysis employs the fraction of jet energy carried by charged particles as a primary discriminator, with residual background estimates derived directly from data. The investigation utilizes 2016 proton-proton collision data collected by CMS, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 16.1 fb$^{-1}$. No significant excess of events was observed beyond the expected background. Consequently, within the framework of the simplified dark matter model considered, SIMPs with masses up to 100 GeV are ruled out, while additional sensitivity is examined for higher mass ranges.

We present the discovery of three transiting low-mass companions orbiting evolved stars: a brown dwarf (TOI-2336b) and two objects situated near the hydrogen-burning mass limit (TOI-1608b and TOI-2521b). Initial identification of these systems was achieved through data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). TOI-2336b possesses a radius of $1.05\pm 0.04\ R_J$, a mass of $69.9\pm 2.3\ M_J$, and an orbital period of 7.71 days. TOI-1608b has a radius of $1.21\pm 0.06\ R_J$, a mass of $90.7\pm 3.7\ M_J$, and an orbital period of 2.47 days. TOI-2521b exhibits a radius of $1.01\pm 0.04\ R_J$, a mass of $77.5\pm 3.3\ M_J$, and an orbital period of 5.56 days. Our analysis indicates that all three low-mass companions are inflated. By fitting a relationship between radius, mass, and incident flux using existing samples of transiting brown dwarfs and low-mass M dwarfs, we identified a positive correlation between flux and radius for both brown dwarfs and low-mass stars; however, this correlation is weaker than that observed in giant planets.

This paper details experiments demonstrating that quantum computers can already tackle certain natural language processing challenges. The study presents examples such as topic classification via both quantum support vector machines and bag-of-words methods, bigram modeling for word sequences and formal concepts, and the resolution of ambiguity in verb-noun combinations. Although the datasets remain limited, the described systems have been executed on actual quantum hardware. The paper outlines these implementations and their outcomes alongside the underlying algorithms and mathematical frameworks.

This study offers a comprehensive analysis of XMM-Newton data for five narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies (NLS1s). All five exhibit very soft X-ray continuum emission characterized by a photon index of $\Gamma\gtrsim 2.5$, leading us to classify them as `ultra-soft' NLS1s in this work. By modeling their optical/UV-X-ray spectral energy distribution (SED) using a reflection-based approach, we detect evidence that the accretion disc surface in these ultra-soft NLS1s exists in a higher ionization state compared to typical Seyfert 1 active galactic nuclei. Our best-fit SED models indicate that, based on available black hole mass measurements, these five ultra-soft NLS1s possess Eddington ratios of $\lambda_{\rm Edd}=1-20$. Furthermore, our models suggest that a substantial portion of the disc energy in these ultra-soft NLS1s is emitted as non-thermal radiation rather than thermal disc emission. Given their extreme characteristics, X-ray observations targeting the iron band for these sources are especially difficult; however, future missions such as Athena will provide clearer insights into the spectral shape within the iron band, allowing for a better distinction between reflection models and other interpretations of their broadband spectra.

Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-based outdoor positioning systems are unsuitable for indoor environments due to inherent limitations. In response, location fingerprinting, which leverages machine learning, has become a practical and effective indoor positioning solution, valued for its simplicity and high accuracy. Historically, shallow learning algorithms dominated this field; however, recent research has shifted toward deep learning methods following their demonstrated superiority over traditional approaches. This paper offers a comprehensive review of deep learning applications in indoor positioning. It begins by examining the pros and cons of various fingerprint types, followed by an analysis, categorization, and comparison of existing literature solutions based on performance metrics. Recognizing data as a critical component, the study also presents a detailed overview of publicly available indoor positioning datasets. Although integrating deep learning has yielded significant performance gains, it has also introduced new challenges and implementation pitfalls, which are thoroughly discussed. The paper concludes with final remarks and an outlook on future research trends.

Students from underrepresented minority (URM) backgrounds face historically entrenched inequities in higher education, particularly within STEM fields that lack diversity. To foster inclusivity and fairness in STEM, it is essential to understand how students from various racial and ethnic groups perform. This study analyzes ten years of data from a large public university to examine trends in major selection, retention, and degree completion among Asian, URM, and White students, alongside their grade point averages (GPAs) for those who persist or leave. The results indicate that URM students are significantly more likely to drop out of most majors than their peers, a disparity that is especially acute in physics and economics. Additionally, URM students consistently achieve lower GPAs than both Asian and White counterparts. Alarmingly, in certain STEM disciplines, the grades earned by URM students who successfully graduate are comparable to those of Asian and White students who abandoned the major. These disturbing patterns suggest a critical shortage of adequate support, mentorship, and guidance for URM students who are already severely disadvantaged. These quantitative findings underscore the urgent need to create equitable and inclusive learning environments to ensure that URM students entering college with significant disadvantages receive the necessary support to excel alongside their peers.

Generating Arithmetic Word Problems (AWPs) via machine methods is difficult because they must accurately express quantities and mathematical relationships while maintaining strict consistency. Machine learning solvers depend heavily on large, annotated datasets containing consistent problems with diverse linguistic variations. While leveraging domain knowledge is essential for verifying consistency, LSTM-based models excel at producing text with varied language structures. To address this, we introduce OLGA, a system designed to create consistent Transfer-Case (TC) word problems involving object transfers between agents. Although we provided a training dataset of consistent 2-agent TC-problems, an LSTM-based generator produced consistent outputs for only about 36% of cases. To ensure quality, we utilized an extension of the previously proposed TC-Ontology to validate problem consistency. Of the remaining 64% of outputs, approximately 40% contained minor errors that were corrected using the same ontology. This validation and repair process relies on constructing an instance-specific representation (ABox) of the auto-generated problem, utilizing sentence classifiers and BERT models trained on problem texts where sentence segments are annotated with ontology class names. Since consistency rates for LSTM-generated 3-agent problems (which are longer) drop significantly, we developed an ontology-based strategy to extend consistent 2-agent problems into consistent 3-agent ones. Consequently, our approach successfully generates a substantial volume of consistent TC-type AWPs involving two or three agents. Furthermore, because the ABox encapsulates all problem information, it enables the generation of various annotations. Applying this methodology to create other types of AWPs represents a promising avenue for future research.

Although machine learning has achieved significant success, it faces limitations when training data is scarce. One promising remedy is incorporating prior knowledge into the training process, a concept known as informed machine learning. This paper offers a structured review of various approaches within this domain. We define informed machine learning and propose a conceptual framework that outlines its components and differentiates it from traditional machine learning. Furthermore, we introduce a taxonomy serving as a classification system for these approaches, considering the origin of knowledge, its representation, and its integration into the machine learning workflow. Utilizing this taxonomy, we survey existing research and explain how diverse knowledge forms—including algebraic equations, logical rules, and simulation outcomes—can be utilized in learning systems. By evaluating numerous studies through this framework, we identify key methodologies in the field of informed machine learning.

While the standard Hawking formula predicts total black hole evaporation, incorporating quantum gravity effects allows us to examine fermion tunnelling from a 5-dimensional rotating black string. In this scenario, the temperature depends not only on the string itself but is also influenced by the emitted fermion's quantum number and the additional spatial dimension. These quantum corrections decelerate the temperature rise, naturally resulting in a stable remnant rather than complete evaporation.

This article presents findings on regular depolarization cascades occurring in periodically perturbed feedforward chains of excitable two-dimensional FitzHugh-Nagumo systems, specifically under strong excitatory forcing at the leading node. The research details a parameter study involving variations in the forcing period, revealing a dynamical transition from basic depolarization to intricate behaviors, notably the onset of mixed-mode oscillations. The work combines rigorous theoretical analysis with meticulous numerical simulations. Specifically, it offers formal proofs regarding the existence and stability of periodic traveling depolarization waves, as well as the presence and propagation of simple mixed-mode oscillations characterized by alternating depolarization and refraction. Extensive numerical exploration uncovers the mechanism behind complex mixed-mode oscillations, which involve numerous large-amplitude voltage spikes separated by occasional small-amplitude resets that do not reach the threshold. Furthermore, detailed numerical analysis sheds light on how this complex behavior propagates downstream, demonstrating an effective filtration property where the network progressively reduces the complexity of mixed-mode oscillations along the chain.

As shared micromobility integrates into our daily lives and surroundings, we anticipate a rapid increase in low-speed transportation options for first- and last-mile journeys. This sector is poised to serve billions of people, offering significant benefits. Consequently, simulations of shared micromobility—including docked bike stations, dockless bike systems, and e-scooters—are viewed as promising solutions for managing the surge in short-distance trips. This paper begins by presenting a comprehensive overview of shared micromobility simulation and its associated validation metrics. It then categorizes research topics, summarizes, and classifies existing studies. Finally, the paper outlines current challenges and future directions for further investigation.

An algorithm is introduced to determine if a finite game qualifies as a weighted potential game (WPG) without prior knowledge of its weights. This algorithm is further utilized to identify the nearest WPG for any given finite game. The study defines the concept and criteria for near weighted potential games (NWPGs), demonstrating their evolutionary equivalence to the original finite game. Leveraging this equivalence, a new method is developed to substitute potential games with NWPGs in game-theoretic control, thereby enhancing the practical application of potential game-based optimization.

Using Numerical Action reconstructions, researchers have traced the paths of galaxy systems (halos) with redshifts ($cz$) below 8,000 km/s since $z=4$. The study focuses on a collection of 9,719 halos drawn from the 2MASS group catalog and Cosmicflows-3. Current distances were calibrated to minimize discrepancies with observed redshifts, with specific compromises made for objects having the most precise distance measurements. The Hubble constant ($H_0$) was varied between 69 and 77 km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, while the matter density parameter ($\Omega_m$) was fixed based on baryon acoustic oscillation data from the Planck Satellite. This approach yielded a best-fit mass-to-light amplitude and modeled the interhalo medium with a uniform density to account for matter outside halos. These solution paths illustrate the formation history of nearby large-scale structures and the emptying of voids. Assuming no local density anomalies, the optimal model yields $H_0 = 73$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with nearly equal matter contributions from interhalo matter (IHM) and halos. By adjusting IHM density to test for local over- or underdensities, a valley of best-fit models emerges along the relation $H_0 = 73.0 (1 + 0.165\delta)$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, a result consistent with Friedmann models featuring distinct internal and external densities. The fraction of matter in IHM observed in n-body simulations aligns roughly with the $H_0=72$ scenario. Additionally, videos were generated to visualize large-scale structure formation complexities, and standard n-body calculations, initiated as tests of NAM solutions and extended to a cosmic scale factor of $a=2$, offer insights into future cosmic evolution.

The MAVEN/NGIMS (Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN/Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer) detects the local influence of gravity waves (GWs) by measuring the regular oscillations of CO$_{2}$ density in the upper atmosphere (120–190 km). These measurements provide valuable insights into GW activity and the atmospheric conditions governing their propagation and dissipation. Observations from MAVEN indicate that GW intensity in this region is governed by saturation processes under isothermal conditions, resulting in an activity level correlated with the inverse of the background temperature.

Recent analysis compares these upper-atmosphere findings with data collected at lower altitudes ($\sim$95–150 km) during aerobraking by the accelerometers on MGS, ODY, and MRO. While an anti-correlation between GW-induced density perturbations and background temperature is plausibly identified in ODY's polar region data, this relationship is absent in the MGS and MRO datasets. Conversely, MRO data from polar regions show a correlation between density perturbations and the Brunt-V\"{a}is\"{a}l\"{a} frequency derived from Global Climate Modeling.

At lower altitudes (100–120 km), although wave saturation may remain dominant, isothermal conditions no longer hold. In such scenarios, theory suggests GW intensity correlates with static stability rather than background temperature. At other latitudes across the three aerobraking datasets, GW-induced relative density perturbations correlate with neither inverse temperature nor static stability. This indicates that, in these cases, GW activity is controlled not only by saturation but also by the effects of wave sources and wind filtering through critical levels.

**Problem Definition:** Emergency department (ED) boarding involves retaining admitted patients within the ED due to a lack of inpatient capacity, often forcing them to compete with new arrivals for resources and degrading emergency care quality. While redirecting patients to alternative specialties or housing (overflowing) is a common mitigation strategy, it can jeopardize inpatient care quality and create operational issues. This study focuses on optimizing inpatient bed assignments to minimize boarding durations without resorting to excessive overflow.

**Methodology:** We model hospital wards using a queuing system featuring multiple customer classes and several server pools. Leveraging real hospital patient flow data, we develop a computationally efficient method to formulate the bed assignment problem, aiming to maximize the joint probability that all waiting patients meet their specific delay targets.

**Results:** By dynamically adjusting overflow rates, the proposed method effectively reduces patient waiting times and alleviates the impact of time-of-day variations on boarding. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms standard practices, including early discharge policies and threshold-based overflowing strategies.

**Managerial Implications:** We offer a practical, data-driven solution for the bed assignment problem that captures essential aspects of patient flow management. Since the resulting optimization model is tractable, this approach serves as a valuable tool for controlling queueing systems with time-sensitive service needs.
This study examines the unit groups, $2$-class groups, $2$-class field towers, and the structures of the second $2$-class groups within certain multiquadratic number fields of degrees $8$ and $16$.

This study introduces SIR-HUXt, a framework that combines sequential importance resampling (SIR) data assimilation with the HUXt solar wind model. Specifically, SIR-HUXt is tailored to ingest time-elongation profiles of Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) fronts within the low heliosphere, utilizing data from missions like STEREO, Parker Solar Probe, and Solar Orbiter. To evaluate its performance, we conducted Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) using a synthetic, fully Earth-directed CME propagating through a uniform ambient solar wind, initialized with mean observed speeds and widths. These experiments covered various observer angles ranging from 20 to 90 degrees behind Earth, including the L5 Lagrange point where ESA's upcoming Vigil monitor will operate for space weather forecasting. Results indicate that SIR-HUXt effectively constrains CME speed and partially constrains longitude; however, CME width remains largely unconstrained, a limitation that requires further investigation to determine if it stems from the specific scenario or is inherent to assimilating time-elongation profiles. Rank histograms confirm that the SIR-HUXt ensembles are well-calibrated, showing no significant bias or dispersion issues. Consequently, tighter constraints on initial CME speed directly enhance predictions for transit time to Earth and arrival velocity. For an L5 observer, SIR-HUXt achieved a 69% reduction in transit time uncertainty and a 63% reduction in arrival speed uncertainty. These findings suggest that SIR-HUXt can enhance the realism of HUXt simulations, thereby reducing uncertainty in hindcast and forecast predictions regarding CME arrival times.

Axion-like particles (ALPs), which can be generated within the Sun and represent a promising candidate for cosmological dark matter, may decay into two photons or interact with matter through Inverse Primakoff (IP) scattering. This study identifies inelastic channels associated with IP processes arising from atomic excitation and ionization. We calculate the corresponding cross-sections by utilizing complete electromagnetic fields derived from atomic charge and current densities, employing robust, well-validated many-body atomic methods. Using these results, we establish constraints on ALP-photon coupling strengths. Our analysis probes and excludes a previously inaccessible parameter space for ALP masses ranging from 1 eV to 1 MeV, which was beyond the reach of prior laboratory experiments. Furthermore, we project the sensitivity potential of upcoming experimental initiatives.

An analytical design is presented for a nonlinear control algorithm tailored to a self-energizing electro-hydraulic brake, where a synthesized nonlinear controller ensures the attainment of the desired closed-loop system dynamics.

Interstellar dust grains with substantial sizes are thought to originate from supernova ejecta and stellar winds, whereas smaller grains may result from the fragmentation of larger ones that have undergone stochastic acceleration. To investigate this acceleration mechanism, we integrated new magnetohydrodynamic (MHD)-particle-in-cell (PIC) techniques into the astrophysical fluid code RAMSES. In this framework, dust grains are modeled as massive "superparticles" subject to aerodynamic drag and Lorentz forces. We conducted various numerical tests to validate the method across different physical scenarios and to demonstrate potential acceleration mechanisms. As a concluding test and basis for future research, we present outcomes from decaying dusty MHD turbulence simulations using grain parameters representative of 1-2 $\mu$m grains in typical cold neutral medium environments. Our findings indicate that under these conditions, both electrically charged and neutral grains can be accelerated significantly beyond their shattering velocities. Although the peak of the gas-grain relative drift velocity distribution is higher for neutral grains, charged grains display an extended exponential tail reaching much greater velocities. Despite this, the distribution shapes suggest that the additional gas-grain coupling provided by the Lorentz force offers grains relative protection against shattering. We also explore the link between these simulations and relatively pristine ~$\mu$m-sized presolar grains that show no signs of significant wear over their lifetimes.

This paper introduces a self-supervised learning approach for multi-object pose estimation. Inferring 3D object understanding from 2D images is a difficult task that involves reconstructing additional dimensions from reduced data. Specifically, determining an object's 3D localization or orientation demands precise reasoning, distinguishing it from simpler tasks like object classification; consequently, the size of the training dataset is critical. However, acquiring large-scale 3D datasets is challenging because 3D annotation is costly and time-intensive. By leveraging image sequences from simple navigation to expand the dataset scale, we can overcome data limitations and facilitate efficient adaptation to new environments. Nevertheless, relying solely on single-image self-annotation by the network limits its training performance. To surpass this self-performance ceiling, we propose a strategy that exploits multiple observations of objects within image sequences: first, global object map landmarks are estimated via network prediction and data association to generate corrected annotations for individual frames. Subsequently, the network undergoes fine-tuning using the dataset augmented with these self-annotated samples, thereby exceeding its initial performance boundaries. We evaluated the proposed method on the KITTI driving scene dataset, demonstrating improved performance in estimating the 3D poses of multiple objects.

Multipartite entity resolution seeks to consolidate records from numerous datasets into unified entities. We formulate a broad category of record linkage tasks within this context as a combinatorial optimization challenge, specifically the multidimensional assignment problem (MAP). Motivating this approach, we demonstrate the benefits of multipartite resolution compared to sequential bipartite matching. Given that the MAP is NP-hard, we employ two heuristic strategies—a Greedy algorithm and very large-scale neighborhood search (VLSNS)—to identify the most probable matches across datasets. We assess and contrast the efficacy of these algorithms and their variants using synthetic data. Computational experiments compare VLSNS against the Greedy algorithm and two genetic algorithm configurations. Crucially, we investigate two re-starting methods for the heuristic search: random-sampling multi-start and deterministic design-based multi-start, finding that the design-based approach becomes increasingly efficient as database size expands. Furthermore, our results indicate that VLSNS, particularly its multi-start variant, surpasses the simple Greedy heuristic, and hybridizing Greedy search with VLSNS yields performance gains. Additionally, incorporating just three extra runs of VLSNS within a multi-start framework enhances the procedure's effectiveness. Finally, we introduce a method for evaluating the complexity of the very large-scale neighborhood search.

Although topological invariants like Chern numbers are essential for categorizing topological phases and predicting unique physical phenomena, their direct spectroscopic measurement has historically been restricted to electronic bands. This study employs inelastic neutron scattering combined with ab initio calculations to detect diverse topological crossings within phonon bands of MnSi and CoSi single crystals. We establish a specific correlation between the Chern numbers of these band-crossing nodes and the modulation of scattering intensity in momentum space surrounding them. With adequate resolution, this approach enables the determination of Chern numbers of any magnitude for topological phonon nodes.

We investigate the non-zero eigenmodes of the modular Hamiltonian within the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate a perturbative method to construct zero eigenmodes for the modular Hamiltonian associated with the excited states introduced by Lashkari et al. (arxiv:1811.05052), leveraging knowledge of the vacuum's non-zero eigenmodes.

We have developed a model for the two-point statistics of biased tracers that integrates dark matter dynamics derived from $N$-body simulations with an analytic Lagrangian bias expansion. Leveraging Aemulus, a suite of $N$-body simulations designed for emulating cosmological observables, we emulate the cosmological dependence of these nonlinear spectra across redshifts ranging from $z = 0$ to $z=2$. Our emulation procedure achieves sub-per-cent accuracy at $k=1\, h {\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ for redshifts targeted by future surveys, with accuracy improving at higher redshifts. We demonstrate that the model effectively describes the statistics of complex tracer populations, including those exhibiting assembly bias and baryonic effects, by reliably fitting their clustering and lensing statistics at $z\simeq 0.4$ up to scales of $k_{\rm max} \approx 0.6\, h\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. Furthermore, we show that the emulator facilitates unbiased cosmological parameter inference in simulated joint analyses of clustering and galaxy--galaxy lensing using data from an independent $N$-body simulation. These findings suggest that our emulator is a promising tool readily applicable to the analysis of both current and forthcoming datasets from galaxy surveys.

We introduce a novel Lagrange multiplier method designed to create positivity-preserving schemes for parabolic equations. This technique employs a space-time Lagrange multiplier alongside Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions to enforce positivity. A predictor-corrector framework is subsequently utilized to generate these schemes: the prediction phase utilizes a standard semi-implicit or implicit method, while the correction phase ensures positivity at negligible computational cost. Furthermore, we offer a modification enabling the construction of schemes that maintain both positivity and mass conservation. This approach is versatile, compatible with any spatial discretization and adaptable to various time-stepping schemes. We derive stability proofs for both first- and second-order methods within a general framework and provide extensive numerical experiments to validate the proposed methodology.

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has underscored the critical challenges and importance of accurately interpreting antibody test results. Achieving a classification strategy with minimal error rates for distinguishing positive from negative samples is difficult when measurement values overlap, and further uncertainty emerges if data complexities are ignored. We address these issues using a mathematical framework that integrates high-dimensional data modeling with optimal decision theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that increasing data dimensionality enhances the separation of positive and negative populations and uncovers nuanced structures that can be mathematically described. By combining these models with optimal decision theory, we develop a classification scheme that outperforms traditional methods, such as confidence intervals and receiver operating characteristic curves, in distinguishing samples. We validate this approach using a multiplex salivary SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin G assay dataset, illustrating three key benefits: (i) improved assay accuracy, reducing classification errors by up to 42% compared to confidence interval methods; (ii) a 40% reduction in indeterminate samples when inconclusive classes are allowed; and (iii) a decreased requirement for antigens needed for classification. This work highlights the potential of mathematical modeling in diagnostic classification and offers a broadly applicable method for public health and clinical environments.

Cell and tissue polarization are essential for morphogenesis throughout biological development and regeneration. Gaining deeper insight into how polarity patterns form requires examining how these patterns reorganize in response to opposing instructive cues, a phenomenon we illustrate through experimentally induced body axis inversions in planarian flatworms. Our dynamically diluted alignment model captures three key processes: the entrainment of cell polarity by a global signal, local cell-cell coupling that aligns polarity among neighbors, and cell turnover which introduces initially unpolarized cells. We demonstrate that in this stochastic framework, a persistent global orienting signal dictates the final mean polarity orientation. By combining numerical simulations with analytical methods, we found that while cell turnover accelerates the reorganization of polarity patterns, neighbor coupling slows it down. We derived a formula for an effective neighbor coupling strength that integrates both effects, revealing that the time required for polarity reorganization depends linearly on this parameter, with no abrupt transitions observed. This finding enables the determination of neighbor coupling strengths based on experimental data. Furthermore, our model corresponds to a dynamic 8-Potts model with annealed site-dilution and offers testable predictions regarding the polarization of dynamic systems, such as the planarian epithelium.

Extracting nonperturbative Transverse Momentum Dependent (TMD) physics is complicated by prescriptions designed to shield the Landau pole, as these entangle long- and short-distance contributions within momentum space. Consequently, varying these prescriptions renders direct comparisons of fit results for underlying nonperturbative components unreliable in isolation. We introduce a model-independent approach that confines momentum-space observables strictly to the perturbative regime. This technique utilizes a collection of integral functionals that operate linearly on terms within the standard position-space operator product expansion (OPE). Systematic artifacts arising from integral truncation can be pushed to higher orders in $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}/k_T$. We demonstrate that this framework allows for the calculation of the cumulative integral of TMD Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) over $k_T \le k_T^\mathrm{cut}$ using collinear PDFs, while incorporating both radiative corrections and evolution effects. This provides a systematic method to correct the naive assumption that TMD PDFs simply integrate to collinear PDFs; for unpolarized quark distributions, we find that selecting renormalization scales near $k_T^\mathrm{cut}$ results in corrections at the percent level. Furthermore, when combined with experimental data and refined perturbative inputs, our integral functionals will facilitate the establishment of model-independent bounds on the nonperturbative OPE contributions to the Collins-Soper kernel and intrinsic TMD distributions.

The study of gamma-ray propagation across cosmological distances at GeV and TeV energies has been a major focus of both theoretical and observational research. Above 100 GeV, the mean free path of these gamma rays is restricted within the cosmic web due to pair production (electrons and positrons) interacting with the cosmic optical and infrared backgrounds. As these secondary electrons and positrons spiral within intergalactic magnetic fields, they cool, potentially leading to global heating or the generation of lower-energy secondary gamma rays. The energy spectrum of gamma rays that survive their journey through the cosmos exhibits absorption features that allow scientists to measure the emissivity of baryonic matter throughout cosmic history, constrain the distance scales of $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, and limit modifications to interaction cross-sections. Significant constraints are placed on the cosmic star-formation history, as well as on predictions from quantum gravity and string theory, such as couplings to hypothetical axion-like particles or Lorentz invariance violations. Recent theoretical and observational breakthroughs suggest a promising multi-wavelength and multi-messenger future for the upcoming generation of gamma-ray observatories.

The Emotion Cause Extraction (ECE) task involves identifying clauses that contain information triggering a specific emotion expressed in a text. We note that a commonly used ECE dataset suffers from a bias where most annotated cause clauses are either immediately preceding their associated emotion clauses or are the emotion clauses themselves. Current ECE models often rely on this positional information and consequently fall victim to this dataset bias. To assess how much existing models depend on clause relative positions, we introduce a new strategy for creating adversarial examples where relative position is no longer a distinguishing feature for cause clauses. Testing these models on such adversarial data reveals a substantial performance decline. To mitigate this bias, we propose a novel graph-based approach that explicitly models emotion-triggering paths by utilizing commonsense knowledge to strengthen semantic connections between candidate and emotion clauses. Experimental results indicate that our method matches the performance of existing state-of-the-art approaches on the original ECE dataset while demonstrating superior robustness against adversarial attacks.

The Chekanov torus represented the inaugural known \emph{exotic} torus, defined as a monotone Lagrangian torus that cannot be transformed into the standard monotone Lagrangian torus via Hamiltonian isotopy. This study investigates the connection between the Chekanov torus within $S^2 \times S^2$ and a monotone Lagrangian torus that predated Chekanov's construction \cite{Chekanov}. We demonstrate that the monotone Lagrangian torus fiber arising from a specific Gelfand--Zeitlin system is Hamiltonian isotopic to the Chekanov torus in $S^2 \times S^2$.

Coughing serves as a prevalent indicator of respiratory and pulmonary conditions, making its detection vital for preventing, evaluating, and managing epidemics like COVID-19. This study introduces a model designed to identify cough events within audio signals. The models were trained using a composite dataset merging ESC-50 with self-recorded cough samples, while the test set comprised inpatient recordings from the respiratory disease department at Ruijin Hospital. Fifteen distinct detection models were constructed based on feature subsets selected via Random Frog, Uninformative Variable Elimination (UVE), and Variable Influence on Projection (VIP) algorithms. The superior model utilized 20 Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) features chosen by UVE and was classified using a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM). This optimal model achieved an accuracy of 94.9%, recall of 97.1%, precision of 93.1%, and an F1-score of 0.95. Its high performance combined with reduced feature dimensionality demonstrates its suitability for deployment on mobile devices like smartphones, thereby enabling remote, non-contact cough detection.

Trees serve as fundamental structures for modeling hierarchical relationships and data organization within networked decision systems. Specifically, an ordered tree is a rooted structure where the sequence of a node's subtrees is critical. In the field of combinatorial optimization, producing these ordered trees is essential for assessing potential combinatorial candidates. This paper introduces an algebraic method for generating ordered trees with $n$ vertices with maximum efficiency, utilizing $\mathcal{O}(n)$ space and achieving an average time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per tree. Computational experiments confirm that this approach generates ordered trees in constant average time, completing the task in approximately 0.1 milliseconds per tree. Given the one-to-one correspondence between this method and other combinatorial classes, it is highly advantageous for generating binary trees with $n$ external nodes, trees with $n$ nodes, valid sequences of $n$ parentheses, triangulated $n$-gons, gambler's sequences, and lattice paths. We anticipate that this scheme will prove valuable in developing algorithms for planning and combinatorial optimization problems involving Catalan numbers.

This work examines the quasi-steady-state assumption within the fundamental mathematical framework of general enzymatic reactions using a strictly quantitative perspective. We rigorously re-derive established findings and introduce a new methodology that eliminates an ambiguous yet prevalent practice. Specifically, we quantitatively delineate the two components of the assumption, apply a straightforward algorithm to scale the associated problem—thereby yielding the required necessary and sufficient conditions—and address other topics, including the dispensability of a third component of the assumption.

This article presents the concept of column adequate tensors within the framework of the tensor complementarity problem (TCP), examining several key properties. As a subclass of nonlinear complementarity problems, the TCP involves functions defined by tensors. We demonstrate both the inheritance and invariant properties of column adequate tensors and prove that, under specific conditions, the problem TCP$(q,\mathcal{A})$ possesses an $\omega$-unique solution.

This paper reports a numerical investigation into the collective behavior of a system of coupled excitable lasers equipped with saturable absorbers. Unlike prior research that utilized real-valued (lossy) coupling, our study focuses exclusively on purely imaginary coupling mediated by evanescent waves. We demonstrate that lasers connected via evanescent coupling achieve synchronization more effectively than those with lossy coupling. Additionally, we find that while disorder-induced localization of excitability occurs off-diagonal even under imaginary coupling, this phenomenon can be disrupted by a non-zero linewidth enhancement factor.

Starting with a Perelman entropy functional and applying the Ricci-DeTurck flow equations, we investigate how Einstein-Hilbert and Einstein-Proca theories behave within Lifshitz geometry as a function of the flow parameter. In the Einstein-Hilbert case, we identify a single consistent fixed point corresponding to flat space-time as the parameter approaches infinity. The inclusion of massive vector fields in the Einstein-Proca theory enriches the system, yet it reaches the same fixed point at an identical rate. This geometric flow, defined by metric coefficients, describes a transition from anisotropic geometry to isotropic flat space-time as the parameter evolves. Specifically, the evolution of Proca fields relies on coefficients that decay to zero as the flow parameter grows, causing these fields to become constant. We derive the evolving Lifshitz metric solution for positive, otherwise arbitrary, critical exponents applicable to spatially anisotropic holographic duals. Our analysis demonstrates that both scalar curvature and matter contributions to the Ricci-DeTurck flow vanish at a fixed point consistent with flat space-time. Consequently, the scalar curvature behavior consistently increases, homogenizing the geometry along the flow. Furthermore, the entropy functional remains positive-definite but decreases throughout the Ricci-DeTurck flow.

This research investigates the gravitational effects of localized scalar field configurations, known as lumps, within higher-derivative gravitational frameworks. Focusing on static, spherically symmetric setups, we derive the linearized spacetime metrics produced by these scalar lumps across various Lagrangians, including those with vanishing (free massive), polynomial, and tachyon potentials characteristic of open string field theory. The analysis extends to multiple gravitational models: Einstein's general relativity, four-derivative gravity, and ghost-free nonlocal gravity. Finally, we evaluate the applicability limits of our findings and suggest potential future uses regarding astrophysical compact objects.

This tutorial examines the primary steps of conducting principal component analysis on multivariate data and achieving dimensionality reduction based on dominant principal components. The underlying computations are demonstrated and executed using a script written in the statistical software package R.

We begin by posing a compelling yet difficult question: if an eyewitness can only remember the suspect's eye features, allowing a forensic artist to create a sketch depicting only the eyes (as seen in the top-left sketch of Fig. 1), can advanced computer vision techniques reconstruct the entire face? More broadly, we ask whether a realistic full-face sketch or image can be estimated even when a significant portion (e.g., over 50%) is missing. Current face completion and generation methods either fail to perform domain transfer learning or struggle with extensive missing areas; for instance, inpainting approaches often result in a blurred generated region when the missing area exceeds 50%. In this paper, we leverage deep learning networks to fill large missing regions (up to 95% missing) and produce high-fidelity faces across different domains. We introduce the recursive generation by bidirectional transformation networks (r-BTN), which recursively generates a complete face or sketch from a small patch. The combination of large missing areas and cross-domain challenges makes it difficult for unidirectional cross-domain learning structures to yield satisfactory results. Conversely, implementing a forward and backward bidirectional learning process between the face and sketch domains allows for the incremental, recursive estimation of missing regions (Fig. 1), producing superior outcomes. Furthermore, r-BTN incorporates an adversarial constraint to promote the generation of realistic faces and sketches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that r-BTN outperforms existing potential solutions.

This study tackles the mobility challenge in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, a factor that causes substantial performance degradation in the practical implementation of fifth-generation (5G) networks. We introduce a new channel prediction technique utilizing the multi-dimensional matrix pencil (MDMP) approach, which estimates path parameters by leveraging the angular-frequency and angular-time domain structures of wideband channels. Additionally, our method incorporates an innovative path pairing strategy that links delay and Doppler components based on the super-resolution capabilities of angle estimation. Unlike previous literature, our approach effectively handles the realistic constraint of time-varying path delays caused by user movement. Theoretically, we demonstrate that in scenarios involving time-varying delays, the prediction error converges to zero as the number of base station antennas increases, provided only two arbitrary channel samples are available. We also establish a lower bound for the required number of antennas to achieve satisfactory performance. Simulations using the 3GPP industrial channel model confirm that the proposed MDMP method nearly matches the performance of stationary scenarios, even at user velocities of 120 km/h and channel state information latencies up to 16 ms.

This paper presents the complete structure of the frame set for the Gabor system $\mathcal{G}(g;\alpha,\beta)$, where the window function $g$ is the Haar function defined as $-\chi_{[-1/2,0)}+\chi_{[0,1/2)}$. The core strategy involves introducing a piecewise linear transformation $\mathcal{M}$ on the unit circle and fully characterizing the structures of its symmetric maximal invariant sets. This transformation is connected to Steinhaus's renowned three-gap theorem, a result that may hold independent interest. Additionally, we refine a classical criterion for Gabor frames, establishing a necessary and sufficient condition for $\mathcal{G}(g;\alpha,\beta)$ to constitute a frame; specifically, this occurs when the symmetric invariant set of $\mathcal{M}$ is empty. Unlike prior studies, this work offers a self-contained framework for analyzing Gabor frames from a novel perspective. The techniques introduced here are original, and all proofs are presented in a way that allows readers to fully understand them without relying on previous literature.

This article introduces the theory of mechanism design and its relevance to engineering challenges. The objective is to present the foundational principles of this theory for control engineers and theorists, alongside current advanced methods in engineering applications. The exposition begins with a concise review of game theory, emphasizing the core concepts essential for understanding mechanism design, followed by a thorough discussion of its principles. Finally, the article examines four major engineering applications: communication networks, power grids, transportation systems, and security infrastructure.

Algorithmic recommendations and decisions have become pervasive in modern society. To ensure transparency and interpretability, many data-driven policies, particularly in public sectors, rely on known deterministic rules. For instance, algorithmic pre-trial risk assessments, which serve as our motivating application, offer relatively straightforward deterministic classification scores and recommendations to assist judges in release decisions. The challenge lies in leveraging data from these existing deterministic policies to learn superior new policies. Unfortunately, prior policy learning methods are inapplicable because they assume existing policies are stochastic rather than deterministic. We propose a robust optimization approach that partially identifies the expected utility of a policy and determines an optimal policy by minimizing worst-case regret. The resulting policy is conservative yet provides a statistical safety guarantee, enabling policymakers to cap the probability of generating outcomes worse than the current policy. We extend this methodology to prevalent scenarios where humans make decisions aided by algorithmic suggestions. Finally, we apply this approach to a unique field experiment involving pre-trial risk assessment tools. Our derived new classification and recommendation rules maintain the transparency and interpretability of the original instrument while potentially achieving better overall outcomes at a reduced cost.

Automatic speech translation for subtitling (SubST) involves converting speech into properly formatted subtitles that adhere to specific display constraints, including the insertion of subtitle breaks. Like standard speech translation (ST), this task typically requires parallel datasets pairing audio with text; however, SubST further demands that the text be annotated with appropriate subtitle segmentation. The scarcity of publicly available corpora with such annotations has historically hindered system development. To address this limitation, we introduce a method for transforming existing ST datasets into SubST resources without manual intervention. By leveraging a multimodal segmenter that utilizes both audio and text inputs, we achieve high-quality automatic segmentation in zero-shot scenarios. Comparative experiments demonstrate that systems trained on these automatically segmented datasets perform comparably to those trained on manually segmented data, validating the effectiveness of our approach.

Spatial constraints limit the quantum operations achievable through local means in distributed multipartite systems. We suggest that indefinite causal structures, resulting from the quantum superposition of distinct spacetime geometries, serve as an independent universal resource for locally implementing any quantum operation across spatially separated systems. Consequently, quantum tasks that are impossible under Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC) alone become feasible locally when this resource is utilized. We demonstrate that by leveraging indefinite causal structure as the exclusive resource, one can perfectly teleport a subsystem's state to a distant lab such that the remote agent accesses the entire initially shared state and can execute any global quantum operation locally. Furthermore, we find that this teleportation process does not consume the indefinite causal structure resource; therefore, the same resource enables the teleportation of the first agent's subsystem back to its original location after the operation is completed. We also show that such bidirectional teleportation is not strictly required for all non-LOCC tasks. Without resorting to teleportation, we present a protocol for the perfect local discrimination of the four Bell states using indefinite causal structure as the sole resource. As immediate applications, we illustrate that other nonlocal tasks—such as locally discriminating states exhibiting "quantum nonlocality without entanglement" and activating bound entangled states—are also achievable through our proposed protocol utilizing indefinite causal structure.

**Background:** In nuclei with significant deformation, the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) exhibits a distinct coupling with the $K = 0$ component of the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR). This interaction produces a double-peak structure in the isoscalar monopole (IS0) strength distribution, characterized by a narrow, low-energy peak induced by deformation and a broader, primary ISGMR component. The energy position of this narrow low-lying IS0 peak depends critically on both the nuclear incompressibility modulus ($K_\infty$) and the coupling strength between IS0 and isoscalar quadrupole (IS2) modes.

**Objective:** This research seeks to examine the two-peaked ISGMR structure in the prolate $^{24}$Mg and oblate $^{28}$Si nuclei to determine which Skyrme-based energy density functional best aligns with experimental observations, thereby providing insights into nuclear incompressibility. Additionally, due to the pronounced IS0/IS2 coupling, the splitting of the ISGQR arising from deformation will be analyzed.

**Methods:** The ISGMR was probed in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si via inelastic $\alpha$-particle scattering using a 196 MeV beam at laboratory angles of $0^\circ$ and $4^\circ$. Data were collected and momentum-analyzed using the K600 magnetic spectrometer at iThemba LABS, achieving an experimental energy resolution of approximately 70 keV (FWHM) that exposed fine structural details within the ISGMR excitation region. IS0 strength distributions were extracted using the Difference-of-Spectrum (DoS) technique. Theoretical predictions were generated using the quasiparticle random-phase approximation (QRPA) against a representative set of Skyrme forces for comparison.

Coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering was initially confirmed experimentally five years ago by the COHERENT collaboration, utilizing neutrinos from the spallation neutron source at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Recent findings from the Dresden-II reactor experiment, which employed a germanium detector, provide the first evidence of this phenomenon using reactor antineutrinos. This study utilizes the new Dresden-II data to place constraints on various beyond-Standard-Model scenarios. Specifically, we examine limitations on neutrino non-standard interactions, neutrino magnetic moments, and multiple models involving light scalar or vector mediators. Furthermore, we quantify the effects of combining these results with COHERENT data (from CsI and Ar targets). This analysis underscores the complementary nature of spallation neutron source and reactor experiments for probing beyond-Standard-Model physics, as well as the benefits of using diverse nuclear targets. Additionally, we investigate potential signals from beyond-Standard-Model scenarios arising from elastic scattering off electrons (which would evade the selection cuts of both COHERENT CsI and Dresden-II), discovering more stringent constraints in specific regions of the parameter space compared to those derived solely from coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering.

We introduce a novel blockade phenomenon arising from the linear coupling of photonic and phononic modes in a hybrid state, termed the hybrid photon-phonon blockade. This effect is demonstrated within a driven nonlinear optomechanical superconducting system, focusing on boson-number correlations across photons, phonons, and hybrid modes in linearly coupled microwave and mechanical resonators containing an inserted superconducting qubit. Our analysis identifies specific system parameters that yield eight distinct combinations of blockade and tunnelling effects—characterized by sub- and super-Poissonian statistics—for these three modes. Notably, we show that the hybrid photon-phonon blockade can emerge through the mixing of individual photonic and phononic modes that individually do not exhibit blockade.

We detail the experimental realization and theoretical framework of a controllable dephasing quantum channel within photonic systems. This channel is achieved by coupling the polarization of light with its spatial distribution, which function as the quantum system and environment, respectively, under the framework of Open Quantum Systems. Our ability to regulate this channel enables the visualization of its impact on a quantum system. Distinct from conventional dephasing channels, our implementation exhibits exotic behavior, characterized by an oscillatory trajectory in the Bloch sphere as a state evolves from pure to mixed. Furthermore, we analyze the evolution of purity and conduct quantum process tomography to determine the $\chi$ matrix representing our channel.

By employing vector fields from the diffeomorphism group on $\mathbb{C}$-multiplied tori and their associated Lie-algebraic frameworks, this work investigates multi-dimensional dispersionless integrable systems that govern conformal structure generating equations in mathematical physics. A novel modification of this Lie-algebraic method, constrained by spatial-dimensional invariance and the meromorphic nature of the underlying differential-geometric structures, is introduced and utilized to demonstrate the complete integrability of various conformal structure generating equations. Specific instances examined include the Einstein-Weyl and modified Einstein-Weyl metric equations, the Dunajski heavenly equation system, the first and second conformal structure generating equations, and the inverse first Shabat reduction heavenly equation. Furthermore, the analysis extends to the modified Plebański, Husain, and general Monge heavenly equations, as well as their multi-dimensional extensions. Additionally, superconformal analogs of the Whitham heavenly equation are constructed.

Magnetic molecules placed on surfaces offer a promising avenue for individually addressing and manipulating spins, provided that long spin excitation lifetimes are achieved for applications in quantum information processing and data storage. Typically, coupling between molecular spins and the conduction electrons of metallic substrates leads to rapid relaxation of spin excitations into the ground state. However, superconducting pairing effects in the substrate can shield excited spins from this decay. This study demonstrates that a gold film with proximity-induced superconductivity can sustain spin excitations in a FeTPP-Cl molecule for over 80 nanoseconds. This duration was established by analyzing the inelastic spin excitations of the FeTPP-Cl molecule's S=5/2 multiplet on gold films deposited on V(100) via scanning tunneling spectroscopy. We observed that the spin lifetime diminishes as the film thickness increases, correlating with the gradual closure of a pair of de Gennes-Saint James resonances within the superconducting gap. These findings clarify the potential of using proximitized gold electrodes to control surface quantum spins, opening new possibilities for tuning spin lifetimes.

The widespread integration of Machine Learning (ML) within security-sensitive domains necessitates transparent and explainable methodologies. Yet, research into comprehending ML models, including Random Forest (RF), remains in its early stages. This study utilizes formal methods and logical reasoning to create a novel, model-specific framework for elucidating RF predictions. Our approach, grounded in Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUC), offers a thorough solution for assessing feature importance across both local and global dimensions, as well as analyzing adversarial samples. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate the superior quality of our feature importance metrics. Furthermore, our adversarial analysis surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, the method generates user-centric reports that facilitate actionable recommendations for real-world applications.

This paper offers a straightforward proof for the existence of an iterative scheme based on two Hilbert spaces, building on the work of Kazmi et al. [K. R. Kazmi, R. Ali, M. Furkan, Hybrid iterative method for split monotone \ldots, Numer Algor, 2017].

The formation of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) droplets has been re-evaluated by incorporating three-loop corrections into the mean field potential's earlier loop factors. This adjustment enhances the stability of QGP droplet formation across various parametrization schemes of the QGP fluid and yields better alignment with lattice QCD results regarding pressure, energy density, and other thermodynamic properties. Consequently, the inclusion of the three-loop contribution more effectively captures the characteristic features of the QGP fluid.
