This study aims to eliminate biases stemming from sampler stochasticity during the inference phase. We evaluate various nested sampler configurations against the widely utilized Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, assessing both their performance on the pulsar timing array parameter space and their computational efficiency on identical datasets. Although consistent parameter estimates are obtained across different sampling algorithms, we recommend implementing two distinct samplers for future robustness checks. This approach will facilitate cross-validation between methods while ensuring realistic execution times.

This paper introduces the Fast Motion Deblurring-Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (FMD-cGAN), a solution designed for blind motion deblurring of single images that yields superior structural similarity and visual quality. While GANs generally face challenges regarding large parameter counts and high computational demands—hindering deployment on resource-constrained devices like mobile units and robots—our approach utilizes a MobileNet architecture featuring depthwise separable convolutions to mitigate these issues. This design significantly reduces model size and inference time without compromising image fidelity, achieving a compression ratio of 3 to 60 times compared to the nearest competitors. The resulting compressed deblurring cGAN not only surpasses closest rivals in speed but also outperforms various state-of-the-art blind motion deblurring models in both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Furthermore, the model is capable of handling real-time deblurring tasks, with experiments on standard datasets demonstrating its effectiveness.

Although considerable research funding has been directed toward learning-based methods for industrial assembly over the last few years, these techniques have not yet been embraced by the industry. We contend that the primary barrier to adoption is the prohibitively vast design space inherent to Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), rather than fundamental algorithmic flaws. Successfully integrating these methods into industrial practice necessitates a paradigm shift away from academic conventions toward an industry-focused approach. This paper establishes criteria for industry-oriented DRL and conducts a comprehensive evaluation comparing DRL from demonstration against a professional industrial integrator using the newly established NIST assembly benchmark. We detail the design decisions, reflecting years of investigation, that allowed our DRL system to consistently surpass the integrator's baseline in both speed and reliability. Furthermore, we present a competition between our DRL system and a human operator on a challenging task involving insertion into a randomly moving target. Our findings indicate that DRL can outperform not only established engineered solutions but also the human motor system, while highlighting substantial potential for future enhancement. Project videos are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/shield-nist.

Let $G$ be a graph and $t$ a nonnegative integer. A mapping $f$ from the vertices of $G$ to $\{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ is termed a $t$-relaxed $k$-coloring if, for every vertex $u \in G$, the count of neighbors $v$ satisfying $f(v) = f(u)$ does not exceed $t$. When such a mapping exists, $G$ is described as $(k,t)$-colorable. The $t$-relaxed chromatic number, denoted $\chi_t(G)$, represents the smallest integer $k$ for which $G$ is $(k,t)$-colorable. A vertex set $S$ in $G$ is defined as $t$-sparse if the subgraph induced by $S$ has a maximum degree no greater than $t$. Consequently, $G$ is $(k,t)$-colorable if and only if its vertex set can be partitioned into $k$ disjoint $t$-sparse sets. Belmonte, Lampis, and Mitsou (2017) previously established that determining the $(k,t)$-colorability of complete multi-partite graphs is NP-complete. This paper establishes tight lower and upper bounds for the $t$-relaxed chromatic number of complete multi-partite graphs and proposes an algorithm to identify maximum $t$-sparse sets in such graphs with a time complexity of $O((t+1)^2)$. Utilizing this algorithm, we demonstrate that the greedy approach for computing $\chi_t(G)$ achieves a 2-approximation and operates in $O(tn)$ time, where $n$ is the number of vertices. Specifically, we prove that for $t \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, the greedy algorithm yields an optimal $t$-relaxed coloring for complete multi-partite graphs. However, for $t \ge 7$, we provide counterexamples showing that the greedy strategy does not always result in an optimal coloring.

The radiative forcings resulting from variations in the concentrations of Earth's five primary natural greenhouse gases—H$_2$O, CO$_2$, O$_3$, N$_2$O, and CH$_4$—along with CF$_4$ and SF$_6$, were assessed for a cloud-free atmosphere. This calculation utilized over 1.5 million spectral lines, some with strengths as weak as $10^{-27}$ cm. In a hypothetical, optically thin atmosphere where absorption bands do not saturate and inter-gas interference is absent, per-molecule forcings are approximately $10^{-22}$ Watts for H$_2$O, CO$_2$, O$_3$, N$_2$O, and CH$_4$, and roughly $10^{-21}$ Watts for CF$_4$ and SF$_6$. However, under current atmospheric conditions, the per-molecule forcings of the abundant gases H$_2$O and CO$_2$ are reduced by four orders of magnitude. The forcings of the less abundant gases, O$_3$, N$_2$O, and CH$_4$, experience less significant suppression, while those of CF$_4$ and SF$_6$ are reduced by less than an order of magnitude due to their extremely low concentrations. Consequently, at present concentrations, the per-molecule forcings of O$_3$, N$_2$O, CH$_4$, CF$_4$, and SF$_6$ are two to four orders of magnitude higher than those of H$_2$O or CO$_2$. Doubling current levels of CO$_2$, N$_2$O, or CH$_4$ results in only a few percent increase in forcing. In contrast, a hundredfold increase in either CF$_4$ or SF$_6$ produces a forcing nearly an order of magnitude smaller than doubling CO$_2$. Significant insights were gained through a harmonic oscillator model used to estimate power radiated per molecule; unlike the strongest bands of the five natural greenhouse gases, the frequency-integrated cross sections of CF$_4$ and SF$_6$ were found to exhibit a noticeable dependence on temperature.

Within special relativity, I suggest that matter conformally couples to a scalar field via its Lagrangian density, applicable to both classical and quantum (statistical) systems. The maximum strength of this scalar-mediated force reaches approximately $1/\Lambda_E^2$, where the cosmological constant $\Lambda_E$ is roughly $2.4\,\rm{meV}$. This strength is roughly $10^{60}$ times greater than Newtonian gravity, given by ${(M_{\mathrm{Pl}}/\Lambda_E)}^2$, with the reduced Planck energy $M_{\mathrm{Pl}}\approx2.4\times 10^{18}\, \rm{GeV}$. However, the discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry inherent in the conformal coupling prevents the existence of a massless scalar field, thereby satisfying the observational constraint that no long-range force has been detected. The force's interaction range is inversely proportional to the square root of the ambient density; consequently, in environments denser than the current cosmic density, the range remains below $1/\Lambda_E \approx 80\, \mu\rm{m}$. General relativity remains valid even when accounting for the energy-momentum tensors of both quintessence and the conformal interaction. The primary objective of this proposal is to resolve the puzzle presented in \cite{hcz2} regarding the identification of the physical frame.

This paper introduces Zecale, a versatile SNARK proof aggregator leveraging recursive SNARK composition. We begin by defining recursive composition, followed by presenting Zecale as a scalable, privacy-preserving solution. Subsequently, we outline potential application types enabled by Zecale and argue that such scalability mechanisms are essential for emulating "cash" functionality within blockchain systems through privacy-preserving state transitions.

We introduce LDP, a lightweight neural architecture search (NAS) framework designed for dense prediction tasks. Building upon a generic pre-defined backbone, LDP utilizes a novel Assisted Tabu Search to enable efficient architecture exploration. Unlike previous NAS approaches that are computationally intensive or limited to specific subtasks, LDP offers speed and versatility across various dense estimation problems. We evaluate LDP's performance on monocular depth estimation, semantic segmentation, and image super-resolution using diverse datasets such as NYU-Depth-v2, KITTI, Cityscapes, COCO-stuff, DIV2K, Set5, Set14, BSD100, and Urban100. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms prior methods on all tested dense prediction tasks while maintaining a model parameter count that is 5% to 315% more compact.

We propose a mixture model based on beta distributions to detect significant correlations among a large number of predictors, $P$. This approach leverages theorems from convex geometry to regulate the error rate in edge detection within graphical models. Our `betaMix` method operates without requiring assumptions regarding the network's structure or its sparsity. Furthermore, the findings presented in this paper are applicable to a broad range of data-generating distributions, encompassing both light-tailed and heavy-tailed spherically symmetric distributions.

The formation of shear bands through strain localization is linked to velocity-weakening instabilities and seismic events. This study simulates steady-state plane-shear flow of numerical granular material (gouge) constrained between parallel boundaries. Testing both constant shear stress and constant strain-rate conditions reveals that these boundary setups produce distinct velocity profiles and friction laws. While the inertial number ($I$) is the primary factor governing the layers' behavior, constant stress conditions also expose dependencies of friction on normal stress and layer thickness. We observe that shear-band localization, which occurs in the quasistatic regime ($I<10^{-3}$) under rate-controlled shear, disappears under stress-controlled loading. Instead, flow halts when the macroscopic friction coefficient nears the quasistatic friction value. Conversely, the inertial regime at higher $I$ values ($I>10^{-3}$) is characterized by distributed shear, alongside friction and porosity that rise with increasing shear rate (a rate-strengthening regime). This finding—that constant stress conditions yield inertial, distributed shear but preclude quasistatic, localized deformation—is explained by the low fluctuations in shear forces at granular contacts during stress-controlled loading. Furthermore, by analyzing porosity inside and outside shear bands, we offer a mechanical explanation for why the transition from quasistatic to inertial shear aligns with the shift from localized to distributed strain.

This paper introduces the concept of a corner element for generalized numerical semigroups, extending the notion of a conductor to higher-dimensional contexts. We explore the properties of this new concept and its relationship with established invariants, while also presenting an algorithm to identify all generalized numerical semigroups sharing a specific corner. Additionally, we establish lower and upper bounds for the count of such semigroups with a fixed corner element.

Stratifications and iterative differential equations serve as analogues to complex linear differential equations within positive characteristic, yet explicit examples of such stratifications remain scarce. This paper aims to construct stratifications on projective and affine curves in positive characteristic and to identify the possible differential Galois groups associated with them. Additionally, it offers partial solutions to the related "differential Abhyankar conjecture," thereby enriching existing literature. The methodology relies on $p$-adic and rigid analytic techniques involving Mumford curves and Mumford groups to build regular singular stratifications and analyze their differential Galois groups. These constructions yield a multitude of stratifications and Galois groups, providing new insights into the tame fundamental groups of affine curves.

This paper introduces a novel approach for lane detection and segmentation utilizing generative models. While traditional methods rely on discriminative models to classify road pixels semantically, our approach models the probability distribution of lanes and road markings by training a generative adversarial network. Leveraging the learned distribution, the system generates context-aware lanes and signs for input images, which are subsequently quantized to identify the nearest class labels. Evaluated on the BDD100K and Baidu ApolloScape datasets, the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques and demonstrates robustness in adverse conditions by successfully reconstructing lanes in scenarios involving fading and occlusion.

This study provides a comprehensive physical analysis of jet launching from a circum-stellar disk within a binary system. Utilizing 3D resistive MHD simulations, we examine both local and global system properties, including angular momentum transport and mass fluxes associated with accretion and ejection. Unlike previous research, this work uniquely incorporates the complete magnetic torque, the presence of an outflow, angular momentum transport via vertical motion, and binary torques. We analyze the specific 3D structure of the system and its response to tidal forces, discovering that a spiral structure evolving within the disk is launched into the outflow; we term this novel feature a "jet spiral wall." These spiral features exhibit synchronized time evolution, with the jet spiral slightly lagging behind the disk spiral. Our results indicate that vertical angular momentum transport plays a significant role in the total budget even in binary systems, a finding also applicable to magnetic torque. However, contributions from the $\phi$-derivative of magnetic pressure and $B_{\phi}B_r$ stresses remain minor. Conversely, the gravity torque generated by the time-dependent 3D Roche potential is essential, serving as the fundamental driver for all 3D effects in our disk-jet system. Quantitatively, we observe that the disk accretion rate in a binary system is $20\%$ higher than that of a single-star disk, while the disk wind mass flux increases by $50\%$.

To determine the count of minimal surfaces sharing a common boundary by analyzing boundary geometry, we introduce a numerical method characterized by both high speed and precision. This approach relies on the method of fundamental solutions. We provide convergence analysis regarding Dirichlet energy and $L^\infty$-error analysis for mean curvature. Notably, every approximate solution generated by our scheme constitutes a smooth surface, marking a distinct departure from prior research that necessitated mesh subdivision.

Achieving consensus among robots in a swarm is a foundational challenge in swarm robotics, focusing on whether group members can agree. The recently introduced contamination problem provides a novel angle by requiring agreement despite adversarial agents that actively attempt to steer the swarm toward a conflicting consensus. This paper seeks a consensus algorithm under this contaminated setting using a top-down methodology: we convert the problem into a centralized two-player game where each participant controls a subset of the swarm, aiming to compel the whole group to converge on their own value. We establish a performance metric for each player and demonstrate a correlation between this metric and the probability of winning. We subsequently present the globally optimal solution for the game, proving that it is unattainable in a distributed environment due to the complex nature of swarm interactions. Consequently, we analyze the problem using a simplified swarm model, comparing the globally optimal strategy against locally optimal ones, with rigorous simulations confirming the superiority of the global approach.

This work employs methods from finite free probability to investigate matrix processes concerning eigenvalues, singular values, and generalized singular values within random matrices. The underlying models are straightforward, with the analysis relying exclusively on expected characteristic polynomials. While several of our findings align with established results in random matrix theory, our primary contribution—pertaining to generalized singular values—appears more comprehensive than standard processes such as those defined by Hermite, Laguerre, or Jacobi polynomials. To validate this, we conducted simulations of the novel process, which demonstrated unique behaviors absent in traditional models while confirming that our analytical techniques accurately capture the true dynamics. Given our ability to compute identical statistics for this new model as for standard ones, these results suggest that further exploration of this area would be both valuable and promising.

This paper demonstrates that the empirical measure of mean-field models adheres to the large deviation principle under either the weak convergence topology or the stronger Wasserstein metric, provided there is a strong exponential integrability condition on the negative part of the interaction potentials. Unlike existing results, our proof establishes this without requiring any continuity or boundedness conditions on the interaction potentials. The argument primarily utilizes the law of large numbers alongside the exponential decoupling inequality for U-statistics developed by de la Peña.

Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) serves as a beneficial matrix factorization method that generates a "parts-based" breakdown of data. Within smart and connected urban settings, Wi-Fi user counts function as a privacy-conscious metric for tracking population mobility. This study employs NMF, enhanced with a new matrix embedding technique, on Wi-Fi user count data collected from the University of Colorado at Boulder Campus to automatically detect patterns of human movement within a Smart and Connected infrastructure context.

The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) has recently identified 12 ultrahigh-energy (UHE) gamma-ray sources ($\varepsilon \ge 100$ TeV) within the Galactic plane, with only a few spatially aligned with pulsar wind nebulae (PWN). This study focuses on a sample of five such sources: two newly discovered LHAASO emitters (LHAASO J1908+0621 and LHAASO J2226+6057) and three previously known GeV-TeV sources, for which X-ray and radio data or upper limits are available. We investigate the multiwavelength emission from these objects under a PWN origin hypothesis, assuming the radiation is driven by the time-dependent spin-down luminosity of their associated pulsars. Utilizing a one-zone, time-dependent leptonic model, we calculate the electron population across various epochs, accounting for radiative (synchrotron and inverse-Compton) and adiabatic cooling processes. Our analysis yields upper limits on the minimum electron Lorentz factor and infers the minimum pair-multiplicity of charged pairs. Additionally, the maximum electron Lorentz factor is constrained by the highest observed photon energies in the sub-PeV range. Specifically for HESS J1640-465, fitting the gamma-ray data necessitates a higher stellar photon energy density than the standard IR/CMB background typically employed in PWN modeling. Finally, we explore potential modifications to the model parameters if particle escape from the nebula is permitted, qualitatively examining the impact of such escape on LHAASO J1908+0621.

For a given Jordan algebra $A$ and a vector space $V$, we provide a description and classification of all Jordan algebras that contain $A$ as a subalgebra with codimension ${\rm dim}_k(V)$, utilizing a non-abelian cohomological structure denoted as ${\mathcal J}_{A}(V, A)$. Every such algebra is isomorphic to a newly defined entity known as the \emph{unified product} $A \, \natural \, V$. Special instances of this unified product include the crossed and twisted products of Jordan algebras, and the specific problems associated with each are examined. Furthermore, we construct the non-abelian cohomology ${\rm H}^2_{\rm nab}(V, A)$, which corresponds to the extensions of $V$ by $A$ for two Jordan algebras. Several applications and examples are presented, including the proof that ${\rm H}^2_{\rm nab}(k, k^n)$ is equivalent to the set of matrices $D \in M_n(k)$ satisfying the equation $2D^3 - 3D^2 + D = 0$.

We introduce a method and software for conducting risk-limiting audits (RLAs) of ballot polls using Bernoulli sampling, where each ballot is selected independently with a probability of $p$. This approach offers multiple benefits: (1) it eliminates the need for a ballot manifest; (2) it allows independent auditing at various locations without requiring a central authority to draw a sample from the entire population or necessitating stratified sampling; and (3) it can commence at polling places on election night, prior to the determination of final margins. Had the reported 2016 U.S. Presidential election margins been accurate, a Bernoulli ballot-polling audit with a 5% risk limit and an initial sampling rate of $p_0 = 1\%$ would have confirmed the results in at least 42 states with a probability of 99% or higher (while other states likely required examining additional ballots). The logistical and security advantages gained by auditing directly at polling places may justify the higher cost of inspecting more ballots compared to alternative methods.

Mixup is a widely used data augmentation strategy for deep neural networks that creates new samples by linearly interpolating input pairs along with their corresponding labels. This approach is recognized for enhancing generalization across numerous learning scenarios and applications. In this study, we first examine Mixup and demonstrate that it implicitly regularizes infinitely many directional derivatives of all orders. Leveraging this new insight, we propose an improved method designed to refine Mixup. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we performed experiments across diverse domains, including images, tabular data, speech, and graphs. Our findings indicate that the proposed method consistently enhances Mixup performance across various datasets and architectures; for example, it achieves a 0.8% increase in ImageNet top-1 accuracy compared to standard Mixup.

We introduce an actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm designed to hedge portfolios comprising securities and over-the-counter derivatives using exclusively historical data. Our methodology is distinguished by several key features: the capacity to utilize various derivatives like forwards, swaps, futures, and options; the integration of trading frictions, including costs and liquidity constraints; versatility across diverse financial portfolios; the handling of realistic, continuous state and action spaces; and adherence to formal risk-adjusted return goals. Crucially, the trained model generates optimal hedges for any initial portfolio and market condition without requiring retraining. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of finite solutions to our Bellman equation and establish the connection to our vanilla Deep Hedging approach.

Recent studies highlight that mathematical reasoning remains a significant hurdle for neural systems, necessitating core competencies such as expression translation, logical reasoning, and the acquisition of mathematical knowledge. This paper illustrates that certain capabilities can be attained by integrating abductive learning with discrete systems pre-programmed with human expertise. Utilizing a recently introduced abductive learning framework on a mathematical reasoning dataset, we present the ABL-Sym algorithm, which fuses Transformer neural models with a symbolic mathematics library. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, ABL-Sym achieves a 9.73% accuracy boost on interpolation tasks and a 47.22% improvement on extrapolation tasks. Online demonstration: http://math.polixir.ai

This study examines the likelihood of scoring a point in the basketball game "Horse." We demonstrate that under Traditional Rules, the optimal strategy involves selecting extremely easy shots. We introduce an alternative set of guidelines known as Pops Rules, which result in optimal shots that are more challenging, thereby creating a more engaging game.

This work introduces $\delta$-type vertex conditions for fourth-order beam operators defined on metric graphs, investigating how specific geometric modifications (graph surgery) influence the spectra of these operators on compact metric graphs. We derive results for a specific class of vertex conditions that serve as an analogue to $\delta$ conditions in quantum graphs, acknowledging that multiple candidates exist for such conditions for beam operators. We establish surgery principles and document the monotonicity properties of the spectrum, accounting for the potential for vertex conditions to shift within the same class following graph alterations. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of these surgery principles by deriving various lower and upper bounds for the eigenvalues.

Process Control Systems (PCSs) serve as the operational backbone of Critical Infrastructures (CIs), making anomaly detection a vital research area for maintaining normal operations. Prior methods have relied on network-level data or ignored process disturbances, creating a risk of misclassifying disturbances as attacks or vice versa. This paper introduces an anomaly detection and diagnostic framework grounded in Multivariate Statistical Process Control (MSPC) designed to differentiate between attacks and disturbances. To achieve this, we extend conventional MSPC to incorporate both process-level and controller-level data. Our approach is evaluated using the Tennessee-Eastman process, demonstrating that it can distinguish disturbances from intrusions to a significant degree. We conclude that the proposed method holds promise for further enhancement by integrating additional data sources.

The Coherent Neutrino-Nucleus Interaction Experiment (CONNIE) employs fully depleted, high-resistivity charge-coupled devices (CCDs) designed to detect the coherent elastic scattering of reactor antineutrinos off silicon nuclei and to investigate physics beyond the Standard Model. Analysis of data collected between 2016 and 2018 established a 95% confidence level upper limit on the coherent scattering rate, thereby imposing tight constraints on simplified Standard Model extensions involving light scalar and vector mediators. In 2019, the experiment ran with an enhanced readout system and a reduced energy threshold of 50 eV. This work outlines the CONNIE detector's performance, presents updated results from the 2019 dataset, and details the recent integration of skipper CCDs into the apparatus.

Achieving seamless human-robot interaction (HRI) and effective cooperative human-robot (HR) teamwork fundamentally depends on precise and timely models of human mental workload (MW). Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) posits that representative physical settings yield corresponding mental processes, implying that higher fidelity in the physical environment enhances modeling accuracy. Virtual Reality (VR) systems offer immersive environments ideal for replicating complex scenarios, especially those involving high risk and stress. While passive biosignal modeling presents a promising noninvasive approach to MW assessment, VR platforms seldom incorporate multimodal psychophysiological feedback or leverage biosignal data for real-time MW modeling. In this study, we introduce a novel VR simulation pipeline, inspired by the NASA Multi-Attribute Task Battery II (MATB-II) architecture, designed to synchronously capture objective performance metrics, subjective evaluations, and passive human biosignals within a simulated hazardous exploration setting. Our system extracts and publishes biofeatures via the Robot Operating System (ROS), enabling the integration of real-time, psychophysiology-based MW models into complete end-to-end systems. Developing a VR simulation pipeline capable of online MW evaluation could serve as a cornerstone for advancing HR systems and VR experiences by allowing these systems to dynamically adjust their behaviors in response to operator mental workload.

We offer a method to decompose a 3-manifold $M$ across diverse settings. When the constituent pieces exhibit specific hyperbolic properties, the manifold $M$ becomes hyperbolic, and its volume is bounded from below by the sum of the suitably defined hyperbolic volumes of these pieces. We provide numerous examples of such hyperbolic pieces and corresponding volumes, including many cases derived from link complements within the 3-sphere.

Consistent with their unconventional characteristics, multi-band alkaline Fe-selenides and, more recently, the heavy-fermion compound CeCu$_{2}$Si$_{2}$, have exhibited signatures of fully-gapped superconductivity with sign-changing gaps. To reconcile these seemingly contradictory properties, a two-orbital pairing state designated as $s\tau_{3}$, featuring a non-trivial matrix structure, was suggested. Driven by the non-trivial and orbital-selective nature of this proposed $s\tau_{3}$ state, we investigated prototypical Josephson junctions where at least one lead exhibits this specific superconducting state. Our analysis, focusing on the limit of two degenerate orbitals and a simple junction hybridization form, uncovered several striking phenomena. Specifically, $s\tau_{3}-N-s\tau_{3}$ and $s\tau_{3}-N-I$ junctions display gapless, purely electron- and hole-like bound states regardless of the global phase difference between the leads. Furthermore, static Josephson currents are absent when both leads are superconducting. These features distinguish $s\tau_{3}$ junctions dramatically from conventional ones. We also determined that these gapless bound states are safeguarded by an orbital-exchange symmetry, though this protection is not topological; consequently, junctions breaking this symmetry, such as $s\tau_{3}-N-s$, exhibit gapped Andreev bound states. Generally, the Josephson effect reappears once the degeneracy between the two orbitals is lifted. Our findings, supported by both analytical and numerical studies of bound states alongside microscopic calculations of the Josephson current, suggest that junctions involving $s\tau_{3}$ pairing in alkaline Fe-selenides will typically possess bound states with a small gap and a significantly suppressed Josephson current.

Variational hybrid quantum-classical algorithms represent a promising avenue for near-term deployment on quantum hardware. These methods leverage a quantum processor to evaluate the cost of a gate sequence more efficiently than classical counterparts, while a classical processor utilizes this data to optimize the sequence's parameters. This work introduces such an algorithm specifically for quantum state diagonalization, a technique vital for applications in condensed matter physics (such as entanglement spectroscopy) and machine learning (including principal component analysis). For a given quantum state $\rho$ and gate sequence $U$, our cost function measures the deviation of $U\rho U^{\dagger}$ from a diagonal form. We employ newly developed short-depth quantum circuits to calculate this cost, where minimizing it yields a gate sequence that approximately diagonalizes $\rho$. Consequently, one can extract approximations of the state's largest eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors. As a proof-of-principle demonstration, we executed this algorithm on Rigetti's quantum computer to diagonalize single-qubit states and used a simulator to determine the entanglement spectrum of the Heisenberg model ground state.

This work presents methods for generating numerous self-dual $\mathbb{Z}_m$-codes and Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-codes of length $2n$, based on existing self-dual $\mathbb{Z}_m$-codes and Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-codes of the same length. As a practical application, we construct extremal Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-codes of length $24$ for $k=4,5,\ldots,20$, as well as extremal Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-codes of length $32$ for $k=4,5,\ldots,10$. Additionally, we develop new extremal Type II $\mathbb{Z}_4$-codes with lengths of $56$ and $64$.

We analyze enhanced dissipation using Hormander's classical framework for second-order hypoelliptic operators [31]. Specifically, we consider a passive scalar within a shear flow, governed by the advection-diffusion equation \[ \partial_t f + b(y) \partial_x f - \nu \Delta f = 0 \] defined on \(\mathbb{T} \times (0,1) \times \mathbb{R}_+\), subject to periodic, Dirichlet, or Neumann boundary conditions in the \(y\)-direction. We show that decay accelerates on the timescale \(T \sim \nu^{-(N+1)/(N+3)}\), where \(N-1\) denotes the highest order of vanishing for the derivative \(b'(y)\) of the shear profile (with \(N=0\) corresponding to monotone shear flows). In the periodic case, our findings align with the established timescale derived by Bedrossian and Coti Zelati [8]. Notably, our results provide new insights specifically for scenarios involving boundaries.

Synthetic Aperture Sonar (SAS) image reconstruction, commonly known as beamforming in the field, involves a set of computationally demanding algorithms designed to generate coherent, high-resolution images from sequential sonar pings that vary spatially. Due to the substantial processing load required, this reconstruction is typically executed topside. Historically, generating real-time imagery within the size, weight, and power (SWaP) limitations of an unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) necessitated significant simplifying assumptions, which inevitably compromised image fidelity. This paper introduces ASASIN, the Advanced Synthetic Aperture Sonar Imagining eNgine, a time-domain backprojection suite optimized for GPUs that enables real-time operation on UUVs without degrading image quality. We detail several optimization techniques employed in ASASIN to achieve this goal. Additionally, the system's signal processing pipeline supports the generation of both 2D and 3D SAS imagery, as demonstrated in our results. Finally, we evaluate ASASIN's performance across various GPU architectures and develop a predictive model for runtime performance, validating its accuracy on both desktop and embedded GPU hardware.

Quantum entanglement represents a specific type of correlation among quantum particles that cannot be enhanced through local operations and classical communication. Consequently, it has been suggested that any increase in entanglement between probes interacting exclusively through a mediator signals that the mediator possesses non-classical properties. Specifically, under particular assumptions about the initial state, a gain in entanglement between probes suggests the presence of quantum coherence within the mediator. However, relaxing these assumptions reveals that certain initial states can generate entanglement between probes even when the mediator remains classical. In such scenarios, initial entanglement between individual probes and the rest of the system effectively "flows" through the classical mediator and becomes localized between the probes. This study provides a theoretical characterization of the maximum possible entanglement gain achievable via a classical mediator and experimentally validates this using liquid-state NMR spectroscopy, demonstrating the optimal growth of quantum correlations between two nuclear spin qubits coupled through a mediator in a classical state. Furthermore, the mediator is actively dephased to underscore its classical nature. Our findings highlight the critical importance of verifying initial state characteristics if entanglement gain is to be used as a metric for detecting non-classical mediators. These methodologies hold potential for applications in quantum optomechanics, quantum biology, and quantum gravity.

Measurements sensitive to the CKM angle $\gamma$ from LHCb are combined. This combination utilizes inputs from time-integrated analyses of tree-level decays including $B^{+}\rightarrow DK^+$, $B^{0} \rightarrow D K^{*0}$, $B^{0} \rightarrow D K^+ \pi^-$, and $B^{+} \rightarrow D K^+\pi^+\pi^-$, alongside results from a time-dependent study of $B_{s}^{0} \rightarrow D_{s}^{\mp}K^{\pm}$ decays. The resulting value is $\gamma = (72.2^{+6.8}_{-7.3})^\circ$, with uncertainties accounting for systematic effects, and the 95.5% confidence level interval is established as $\gamma \in [55.9,85.2]^\circ$. A second combination is also examined, incorporating additional data from $B^{+} \rightarrow D \pi^+$ and $B^{+} \rightarrow D \pi^+\pi^-\pi^+$ decays, which produces consistent outcomes.

The Hubble tension has challenged standard cosmological models. One proposed solution involves local variations in the expansion rate within an inhomogeneous universe, where spatial averaging over a finite region is used to define a local Friedmann spacetime. However, it remains uncertain whether this averaging concept is gauge invariant, meaning it is unclear if results derived in a specific gauge hold physical significance. This paper addresses that question by examining the gauge invariance of spatial averaging in cosmology. By analyzing the spatial average within gauge-invariant cosmological perturbation theory, we demonstrate that the answer is affirmative.

Socially assistive robots (SAR) demonstrate significant promise for enhancing the social and educational growth of children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD). As SARs prove to be a viable complement to human support, researchers have increasingly investigated their long-term effects within real-world settings, particularly the home. A primary computational hurdle in this domain is personalization, which is essential for allowing SAR systems to tailor their interactions to each child's evolving and unique requirements. To address this, we developed a hierarchical human-robot learning framework (hHRL) comprising five controllers—disclosure, promise, instruction, feedback, and inquiry—governed by a meta-controller that employs reinforcement learning. This system adjusts instruction difficulty and robot feedback in response to individual learning patterns. We tested and evaluated this method in a home-based study involving 17 children with ASD aged 3 to 7 over a period of several months. The results indicate that the fully autonomous SAR system successfully customized its instruction and feedback to match each child's proficiency levels. Consequently, all participants exhibited progress in targeted skills and maintained long-term retention of the learned material. Furthermore, children remained engaged for most of the intervention, and families reported the system as both useful and adaptable. Overall, these findings confirm that autonomous, personalized SAR interventions are feasible and effective for delivering sustained developmental support to children with varied learning needs in the home environment.

We provide a theoretical investigation into the optical behavior of a nonlinear oscillator created by linking the local surface plasmon resonance of a metal nanoparticle with excitonic states in a monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenide. Our findings indicate that this hybrid system displays pronounced anharmonicity in its lower energy states, forecasting a nonlinearity enhancement of approximately seven orders of magnitude compared to silicon photonic crystal cavities. Furthermore, we establish that the system manifests significant quantum characteristics, including antibunching and non-Gaussianity. Potential applications for arrays of these nanoscale nonlinear oscillators include the development of innovative optical metamaterials, while a single nanoparticle-monolayer unit could be integrated with an optical resonator to facilitate efficient coupling between propagating fields and the system.

The efficiency of enumerating every solution to an instance of Langford's Problem depends heavily on the chosen model and search strategy. This study evaluates a wide range of models, each derived from two fundamental perspectives. Empirical results indicate that a channelled model utilizing a static branching order on one of these perspectives yields superior performance among the tested options. Notably, one base model demonstrates high effectiveness for propagation, whereas the other serves as a robust mechanism for defining a static search order.

Global circulation models (GCMs) within the CMIP6 framework exhibit an equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) ranging from 1.83°C to 5.67°C. These 38 models are categorized into three ECS groups—low (1.80–3.00°C), medium (3.01–4.50°C), and high (4.51–6.00°C)—and evaluated against ERA5-T2m surface temperature records spanning 1980–1990 to 2011–2021. Results indicate that every model with an ECS exceeding 3.0°C overestimates observed global surface warming. Furthermore, spatial t-statistics show that data-model agreement is rejected over 60% of the Earth's surface when using low-ECS models, rising to 81% for high-ECS models. Consequently, both high and medium-ECS models are deemed unsuitable for predictive purposes. While low-ECS models are not entirely satisfactory, they are considered non-threatening, as projections for 2050 suggest moderate warming of less than approximately 2°C relative to preindustrial levels.

Our results demonstrate that axial inverse magnetic catalysis (AIMC), associated with $U(1)$ axial symmetry, arises near the chiral crossover region in thermomagnetic QCD featuring 2 + 1 flavors at the physical point. This phenomenon correlates with chiral inverse magnetic catalysis (CIMC) affecting the $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ symmetry. Using a Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model with 2 + 1 quark flavors, we explicitly observe AIMC, noting that introduced anomalous quark magnetic moments are essential for driving both CIMC and AIMC. Our findings are briefly testable on the lattice, and we also outline potential phenomenological and cosmological implications.

This study employs a Soft-Sphere Discrete Element Method code to model the transmission and attenuation of seismic waves. We apply these findings to various space missions involving surface contact with small celestial bodies, including the seismic waves generated by hypervelocity impacts from the DART and Hayabusa2 missions once shock waves transition into seismic waves. Our results indicate that even at extremely low pressures found within asteroid interiors, seismic wave speeds can reach hundreds of meters per second, contingent on the impact velocity. Consistent with experimental data, our simulations demonstrate that wave velocity scales directly with $P^{1/6}$, where $P$ represents total pressure (the sum of confining and wave-induced pressures). Regardless of system pressure or impact velocity within the investigated range, energy dissipation remains exceptionally high. These insights enable us to predict the potential for seismic waves to mobilize surface particles upon spacecraft contact. Furthermore, this rapid energy loss suggests that hypervelocity impacts likely disturb only the outer layer of self-gravitating aggregates, facilitating segregation and other processes that could generate a layered structure, for which observational evidence already exists.

Gas giant atmospheres are believed to be inhomogeneous because of weather and patchy cloud formations. This study utilized two full nights of coronagraphic data from the CHARIS integral field spectrograph, operated via the SCExAO adaptive optics system on the Subaru Telescope, to examine the HR 8799 planets for spectrophotometric variations. While no significant variability was detected, we established the tightest upper limits for HR 8799 c and d to date. According to injection-recovery simulations, our setup had a 50% probability of detecting H-band photometric variations as small as 10% for HR 8799 c and 30% for HR 8799 d; furthermore, we anticipated a 50% chance of recovering 20% variability in the H/K flux ratio for HR 8799 c. By merging datasets from both nights, we generated some of the most precise spectra available for HR 8799 c, d, and e. Analysis using a grid of cloudy radiative-convective-thermochemical equilibrium models indicates that all three planets exhibit supersolar metallicity and effective temperatures near 1100 K. Nevertheless, our high signal-to-noise spectra reveal that HR 8799 d possesses a distinct spectrum compared to HR 8799 c, suggesting it may feature more vertically extended and uniform clouds, thereby indicating the planets are not identical.

Fast Fourier Transform-based phase screen simulations yield accurate results only when the screen size ($G$) significantly exceeds the outer scale parameter ($L_0$); otherwise, they fail to correctly model both low and high-frequency turbulence-induced phase distortions. While sub-harmonic compensation is a prevalent technique for low-frequency correction, it remains ineffective across all screen-to-outer-scale ratios ($G/L_0$). Traditional sub-harmonic methods introduce unequal sampling or weight calculations during low-frequency sub-harmonic addition and patch normalization. To address these limitations, we have adapted the sub-harmonic approach by incorporating a Gaussian phase autocorrelation matrix. Our results demonstrate that the maximum relative error in the structure function compared to theoretical values remains between 0.5% and 3% for a $G/L_0$ ratio of 1/1000, even for screen diameters up to 100 meters.

Spatial search on graphs represents a key application of quantum walks. Demonstrating the superiority of quantum-walk-based search over random-walk-based search remains a challenging problem that has been tackled through various approaches. Typically, graph symmetries facilitate the calculation of computational complexity; Johnson graphs are particularly notable in this context due to their regularity, Hamilton-connectedness, and vertex- and distance-transitivity. This study demonstrates that continuous-time quantum walk achieves spatial search on Johnson graphs with the Grover lower bound of $\pi\sqrt{N}/2$ and an asymptotic success probability of $1$ for every fixed diameter, where $N$ denotes the number of vertices. The provided proof is mathematically rigorous and applicable to other graph classes.

Biomolecular condensates, largely driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), are increasingly acknowledged through extensive experimental research as being critical to biology, medicine, and biophysics. Amidst these findings, analytical models have proven to be a powerful and manageable instrument in recent theoretical work regarding how LLPS governs the formation and breakdown of condensates. This process typically, though not always, entails intrinsically disordered proteins participating in multivalent interactions dictated by their amino acid sequences. To assist researchers in utilizing these theoretical approaches, we present a practical guide to computational methods designed to derive sequence-specific LLPS characteristics from analytical frameworks. The numerical techniques discussed cover determining spinodal and binodal phase boundaries from a general free energy function using random phase approximation examples from polymer theory, constructing tie lines for multi-component LLPS, and simulating multiple-chain heteropolymeric systems via field-theoretic methods with complex Langevin dynamics. Furthermore, since accurate physical insights often depend on comparing analytical theories with explicit-chain predictions, we also briefly describe a widely used approach for coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of sequence-specific LLPS.

Selecting confounders is arguably the most critical phase in designing observational studies. Various criteria, each with distinct goals and methodologies, have been suggested, sparking ongoing debate regarding their validity and practical utility. This paper offers a comprehensive synthesis of these criteria and the underlying assumptions. We outline the specific objectives that confounder selection methods strive to meet and examine the degree of structural knowledge necessary for different approaches. Furthermore, we address the limitations of current methods and discuss their implications for practitioners.

This paper examines and broadens existing literature on spacetime topology by leveraging the characteristics of the codimension 2 null cut locus. The findings are categorized into two groups based on the assumption of horizon presence, with applications including spacetimes within the asymptotically (locally) AdS framework.

We outline the procedure for generating three-dimensional (3D) films of the Northern Lights or Aurorae Borealis using real-time data captured by two remote, high-resolution fisheye cameras. By performing astrometric reconstruction of visible stars, we model and correct the optical mapping of each camera to ensure precise alignment between the two image sets. Sample videos of the resulting movies are available at http://www.iap.fr/aurora3d.

We demonstrate that introducing Vector-Like Quarks (VLQs) with top-quark quantum numbers, in conjunction with the pseudo-scalar sector of a Type-II Two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM-II), can alleviate the tight lower bound of approximately 580 GeV on the charged Higgs boson ($H^\pm$) mass derived from $B$-physics data. This conclusion holds for both singlet and doublet representations of VLQs, allowing the minimum permissible $m_{H^\pm}$ to drop as low as 80 GeV. Such a reduction results from cancellations within $b\to s\gamma$ processes between contributions from the VLQs and the $H^\pm$ boson. Additionally, to facilitate the exploration of the parameter space where this mechanism is most potent, we provide calculations for production cross-sections and decay rates involving a top-partner VLQ ($T$) and the 2HDM-II Higgs states, particularly $H^\pm$. These findings aim to direct experimental searches for extended Higgs and quark sectors at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Notably, we emphasize the scenario of VLQ pair production ($pp\to T\bar T$) followed by the decay $T\to H^\pm b$, where the subsequent decay of $H^\pm$ into $\tau\nu$ or $tb$ pairs depends on whether $m_{H^\pm}$ is below or above the top-quark mass $m_t$, respectively.

Experimental characterization of two-dimensional stealthy hyperuniform distributions of rigid scatterers within a waveguide reveals wave transport properties for scalar waves in airborne audible acoustics. The non-resonant nature of these scatterers enables a direct correlation between transport properties and the geometric point distribution via the structure factor. Transport behavior is analyzed as a function of the pattern's stealthiness ($\chi$) and contrasted with disordered materials in the diffusive regime, which are described by Ohm's law using the mean free path. Both theoretical and numerical analyses identify distinct scattering regimes—including transparent regions, isotropic band gaps, and anisotropic scattering—as functions of $\chi$. Furthermore, the experimental investigation uncovers the robustness of these scattering regimes against losses, which are inherent in audible acoustics.

For $M \geq 2$ distributions defined on a general measurable space, we propose a nonparametric (kernel-based) metric for multi-sample dissimilarity, termed KMD, which quantifies the disparity among these distributions. The population KMD ranges from 0 to 1, yielding 0 exclusively when all $M$ distributions are identical and 1 when they are mutually singular. Additionally, KMD shares key characteristics with $f$-divergences, including invariance under bijective transformations and adherence to the data processing inequality. A sample estimator of KMD, derived from independent observations across the $M$ distributions, can be calculated in near-linear time (modulo logarithmic terms) using $k$-nearest neighbor graphs for any fixed $k \geq 1$. We establish a straightforward test for the equality of $M$ distributions utilizing the sample KMD, which is consistent against any alternative where at least two distributions differ. Furthermore, we demonstrate central limit theorems for the sample KMD, fully characterize the test's asymptotic power and detection threshold, and illustrate the method's utility through both real and synthetic data applications. The approach is also available in an R package.

The brane setup $(F1,D2,D8)$, which supports a $Lif_4^{(2)}\times S^1\times S^5$ geometry, represents a recognized Lifshitz vacuum in type IIA theory sustained by a massive $B_{\mu\nu}$ field. This configuration permits exact infrared excitations that interact with the massless modes of fundamental strings. Consequently, these massless modes drive the solutions toward a dilatonic $Lif_4^{(3)}\times S^1\times S^5$ vacuum in the infrared limit. We investigate the entanglement entropy on the boundary of this spacetime for both strip and disc subsystems. Surprisingly, we find that the net entropy density of the excitations at first order remains independent of the characteristic size of the subsystems. We contextualize these findings within the framework of the first law of entanglement thermodynamics.

This study examines timelike geodesics and periapsis precession within the Fisher-Janis-Newman-Winicour-Wyman spacetime, which models a naked singularity in the Einstein-massless scalar framework. We revisit prior findings by relaxing constraints on the eccentricity of bound orbits and the semilatus rectum. Our results indicate that negative periapsis precession arises when the spacetime significantly departs from the Schwarzschild metric. Specifically, for orbits with low eccentricity, negative precession occurs when the deviation parameter $\gamma$ is less than $1/2$. Additionally, we derive analytical solutions for the specific cases where $\gamma = 0, 1/2,$ and $1/4$, demonstrating that negative precession does not occur in the $\gamma = 1/2$ scenario.

This work establishes uncertainty relations that set upper bounds on the velocity of evolutionary dynamics, whether driven solely by selection or by both selection and mutation, as described by the replicator and replicator-mutator equations. The derived speed limits indicate that greater population diversity facilitates faster evolutionary progress. Specifically, uncertainty in the fitness function is identified as a requisite condition for rapid evolution. Consequently, these findings extend Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection to mutational dynamics by formulating evolutionary rate constraints as uncertainty relations.

The graphene/SiC interface has recently become a flexible platform for growing otherwise unstable, monoelemental two-dimensional (2D) layers through intercalation. These layers, inherently capped within a van der Waals heterostructure by overhead graphene, form a new category of quantum materials exhibiting distinctive properties that differ from their bulk parent crystals. Intercalated silver serves as a prime example, where 2D quantum confinement and the breaking of inversion symmetry drive a transition from metal to semiconductor. Nevertheless, knowledge regarding the associated unoccupied states remains limited, and precise control of the Fermi level position across the bandgap is highly desirable. In this work, we achieve n-type doping of a graphene/2D-Ag/SiC heterostack via in situ potassium deposition and investigate its band structure using synchrotron-based angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy. Although the induced carrier densities, approximately $10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$, are insufficient to trigger the onset of the silver conduction band, the graphene band alignment shifts relative to the rigidly displaced Ag valence band and substrate core levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate an ordered potassium adlayer ($2\times 2$ relative to graphene) featuring free-electron-like dispersion. This configuration suppresses plasmaron quasiparticles in graphene by enhancing the metalization of the heterostack. Our findings establish surface charge-transfer doping as an effective method for tuning the band alignment and electronic characteristics of van der Waals heterostructures composed of graphene and a novel class of monolayered quantum materials.

This research investigates the existence of distance-transitive graphs derived from the coset actions of $G_2(q)$ on either the subfield subgroup $G_2(\sqrt{q})$ or the Ree subgroup $^2G_2(q)$. The findings indicate that no such graphs exist, regardless of whether the groups are extended by outer automorphisms of $G_2(q)$.

We establish chiral Ward identities for lattice QCD utilizing Wilson quarks, applicable to systems with $N_\mathrm{f} \geq 3$ flavors, small lattice volumes, Schrödinger functional boundary conditions, and negligible quark masses. These identities link the axial transformation of the non-singlet pseudoscalar density to the scalar density, thereby facilitating the non-perturbative calculation of the scale-independent renormalization parameter ratio $Z_\mathrm{S}/Z_\mathrm{P}$. Our findings for $N_\mathrm{f}=3$ QCD employ tree-level Symanzik-improved gluons and Wilson-Clover quarks across bare gauge couplings spanning the typical range used in large-volume $N_\mathrm{f} = 2+1$ simulations with Wilson fermions at lattice spacings under $0.1\,$fm. The achieved precision ranges between 0.3\% and 1\%, rising to 2\% for the coarsest lattice configuration. Finally, we examine the application of the $Z_\mathrm{S}/Z_\mathrm{P}$ ratio in non-perturbative computations of $\mathrm{O}(a)$ improved renormalized quark masses.

The task of keyphrase generation involves creating phrases that most accurately represent a specific document. While existing methods in academic fields primarily rely on article titles and abstracts, this study investigates whether incorporating data from the full text or semantically similar papers enhances neural keyphrase generation. Our findings indicate that including sentences from the full text, especially via extractive summaries, substantially improves the model's ability to generate keyphrases that are either present in or absent from the source material. This conclusion is supported by experiments using three established models and the Longformer Encoder-Decoder (LED) transformer, which is optimized for longer documents. Furthermore, we introduce FullTextKP, a new large-scale dataset that distinguishes itself by including the complete article text alongside titles and abstracts. The source code is available at https://github.com/kgarg8/FullTextKP.

Building upon recent advancements regarding lower Ricci curvature bounds in quantum systems, we present two noncommutative analogues of curvature-dimension inequalities tailored for symmetric quantum Markov semigroups on matrix algebras. Assuming these curvature-dimension conditions hold, we establish a set of dimension-dependent functional inequalities, derive a noncommutative version of the Bonnet-Myers theorem, and demonstrate the concavity of entropy power within this framework. Furthermore, we illustrate these concepts with examples that meet specific curvature-dimension criteria, such as Schur multipliers on matrix algebras, Herz-Schur multipliers on group algebras, and depolarizing semigroups.

Predicting ad click-through rates (CTR) is a fundamental challenge for large-scale advertising platforms. Since ad clicks represent a major form of user interaction and serve as the primary indicator of ad utility, they are critical in cost-per-click models where advertiser charges depend directly on click frequency. Consequently, developing robust CTR models represents a substantial investment for most internet advertising firms. Addressing these challenges requires machine learning techniques optimized for online learning that extend beyond mere accuracy gains, focusing instead on efficiency, reproducibility, calibration, and credit attribution. This paper presents a case study of practical methods implemented in Google's search ads CTR model, offering an industry perspective on key areas of current machine learning research. It demonstrates how novel ML techniques are rigorously evaluated and effectively integrated into large-scale industrial environments.

This work establishes a Chern-Weil theorem and a Hilbert-Samuel formula applicable to a broad category of singular plurisubharmonic metrics on a line bundle defined over a smooth projective complex variety. The derivation relies on b-divisor theory and the multiplier ideal volume function. We extend these findings to the line bundle associated with Siegel-Jacobi forms over the universal abelian variety, equipped with its canonical invariant metric. This outcome generalizes the second author's prior result concerning the universal family of elliptic curves to higher degrees.

We propose leveraging gradients to identify adversarial and out-of-distribution samples. To probe a neural network's effective expressivity, we introduce confounding labels—distinct from those used during training—into the gradient generation process. Gradients illustrate the magnitude of change necessary for a model to correctly represent specific inputs, offering insights into the model's representational capabilities, which are shaped by both architectural design and training data. By employing a differently designed label, our method eliminates the reliance on ground truth labels when generating gradients during inference. We demonstrate that this gradient-based approach detects input anomalies by assessing the model's effective expressivity without requiring hyperparameter tuning or extra processing, ultimately outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques for detecting adversarial and out-of-distribution inputs.

Recent years have seen deep learning surpass traditional methods in numerous machine learning applications, particularly in time series forecasting—a critical area within data mining. These neural networks excel by automatically capturing temporal dependencies, making them a robust solution. However, choosing the optimal architecture and its parameters remains a complex, expertise-intensive challenge, highlighting the need for further research into the suitability of various models for specific forecasting tasks. This study addresses two primary objectives: conducting a comprehensive review of recent deep learning advancements in time series forecasting and performing an experimental comparison of the most popular architectures. We analyze seven distinct deep learning models based on their accuracy and efficiency, evaluating performance across diverse architectural configurations and hyperparameters. The research utilizes over 50,000 time series datasets spanning 12 different forecasting problems. By training more than 38,000 models, this work presents the most extensive deep learning analysis for time series forecasting to date. The findings indicate that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are the top performers. While LSTMs deliver the highest accuracy, CNNs offer comparable performance with greater stability across varying parameter settings and improved computational efficiency.

We examine networks comprising two node categories: hyperconnected "center" nodes (v-nodes) that interact extensively through "satellite" nodes (u-nodes). This centralized architecture, common in gene networks, forms a bow-tie structure with distinct properties. Specifically, this layout generates feedback loops capable of producing any desired patterning dynamics, whether periodic or chaotic, and establishes multiple equilibrium states. We demonstrate that activating or silencing a single node can abruptly shift the network's attractor, even when that node has weak connectivity. We differentiate between two dynamic regimes: "power of center" (PC), where satellite response is rapid, and "satellite power" (SP), where center response is rapid. Using a simplified network model, we show that centralized networks exhibit greater robustness against time-dependent perturbations in the PC regime compared to the SP regime. In theoretical molecular biology, these models can elucidate a non-trivial connection between the architecture of protein-DNA and protein-protein interaction networks and the controllability of cellular process dynamics over space and time.

This editorial establishes the quantum field theoretic framework necessary for the existence of Elko and mass dimension one fermions. Beyond introducing Elko and its corresponding quantum field, this work may also pave the way for a novel class of spin-1/2 fermions and bosons. As argued in this volume, these new particles represent first-principle candidates for dark matter.

Stellar rotation is a complex function of mass, metallicity, and age, which can be influenced by binarity. To understand the importance of these parameters in main sequence stars, we have assembled a sample of observations that spans a range of these parameters using a combination of observations from The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and the Kepler Space Telescope. We find that while we can measure rotation periods and identify other classes of stellar variability (e.g., pulsations) from TESS lightcurves, instrument systematics prevent the detection of rotation signals longer than the TESS orbital period of 13.7 days. Due to this detection limit, we also utilize rotation periods constrained using rotational velocities measured by the APOGEE spectroscopic survey and radii estimated using the Gaia mission for both TESS and Kepler stars. From these rotation periods, we 1) find we can track rotational evolution along discrete mass tracks as a function of stellar age, 2) find we are unable to recover trends between rotation and metallicity that were observed by previous studies, and 3) note that our sample reveals that wide binary companions do not affect rotation, while close binary companions cause stars to exhibit more rapid rotation than single stars.

This study utilizes inverse design techniques to create two-dimensional plasma metamaterial (PMM) devices. By employing backpropagated finite difference frequency domain (FDFD) simulations, we engineered waveguides and demultiplexers capable of operating in both transverse electric (TE) and transverse magnetic (TM) modes. These devices, constructed from plasma elements with densities suitable for approximately 7 GHz operation, successfully demonstrate waveguiding and demultiplexing functions. The achievable plasma densities facilitate future in-situ training and experimental implementation. Additionally, we investigated the potential of PMMs for nonlinear Boolean operations within optical computing, successfully realizing functionally complete logical gates (OR and AND) using the TM mode.

The geospace environment is inherently volatile and driven by dynamic forces, with space weather exerting significant influence on Earth's magnetosphere. This interaction triggers a complex and poorly understood response in the thermosphere, notably affecting the evolution of neutral mass density. While numerous models utilize space weather drivers to predict density variations, they often suffer from high computational costs or lack accuracy under specific conditions. To address these limitations, this study employs a probabilistic machine learning (ML) approach to develop an efficient surrogate for the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIE-GCM), a physics-based thermosphere model. By leveraging principal component analysis to reduce dimensionality and recurrent neural networks to capture dynamic behavior, the proposed method offers significantly faster performance than traditional numerical simulations. The resulting reduced order probabilistic emulator (ROPE) utilizes Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to forecast time-series data in the reduced state space, generating probability distributions for future density. Results indicate that the TIE-GCM ROPE matches the error rates of previous linear methods across available datasets while enhancing storm-time modeling. Furthermore, a satellite propagation analysis of the major November 2003 storm demonstrates that the TIE-GCM ROPE captures satellite positions with a bias of less than 5 km, whereas linear approaches, which provide only point estimates, exhibit biases ranging from 7 to 18 km.

The recent identification of extraordinary-log universality has sparked significant interest in both classical and quantum boundary critical phenomena. However, despite extensive research, the existence of quantum extraordinary-log universality remains highly debated. In this work, we investigate the quantum edge criticality of a two-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model with emergent bulk criticality using quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Above an insulating bulk, the open boundaries undergo a Kosterlitz-Thouless-like transition into a superfluid phase when edge hopping strength is sufficiently increased. At the bulk critical point, the edges display extraordinary, ordinary, and special critical phases. Specifically, within the extraordinary phase, finite-size scaling of two-point correlations and superfluid stiffness involves logarithms, demonstrating a classical-quantum correspondence for extraordinary-log universality. Furthermore, thanks to modern quantum emulators for interacting lattice bosons, these edge critical phases may soon be realized experimentally.

James' submodule theorem serves as a cornerstone in the representation theory of finite general linear groups and symmetric groups. This note explores an analogous version of the theorem for a general finite group possessing a split $BN$-pair. This approach yields a distinguished composition factor of the Steinberg module, originally identified by Hiss through a distinct methodology. Determining the dimension of this specific composition factor remains a significant open problem.

Research indicates that coherent phonons serve as a powerful instrument for manipulating and improving the optoelectronic and transport characteristics of nanostructured materials. Recent investigations have demonstrated that the interaction between acoustic phonons and rapidly moving carriers in semiconductor heterostructures can trigger electron-phonon instabilities, leading to both standard and induced Cherenkov effects; however, the mechanisms driving these instabilities remain largely obscure. This study reveals that, beyond Cherenkov instability, other supersonic phenomena can occur during non-equilibrium charge transport in miniband semiconductor superlattices (SLs) when driven by an acoustic plane wave. By employing semiclassical nonperturbative techniques alongside bifurcation theory, we identify the conditions under which dynamical instabilities arise due to the emission of specific SL phonons by supersonic electrons and their subsequent feedback on those electrons. Significantly, the radiation mechanism aligns with the Ginzburg-Frank-Tamm theory, manifesting as either normal or anomalous Doppler effects. We also examine induced Doppler effects in the context of electron bunch formation within the spatially periodic structure of the SL. When the acoustic wave amplitude surpasses a specific threshold, these dynamical instabilities manifest as drift velocity reversals, resonances in sound attenuation, and absolute negative mobility. Furthermore, we show that these newly identified superluminal Doppler phenomena enable tunable broadband amplification and the generation of GHz-THz electromagnetic waves, laying the foundation for the creation of innovative phononic devices.

Given the high cosmic temperature at the onset of inflation, cosmological scalar perturbations are expected to adhere to a thermal distribution. This study employs the Fubini-study method to examine how this thermal contribution, defined by the parameter $\kappa_{0}$, influences the evolution of cosmological complexity ($\mathcal{C}_{FS}$). Our findings indicate that incorporating thermal effects causes the Universe to "decomplex" initially as scalar perturbation modes exit the horizon during the de Sitter (dS) phase, with $\mathcal{C}_{FS}$ reaching a minimum near $\pi/4$. If $\mathcal{C}_{FS}$ attains this minimum within the dS era—occurring with a small $\kappa_0$ or a sufficiently large e-folding number for a larger $\kappa_0$—it rebounds and increases. Upon transitioning from the dS to the radiation-dominated (RD) phase, $\mathcal{C}_{FS}$ declines, crosses its minimum again, and subsequently rises until the mode reenters the horizon. Conversely, for sufficiently large $\kappa_0$, $\mathcal{C}_{FS}$ decreases without reaching its minimum during the dS era and begins increasing immediately after the shift to the RD phase. During the RD era, as the mode reenters the horizon, $\mathcal{C}_{FS}$ oscillates around $\kappa_{0}$. These dynamics contrast sharply with the zero-temperature scenario, where complexity rises during the dS phase and falls during the RD era until horizon reentry. Consequently, our results demonstrate that thermal effects qualitatively alter the evolutionary trajectory of cosmological complexity.

Research has confirmed that only a minor subset of neoantigens displayed by MHC class I molecules on cell surfaces are capable of triggering T cells, a constraint primarily due to the binding specificity between the T cell receptor (TCR) and the peptide-MHC (pMHC) complex. Predicting T cell binding to neoantigens remains a difficult and unsolved challenge. To address this, we introduce ATMTCR, an attentive-mask contrastive learning model designed to infer TCR-antigen binding specificity. The model employs a Transformer encoder to convert each input TCR sequence into a latent representation, followed by masking a proportion of residues guided by attention weights to create a contrastive view. By pretraining on extensive datasets of TCR CDR3 sequences, we demonstrated that contrastive learning markedly enhances the prediction accuracy of TCR binding to pMHC complexes. In addition to identifying critical amino acids and their positions within the TCR sequence, our model captures high-order semantic information governing TCR-antigen binding specificity. Evaluation across two independent datasets revealed that our method outperforms other existing algorithms. Furthermore, the analysis of attention weights allowed us to effectively pinpoint important amino acids and their positional preferences, thereby demonstrating the interpretability of the proposed model.

The paper proves several characterizations of complex ellipsoids within the class of convex bodies in Cn, focusing on their sections and projections. Furthermore, characterizing complex symmetry using analogous methods serves as a vital instrument.

This research investigates a parallel server system with two classes and two servers under a newly defined extended heavy traffic regime. In this regime, the underlying "static allocation" linear program (LP) is critical, yet a unique solution is not required. The primary contribution is the development of policies that asymptotically attain a lower bound on the expected discounted linear combination of diffusion-scaled queue lengths, established in reference [1], thereby rendering these policies asymptotically optimal (AO).

Each extreme point of the LP corresponds to a specific control mode, defined as a set of active class-server pairs. When multiple LP solutions exist, these modes can be chosen dynamically. The study demonstrates that achieving asymptotic optimality requires either a single mode or two modes; in the two-mode scenario, a switching point exists within the normalized workload domain, defined by a free boundary problem. These policies are constructed by identifying pairs of elementary policies and transitioning between them at this boundary. Furthermore, this work presents the first instance in heavy traffic theory where the weak limits under an AO policy follow a diffusion process characterized by discontinuous drift and diffusion coefficients.

This study examines model estimation and reward-free learning within episodic Block MDPs, where decision-makers observe rich contexts derived from a limited set of latent states. We first address the task of estimating the latent state decoding function—the mapping from observations to latent states—using data collected under a fixed behavior policy. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound on the estimation error rate and propose an algorithm that achieves this fundamental limit; notably, this algorithm also estimates all MDP components. Subsequently, we analyze reward-free learning of near-optimal policies. Leveraging our efficient model estimation method, we demonstrate the ability to infer policies that converge to the optimal solution at the fastest possible rate as sample size increases. Our analysis further reveals necessary and sufficient conditions under which the block structure reduces sample complexity for identifying near-optimal policies. When these conditions hold, the minimax sample complexity improves by a factor of $n$, representing the number of possible contexts.

Warm absorbers detected in over 50% of nearby active galactic nuclei (AGN) serve as indicators of ionized outflows situated at parsec-scale distances from the central source. When the minimum inferred ionization parameters indicate plasma temperatures around $10^4$ K, the gas transitions from a bound to an unbound state if heated to approximately $10^6$ K at greater radii. Recent work by Dannen et al. reveals that under such conditions, thermally driven wind solutions become unstable, often forming dense clumps due to thermal instability. To investigate the observational implications of these findings, we calculated line profiles using the one-dimensional simulations presented by Dannen et al. We demonstrate how line profiles, even from a simple steady-state wind, vary with the ionization energy (IE) of absorbing ions, reflecting the wind's ionization stratification. To categorize the variety of line shapes, we classified them into four groups: weak Gaussians, saturated boxy profiles with and without extended blue wings, and broad weak profiles. Ions with the highest IE, which sample the fastest-moving regions, produce the lines in the latter two categories. Their maximum blueshifts align with the peak flow velocities found in both steady-state and clumpy thermally unstable models. Conversely, in thermally stable models, the maximum blueshifts of high-IE lines can be less than half the actual solution velocities. Furthermore, clumpy solutions can create distinct absorption troughs at widely separated velocities.

APOGEE is a high-resolution (R ~22,000), near-infrared, multi-epoch spectroscopic survey of the Milky Way. The second generation of the project, APOGEE-2, expanded the survey into the Southern Hemisphere via APOGEE-2S.
