This expansion allowed APOGEE to conduct a comprehensive panoramic mapping of the galaxy's primary regions; notably, by observing in the H-band, APOGEE can uniquely investigate dust-obscured inner Milky Way regions that are optimally accessed from the South. This paper details the targeting strategy for APOGEE-2S, focusing on documenting modifications to the original, previously published plan. It explains the rationale behind these changes and evaluates their effectiveness in meeting scientific goals. Anticipating this to be the final publication detailing APOGEE targeting, we provide a complete accounting of all relevant information through the conclusion of the APOGEE-2S project. This includes major survey programs exploring significant stellar populations and galactic regions, as well as a comprehensive list of programs contributing to the APOGEE database through time allocations from the Chilean National Time Allocation Committee (CNTAC) and the Carnegie Institution for Science (CIS). This work was presented alongside a companion article by R. Beaton et al. (submitted; AAS29028), which outlines the final target selection strategy adopted for APOGEE-2 in the Northern Hemisphere.

The full physical comprehension of optimizing thermodynamic work remains a significant unresolved challenge in stochastic thermodynamics. We tackle this problem by applying the Hamiltonian framework of linear response theory within the context of finite-time, weak processes. We derive and analyze the associated Euler-Lagrange equation, demonstrating its key characteristics through the standard case of driven Brownian motion in an overdamped regime. Our results indicate that the optimal protocols derived either converge to exact stochastic thermodynamic solutions in the appropriate limit or are identical to them, exhibiting the characteristic jumps. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates that jumps at the process boundaries serve as an effective optimization strategy for fast yet weak processes across all driven systems. Finally, we reveal that these fast-but-weak optimal protocols possess time-reversal symmetry, a feature previously obscured in exact solutions far from equilibrium.

Collecting, aggregating, and sharing personal information is essential for advancing machine learning applications that serve societal needs. Nevertheless, anecdotal accounts and survey data indicate that the general public often feels displeased or even enraged by current, legally permissible data collection methods. This discrepancy suggests that existing personal data markets fail to align with the norms held by ordinary individuals. Consequently, this study experimentally investigates whether market transactions within a typical online setting are acceptable when judged by laypeople. The findings reveal that a significant majority of participants declined to engage in data pricing activities, even in a commercial environment where market principles usually prevail. Among those who did assign a value to their data, the median price was roughly ten times higher than prevailing market rates. These outcomes challenge the "notice and consent" framework currently employed by technology companies and government regulators to assess data flows. Furthermore, the results highlight a fundamental conceptual gap between cultural and legal expectations concerning the utilization of personal data.

Simulations of low-Reynolds number elastoinertial turbulence (EIT) in polymer solutions reveal localized fluctuations in polymer stretch. These patterns closely resemble structures identified through linear stability and resolvent analyses, specifically Tollmien-Schlichting (TS) modes, which form critical-layer configurations where the mean fluid velocity matches the wave speed. Further computations of self-sustained nonlinear TS waves demonstrate that stagnation points within this critical layer produce sheets of significant polymer stretch, suggesting these kinematic features serve as the origin of analogous structures observed in EIT.

This document presents a selection of recent ATLAS and CMS measurements focusing on single top quark production and associated top-antitop quark pair production alongside a $W$, $Z$, or photon ($\gamma$) boson. These analyses primarily utilize proton-proton collision data from the LHC's Run 2, collected at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, with integrated luminosities reaching up to 77.5 fb$^{-1}$. Additionally, a combined analysis of single top quark measurements from both experiments using the full Run 1 dataset at $\sqrt{s}=7,8$ TeV is featured. These studies investigate Standard Model couplings between top quarks and gauge bosons and provide sensitivity to various anomalous non-Standard-Model effects.

We report high-resolution (0.3", equivalent to 16 AU) and high signal-to-noise Submillimeter Array observations of the 870 micrometer (345 GHz) continuum and CO J=3--2 line emission from the protoplanetary disk surrounding TW Hya. By combining continuum and line radiative transfer calculations with the multiwavelength spectral energy distribution, we analyzed these data using simple two-dimensional parametric disk models. Assuming a radially invariant dust population and a vertically integrated gas-to-dust mass ratio, we could not simultaneously fit both the CO and dust observations with models featuring either a single, distinct outer boundary or a smooth exponential taper at large radii. Instead, our results indicate that millimeter-sized dust grains in the TW Hya disk exhibit a relatively sharp edge near 60 AU, whereas CO emission (along with optical/infrared scattered light) extends to a significantly larger radius of at least 215 AU. We discuss potential explanations for this radial distribution of millimeter-sized dust and the apparent discrepancy between CO and dust sizes, suggesting that these features may signal substructure within the dust disk or represent natural outcomes of solid growth and radial drift expected in older pre-main sequence systems like TW Hya.

Current visually-induced audio generation methods rely on sampling brief, low-quality, single-class sounds, with state-of-the-art models requiring minutes to generate just one second of audio on high-end GPUs. This work introduces a single model that produces high-fidelity, visually relevant sounds from open-domain video frames in real-time on a single GPU. We train a transformer to sample a new spectrogram from a pre-trained codebook using video features. This codebook was created via a VQGAN variant optimized for a compact sampling space using a novel spectrogram-based perceptual loss. A window-based GAN then converts the generated spectrogram into a waveform, significantly accelerating the process. Addressing the lack of automatic evaluation metrics for spectrograms, we developed a new suite of metrics based on a novel sound classifier, Melception, designed to assess fidelity and relevance in open-domain samples. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations on both small and large datasets confirm our model's performance, showing substantial improvements over state-of-the-art approaches in quality, compactness, and speed. Code, demos, and samples are available at v-iashin.github.io/SpecVQGAN.

This paper introduces a new mechanism for managing the unfolding of definitions within dependent type theory. Conventional proof assistants typically allow users to dictate globally whether specific definitions should or should not be unfolded throughout a development. While unfolding is often required to reason about definitions, excessive unfolding can lead to fragile proofs and proof goals that become computationally intractable. In our proposed system, definitions remain unfolded by default, with users retaining the ability to unfold them selectively on a local basis. We substantiate this approach by elaborating our system to a core type theory that incorporates extension types—a connective originally developed in homotopy type theory. Furthermore, we establish a normalization theorem for our core calculus and have implemented the system in the cooltt proof assistant, thereby offering both theoretical validation and practical demonstration of its efficacy.

We present a linear-time algorithm to determine the diameter of AT-free graphs. Additionally, we refine the definition of polar sets and establish novel properties for polar sets within (weak) dominating pair graphs. By leveraging existing reductions that map the problems of identifying simplicial vertices and locating triangles in general graphs to the task of finding diameters in AT-free graphs, we demonstrate that these problems can be solved in O(n^2) time. Consequently, we enhance the known run-time complexities for various graph-theoretical problems.

The era of complexity has arrived, fundamentally altering the landscape of science. Surprisingly, a critical examination of the explanations for these shifts yields largely discouraging results, as most responses focus on properties—such as non-linearity—that have long been central to scientific inquiry. This article serves as the preface to the special issue "Grasping Complexity" in the journal "Computers and Mathematics with Applications." It explores the reasons behind this shift in scientific eras, outlines the primary transformations in scientific practice, and provides a concise overview of the contributions within the issue.

Quantum physics presents numerous unexpected phenomena. Two notable examples are the challenge to locality suggested by Bell's Theorem and the potential of quantum computation, which questions the complexity-theoretic Church-Turing thesis. In each instance, the astonishment might stem from uncritically accepting a rigid arrow-of-time assumption, potentially valid only within the classical realm. This hypothesis has frequently been discussed regarding Bell's Theorem, and the argument related to quantum computation is outlined below. Future progress requires developing models that discard this stringent arrow-of-time constraint in favor of a weaker alternative.

Optimizing gaze recognition can substantially minimize eye movement data, thereby enhancing the comprehension of visual and cognitive processing, which is a critical prerequisite for eye-based interactions in virtual reality (VR). Nevertheless, the three-dimensional nature of VR environments introduces novel challenges for current recognition algorithms. Utilizing seven evaluation metrics and an Overall score (the average of seven normalized values), we determined the optimal parameters for three established algorithms—Velocity-Threshold Identification, Dispersion-Threshold Identification, and Velocity & Dispersion-Threshold Identification—as well as our proposed modified Velocity & Dispersion-Threshold Identification algorithm. A comparative analysis of these four algorithms with their optimized parameters reveals that our modified approach yields superior performance. Additionally, we conducted a preliminary investigation into how interface complexity affects classification outcomes, finding that the algorithms demonstrate low sensitivity to such variations.

Phase-change memory (PCM) architectures utilize multiple banks to handle memory requests concurrently. However, performance degrades when multiple requests target the same bank, as they must be processed sequentially. We note that contemporary PCM banks consist of largely independent partitions that share only limited global peripherals, specifically sense amplifiers for reading and write drivers for writing. Leveraging this structure, we present PALP, a mechanism that facilitates partition-level parallelism within each bank by utilizing the memory controller's scheduling logic. PALP offers three key contributions: first, we define novel PCM commands to enable partition-level parallelism and mitigate read-write conflicts with minimal modifications to PCM logic and interfaces; second, we suggest simple circuit adjustments to create an alternative write driver mode that, alongside sense amplifiers, resolves read-read conflicts; third, we introduce a new scheduling strategy that prioritizes requests capable of exploiting partition-level parallelism, including those with long outstanding times, while ensuring starvation-freedom and adherence to the PCM's running-average-power-limit (RAPL). Evaluation using MiBench and SPEC CPU2017 workloads demonstrates that PALP reduces average PCM access latency by 23% and enhances overall system performance by 28% compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This article aims to derive initial-order differential subordination relationships for specific Carath\'{e}odory functions that exhibit favorable geometric characteristics. Additionally, we identify multiple implications to demonstrate that the normalized analytic function falls within diverse subclasses of starlike functions.

This paper demonstrates that, under conditions of sufficiently strong atomic interactions, analytical solutions for current-carrying nonlinear Bloch states at the Brillouin zone edge can be derived for a model of spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) with symmetric spin interactions situated in optical lattices. These straightforward yet general exact solutions offer an analytical proof of several unique properties that have no counterparts in standard BEC lattice systems or in uniform spin-orbit-coupled BEC systems. Furthermore, this work serves as an analytical case study for elucidating the superfluid and other associated characteristics of spin-orbit-coupled BEC lattice systems.

We describe the semigroups of mappings that either preserve orientation or both preserve and reverse it on a finite cycle by analyzing their behavior on oriented triples and quadruples. This analysis provides a proof demonstrating that the latter semigroup is identical to the semigroup of all mappings that maintain the intersections of chords on the associated circle.

The findings regarding the initial boundary value problem for Einstein's vacuum field equations, presented in \cite{friedrich:nagy}, depend on a distinctive gauge choice. One of the defining gauge source functions corresponds to the mean extrinsic curvature of the time-like leaves within a foliation that encompasses the boundary and its surrounding neighborhood. The remaining functions govern the evolution of a frame field and coordinates on these leaves. Generally, their combined effect is necessary to regulate the evolution of the leaves within the context of the reduced field equations. This article derives the hyperbolic equations implicit in this gauge, demonstrating that they are independent of the Einstein equations and are well-defined across arbitrary space-times. The analysis becomes more straightforward when boundary conditions specifying constant mean extrinsic curvature are imposed, and it simplifies further if the boundary is required to be totally geodesic.

Integrin serves as a critical transmembrane receptor protein that remodels the actin network and secures the cell membrane to the extracellular matrix through mechanochemical mechanisms. It facilitates the aggregation of specific lipids and lipid-anchored proteins—a process vital for a particular form of endocytosis—within active regions driven by integrin activity. To investigate this, we introduce a minimal, exactly solvable model that captures the interaction between the stochastic switching of integrins between on and off states and the inherent dynamics of the membrane. Our analysis yields an analytic formula for membrane deformation and local velocity, elucidating how a single integrin drives lipid clustering. We find that deformation, velocity, and lipid clustering evolve in a nonmonotonic manner, with their dependencies on stochastic shuttling timescales and membrane characteristics clearly defined.

Recent and forthcoming 3GPP 5G New Radio (NR) specifications incorporate features designed to deliver connectivity across diverse verticals, specifically targeting automotive, rail, and aviation sectors. Currently, NR is undergoing enhancements and introducing new radio access network capabilities to ensure fast, reliable, and unrestricted connectivity for transport applications. This article examines the critical characteristics and requirements of various services aimed at making the transport industry more sustainable, economically viable, safe, and secure. These needs will be addressed by emerging and novel 5G NR features, such as precise positioning, reference signal architectures for multi-point transmission and reception, service-specific scheduling configurations, and service quality prediction.

Research into quarkonium production during heavy-ion collisions serves as a tool for investigating the properties of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP). The suppression and regeneration of bound quarkonium states reflect medium characteristics, while alterations in quarkonium polarization observed in Pb-Pb collisions compared to pp collisions can offer deeper insights into the suppression and regeneration mechanisms within the QGP. Furthermore, quarkonia provide sensitivity to the initial phases of heavy-ion collisions, and data from photonuclear collisions can help restrict the nuclear gluon distribution at low Bjorken-$x$. This paper examines recent quarkonium measurements conducted by the ALICE collaboration in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}~=~5.02$ TeV. We present preliminary results on the inclusive J/$\psi$ nuclear modification factor ($R_{\rm AA}$) across both forward and midrapidity regions. Additionally, we discuss the first-ever measurement of J/$\psi$ polarization in Pb-Pb collisions, along with preliminary findings on the coherent J/$\psi$ photoproduction cross section.

Bayesian optimization (BO) is highly effective for optimizing black-box functions that incur expensive evaluation costs, a scenario common in fields ranging from hyperparameter tuning and drug discovery to robotics. BO operates by using a Bayesian surrogate model to sequentially choose query points, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation within the search space. While most current approaches depend on a single Gaussian process (GP) surrogate with a kernel form often chosen via prior domain knowledge, this paper proposes an alternative using an ensemble (E) of GPs. This ensemble adaptively selects the best-fitting surrogate model in real-time, creating a GP mixture posterior with greater expressive power. The method employs Thompson sampling (TS) to determine the next evaluation input based on this ensemble GP posterior, a process that eliminates the need for additional design parameters. To ensure scalability, the approach utilizes random feature-based kernel approximation for each GP model, and the resulting EGP-TS framework supports parallel execution. Furthermore, the paper provides theoretical analysis on Bayesian regret to prove the convergence of EGP-TS to the global optimum in both sequential and parallel contexts. Empirical evaluations on synthetic functions and real-world applications demonstrate the advantages of this proposed method.

A linear regression algorithm is employed on a digital-supermode distributed Bragg reflector laser to optimize wavelength switching times. By using feedback from a digital coherent receiver to update the pre-emphasis weights for laser section currents, the method enables in-situ calculation, eliminating the need for manual adjustments. Testing on a representative subset of channels demonstrates that this commercially available laser can reconfigure over 6.05 THz (supporting 122 channels) in under 10 ns.

We introduce a novel approach for formulating simple, exact equations that characterize gravitational solutions, specifically black holes and their quasinormal modes. More specifically, we derive the complete set of functional and Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz non-linear integral equations rooted in quantum integrability. In doing so, we demonstrate that quasinormal modes satisfy various equivalent exact quantization conditions and correspond to Bethe roots. By numerically solving these integral equations and comparing the outcomes with alternative methods, we conclusively validate the approach's simplicity, precision, and efficacy. Moreover, this technique bridges previously unconnected disciplines and establishes a foundation for innovative research directions within gravity and gauge theories.

We conduct a systematic investigation into the correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion framework using lattice QCD. We achieve strong signal quality for all Wick contractions of quark fields except one. This study examines how our results vary with quark mass and evaluates the significance of correlations between the quark and antiquark inside the pion. Furthermore, we compare our lattice findings with predictions derived from chiral perturbation theory.

Experimental precision data regarding energy-level differences in hydrogen-like atoms, particularly the 1S-2S transitions in hydrogen and deuterium, underscore the need to formulate a reduced Dirac equation (RDE) that utilizes reduced mass instead of the standard electron mass. The RDE's theoretical foundation rests on two symmetries: invariance under space-time inversion and pure space inversion. Utilizing the RDE within a covariant quantum electrodynamics framework, the Lamb shift is calculated at the one-loop level as a radiative correction to a bound electron in an off-mass-shell state. This novel method eliminates infrared divergences. Consequently, although the overall calculation has limited precision, it is streamlined, entirely free of divergences and ambiguity.

Interactions among quasiparticles are fundamentally critical, as they dictate the macroscopic characteristics of quantum materials. A prime illustration is superconductivity, which stems from attractive electron-electron interactions mediated by phonons or other exotic fluctuations. In this study, we incorporate mobile exciton impurities into a two-dimensional electron gas to examine the interactions between the resulting Fermi polaron quasiparticles. Utilizing multi-dimensional coherent spectroscopy on monolayer WS$_2$ offers an optimal environment for analyzing polaron-polaron interactions, leveraging the system's trion fine structure and valley-specific optical selection rules. At low electron doping levels, we observe that the primary interactions occur between polaron states dressed by the same Fermi sea. In the absence of bound polaron pairs (bipolarons), a minimal microscopic model demonstrates that these interactions arise from a phase-space filling effect, where excitons compete for identical electrons. Furthermore, we uncover a bipolaron bound state featuring a significantly large binding energy, formed by excitons from different valleys cooperatively binding to the same electron. This research establishes a foundation for investigating and comprehending strong electron correlation effects in two-dimensional layered systems, such as moiré superlattices.

We introduce a methodology for generating phase portraits of stochastic systems. By decomposing the dynamics described by the Fokker-Planck equation into convective and diffusive components, we demonstrate that stable and unstable fixed points within the convective field align with the maxima and minima of the stationary probability distribution, provided the probability current is zero at these locations. Consequently, stochastic phase portraits, which visualize the convective field, reveal these distributional extrema and facilitate the identification of stochastic bifurcations that alter the count and stability of such extrema. Furthermore, we establish that limit cycles in these portraits signify ridges of the probability distribution and uncover a new class of stochastic bifurcations characterized by a probability maximum migrating to the system's boundary via a gap between the two nullclines of the convective field.

Semantic segmentation networks are typically trained once and remain static during deployment, leading to frequent misclassifications when the operational data distribution diverges from the training set. To address this, we propose adapting the neural network to the robot's environment during deployment without requiring external supervision. By utilizing complementary data representations, we create a supervision signal through the probabilistic accumulation of consecutive 2D semantic predictions into a volumetric 3D map. The network is then trained on renderings of this accumulated map, which resolves ambiguities and enforces multi-view consistency via the 3D representation. Unlike traditional scene adaptation techniques, our approach aims to preserve previously acquired knowledge by employing a continual learning strategy with experience replay. Extensive experiments on the ScanNet dataset and in-house RGB-D sensor data demonstrate successful adaptation to real-world indoor scenes. Our method achieves an average segmentation accuracy improvement of 9.9% over fixed pre-trained networks while successfully retaining knowledge from the original pre-training dataset.

An analysis of differential cross sections and photon-beam asymmetries for the $\gamma p \to K^+\Lambda(1520)$ reaction was conducted using a tree-level effective Lagrangian framework. The reaction amplitudes were constructed by incorporating $t$-channel $K$ and $K^\ast$ exchanges, $u$-channel $\Lambda$ exchange, $s$-channel nucleon exchange, and the interaction current, alongside a minimal set of $s$-channel nucleon resonances. The findings indicate that experimental data are accurately reproduced by including either the $N(2060)5/2^-$ or $N(2120)3/2^-$ resonance. In both scenarios, the contact term and $K$ exchange contribute significantly; however, while $K^\ast$ and $\Lambda$ exchanges are negligible when the former resonance is included, they play a considerable role in the latter. Future measurements of target asymmetries are recommended to precisely determine the resonance contributions and elucidate the specific roles of the $K^\ast$ and $\Lambda$ exchanges in this reaction.

Conventional approaches to Bayesian estimation for sparse blind deconvolution typically rely on Bernoulli-Gaussian (BG) priors to represent sparse sequences and employ Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques for parameter estimation. However, the discrete characteristics of the BG model induce computational bottlenecks, hindering efficient probability space exploration even with advanced sampler schemes. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an alternative MCMC framework that models sparse sequences using a Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) prior. By deriving effective Gibbs samplers for this prior, we show that the computational overhead of the BG model is eliminated by shifting the problem into a fully continuous-valued domain. Furthermore, we integrate both time and frequency domain constraints on the convolving sequences. The efficacy of our proposed methods is validated through extensive simulations, alongside a characterization of the computational advantages over existing BG-based approaches.

Metal-poor stars are crucial for comprehending galaxy formation and evolution, as remnants of early mergers may be detectable within their abundance distributions, kinematics, and orbital parameters. This study presents preliminary findings from an ongoing chemo-kinematic analysis of metal-poor stars ([Fe/H] $\leq$ -1.0) observed by the GALAH spectroscopic survey. We employed unsupervised machine learning techniques, including hierarchical clustering, k-means analysis, and correlation matrices, to examine both chemical and orbital data. Our ultimate objective is to identify the most effective method for distinguishing between various Galactic stellar populations and groups resulting from merger events, such as Gaia-Enceladus and Sequoia.

The spectral/hp element method integrates the geometric adaptability of traditional h-type finite elements with the advantageous numerical characteristics of spectral approaches by utilizing high-order piecewise polynomial basis functions on relatively coarse meshes. Spatial discretization relies on orthogonal polynomials, such as Legendre or Chebyshev polynomials, which are adapted to ensure C0-continuity. Both theoretically and computationally, elevating the polynomial degree $p$ yields high-precision results and rapid convergence; specifically, under suitable regularity conditions, the method achieves exponential error reduction between numerical approximations and exact solutions. This approach has been extensively utilized in numerous simulation studies covering both fundamental and practical engineering flows. The present paper outlines the formulation of the spectral/hp element method and reviews its application in computational fluid dynamics, with a specific emphasis on transitional flows and ocean engineering. Additionally, the discussion addresses key challenges that must be resolved to extend the method's applicability to more complex scientific and engineering problems.

This study examines the survival probability and the distribution of first-passage times for a system consisting of a periodic array of absorbing pillars situated between two parallel reflecting boundaries. By approximating the periodic unit cell as a cylindrical tube with a single pillar, we derive an exact solution to the modified Helmholtz equation using a mode matching technique. This solution yields the Laplace transform of the survival probability and elucidates the influence of key geometric parameters, including the pillar's height and radius, the spacing between pillars, and the distance between the confining planes. The model facilitates an analysis of various asymptotic regimes within the first-passage time probability density. Specifically, in scenarios where the distance between confining planes is large, we demonstrate that the mean first-passage time significantly exceeds the typical time, rendering it uninformative. Furthermore, we highlight the limitations of the capacitance approximation regarding the principal eigenvalue of the Laplace operator. Finally, the discussion includes practical implications and directions for future research.

The transmission speed of any physical signal, whether classical or quantum, is fundamentally capped by the speed of light, meaning quantum mechanics cannot accelerate localized information transfer. However, when information is not confined to the sender but is instead distributed across space via spatial coherence, the speed of information acquisition and transmission can be enhanced. This study demonstrates a quantum mechanical advantage in transmitting globally encoded information, proving a quadratic improvement in information speed for quantum carriers compared to classical ones. These findings are particularly applicable to scenarios involving information sources with limited power, such as those restricted by a finite number of transmittable signals per unit of time.

We address a two-stage robust facility location problem set within a metric space, characterized by uncertain demand. In the initial stage, the decision-maker determines the integer supply units for each facility to meet potentially varying second-stage demands, aiming to minimize the total cost comprising first-stage supply expenses and the worst-case cost of satisfying second-stage demands across all scenarios. Second-stage actions are limited strictly to assignment decisions, with no option to augment supply capacity dynamically. This constraint distinguishes our approach from prior research on two-stage robust facility location and set covering issues. We adopt an implicit uncertainty model defined by an exponential number of demand scenarios, bounded by a parameter $k$ representing the maximum number of second-stage clients. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that limiting second-stage assignment decisions to a fixed, static fractional allocation for each client—regardless of the specific scenario—yields an $O(\log k/\log \log k)$-approximation for the problem. Furthermore, the optimal static assignment can be computed efficiently, thereby securing this approximation guarantee.

This work examines the actions of the Möbius group on two sub-populations within the solvable chimera model introduced by Abrams et al. The global dynamics are described by two coupled Watanabe-Strogatz systems, one corresponding to each sub-population. Initially, the asymptotic behavior of the model appears straightforward; for example, in stable chimera states, oscillator distributions seem to undergo simple rotations after a sufficiently long time. However, a deeper analysis reveals that the dynamics are more complex than what is apparent from the evolution of oscillator phase densities. To obtain a complete understanding, one must study the dynamics on the transformation group acting on these densities. This approach highlights the influence of a "hidden" variable that remains invisible at the macroscopic level.

We utilized COVID-Twitter-BERT and RoBERTa models to detect informative tweets related to COVID-19, further enhancing their robustness through adversarial training. The ensemble combining these two models achieved a positive class F1-score of 0.9096 on the test data from the WNUT-2020 Task 2, securing the first position on the leaderboard. Additionally, ensembles of models trained with adversarial training yielded comparable results.

We report the identification of a remarkable dimming episode in a cool supergiant star, designated M51-DS1, located in the nearby spiral galaxy M51. Discovered during a Hubble Space Telescope (HST) survey targeting failed supernovae, this supergiant, likely linked to a young stellar population ($\lesssim6$ Myr), exhibited significant variability (amplitude $\Delta F814W\approx0.7$ mag) across HST images taken from 1995 to 2016. Subsequently, the star dimmed by more than 2 mag in the $F814W$ band between late 2017 and mid-2019. However, follow-up observations in 2021 revealed a rebrightening, which excludes the possibility of a failed supernova. Before this event, the star was luminous and red, with an absolute magnitude $M_{F814W}\lesssim-7.6$ mag and colors ranging from $F606W-F814W=1.9$ to $2.2$ mag. Modeling of the pre-dimming spectral energy distribution suggests a highly reddened, very luminous star ($\log[L/L_{\odot}] = 5.4$ - $5.7$) with an effective temperature of $\approx3700$ - $4700$ K, consistent with a cool yellow or post-red supergiant (RSG) having an initial mass of $\approx26$ - $40$ $M_{\odot}$. Nevertheless, uncertainties regarding local and circumstellar extinction remain; near-IR data are also compatible with an RSG that is cooler ($T_{\mathrm{eff}}\lesssim3700$ K) and slightly less luminous ($\log[L/L_{\odot}] = 5.2$ - $5.3$), implying an initial mass of $\approx19$ - $22$ $M_{\odot}$. In both scenarios, the dimming is likely caused by an unusual episode of enhanced mass loss that temporarily obscured the star, possibly representing an extreme version of the 2019–2020 "Great Dimming" of Betelgeuse. Given growing evidence that massive evolved stars frequently display variability that mimics disappearing stars, our findings underscore a significant challenge in distinguishing true failed supernovae.

This study develops and estimates a dynamic equilibrium model analyzing how risky entrepreneurs make borrowing and saving choices within both formal and local informal credit markets. Households can access an exogenous formal credit market alongside an informal one where interest rates are endogenously set by local credit supply and demand. Using Thai village data from a period of formal credit market expansion, the model is estimated via Simulated Maximum Likelihood. The results indicate that a 49% drop in fixed costs led to a 36% rise in the share of households borrowing formally, while doubling collateralized borrowing limits reduced informal interest rates by 24%. The findings show that while more productive households gained from expanded borrowing access, less productive households suffered welfare losses due to reduced savings opportunities. Overall, the net gains are smaller than those predicted by models that ignore the informal credit market.

Literature reports indicate that energy levels in thin Bi films on surfaces are equidistant, implying a harmonic oscillator framework; however, this conclusion is not definitive. Given that measurements are limited to finite energy ranges and possess inherent uncertainty, alternative explanations exist. This study reviews isospectral potentials and evaluates the validity of the harmonic oscillator hypothesis against recent data. Initially, we model experimental findings using a harmonic oscillator to derive realistic parameters for the quantum well's size and depth. Subsequently, we employ the shift-operator method to compute anharmonic, non-polynomial potentials capable of generating partially equidistant spectra, discussing various potential types and their modeling utility. Furthermore, utilizing $n$th order perturbation theory, we demonstrate that polynomial potentials cannot yield exactly equidistant eigenenergies unless they correspond to the harmonic oscillator potential. Ultimately, this work aims to delineate the limits of conclusions that can be drawn from experimental determinations of energy levels.

This study investigates striped patterns generated by magnetic impurities in optimally doped d-wave superconductors (DSCs) through self-consistent solutions of the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations using the $t-t^{\prime }-U-V$ model. For a single impurity, the stable ground state manifests as a modulated checkerboard pattern. In the presence of two impurities, stripe-like structures within the order parameters emerge as a result of impurity pinning. Both the DSC and charge order modulations exhibit a period of four lattice constants (4$a$), which is exactly half the period observed in the coexisting spin order. Notably, introducing three or more impurities can lead to more intricate striped morphologies driven by quantum interference. Future experimental investigations involving magnetic impurity substitution in DSCs are anticipated to validate these findings.

The 331 model incorporating right-handed neutrinos is re-evaluated to study CP violation within the quark sector. Following spontaneous symmetry breaking, the masses and physical properties of the particle spectrum are determined. The fermion content of this model is expanded to include exotic quarks possessing known electric charges and masses set at the TeV scale. These exotic quarks generate additional CP violation through their interactions with Standard Model quarks, mediated by charged gauge bosons also fixed at the TeV scale. A new discrete $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetry is implemented to ensure the stability of a scalar field, making it a viable dark matter candidate. This scalar field couples at tree level to the $Z^{\prime}$ gauge boson, which serves as a dark matter portal. Calculations of the relic density for this scalar field yield a mass solution consistent with observed dark matter limits. Finally, the allowed region in the parameter space of dark matter mass versus $Z^{\prime}$ mass is derived, incorporating constraints from the PANDAX2017, XENON1T(2t.y), and LUX experiments.

A primary limitation of the Volume-Of-Fluid (VOF) method is that the disintegration of thin liquid films or filaments is predominantly driven by numerical artifacts rather than physical mechanisms. In the VOF framework, film rupture typically occurs when thickness approaches the grid scale; consequently, refining the mesh delays these breakup events. Furthermore, because the method conserves mass, the fragmentation of thin filaments generates numerous droplets, preventing the desired convergence of the droplet size distribution even as the grid is refined. This study introduces a new algorithm designed to identify and perforate slender structures. First, thin films or ligaments are detected by calculating quadratic moments of an indicator derived from the volume fraction. A multiscale strategy enables the selection of a critical film thickness that remains independent of mesh resolution. Subsequently, breakup is triggered by creating holes in the films before their thickness diminishes to the grid size. We demonstrate that this approach enhances the convergence of both the droplet size distribution and enstrophy with respect to grid refinement.

This study re-examines the $L_\mu - L_\tau$ extension of the Standard Model, which offers a potential explanation for both anomalies observed in semileptonic $B$ meson decays and the characteristics of dark matter (DM). When the kinetic mixing between the $Z^\prime$ gauge boson and the photon is zero at high energy scales, the region of parameter space favored by $B$ anomalies is ruled out due to conflicting low-energy flavor constraints and strict limits from direct DM detection experiments; this occurs because such a setup induces significant DM-SM couplings during low-momentum scattering. However, the situation changes if the kinetic mixing vanishes at low energy scales instead. In this alternative scenario, the scattering rate for low-momentum DM is sufficiently suppressed, thereby relaxing constraints from direct detection experiments. Consequently, we identify a reopened parameter space region where both the $B$ anomalies and the nature of dark matter can be explained simultaneously.

This study presents a label-free assessment of drug responses in human breast (MCF-7) and colon (HT-29) cancer spheroids using dynamic optical coherence tomography (OCT). MCF-7 spheroids were treated with paclitaxel (PTX/Taxol), while HT-29 spheroids received SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan. Treatments were administered at concentrations of 0 (control), 0.1, 1, and 10 μM over durations of 1, 3, and 6 days. Samples underwent repeated raster scanning, and two dynamic OCT algorithms—logarithmic intensity variance (LIV) and late OCT correlation decay speed (OCDSl)—were employed to visualize tissue and cellular dynamics. Both LIV and OCDSl imaging clearly revealed and quantitatively analyzed distinct drug response patterns for each spheroid type. For both cell types, structural degradation alongside reductions in LIV and OCDSl values were observed, suggesting potentially different mechanisms of drug action. These findings indicate that dynamic OCT is effective for highlighting drug response patterns and facilitating anti-cancer drug testing.

In recent years, deep unfolding networks (DUNs) have gained significant attention for image compressed sensing (CS) by integrating optimization solvers with deep neural networks. However, current DUNs face two main challenges: 1) the reliance on simple stacked convolutional networks for each iteration restricts model expressiveness, and 2) fixed hyperparameters after training reduce adaptability across different input contents. To address these issues, this paper introduces FHDUN, a novel fast hierarchical DUN based on the unfolded Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA). FHDUN employs a hierarchical unfolding architecture to jointly extract richer contextual priors from multi-scale spaces. Additionally, a series of hyperparameter generation networks are incorporated to dynamically optimize hyperparameters based on input content, thereby enhancing adaptability. Leveraging the acceleration inherent in FISTA, an embedded acceleration module reduces the required iterative loops by over 50% compared to recent DUNs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FHDUN outperforms existing state-of-the-art CS methods while requiring fewer iterations.

Recurrent networks represent some of the most potent and promising artificial neural network algorithms for handling sequential data, including natural language, audio, and time series. Unlike conventional feed-forward networks, recurrent networks possess an inherent feedback loop that enables the storage of temporal context and the propagation of state information across entire event sequences. This capability facilitates state-of-the-art performance in critical tasks such as language modeling, stock market forecasting, image captioning, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. Nevertheless, training fully connected recurrent networks and managing gradient flow remain complex challenges. Numerous studies have been conducted to address these limitations. This article aims to provide a concise overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and practical techniques for training fully recurrent neural networks. This review was conducted as part of the IPO studio software module titled "Multiple Object Tracking."

How are symmetries encoded in quasicrystals? To compensate for the absence of translational symmetry, quasicrystals exhibit non-crystallographic symmetries, such as 5- and 8-fold rotations in two-dimensional space. This phenomenon originates from the extended crystallographic group of high-dimensional lattices projected onto physical space via a finite perpendicular window. A key question is how the translation operation in high dimensions influences quasicrystals following this projection. We address this by demonstrating that a simple translation within a four-dimensional hypercubic lattice fully determines a specific rotational symmetry in two-dimensional quasicrystals. Specifically, by categorizing translations in this four-dimensional lattice, we discuss new types of quasicrystals featuring 2, 4, and 8-fold rotational symmetries. This reveals that translation in a high-dimensional lattice is intrinsically linked to the rotational symmetry of the resulting quasicrystal. Furthermore, in the context of multi-frequency driven systems, this approach offers a novel method for discovering new quasicrystals projected from high-dimensional Floquet lattices.

Human brain activity relies on electrochemical processes that require invasive methods for direct measurement. Consequently, medical and research fields rely on non-invasive techniques to capture quantities such as electric potential differences (EEG) and magnetic flux density (MEG). However, reconstructing neuronal currents from these measurements constitutes a severely ill-posed problem, despite its visualization being a primary tool in cognitive neuroscience. In this work, we develop a novel vector-valued spline method grounded in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This approach utilizes an isotropic multiple-shell model for head geometry and a quasi-static framework for electro-magnetic modeling. Building upon previous spline techniques, the proposed method retains classical minimum norm properties while minimizing the (infinite-dimensional) Tikhonov-Phillips functional to address the instability inherent in the inverse problem. This optimization simplifies to solving a finite-dimensional system of linear equations without discarding information, yielding a unique solution that accounts for the fact that only the harmonic and solenoidal components of the current influence the measurements. Furthermore, we demonstrate a convergence result, proving that the vector spline solution approaches the data generator as the number of measurements grows. When applied to synthetic test cases with irregularly distributed data, the method performs effectively. Numerical results, incorporating various parameter choice strategies and testing both with and without added Gaussian white noise, show that vector splines outperform earlier scalar spline approaches in terms of normalized root mean square error. Finally, the method produces results consistent with physiological expectations when applied to real-world data.

This work introduces GCIS, a grammar compression algorithm founded on Nong et al.'s 2009 induced suffix sorting algorithm (SAIS). The method leverages the factorization generated by SAIS during suffix sorting, substituting these factors with non-terminals within a context-free grammar. This process is applied recursively to the resulting shorter sequence of non-terminals. The final grammar is encoded by utilizing redundancies, specifically common prefixes among rule right-hand sides, which are ordered according to SAIS. GCIS achieves competitive compression ratios with minimal time and space requirements. Experimental results on diverse text sizes—from moderate to very large and repetitive—demonstrate that GCIS outperforms established compressors like Gzip, 7-Zip, and RePair, the latter being the benchmark for grammar compression. Although GCIS exhibits slower decompression speeds, grammar-based compressors offer the advantage of direct substring access in compressed form without full decompression. GCIS proves to be a strong candidate for this use case, competing effectively with other RePair-based solutions. Furthermore, the algorithm's inherent relationship with SAIS allows it to serve as an efficient intermediate structure for constructing the suffix array and LCP array during text decompression.

This study extends the concept of classical parking functions by incorporating randomness and a novel parking protocol, drawing inspiration from the paper "Parking Functions: Choose your own adventure" by Carlson, Christensen, Harris, Jones, and Rodríguez (arXiv:2001.04817). Key findings include a proof that the likelihood of forming a parking function from an $n$-length preference vector remains constant regardless of the probabilistic parameter $p$. The analysis further investigates the characteristics of preference vectors conditioned on being parking functions and examines how $p$ influences these properties. A focal point of the research is the case where $p=1/2$, which reveals a sharp transition in specific parking statistics. Additionally, the paper outlines several combinatorial implications of the proposed protocol, notably offering a combinatorial interpretation for the array in OEIS A220884 as the expected count of preference sequences with specific traits regarding occupied spots; this resolves an open problem by Novelli and Thibon from 2020 (arXiv:1209.5959). Finally, the results are linked to other weighted phenomena in combinatorics, alongside suggestions for future research avenues.

This paper investigates two distinct tiling patterns for a honeycomb strip, deriving closed-form expressions for their counts. Additionally, we establish new identities linking tribonacci numbers, Padovan numbers, and Narayana's cow sequence, alongside offering combinatorial proofs for several existing identities concerning these numerical series.

Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) represents a framework for adapting predictive models to downstream optimization tasks by leveraging their outputs to enhance task performance. A primary technical hurdle in DFL is the need to differentiate through the optimization process, a challenge complicated by discontinuous solutions and other complexities. Previous research has largely circumvented this by manually designing task-specific surrogate functions that yield informative gradients upon differentiation. However, the necessity of handcrafting these surrogates for every new task restricts the applicability of DFL. Furthermore, these surrogates often lack convexity guarantees, potentially causing the training of predictive models to converge to suboptimal local minima. This paper eliminates the reliance on surrogates entirely, opting instead to learn loss functions that encode task-specific information. To our knowledge, this is the first method to completely substitute the optimization component of decision-focused learning with an automatically learned loss function. Our approach (a) relies solely on access to a black-box oracle capable of solving the optimization problem, ensuring broad generalizability, and (b) is convex by design, facilitating straightforward optimization. We assess our method across three resource allocation problems from existing literature, demonstrating that it surpasses standard learning approaches that ignore task structure in all three domains and also outperforms hand-crafted surrogates found in prior work.

Developers often rely on APIs to execute specific tasks, such as processing Excel files or handling text files line-by-line. Automatically generating API usage sequences from natural language queries could significantly accelerate and streamline application development. Current methods typically employ information retrieval models to match API sequences with queries or utilize RNN-based encoder-decoder architectures. However, the retrieval approach treats queries and API names merely as bags of words, failing to grasp query semantics deeply. Meanwhile, the RNN approach encodes user queries into fixed-length context vectors using a neural language model to generate sequences.

This study investigates the efficacy of recent Pre-trained Transformer Models (PTMs) for API learning tasks. These models are unsupervisedly trained on vast natural language corpora to capture contextual knowledge and have proven successful in various NLP domains, yet their potential for API sequence generation remains unexplored. We empirically evaluate PTMs using a dataset comprising 7 million annotations sourced from GitHub, which was also utilized for assessing prior methods. Our findings indicate that PTMs produce more accurate API sequences, outperforming related techniques by approximately 11%. Additionally, we identified two distinct tokenization strategies that substantially enhance PTM performance in this specific task.

We establish several findings regarding the magnitude and configuration of subsets within vector spaces over finite fields that contain an excessive number of mutually orthogonal vector pairs. Specifically, we derive precise finite field analogues of a Rosenfeld theorem and an approximate version of a Berlekamp theorem.

Quadratic algebras extend the concept of Lie algebras and encompass the symmetry algebras of two-dimensional second-order superintegrable systems as specific instances. These superintegrable systems represent exactly solvable models within both classical and quantum mechanics. Distinct superintegrable systems and their associated quadratic algebras can be linked through geometric contractions derived from B\^ocher contractions of the conformal Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(4,\mathbb{C})$ onto itself. In two dimensions, quadratic algebras are categorized into nondegenerate and degenerate types; geometrically, these correspond to three-parameter and one-parameter potentials, respectively. In a prior study, we classified all abstract parameter-free nondegenerate quadratic algebras using canonical forms, identified which could be realized as quadratic algebras for 2D nondegenerate superintegrable systems on constant curvature and Darboux spaces, and examined the connection between B\^ocher contractions of these systems and abstract contractions of free quadratic algebras. This paper conducts a parallel investigation into abstract parameter-free degenerate quadratic algebras and their potential geometric realizations. We demonstrate that the only free degenerate quadratic algebras constructible in phase space are those originating from superintegrability. Furthermore, we classify all B\^ocher contractions linking degenerate superintegrable systems and, independently, all abstract contractions connecting free degenerate quadratic algebras. Finally, we highlight the rare exceptions where abstract contractions fail to be realized by geometric B\^ocher contractions.

This work addresses the challenge of \emph{timely} private information retrieval (PIR) across $N$ non-colluding servers that hold replicated and continuously updated data. The objective is for a user to retrieve one of $M$ messages without revealing the message's identity, ensuring the retrieval process is executed promptly. To quantify this timeliness, we employ the \emph{age of information} (AoI) metric. Notably, under conditions of \emph{asymmetric traffic}, the timely PIR problem is equivalent to minimizing AoI while satisfying PIR constraints. We explicitly derive the optimal tradeoff between PIR rate and AoI (specifically peak or average AoI) for the scenario where $N=2$ and $M=3$. Additionally, we offer structural insights applicable to the general case with arbitrary $N$ and $M$.

This paper introduces novel analytic formulas, expressed through hypergeometric functions, for the one-loop contributions to the Higgs decay channel $H \rightarrow Z\gamma$. The computations adhere to the tensor one-loop reduction methodology outlined by A.~I.~Davydychev in Phys.\ Lett.\ B {\bf 263} (1991) 107. Furthermore, this work presents one-loop form factors for the decay process that remain valid across any arbitrary space-time dimension $d$ for the first time.

The rapid surge in real-world video data, characterized by highly diverse and evolving topics, naturally results in a long-tailed distribution across categories, highlighting the necessity for Video Long-Tailed Recognition (VLTR). This study addresses the challenges inherent in VLTR and outlines strategies to overcome them. Specifically, we tackle three key issues: (1) the impracticality of retraining entire models to extract high-quality features, (2) the high cost associated with acquiring frame-level labels, and (3) the bias introduced by long-tailed data distributions. However, most current VLTR approaches rely on image-level features from pretrained models that are often task-irrelevant, while learning from video-level labels. To address these limitations regarding (1) task-irrelevant features and (2) video-level labels, we introduce two complementary learnable feature aggregators. The learnable layers within each aggregator generate task-relevant representations, while the aggregators themselves synthesize snippet-wise knowledge into comprehensive video representations. Furthermore, we propose Minority-Oriented Vicinity Expansion (MOVE), which explicitly incorporates class frequency to approximate vicinity distributions, thereby mitigating (3) biased training. By integrating these solutions, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the large-scale VideoLT dataset and the synthetically imbalanced Imbalanced-MiniKinetics200. When utilizing VideoLT features from ResNet-50, our approach delivers 18% and 58% relative improvements over the previous state-of-the-art for head and tail classes, respectively.

We examine a relative projective line defined over a Berkovich space with base $\mathbf{Z}$, where the fibers correspond to projective lines over various valued fields, along with a polarized endomorphism acting on this line. We demonstrate that the family of equilibrium measures, derived from restricting the endomorphism to individual fibers, exhibits continuity. Furthermore, this conclusion remains valid if $\mathbf{Z}$ is substituted by a complete valued field, a hybrid field, a discrete valuation ring, or the ring of integers of a number field.

We introduce, for the first time, an off-shell supersymmetric continuous spin gauge theory within 4-dimensional Minkowski spacetime, utilizing both constrained and unconstrained Lagrangian frameworks. Extending existing on-shell descriptions [1], we utilize an auxiliary field to ensure the algebra of supersymmetry transformations closes off-shell. The resulting 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ massless continuous spin supermultiplet is defined as $(\mathrm{\Phi}, \mathrm{H} \,; \mathrm{\Psi})$, consisting of complex scalar continuous spin gauge fields $\mathrm{\Phi}$ (dynamical) and $\mathrm{H}$ (non-dynamical), alongside a Dirac continuous spin gauge field $\mathrm{\Psi}$. Specifically, we show that in a limiting case, this off-shell continuous spin supermultiplet yields the off-shell supersymmetry transformations for the known scalar supermultiplet $(\,{\scriptstyle 0}\,,\, {\scriptstyle 1/2}\,)$, as well as all integer-spin supermultiplets $(\,s\,,\, s\, {\scriptstyle +\, 1/2}\,)$ with $s\geqslant1$, and all half-integer spin supermultiplets $(\, s\, {\scriptstyle -\, 1/2}\,,\, s \,\,)$ with $s\geqslant1$.

For a prime $p$, a finite $p$-group of order $p^n$ is said to have maximal class when its nilpotency class is $n-1$. This work investigates saturated fusion systems defined on maximal class $p$-groups, specifically those with order $p^k$ where $k \ge 4$. According to the Alperin-Goldschmidt Theorem for fusion systems, such a system $\mathcal{F}$ is completely characterized by the automorphisms of the group $S$ itself and its $\mathcal{F}$-essential subgroups. An $\mathcal{F}$-essential subgroup is termed an "$\mathcal{F}$-pearl" if it has order $p^2$ or is non-abelian of order $p^3$. A central technical result establishes that every $\mathcal{F}$-essential subgroup is either an $\mathcal{F}$-pearl or one of two specific maximal subgroups of $S$. While this finding is straightforward for $p=2$ (based on work by Díaz, Ruiz, and Viruel) and $p=3$ (via Parker and Semeraro), the primary contribution addresses the case $p \ge 5$, where a classification of maximal class $p$-groups is currently unavailable. The main theorem characterizes all reduced saturated fusion systems on maximal class $p$-groups of order at least $p^4$, deriving from two broader theorems that classify systems on exceptional and non-exceptional groups without restriction to the reduced case. Consequently, a key corollary states that if $O_p(\mathcal{F}) = 1$, then $\mathcal{F}$ must contain $\mathcal{F}$-pearls, or $S$ must be isomorphic to a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\mathrm{G}_2(p)$ for $p \ge 5$, with the corresponding fusion systems explicitly detailed.

The recently introduced Collaborative Metric Learning (CML) framework has garnered significant attention within recommendation systems due to its simplicity and efficacy. Conventional CML research primarily relies on \textit{negative sampling} to mitigate the computational costs associated with pairwise calculations. However, through theoretical analysis, this work reveals that negative sampling induces a biased estimation of generalization error. Specifically, we demonstrate that sampling-based CML introduces a bias term into the generalization bound, measured by the per-user \textit{Total Variance} (TV) between the distribution created by negative sampling and the true data distribution. Consequently, minimizing the sampling-based CML loss function fails to guarantee a low generalization error, even with ample training data. Furthermore, we show that this bias term disappears when negative sampling is omitted. Inspired by these findings, we propose \textit{Sampling-Free Collaborative Metric Learning} (SFCML), an efficient alternative that eliminates sampling bias in practice. Finally, extensive experiments across seven benchmark datasets validate the superiority of our proposed algorithm.

Existing research has laid a robust groundwork for neural set functions, developing architectures that maintain essential set properties like permutation invariance. Later studies emphasized the benefits of Mini-Batch Consistency (MBC), which enables sequential processing of set partitions—such as streaming data chunks—while ensuring output consistency, though few MBC-compatible architectures currently exist. We introduce a framework capable of transforming any non-MBC model into an MBC-compliant one, thereby allowing all set functions to operate universally within an MBC context (UMBC). Furthermore, we develop a Monte Carlo dropout approach facilitated by our framework, enabling uncertainty estimation on streaming sets without requiring full-set visibility. We validate UMBC through theoretical proofs, unit tests, and extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments on Gaussian data, point cloud classification (both clean and corrupted), and amortized clustering on ImageNet. Additionally, we examine the probabilistic calibration of set-functions under test-time distributional shifts. Our findings highlight the practical value of universal mini-batch consistency and reveal that our dropout strategy enhances uncertainty calibration.

We investigate quantum phases and transitions within a one-dimensional interacting fermion system characterized by a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis (LSM) type anomaly. Specifically, we demonstrate a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem showing that inversion symmetry mandates any symmetry-preserving gapped ground state to take the form of a Kitaev chain. Alternatively, applying the Jordan-Wigner transformation reveals that this system corresponds to a spin model where gapped ground states must spontaneously break either inversion symmetry or the Ising symmetry linked to fermion parity. Utilizing analytical techniques and variational matrix product state simulations, we construct a phase diagram and analyze the critical behaviors of the resulting quantum phase transitions through entanglement entropy, energy variance, and finite-size scaling of order parameters. Notably, we identify continuous transitions between distinct ordered phases that lie outside the Ginzburg-Landau-Wilson framework, analogous to deconfined quantum critical points in two spatial dimensions. We establish that this one-dimensional deconfined criticality is governed by Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, allowing us to extract the Luttinger parameter and critical exponents. Furthermore, we discover a gapless phase separating two ordered phases that cannot be characterized by a U(1) Luttinger liquid.

As a local, unitary, and Lorentz-invariant quantum field theory, the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics maintains symmetry under the combined operations of Charge, Parity, and Time Reversal (CPT). This principle necessitates that particles and antiparticles share identical magnitudes for their fundamental properties. Recent Penning-trap experiments have subjected these CPT tenets to rigorous testing by measuring mass asymmetries between matter and antimatter. Building on these developments, this study contrasts CPT invariance constraints derived from kaon systems with those obtained from Penning-trap measurements. By employing a straightforward yet robust argument regarding the mass decomposition of hadrons, we demonstrate that limits on quark-antiquark mass differences inferred from kaon oscillations vastly exceed the sensitivity of Penning-trap experiments. Furthermore, we explore potential reinterpretations of the Standard Model should these precision experiments reveal CPT violation. Our analysis indicates that such scenarios are generally highly unconventional and demand substantial fine-tuning to uphold micro-causality.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Computer Vision (CV) have recently reached the forefront of technological advancement, with innovations emerging daily. When combined with increasingly capable drone systems, these technologies have driven a heightened demand for autonomous surveillance. This overview introduces the Automated Logging Drone (ALD) project and illustrates potential applications, highlighting how the system can be further refined and enhanced with additional features.

Information retrieval (IR) systems commonly employ ranked lists to display content deemed relevant to user needs. Fairness has emerged as a critical dimension in evaluating these rankings, complementing established metrics of accuracy and utility to offer a more comprehensive view of system behavior. Although numerous metrics have recently been introduced to quantify the fairness of rankings—especially concerning specific groups of content providers—there remains a significant lack of comparative analysis within the IR domain. Consequently, practitioners have limited guidance on selecting appropriate fairness metrics for specific scenarios or understanding the degree of agreement among these metrics when applied to real-world data. This paper addresses this gap by presenting several existing fair ranking metrics within a unified notation to facilitate a direct comparison of their assumptions, objectives, and design choices. We further conduct an empirical evaluation of these metrics across multiple datasets that encompass both search and recommendation tasks.

The evolution of protoplanetary disks is constrained by analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha and discuss their implications for population studies of classical T Tauri stars. Comparing mass accretion rates derived from fitting UV-to-near-infrared spectra in recent X-Shooter observations with those measured 11 years prior using the same instrument, we find that XX Cha exhibits nearly 2 dex of accretion variability between 2010 and 2021. While the specific timescales of this variation remain uncertain, XX Cha demonstrates extreme accretion variability for a classical T Tauri star. If such behavior is common among these stars, potentially occurring on timescales longer than previously investigated, it could significantly influence disk evolution models constrained by the observed spread in accretion rates. Finally, we note that earlier studies relying on spectral lines to assess accretion variability may have underestimated the fluctuations in certain targets.

This research examines service scheduling within a slotted framework where agents arrive with requests following a Bernoulli process and must depart within two slots. Service costs are quadratic relative to service rates, and quadratic waiting costs are also factored in. The problems are modeled as average cost Markov decision processes (MDPs). Although the system is linear with quadratic costs, it features state-dependent control and a non-standard cost function structure when fixed waiting costs are considered, which complicates optimization. We characterize the optimal policy and demonstrate that it is linearly dependent on the system state. Additionally, we analyze scenarios where agents make independent scheduling decisions to minimize their own costs, framing these as stochastic games. We derive the Nash equilibria for these games. To handle unknown system parameters, we propose an estimation algorithm and establish bounds on the difference between the actual incurred cost and the cost calculated using estimated parameters.

It is widely accepted that topological superconductivity, a previously unattainable state of quantum matter, can be realized by inducing superconductivity within topological materials. In pursuit of these superconductors, certain topological insulators (such as Bi$_2$Se$_3$) have been successfully converted into superconductors via metal-ion intercalation (e.g., Cu, Pd, Sr, Nb). Superconductivity can also be triggered in topological materials through applied pressure, as demonstrated by a pressure-induced superconducting phase in Bi$_2$Se$_3$. However, none of these approaches have yielded conclusive evidence of topological superconductivity. This review explores an alternative method for inducing superconductivity in non-superconducting topological materials: creating a mesoscopic interface between the material and a non-superconducting, normal metallic tip, which results in a superconducting state at the interface. This phenomenon, termed the tip-induced superconducting (TISC) phase, was first observed in 2014 on Cd$_3$As$_2$ at IISER Mohali, India, and has since been identified in numerous other topological materials. Because the TISC phase exists only within a confined region under a mesoscopic point contact, conventional bulk characterization techniques are ineffective for detecting or confirming it. Conversely, this point contact geometry is optimal for probing temperature- and magnetic field-dependent superconducting energy gaps and critical currents. We will examine the experimental signatures necessary to confirm superconductivity when standard "text-book" detection methods are inapplicable, and subsequently review various systems where a TISC phase can be realized.

Mechanical topological insulators have garnered significant interest in recent years. Typically, topologically protected modes are predicted for infinite, periodic phononic systems by analyzing bulk-band dispersion and Berry curvature to estimate metrics like group velocity and energy isolation. However, real-world systems are finite in size and driven by excitations with finite bandwidths, as dictated by the Fourier uncertainty principle. Consequently, dynamics predicted for ideal infinite systems at a specific frequency diverge from those observed in practical systems driven across a finite bandwidth. In this study, we show that propagating topological waves in a valley Hall system can be understood through the underlying linear degenerate modal basis. We demonstrate that these waves consist of a small subset of closely spaced modes with nontrivial phase differences, allowing for the creation of analytical reduced-order models that accurately represent topological wave behavior. This insight is then used to predict the true group velocity of propagating topological waves relative to input signal bandwidth and frequency by aligning individual mode contributions with the supercell dispersion diagram of a semi-infinite system. Furthermore, we show that damped topological waves can be analyzed using a modal superposition framework, employing the damped modal spectrum to characterize variations in group velocity and predict edge-to-bulk transitions. Thus, this work establishes a framework for accurately characterizing both undamped and damped topological wave propagation in quantum valley Hall systems using classical dynamics.

This study investigates how individuals adjust income redistribution in contexts where the extent to which luck influences opportunities and results is uncertain. We surveyed a representative U.S. sample, asking participants to make redistribution choices after observing worker outcomes and distinguishing whether luck amplified effort ("lucky opportunities") or directly determined income ("lucky outcomes"). The results show that people reduce their redistribution efforts and become less responsive to shifts in luck's significance when "lucky opportunities" are present. These insights inform models aiming to predict redistribution attitudes and offer an explanation for the divergence between laboratory findings on support for redistribution and actual U.S. inequality trends.

While training classifiers with fairness constraints like group fairness helps regularize prediction disparities between groups, these constraints often fail to generalize during evaluation. To enhance the generalizability of fair classifiers, we introduce "fair mixup," a novel data augmentation technique that enforces fairness by regularizing models along interpolated paths between groups. Leveraging mixup, a robust augmentation method, we generate these interpolates to achieve fairness. Our analysis and empirical results across tabular, vision, and language benchmarks demonstrate that fair mixup significantly improves the generalization of both accuracy and fairness metrics.

This study introduces a Spiking Convolutional Neural Network (SCNN) featuring retinal foveal-pit inspired Difference of Gaussian filters and rank-order encoding. The model was trained using a backpropagation variant adapted for spiking neurons via the Nengo library. Performance was assessed on two public datasets for digit and vehicle recognition, achieving up to 90% accuracy with cross-entropy loss. This represents a significant improvement over the 57% accuracy obtained by classification without neural filtering. Overall, this proof-of-concept demonstrates that biologically plausible filtering effectively handles noisy inputs, such as those in the vehicle recognition task. Future work will enhance the SCNN by incorporating lateral inhibition-based redundancy reduction before rank-ordering to further boost classification accuracy.

We introduce a syntactic dependency treebank featuring naturalistic English data from both children and child-directed speech (MacWhinney, 2000). Our annotation scheme primarily adheres to the Universal Dependencies (UD) guidelines (Zeman et al., 2022), incorporating specific extensions to capture lexical and syntactic features distinct to conversational speech as opposed to written text. Compared to other UD-style spoken treebanks and existing dependency corpora focused on child-parent interactions, our dataset is significantly larger, comprising 44,744 utterances and 233,907 words. It includes speech from 10 children spanning a broad age range of 18 to 66 months. This resource allows us to investigate: (1) the performance of state-of-the-art dependency parsers designed for written domains when applied to spontaneous conversations involving different interlocutors; and (2) the correlation between parser accuracy and a child's developmental stage. To address these inquiries, we are currently conducting comprehensive evaluations using both graph-based and transition-based parsers with varied hyperparameter settings, trained on three distinct types of out-of-domain written text: news articles, tweets, and learner data.

In production natural language understanding (NLU) systems, users' changing requirements drive the addition of new features, which are represented by new symbols in the meaning space. This expansion necessitates more training data, leading to continuously growing datasets. We introduce the first systematic study of this incremental symbol learning context. Our findings expose a critical issue in developing broad-coverage NLU systems: as the overall dataset expands, performance on newly introduced symbols often declines unless their specific training data is proportionally increased, indicating that learning new symbols becomes harder with larger datasets. We demonstrate that this pattern persists across multiple mainstream models on two prevalent NLU tasks: intent recognition and semantic parsing. While class imbalance is not the only factor, we identify that the trend is closely linked to a phenomenon we term "source signal dilution," where robust lexical indicators for new symbols are weakened as the dataset grows. Selectively removing training examples to mitigate this dilution frequently reverses the negative trend, highlighting the heavy dependence of current neural NLU models on straightforward lexical cues. The code, models, and data are accessible at https://aka.ms/nlu-incremental-symbol-learning.

We situate Musial and Sagher's notion of HK$_r$-integration within the framework of approximate Henstock--Kurzweil integration theory. By imposing the condition that the indefinite HK$_r$-integral must be continuous, the concept becomes a subset of the classical Denjoy--Khintchine integral. Furthermore, we offer a direct proof establishing that this inclusion is strict.

This study introduces a reduced-bias estimator for the Extreme Value Index (EVI) tailored to Pareto-type (heavy-tailed) distributions, derived via the weighted least squares approach.
