This study introduces a straightforward technique utilizing a thin-film contact thermometer based on the phase-change material Ge2Sb2Te5 to accurately map thermal contours from the nanoscale to the microscale. Ge2Sb2Te5 exhibits a crystalline transition at its glass transition temperature (Tg), accompanied by significant shifts in electrical conductivity, optical reflectivity, and density. Using this method, we mapped the surface temperatures of both a nanowire and an embedded micro-heater on the same chip, successfully capturing temperature contours that differ in scale by three orders of magnitude. Thanks to the continuous nature of the thin film, the technique achieves a spatial resolution as fine as 20 nanometers.

The $n$-vector spin model, for which the self-avoiding walk (SAW) represents a special case in the $n \rightarrow 0$ limit, possesses an upper critical dimension of four spatial dimensions. We employed an irreversible Berretti-Sokal algorithm to simulate SAWs on 4D hypercubic lattices with periodic boundary conditions, reaching a linear size of $L=768$. By analyzing the unwrapped end-to-end distance, we determined the critical fugacity to be $z_c= 0.147 \, 622 \, 380(2)$, a value that improves upon the previous result ($z_c=0.147 \, 622 \, 3(1)$) by a factor of 50. This enhanced precision allows for a systematic investigation of the finite-size scaling behavior of 4D SAW across various physical quantities. Our findings reveal that near $z_c$, the free energy scaling comprises both a Gaussian fixed-point term and a component responsible for multiplicative logarithmic corrections. Specifically, we observe that the critical magnetic susceptibility and specific heat diverge logarithmically as $\chi \sim L^2 (\ln L)^{2 \hat{y}_h}$ and $C \sim (\ln L)^{2 \hat{y}_t}$, respectively. The resulting logarithmic exponents, $\hat{y}_h=0.252(2)$ and $\hat{y}_t=0.25(2)$, align excellently with field-theoretical predictions of $\hat{y}_h=\hat{y}_t=1/4$. Consequently, these results offer robust support for the recently proposed finite-size scaling form applicable to O$(n)$ universality classes at four dimensions.

This paper presents a multi-classifier approach designed to enhance concatenate-based neural networks like ResNet and DenseNet, specifically to reduce the burden on the final classifier. We detail the classifier architecture, which aggregates features generated between network stages, and specify the constituent layers and activation functions used to compute individual classification scores. Instead of Softmax, we employ L2 normalization to derive these scores. Additionally, we identify conditions that facilitate improved convergence. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed classifiers significantly boost accuracy, outperforming original models in both efficacy and convergence speed. Furthermore, the method is highly versatile, applicable to all classification tasks involving concatenate-designed network architectures.

Matrix product states are established as efficient tools for determining ground states of local, gapped Hamiltonians, especially within one-dimensional systems. We present the multi-targeted density matrix renormalization group approach, which operates on a bundled matrix product state containing numerous excitations. By employing a block or banded Lanczos algorithm, this method enables the simultaneous variational optimization of the entire excitation bundle. Demonstrations on a Heisenberg model and other relevant scenarios show that a vast number of excitations can be achieved with a low bond dimension, yielding highly reliable local observables across the chain.

Comparisons of high-precision optical atomic clocks \cite{Ludlow2015} are crucial for advancing fundamental physics tests \cite{Safronova2018}, relativistic geodesy \cite{McGrew2018, Grotti2018, Delva2019}, and the forthcoming redefinition of the SI second \cite{Riehle2018}. However, the utility of these applications is currently constrained by the statistical precision achievable in interspecies comparison measurements. The stability of individual clocks is capped by the finite coherence time of the optical local oscillator (OLO), which dictates the maximum duration for atomic interrogation. In this work, we experimentally validate differential spectroscopy \cite{Hume2016}, a comparison protocol that allows interrogation to extend beyond the OLO coherence time. By phase-coherently linking a zero-dead-time (ZDT) \cite{Schioppo2017} ytterbium optical lattice clock with an Al$^+$ single-ion clock through an optical frequency comb and executing synchronized Ramsey spectroscopy, we achieve an improvement in comparison instability of nearly an order of magnitude compared to our prior results \cite{network2020frequency}. To the best of our knowledge, this establishes the most stable interspecies clock comparison reported to date.

This study examines the development, accretion, and expansion of supermassive black holes during the early universe. Utilizing the Bondi accretion model, the accretion rate ${\dot M}$ is determined. Beginning with seed black holes of approximately $10^2-10^3M_{\odot}$, super-Eddington accretion drives the Bondi rate to evolve these into supermassive black holes weighing between $10^9-10^{10}M_{\odot}$ within a young quasar lifespan of roughly $10^5-10^6$ years.

Currently, target recognition techniques are vital across numerous domains. However, existing methods relying on target image data are hindered by image quality issues and the time required for image reconstruction. This paper introduces a new imaging-free target recognition approach that integrates ghost imaging (GI) with generative adversarial networks (GAN). Leveraging the GI mechanism, the target is illuminated by a sequence of random speckles, while a resolution-less bucket detector captures the echo signals. These continuous detection results form a bucket signal array, which serves as the training sample for the GAN. Subsequently, a conditional GAN maps the bucket signal array to specific target categories. In practical deployment, the speckle sequence used during training illuminates the target, and the resulting bucket signal array is fed into the GAN for recognition. This proposed method addresses the limitations of traditional image-based recognition techniques and offers a degree of turbulence resistance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the method achieves promising performance.

Although log-linear models are widely used in empirical studies, managing zeros in the dependent variable remains a contentious problem. This paper resolves this ambiguity by introducing a novel class of estimators known as iterated Ordinary Least Squares (iOLS), which handles the logarithm of zero. This family encompasses standard methods like log-linear and Poisson regressions, provides multiple computational benefits, and aligns with the proper implementation of the $\log(Y+1)$ transformation. The approach is further extended to accommodate endogenous regressors (i2SLS) and resolves frequent limitations associated with Poisson models, including the inclusion of numerous fixed effects. Additionally, specification tests are developed to assist researchers in choosing among competing estimators. The proposed methods are demonstrated through numerical simulations and replications of seminal studies.

Generating a diverse set of feasible solutions by efficiently sampling from constraint manifolds remains a fundamental challenge. We address scenarios where a problem is factored, meaning the underlying nonlinear program is decomposed into differentiable equality and inequality constraints, each relying on a specific subset of variables. Such decomposable problems are central to efficient and robust sequential robot manipulation planning. Both naive sequential conditional sampling of individual variables and fully joint sampling of all variables simultaneously (e.g., via optimization) can prove highly inefficient and non-robust. Consequently, we introduce a novel framework designed to learn how to decompose the overall problem into smaller, sequential sampling tasks. Specifically, we employ Monte-Carlo Tree Search to learn optimal assignment orders for variable subsets, thereby minimizing the computational time required to generate feasible full samples. This approach enables the efficient computation of diverse, valid robot configurations for mode-switches in sequential manipulation tasks, serving as waypoints for subsequent trajectory optimization or sampling-based motion planning algorithms. We demonstrate that the learning method rapidly converges to the optimal sampling strategy for a given problem, outperforming user-defined orderings or fully joint optimization while delivering superior sample diversity.

We provide a significantly more concise and straightforward proof of H. B. Neumann's result, which is briefly stated as follows: For any well-ordered subset, A, within a totally ordered semigroup, the collection of all products formed by any finite number of elements from A is also well-ordered. Furthermore, for every element t, only a finite number of such products equal t.

This study investigates sea surface synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images through an inverse problem framework designed to enhance Radon domain information for precise ship wake detection. This enhancement is realized by emphasizing linear features within the imagery. To address the inverse problem, we introduce a penalty function that integrates the dual-tree complex wavelet transform (DT-CWT) with a non-convex Cauchy penalty. Utilizing the forward-backward (FB) splitting algorithm to solve this problem yields improved images in the Radon domain. The proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art ship wake detection techniques across various performance metrics. Notably, detection accuracy for ship wakes in SAR images spanning different frequency bands and spatial resolutions exceeds 90%, representing a 7% improvement over the second-best method.

This study establishes two findings regarding uniform confidence intervals for the tail index and extreme quantile. Initially, we demonstrate that creating a length-optimal confidence interval with accurate uniform coverage across a local non-parametric family of tail distributions is unfeasible. Consequently, acknowledging this limitation, we develop honest confidence intervals that ensure uniform validity by integrating the worst-case bias within the local non-parametric framework. We apply this methodology to both simulated data and an actual dataset of National Vital Statistics sourced from the National Center for Health Statistics.

Salient object detection in optical remote sensing images (RSI-SOD) presents a significant challenge due to the intricate scale and shape variations, as well as the unpredictability of object locations. While current SOD techniques perform adequately on natural scenes, they struggle to adapt to the unique characteristics of remote sensing imagery. To address this, we introduce AGNet, a novel Attention Guided Network designed for RSI-SOD, which comprises a position enhancement stage and a detail refinement stage. The position enhancement stage leverages both semantic and contextual attention modules to precisely estimate the approximate locations of salient objects. Subsequently, the detail refinement stage employs a self-refinement module to iteratively improve predictions, guided by both attention and reverse attention mechanisms. Furthermore, a hybrid loss function is utilized during training to enhance model performance across pixel, regional, and statistical dimensions. Comprehensive experiments on two leading benchmarks confirm that AGNet delivers competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art methods. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/NuaaYH/AGNet.

Gaussian Process (GP)-based surrogate models possess the intrinsic ability to handle anomalies stemming from sparse, missing, or inconsistent data within the digital twin's modeling and simulation modules, particularly for accident-tolerant fuel (ATF) concepts. However, GPs struggle with accuracy when high-fidelity experimental data is scarce and face difficulties approximating functions with more than 20 dimensions. Additionally, noise, erroneous observations, and outliers pose significant challenges for advanced ATF applications, especially since governing differential equations for long-term ATF candidates are empirical and data availability remains a constraint. In contrast, Physics-Informed Multi-Fidelity Kriging (MFK) proves valuable for identifying and predicting necessary material properties, offering a robust solution for scenarios involving low-fidelity physics and limited high-fidelity data—conditions typical of ATF development. This chapter examines the MFK methodology and applies it to experimental thermal conductivity data for ATF, demonstrating its superiority over conventional Kriging when dealing with small datasets. The resulting mathematical models facilitate seamless integration with subsequent analyses, such as uncertainty quantification and sensitivity studies, making them suitable for fundamental research and diverse product development sectors. Ultimately, this chapter aims to demonstrate the capability of MFK surrogates when embedded within a digital twin system for ATF applications.

As plug-in electric vehicle (PEV) adoption grows and fast-charging capabilities advance, these vehicles significantly disrupt power delivery systems. Their high power density and impulsive nature render traditional load impact assessment techniques inadequate. This study introduces an integrated approach to evaluate the long-term effects of PEV charging on the temporal response and depreciation of grid assets within sub-transmission and distribution networks (below 69kV). Unlike conventional methods, this proposed framework incorporates dynamical system models of grid assets into Time-Series (TS) analysis and utilizes Monte-Carlo simulations to capture stochastic charging patterns, offering a more robust and precise assessment. Furthermore, the formulation for the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of grid assets is recalibrated under this methodology. Ultimately, the findings will empower utilities to quantify both capital and operational costs associated with grid assets across various levels of PEV penetration and over any specified time horizon.

This study introduces a new framework designed to forecast traffic flow bandwidth proactively. A prevalent challenge in contemporary network management systems is the temporal gap between the moment a decision is made and when countermeasures are executed, during which network conditions change. This approach transforms raw traffic packets into feature-rich flows and utilizes machine learning models—specifically Decision Trees, Random Forests, XGBoost, and Deep Neural Networks—to predict bandwidth for the next time interval for each flow. By supplying these predictions to management systems rather than relying on current bandwidth data, operators can make decisions based on a more accurate representation of the network state. The framework was tested on 981,774 flows across 15 distinct time windows ranging from 0.03s to 4s. Results demonstrate that Random Forest outperforms other models in reliability and accuracy, reducing mean absolute error by 19.73% and root mean square error by 18.00% compared to using current bandwidth. Consequently, the experimental evidence suggests that this framework enables network management systems to make better-informed decisions by leveraging predicted network states.

This paper proposes integrating coinduction into the computational framework of natural language understanding (NLU). We contend that this approach will establish a foundation for more realistic, computationally robust, and scalable models of dialogue, syntax, and semantics. Because bottom-up, inductively built semantic and syntactic structures are fragile and fail to adequately capture the meaning of lengthy sentences or authentic dialogues, NLU requires a new theoretical basis. Coinduction, which relies on top-down constraints, has proven effective in designing operating systems and programming languages. Furthermore, its implicit presence in text mining, machine translation, and certain models of intensionality and modality suggests its viability, a point supported by high-level formalizations presented in this article.

Since coinduction and induction can coexist, they offer a unified conceptual model and common language for NLU research, an opportunity particularly evident in studies of compositionality. The article illustrates several instances where induction and coinduction appear together in natural language processing. We argue that the individual limitations of each method can be mitigated in empirical contexts through their combination, though an open challenge remains in developing a theory governing their joint application.

This study examines the structural characteristics and dynamical stability of C$_3$N$_2$ with hydrogen as an interstitial guest. The analysis employed density functional theory (DFT) via the Quantum Espresso software, utilizing the generalized gradient approximation. Our results indicate that the presence of the guest atom barely alters the host's lattice constant, confirming that C$_3$N$_2$ retains its dynamical stability upon the insertion of a single atom into its cage-like framework. Furthermore, we determined that the guest's vibrational modes are low-frequency, which consequently reduces the acoustic bandwidth of C$_3$N$_2$.

Time-frequency (T-F) analysis and processing of nonstationary signals are frequently conducted in the T-F domain derived from the discrete Gabor transform (DGT). However, windowing effects in the DGT result in a spread representation that can compromise analysis and processing performance. To achieve better localization, researchers have explored sparsity-aware techniques based on the $\ell_1$-norm; yet, these approaches require discretizing continuous parameters onto a grid, leading to model mismatch. This paper introduces a method for estimating sparse T-F representations using the atomic norm, which facilitates sparse optimization without the need to discretize continuous parameters. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method yields a sparser T-F representation compared to conventional approaches.

This paper examines the Coupon Collector's Problem, a scenario where a collector seeks to gather a complete set of items—such as coupons, baseball cards, or other trinkets found within chip bags or soda bottles. Since the specific item obtained is unknown until the product is opened, the study investigates the mean and variance of $N$, the number of items required to finish the collection. Various analytical methods are employed, some applicable only when all coupons have equal collection probabilities, while others extend to unequal probabilities, reflecting real-world conditions more accurately.

The unresolved connection between electron-phonon ($e$-ph) interactions and charge-density-wave (CDW) order in bismuthate-based high-temperature superconductors is investigated here through advanced, nonperturbative hybrid quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the parent material, BaBiO$_3$. Our approach incorporates Bi $6s$ and O $2p_\sigma$ orbitals and couples them to Bi-O bond-stretching optical phonons by modulating the Bi-O hopping integral. Leveraging recently developed, efficient, and scalable algorithms, we conducted simulations on extensive three-dimensional clusters containing up to 4000 orbitals. These simulations utilized model parameters derived directly from $\textit{ab initio}$ electronic structure calculations, alongside a physically grounded phonon energy of $\hbar\Omega_0 = 60 \ {\rm meV}$. Our findings indicate that coupling to these bond-stretching modes is adequate to explain the observed CDW transition, even though density functional theory predicts a relatively weak dimensionless coupling for this branch. Furthermore, the transition does not align with the weak-coupling Peierls framework, despite the noninteracting Fermi surface being well-nested at the CDW ordering vector. These results underscore the complexity of $e$-ph interactions that are off-diagonal in orbital space and imply that such interactions are pivotal in defining the bismuthate phase diagram.

Various mechanisms can boost dark matter, generating signals distinct from those of standard dark matter. We demonstrate that the semi-annihilation process $\chi\chi\to\bar{\chi}\nu$ yields signatures unique to itself and different from other semi-annihilation or conventional dark matter annihilation scenarios. Since the boosted dark matter resulting from this semi-annihilation is interpreted as a high-energy neutrino, the combined flux of the dark matter and the associated neutrino creates two peaks in the energy spectrum near the dark matter mass. Furthermore, we show that future large-volume neutrino observatories, such as the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment and Hyper-Kamiokande, will be capable of detecting both particles produced within the Sun.

Theoretical analysis reveals that a specific class of asymptotically stable skin-effect lattices, characterized by nonnormal Toeplitz operators $H_g$ with a positive "numerical ordinate" $\omega(H_g)>0$, exhibits a phenomenon of topological directed amplification for certain initial perturbations. Although global dissipation is present, the nonnormal temporal evolution displays a counterintuitive transient phase where edge states are amplified; this behavior, which diverges sharply from the asymptotic limit, remains hidden in standard spectral analyses of $H_g$. The "pseudospectrum" offers a consistent framework to describe this effect, while the {\it Kreiss constant} provides a quantitative measure of the maximum power amplification. Furthermore, the singular value decomposition of the propagator $e^{-i H_g t}$ yields a method to identify the optimal initial condition for achieving peak amplification power. Finally, it is predicted that the interaction between nonnormality and nonlinearity within a skin-effect laser array could enable narrow-emission spectra alongside scalable, stable output power.

This paper leverages the value function reformulation of bilevel optimization to derive duality results. Our methodology extends Fenchel-Lagrange-type duality to address this specific problem class. We begin by reviewing standard duality theorems to demonstrate their inapplicability here. Subsequently, utilizing the concept of partial calmness, we prove both weak and strong duality theorems, specifically examining Lagrange, Fenchel-Lagrange, and Toland-Fenchel-Lagrange duality frameworks under appropriate conditions. Third, by applying regularization techniques to the bilevel program, we derive sufficient conditions for strong duality under a generalized Slater-type condition, doing so without requiring convexity or the partial calmness assumption. Finally, we establish a strong duality result for bilevel optimization problems featuring geometric constraints, even in the absence of the Slater condition.

This study presents the design and analysis of a coupled discontinuous Galerkin finite element method and boundary element method for solving the three-dimensional Helmholtz equation with variable coefficients. The coupling is implemented using a mortar variable linked to an impedance trace along a smooth interface. The resulting method exhibits a block structure featuring nonsingular subblocks. We establish the quasi-optimality of both the $h$- and $p$-versions of the scheme, contingent upon a threshold condition regarding the approximability of the discrete spaces. A key component of this analysis is a newly developed discontinuous-to-continuous reconstruction operator designed for tetrahedral meshes with curved faces.

We introduce a method for simultaneously recovering the electromagnetic and acoustic material properties within a medium $\Omega$ by utilizing photo-acoustic pressure data recorded at a single boundary point of $\Omega$. This pressure, denoted as $p^{\star}\left(x, s, \omega \right)$, arises from plasmonic nanoparticles and depends on a fixed observation point $x \in \partial \Omega$, a time interval $s$, and a frequency band $\omega$. We demonstrate that this limited data is sufficient to determine the sound speed, mass density, and permittivity throughout $\Omega$. Specifically, analyzing the temporal behavior of the measured pressure allows us to estimate travel times to interior points; applying the eikonal equation then yields the acoustic propagation speed. Furthermore, we reconstruct the internal acoustic Green's function. By examining the singularities of this function, we derive integrals along geodesics of the logarithmic gradient of the mass density for internal points. Solving this internal integral-geometric problem enables us to recover the mass density distribution inside $\Omega$. Finally, by analyzing the frequency dependence of $p^{\star}\left(x, s, \omega \right)$, we identify plasmonic resonances to reconstruct the permittivity within the medium.

Imperfections in the ideal atomic structure of crystals significantly influence their properties, and the diffusion of these defects drives numerous microstructural transformations in solids. Yet, directly observing point defect diffusion remains challenging due to the difficulties in imaging non-periodic structures and the inherent timescales of the diffusion process. In this study, rather than capturing thermal diffusion, we utilize a 60 kV scanning transmission electron microscope to induce and track the migration of a divacancy within a graphene lattice. This beam-activated migration occurs on a timescale that enables us to record substantial portions of the defect's trajectory and structural evolution. By combining low-voltage operation with ultra-high vacuum conditions, we maintain defect stability across extended imaging sequences, achieving the first direct observation of point defect diffusion in a crystalline material.

This paper introduces a method for compiling the surface code into two-body parity measurements, referred to as "pair measurements," which are executed along the edges of a Cairo pentagonal tiling. The proposed circuit outperforms the previous approach by Chao et al. by reducing the number of pair measurements required per four-body stabilizer measurement from six to five, and decreasing the time steps per stabilizer round from ten to six. Through Monte Carlo sampling, I demonstrate that these optimizations raise the surface code's threshold when compiled into pair measurements from approximately 0.2% to 0.4%. Furthermore, at a physical gate error rate of 0.1%, the teraquop footprint improves from roughly 6,000 qubits to about 3,000 qubits. However, I also find that Chao et al.'s construction yields a smaller teraquop footprint for physical gate error rates below approximately 0.03%, a limitation in my approach caused by bidirectional hook errors. Additionally, when compared to the planar honeycomb code, this work notably narrows the performance gap between the surface code and the honeycomb code during pair measurement compilation; nevertheless, the honeycomb code remains more efficient, boasting a threshold of approximately 0.8% and a teraquop footprint of roughly 1,000 qubits at a 0.1% physical gate error rate.

Battleships is a traditional two-player board game originating from World War I. While numerous digital versions exist, they share significant limitations, particularly regarding fairness and their reliance on a third-party trust model. This paper presents an implementation of a fair, denial-of-service-resistant system where the honest winner receives their deposit immediately. The solution leverages a permissionless Blockchain capable of executing Turing-complete smart contracts.

Over the past few years, the expander decomposition technique has been instrumental in creating numerous graph algorithms, significantly advancing long-standing complexity limits. This powerful tool has fostered two prevailing beliefs within the community: (1) that most problems exhibit similar difficulty on worst-case graphs as they do on expanders, and (2) that expander decompositions hold the key to overcoming the remaining barriers in fine-grained complexity. This study aims to evaluate the validity of these claims across specific problems. To do so, we introduce the concept of worst-case-to-expander-case self-reductions and construct a series of such reductions for fundamental graph problems, thereby confirming belief (1) for instances like $k$-Clique, $4$-Cycle, Maximum Cardinality Matching, Vertex-Cover, and Minimum Dominating Set. Surprisingly, for the majority (though not all) of these problems, the proof relies on simple gadget reductions rather than expander decompositions; this demonstrates that the "hammer" of expander decomposition is often ineffective against these problems and refutes belief (2).

Forms are ubiquitous documents in daily life that convey substantial information through both their textual content and organizational layout. To enable the automatic processing of these forms, two essential steps following initial optical character recognition (OCR) are word grouping and relation extraction. Word grouping involves clustering words that constitute the same semantic entity, while relation extraction aims to identify connections between these entities. Although previous studies have addressed these as separate tasks, they are inherently correlated and mutually reinforcing. The grouping phase refines the representation of entities, while the linking phase provides feedback to improve grouping accuracy. Consequently, we extract multimodal features from both text and layout data to construct an end-to-end model using multitask learning, thereby integrating word grouping and relation extraction to boost performance in both areas. Our proposed method was evaluated on the FUNSD benchmark, a real-world, fully-annotated dataset of noisy scans, and extensive experiments confirm its effectiveness.

Non-native English speakers often face significant confusion during restaurant ordering processes, particularly at establishments like Subway, due to unfamiliarity with specific ingredient terms or proper nouns. To address this challenge, we developed a bilingual dialogue system that simultaneously supports Chinese (Mandarin) and English, allowing users to switch languages freely during the conversation. Specifically designed for Subway ordering, our system, named BilDOS, incorporates three core components: a Discriminator module that identifies the language of user input, a Translator module that converts non-English inputs into English, and a Dialogue Manager module that detects user intent, manages outliers by issuing clarification requests, maps detected intents and keywords to specific intent classes, tracks the current stage of the ordering process, prompts for necessary details, finalizes order information upon completion, and initiates an evaluation process once the interaction ends.

Quaternions, split quaternions, and hybrid numbers are established mathematical systems utilized for geometric modeling in both Euclidean and Lorentz spaces. These systems can be derived from quadratic forms. This article investigates the method for identifying the specific number system associated with any given quadratic form. Consequently, the study yields the corresponding bilinear form, vector product, skew-symmetric matrix, and rotation matrices for any such system.

Significant work has been undertaken to evaluate the benefits of acquiring additional decay-data measurements for the primary fission-product contributors to decay heat in neutron-irradiated fissile fuel and associated actinides using Total Absorption Gamma-ray Spectroscopy (TAGS/TAS) and Discrete Gamma-ray Spectroscopy (DGS). This review builds upon comparable efforts conducted under the OECD/WPEC-Subgroup 25 (2005-2007) and the International Atomic Energy Agency (2010, 2014), incorporating various highly pertinent TAGS measurements resulting from those assessments. We provide recommendations for new decay-data evaluations, alongside potential requirements for total absorption and discrete high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy studies encompassing roughly 120 fission products and several isomeric states.

This study examines two non-interacting two-level emitters weakly coupled to a one-dimensional non-linear wave guide. The wave guide's Kerr-like non-linearity supports, alongside a scattering continuum, a two-body bound state, thereby modeling a bath with a complex mode structure. By solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for emitters initially in excited states, we analyze their radiation dynamics. When the two-emitter energy is tuned to resonate with a two-body bound state, the observed dynamics span exponential decay, fractional populations, and Rabi oscillations. We further investigate how these dynamics depend on emitter detuning and separation distance. Approximate reduced Hilbert space formulations reveal effective interactions dependent on emitter separation and momentum, clarifying the physical mechanisms and highlighting features unique to the non-linear wave guide. Our theoretical results are applicable to various experimental platforms and can be tested with current technology. Additionally, these weak-coupling Schrödinger equation results offer essential insights for developing master equation approaches.

We assess the determinant of a matrix composed of elliptic hypergeometric terms, structured similarly to Sylvester matrices. While a hypergeometric evaluation for such matrices was previously established by Feng, Krattenthaler, and Xu within approximation theory, our work provides an elliptic extension incorporating two extra parameters alongside the standard base $q$ and nome $p$. Furthermore, we derive a transformation formula that converts an elliptic determinant into a scalar multiple of another, introducing two additional parameters. The proofs for both the evaluation and the transformation rely on an elliptic determinant lemma by Warnaar, as well as the application of two $C_n$ elliptic formulas that generalize Frenkel and Turaev's $_{10}V_9$ summation and $_{12}V_{11}$ transformation results, contributions by Warnaar, Rosengren, Rains, Coskun, and Gustafson.

This study analyzes and models the cholera epidemics that impacted South Sudan, the world's newest nation, during 2014 and 2015. South Sudan likely presents one of the most challenging environments for adapting deterministic mathematical cholera models, given its unstable socio-political climate, which significantly disrupts human mobility and sanitary conditions, thereby elevating the risk of major outbreaks. Although the static gravity model has limitations in capturing the chaotic human movement within South Sudan, the calibrated SIRB model—which utilizes the Ensemble Kalman Filter for data assimilation—successfully reproduces epidemic dynamics in counties with the highest infection rates. This demonstrates the methodology's potential for forecasting future outbreaks.

Although the instability of deep learning models is a well-established issue in the machine learning community, its impact on healthcare applications remains poorly understood. This study examines the stability of various model architectures trained on electronic health records, focusing on outpatient prediction tasks. Our findings reveal that repeated training runs of the same model on identical data can yield significantly different patient-level outcomes, despite global performance metrics remaining consistent. To address this, we introduce two metrics for quantifying the effects of training randomness and propose strategies to enhance model stability.

Spectro-astrometry was employed to examine the low-velocity component (LVC) of optical forbidden emission from the T Tauri stars RU Lupi and AS 205 N. Both objects also exhibit high-velocity forbidden emission (HVC), indicative of a jet. While AS 205 N displays a complex outflow system, RU Lupi shows an [O I] 6300 and [S II] 6716, 6731 LVC narrow component (NC) aligned with the HVC's position angle (PA) but possessing a distinct velocity gradient. Specifically, in RU Lupi, the displacement from the star along the rotation axis diminishes as velocity increases. Based on the NC's PA and velocity gradient, researchers infer that this component traces a wide-angle magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk wind, ruling out a photoevaporative wind. This conclusion aligns with prior spectro-astrometric findings regarding the CO fundamental line. The observed reduction in offset with increasing velocity suggests that the wind's height grows with the disk radius. Furthermore, this study provides one of the initial measurements of the spatial extent of the forbidden emission line LVC NC (approximately 40 au for RU Lupi in [S II] 6731 and [O I] 6300 lines; ~8 au in [S II] 6731) and offers the first direct confirmation that the LVC narrow component can trace an MHD disk wind.

The main goal of a safe navigation algorithm is to steer an object from its starting point to a destination while preventing collisions with obstacles along the route; effective obstacle avoidance strategies are essential for ensuring safety in dynamic settings. This report introduces three distinct strategies for safe navigation in such environments. The Biologically-Inspired Navigation Algorithm (BINA) excels in minimizing avoidance time, whereas the Equidistant Based Navigation Algorithm (ENA) successfully manages navigation tasks within uncertain dynamic conditions. Additionally, the Navigation Algorithm based on an Integrated Environment Representation (NAIER) enables objects to find safe paths through obstacles in unknown dynamic environments in a manner reminiscent of human behavior. Extensive simulations and experiments involving a real non-holonomic mobile robot validate the performance and characteristics of these proposed algorithms. Furthermore, the algorithms have been deployed on two real-world control systems: an intelligent wheelchair and a robotic hospital bed. Tests with SAM and Flexbed demonstrate that these algorithms effectively handle complex real-time scenarios. Notably, the proposed methods are cost-efficient and easy to implement in real-time applications. This paper also includes an additional study on a networked multi-robot formation building algorithm, proposing a constructive and straightforward decentralized control method for forming groups of objects with random initial positions. Moreover, the challenge of forming structures with anonymous objects is addressed. This randomized decentralized navigation algorithm guarantees convergence to a desired configuration with a probability of one.

Although not ancient, the history of the maximum-power heat engine efficiency formula has been turbulent. Over a decade after Curzon and Ahlborn published their seminal 1975 article, researchers rediscovered two earlier works from 1957 by Chambadal and Novikov. Subsequently, the name of Yvon emerged from a 1955 conference paper referencing this famous relation. Through a historical study of French books that were long out of print and never translated, this paper reveals that Henri B. Reitlinger actually first proposed this relation in 1929.

An explicit free basis is used to determine the first-order flex space of the bar-joint framework $G_P$ corresponding to a parallelogram tiling $P$. The findings are applied to braced parallelogram frameworks and quasicrystal frameworks linked to multigrids as defined by de Bruijn and Beenker. Specifically, the work characterizes rigid bracing patterns, identifies quasicrystal frameworks with finite-dimensional flex spaces, and establishes a zero mode spectrum.

Gossip protocols have been suggested as a resilient and efficient approach for spreading information across extensive networks. This paper introduces a compositional analysis method designed to examine formal probabilistic models of gossip protocols, which are defined within a simple probabilistic timed process calculus tailored for wireless sensor networks. We enhance this calculus with a simulation framework that enables the comparison of probabilistic protocols exhibiting similar behaviors within a defined tolerance. Utilizing this framework, we demonstrate several algebraic laws that prove highly effective for estimating the performance of gossip networks, covering scenarios with and without communication collisions, as well as randomized gossip networks. Our simulation theory represents an asymmetric variant of the weak bisimulation metric, retaining most characteristics of the original definition. However, this asymmetric version is especially well-suited for analyzing protocols where the systems in question are not approximately equivalent, such as gossip protocols.

Sensemaking and narrative are fundamentally intertwined concepts that explain how individuals comprehend their environment. Sensemaking involves organizing and linking current information with past knowledge and inferences, whereas narratives serve as essential structures created through this process to offer a more comprehensive view of the world than any single piece of information could provide. Both mechanisms are crucial for human interpretation and hold significant value for computational systems aiming to replicate these abilities. This paper examines theories of sensemaking and narrative regarding how people construct understanding from encountered data, along with the connections between these research areas. We emphasize visual storytelling as a specific computational task that can be improved by integrating sensemaking and narrative components. Furthermore, we outline our visual storytelling system that utilizes these approaches and present examples from its current implementation.

Creating assistive interfaces for robots that accept arbitrary, high-dimensional, and noisy inputs—such as webcam-captured eye gaze—poses significant challenges, particularly when no natural default interface exists to infer user intent. Reinforcement learning (RL) leveraging online user feedback offers a promising solution by allowing the system to adapt to individual users; however, this method often demands extensive human-in-the-loop data, especially when feedback is sparse. We introduce a hierarchical approach that learns efficiently from limited feedback by first using offline pre-training to construct a latent space of useful, high-level robot behaviors. This foundation allows the system to concentrate online feedback efforts on mapping user inputs to these high-level behaviors. Our core insight is that a pre-trained policy enables the system to extract more value from sparse rewards compared to a naive RL algorithm: it leverages successful task executions to retrospectively relabel unsuccessful ones, thereby inferring the user's intended actions. We validate this method through a user study involving 12 participants performing tasks in three simulated robotic manipulation scenarios (flipping light switches, opening a shelf door, and rotating a valve) using eye gaze via webcam. Results demonstrate that our approach successfully maps 128-dimensional gaze features to 7-dimensional joint torques from sparse rewards within under 10 minutes of online training. Furthermore, the method seamlessly accommodates diverse gaze strategies from users and adapts effectively to distributional shifts across inputs, tasks, and environments.

Let $\vee^k A$ denote the $k$-th symmetric tensor power of a matrix $A \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$. As established in \cite{IAM}, the normalized trace of $\vee^k A$ can be represented as an integral over the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{n}$ in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ (equipped with the normalized Euclidean surface measure $\sigma$) involving the $k$-th powers of $A$'s numerical values. This paper first leverages such an integral representation to define a family of unitarily invariant norms on $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, subsequently investigating their relationships with the Schatten-norms of $\vee^k A$. Furthermore, we establish a link between the analysis of symmetric gauge functions and complete symmetric polynomials. Finally, building upon the work of R. Bhatia and J. Holbrook (\cite{hol}) and insights from R. Bhatia regarding weakly unitarily invariant norms (\cite{bhatia}), we derive an explicit formula for the weakly unitarily invariant norm associated with the $L^4$-norm on $C(\mathbb{S}^{n})$. Our findings extend the results of Bhatia and Holbrook and offer a methodological framework for computing weakly unitarily invariant norms on $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ linked to $L^{2k}$-norms on $C(\mathbb{S}^{n})$.

Let $R$ be a ring and consider a left $R$-module $M$ possessing two direct sum decompositions, $M = A \oplus (\bigoplus_{i \in I} C_i)$ and $M = B \oplus (\bigoplus_{j \in J} D_j)$, where the submodules $A$, $B$, and each $D_j$ are finitely generated, while the index sets $I$ and $J$ may be infinite. We demonstrate that there exist finite subsets $I_0 \subseteq I$ and $J_0 \subseteq J$, along with a direct summand $Y$ of $\bigoplus_{i \in I_0} C_i$, such that $A \oplus Y = B \oplus (\bigoplus_{j \in J_0} D_j)$. Following this, we discuss potential generalizations of this finding, limitations thereof, and related inquiries.

Although Neural Network (NN) based image compression codecs have recently surpassed classic state-of-the-art methods like BPG (which relies on HEVC intra), they typically suffer from high computational complexity and restricted parallel processing capabilities. This study introduces a conditional separation principle designed to enhance parallelization and reduce computational demands within NN codecs. We propose the Conditional Color Separation (CCS) codec, which applies this principle by dividing image color components into primary and non-primary groups. Each group is processed independently using jointly trained networks. This methodology enables parallel processing of individual components, offers flexibility in channel selection, and significantly lowers overall complexity. Compared to our baseline model against BPG, the CCS codec achieves over 40% memory reduction, 2x faster encoding, and 22% faster decoding speeds, with merely a 4% loss in RGB PSNR (BD-rate).

We introduce a minimal equilateral triangular lattice framework used to derive electron and exciton band structures for semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenides. By explicitly accounting for exchange interactions, this model effectively spans the range from Wannier to Frenkel excitons. Single-particle contributions are derived from a nearest-neighbor tight-binding approach parameterized by effective mass and spin-orbit coupling. Direct-space solutions to the characteristic equation align qualitatively with first-principles calculations, demonstrating the limitations of the two-dimensional hydrogen model in describing the lowest-energy exciton bands. Furthermore, the model validates the absence of subshell degeneracy and indicates that the A-B exciton splitting is governed by both the electrostatic environment and spin-orbit interactions.

While most monocular depth sensing approaches rely on conventionally captured images that ignore scene content, animal eyes utilize rapid mechanical movements known as saccades to direct high-resolution foveal imaging toward specific areas. This paper introduces the SaccadeCam framework, which adaptively allocates resolution to regions of interest. We propose a self-supervised algorithm for this adaptive resolution and demonstrate end-to-end learning for monocular depth estimation, alongside preliminary results from a physical SaccadeCam hardware prototype.

Unique Assembly Verification (UAV) stands as one of the most foundational and extensively researched challenges in Tile Self-Assembly. This algorithmic inquiry determines whether a specific tile system assembles exclusively into a designated structure. The complexity of UAV within the 2-Handed Assembly Model (2HAM) at constant temperatures has remained an unresolved question since the model's inception. While it was previously established that the problem resides in the coNP class and falls within P at a temperature of one ($\tau=1$), its general complexity is known to be difficult for various model extensions, such as those involving a third dimension or variable temperatures, yet the core version persisted as an open problem.

In this study, we demonstrate that the UAV problem in the 2HAM remains computationally hard even at a low constant temperature of $\tau = 2$, thereby resolving a complexity question that has been open since 2013. Furthermore, our findings establish that UAV is coNP-complete in the staged self-assembly model with a single bin and stage (an issue open since 2007) and in the q-tile model (open since 2004). Our reduction relies on Monotone Planar 3-SAT with Neighboring Variable Pairs, a specialized NP-hard variant of 3SAT. We also present a positive result indicating that UAV can be solved in polynomial time if the target assembly is guaranteed to have a tree-shaped bond graph, meaning it contains no cycles. Specifically, we offer an $\mathcal{O}(n^5)$ algorithm for UAV on tree-bonded assemblies at a fixed temperature of 2, and an $\mathcal{O}(n^5\log \tau)$ algorithm when the temperature is provided as part of the input.

Commonsense knowledge (CSK) regarding concepts and their attributes is valuable for AI systems, including resilient chatbots. Earlier initiatives such as ConceptNet and TupleKB assembled extensive CSK datasets but were limited to Subject-Predicate-Object (SPO) triples featuring simple concepts for subjects and monolithic strings for predicates and objects. Furthermore, these prior efforts typically prioritized either precision or recall, rarely balancing both objectives. This paper introduces Ascent, a methodology for automatically constructing a large-scale CSK knowledge base that offers enhanced expressiveness and superior precision and recall compared to previous works. Ascent extends beyond standard triples by incorporating composite concepts through subgroups and aspects, as well as refining assertions with semantic facets to capture temporal and spatial validity and additional qualifiers. By combining open information extraction with targeted cleaning via language models, Ascent achieves a knowledge base of greater size and quality, as demonstrated by intrinsic evaluations. Extrinsic evaluations on question-answering tasks further highlight its advantages. Resources, including a web interface, data, and code, are available at https://ascent.mpi-inf.mpg.de/.

We extend the standard Dirac-Bloch equation framework, typically employed to calculate the nonlinear optical response of 2D materials under spatially uniform optical excitation, to accommodate structured light pulses. Specifically, we derive the general form of these equations for a spatially inhomogeneous field acting on graphene-like materials. As a practical demonstration of our approach, we explicitly analyze the interaction between angular momentum-carrying optical pulses and graphene.

We examine separable 2D discrete Schrödinger operators constructed from 1D almost Mathieu operators. For fixed Diophantine frequencies, we demonstrate that when the coupling is sufficiently small, the resulting spectrum forms an interval. This finding complements J. Bourgain's result, which showed that for fixed couplings, the spectrum exhibits gaps for certain Diophantine frequencies (specifically those with positive measure). Our findings extend to separable multidimensional discrete Schrödinger operators generated by 1D quasiperiodic operators, provided their potentials are analytic and their frequencies are Diophantine. The proof relies on analyzing the thickness of the spectrum of the almost Mathieu operator and applies the Newhouse Gap Lemma regarding sums of Cantor sets.

This work serves as the initial segment of a series focusing on the generalizations and applications of fundamental theorems within variational bifurcation theory. By employing parameterized splitting theorems from Morse theory, we extend several renowned bifurcation results for potential operators by relaxing standard differentiability requirements on the associated functionals. This approach facilitates the study of bifurcation in quasi-linear elliptic boundary value problems.

A significant advancement by Guth, Iosevich, Ou, and Wang (2019) regarding the Falconer distance problem establishes that for any compact set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$, a Hausdorff dimension exceeding $\frac{5}{4}$ ensures the distance set $\Delta(A)$ possesses positive Lebesgue measure. Shortly thereafter, Murphy, Petridis, Pham, Rudnev, and Stevens (2022) extended this finding to prime fields, demonstrating that for subsets $E\subset\mathbb{F}_p^2$ with cardinality $|E|\gg p^{5/4}$, a substantial number of points $x\in E$ exhibit at least $cp$ distinct distances. The primary objective of this paper is to generalize these results within a broad framework of pinned trees, drawing inspiration from the recent contributions of Ou and Taylor (2021).

Image resizing is a fundamental operation in image processing, with existing literature offering numerous methods that are typically specialized for either upscaling or downscaling. This paper addresses the problem on a continuous scale, independent of whether the target size is larger or smaller, by globally approximating the underlying continuous image using tensor product Lagrange polynomials interpolated at a grid of Chebyshev zeros of the first kind. This well-established approximation technique is widely utilized across various applications due to the optimal behavior of its associated Lebesgue constants. We demonstrate that Lagrange-Chebyshev interpolation is highly effective for resizing arbitrary digital images in both directions. Performance evaluations using SSIM and PSNR metrics reveal that the proposed method performs almost comparably to the classical Bicubic method during upscaling, with slightly superior results. However, in downscaling scenarios, it significantly outperforms both Bicubic and other recent approaches. Furthermore, for downscaling cases involving an odd scale factor, we provide an estimate of the mean squared error, proving it is theoretically zero in the absence of noise or initial artifacts; consequently, the PSNR becomes infinite and the SSIM reaches one.

Despite significant advancements in Video Instance Segmentation (VIS), existing methods often fail to generate masks with high-quality, precise boundary details. Additionally, predicted segmentations frequently exhibit temporal instability, indicating a lack of effective utilization of temporal consistency cues. This paper addresses these challenges by aiming to produce highly detailed and temporally stable mask predictions. We introduce the Video Mask Transfiner (VMT), which utilizes a highly efficient video transformer to extract fine-grained, high-resolution features. VMT identifies and clusters sparse, error-prone spatio-temporal regions within each tracklet, refining them through a combination of local and instance-level cues. Furthermore, we recognize that the coarse boundary annotations in the popular YouTube-VIS dataset are a primary bottleneck. Leveraging the VMT architecture, we develop an automated annotation refinement strategy based on iterative training and self-correction. To support the evaluation of high-quality mask predictions, we present the HQ-YTVIS dataset, which includes a manually re-annotated test set and our automatically refined training data. We evaluate VMT against recent state-of-the-art methods on the HQ-YTVIS, as well as the YouTube-VIS, OVIS, and BDD100K MOTS benchmarks. Experimental results clearly demonstrate the method's efficacy and effectiveness in segmenting complex and dynamic objects by capturing precise details.

We introduce classical and quantum algorithms grounded in spectral techniques to address a challenge in tensor principal component analysis. The proposed quantum approach delivers a quartic speedup alongside exponentially reduced space requirements compared to the fastest classical spectral method, and it offers a super-polynomial advantage over classical algorithms restricted to polynomial space. Our classical methods differ slightly from those recently detailed in Ref. 1; specifically, we achieve an enhanced recovery threshold and ensure functionality for both even and odd order tensors. These findings indicate that large-scale inference tasks represent a promising avenue for future quantum computing applications.

Radio orbital angular momentum (OAM) communications depend on precise alignment between transmit and receive beam directions. Consequently, a critical capability of OAM receivers is the reliable estimation of the angle of arrival (AoA) for multi-mode OAM beams. Addressing the constraints of current AoA estimation methods, this paper introduces a more practical approach that applies the Estimating Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariance Techniques (ESPRIT) algorithm multiple times to received training signals within both OAM and frequency domains. This proposed technique, termed the mode-frequency (M-F) multi-time (MT)-ESPRIT algorithm, significantly reduces misalignment errors in real-world OAM channels, enabling performance levels that closely match those of ideally aligned systems.

This study measures the production cross section of top quark pairs accompanied by a photon in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Utilizing a data set with an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS experiment during the LHC's 2016–2018 run, the analysis defines a fiducial region at the particle level. Event selection requires an isolated, high-energy lepton, at least three jets from quark hadronization (with at least one b-tagged jet), and an isolated photon. The inclusive fiducial $\mathrm{t\overline{t}}\gamma$ cross section, for photons with transverse momentum exceeding 20 GeV and pseudorapidity $|\eta| < 1.4442$, is determined to be $798 \pm 7$ (stat) $\pm 48$ (syst) fb, consistent with next-to-leading order standard model predictions. Additionally, differential cross sections are measured across various kinematic variables and analyzed within the standard model effective field theory (EFT) framework, yielding the current most stringent direct constraints on anomalous electromagnetic dipole moment interactions between the top quark and the photon.

The Hilbert metric serves as a distance measure for points contained within a convex body, extending the Cayley-Klein model of hyperbolic geometry to arbitrary convex sets and offering various applications in the study and manipulation of such bodies. This paper investigates the geometric and combinatorial characteristics of Voronoi diagrams formed by point sites under the Hilbert metric. For any convex polygon $K$ with $m$ edges, we introduce two algorithms—one randomized and one deterministic—to compute the Voronoi diagram of an $n$-point set within the Hilbert metric defined by $K$. The randomized approach achieves an expected time complexity of $O(m n + n (\log n)(\log m n))$, while the deterministic method operates in $O(m n \log n)$ time; both require $O(m n)$ space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the worst-case combinatorial complexity of these diagrams is $\Theta(m n)$.

Sparsely gated Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures have demonstrated compute-efficient scaling for multilingual machine translation, yet they suffer from severe overfitting on low-resource tasks. This work introduces effective regularization techniques—including dropout applied to MoE layers in EOM and FOM, Conditional MoE Routing, and Curriculum Learning—that mitigate overfitting and enhance low-resource performance without degrading results on high-resource tasks. Evaluated on a large-scale multilingual machine translation benchmark, these strategies yield approximately a +1 chrF++ gain for very low-resource language pairs. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the learned MoE routing mechanisms to better comprehend the impact of our regularization approaches and identify avenues for further improvement.

An ortho-unit polygon is defined as an orthogonal polygon whose vertices possess integer coordinates and whose edges all measure a length of one. This paper establishes that for any ortho-unit polygon with $n \geq 12$ vertices, it can be fully guarded using no more than $\lfloor \frac{n-4}{8} \rfloor$ guards.

We demonstrate that every spectral set in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2qr}$, where $p$, $q$, and $r$ are prime numbers, forms a tiling. By integrating this finding with a recent result by Malikiosis, we establish that Fuglede's conjecture is valid for $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2qr}$.

The Fermi liquid exhibits an emergent low-energy symmetry reflecting charge conservation at every momentum point on the Ferm surface. Else, Thorngren, and Senthil (ETS) recently proposed that this emergent symmetry possesses a distinct 't Hooft anomaly. We present a straightforward derivation of the ETS anomaly by leveraging the chiral anomaly of Weyl fermions.

We establish estimates for the Hessian of two smooth functions defined on the Grassmannian manifold. Utilizing these estimates, we derive curvature bounds for minimal submanifolds in Euclidean space through the Gauss map. Consequently, the Bernstein-type theorem previously established by Jost and the first author can be enhanced.

AT 2019avd is an enigmatic nuclear transient observed across infrared to soft X-ray wavelengths. The source exhibited two successive flares in the optical and infrared bands, with the second flare monitored by X-ray programs. UVOT/Swift photometry of this second flare identified two plateaus: one following the peak and another appearing approximately 240 days later. Concurrent NICER and XRT/Swift observations revealed two X-ray emission declines: one coinciding with the initial optical plateau and another occurring 70–90 days after the optical/UV decline. These findings suggest that the optical/UV emission was not primarily due to X-ray reprocessing. Additionally, a time lag of roughly 16–34 days between optical and UV signals indicates that the optical emission likely arises from UV reprocessing by gas located 0.1–0.3 parsecs away. We also report the first VLA and VLBA detections of the source at various frequencies and stages of the second flare. Radio band characteristics—including a steep spectrum transitioning to a late-time inverted spectrum, high brightness temperature, and a radio-loud state—suggest the formation of a nascent compact jet. Based on these multiwavelength properties, we propose that a tidal disruption event (TDE) triggered the black hole's activity at the first flare, leading to a super-Eddington accretion disk that settled into a sub-Eddington state by the end of the second flare, thereby enabling the launch of the radio jet.

**Context:** Software engineering education must prioritize empirical research methods to equip students with the field-based evidence that both researchers and practitioners depend on. Typically, the master's thesis represents the final and most practical application of this training within a student's academic journey.

**Problem:** Conducting thesis work in collaboration with industry demands a delicate equilibrium between academic and practical stakeholder concerns. While achieving high-impact empirical results within a standard thesis timeline is possible, it remains challenging; striving for practical industrial value often compromises academic rigor. Although methods like Design Science Research (DSR) offer a constructive approach, applying them successfully in thesis projects is consistently difficult.

**Principle Solution Idea:** DSR facilitates the necessary balance by accommodating both knowledge inquiries and design activities. However, there is a scarcity of guidance on implementing this method effectively within a master's thesis context. To address this, we supplement existing DSR descriptions with pragmatic advice drawn from our own experience, aimed at students, examiners, and supervisors in both academic and industrial sectors to support the execution of design science theses in industry collaborations.

**Method:** This paper utilizes the Design Science Research methodology itself. Drawing on an analysis of 12 design science theses completed over the past seven years, we identify common pitfalls and best practices by examining student-supervisor dynamics, supervisor-industry interactions, examiner feedback, and reviewer comments on resulting publications.

**Results:** We offer specific recommendations for defining research questions, organizing reports, and planning and executing empirical work alongside practitioners.

We develop a regular sampling theory for continuous frames with a unitary structure within the range of their analysis operator. This unitary structure corresponds to a unitary representation of a locally compact abelian group acting on a separable Hilbert space. The sampling process is defined using specific discrete convolution systems that extend conventional sampling frameworks, where "regular sampling" signifies that samples are acquired at a countable discrete subgroup.

The interaction between cellular proliferation and cell-cell communication is vital for the aggregation, expansion of bacterial colonies, and the self-organization of tissues. To explore this relationship, we examine the collective behavior of dividing chemotactic colonies by analyzing their large-scale, long-term dynamics using a renormalization group (RG) framework. Our analysis demonstrates that fluctuations at macroscopic scales generate a pertinent yet unconventional chemotactic interaction driven by polarity, even in the absence of such a mechanism at the microscopic level. This phenomenon arises from the combination of the established Keller–Segel (KS) chemotactic nonlinearity with cellular birth and death processes. At the one-loop level, the RG flow equations yield no stable fixed point. Furthermore, we establish a link between the dynamics studied here and the celebrated Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) equation featuring long-range correlated noise, suggesting the presence of a strong-coupling, nonperturbative fixed point.

We numerically examine free and self-interacting ultralight scalar fields surrounding black holes within the framework of General Relativity. Specifically, we analyze complex scalar fields $\Phi$ governed by a quartic potential $V \propto \lambda |\Phi|^4$, neglecting black hole spin to isolate the impact of self-interactions on boson clouds. Employing the spectral solver Kadath, we calculate quasi-equilibrium states of the dominant eigenmodes, accounting for their backreaction on the spacetime metric. For coupling constants in the range $-10^{-2} \lesssim \lambda \lesssim 10^{-2}$, we determine that the mass of the self-interacting cloud can reach approximately $70\%$ higher than that of a free cloud; however, the resulting backreaction on the metric remains minimal, at roughly $1\%$, due to the low density of these bosonic structures. Within this parameter regime, we identify approximate quadratic relationships between the cloud mass and $\lambda$, as well as between the scalar field amplitude and the coupling between these two variables. Conversely, for $\lambda$ values exceeding this range, the eigenfrequencies deviate significantly from the free-test-field inputs required for our numerical setup, rendering the results physically unreliable despite their mathematical convergence. This effectively delineates the limits of $\lambda$ where the free scalar field solution adequately approximates self-interacting configurations. Our study represents one of the initial nonperturbative investigations into self-interacting bosonic clouds around black holes, offering fresh insights into nonlinear regimes, resolving technical hurdles, and defining specific constraints. Furthermore, our findings serve as valuable inputs for fully dynamical numerical relativity simulations and future studies involving spinning black holes and real scalar fields.

This brief article provides explicit formulas for the roots of a quartic equation with four real solutions. While a general quartic root expression can be found on Wikipedia, this piece offers an optimized and more concise formula specifically for cases where all roots are real.

Extracting road networks from aerial and satellite imagery remains a persistent challenge. Current approaches typically rely on pixel-level segmentation followed by vectorization or iterative graph construction via next-move prediction; however, both methods suffer from significant limitations, including high computational demands and incomplete results. In contrast, we introduce a method that directly generates the final road graph in a single pass. Our approach integrates a Fully Convolutional Network to identify key features like intersections, dead ends, and turns with a Graph Neural Network that predicts connections between these nodes. This strategy offers greater efficiency than iterative techniques and streamlines training by eliminating the need for pre-defined starting locations while maintaining an end-to-end workflow. Evaluated on the RoadTracer dataset, our method achieves competitive performance and demonstrates superior speed compared to existing solutions, enabling the possibility of real-time processing on embedded devices during flight.

Offering clear, user-friendly rationales for recommendations can enhance comprehension of suggested items, improve system usability, and foster user trust. While natural language generation is a standard method for achieving this, prior research has predominantly relied on recurrent neural networks, leaving the potentially more powerful pre-trained Transformer models largely unexplored. A key challenge arises because user and item IDs, crucial identifiers in recommender systems, exist in a different semantic space than the words these pre-trained models were originally trained on; thus, effectively integrating these IDs remains a critical problem. Drawing inspiration from recent advances in prompt learning, we propose two approaches: replacing IDs with alternative words (discrete prompt learning) and directly injecting ID vectors into pre-trained models (continuous prompt learning). In the latter scenario, since ID vectors are randomly initialized while the model has been pre-trained on extensive corpora, they operate at different learning stages. To address this discrepancy, we introduce two training strategies: sequential tuning and using recommendation as regularization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our continuous prompt learning method, when equipped with these strategies, consistently surpasses strong baselines across three explainable recommendation datasets.

Generating realistic, long-term human motion sequences within real-world environments holds significant potential for various applications. However, existing scene-aware motion synthesis methods are often restricted by predefined target objects or positions, which curtails the variety of human-scene interactions in the resulting motions. This paper addresses the challenge of creating diverse, scene-aware human motions guided by specific action sequences. To accomplish this, we break down the diversity of such motions into three distinct dimensions: interaction diversity (such as sitting on various objects with different postures), path diversity (navigating to target locations via different routes), and motion diversity (exhibiting varied body movements during transit). Building on this factorized approach, we introduce a hierarchical framework where each sub-module specializes in modeling one of these aspects. We evaluate our framework using two demanding datasets for scene-aware human motion synthesis. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses previous approaches in both diversity and naturalness.

An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) operates as a supervised learning algorithm where parameters are refined through repeated iterations of processing inputs, comparing results against expected labels, and adjusting the parameters accordingly. Drawing inspiration from recent work by Boer and Kramer (2020), we explore a distinct scenario: what if an observer can monitor the evolution of ANN parameters across numerous iterations while remaining unaware of the underlying dataset? This situation might arise, for example, if an adversary intercepts a multi-party computation of ANN parameters, thereby gaining access to intermediate values. The central question is whether such an observer can construct a system of equations and solve it to reconstruct the original dataset.
We demonstrate that atomic polyadic algebras of infinite dimensions are fully representable.

In practical quantum information processing, measurement readout stages often suffer from noise that affects individual qubits as well as multiple qubits collectively, a phenomenon known as crosstalk. This study introduces a framework to mitigate both single-qubit and crosstalk measurement errors. The proposed protocol involves two stages: quantum pre-processing, which applies local unitary transformations prior to measurement, and classical post-processing, which adjusts the outcomes to recover noise-free data. These local unitaries are constructed by characterizing the noisy measurement apparatus using quantum detector tomography. We demonstrate that this protocol can suppress multi-qubit measurement error rates to the single-qubit level, reducing errors to the percent range. Implemented on the IBMQ Sydney platform, the protocol was applied to certify entanglement-generating circuits. Results confirm that the mitigation effectively eliminates measurement errors, enabling the efficient certification of these circuits.

While distributed algorithms offer greater flexibility than centralized approaches for resource allocation tasks, such as those in cyber-physical systems, their decentralized structure often exposes them to man-in-the-middle attacks, particularly during communication between price-taking agents and a central coordinator. To address this, we introduce a resilient strategy within the framework of primal-dual distributed optimization. We develop a robust optimization model that specifically addresses Byzantine attacks on the communication links between agents and the coordinator. Furthermore, we present a resilient primal-dual algorithm leveraging advanced robust statistics techniques. Analysis demonstrates that this algorithm converges to a neighborhood of the robust optimization solution, with the neighborhood's radius scaling proportionally to the fraction of compromised communication channels.

This study extends Buchert's averaged equations, originally presented in *Gen. Rel. Grav.* 32, 105 (2000) and *Gen. Rel. Grav.* 33, 1381 (2001), to the LRS class II dust model by averaging the entirety of the Einstein equations rather than solely their trace component. We derive the corresponding averaged equations and examine the influence of backreaction on expansion and shear scalars within an approximate LTB framework. Finally, we suggest a method to close the resulting system of averaged equations.

The advent of electronic health records (EHR) offers a way to complement costly and logistically challenging randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with accessible real-world evidence. This study leverages EHR data to build synthetic control arms for single-arm trials that lack a control group. We introduce a novel nonparametric Bayesian common atoms mixture model capable of identifying equivalent population strata within both the EHR and the treatment arm. By resampling the EHR data, we generate patient populations that mirror those in the single-arm trial; this resampling is executed using a density-free importance sampling approach. With a synthetic control arm established, treatment effect inference can be performed using standard RCT methods, or alternatively, through straightforward model-based inference enabled by our proposed Bayesian framework. Simulation results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing alternatives. We further apply this approach to enhance single-arm glioblastoma studies by creating a synthetic control arm derived from historical trials.

Burchnall's approach to inverting the Feldheim-Watson linearization formula for Hermite polynomials has been generalized to encompass the entire Askey-scheme and its $q$-analogue. These derived expansion formulas are explicitly detailed for various families associated with measures of infinite support, notably the Wilson and Askey-Wilson polynomials. An integrated formulation enables the derivation of alternative expressions for orthogonal polynomials under modified weights, yielding expansions for Hermite, Laguerre, Meixner, Charlier, Meixner-Pollaczek, big $q$-Jacobi, and big $q$-Laguerre polynomials. Furthermore, we demonstrate that expansions can be obtained for orthogonal polynomials linked to the Toda-modification of the weight for classical families—specifically Hermite, Laguerre, Charlier, Meixner, Meixner-Pollaczek, and Krawtchouk polynomials—that correspond to known explicit solutions of the Toda lattice.

Broken inversion symmetry in 2D materials introduces a distinct degree of freedom known as valley pseudospin, which identifies whether conducting carriers occupy one of the two energy-degenerate crystal momenta, $K$ or $K'$. Previous research has demonstrated that circularly-polarized light can induce near-100% valley polarization, paving the path for valley-based transistors. However, realizing these devices practically remains difficult due to the challenge of switching valley polarization, largely constrained by short coherence lifetimes. Advances in ultrashort laser technology now enable the generation of attosecond pulse trains with precisely controlled phases and polarizations. Leveraging this capability, we propose a coherent control protocol capable of activating, deactivating, and switching valley polarization on timescales faster than both electronic and valley decoherence, effectively creating an ultrafast optical valley switch. We theoretically validate this protocol for monolayer hBN and MoS$_2$ using first-principles calculations. Furthermore, by employing two time-delayed linearly-polarized pulses with orthogonal orientations, we demonstrate a method to extract the electronic dephasing time $T_2$ from valley Hall conductivity.

This study examines the spectral time variations of candidate luminous blue variable (cLBV) stars within two low-metallicity blue compact dwarf galaxies: DDO 68 and PHL 293B. The cLBV in DDO 68, situated in HII region #3, exhibited a significant outburst between 2008 and 2010, characterized by an Halpha luminosity increase exceeding 1000 times.
