In instances involving very heavy multi-TeV sneutrinos, these corrections mirror those from stops at the one-loop level. Furthermore, we demonstrate that general gauge mediation combined with the inverse seesaw model naturally supports a 125 GeV Higgs boson alongside stops at the TeV scale.

This study examines evolving wormhole configurations within third-order Lovelock gravity, specifically investigating whether these solutions adhere to energy conditions. By employing a generalized Friedmann-Robertson-Walker spacetime and imposing a constraint on the Ricci scalar—which remains independent of the radial coordinate $r$ in standard cosmological models and depends solely on time—we derive dynamic wormhole geometries. These solutions expand within an inflationary background, allowing us to analyze how higher-order Lovelock terms influence their dynamics. Our findings indicate that with appropriate third-order Lovelock coefficients, wormhole solutions exist that satisfy the weak energy condition (WEC), including cases where the WEC holds throughout the entire evolution of the wormhole.

To directly measure the muon component of extensive air showers with energies exceeding $10^{16.5}$ eV, the Pierre Auger Observatory is installing an underground muon detector (UMD). This system comprises 219 modules, each covering 10 $\mathrm{m^2}$ and divided into 64 scintillators linked to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). Accessing the muon content directly enables research into the composition of primary cosmic rays and high-energy hadronic interactions in the forward region. Since muon density fluctuates significantly—from tens of muons per $\mathrm{m^2}$ near the shower axis intersection to less than one per $\mathrm{m^2}$ at greater distances—the read-out electronics employ two simultaneous acquisition modes to cover the required dynamic range: a binary mode for counting individual muons and an ADC mode for measuring high densities. This paper details the end-to-end calibration of the UMD modules. The process begins with calibrating the SiPMs via the binary channel, followed by calibrating the ADC channel using atmospheric muons recorded concurrently with shower data. The study presents and discusses laboratory and field measurements developed to implement the full calibration chain for both channels. The resulting procedure is robust enough to handle the large number of channels in the UMD, ensuring reliable operation under varying environmental conditions over several years.

User-generated reviews on app stores and social media platforms serve as vital resources for developers, with their analysis proving beneficial across various software engineering domains, such as requirements engineering and testing. However, automatic review classification traditionally demands substantial manual effort to curate labeled datasets. This requirement hinders extensibility; whenever the classification goal shifts—whether to distinguish bugs from usability issues or to analyze sentiment—new data must be labeled, limiting the practical adaptability of existing models to novel tasks. Although recent pre-trained neural language models (PTMs), trained unsupervised on vast corpora, have achieved success in similar NLP tasks, their potential for app review classification remains underexplored.

The objective of this study is to evaluate the advantages of PTMs over existing models for app review classification and to assess their transferability across diverse settings. Our method involves an empirical analysis of PTM accuracy and time efficiency relative to prior approaches using six datasets from the literature. We further investigate the performance of domain-specific PTMs trained directly on app reviews. To comprehensively evaluate PTMs, we conduct studies covering binary and multi-class classification, zero-shot classification (for new labels), multi-task learning, and reviews sourced from different platforms. The datasets consist of manually labeled reviews from the Google Play Store, Apple App Store, and Twitter. Performance will be measured using Micro and Macro Precision, Recall, and F1-scores, alongside the time required for training and inference.

Recent years have seen Bayesian methods suggested as a remedy for various challenges in quantum state and process tomography. However, current state-of-the-art Bayesian solutions face three major hurdles: numerical intractability, the absence of informative prior distributions, and a failure to track time-dependent processes. This work addresses each of these issues. First, we employ modern statistical techniques, building on the pioneering work of Huszár and Houlsby and Ferrie, to render Bayesian tomography numerically feasible, enabling practical computation of Bayesian point and region estimators for quantum states and channels. Second, we introduce the first prior distributions for quantum states and channels that incorporate valuable experimental insights. Finally, we devise a method capable of tracking time-dependent states and estimating the drift and diffusion processes influencing them. We also provide source code and animated visual demonstrations of our methods.

These lecture notes were developed for a graduate-level quantum simulation course at Leibniz University Hannover in 2013. The initial section covers advanced techniques for numerically modeling many-body quantum systems, highlighting successful applications alongside the inherent constraints imposed by the exponential complexity of such problems. The second part demonstrates how highly controllable quantum platforms, specifically ultracold atoms, can bypass the limitations of classical simulation approaches. I examine various theoretical and experimental breakthroughs and sketch the path forward for future advancements.

This study addresses static output feedback control for Linear Quadratic Regulator problems with structured constraints under the assumption of unknown system parameters. To solve this model-free problem, we propose a policy gradient algorithm based on the gradient projection method, demonstrating its global convergence to $\varepsilon$-stationary points. Furthermore, we introduce a variance reduction technique, proving both theoretically and numerically that it substantially lowers variance in gradient estimation. Our numerical experiments also confirm that this model-free approach effectively resolves the problem.

We investigate cluster synchronization within networks and introduce a canonical transformation designed for the simultaneous block diagonalization of matrices, which serves as the foundation for analyzing the stability of cluster synchronous solutions. This methodology offers multiple benefits: (1) it decomposes the stability challenge into lower-dimensional subproblems while retaining physically significant data; (2) it enables the examination of stability across both orbital and equitable partitions of network nodes; and (3) it yields a problem parametrization involving a limited set of parameters. Regarding the final point, we demonstrate how the canonical transformation isolates the system into blocks that maintain essential physical characteristics of the original dynamics. Furthermore, we apply our proposed algorithm to evaluate various real-world networks of interest, revealing that it executes more rapidly than competing algorithms found in existing literature.

Neural network-based embeddings have become the standard method for generating text vectors that capture lexical and semantic similarities and differences. Typically, current encoding techniques treat punctuation as negligible, either discarding it during preprocessing or handling it as a fixed token. However, punctuation significantly influences sentence meaning, as illustrated by the distinction between "Let's eat grandma" and "Let's eat, grandma." We hypothesize that a representation model sensitive to punctuation will enhance downstream task performance. To this end, we propose a model-agnostic approach that integrates both syntactic and contextual data to boost sentiment classification results. We validate our findings through experiments on public datasets and present case studies demonstrating that our model generates representations that account for sentence-level punctuation.

General relativity ensures a unique mapping between static neutron star (NS) observables—measurable via multi-messenger astronomy, such as mass-radius relations and tidal deformability—and the equation of state (EoS) of beta-equilibrated matter. While it is established that these static characteristics alone cannot distinguish conventional NSs from hybrid stars, assuming the core contains only neutrons and protons allows the lepton fraction to be uniquely determined by chemical equilibrium. Employing a straightforward analytical approach based on a polynomial expansion of the EoS, we demonstrate that the beta-equilibrium equation can yield multiple solutions, resulting in an inherent ambiguity regarding the internal composition of NSs, even under the purely nucleonic assumption. Furthermore, we find that additional empirical data on symmetric matter at high densities is largely ineffective in resolving this composition uncertainty when measurement errors are considered. Consequently, only constraints on the high-density symmetry energy can significantly aid in deciphering the core composition. Our findings establish a lower bound on the uncertainty achievable for NS core composition through both astrophysical and terrestrial experiments.

The Speech processing Universal PERformance Benchmark (SUPERB) has driven significant research into speech representation learning by evaluating shared self-supervised learning (SSL) models across diverse downstream tasks with minimal architectural changes and limited data. SUPERB demonstrates that these SSL upstream models enhance downstream performance through slight adaptation. As this paradigm of combining self-supervised upstream models with downstream tasks gains traction, assessing the adversarial robustness of such frameworks has become a top priority. This paper presents the first investigation into the adversarial vulnerabilities of this paradigm under attacks from both zero-knowledge and limited-knowledge adversaries. Experimental findings reveal that the SUPERB-based paradigm is highly susceptible to limited-knowledge adversaries, while attacks generated by zero-knowledge adversaries exhibit transferability. Furthermore, the XAB test confirms the imperceptibility of the crafted adversarial examples.

Acquiring extensive datasets and performing expensive manual annotations are essential for training facial emotion recognition models, yet these requirements present significant challenges. To address this, we introduced Facegame, a gamified system that generates annotated facial emotion data without requiring explicit human labeling. In this game, players attempt to mimic a target face displaying a specific basic emotion. Each round produces a new dataset comprising facial features and landmarks, pre-annotated with the corresponding emotion label. This methodology establishes a robust, sustainable, and continuous machine learning training pipeline. Experimental evaluation of Facegame highlighted several key contributions to affective computing. First, the gamified collection process yielded a diverse range of facial expressions for each basic emotion, leveraging the natural variability in players' expressions and abilities. We observed enhanced accuracy when this data augmented established "in-the-wild" datasets for training emotion recognition models. Second, the natural language instructions used in Facegame offer a novel approach to interpretable explainability applicable to various facial emotion recognition systems. Finally, repeated gameplay led to significant improvements in players' skills regarding facial emotion perception and expression.

We develop generalized coherent states for the rationally extended Scarf-I potential and examine their statistical and geometrical characteristics. Particular focus is placed on analyzing the spatio-temporal features of these states through the quantum carpet pattern and the auto-correlation function. This investigation seeks to identify the signature of the "rationalisation" applied to standard potentials and their associated classical orthogonal polynomials.

Accreting black holes (BHs) emit relativistic, collimated jets across a vast range of masses and luminosities, implying that the underlying jet-launching mechanism is universal, robust, and independent of scale. While theoretical models and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations identify large-scale poloidal magnetic flux as the essential component for jet formation, the origin of this flux remains unclear; specifically, it is debated whether it forms locally or is advected inward from the surrounding medium. In this study, we employ the GPU-accelerated GRMHD code H-AMR to investigate global 3D black hole accretion at exceptionally high resolutions, comparable to those typically used in local shearing box simulations. We show that turbulence within an extended radial accretion disc can generate large-scale poloidal magnetic flux in situ, even beginning with a purely toroidal magnetic field. This flux accumulates near the black hole until it becomes dynamically significant, creating a magnetically arrested disc (MAD) that drives relativistic jets exceeding the power of the accretion flow itself. Compared to prior GRMHD simulations using toroidal fields, these jets are 10,000 times more powerful. Furthermore, the jets remain stable against significant kink or pinch instabilities, accelerate to Lorentz factors of $\gamma \sim 10$ over three orders of magnitude in distance, and exhibit a collimation profile consistent with observations of the M87 jet.

Let $\Gamma$ denote a sofic group, $\Sigma$ a sofic approximation sequence for $\Gamma$, and $X$ a $\Gamma$-subshift possessing nonnegative sofic topological entropy relative to $\Sigma$. Assuming $X$ is a shift of finite type or, more broadly, adheres to the topological Markov property, we demonstrate that for any sufficiently regular potential $f \colon X \to \mathbb{R}$, any translation-invariant Borel probability measure on $X$ that maximizes the measure-theoretical sofic pressure of $f$ with respect to $\Sigma$ constitutes a Gibbs state with respect to $f$. This finding generalizes the classical Lanford-Ruelle theorem, along with earlier extensions by Moulin Ollagnier, Pinchon, Tempelman, and others, to the context of sofic groups.

Building on this primary result, we establish a criterion for the uniqueness of an equilibrium measure and provide sufficient conditions ensuring that equilibrium states remain independent of the specific sofic approximation sequence selected. Furthermore, we prove that for any group-shift over a sofic group, the Haar measure is the unique measure of maximal sofic entropy for every sofic approximation sequence, provided the homoclinic group is dense.

In terms of exposition, we offer a concise proof of Chung's variational principle regarding sofic topological pressure.

Sea lice pose significant health risks to both wild and farmed salmon, creating substantial economic challenges for aquaculture operations. Due to their free-living larval stage, these parasites can travel tens of kilometers across the ocean, linking salmon farm populations and making isolated control efforts ineffective. This paper introduces a straightforward analytical framework to model sea lice dispersal between two farms. The model determines the distribution of arrival times for dispersing lice and quantifies cross-infection levels. Furthermore, we integrate numerical hydrodynamic data with a particle tracking system to simulate lice movement between farms in the Broughton Archipelago, BC. These simulations allow us to calibrate the analytical model and derive realistic parameter estimates. Our results indicate that an intermediate distance between farms often maximizes cross-infection rates, and that rising temperatures will likely exacerbate the level of cross-infection.

This work introduces a hybrid image classifier that combines mode-selective image upconversion, single-pixel photodetection, and deep learning to efficiently process vast numbers of pixels. By leveraging partial Fourier transforms to capture signature features across both the original and Fourier domains, the system markedly enhances classification accuracy and robustness. Evaluated on MNIST handwritten digits, the method elevates accuracy from 81.25% to 99.23% and maintains an 83% accuracy rate even on heavily contaminated images with a signal-to-noise ratio of -17 dB. This approach holds significant potential for applications including rapid lidar data analysis, high-resolution image recognition, identification of occluded targets, and atmospheric monitoring.

This letter introduces a 3-dimensional, energy-efficient deployment strategy for multiple aerial access points (AAPs) serving as flying base stations to support uplink communications from ground user equipment (UE). We analytically derive the globally optimal vertical positions of AAPs by accounting for inter-cell interference and AAP energy usage, while determining their horizontal locations to maximize coverage packing density through a new regular polygon-based algorithm. Additionally, we identify the maximum count of non-interfering AAPs feasible within the target area. Numerical simulations are conducted to verify the impact of AAP energy consumption on the optimal placement and confirm our analytical results.

Mathematical word problems serve as a natural abstraction for various quantitative reasoning tasks, including interpreting financial news, sports outcomes, and war casualties. Addressing these problems necessitates a grasp of multiple mathematical principles, such as dimensional analysis and subset relationships. This paper introduces declarative rules that dictate the conversion of natural language descriptions of these concepts into mathematical expressions. We subsequently propose a framework for integrating this declarative knowledge into word problem solving. Our approach learns to translate arithmetic word problem text into math expressions by identifying the pertinent declarative knowledge required for each step of the solution. This strategy enables the handling of multiple concepts within a single problem while ensuring the interpretability of the resulting expression. By modeling the mapping to declarative knowledge as a latent variable, our method eliminates the requirement for costly annotations. Experimental results indicate that our domain-knowledge-based solver surpasses all other systems and demonstrates superior generalization, particularly in realistic scenarios where training and test data distributions differ.

We merge two prominent optimization techniques—variational optimization and evolutionary algorithms—to develop learning methods for generative models. This integration is specifically tailored for models with discrete latents by employing truncated posteriors as the variational distribution family, where the parameters consist of sets of latent states. By treating these states as individual genomes and utilizing the variational lower bound as a fitness metric, we can execute the variational loop through evolutionary algorithms. These truncated posteriors offer high flexibility, demonstrating that evolutionary algorithms can both efficiently and effectively optimize the variational bound. Moreover, this variational loop functions as a general-purpose "black box" method, eliminating the need for analytical derivations. To validate its broad applicability, we applied this approach to three distinct generative models: noisy-OR Bayes Nets, Binary Sparse Coding, and Spike-and-Slab Sparse Coding. We further assessed the effectiveness and efficiency of this novel variational strategy using standard competitive benchmarks for image denoising and inpainting. These benchmarks enable quantitative comparisons against a diverse array of techniques, including probabilistic methods, deep deterministic and generative networks, and non-local image processing approaches. Notably, within the "zero-shot" learning category (training solely on corrupted images), our evolutionary variational algorithm achieved significant improvements over the state-of-the-art in numerous benchmark scenarios. Specifically, for a well-known inpainting benchmark, it attained state-of-the-art performance across all algorithm categories despite training exclusively on corrupted images. Overall, our findings underscore the critical role of advancing optimization methods for generative models to drive performance gains.

This study employs the variational quantum Monte Carlo (VMC) approach to investigate how ground-state properties of quasi-one-dimensional paramagnetic electron fluids vary with wire width ($b$) and electron density ($r_\text{s}$). While the transition to a quasi-Wigner crystal phase is density-dependent and occurs at low densities, we specifically examine how wire width influences the shift in the dominant peak of the static structure factor from $k=2k_\text{F}$ to $k=4k_\text{F}$. Our results indicate that at a constant electron density, this crossover in the charge structure factor happens as the wire width decreases. We propose that this transition arises from the interplay between $r_\text{s}$ and the condition $b<r_\text{s}$, with finite-width correlation effects manifesting as changes in the peak heights of both charge and spin structure factors. By fitting the dominant peaks using functions derived from our finite-width theory and bosonization insights, we achieve a strong agreement with the VMC data. The distinct peaks observed at $4k_\text{F}$ (charge) and $2k_\text{F}$ (spin) signal a complete separation of charge and spin degrees of freedom. Additionally, we find that the electron correlation energy and the Tomonaga-Luttinger parameter $K_{\rho}$ exhibit significant dependence on wire width.

Recent years have seen a surge in data volumes within academic institutions, especially concerning undergraduate research, where students often rely on manual empirical techniques for keyword selection while overlooking established technical methods. Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), exemplified by the Platform for Integrated Research and Academic Work with Responsibility (PILAR)—which catalogs project metadata such as titles, abstracts, and keywords—have become increasingly vital for managing this information. This study analyzed PILAR records using unsupervised machine learning algorithms, evaluating nine distinct models across a dataset of 7,430 research project entries. Among the approaches tested, the TF-IDF method proved most effective for keyword extraction, achieving 72% accuracy and an average processing time of 0.4786 seconds (SD 0.0501) per thesis file.

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has delivered photometric light curves for stars spanning almost the entire sky, enabling asteroseismology to be applied to an unprecedented number of potential solar-like oscillators. Our objective is to compile a catalogue of TESS-observed solar-like oscillators using the 120-second and 20-second cadence modes. This catalogue focuses on stars oscillating at frequencies exceeding the Nyquist limit of TESS's 30-minute cadence, thereby covering both main sequence and subgiant evolutionary stages. We aim to estimate the global asteroseismic parameters $
u_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $\Delta
u$. To achieve this, we utilize a novel probabilistic detection algorithm on the 120-second and 20-second light curves of more than 250,000 stars, identifying targets exhibiting characteristic signatures of solar-like oscillations. Following a manual vetting process to confirm these oscillations, we derive $
u_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $\Delta
u$ using the algorithm's computed probability densities. The resulting catalogue contains 4,177 solar-like oscillators, with $\Delta
u$ and $
u_{\mathrm{max}}$ reported for 98% of the total sample. The data reveals extensive coverage of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, including the red giant branch, subgiant regime, and main sequence. Cross-referencing with external databases indicates that 25 of the detected oscillators belong to spectroscopic binaries, while 28 are confirmed planet host stars. These findings offer the potential for precise, independent asteroseismic constraints on these targets and future TESS candidates of interest.

A rigorous theoretical study examines the nonlinear propagation of dust-ion-acoustic shock waves within a multi-component magnetized pair-ion plasma. This plasma consists of inertial warm positive and negative ions, inertialess non-thermal electrons and positrons, and static, negatively charged, massive dust grains. Utilizing the reductive perturbation method, the Burgers' equation is derived. The model indicates that the presence of static, negatively charged, massive dust grains allows for both positive and negative shock structures. It is observed that increasing ion kinematic viscosity reduces the steepness of both positive and negative shock profiles without altering their height, whereas higher electron temperatures enhance the shock amplitude. Furthermore, an increase in the oblique angle and the positron number density both lead to an increase in the height of the positive shock profile. Finally, the practical applications of these findings are briefly discussed.

This study introduces the lowest-order hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin schemes with numerical integration, labeled HDG-P0, designed for the reaction-diffusion equation and generalized Stokes equations across two and three dimensions. The term "lowest order" refers to the use of piecewise constant functions on the mesh skeleton for the global HDG facet degrees of freedom. We provide an optimal a priori error analysis for these HDG-P0 schemes, addressing a gap in existing literature regarding HDG discretizations that incorporate numerical integration. Additionally, we develop optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners for the statically condensed HDG-P0 linear systems. In both analytical developments, we first demonstrate that the statically condensed HDG system is equivalent to a slightly modified nonconforming Crouzeix-Raviart (CR) discretization. Specifically, the global piecewise-constant HDG space on the mesh skeleton maps one-to-one with the nonconforming CR piecewise-linear space defined over the entire mesh. This equivalence enables the application of established nonconforming geometric multigrid theory to precondition the condensed HDG system. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions are included to validate the theoretical results.

We present a novel torsional oscillator designed for investigating quantum fluids at approximately 100 Hz frequencies, with the capability to achieve velocities of several cm/s. Achieving these speeds necessitates an amplitude greater than 100 $\mu m$, a magnitude that renders conventional capacitor-driven devices unsuitable. This work details the new geometric configuration, outlines the design process, and reports on initial performance evaluations.

The LISA mission will employ quadrant photoreceivers as front-end sensors for its phasemeter, which measures the motion of drag-free test masses regarding both angular orientation and separation. To characterize these photoreceivers, a laboratory testbed has been established, where several limiting noise sources have been identified and their contributions quantified through measurement or data derivation. We have constructed a photoreceiver featuring a 0.5 mm diameter quadrant photodiode, achieving an equivalent input current noise of less than 1.8 pA/√Hz below 20 MHz, with a 3dB bandwidth of 34 MHz.

Achieving optimal oxygen distribution stands as a critical energy management challenge within the contemporary iron and steel sector. Typically, energy supply aligns with manufacturing process demand; however, frequent fluctuations in this balance occur due to inherent uncertainties in production. This study introduces an oxygen distribution model designed to handle uncertain demands, utilizing a two-stage robust optimization (TSRO) framework equipped with a budget-based uncertainty set. This approach safeguards initial distribution decisions while minimizing conservatism. The primary objective of the TSRO model is to determine "wait-and-see" decisions that maximize production profits alongside "here-and-now" decisions that reduce operational instability and penalties for surplus or shortage. To model energy demand uncertainty, we employed a Gaussian process (GP)-based time series model to forecast continuous process demands and a capacity-constrained scheduling model to generate multi-scenario demands for discrete processes. Extensive computational experiments were conducted on the TSRO and its components using synthetic instances derived from historical data. The validation and analysis results are encouraging, demonstrating that our approach is effective for addressing industrial cases characterized by uncertainty.

A novel regime of proton-driven plasma wakefield acceleration has been identified, characterized by plasma nonlinearity that boosts the phase velocity of the excited wave above the speed of the protons. When the beam charge significantly exceeds the minimum required to generate a nonlinear wave, the longitudinal plasma density profile can be tailored to match the wave speed closely to the speed of light. Consequently, this configuration enables the acceleration of electrons or positrons to approximately 200 GeV using a 400 GeV proton driver.

Solar modeling has historically been divided into "internal" and "surface" approaches due to the absence of tools capable of bridging the vast disparities in spatial and temporal scales, as well as the distinct environments and dominant physical mechanisms involved. Recent efforts have focused on overcoming this separation. This study tackles the remaining challenges in linking internal convection zone and dynamo simulations with the solar surface by conducting a proof-of-concept, high-resolution global simulation of the Sun's convection zone using the task-based DISPATCH code framework. We introduce a novel "volleyball" mesh decomposition, featuring Cartesian patches tessellated onto a sphere without singularities. Utilizing an entropy-based HLLS approximate Riemann solver for global magneto-hydrodynamic modeling, the simulation spans 0.655 to 0.995 R$_\odot$ with an initial ambient magnetic field of 0.1 Gauss. The results show the development of convective motions characterized by complex, turbulent structures. Furthermore, small-scale dynamo action twists the ambient magnetic field, locally amplifying its magnitude by over two orders of magnitude within the initial simulation period.

A Lorentz surface in $\mathbb R^4_2$ is classified as being of general type when its associated null curves are non-degenerate. Such surfaces possess both canonical isothermal and canonical isotropic coordinates. It is established that the Gauss curvature $K$ and the normal curvature $\varkappa$, viewed as functions within these canonical coordinates, obey a system of two fundamental partial differential equations. By employing Weierstrass-type representations for the corresponding null curves, we explicitly resolve this system of PDEs, representing any solution through four real functions of a single variable. Furthermore, we derive the transformation rules for these functions under a proper motion in $\mathbb R^4_2$ within the context of the null curve's Weierstrass representation. Leveraging these rules, we determine the relationship between two sets of four real functions that generate the same solution to the natural PDE system.

Marginal problems emerge across numerous disciplines, fundamentally centered on determining the compatibility of partial information with a joint probability distribution. Consequently, characterizing marginal sets through quantifier elimination and polyhedral projection techniques is of primary significance. This study begins by reviewing polyhedral projection algorithms with a specific emphasis on their utility in information theory; alongside established methods, it introduces a novel geometric algorithm that traverses the face lattice of the polyhedron within the projection space. A key application of this approach lies in quantum non-locality, where marginal problems are critical for computing Bell inequalities. By applying these algorithms, the research identifies numerous tight entropic Bell inequalities for tripartite Bell scenarios and more intricate networks relevant to causal inference. Finally, the utility of these inequalities as nonlocality witnesses is evaluated by searching for quantum states that violate them.

This paper introduces a straightforward and flexible approach for simulating the photon statistics of multimode Gaussian states, utilizing automatic differentiation applied to generating functions. The authors derive generating functions for photon number distributions, cumulative probabilities, moments, and factorial moments, while also providing related formulas for photon-added and photon-subtracted multimode Gaussian states. Numerical simulations are performed using the PyTorch machine learning framework to handle automatic differentiation. The study demonstrates that this method is highly effective for practical simulations of quantum optical experiments under realistic conditions involving low photon numbers and various imperfections. As a specific application, the detection probabilities of a recent multipartite time-bin coding quantum key distribution system are calculated and compared against experimental data.

Gesture-based authentication has become a non-intrusive and effective method for verifying users on mobile devices. While these techniques traditionally depended on classical machine learning, recent efforts have shifted toward deep learning approaches. Although previous studies indicate that deep learning models are susceptible to adversarial attacks, there remains a significant gap in research concerning adversarial threats within behavioral biometrics. This study addresses this gap by collecting tri-axial accelerometer gesture data (TAGD) from 46 participants to evaluate both classical and deep learning classifiers, specifically support vector machines (SVM) and convolutional neural networks (CNN). We simulate a realistic adversarial scenario where the attacker possesses genuine TAGD data but lacks knowledge of the authentication model. By employing a deep convolutional generative adversarial network (DC-GAN) to generate adversarial samples, we demonstrate that our deep learning model exhibits unexpected robustness against this specific attack vector.

This study examines matter-antimatter asymmetry through a gravitational baryogenesis mechanism set within the Dvali-Gabadadze-Porrati (DGP) brane cosmology framework. Utilizing a flat Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric in the DGP brane model, we demonstrate that in a radiation-dominated universe ($w = 1/3$), the ratio of baryon number density to entropy generated by gravitational baryogenesis is non-zero, differing from the predictions of standard general relativity. Furthermore, we analyze this baryon-to-entropy ratio in the context of observational constraints specific to DGP cosmology.

We examine the collective scattering of coherent light by a thermal alkali-metal vapor at temperatures between 350 K and 450 K, which corresponds to average atomic separations ranging from $0.7 \lambda$ to $0.1 \lambda$. We construct a theoretical framework modeling the atomic ensemble as a system of coherent, interacting, and radiating dipoles. Our findings demonstrate that the two-time second-order correlation function for a thermal ensemble can be represented as an average over randomly positioned atomic pairs. The proposed model yields results that align well with experimental data. Additionally, we illustrate how adjusting experimental parameters can enable the exploration of various photon statistics regimes.

Long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) linked to supernovae (SNe) are thought to stem from the core collapse of massive stars, while short-duration GRBs connected to compact star mergers are anticipated to be accompanied by kilonovae. GRB 21127A, lasting approximately 84 seconds, featured an initial short, hard spike followed by extended soft gamma-ray emission at a redshift of $z=0.228$. Follow-up optical observations conducted with BOOTES, LCOGT, and the Lijiang 2.4m telescope failed to detect any associated supernova signature, even establishing very stringent limits for such a low redshift. Observations of the host galaxy within a large error circle yielded a rough estimate of the GRB's physical offset from the galactic center at $20.47 \pm 14.47$ kpc. These characteristics mirror those of GRB 060614 and indicate that the progenitor of GRB 211227A is unlikely to be the death of a massive star. Consequently, we propose that GRB 211227A originates from a compact star merger. Calculating pseudo-kilonova emission using typical parameters reveals that any such signal would be too faint to detect. This scenario naturally accounts for the observed prompt emission characteristics, the absence of both supernova and kilonova signals, and the significant physical distance from the galaxy center.

This paper introduces TrollHunter2020, a real-time detection system deployed to identify trolling narratives on Twitter throughout the 2020 U.S. elections. These narratives serve as alternative interpretations of polarizing events, often aimed at executing information operations or inciting emotional reactions. Identifying such narratives is crucial for maintaining constructive discourse and curbing misinformation on the platform. However, traditional detection methods require substantial time and data, which may be unavailable during the fast-paced, high-stakes environment of an election cycle. To address this, we developed TrollHunter2020 to detect trolls in real-time across dozens of trending topics and hashtags related to candidate debates, election night, and the post-election period. The system collects trending data and applies correspondence analysis to uncover significant relationships between the primary nouns and verbs used in constructing these narratives as they appear. Our findings indicate that TrollHunter2020 successfully identifies emerging trolling narratives at the very early stages of polarizing events. We further discuss the tool's effectiveness in detecting information operations early and its potential implications for fostering constructive discourse around contentious issues on the platform.

This article proposes a conjectural uniform error term for the Chebotarev-Sato-Tate distribution concerning abelian surfaces that are $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous to a product of non-CM-elliptic curves which are not $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-isogenous to one another, a result previously established by the author in \cite[Theorem 1.1]{Amri22}. As a direct consequence, we offer a straightforward proof of the generalized Lang-Trotter conjecture, which was recently formulated and examined in \cite{Chen}.

For a long time, Maxwell's boundary conditions (MBCs) were recognized as inadequate for predicting the optical responses of spatially dispersive media. Consequently, supplementing MBCs with additional boundary conditions (ABCs) has become a common, though debated, approach. This study resolves the issue of ABCs by examining nuanced physical properties of surfaces. A general theoretical framework is introduced to analyze light-matter interactions at the boundaries of any medium and is applied to the classic problem of exciton polaritons. We demonstrate that while ABCs can always be tailored to align with this theory, they should not be interpreted as intrinsic surface properties; instead, such characteristics are encapsulated by a *surface response function* (SRF). In contrast to ABCs, an SRF fundamentally describes non-local boundary effects, and we propose methods for experimentally determining the spatial profile of this function.

This paper introduces the JSON Stats Analyzer, a free, open-source, web-based JavaScript tool designed for analyzing JSON documents. We detail the tool's functionality and demonstrate its application using eleven JSON documents selected from Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 levels of our proposed taxonomy. This taxonomy classifies JSON documents based on their size, content, redundancy, and nesting patterns. For each document analyzed, we provide its definition, structural characteristics, and a visual representation of its structure along with summary statistics.

This paper revisits the characterization of incentive-compatible single-parameter mechanisms originally presented by Archer & Tardos (2001). We contend that the purported uniqueness result, known as "Myerson's Lemma," was not adequately proven. We offer a straightforward proof of uniqueness that harmonizes the treatment of two distinct classes of allocation functions prevalent in the literature, demonstrating that the general case follows from an underappreciated result in real function theory. Furthermore, we establish that our approach is more elementary than prior methods. Finally, by extending our characterization to higher dimensions, we derive alternative proofs for revenue equivalence in both multiunit and combinatorial auctions.

Text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis with accents aims to produce L2-accented speech as a variation of standard L1 speech. Controlling accent intensity during this process has become a significant and increasingly popular research area. While recent approaches utilize a speaker-adversarial loss to separate speaker and accent features, adjusting the loss weight to manage intensity, these methods suffer from a lack of interpretability and fail to establish a direct link between the control parameter and natural accent strength. To address this, this paper introduces a novel, explicit, and intuitive scheme for accent intensity control. Specifically, we extract the "goodness of pronunciation" (GoP) posterior probability from an L1 speech recognition model to quantify phoneme-level accent intensity, and then integrate this into a FastSpeech2-based model named Ai-TTS for generation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses baseline models in both accent rendering quality and intensity control.

We have developed efficient emulators for calculating the infinite nuclear matter equation of state from first principles. These emulators utilize the subspace-projected coupled-cluster method, employing a newly created algorithm termed "small-batch voting." This algorithm removes spurious states that can arise when emulating quantum many-body methods using non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. The resulting efficiency and accuracy enable a rigorous statistical analysis, allowing us to investigate nuclear matter predictions across more than one million parametrizations of a chiral interaction model that includes explicit $\Delta$-isobars at next-to-next-to leading order. By constraining the low-energy coupling constants of this chiral interaction with nucleon-nucleon scattering phase shifts and bound-state observables of light nuclei up to helium-4, we apply history matching to determine non-implausible domains. Within these identified domains, we conduct a Bayesian analysis using sampling/importance resampling with various likelihood calibrations to examine correlations among interaction parameters, calibration observables in light nuclei, and nuclear matter saturation properties.

This paper introduces PrivateSNN, a method designed to achieve both privacy and energy efficiency in neural systems by constructing low-power Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) from pre-trained Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) without exposing sensitive dataset information. We address two specific leakage vulnerabilities: data leakage, which occurs when real training data is accessed during the ANN-to-SNN conversion, and class leakage, where network parameters allow the reconstruction of class-related features. To mitigate data leakage, we generate synthetic images from the pre-trained ANNs and utilize them for the conversion process. However, because standard conversion preserves weight values (or scaled versions), the resulting SNNs remain susceptible to class leakage. We resolve this by encrypting SNN weights through training with a temporal spike-based learning rule, which renders the parameters difficult to interpret in the spatial domain. Our results demonstrate that PrivateSNN effectively eliminates both leakage types while incurring only a minor performance decrease (less than ~2%) and achieving a substantial energy-efficiency improvement (approximately 55x) over standard ANNs. Extensive experiments across CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet datasets underscore the critical importance of privacy-preserving SNN training.

For integers $k \geq 2$ and $a > 1$, we denote $N_k(a)$ as the count of multinomial coefficients with $k$ terms that equal $a$. This paper investigates the behavior of $N_k(a)$, demonstrating that both its average and normal orders are $k(k-1)$. Furthermore, we establish that $N_k(a) = O\left((\log a/\log\log a)^{k-1}\right)$ and present several conjectures concerning extreme values where $N_k(a)$ is large.

This study extends our previous investigation [K. Haydukivska et al., J. Mol. Liq., 2021, 328, 115456] into the asymmetric behavior of pom-pom polymers, which feature two branching points at the termini of a linear backbone with side arms of lengths $f_1$ and $f_2$ (where $f_1 \neq f_2$). We examine these structures under good solvent conditions at infinite dilution using a combination of analytical methods based on direct polymer renormalization and computer simulations via dissipative particle dynamics and Monte Carlo techniques. Our analysis focuses on how molecular asymmetry influences average polymer conformations. We provide quantitative estimates for universal size and shape parameters of both the individual branches and the entire molecules, expressed as functions of $f_1$ and $f_2$. Specifically, we calculate the ratio of gyration radii between asymmetric and symmetric pom-pom topologies with identical molecular weights, demonstrating that asymmetry effectively increases the molecular size. Furthermore, we define and analyze an asymmetry factor and quantify the shift in the center of mass induced by side stars, offering additional metrics to characterize the asymmetry of pom-pom architectures.

Establishing the finite-temperature atomic structure of the hybrid perovskite MAPbI3 remains a significant challenge for both experimental and theoretical approaches. Molecular dynamics (MD) emerges as a potent computational tool capable of resolving this structure, though the outcomes vary depending on the density functional approximation (DFA) used in *ab initio* MD or the force field employed in classical MD. This study consistently compares structural configurations at 250K and 400K derived from various DFAs and force fields. Key analyses include the symmetry of the PbI3 framework and the relative arrangement of adjacent organic molecules within it. By utilizing the distribution function of these molecules, we map an effective energy landscape governing single-molecule rotation, which is accurately represented by a pair of cubic harmonics. Furthermore, existing literature data are examined and contrasted with the structures generated by the different methods. While the variability in experimental data currently prevents the definitive selection of a single "best" method, several promising candidates and notable outliers have been identified.

This study demonstrates the spin reversal of the $Fe^{3+}$ sublattice and the spin-canting of $Fe^{3+}$ ions across the magnetic compensation temperature ($T_{Comp}$) in polycrystalline $Y_{1.5}Gd_{1.5}Fe_{5}O_{12}$ (YGdIG) using in-field $^{57}Fe$ Mössbauer spectroscopy. These findings are supported by hard x-ray x-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) measurements, which also reveal the spin reversal of both $Fe^{3+}$ and $Gd^{3+}$ sublattices. Furthermore, the analysis of the effective internal hyperfine field ($H_{eff}$) and the relative intensities of absorption lines within the sextet from in-field $^{57}Fe$ Mössbauer data unambiguously confirms the signatures of $Fe^{3+}$ spin reversal, their continuous transition, and the field-induced spin-canting of the $Fe^{3+}$ sublattices across $T_{Comp}$. Additionally, the Fe K-edge and Gd $L_3$-edge XMCD signals exhibit extra spectral features linked to the magnetic ordering of $Gd^{3+}$ and $Fe^{3+}$, respectively, allowing for the extraction of information from both sublattices through a single-edge analysis. The temperature-dependent evolution of magnetic moments derived from either the Fe K- or Gd $L_3$-edge aligns well with values obtained from bulk magnetization measurements of both YGdIG and YIG ($Y_{3}Fe_{5}O_{12}$). Collectively, these measurements open new pathways for investigating the magnetic behavior of such complex systems across the compensation point.

Microwave cavity resonators are essential elements in numerous quantum technologies and offer a viable platform for hybrid quantum systems, largely because their open design allows for the integration of various subsystems within the cavity. However, incorporating auxiliary structures to support these subsystems poses challenges, as predicting their impact on cavity modes is difficult without prior knowledge of material behavior in the microwave spectrum. This understanding is particularly vital when precise frequency matching and limited tuning are required, such as aligning microwave modes with atomic resonances. In this study, we examine microwave cavity modes in the presence of three common, machinable polymers, focusing specifically on shifts in resonance and energy dissipation. We illustrate how derived dielectric coefficients and loss tangent parameters can guide cavity design by applying them to a test case: matching a polymer-filled 3D microwave cavity to a hyperfine transition in rubidium.

We present a theoretical framework for the interfacial spin Seebeck effect (SSE) in easy-axis antiferromagnets at low temperatures and long wavelengths. The field-induced spin-flop (SF) transition in N\'eel order marks a qualitative shift in SSE behavior: below the SF point, two spin carriers with opposing magnetic moments exist, with those polarized along the field constituting a majority magnon band. Conversely, above the SF point, the low-energy, ferromagnetic-like mode exhibits a magnetic moment opposite to the field direction. This mechanism causes the SSE to reverse sign across the SF transition, consistent with recent experimental findings on Cr$_2$O$_3$/Pt and Cr$_2$O$_3$/Ta devices [Li $\textit{et al.,}$ $\textit{Nature}$ $\textbf{578,}$ 70 (2020)]. According to our model, the SSE arises from a N\'eel spin current below the SF and a magnetic spin current above it. By utilizing the ratio of the associated N\'eel to magnetic spin-mixing conductances as a single constant fitting parameter, we successfully replicate the experimental data's field dependence and partially account for the temperature dependence of the relative SSE jump across the SF.

This study tackles trajectory tracking for an autonomous tractor-trailer system through a decentralized control strategy. A fully decentralized model predictive controller is developed, treating inter-subsystem interactions as perturbations rather than accounting for them directly. To ensure robustness against discrepancies between the nominal model and the actual system, a tube-based method is introduced. Following each new measurement, nonlinear moving horizon estimation updates the state and parameter estimates, which are then supplied to a robust tube-based decentralized nonlinear model predictive controller. This control framework successfully guides the tractor-trailer along any desired path with high precision, maintaining robustness against ignored subsystem couplings and environmental disturbances. Experimental validation confirms accurate trajectory tracking performance on a uneven grass surface.

Carbon, the fourth most abundant element in the universe, becomes a metallic fluid with transient covalent bonds upon melting; however, its elusive liquid-liquid phase transitions have been difficult to capture. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) simulations involving up to 108 atoms via molecular dynamics, alongside a neutral pseudo-atom method that treats multi-atom effects through ion-ion correlation functionals, both utilizing electron-electron exchange-correlation functionals for many-body interactions. Using these approaches, we demonstrate that liquid carbon undergoes multiple liquid-liquid transitions associated with shifts in coordination number within the density range of 3 g/cm³ to approximately 6 g/cm³, specifically when a coordination number of 12 is achieved. These transitions vanish at temperatures exceeding 4 eV. Furthermore, the calculated pressures and transition densities exhibit sensitivity to the specific exchange-correlation functionals applied. Notably, we find that a simple metallic model accurately predicts structure factors and thermodynamics without requiring covalent-bonding features. Additionally, the ion-ion structure factor at these densities and temperatures reveals a subpeak linked to twice the Fermi wavevector, which constrains the fluid in momentum space. Dominant Friedel oscillations within the pair interactions correlate the ions and drive the observed multiple liquid-liquid phase transitions. Our findings suggest that liquid carbon represents a class of fluids where structure is ordered by long-range Friedel oscillations in pair potentials. These results are vital for terrestrial and astrophysical research, inertial fusion utilizing carbon drivers, refined shock experiments, and the discovery of new carbon-based materials.

Fission data serve as critical inputs for reaction networks used in nucleosynthesis simulations and nuclear forensics. For these applications, alongside the modeling of multi-chance fission, the fission characteristics of odd-mass nuclei are equally vital as those of even-even nuclei. Theoretical frameworks aiming to explicitly model fission dynamics usually rely on variations of nuclear mean-field theory. Consequently, handling systems with an odd number of particles becomes significantly more complex, both formally and computationally. This study employs the blocking prescription within Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory, utilizing Skyrme energy functionals, to calculate the deformation properties of odd-mass uranium isotopes. We demonstrate that the resulting fission fragment distributions are highly sensitive to the spin of the odd neutron. Furthermore, by directly computing the spin distribution of the fissioning nucleus, we propose a rigorous methodology for predicting charge and mass distributions in odd-mass nuclei.

This study examines the market microstructure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), the leading form of blockchain-based decentralized exchanges. Our findings indicate that AMM execution mechanisms cause value erosion for liquidity providers when token exchange rates are volatile. Consequently, AMMs are only viable when token pairs serve high personal utility for investors or when the prices of the tokens in the pair are highly correlated. While a pricing curve with greater curvature mitigates arbitrage risks, it simultaneously diminishes investor surplus. Furthermore, combining multiple tokens into a pool intensifies the arbitrage issue. We substantiate these key model implications with statistical evidence derived from transaction-level data of AMMs.

This paper addresses the partial gathering problem for mobile agents within synchronous dynamic bidirectional ring networks. Defined by a parameter $g$ (where $g < k$ and $k$ is the total number of agents), the problem requires agents to reach a state where every node contains either zero or at least $g$ agents. While previous research focused on static graphs, this study extends the investigation to dynamic environments, specifically 1-interval connected rings where a single link may fail at each time step. By examining the relationship between $k$ and $g$, we fully characterize the solvability of the problem and evaluate the move complexity of our proposed algorithms. We establish that $g$-partial gathering is impossible if $k \leq 2g$. For the range $2g + 1 \leq k \leq 3g - 2$, the problem is solvable with $O(n \log g)$ time and $O(gn \log g)$ total moves. When $3g - 1 \leq k \leq 8g - 4$, solvability is achieved with $O(n)$ time and $O(kn)$ moves; given that $k = O(g)$ in this interval, the move complexity simplifies to $O(gn)$. Furthermore, for $k \geq 8g - 3$, the problem is solvable in $O(n)$ time with $O(gn)$ total moves. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that partial gathering is feasible in dynamic rings whenever $k \geq 2g + 1$. Additionally, we prove that solving partial (or total) gathering necessitates at least $\Omega(gn)$ moves. Consequently, when $k \geq 3g - 1$, the partial gathering problem can be resolved with an asymptotically optimal total of $O(gn)$ moves.

Human learning often relies on small-group learning, where students collaborate toward shared goals by articulating their understanding, comparing perspectives, and assisting one another in resolving issues. This paper explores whether such a human-centric approach can enhance machine learning by introducing a novel framework called Small-Group Learning (SGL). In SGL, a collection of machine learning models with diverse architectures cooperate to improve performance by capitalizing on their respective strengths. Specifically, each model generates a pseudo-labeled dataset using its current state and subsequently retrains itself using pseudo-labels produced by other models. The framework is structured as a multi-level optimization process involving three distinct stages: independent model training and pseudo-labeling, retraining using cross-generated pseudo-labeled data, and architectural refinement through validation loss minimization. An efficient algorithm has been devised to address this complex optimization problem. The SGL framework was applied to neural architecture search, and experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets confirm its efficacy.

This paper explores applications of our previous research to investigate specific Galois groups and splitting fields of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}\left(X_0(N)\right)$, employing Hilbert's irreducibility theorem and modular forms. Furthermore, we examine the computational dimensions of this problem utilizing the software systems MAGMA and SAGE.

Although multiple sources acknowledge WaveNet's capability to produce high-quality speech, no prior research has examined the interpretation or visualization of trained WaveNet models. This study explores whether WaveNet achieves speech understanding by unsupervisedly learning an acoustically meaningful latent representation within its receptive field and seeks to elucidate the mechanism behind its feature extraction. Utilizing singular value decomposition and linear regression analysis on activations alongside known acoustic features (such as F0), the research identifies three key findings: (1) activations in deeper layers exhibit strong correlations with spectral features; (2) WaveNet explicitly extracts pitch information despite being trained solely to predict the next audio sample; and (3) this feature analysis relies on the conversion of the latent signal representation between baseband and wideband components.

To highlight discrepancies between current theory and the latest GW170817 neutron star observations, we focus on the impact of the nucleon radius within the existing theoretical framework. We argue that the nucleon radius effect is significant and that the mass radius should replace the charge radius in calculations. Based on recent measurements, we set the nucleon mass radius to $r_m = 0.55\pm0.09$ fm and incorporate it as an input into the "Excluded Volume Effects" model within the nuclear matter equation of state. This approach yields a novel neutron star mass-radius relation that aligns with the GW170817 observational data.

Determining the conditions under which universal exchange-only computation is feasible for qudits encoded in $d$-state systems with $d>2$ remains an open challenge in quantum information theory. This issue can be framed through representation theory: quantum mechanical swaps arising from exchange interactions correspond to transpositions in a symmetric group, each $d$-state system maps to the fundamental representation of $SU(d)$, and each encoded qudit corresponds to an irreducible representation of a Lie algebra generated by these transpositions. To address this, we first establish a mathematical definition of exchange-only universality as a mapping from the special unitary algebra on a product of qudits to a representation of a Lie algebra generated by transpositions, confirming its consistency with quantum computing constraints. We then characterize families of qudits that admit such universality. Since irreducible representations for qudits are canonically labeled by partitions, this aids our analysis. Specifically, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for universality involving one or two qudits based on arithmetic properties of their associated partitions, and conditions for arbitrarily many qudits using Littlewood--Richardson coefficients. Key findings include the proof that universal families of multiple qudits are upward closed, that universality is assured with a sufficient number of qudits, and that any non-universal family can achieve universality by adding at most five ancillae. Additionally, we present results for 2-state systems as a special case.

This work investigates new simulation-like preorders designed for quotienting nondeterministic B\"uchi automata. We introduce fixed-word delayed simulation, a novel preorder that is coarser than delayed simulation. We contend that fixed-word simulation represents the coarsest forward simulation-like preorder suitable for automaton quotienting, thereby deepening our comprehension of the boundaries of this technique. Furthermore, we demonstrate that determining fixed-word simulation is PSPACE-complete. From a practical standpoint, we propose proxy simulations, which are new polynomial-time computable preorders that are sound for quotienting. Specifically, quotients generated by delayed proxy simulation can be significantly smaller—by an arbitrarily large factor—than those produced by direct backward simulation. These proxy simulations are derived from a theory of refinement transformers, where a refinement transformer maps preorders in a non-decreasing manner while maintaining specific properties. Finally, we examine the general conditions under which refinement transformers remain sound for quotienting.

Variations in the glacier calving front significantly impact the flow dynamics of entire glacier systems, making precise monitoring of its position crucial. However, manually outlining this front in SAR images is a challenging, time-consuming, and subjective endeavor. While convolutional neural networks have demonstrated promising potential for automating glacier segmentation in SAR imagery, warranting further investigation, this study introduces a novel two-stage approach that incorporates uncertainty estimation within an Uncertainty Optimization framework. By integrating dropout as a random sampling layer into a U-Net architecture, we construct a probabilistic Bayesian Neural Network. Multiple forward passes generate a sampling distribution that quantifies model uncertainty for every pixel in the segmentation mask. This additional uncertainty map provides valuable guidance for experts during manual data annotation. Moreover, incorporating the uncertainty map as input to the network yields a Dice similarity score of 95.24%, representing a notable enhancement in segmentation performance compared to existing deterministic U-Net-based pipelines for glacier segmentation.

Narrow-band Internet of Things (NB-IoT) is a Low-Power Wide-Area Network (LPWAN) technology initially introduced by 3GPP Release 13 to facilitate cost-effective, energy-efficient, and extensive cellular connectivity for IoT applications. As the requirement for over-the-air services expands and the count of connected wireless devices approaches 100 billion, wireless spectrum is becoming increasingly limited, creating a need for innovative methods to maximize device density within constrained spectral resources to meet growing service demands. Therefore, it is crucial for researchers to devise efficient solutions that uphold NB-IoT Quality of Service (QoS) standards within the 5th Generation (5G) and future network frameworks. This research aims to enhance the capacity and data rates for NB-IoT in post-5G networks by proposing a Symbol Time Compression (STC) technique. The suggested method reduces the bandwidth occupied by each device without compromising system complexity, data throughput, or Bit Error Rate (BER) performance. While STC has been previously proposed to halve bandwidth usage and improve Peak-to-Average Power Ratio (PAPR) when used with conventional Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM), this study introduces a specific STC-based approach that utilizes unused bandwidth to double the number of connected devices while maintaining system performance and low complexity. Additionally, the $\mu$-law companding technique is employed to further reduce the PAPR of transmitted signals. Simulation results indicate that this proposed approach, incorporating $\mu$-law companding, doubles the transmitted data capacity and lowers the PAPR by 3.22 dB, all while preserving the original system complexity and BER.

Image classification is a pivotal task across many machine learning domains. Recently, numerous methods leveraging quantum machine learning and diverse quantum image encoding strategies have emerged. This paper investigates how three distinct quantum image encoding techniques influence the performance of a convolution-inspired hybrid quantum-classical algorithm known as the quanvolutional neural network (QNN). Additionally, we analyze the impact of variational, or trainable, quantum circuits on classification outcomes. Our findings suggest that certain encodings are more compatible with variational circuits. However, we also observe that no single encoding is universally superior; rather, the optimal choice depends on the specific constraints of the application.

Based on extensive transition strength calculations using the shell model, magnetic dipole strength functions have been established for germanium isotopes ranging from $N = Z = 32$ to $N = 48$. The study examines how these strengths evolve with increasing neutron numbers within the $1g_{9/2}$ orbital, revealing a bimodal structure characterized by a low-energy enhancement and a resonance associated with the scissors mode. This low-energy enhancement is most pronounced near closed shells, particularly when the $1g_{9/2}$ orbital is nearly full, whereas the scissors-like resonance peaks in the middle of the open shell, aligning with the observed magnitudes of electric quadrupole transition strengths. These findings corroborate earlier results from iron isotopes and confirm that the occurrence and correlation of these two low-lying magnetic dipole modes represent a global structural feature.

To advance the understanding of timing systematics in pixelized readout chips and to support future fast timing detectors for 4D tracking at the HL-LHC, we conducted a detailed analysis of the Timepix3 hybrid pixel detector developed by the Medipix collaboration. Our investigation employed three distinct measurement methods: test pulses, testbeam data, and a custom-built laser setup. Both the testbeam and laser measurements revealed a consistent structure for the average delay across the pixel matrix for various Timepix3 chips, with a maximum variation of approximately 4 ns. This variation is significant relative to the 1.56 ns time bins. Applying a per-pixel correction for this delay improved the time resolution by an average of 159 ps, depending on the specific sensor. After accounting for timewalk and average pixel delay, the best achieved time resolution for a single Timepix3 chip with a 200 $\mu\text{m}$ planar silicon sensor was $686.4 \pm 0.2$ ps, compared to $892.9 \pm 0.3$ ps without corrections. However, this value still falls short of the naively expected 451 ps. Our laser setup identified the source of the remaining delay as a combination of signal propagation and variations in the fast oscillator's start-up time within the pixels. These findings underscore the necessity for next-generation pixel detectors to correct for such systematic timing effects to achieve the enhanced time resolution required for HL-LHC 4D tracking.

We investigate the asymptotic behavior of the Mixmaster Universe near the cosmological singularity within $f(R)$ gravity, incorporating quadratic corrections to the Ricci scalar $R$. This analysis utilizes a scalar-tensor framework and Misner-Chitr\'e-like variables, modeling the dynamics as a billiard ball moving in a specific domain of half-Poincar\'e space. The shape of the potential well is dictated by the model's spatial curvature and the specific form of the self-interacting scalar field potential. We show that these potential walls define an open domain within the configuration space, permitting the point-universe to access the boundary of the corresponding Lobachevsky space. Consequently, we establish the existence of a stable final Kasner regime during Mixmaster evolution, indicating the suppression of chaos near the singularity. The significance of this work stems from the general applicability of the dynamics, which extends directly to the BKL conjecture, and the interpretation of the modified gravity theory as the leading-order correction to the Einstein-Hilbert action via a Taylor expansion of a generic $f(R)$ function (provided a curvature cut-off is applied).

Recent breakthroughs in deep generative modeling have driven substantial progress in natural language generation (NLG). Integrating entities into neural generation frameworks has proven highly effective, aiding in both summary topic inference and the creation of coherent text. To further amplify the utility of entities within NLG, this paper proposes modeling entity types during the decoding stage to ensure precise generation of contextual words. We introduce a novel NLG model designed to produce target sequences from a provided list of entities. This model employs a multi-step decoder that incorporates entity types directly into the entity mention generation process. Experimental results on two public news datasets indicate that this type injection approach outperforms existing baselines that rely on type embedding concatenation.

The expansion of Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) through wearable and non-wearable Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) holds the promise of enhancing diagnostic quality and enabling prompt treatment for diverse medical conditions. However, the widespread adoption of IoMT also elevates the risk of malicious activities, which can result in severe consequences such as personal data theft, data breaches, and compromised medical devices, thereby endangering human lives. These devices generate vast amounts of data reflecting user behavior patterns, ranging from personal and social activities to daily health monitoring. Consequently, anomalies may arise due to various factors, including unexpected user actions, faulty sensors, or irregular data from compromised devices. Addressing this challenge requires an urgent development of a framework to secure smart healthcare infrastructure capable of detecting and mitigating such anomalies. This paper introduces an anomaly detection model for RPM leveraging IoMT and smart home devices. We propose a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based approach that analyzes normal user behavior within an RPM context involving both smart home and health devices to identify deviations. A testbed comprising multiple IoMT devices and home sensors was designed to collect data, which was then used to train the HMM model using network and behavioral data. The proposed HMM-based model demonstrated an accuracy of over 98% in identifying anomalies within the RPM context.

Although measuring thermal transients via source-drain voltage is a standard technique for characterizing silicon semiconductors, its direct applicability to silicon carbide (SiC) devices remains questionable. This study conducts a thorough assessment of its accuracy, resolution, and stability to determine its viability for extracting structural information from SiC MOSFETs using source-drain voltage as a temperature-sensitive electrical parameter. The characterization methodology comprises two primary procedures involving critical testing variables, such as gate voltages and sensing and heating currents. Furthermore, the impacts of these parameters on both static and dynamic performance are examined to establish a reproducible guideline for thermal transient measurements in SiC MOSFETs.

The receptive fields of V1 cortical cells exhibit significant heterogeneity, functioning as spatially varying operators that differentiate the stimulus image. A lightness and color constancy image can be reconstructed by solving the associated inverse problem, formulated as a Poisson equation with these heterogeneous differential operators. At the neural level, short-range connectivity weights represent the point-wise adapted fundamental solution to this Poisson problem. Furthermore, homogenization techniques provide initial evidence that the results converge toward homogeneous reconstructions.

Human inputs and preferences play a critical role when users interact with autonomous cyber or cyber-physical systems, particularly in scenarios requiring the system's behavior to align with user desires. Cumulative prospect theory (CPT) offers an empirically validated framework for modeling the human tendency to perceive gains and losses asymmetrically. This paper addresses a setting where an autonomous agent must learn behaviors within an unknown environment. While traditional reinforcement learning optimizes expected utility through repeated interactions, we propose optimizing a CPT-based cost to better mimic human behavior. We define the CPT-value of an action taken in a specific state and prove the convergence of an iterative dynamic programming method for estimating this value. Furthermore, we present two algorithms that enable agents to learn policies optimizing CPT-value, evaluating them in environments requiring target state acquisition while avoiding obstacles. Our results demonstrate that agents using these algorithms exhibit behaviors more closely aligned with human users in identical settings and significantly outperform baselines that optimize expected utility.

It is well-established that a distributive lattice of commuting congruences on a universal algebra A is a fundamental component of its sheaf representation. Gehrke and van Gool (J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 2018) recently characterized sheaf representations of universal algebras over stably compact spaces arising from this framework, highlighting the pivotal role of softness. In this paper, we broaden this theory by substituting algebraic varieties with Barr-exact categories, thereby including various "non-algebraic" instances. Our methodology relies on the concept of K-sheaves: intuitively, while standard sheaves are defined on open sets, K-sheaves are defined on compact ones. We consistently employ sheaves on complete lattices instead of topological spaces, enabling point-free sheaf representations where spaces are substituted with frames. These findings facilitate the construction of sheaf representations for the dual of the category of compact ordered spaces and allow for the recovery of Banaschewski and Vermeulen's point-free sheaf representation of commutative Gelfand rings (Quaest. Math., 2011).

Securing and maintaining employment is fundamental to societal participation and economic stability. However, the criteria and processes for job eligibility are shifting rapidly due to the rise of data-driven Automated Hiring Systems (AHSs). While concerns exist regarding the opacity of these systems and their potential to restrict access for certain demographics, many AHSs assert that they identify and counteract discriminatory practices to foster diversity and inclusion. Despite their expanding global adoption, these claims of bias mitigation remain largely unexamined; when they are evaluated, the analysis is almost exclusively conducted from a US socio-legal viewpoint. This paper offers an alternative perspective by critically analyzing three widely used UK AHSs—HireVue, Pymetrics, and Applied—to understand how they conceptualize and address bias and discrimination. Drawing on publicly available documentation, we outline the design, validation, and auditing mechanisms for bias within these tools, exposing underlying assumptions and limitations, before contextualizing them within the UK's socio-legal framework. The UK possesses a distinct legal landscape compared to the US, particularly regarding employment and equality laws as well as data protection regulations. We argue that these differences are crucial for addressing transparency issues and may pose significant challenges to definitively embedding bias mitigation that complies with EU legal standards. This is a critical issue because AHSs, especially those developed in the US, risk obscuring rather than resolving systemic workplace discrimination.
A concise overview of physics extending beyond the Standard Model.

Stone-type duality theorems serve as vital instruments in logic by establishing connections between algebraic and relational/topological models. Beyond offering elegant abstraction, these theorems elevate soundness and completeness to a categorical equivalence, creating a unified framework that integrates both algebraic and topological methodologies. This work provides a systematic exposition of Stone-type duality for structures interpreting bunched logics, beginning with the most basic systems, recovering standard BI and Boolean BI (BBI), and extending to both classical and intuitionistic Separation Logic. The analysis demonstrates uniformity and modularity by encompassing bunched logics derived from BI and BBI through extensions with modalities and multiplicative connectives representing disjunction, negation, and falsum. This scope includes the logic of separating modalities (LSM), De Morgan BI (DMBI), Classical BI (CBI), and the sub-classical family extending Bi-intuitionistic (B)BI (Bi(B)BI).
