This presentation outlines a straightforward method for systematically altering the basis at the one-loop level, accounting for shifts arising from evanescent operators. As a demonstration, we utilize this approach to derive the one-loop basis transformation connecting the BMU basis, which is advantageous for NLO QCD computations, to the JMS basis employed in matching to the SMEFT.

We demonstrate the equivalence between two holographic methods for calculating the butterfly velocity within higher-derivative theories characterized by Lagrangians formed from arbitrary contractions of curvature tensors. The butterfly velocity quantifies the propagation speed of local perturbations in chaotic many-body systems and is derived from the out-of-time-order correlator. This correlation facilitates a holographic approach where the velocity is determined by a localized shockwave on the horizon of a dual black hole. Alternatively, a second holographic method employs entanglement wedge reconstruction to establish a concept of operator size and derives the velocity from specific extremal surfaces. Through direct calculation, we confirm that these two velocities coincide exactly in the specified class of gravitational theories. Furthermore, we provide evidence suggesting this equivalence extends to all gravitational theories. In the process, we establish several general results concerning shockwave spacetimes.

We investigate long-wavelength correlation functions for massive scalar fields within de Sitter spacetime. In the context of a theory featuring quartic self-interaction, we compute the two-point function up to the two-loop level. A comparison between our findings and both the Hartree-Fock approximation and the stochastic approach reveals that the former only sums cactus-type diagrams, while the latter incorporates sunset diagrams as well and yields the correct outcome. Furthermore, we show that the long-wavelength expectation value of the commutator of two fields vanishes for both spacelike and timelike separated points.

Using resistive MHD equations, the nonlinear dynamo effect of tearing modes is derived and partitioned into components parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field. Initially, considering a force-free plasma, the parallel dynamo effect is observed to drive opposing current densities on either side of the rational surface, resulting in a completely flattened $\lambda = \boldsymbol{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}/|\boldsymbol{B}|^2$ profile in that region. Given the abundance of rational surfaces in turbulent plasma, this suggests a tendency for the plasma to relax into a Taylor state. Conversely, slightly away from these surfaces, the parallel dynamo effect diminishes, causing the nonlinear dynamo form to approximate the quasilinear form. Upon including the pressure gradient, it is found that the parallel dynamo effect flattens the $\boldsymbol{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}$ profile rather than the $\lambda$ profile. Furthermore, the perpendicular dynamo effect of tearing modes is shown to eliminate the pressure gradient near the rational surface. Additionally, these findings provide further support for the assumption of a flat current density within magnetic islands in tearing mode theory.

In Self-Amplified Spontaneous Emission Free Electron Laser (SASE FEL) short-pulse schemes, pulse duration is typically constrained by the FEL coherence time, which spans a few hundred attoseconds for hard X-rays and enters the femtosecond range for XUV and soft X-rays. This paper introduces a modified chirp-taper scheme designed to surpass this coherence time limitation. Numerical simulations for the XUV and soft X-ray FEL facility FLASH indicate that pulses lasting a few hundred attoseconds can be generated in the 2–10 nm wavelength range, achieving peak powers of hundreds of megawatts. With a repetition rate of several thousand pulses per second, this approach offers a distinctive source for attosecond science.

This study explores the application of slowly varying functions, defined in the sense of Karamata, to the theory of Markov branching processes. We focus on the critical scenario where the infinitesimal generating function possesses an infinite second moment yet exhibits regular variation with a specific remainder term. Furthermore, we enhance the Basic Lemma within the framework of critical Markov branching processes and sharpen established limit theorems.

Although the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with evolving IoV architectures. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for enhancing data privacy and security within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant potential through its secure, decentralized, and auditable mechanisms for data recording and sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application and implementation of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. Additionally, it examines potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research directions associated with these frameworks. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for developing modern Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions to address various data privacy issues and scenarios in IoVs.

Utilizing photometric redshifts and statistical background subtraction, we measured stellar mass functions within galaxy groups of $4.5$–$8\times10^{13}~\mathrm{M}_\odot$ at redshifts $1<z<1.5$. These groups, drawn from the COSMOS and SXDF fields, were identified through X-ray imaging and sparse spectroscopy. We calculated stellar mass functions for star-forming and quiescent galaxies separately, distinguishing them via rest-frame $UVJ$ colours. From these distributions, we derived the quiescent fraction and the quiescent fraction excess (QFE) relative to the field as a function of stellar mass. The QFE rises with stellar mass, mirroring trends seen in more massive clusters at the same redshift range, which contrasts with the apparent independence of stellar mass and environment on quiescent fractions at $z\sim 0$. Comparing our findings with higher-mass clusters at similar redshifts and lower redshifts, we identified a robust dependence of QFE on halo mass at fixed stellar mass. This relationship is well described by a logarithmic slope of $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{QFE})/\mathrm{d}\log(M_{\mathrm{halo}}) \sim 0.24 \pm 0.04$ across all stellar mass and redshift bins. This result aligns qualitatively with the BAHAMAS hydrodynamic simulations but conflicts with observed QFE trends against stellar mass. We tested two toy models: one assuming quenching begins only after accretion onto the main progenitor ("no pre-processing") and another where it starts upon becoming a satellite ("pre-processing"). The required delay times appear to depend on halo mass, with a significantly stronger dependence needed in the absence of pre-processing. Ultimately, our results support models indicating that environmental quenching initiates in low-mass haloes ($<10^{14}M_\odot$) at $z>1$.

This note examines the computational model defined by photonic circuits, which feature edges traversed by photons within a single time-bin and vertices represented by idealized, lossless beam splitters and phase shifters. The circuit framework is abstracted as the symmetric monoidal category of unitary matrices acting on the bosonic Fock space of multimode photons. Additionally, a diagrammatic language is introduced to facilitate the comprehension and creation of photonic algorithms, effectively capturing the categorical properties of this representation. As practical demonstrations of the formalism, the boson sampling scheme and the Knill-Laflamme-Milburn protocol are implemented on a single-rail photonic computer, alongside an investigation into a parity-based model for qudits.

This survey examines dynamic epistemic logics that include modalities for quantifying over changes in information. We provide complete axiomatizations for these logics, with a specific emphasis on axioms addressing the interplay between knowledge and such quantifiers. Additionally, we discuss their relative expressivity, decidability, and the complexity associated with model checking and satisfiability, along with their applications. The survey concludes by highlighting open problems and emerging research directions.

This study investigates the ground-state phase diagram of an $S=1/2$ two-leg ladder featuring varied leg interactions. The nearest-neighbor spin interactions along the $a$ and $b$ legs are characterized by $xy$ and $z$ components denoted as $J_{{\rm l},a}$ and $\Delta_{\rm l} J_{{\rm l},a}$ (and $J_{{\rm l},b}$ and $\Delta_{\rm l} J_{{\rm l},b}$), respectively. Conversely, the uniform rung interactions are defined by $\Gamma_{\rm r} J_{{\rm r}}$ for the $xy$ component and $J_{{\rm r}}$ for the $z$ component, where $\Delta_{\rm l}$ and $\Gamma_{\rm r}$ represent the $XXZ$ anisotropy parameters for the legs and rungs. The system exhibits frustration when $J_{{\rm l},a} J_{{\rm l},b}<0$, regardless of the sign of $J_{\rm r}$. Numerical analysis determines the phase diagram within the $\Delta_{\rm l}$ ($|\Delta_{\rm l}| \leq 1.0$) versus $J_{{\rm l},b}$ ($-2.0\leq J_{{\rm l},b}\leq 3.0$) plane, assuming fixed parameters of $J_{{\rm l},a}=0.2$, $J_{{\rm r}}=-1.0$, and $\Gamma_{\rm r} = 0.5$. This determination combines physical intuition with level spectroscopy and phenomenological renormalization-group methods applied to exact diagonalization data. The resulting diagram identifies ferromagnetic, Haldane, Néel, nematic Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL), partial ferrimagnetic, and $XY1$ phases. Notably, the nematic TLL phase emerges in both the strong-rung frustrated and unfrustrated regimes. First-order perturbative calculations from the strong rung coupling limit clarify the diagram's features, while density-matrix renormalization-group (DMRG) computations of energy gaps, local magnetization, and spin correlation functions further validate the findings.

In the field of medical image processing, manufacturers often safeguard their intellectual property by distributing only compiled binary software, which is resistant to analysis by potential adversaries. This paper examines the effectiveness of this strategy in protecting image processing algorithms, specifically focusing on whether machine learning can reverse-engineer the generation of mono-energetic images and iodine maps from dual-energy CT data. Our findings demonstrate that both tasks can be approximated with extremely high accuracy using data from a single image slice, achieving a structural similarity index exceeding 0.98 across all tested scenarios.

The evolution of remote sensing has generated petabytes of raster data, which is frequently integrated with high-resolution vector datasets, such as city boundaries. A prevalent operation in this context is zonal statistics, which calculates metrics for each polygon within a vector dataset. This paper reframes the zonal statistics challenge as a join problem and introduces a new distributed system capable of scaling to handle petabytes of both raster and vector information. Unlike traditional approaches, our method eliminates the need for preprocessing or indexing, making it ideally suited for the ad-hoc queries typically required by researchers. We developed a theoretical cost model that demonstrates the algorithm's superiority over baseline methods. Additionally, extensive experiments were conducted on large-scale satellite data containing up to a trillion pixels and vector data with up to hundreds of millions of edges. These results confirm that our approach scales effectively to massive datasets, achieving performance improvements of up to two orders of magnitude compared to Rasdaman and Google Earth Engine.

We present an example of a spacetime featuring a continuous metric that is globally hyperbolic and displays causal bubbling, with the metric decomposing orthogonally into timelike and spacelike components. This example is examined within the framework of energy conditions and the recently proposed synthetic timelike curvature-dimension (TCD) condition. Specifically, we note that the TCD condition alone is insufficient to preclude causal bubbling.

This research examines a mathematical model of a perturbed, stratified mean shear flow incorporating turbulent viscosity eddy coefficients. Utilizing the standard Boussinesq approximation for buoyancy-driven natural convection, we disregard the effects of turbulent diffusivity eddy coefficients. The resulting model for vertical velocity perturbations, which accounts for both vertical and horizontal viscosity, yields a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein (TG) differential equation. When considering only horizontal viscosity, we derive a modified TG equation that maintains the same order as the classical inviscid formulation. Assuming slowly varying Brunt-Väisälä frequencies and background horizontal velocities, we analyze the geometrical and physical optics approximations of this modified equation via the WKB method. Finally, we explore the behavior of these asymptotic solutions in the vicinity of turning point singularities and critical levels.

We examine the "Complexity=Action" (CA) conjecture within the context of Born-Infeld (BI) gravity, calculating the action's growth rate inside the Wheeler-DeWitt (WDW) patch, which corresponds to the complexity growth of the dual holographic boundary state. To determine the accurate on-shell action, we apply a direct variational method to identify the appropriate boundary and corner terms. Our results indicate that the late-time behavior of holographic complexity aligns with the anticipated two times the energy.

The Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST) at the Cerro-Chajnantor Atacama Telescope Prime (CCAT-prime) Facility will serve as the host for Prime-Cam, a cutting-edge first-generation camera equipped with multi-wavelength imaging polarimeters and spectroscopic tools designed for intensity mapping during the Epoch of Reionization. This article introduces the 850 GHz (350 micron) instrument module, which represents the highest frequency component of Prime-Cam and offers unique capabilities for astronomical and cosmological surveys. By leveraging the exceptional atmospheric transparency available at the 5,600-meter elevation of Cerro Chajnantor, this module will cover a 1.1-degree field of view and deploy approximately 40,000 Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) coupled with Silicon platelet feedhorns, both manufactured at NIST. This setup will deliver unprecedented broadband intensity and polarization measurement precision. The 850 GHz module is essential for investigating critical astrophysical inquiries concerning galaxy formation, Big Bang cosmology, and star formation within our Galaxy. The paper outlines the module's design rationale and overall architecture, along with results from initial laboratory characterization.

Applying the standard finite element method (FEM) to general partial differential equations reveals that round-off error scales proportionally to $N^{\beta_{\rm R}}$, where $N$ represents the number of degrees of freedom (DoFs) and $\beta_{\rm R}$ is a specific coefficient. We introduce a technique utilizing a limited number of inexpensive numerical experiments to identify both $\beta_{\rm R}$ and the proportionality coefficient across different space dimensions and FEM software. Leveraging these derived coefficients, the approach outlined in \cite{liu386balancing} for forecasting the maximum attainable accuracy $E_{\rm min}$ and the corresponding optimal DoF count $N_{\rm opt}$ is generalized to broader problem sets. This extended strategy enables precise prediction of $E_{\rm min}$ for general scenarios, typically decreasing the computational time required to achieve the highest accuracy by 60\%--90\%.

Causal phenomena linked to rare events are prevalent in numerous engineering challenges, including risk-sensitive safety analysis, accident prevention, and extreme value theory. Nevertheless, existing causal discovery techniques frequently fail to detect causal relationships between random variables in dynamic environments that only emerge during low-probability realizations. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new statistical independence test designed for data derived from time-invariant dynamical systems where rare yet impactful events occur. Specifically, we leverage the time-invariance of the underlying data to create a superimposed dataset comprising system states preceding rare events across various timesteps. Subsequently, we develop a conditional independence test applied to this reorganized data. We establish non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds ensuring the consistency of our approach and demonstrate its efficacy on diverse simulated and real-world datasets, such as incident records from the Caltrans Performance Measurement System (PeMS). The code and datasets supporting these experiments are publicly accessible.

Quantum electrodynamics now enters a regime where the coupling between light and matter exceeds their intrinsic energies, known as deep-strong coupling (DSC). This state challenges conventional physical assumptions and generates electromagnetic nonlinearities distinct from those found in natural materials. In this DSC regime, excitations behave as photons with a linear energy spectrum until a critical number is reached, at which point the system abruptly becomes strongly anharmonic. This creates an effective, extremely high-order nonlinearity dependent on intensity. Such behavior facilitates N-photon blockade (where N is very large), paving the way for novel quantum light sources. Specifically, this nonlinearity serves as the foundation for a new gain medium; when incorporated into a laser or maser, it produces large Fock states instead of coherent states. These Fock states could theoretically possess photon numbers orders of magnitude greater than any previously achieved and remain protected from dissipation through a novel equilibrium between nonlinear gain and linear loss. The text concludes by outlining potential pathways for the experimental realization of these phenomena.

This paper presents novel data structures designed to facilitate robust regression via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) by employing importance sampling, where gradients are sampled with probability proportional to their norms. While SGD is a staple in large-scale machine learning, its convergence can be sluggish due to the high variance inherent in uniform sampling. Conversely, importance sampling drastically reduces variance but is typically hard to implement because calculating sampling probabilities necessitates multiple data passes, a scenario where standard gradient descent (GD) might otherwise be applied. We propose an algorithm that approximately samples $T$ gradients of dimension $d$ from a near-optimal importance sampling distribution for robust regression across $n$ data rows. Consequently, our method executes $T$ steps of importance-sampled SGD while maintaining sublinear space complexity and requiring only a single pass over the data. Furthermore, these techniques are applicable to importance sampling in second-order optimization.

Reconstructing high-resolution images from low-resolution data containing clipped noise is algorithmically difficult because the problem is ill-posed. Existing solutions have rarely addressed this challenge, and current methods typically rely on simplistic regularizers. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of two adaptive regularizers grounded in anisotropic diffusion concepts. In addition to assessing the classical edge-enhancing anisotropic diffusion regularizer, we present a new non-local variant featuring one-sided differences, which we call "sector diffusion," that delivers superior performance. We integrate this approach with all six variations of the standard super-resolution observation model, which stem from permuting its three operators for warping, blurring, and downsampling. Notably, evaluation within a practically relevant noisy environment yields a ranking that differs from the noise-free results reported in our previous work (SSVM 2017).

Recommender systems are increasingly under scrutiny due to their expanding influence on the opportunities available to individuals. Existing fairness audits are restricted to broad parity checks across sensitive groups. We introduce an audit based on envy-freeness, a finer-grained metric that aligns with individual preferences, ensuring that every user prefers their own recommendations over those of others. Because verifying envy-free conditions requires estimating user preferences beyond their current recommendation history, we frame the audit as a novel pure exploration problem within multi-armed bandits. We present a sample-efficient algorithm with theoretical assurances that it will not degrade user experience, alongside an analysis of the trade-offs observed on real-world recommendation datasets.

This study introduces an inference procedure designed to yield consistent parameter estimators for modal regression models when covariates are subject to measurement error. Additionally, a score-based diagnostic tool utilizing parametric bootstrapping is created to evaluate the validity of parametric assumptions within the regression framework. Both the proposed estimation technique and the diagnostic method are tested on synthetic data from simulation studies as well as real-world datasets to showcase their practical application and efficacy. These empirical cases highlight the critical necessity of properly addressing measurement error in error-prone covariates when determining associations between responses and covariates using modal regression, a model particularly effective for skewed and heavy-tailed response distributions.

This paper introduces "strong reduction," a novel conformance relation tailored for partial, nondeterministic finite state machines. This relation complements existing frameworks by specifically addressing model-based testing for systems where input availability depends on the current state, such as graphical user interfaces or mechanically toggleable systems. We propose a new algorithm that generates complete test suites based on strong reduction, executed under a grey-box testing paradigm. In this approach, the algorithm assumes knowledge of which inputs are enabled or disabled based on the system state, while keeping the internal implementation states hidden as in black-box testing. The algorithm leverages this state-dependent information to ensure the resulting test suite size grows linearly with the reference model's state space. Furthermore, examples demonstrate that this method can significantly reduce test suite sizes compared to traditional black-box testing approaches for strong reduction.

This study applies the Page and Wootters quantum description of time to the near-horizon region of a black hole. It demonstrates that this quantization method—a modified version of the PaW approach proposed in [21]—cannot be fully applied to this specific quantum region. Even with existing literature modifications, the PaW approach remains controversial regarding time evolution, the flow of time, the measurement problem, the recording of near-horizon history, and a consistent definition of the arrow of time within this area. Furthermore, the investigation into clock ambiguity results in a unique definition of a clock specifically for the black hole's near-horizon region.

We employ the $4-\epsilon$ expansion to investigate fixed points in $2+1$ dimensional $\mathcal{N}$=1 Wess-Zumino models featuring $N_{\Phi}$ scalar superfields coupled via a cubic superpotential. For $N_{\Phi}=3$, we categorize all perturbatively unitary SUSY fixed points. When $N_{\Phi}=4$ and $N_{\Phi}=5$, our focus shifts to irreducible fixed points where scalar superfields constitute a single irreducible representation of the symmetry group. In the $N_{\Phi}=4$ scenario, we demonstrate that the S5 invariant super Potts model is the unique irreducible fixed point with fully interacting scalar superfields. For $N_{\Phi}=5$, we examine all Lie subgroups of O(5) and utilize the GAP computational algebra system to analyze finite subgroups of O(5) up to order 800, identifying three fully interacting irreducible fixed points. Notably, a subgroup of O(5) displaying O(3)/Z2 symmetry leads to a new family of models characterized by $N_{\Phi}=\frac{\rm N(N-1)}{2}-1$ and O(N)/Z2 symmetry, valid for any integer $N \geq 3$.

While current state-of-the-art speaker verification systems primarily rely on speech enhancement techniques utilizing deeper and wider neural networks to boost performance, this paper introduces an alternative strategy. It aims to enhance model resolution by integrating attention-based dynamic kernels within a convolutional neural network, allowing parameters to adapt based on input features. Furthermore, channel attention and multi-layer feature aggregation are employed to distill these kernel attention weights, facilitating the learning of global speech characteristics. This method offers an efficient way to increase representational capacity even with limited data, as the model structures self-adapt to specific inputs. On the VoxCeleb1 test set, the proposed dynamic convolutional model achieved an EER of 1.62% and a miniDCF of 0.18, representing a 17% relative improvement over ECAPA-TDNN.

Effective commonsense reasoning systems must generalize across a wide range of reasoning scenarios. However, current state-of-the-art methods often rely on costly data annotations and overfit to specific benchmarks, failing to acquire general semantic reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, zero-shot question answering (QA) systems have emerged as a robust solution by converting commonsense knowledge graphs (KGs) into synthetic QA samples for training. Given the growing variety of commonsense KGs, this paper seeks to expand zero-shot transfer learning into multi-source environments, allowing different KGs to work synergistically. To achieve this, we introduce a modular knowledge aggregation approach designed to reduce knowledge loss caused by interference between sources, establishing a new zero-shot commonsense reasoning framework. Experiments across five commonsense reasoning benchmarks validate the framework's effectiveness, demonstrating performance improvements when leveraging multiple knowledge graphs.

Smishing, short for SMS phishing, is a social engineering tactic involving fabricated text messages designed to entice recipients into interaction. These deceptive messages typically seek to steal credentials, install malware, or initiate further attacks by prompting users to reply, click malicious links leading to phishing sites, or call specific numbers. Daily, thousands of mobile users fall victim to smishing. Drawing on prior research regarding robocalls by Tu et al. (USENIX Security, 2019) and USB drive exploits by Tischer et al. (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2016), this study explores the underlying reasons for smishing's success. Consequently, we conducted experiments by sending eight fake SMS messages to 265 participants, tracking their CLICK, REPLY, and CALL behaviors and collecting survey feedback. The results indicate that 16.92% of participants potentially succumbed to the initial attack. To assess repeat vulnerability, a randomly selected subset of users was targeted with a second, distinct smishing campaign, resulting in another 12.82% falling for the deception. Through logistic regression analysis, we determined that the combination of REPLY and CLICK actions significantly increased the likelihood of a response compared to CLICK alone. Furthermore, a statistically significant rise in response rates was observed when comparing Facebook and Walmart scenarios against an IRS baseline.

This research investigates the valence crossover and strong electron-phonon coupling in EuPd$_2$Si$_2$ using polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy. At low temperatures, the fully-symmetric phonon mode displays a markedly asymmetric lineshape, which signals a Fano-type interaction between this mode and a continuum of electron-hole excitations. Furthermore, anomalies in both the frequency and linewidth of the phonon modes occur across the valence-crossover temperature, implying a coupling between valence fluctuations and lattice vibrations. Notably, two specific phonon modes exhibit a significantly enhanced Gr\"uneisen parameter, indicating proximity to a critical elasticity regime. Finally, density functional theory calculations are employed to assess the relative contributions of structural versus valence changes to these phonon anomalies.

This study explores visual cross-embodiment imitation, where agents acquire policies from videos of others (like humans) performing identical tasks despite significant variations in physical form, movement, and end-effector dynamics. We demonstrate the ability to automatically derive robust, vision-based reward functions from these cross-embodiment demonstrations. Specifically, we introduce a self-supervised Cross-embodiment Inverse Reinforcement Learning (XIRL) framework that utilizes temporal cycle-consistency constraints to extract deep visual embeddings representing task progression from offline videos of multiple experts executing the same task with different physical constraints. Previously, generating rewards from self-supervised embeddings usually necessitated alignment with a reference trajectory, which is often unattainable given stark embodiment disparities. Our empirical results show that if embeddings effectively capture task progress, the negative distance between the current and goal states within the learned embedding space serves as an effective reward for training policies via reinforcement learning. We observe that our learned reward function not only performs well on embodiments encountered during training but also generalizes to completely novel embodiments. Furthermore, when transferring real-world human demonstrations to a simulated robot, XIRL exhibits superior sample efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Qualitative results, code, and datasets are accessible at https://x-irl.github.io.

Social media echo chambers pose a critical threat, recently exacerbating responses to the COVID-19 pandemic by fostering conspiracy theories, vaccine hesitancy, and reduced adherence to mask mandates and social distancing. This issue is deeply intertwined with political polarization and the dissemination of misinformation. An echo chamber is characterized as a user network where individuals exclusively engage with viewpoints that reinforce their existing beliefs while dismissing or discrediting opposing perspectives. This survey investigates the echo chamber phenomenon through a social computing lens, aiming to outline potential solutions. By reviewing related literature, we analyze the defining attributes of echo chambers and their impact on both individuals and society. Furthermore, we elucidate the algorithmic and psychological mechanisms driving their formation, specifically the bias inherent in social media recommender systems and internal biases such as confirmation bias and homophily. While mitigating internal biases remains difficult, significant efforts have been directed toward addressing algorithmic bias; these systems often exploit user predispositions to personalize content, thereby increasing engagement and ad revenue. Consequently, this study explores various computational strategies for detecting and preventing echo chambers, with a primary focus on modifications to recommender systems.

Chikungunya represents a rapidly spreading, emerging global threat to health security. Numerous studies have sought to forecast its incidence rates, including an extensive analysis by DARPA covering data from 2014 to 2017 on suspected cases, confirmed cases, fatalities, population figures, and incidence rates across various nations. This project analyzed the DARPA dataset and expanded upon it by integrating weather features—such as temperature, humidity, dew point, wind, and pressure—along with geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) for each country. These additional variables were retrieved from different APIs for the years 2014 to 2016. Once a comprehensive dataset was compiled, Linear Regression was employed to predict the incidence rate, with the model's accuracy and error rate subsequently calculated.

DRAM serves as the primary memory technology in contemporary computing architectures. These systems utilize a memory controller to communicate with DRAM through specific commands, which the DRAM executes using internal components like access transistors and sense amplifiers. However, these components are governed by fixed internal timings associated with each command. This rigidity restricts the range of operations DRAM can perform and impedes the development of novel features aimed at enhancing reliability, performance, and energy efficiency. To address these constraints, we propose making DRAM internal timings programmable to dynamically control in-DRAM components. Consequently, we have designed CODIC, an economical DRAM substrate that allows fine-grained adjustment of four critical, previously fixed internal timings. CODIC was implemented with minimal modifications to both the DRAM chip and the DDRx interface. To illustrate CODIC's capabilities, we introduced two novel security mechanisms: (1) a more robust DRAM Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) with significantly higher throughput than existing solutions, and (2) the first cold boot attack prevention method that incurs no runtime performance or energy overhead.

Over recent decades, boson stars have garnered significant interest as straightforward, self-consistent models of compact objects and as self-gravitating structures potentially arising from dark-matter theories. Direct electromagnetic detection of these hypothetical entities is improbable because their bosonic components are expected to interact weakly with ordinary matter and radiation. Nevertheless, binary boson star systems could form and merge, emitting gravitational waves that might differentiate them from binaries consisting of black holes or neutron stars. This study investigates the merger of two boson stars by numerically solving the fully relativistic Einstein-Klein-Gordon equations for a complex scalar field featuring a solitonic potential, which produces highly compact configurations. Due to the steep mass-radius relationship, we can analyze the dynamics and gravitational radiation of unequal-mass binary boson stars with mass ratios reaching approximately $q\approx23$, avoiding the challenges typically associated with evolving high-ratio binary black holes. Consistent with prior research on equal-mass mergers, our simulations show that the final state is either a nonspinning boson star or a spinning black hole, contingent upon the initial masses and the system's angular momentum. We find no evidence of synchronized scalar clouds forming around the remnant black holes or boson stars. Notably, unlike in equal-mass scenarios, one mechanism for angular momentum dissipation becomes asymmetric, resulting in substantial kick velocities (up to several $10^4\,{\rm km/s}$) that could lead to wandering remnant boson stars. Finally, we compare the predicted gravitational wave signatures of boson star binaries with those of black hole binaries and discuss the feasibility of detecting these differences using ground-based interferometers.

This study examines automorphism ensemble decoding (AED) applied to quasi-cyclic (QC) low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Since belief propagation (BP) decoding on standard factor graphs remains invariant under quasi-cyclic automorphisms, it inherently fails to benefit from AED. However, by introducing minor modifications to the parity-check matrix at the receiver—without altering the transmitted code—we can disrupt this symmetry. This approach enables improved error-correction performance through an ensemble of identical BP decoders while maintaining the worst-case decoding latency. The method was validated using LDPC codes from CCSDS, 802.11n, and 5G standards, achieving a 0.2 to 0.3 dB gain over conventional BP decoding. Furthermore, compared to saturated BP (SBP) with similar performance, the proposed algorithm reduces average decoding latency by a factor of more than eight.

This study introduces a novel approach for sequentially training deep neural networks across multiple tasks, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting while enabling rapid adaptation to unseen tasks. Building upon prior research regarding network masking (Wortsman et al., 2020), we demonstrate that learning a linear combination of a limited set of task-specific masks (termed "impressions") on a randomly initialized backbone is sufficient to maintain accuracy on previously learned tasks and achieve high performance on new ones. Unlike previous techniques, our method avoids generating dedicated masks or contexts for every new task, instead utilizing transfer learning to minimize per-task parameter overhead. We illustrate that combining individual impressions—each of which performs poorly in isolation—can yield results comparable to a dedicated mask. Furthermore, even homogeneous masks from the same task can approach the performance of heterogeneous combinations when a sufficient number of impressions are aggregated. Our approach scales more efficiently than existing methods, often requiring orders of magnitude fewer parameters and functioning without modification even when task identity is unknown. Additionally, in scenarios where task labels are absent at inference, our algorithm offers a frequently superior alternative to the entropy-based task-inference methods proposed by Wortsman et al. (2020). We validate our method using various well-known image classification datasets and architectures.

This study combines theoretical and experimental approaches to examine dielectronic recombination (DR) leading to doubly excited $3l3l'$ (LMM) states in Fe XVII, a critical process for generating soft X-ray lines in this common ion. Employing two distinct electron beam ion traps (EBITs) alongside complementary methods for sample preparation and purity assessment, we observed minimal contamination, enabling precise electron density diagnostics in both devices. Our experimental data on resonant energies and strengths were benchmarked against prior independent storage ring studies, as well as results from configuration interaction, multiconfiguration Dirac-Fock, and many-body perturbation theory calculations. The many-body perturbation theory approach demonstrated exceptional predictive accuracy when compared with the combined experimental datasets. Based on these findings, we derived DR rate coefficients that reveal significant differences from values currently listed in the OPEN-ADAS and AtomDB databases.

This paper examines the spectra of associative locally matrix algebras, which need not be unital or possess countable dimensions. We identify every possible spectrum for these algebras and provide a novel proof of the Dixmier-Baranov Theorem. Furthermore, leveraging our spectral characterization, we establish the embeddings of locally matrix algebras.

Advanced optical oscillators utilizing cryogenic reference cavities are currently constrained by the Brownian thermal noise resulting from the mechanical dissipation of mirror coatings. Recently, crystalline Al$_{1-x}$Ga$_{x}$As/GaAs coatings have appeared as a viable option for reducing this thermal noise. This study details measurements of frequency noise in two fully crystalline cryogenic cavities featuring Al$_{0.92}$Ga$_{0.08}$As/GaAs optical layers. We document previously unobserved birefringent noise caused by anti-correlated frequency fluctuations between the polarization modes of these crystalline coatings and determine the variables influencing its strength. A comparison of the birefringent noise across the two cavities reveals phenomenological scaling laws with respect to intracavity power and mode area. We also implement an interrogation method that eliminates this noise by simultaneously probing both polarization modes. While the residual noise after cancellation exceeds the thermal noise limits of both cavities, it remains lower than the instabilities previously recorded in equivalent resonators with dielectric coatings. Although the origin of these new noise mechanisms is not yet clear, we demonstrate that crystalline coatings can achieve stability and sensitivity comparable to those using dielectric coatings.

By definition, critical models are expected to exhibit slow correlation decay for local observables while maintaining some mixing for macroscopic ones. A robust interpretation of this mixing property is that altering boundary conditions does not induce a singular effect on the system's interior, even in the asymptotic limit. This paper establishes that result for the wired uniform spanning tree and the Temperleyan dimer model.

Gerrymandering involves distorting elections through the manipulation of voting district boundaries; while historically significant, it has proven analytically challenging to verify. We introduce a method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo with Simulated Annealing to quantify the degree of unfairness in districting plans. Our approach yielded promising results when applied to Texas, utilizing a redistricting Markov Chain enhanced by Simulated Annealing to achieve accelerated outcomes. This demonstrates robust evidence that Simulated Annealing effectively generates representative voting distributions rapidly for large-scale elections and successfully identifies unfair biases in enacted districting schemes.

This study focuses on three-dimensional complete manifolds where the scalar curvature is bounded below. A primary objective is to formulate a sharp comparison theorem for the bottom spectrum, modeled after Cheng's classical result. Additionally, the paper aims to derive geometric insights, including volume estimates, based on scalar curvature when the Ricci curvature is asymptotically nonnegative and the scalar curvature is positive. Specifically, if the scalar curvature decays at a rate no faster than linear, the manifold cannot support a positive Green's function. Furthermore, when the scalar curvature is bounded below by a positive constant, the volume of unit balls is shown to be upper-bounded by the scalar curvature's lower bound at infinity; notably, in the case of nonnegative Ricci curvature, the manifold's volume exhibits linear growth, thereby affirmatively answering a question posed by Gromov for dimension three. Finally, volume estimates are also provided for scenarios where the scalar curvature decays polynomially.

Building upon the research presented in (1), this report initially revisits the definitions and notation established therein, offering derivations for the precise mathematical formulation of an SIS epidemic on a hypergraph. It subsequently extends the findings of (1) to a broader class of models that includes both SIS and SIR dynamics. Exact differential equations governing the expected population values for each state are derived. By concentrating on Bi-uniform hypergraphs, appropriate approximations are applied to generate numerical solutions, which are then validated against stochastic simulations across various system configurations.

Identifying Software Vulnerabilities (SVs) in code commits is increasingly recommended to provide early warnings of security risks. However, there is a significant gap in assessing vulnerability-contributing commits immediately after detection to offer timely insights into exploitability, impact, and severity, which are crucial for planning and prioritizing mitigation efforts. To address this, we introduce DeepCVA, a novel deep multi-task learning model designed to automate seven Commit-level Vulnerability Assessment tasks simultaneously, grounded in Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) metrics. We evaluated the model's effectiveness and efficiency through large-scale experiments involving 1,229 vulnerability-contributing commits with 542 distinct SVs across 246 real-world software projects. Results indicate that DeepCVA outperforms many supervised and unsupervised baseline models, achieving a 38% to 59.8% higher Matthews Correlation Coefficient. Additionally, DeepCVA requires 6.3 times less training and validation time than seven cumulative assessment models, significantly reducing maintenance costs. Overall, DeepCVA represents the first effective and efficient solution for automatically assessing SVs early in the software development lifecycle.

We present three distinct transformations connecting Hermitian and non-Hermitian quantum systems at criticality, which are governed by conformal field theories (CFTs). The first transformation maintains both the physical spectrum (PS) and the entanglement spectrum (ES); consequently, the central charges derived from the logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy remain identical for both system types. The second transformation preserves the PS but alters the ES, resulting in distinct entanglement entropy scalings and different central charges. We illustrate this using the dilation method applied to free fermions, showing that a non-Hermitian system with central charge $c=-2$ can be mapped to a Hermitian system with $c=1$. Finally, we examine Galois conjugation in the Fibonacci model under the parameter shift $\phi \to -1/\phi$. This transformation affects neither the PS nor the ES, linking the tricritical Ising model and 3-state Potts model to the Lee-Yang model. Through the scaling properties of entanglement entropy, this relationship reveals negative central charges for these models.

Given the inherent complexity of cancer, researchers employ clustering algorithms to unravel observed heterogeneity and pinpoint treatable subtypes. Although kernel-based clustering methods can incorporate multiple input matrices—a crucial capability for multidimensional diseases like cancer—their results are often difficult to evaluate, leaving the specific contribution of each data source unclear. This paper introduces an extension to multiple kernel learning clustering that characterizes identified patient clusters by highlighting the features with the greatest impact. Specifically, we integrate feature clustering with multiple kernel dimensionality reduction to create FIPPA, a metric quantifying the influence of feature clusters on patient clusters. In our application across various cancer types using four distinct data modalities, we aimed to identify integrative subtypes and determine their key molecular drivers. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard metrics, such as survival analysis, while also providing interpretable insights into the molecular foundations of these subtypes through high-impact features. This capability aids in validating potential cancer subtypes and generating new hypotheses regarding individual patient groups, with applicability extending to other disease phenotypes.
We conduct a canonical analysis of the recently discovered non-relativistic string action (arXiv:2107.00642 [hep-th]) and examine its gauge-fixed formulation.

Point cloud super-resolution is a critical challenge in 3D reconstruction and data comprehension, aiming to transform low-resolution inputs into high-resolution outputs rich in detail. This paper introduces a data-driven approach leveraging graph networks and adversarial losses. The core strategy involves exploiting local point cloud similarities and drawing analogies between the low-resolution input and the high-resolution target. To address local similarity, we developed a deep network utilizing graph convolution. Regarding the input-output analogy, we integrated residual connections into the graph convolution and established a skip connection between the input and output layers. The model is trained using an innovative loss function that combines Chamfer Distance (CD) with graph adversarial loss, enabling the automatic capture of high-resolution point cloud characteristics without manual intervention. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results and exhibiting strong generalization capabilities on unseen data.

Millisecond pulsars are considered the primary origin of gamma-ray emissions within globular clusters, yet the distinct roles of two mechanisms—curvature radiation arising from pulsar magnetospheres and inverse Compton scattering involving relativistic pairs ejected into the cluster environment—have remained ambiguous. To clarify this, we analyzed 8 years of $\textit{Fermi}$-LAT data from 157 Milky Way globular clusters to detect signatures of inverse Compton emission. We observed a moderately significant (3.8$\sigma$) correlation between gamma-ray luminosities and photon field energy densities, though this could alternatively stem from a hidden relationship between photon densities and stellar encounter frequencies. When examined collectively, the gamma-ray spectra of these clusters decompose into two distinct parts: an exponentially cut-off power law and a pure power law. The latter, detected at an 8.2$\sigma$ significance with a spectral index of $2.79 \pm 0.25$, is best explained as inverse Compton emission from cosmic-ray electrons and positrons supplied by millisecond pulsars. Furthermore, the luminosity of this power-law component is comparable to, or slightly less than, that of the curvature component, implying that the fraction of pulsar spin-down power channeled into relativistic leptons is roughly equivalent to the fraction emitted as prompt magnetospheric radiation.
